questions.loText: Assess the causes of covered interest rate parity violations after the financial crisis of 2008.
questions.reading: LTR-16: Covered Interest Parity Lost: Understanding the Cross-Currency Basis
questions.topic: Covered Interest Parity Lost: Understanding the Cross-Currency Basis
questions.source: New • built from GARP Ch.17, Sections 17.1 and 17.2
questions.question: An FX strategist compares the three-year cross-currency basis against the US dollar across jurisdictions, quoted as in the reading’s graphs on the non-dollar currency (negative when dollars are dearer through swaps than in the cash market). In Japan, banks fund dollar lending with yen deposits through FX swaps and life insurers hedge most of their US dollar bonds. In Australia, banks fund a large Australian dollar mortgage book partly by borrowing abroad and swapping the proceeds into Australian dollars, while Australian institutional investors hedge their foreign assets. Which statement is consistent with the reading?

options.text: Both bases are negative, because after the crisis the US dollar commands the same premium against every currency.
The JPY basis is positive, because Japanese banks act mainly as arbitrageurs that supply dollars in the swap market.

The JPY basis is negative because Japanese banks and insurers both borrow dollars through swaps; the AUD basis is positive because Australian banks lend dollars in the swap market and offset investors’ hedging demand.
The AUD basis is negative, because Australian banks add to institutional investors’ demand for dollars through swaps.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Japan**

Banks use yen deposits to fund dollar lending through swaps, and life insurers hedge dollar bonds: both borrow dollars through swaps, so they compete for swapped dollars. Dollar borrowing via swaps is in higher demand and dearer than in the cash market: a negative quoted basis.

**Step 2 – Australia**

Banks with a mortgage book larger than their deposit base borrow abroad and swap into Australian dollars, so in the swap market they lend dollars. That offsets investors’ hedging demand, and the basis is positive.

⇒ The sign follows the net hedging position against the dollar, with banks as the swing factor.

**Interpretation**

Sweden looks like Japan against the dollar but like Australia against the euro, because the euro swap market is the marginal funding source for Swedish banks. Pick the right currency pair before reading the sign.

**LO:** LTR-16 c: Assess the causes of covered interest rate parity violations after the financial crisis of 2008. • **Reference:** Borio, McCauley, McGuire and Sushko (2016), GARP Ch.17, 17.1 Demand for Currency Hedges; 17.2 The Currency Basis in the Cross Section

**Source:** Written new for the Liquidity and Treasury Risk P1–P3 workbook (question LTR-16 c.6), built from GARP Ch.17, Sections 17.1 and 17.2.

a.reason: Absolute claim: the reading shows a positive Australian dollar basis.

b.reason: Role misassignment: Japanese banks are hedgers adding to dollar demand; their reliance on swaps reduced their arbitrage capacity.

d.reason: Reverses Australian banks’ role: they offset investors, which is why Australia is the exception.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Explain and calculate liquidity trading risk via cost of liquidation and liquidity-adjusted VaR (LVaR).
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-1 a Q1
questions.question:
A junior risk analyst at a Tokyo securities house is preparing a briefing for newly hired analysts on what drives the cost of unwinding trading positions in JPY-denominated instruments. The draft contains the following statements:

I. For an instrument with a market maker, the bid and offer quotes are the same up to the market maker’s size limit; beyond that size the bid tends to fall and the offer tends to rise as the trade gets larger.

II. For a retail customer dealing at a bank branch, the quoted spread on a foreign exchange transaction tends to widen as the transaction size increases, mirroring the pattern seen between sophisticated institutions.

III. Even where no market maker quotes an instrument, there is an implicit bid-offer spread, because the price a dealer offers depends on which side of the trade the institution wants to take.

IV. The price at which a position can be sold depends on the mid-market price, the quantity sold, and the economic environment, but not on how quickly the sale must be completed, because speed affects only market risk.

Which of the statements should the analyst retain in the briefing?

options.text: I only
I, II, and III only
I and III only
I, III, and IV only

questions.solution:
Tokyo securities house briefing: which statements about drivers of liquidity trading risk to retain.

**Concept and theory**

Liquidity trading risk is the risk that a trading position cannot be unwound at short notice at, or close to, its fair (mid-market) value. GARP stresses that solvency (assets exceed liabilities) and liquidity (the ability to make cash payments as they fall due) are different, and that in trading, a liquid position is one that can be unwound quickly. The price realised on a sale depends on four things: (1) the mid-market price or an estimate of value, (2) how much of the asset is to be sold, (3) how quickly it must be sold, and (4) the economic environment. GARP’s house-sale analogy makes the speed point: in a slow market, a seller who must sell immediately has to cut the price well below estimated value.

The bid-offer spread is the main channel. A financial institution sells at the bid and buys at the offer. A dealer’s quote is good only up to a certain size; above it the spread widens because hedging a bigger trade is harder. In GARP’s Figure 1.1 the bid and offer are the same up to the market maker’s size limit and then diverge: the bid falls and the offer rises with size. Where there is no market maker, an implicit spread still exists, because the dealer’s price depends on which side the institution wants to take. GARP adds an important contrast: in the retail market, spreads can show the opposite pattern, with a larger transaction getting a better quote.

| Market | Spread as trade size grows |
|---|---|
| Institutional, with market maker | Constant up to size limit, then widens |
| Institutional, no market maker | Implicit spread, depends on side of trade |
| Retail (bank branch) | Sometimes narrows (better quote) |

**Applying it to this question**

Test each statement against GARP Section 1.1. Statement I reproduces Figure 1.1: same bid and offer up to the size limit, then diverging. True. Statement II claims that retail spreads widen with size, mirroring the institutional pattern; GARP says the retail market sometimes shows the opposite pattern. False. Statement III is GARP’s implicit spread point. True. Statement IV lists three of the four determinants but deletes “how quickly it is to be sold”. False. The analyst should keep I and III only.

**Fragile fact.** Direction by market: institutional spreads widen beyond the market maker’s size limit; retail quotes can improve with size. There are four determinants of sale price, and speed is one of them.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 66.a, verbatim):** Explain and calculate liquidity trading risk via cost of liquidation and liquidity-adjusted VaR (LVaR).

**GARP:** Chapter 1, Section 1.1 Liquidity Trading Risk (Figure 1.1 and surrounding text). **GARP** **vs Schweser:** none of substance; Schweser condenses the same points and omits the retail contrast (GARP-only detail).

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-1 a, where it is Q1 of 9.

a.reason: (Scope or condition error). Keeping only I means rejecting III, which reflects the belief that a bid-offer spread exists only when a market maker quotes. GARP says the spread is still there implicitly. A would be right only if the stem asked which statement describes quotes from a market maker specifically.

b.reason: (Polarity flip). B adds Statement II, which reverses GARP’s retail observation: an individual at a branch is likely to get a better quote as size rises. B would be right only if II said retail spreads “sometimes narrow” as size increases.

c.reason: C keeps exactly the two statements GARP supports: the market maker’s size limit followed by widening quotes (Figure 1.1), and the implicit bid-offer spread that exists even with no market maker because the price depends on which side of the trade is taken.

d.reason: (Scope or condition error). D adds Statement IV, which drops one of the four determinants of sale price (speed of sale). Speed matters directly for liquidity: an immediate sale needs a price cut. D would be right only if IV listed all four determinants, including how quickly the asset must be sold.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Explain and calculate liquidity trading risk via cost of liquidation and liquidity-adjusted VaR (LVaR).
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-1 a Q2
questions.question:
A treasury analyst at an Australian bank is estimating how much it would cost to close out three trading positions in normal market conditions. Spreads are assumed constant at today’s quotes.

| Position | Direction | Units (million) | Bid (AUD) | Offer (AUD) | Daily price vol (%) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Stock P | Long | 4.0 | 31.80 | 32.20 | 1.4 |
| Stock Q | Short | 1.5 | 12.35 | 12.65 | 2.1 |
| Property trust R | Long | 9.0 | 4.46 | 4.54 | 0.9 |

Which of the following is closest to the cost of liquidation of the three positions in a normal market?

options.text: AUD 1.385 million
AUD 0.935 million
AUD 2.770 million
AUD 1.160 million

questions.solution:
Australian bank: normal-market cost of liquidating three positions, one of them short.

**Concept and theory**

GARP measures market liquidity by the bid-offer spread, either in dollars or as a proportion of price:

p $= \text{Offer} -$ Bid, s $= \frac{\text{Offer} - \text{Bid}}{\text{Mid-market price}}$ , Mid $= \frac{\text{Bid} + \text{Offer}}{2}$ .

The mid-market price is treated as the fair price. A sell trade is done at the bid and a buy trade at the offer, each half a spread away from mid. Liquidating a position of mid-market value $\alpha$ therefore costs s$\alpha$/2. For a book of n positions in normal market conditions (GARP equation 1.1):

Cost of liquidation (normal market) $= \sum_{\text{i}=1}^{\text{n}} \frac{\text{s}_{\text{i}} \alpha_{\text{i}}}{2}$ ,

where $\text{s}_{\text{i}}$ is the normal-market proportional spread of instrument i and $\alpha_{\text{i}}$ is the dollar (mid-market) value of the position. Because $\text{s}_{\text{i}}\alpha_{\text{i}} = (\text{p}_{\text{i}}$/Mid$_{\text{i}})(\text{Mid}_{\text{i}} \times\text{units}_{\text{i}}) = \text{p}_{\text{i}} \times\text{units}_{\text{i}}$, the cost can be computed equally well as half the dollar spread times the number of units. Two features matter for traps. First, the cost applies to a short position too: closing a short means buying at the offer, again half a spread above mid. GARP’s Practice Question 1.3 (a short and a long position) makes this point. Second, costs add across positions; they never net, because each unwind loses half a spread whatever its direction. The measure assumes market prices do not change; it is a pure transaction-cost measure, separate from VaR.

**Applying it to this question**

Dollar route (equivalent to $\text{s}_{\text{i}}\alpha_{\text{i}}$/2):

P: 0.5 × (32.20 − 31.80) × 4.0m = 0.5 × 0.40 × 4.0m = 0.800m

Q (short): 0.5 × (12.65 − 12.35) × 1.5m = 0.5 × 0.30 × 1.5m = 0.225m

R: 0.5 × (4.54 − 4.46) × 9.0m = 0.5 × 0.08 × 9.0m = 0.360m

Total = 0.800 + 0.225 + 0.360 = 1.385m

Check by the proportional route for P: Mid = 32.00, s = 0.40/32.00 = 0.0125, $\alpha=$ 128m, cost = 0.0125 × 128/2 = 0.800m. The total cost of exiting all three positions at normal-market spreads is AUD 1.385 million. The daily price volatilities are irrelevant: they feed VaR, not the cost of liquidation, which assumes prices do not move.

**Fragile fact.** Halve the spread, and add every position’s cost, longs and shorts alike; the denominator of s is the mid, not the bid or offer.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 66.a, verbatim):** Explain and calculate liquidity trading risk via cost of liquidation and liquidity-adjusted VaR (LVaR).

**GARP:** Chapter 1, Section 1.1.2 Measuring Market Liquidity, equation (1.1) and Example 1.1. **GARP vs Schweser:** none; Schweser gives the same formula (its equation images are missing in the text file, but its worked example and quiz use s$\alpha$/2).

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-1 a, where it is Q2 of 9.

a.reason: A applies GARP’s equation 1.1, half the proportional spread times mid-market value, to every position, including the short, and adds the three costs.

b.reason: (Sign error). AUD 0.935 million nets the short against the longs: 0.800 − 0.225 + 0.360. Closing a short is a purchase at the offer and costs half a spread, so it adds. B would be right only if the short were a hedge that is not being unwound and its cost were somehow refunded, which never happens in this measure.

c.reason: (Dropped term). AUD 2.770 million omits the one-half: 2 × 1.385. It charges the whole spread, as if the positions were bought at the offer and sold at the bid in one round trip. C would be right only for a round-trip cost measured from bid to offer.

d.reason: (Scope or condition error). AUD 1.160 million leaves out Stock Q (0.800 + 0.360), treating only long positions as costly to unwind. D would be right only if the stem asked for the cost of liquidating the long positions alone.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Explain and calculate liquidity trading risk via cost of liquidation and liquidity-adjusted VaR (LVaR).
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-1 a Q3
questions.question: The CRO of a Toronto-based investment dealer is reviewing a proposal from the head of the equity desk. The desk holds CAD 900 million spread across 45 mid-cap names. The desk head proposes consolidating the book into 6 large positions, arguing that monitoring costs would fall and that the desk’s market risk VaR would barely change. Which of the following best describes the effect of the proposal on the desk’s liquidity trading risk?

options.text: It is acceptable, because spreading a book across many names reduces liquidity trading risk in the same way that it reduces market risk, and the 6 names remain diversified.
It is acceptable, because the proportional spread $\text{s}_{\text{i}}$ used in the cost of liquidation is a property of each instrument and does not depend on the size of the position held.
It reduces liquidity trading risk, provided each large position is later sold in a single block, because a fast sale minimises the time the desk is exposed to price moves.

It is likely to increase liquidity trading risk, because $\text{s}_{\text{i}}$ rises with the size of position i; holding many small positions and limiting the size of any one position tend to reduce it.

questions.solution:
Toronto dealer: effect of consolidating 45 names into 6 large positions on liquidity trading risk.

**Concept and theory**

Equation 1.1 shows that the cost of liquidation is driven by $\text{s}_{\text{i}}$ and $\alpha_{\text{i}}$ for each position. The crucial point is that $\text{s}_{\text{i}}$ is not a fixed property of the instrument: GARP states that $\text{s}_{\text{i}}$ increases with the size of position i. This follows from the market maker’s size limit. Beyond that limit, the bid falls and the offer rises as the trade gets larger, because the dealer finds a bigger exposure harder to hedge.

This produces an asymmetry with market risk that GARP states directly: although diversification reduces market risk, it does not necessarily reduce liquidity trading risk. Market risk is reduced by imperfect correlation between price moves, so combining positions in different names cancels some risk. Liquidation costs do not cancel. Each unwind costs half a spread, and in a crisis spreads tend to widen together. What reduces liquidity trading risk is the size of each individual position relative to what the market can absorb. GARP concludes that holding many small positions rather than a few large ones tends to entail less liquidity risk, and that setting limits on the size of any one position is one way of reducing liquidity trading risk.

Large positions are also vulnerable to predatory trading: if others expect a large holder to sell, they short in advance, making it harder to exit at competitive prices. GARP’s remedy is confidentiality and, for large positions, a slow unwind, not a block sale.

| Lever | Market risk | Liquidity trading risk |
|---|---|---|
| More names (diversification) | Reduced | Not necessarily reduced |
| Smaller individual positions | Little effect | Reduced $\text{(s}_{\text{i}}$ smaller) |
| Size limits per position | Little effect | Reduced |

**Applying it to this question**

The proposal raises the size of each position about sevenfold on average (CAD 900m over 6 names versus 45). Since $\text{s}_{\text{i}}$ rises with position size, the cost of exiting each position, and of the book as a whole, is likely to rise. The desk head’s VaR argument concerns market risk, which is a different risk; it does not answer the liquidity question. The deciding fact is GARP’s statement that $\text{s}_{\text{i}}$ increases with position size and that many small positions entail less liquidity risk.

**Fragile fact.** Diversification reduces market risk, not necessarily liquidity trading risk; $\text{s}_{\text{i}}$ rises with position size.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 66.a, verbatim):** Explain and calculate liquidity trading risk via cost of liquidation and liquidity-adjusted VaR (LVaR).

**GARP:** Chapter 1, Section 1.1.2 Measuring Market Liquidity (text after equation 1.1) and Section 1.1 on predatory trading. **GARP vs Schweser:** none; Schweser states that larger positions create more liquidity risk and that size limits and many smaller positions reduce it, but it omits GARP’s explicit diversification contrast.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-1 a, where it is Q3 of 9.

a.reason: (Sibling swap). A gives liquidity trading risk a property of market risk. GARP says that diversification reduces market risk but does not necessarily reduce liquidity trading risk. A would be right only if the question asked about the effect on market risk of spreading the book across names.

b.reason: (Scope or condition error). B treats $\text{s}_{\text{i}}$ as independent of size. That holds only for trades below the market maker’s size limit (for example, a tiny holding in a deep Treasury market). For large positions, $\text{s}_{\text{i}}$ widens with size. B would be right only if every position stayed well within dealers’ size limits.

c.reason: (Polarity flip). C reverses the speed trade-off for spreads. Selling a large position quickly in one block faces a wide spread and invites predatory trading; a fast sale reduces exposure to mid-market moves, not spread cost. C would be right only for a position small enough that its spread did not depend on trade size.

d.reason: D restates GARP: $\text{s}_{\text{i}}$ increases with the size of position i; many small positions entail less liquidity risk; position-size limits reduce liquidity trading risk.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Explain and calculate liquidity trading risk via cost of liquidation and liquidity-adjusted VaR (LVaR).
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-1 a Q4
questions.question:
A risk consultant engaged by a Singapore bank is estimating the cost of liquidating two positions in a stressed market at the 99% confidence level. Dollar bid-offer spreads are assumed normally distributed and perfectly correlated across positions; use $\lambda=$ 2.326.

| Position | Units (m) | Mid (SGD) | Mean spread | SD spread | Today’s spread | Daily vol (%) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Stock K | 3.0 | 24.00 | 0.120 | 0.200 | 0.10 | 1.6 |
| REIT L | 20.0 | 2.50 | 0.020 | 0.015 | 0.02 | 1.1 |

(Mean, SD and today’s spreads are dollar spreads in SGD per unit.) Which of the following is closest to the stressed-market cost of liquidation?

options.text: SGD 0.380 million
SGD 1.427 million
SGD 1.120 million
SGD 2.853 million

questions.solution:
Singapore bank: stressed-market cost of liquidation at 99% from dollar spread statistics.

**Concept and theory**

The normal-market measure uses a single typical spread. In a stressed market, spreads widen, so GARP models each instrument’s proportional spread as a random variable with mean $\mu_{\text{i}}$ and standard deviation $\sigma_{\text{i}}$, and uses a “worst case” spread at a chosen confidence level (GARP equation 1.2):

Cost of liquidation (stressed market) $= \sum_{\text{i}=1}^{\text{n}} \frac{(\mu_{\text{i}} + \lambda\sigma_{\text{i}}) \alpha_{\text{i}}}{2}$ .

Here $\mu_{\text{i}}$ and $\sigma_{\text{i}}$ are the mean and standard deviation of the proportional spread, $\alpha_{\text{i}}$ is the mid-market value of position i, and $\lambda$ is the confidence parameter for the spread. With normal spreads, a one-tailed 99% worst case gives $\lambda=$ 2.326 (only wider spreads hurt, so the tail is one-sided). Schweser labels the same parameter $\gamma$.

When the data come as dollar spreads, convert by dividing by the mid-market price: $\mu_{\text{i}} =$ $\bar{\text{p}}_{\text{i}}$/Mid$_{\text{i}}$ and $\sigma_{\text{i}} = \text{sd}(\text{p}_{\text{i}})$/Mid$_{\text{i}}$. Equivalently, since $\alpha_{\text{i}} = \text{Mid}_{\text{i}} \times\text{units}_{\text{i}}$, the cost is half of ($\bar{\text{p}}_{\text{i}} + \lambda$ sd$(\text{p}_{\text{i}}))$ times the number of units. Summing the position costs assumes spreads are perfectly correlated, which GARP argues is realistic because spreads widen together when liquidity is tight. In GARP’s Example 1.2, the stressed cost at 99% is almost five times the normal-market cost.

**Applying it to this question**

Formula first: Cost $= \sum_{\text{i}}$ 0.5 $\alpha_{\text{i}}(\mu_{\text{i}} +$ 2.326 $\sigma_{\text{i}})$.

$\alpha_{\text{K}} =$ 3.0m × 24.00 = 72.0m, $\mu_{\text{K}} =$ 0.120/24.00 = 0.005000, $\sigma_{\text{K}} =$ 0.200/24.00 = 0.008333

$\alpha_{\text{L}} =$ 20.0m × 2.50 = 50.0m, $\mu_{\text{L}} =$ 0.020/2.50 = 0.008000, $\sigma_{\text{L}} =$ 0.015/2.50 = 0.006000

$\text{Cost}_{\text{K}} =$ 0.5 × 72.0 × (0.005000 + 2.326 × 0.008333) = 0.5 × 72.0 × 0.024383 = 0.8778m

$\text{Cost}_{\text{L}} =$ 0.5 × 50.0 × (0.008000 + 2.326 × 0.006000) = 0.5 × 50.0 × 0.021956 = 0.5489m

Total = 0.8778 + 0.5489 = 1.4267m ≈ SGD 1.427 million

Check via units: 0.5 × 3.0m × (0.120 + 2.326 × 0.200) = 0.5 × 3.0 × 0.5852 = 0.8778m. Today’s quoted spreads and daily price volatilities are irrelevant: the stressed measure uses the distribution of spreads, and price volatility belongs to VaR.

**Fragile fact.** Use the distribution of spreads ($\mu+ \lambda\sigma$), not today’s quote; divide dollar spreads by the mid; 99% one-tailed gives $\lambda=$ 2.326.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 66.a, verbatim):** Explain and calculate liquidity trading risk via cost of liquidation and liquidity-adjusted VaR (LVaR).

**GARP:** Chapter 1, Section 1.1.2 Measuring Market Liquidity, equation (1.2) and Example 1.2. **GARP vs Schweser:** notation only: GARP uses $\lambda$, Schweser uses $\gamma$ for the spread confidence parameter. Schweser’s worked example uses a one-tailed 1.645 at 95%.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-1 a, where it is Q4 of 9.

a.reason: (Dropped term). SGD 0.380 million omits $\lambda\sigma_{\text{i}}$: 0.5 × (72.0 × 0.005 + 50.0 × 0.008) = 0.5 × (0.36 + 0.40). That is the normal-market cost using mean spreads. A would be right only if the question asked for the expected (mean-spread) cost of liquidation.

b.reason: B is equation 1.2 at $\lambda=$ 2.326: half of each position’s 99% worst-case proportional spread times its mid-market value, summed under perfect correlation.

c.reason: (Wrong percentile). SGD 1.120 million uses $\lambda=$ 1.645 (95%): 0.5 × 3.0 × (0.120 + 1.645 × 0.200) + 0.5 × 20.0 × (0.020 + 1.645 × 0.015) = 0.6735 + 0.4468. C would be right if the stem specified a 95% confidence level.

d.reason: (Dropped term). SGD 2.853 million omits the one-half: 2 × 1.4267. It charges the full worst-case spread rather than the half-spread lost when trading away from mid. D would be right only for a full round-trip (offer-to-bid) cost.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Explain and calculate liquidity trading risk via cost of liquidation and liquidity-adjusted VaR (LVaR).
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-1 a Q5
questions.question: An internal auditor at a Frankfurt-based bank is validating the model used to compute the stressed-market cost of liquidating the bank’s EUR trading book, $\sum_{\text{i}}(\mu_{\text{i}} + \lambda\sigma_{\text{i}})\alpha_{\text{i}}$/2 with $\lambda=$ 2.326. The documentation assumes normally distributed spreads and sums the position-level costs. The auditor’s back-testing shows that, for the bank’s high-yield bond category, the 99th percentile of the proportional spread lies 3.6 standard deviations above its mean. Which of the following conclusions is most appropriate?

options.text: Summing position-level costs is overly conservative, because it assumes spreads are perfectly correlated, whereas in tight markets spreads in different instruments tend to widen independently.
$\lambda$ should remain 2.326 for every instrument, because the 99% confidence level fixes $\lambda$ regardless of the empirical distribution of spreads.
For the high-yield bond category, setting $\lambda$ equal to 3.6 is appropriate, because $\lambda$ can reflect the empirical distribution of spreads rather than the normal distribution.
The cost measure should be expected to rise as the assumed liquidation period lengthens, because a longer period exposes the book to wider spreads.

questions.solution:
Frankfurt bank audit: assumptions behind the stressed-market cost of liquidation.

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s stressed-market measure, $\sum_{\text{i}}(\mu_{\text{i}} + \lambda\sigma_{\text{i}})\alpha_{\text{i}}$/2, rests on three modelling choices, and GARP comments on each.

Distribution of spreads and the choice of $\lambda$. If spreads are normal, a 99% one-tailed worst case gives $\lambda=$ 2.326. GARP notes that in practice spreads are not normally distributed, and it may be appropriate to use a $\lambda$ that reflects their empirical distribution. Its own illustration: if the 99th percentile of the distribution for a category of instruments is 3.6 standard deviations above the mean, $\lambda$ can be set to 3.6 for those instruments. So $\lambda$ is a calibrated parameter, not a fixed constant tied to the normal table.

Correlation. Summing position-level costs assumes spreads in all instruments are perfectly correlated. GARP states that this may seem overly conservative but is not: when liquidity is tight and spreads widen, they tend to do so for all instruments together.

Liquidation horizon. The spread depends on how quickly a position is liquidated. Both measures in equations 1.1 and 1.2 are therefore likely to be decreasing functions of the time period assumed for liquidation: a slower sale meets narrower spreads. GARP also recommends calculating both measures regularly to monitor changes in the book’s liquidity.

| Assumption | GARP’s view |
|---|---|
| Normal spreads, $\lambda=$ 2.326 | May be replaced by an empirical $\lambda$ (for example 3.6) |
| Perfect correlation (sum of costs) | Not overly conservative; spreads widen together |
| Liquidation period | Longer period, lower cost (decreasing function) |

**Applying it to this question**

The stem gives the auditor’s key finding: for high-yield bonds the empirical 99th percentile lies 3.6 standard deviations above the mean, not 2.326. That is exactly GARP’s case for setting $\lambda=$ 3.6 for that category. Keeping 2.326 would understate the worst-case spread for fat-tailed instruments. The summation and horizon features are not defects, and statements A and D misstate them.

**Fragile fact.** The perfect-correlation assumption is not overly conservative; the cost measures decrease as the liquidation period lengthens; $\lambda$ may be set empirically (3.6 in GARP’s example).

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 66.a, verbatim):** Explain and calculate liquidity trading risk via cost of liquidation and liquidity-adjusted VaR (LVaR).

**GARP:** Chapter 1, Section 1.1.2 Measuring Market Liquidity (text after Example 1.2). **GARP** **vs Schweser:** Schweser says the equation assumes a “strong positive correlation”; GARP says perfectly correlated. Schweser omits the empirical-$\lambda$ (3.6) point and the liquidation-period point, so those facts are GARP-only.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-1 a, where it is Q5 of 9.

a.reason: (Polarity flip). A reverses GARP’s conclusion. GARP says the perfect-correlation assumption “may seem overly conservative, but it is not”, because spreads widen together when liquidity is tight. A would be right only if spreads behaved independently in stressed markets, which GARP rejects.

b.reason: (Absolute claim). B makes $\lambda$ fixed for every instrument whatever the evidence. GARP explicitly allows $\lambda$ to reflect the empirical distribution. B would be right only if spreads were known to be normally distributed for every instrument.

c.reason: C matches GARP’s text: where the 99 percentile point of the spread distribution for a category of instruments is 3.6 standard deviations above the mean, $\lambda$ can be set to 3.6 for those instruments.

d.reason: (Polarity flip). D reverses the horizon effect. GARP states that the measures are likely to be decreasing functions of the liquidation period, since slower liquidation meets narrower spreads. D would be right if the question asked about the effect of a shorter liquidation period.

questions.loText: Explain and calculate liquidity trading risk via cost of liquidation and liquidity-adjusted VaR (LVaR).
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-1 a Q6
questions.question:
A portfolio manager at a Sao Paulo asset manager reports liquidity-adjusted VaR, defined as regular VaR plus the cost of unwinding positions in a stressed market. Spreads are assumed normally distributed and perfectly correlated; use $\lambda=$ 2.326.

- One-day 99% VaR of the two-position portfolio: BRL 3.10 million.
- Standalone one-day 99% VaR: position X BRL 2.60 million; position Y BRL 1.70 million.

| Position | Mid-market value (BRL m) | Mean proportional spread | SD proportional spread |
|---|---|---|---|
| X | 60 | 0.004 | 0.003 |
| Y | 25 | 0.012 | 0.010 |

Which of the following is closest to the portfolio’s liquidity-adjusted VaR?

options.text: BRL 3.870 million
BRL 3.370 million
BRL 4.640 million
BRL 5.070 million

questions.solution:
Sao Paulo asset manager: LVaR as portfolio VaR plus stressed-market cost of unwinding.

**Concept and theory**

Market VaR estimates a worst-case change in the mark-to-market value of the trading book. The cost-of-liquidation measures estimate what it would cost to exit the book if market prices did not change. The two capture different risks, and some researchers (Bangia, Diebold, Schuermann and Stroughair, cited by GARP) combine them into a liquidity-adjusted VaR. GARP gives two definitions:

LVaR (normal) $= \text{VaR} + \sum_{\text{i}=1}^{\text{n}} \frac{\text{s}_{\text{i}}\alpha_{\text{i}}}{2}$ (equation 1.3)

LVaR (stressed) $= \text{VaR} + \sum_{\text{i}=1}^{\text{n}} \frac{(\mu_{\text{i}} + \lambda\sigma_{\text{i}})\alpha_{\text{i}}}{2}$

Symbols are as before: $\text{s}_{\text{i}}$ is the normal-market proportional spread, $\mu_{\text{i}}$ and $\sigma_{\text{i}}$ are the mean and standard deviation of the proportional spread, $\alpha_{\text{i}}$ is the mid-market value, and $\lambda$ is the spread confidence parameter.

The two pieces aggregate differently. VaR is a portfolio measure: the VaR of the whole book reflects diversification across positions, so the relevant input is the portfolio VaR, not the sum of standalone VaRs. The liquidity add-on is a sum of position-level costs, because it assumes spreads are perfectly correlated (they widen together when liquidity is tight), and because each unwind’s half-spread cost cannot be offset by another’s. The adjustment always increases VaR: the cost of liquidation is an additional loss.

**Applying it to this question**

Formula: LVaR $= \text{VaR}_{\text{portfolio}} + \sum_{\text{i}}$ 0.5 $\alpha_{\text{i}}(\mu_{\text{i}} +$ 2.326 $\sigma_{\text{i}})$.

$\text{Cost}_{\text{X}} =$ 0.5 × 60 × (0.004 + 2.326 × 0.003) = 0.5 × 60 × 0.010978 = 0.32934m

$\text{Cost}_{\text{Y}} =$ 0.5 × 25 × (0.012 + 2.326 × 0.010) = 0.5 × 25 × 0.035260 = 0.44075m

Liquidity add-on = 0.32934 + 0.44075 = 0.77009m

LVaR = 3.10 + 0.77009 = 3.87009m ≈ BRL 3.870 million

The standalone VaRs (BRL 2.60m and 1.70m) are irrelevant inputs: the stem defines LVaR on the portfolio’s VaR, which already reflects diversification between X and Y.

**Fragile fact.** VaR enters at the portfolio level (diversified); the liquidity add-on is a straight sum of half-spread costs; the stressed version uses $\mu+ \lambda\sigma$.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 66.a, verbatim):** Explain and calculate liquidity trading risk via cost of liquidation and liquidity-adjusted VaR (LVaR).

**GARP:** Chapter 1, Section 1.1.3 Liquidity-Adjusted VaR, equation (1.3) and the stressed-market version that follows it (footnote 1, Bangia et al.). **GARP vs Schweser:** none; Schweser states that VaR can be adjusted for the cost of unwinding in both normal and stressed markets (its equation images are missing from the text file).

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-1 a, where it is Q6 of 9.

a.reason: A follows the stressed-market definition of LVaR exactly: regular (portfolio) VaR plus the sum of half of each position’s worst-case proportional spread times its mid-market value.

b.reason: (Dropped term). BRL 3.370 million omits $\lambda\sigma_{\text{i}}$: 3.10 + 0.5 × (60 × 0.004 + 25 × 0.012) = 3.10 + 0.27. This is LVaR under the normal-market definition (equation 1.3) with mean spreads. B would be right if the firm defined LVaR with the normal-market cost.

c.reason: (Dropped term). BRL 4.640 million omits the one-half on the liquidity add-on: 3.10 + 2 × 0.77009. C would be right only if an unwind crossed the full spread rather than half of it.

d.reason: (Wrong input twin). BRL 5.070 million uses the sum of standalone VaRs (2.60 + 1.70 = 4.30) instead of the portfolio VaR: 4.30 + 0.77. D would be right only if the stem defined LVaR on undiversified (summed) VaR.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Explain and calculate liquidity trading risk via cost of liquidation and liquidity-adjusted VaR (LVaR).
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-1 a Q7
questions.question: A member of the board risk committee at a London-based bank asks the head of market risk to explain the bank’s new liquidity-adjusted VaR (LVaR) report for its GBP trading book. Which of the following explanations is most accurate?

options.text: The cost of liquidation already captures adverse moves in mid-market prices, so adding it to VaR double counts market risk; LVaR is useful only as a cross-check on VaR.
Defining LVaR with the stressed-market cost of liquidation produces a lower figure than defining it with the normal-market cost, because the stressed measure uses only the mean spread.
The liquidity adjustment in LVaR equals the full proportional bid-offer spread times the value of each position, because closing a position means crossing the whole spread.
VaR estimates a worst-case change in mark-to-market value, while the cost-of-liquidation measures assume market prices do not change; LVaR adds the cost of unwinding to VaR to combine the two.

questions.solution:
London bank board question: what LVaR combines and why.

**Concept and theory**

GARP introduces liquidity-adjusted VaR by contrasting two measurement tools. Market VaR is designed to estimate a “worst case” change in the mark-to-market valuation of the trading book: it is about prices moving. The cost-of-liquidation measures (equations 1.1 and 1.2) are designed to estimate the cost of liquidating the book if market prices do not change: they are about the half-spread lost when trading away from mid. Because the two measures deal with different risks, some researchers have suggested combining them into one number.

GARP gives two versions:

LVaR $= \text{VaR} + \sum_{\text{i}=1}^{\text{n}} \frac{\text{s}_{\text{i}}\alpha_{\text{i}}}{2} \text{or LVaR} = \text{VaR} + \sum_{\text{i}=1}^{\text{n}} \frac{(\mu_{\text{i}} + \lambda\sigma_{\text{i}})\alpha_{\text{i}}}{2}$ .

The first adds the normal-market cost of unwinding; the second adds the stressed-market cost. Since $\mu_{\text{i}} + \lambda\sigma_{\text{i}} > \mu_{\text{i}}$ for any positive $\lambda$ and $\sigma_{\text{i}}$, the stressed version is larger. Schweser’s Professor’s Note makes the same directional point: the confidence parameter times spread volatility is added to the mean spread because the liquidity adjustment increases VaR. In each case the cost is half the spread, because a sale at the bid (or a purchase at the offer) is half a spread from the mid-market fair price.

GARP also links LVaR to execution: a trader unwinding a large position might minimise VaR after trading costs, which is “something similar” to LVaR (Section 1.1.4).

**Applying it to this question**

The board member asks what the report means. The deciding facts are (i) VaR and the cost-of-liquidation measures address different risks, the latter assuming no price change, and (ii) LVaR is VaR plus the cost of unwinding in normal or stressed markets. Only D states both.

**Fragile fact.** The cost-of-liquidation measures assume no price change; LVaR adds them to VaR; the stressed version is always the larger.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 66.a, verbatim):** Explain and calculate liquidity trading risk via cost of liquidation and liquidity-adjusted VaR (LVaR).

**GARP:** Chapter 1, Section 1.1.3 Liquidity-Adjusted VaR. **GARP vs Schweser:** none; Schweser’s Professor’s Note confirms that adding $\gamma\sigma$ raises VaR (Schweser $\gamma$ is GARP $\lambda$).

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-1 a, where it is Q7 of 9.

GARP says the cost measures are computed as if market prices do not change, so there is no double counting. A would be right only if the liquidation cost were modelled to include adverse mid-market moves.

The stressed cost uses $\mu_{\text{i}} + \lambda\sigma_{\text{i}}$, not the mean alone, so stressed LVaR is the higher figure. B would be right if “stressed” and “normal” were swapped and the normal measure used the mean spread.

questions.question: A risk consultant at a Shanghai securities firm is reviewing a plan to unwind a large CNY position over n days. The desk chooses daily quantities to minimise the unwind cost that will not be exceeded at a chosen confidence level, combining bid-offer costs (which rise with the quantity traded per day) and the risk of adverse moves in the mid-market price. Which of the following statements about the optimal plan is most accurate?

options.text: At a high confidence level, the desk should sell exactly 1/n of the position each day, because equal daily trades minimise total bid-offer costs.
The desk should trade more than 1/n of the position on day 1, and lowering the confidence level makes the amounts traded each day less variable.
Unwinding quickly lowers the bid-offer cost but raises exposure to mid-market moves, so a slower unwind is preferred when the spread is very sensitive to daily volume.
As the confidence level falls toward 50%, the desk cares only about the standard deviation of costs, so the whole position should be sold on day 1.

questions.solution:
Shanghai securities firm: properties of the optimal multi-day unwind plan.

**Concept and theory**

GARP Section 1.1.4 (based on Almgren and Chriss, 2001) treats the unwinding of a large position as a trade-off. Unwinding quickly means large daily trades, so the bid-offer spread faced is large, but the position is held for only a short time, so the potential loss from the mid-market price moving against the trader is small. Unwinding slowly means smaller daily trades and narrower spreads, but more days of exposure to adverse price moves.

Formally, a position of V units is sold over n days with $\text{q}_{\text{i}}$ units on day i, leaving $\text{x}_{\text{i}} = \text{x}_{\text{i}}-_{1} - \text{q}_{\text{i}}$ (with $\text{x}_{0} =$ V). The dollar spread when q units trade in a day is p$(\text{q})$, rising in q. The trader chooses the $\text{q}_{\text{i}}$ to minimise the unwind cost not exceeded at the chosen confidence level:

$\lambda\sqrt{\sum_{\text{i}=1}^{\text{n}} \sigma^{2}\text{x}^{2}_{\text{i}}} + \sum_{\text{i}=1}^{\text{n}} \frac{\text{q}_{\text{i}} \text{p}(\text{q}_{\text{i}})}{2}$ subject to $\sum_{\text{i}=1}^{\text{n}} \text{q}_{\text{i}} =$ V.

GARP’s Example 1.3 (100 million units over five days) gives three lessons:

| Confidence level | Amounts traded, days 1 to 5 (million units) |
|---|---|
| 95% | 48.9, 30.0, 14.1, 5.1, 1.9 |
| 75% | 36.1, 26.2, 17.7, 11.6, 8.4 |
| 50% | 20, 20, 20, 20, 20 |

(1) More than 1/n of the position should be traded on day 1, because the longer any part is held, the greater the risk of adverse moves. (2) As the confidence level falls, the amounts traded show less variability. (3) At 50%, $\lambda=$ 0: the trader cares only about expected costs, not the standard deviation of costs, and trades equal amounts each day.

**Applying it to this question**

The plan minimises a confidence-level cost, so lesson (1) applies: front-load, more than 1/n on day 1. Lesson (2) says that lowering the confidence level flattens the schedule. Statement B contains both facts and nothing false.

**Fragile fact.** Quick unwind: high spread cost, low market risk. Optimal plans front-load (more than 1/n on day 1). At 50%, equal amounts.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 66.a, verbatim):** Explain and calculate liquidity trading risk via cost of liquidation and liquidity-adjusted VaR (LVaR).

**GARP:** Chapter 1, Section 1.1.4 Unwinding a Position Optimally, Example 1.3, and chapter Summary. **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser covers the quick versus slow trade-off but its equations are missing from the text file and it omits Example 1.3; the front-loading and confidence-level facts are GARP-only. **Source caution:** GARP’s optimisation formulas are garbled in the text extraction; the objective shown above was reconstructed and verified by reproducing Example 1.3’s published amounts exactly.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-1 a, where it is Q8 of 9.

a.reason: (Scope or condition error). Equal 1/n trades are optimal only at the 50% confidence level, where the market-risk term vanishes. A moves that condition to a high confidence level. A would be right if the stem said the desk minimised only expected costs (50%).

b.reason: B restates GARP’s conclusions from Example 1.3: more than 1/n is traded on the first day, and as the VaR confidence level is reduced, the amounts traded per day show less variability.

c.reason: (Polarity flip). C reverses the speed effect on spreads. A quick unwind raises bid-offer costs and lowers market-risk exposure (GARP Summary). C would be right if it said “unwinding slowly lowers the bid-offer cost but raises exposure to mid-market moves”.

d.reason: (Sibling swap). D attributes to the 50% case the opposite concern. At 50% the trader is interested only in expected costs, not the standard deviation of costs, and trades equal amounts. Front-loading comes from the variance term, which matters more at higher confidence. D would be right only if it described a very high confidence level and said “more on day 1”, not “the whole position”.

questions.question:
A treasury analyst at a US bank must unwind a position of 10 million units of an asset over two days. Trading takes place at the beginning of each day, daily mid-market price changes are normal and independent, and the dollar bid-offer spread when q million units are traded in one day is p$(\text{q}) = \text{a} + \text{b e}^{\text{cq}}$.

| Input | Value |
|---|---|
| a, b, c | 0.10, 0.04, 0.10 (q in millions) |
| Standard deviation of price change per day | USD 0.08 per unit |
| Confidence parameter $\lambda$ (95%) | 1.645 |
| Average daily market volume | 25 million units |
| Plan Y | sell 7 million units on day 1, 3 million on day 2 |

Which of the following is closest to the 95% unwind cost measure (bid-offer costs plus the market-risk term) that the analyst would minimise, evaluated for Plan Y?

options.text: USD 0.863 million
USD 2.121 million
USD 1.258 million
USD 2.237 million

questions.solution:
US bank: evaluate the 95% unwind cost measure for a two-day plan (7 then 3 million units).

**Concept and theory**

GARP models the unwind of V units over n days using dollar spreads, because the spread depends on the quantity traded each day. Define $\text{q}_{\text{i}}$ as the units traded on day i and $\text{x}_{\text{i}}$ as the position at the end of day i, so $\text{x}_{\text{i}} = \text{x}_{\text{i}}-_{1} - \text{q}_{\text{i}} \text{with x}_{0} =$ V, and $\text{x}_{\text{n}} =$ 0. Each trade costs half the dollar spread p$(\text{q}_{\text{i}})$ per unit, so total bid-offer costs are $\sum_{\text{i}} \text{q}_{\text{i}}$ p$(\text{q}_{\text{i}})$/2.

For market risk, mid-market price changes are normal with standard deviation $\sigma$ per day and independent across days. Because trading takes place at the beginning of each day, the position exposed during day i is $\text{x}_{\text{i}}$, and the variance of the value change on day i is $\sigma^{2}\text{x}^{2}_{\text{i}}$. Summing over independent days gives a total variance of $\sum_{\text{i}} \sigma^{2}\text{x}^{2}_{\text{i}}$. The trader minimises

$$\underbrace{\lambda\sqrt{\sum_{\text{i}=1}^{\text{n}} \sigma^{2}\text{x}_{\text{i}}^{2}}}_{\text{market-risk term}} + \underbrace{\sum_{\text{i}=1}^{\text{n}} \frac{\text{q}_{\text{i}}\,\text{p}(\text{q}_{\text{i}})}{2}}_{\text{bid-offer costs}}, \qquad \text{p}(\text{q}) = \text{a} + \text{b}\,\text{e}^{\text{cq}},$$

subject to $\sum\text{q}_{\text{i}} =$ V. Here $\lambda$ is the confidence parameter (1.645 at 95%, 2.326 at 99%), and a, b, c describe how the dollar spread widens with daily volume. GARP calls this minimising VaR after trading costs, which is similar to the LVaR measure in equation (1.3). The front-loading result arises because selling more on day 1 shrinks the later $\text{x}_{\text{i}}$ and therefore the market-risk term, at the price of a wider spread on day 1.

**Applying it to this question**

Plan Y: $\text{q}_{1} =$ 7, $\text{q}_{2} =$ 3, so $\text{x}_{1} =$ 10 − 7 = 3 and $\text{x}_{2} =$ 0 (units in millions).

p(7) = 0.10 + 0.04 $\text{e}^{0.7} =$ 0.10 + 0.04 × 2.01375 = 0.18055

p(3) = 0.10 + 0.04 $\text{e}^{0.3} =$ 0.10 + 0.04 × 1.34986 = 0.15399

Bid-offer costs $= \frac{1}{2} ($7 × 0.18055$) + \frac{1}{2} ($3 × 0.15399) = 0.63193 + 0.23099 = 0.86292

Market-risk term = 1.645 $\times\sqrt{0.08^{2} \times(3^{2} + 0^{2})} =$ 1.645 × 0.08 × 3 = 0.39480

Unwind cost measure = 0.86292 + 0.39480 = 1.25772 ≈ USD 1.258 million

With 95% confidence, unwinding under Plan Y should cost no more than about USD 1.26 million. For comparison, an equal 5/5 split gives 0.82974 + 0.65800 = 1.48774, so the front-loaded plan is better here. The average daily market volume (25 million units) is irrelevant: the spread function already maps daily quantity to spread.

**Fragile fact.** With trading at the start of each day, the exposure on day i is the end-of-day position $\text{x}_{\text{i}}$ (so $\text{x}_{\text{n}} =$ 0); halve the dollar spread; the variance terms sum before the square root.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 66.a, verbatim):** Explain and calculate liquidity trading risk via cost of liquidation and liquidity-adjusted VaR (LVaR).

**GARP:** Chapter 1, Section 1.1.4 Unwinding a Position Optimally, and Example 1.3. **GARP** **vs Schweser:** Schweser mentions the equations but they are missing from its text file, so this content is GARP-based. **Source caution:** the GARP text extraction garbles the bid-offer cost and objective formulas; they were reconstructed from the surviving text (“each trade costs half the bid-offer spread”, variance on day i of $\sigma^{2}\text{x}^{2}_{\text{i}}$, trading at the beginning of a day) and verified by reproducing Example 1.3’s amounts (48.9, 30.0, 14.1, 5.1, 1.9 at 95%) exactly.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-1 a, where it is Q9 of 9.

a.reason: (Intermediate result). USD 0.863 million is the bid-offer component alone (0.63193 + 0.23099); the market-risk term 0.39480 was not added. A would be right if the question asked for expected bid-offer costs only (the 50% case, $\lambda=$ 0).

b.reason: (Dropped term). USD 2.121 million omits the one-half on trading costs: 7 × 0.18055 + 3 × 0.15399 = 1.72585, plus 0.39480. B would be right only if each trade cost the full spread.

c.reason: C applies GARP’s objective with end-of-day positions $\text{(x}_{1} =$ 3, $\text{x}_{2} =$ 0), half the dollar spread on each day’s trade, and $\lambda=$ 1.645.

d.reason: (Wrong input twin). USD 2.237 million uses start-of-day positions (10 and 3) instead of end-of-day positions (3 and 0): 1.645 × 0.08 $\times\sqrt{10^{2} + 3^{2}} =$ 1.645 × 0.08 × 10.44031 = 1.37394, plus 0.86292. Because trading occurs at the beginning of each day, the 7 million sold on day 1 is never exposed to day 1’s price move. D would be right if trading took place at the end of each day.

questions.question: A member of the board risk committee of a Brazilian mortgage lender is reviewing the lender’s year-end balance sheet. Assets of BRL 60 billion consist mainly of residential mortgages that cannot be sold quickly. The assets are financed 88% by deposits and short-term borrowings and 12% by equity. The average loan-to-value ratio of the mortgage book is 64%. A stress scenario assumes that 30% of depositors withdraw their funds within two weeks. Which of the following best describes the lender’s position under this scenario?

options.text: The lender becomes insolvent as soon as the withdrawals begin, because each withdrawal reduces equity, so the scenario is a test of solvency rather than of liquidity.
The lender faces little funding risk, because a lender with positive equity can always raise enough cash at short notice by borrowing against its mortgage assets.
The lender is solvent, since assets exceed liabilities, but it could still fail if it cannot turn its illiquid mortgages into cash quickly enough to meet the withdrawals.
The scenario mainly measures liquidity trading risk, so it is best quantified as the cost of unwinding the mortgage book at the normal-market bid-offer spread.

questions.solution:
Brazilian mortgage lender, 88% deposit and short-term funded, 30% withdrawal stress: solvency versus liquidity.

**Concept and theory**

GARP opens the chapter by separating two ideas that are often confused. Solvency means a company has more assets than liabilities, so its equity is positive. Liquidity means the company can make cash payments as they become due. Liquidity funding risk, the subject of Section 1.2, is the risk to a financial institution’s ability to meet its cash needs as they arise. The two can diverge sharply: GARP stresses that institutions that are solvent can, and sometimes do, fail because of liquidity problems.

GARP’s illustration is a bank whose assets are mostly illiquid mortgages, financed 90% with deposits and 10% with equity. That bank is comfortably solvent, yet it could fail if 25% of depositors suddenly decided to withdraw their funds, because the mortgages cannot be turned into cash fast enough. Northern Rock is GARP’s real-world example: the regulator judged it solvent, but it could not fund itself.

|  | Solvency | Liquidity (funding) |
|---|---|---|
| Question asked | Do assets exceed liabilities? | Can cash be paid when due? |
| Balance-sheet test | Equity > 0 | Cash and convertible assets versus outflows |
| Effect of a deposit withdrawal | None (assets and liabilities both fall) | Drains cash immediately |

A withdrawal reduces a liability (the deposit) and an asset (cash) by the same amount, so equity is unchanged. What changes is the stock of cash available for the next withdrawal.

**Applying it to this question**

Assets of BRL 60 billion are funded 12% by equity, so equity is about BRL 7.2 billion and positive: the lender is solvent. The stress is a 30% deposit withdrawal within two weeks, while the assets are mortgages that “cannot be sold quickly”. This is GARP’s 90/10 bank with a run, in different numbers. The 64% loan-to-value ratio is an irrelevant input: it speaks to credit risk on the mortgages, not to whether they can be converted to cash in two weeks.

**Fragile fact.** A run leaves equity unchanged; it drains cash. A solvent firm can fail for liquidity reasons, and the reverse does not follow.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 66.b, verbatim):** Identify examples of liquidity funding risk, funding sources, and lessons learned from real cases: Northern Rock, Ashanti Goldfields, and Metallgesellschaft.

**GARP:** Chapter 1, introduction (solvency versus liquidity; the 90%/10% mortgage bank) and Section 1.2, Liquidity Funding Risk. **GARP vs Schweser:** none. Schweser defines funding risk the same way but omits the 90/10 illustration.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-1 b, where it is Q1 of 14.

a.reason: (Sibling swap: solvency for liquidity). A withdrawal lowers cash and deposits by the same amount, so it does not reduce equity. Treating a run as a solvency event confuses the two concepts that GARP separates. A would be right only if the scenario were a credit loss on the mortgages large enough to wipe out the 12% equity.

b.reason: (Absolute claim). GARP explains that in stressed conditions lenders become risk averse, charge more, shorten maturities, and sometimes refuse to lend at all. Positive equity guarantees nothing about access to cash. B would be closer to right only under unstressed markets, where GARP says a creditworthy bank usually has no problem borrowing.

c.reason: C states both halves of GARP’s point: the lender is solvent (assets exceed liabilities), yet it can still fail because illiquid mortgages cannot be converted into cash quickly enough to meet withdrawals. GARP says solvent institutions can and sometimes do fail because of liquidity problems.

d.reason: (Sibling swap: trading risk for funding risk). Liquidity trading risk concerns how easily trading-book positions can be unwound, measured by bid-offer costs. The scenario is about meeting cash outflows on the funding side, which is liquidity funding risk. Even where asset sales are used, GARP says the analysis should use stressed, not normal, conditions. D would fit a question about the cost of unwinding a traded portfolio.

questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a Japanese regional bank is preparing a report for the asset-liability committee on what can cause liquidity funding problems. The bank funds JPY 2.4 trillion of loans, about 70% of which have maturities beyond five years. The analyst drafts the following statements:

I. A flight to quality across the economy can leave investors reluctant to provide funding wherever there is any credit risk at all.

II. Overly aggressive funding decisions, such as using short-term instruments to fund long-term needs, create a liquidity mismatch.

III. Poor financial performance can undermine confidence, leading to a loss of deposits and difficulty in rolling over funding.

IV. Financing long-term loans with long-term bonds and equity, so that funding outlasts the assets, is a leading cause of funding problems.

Which of the statements correctly identify causes of liquidity funding problems?

options.text: I, II, and III only
II and III only
I, II, III, and IV
II, III, and IV only

questions.solution:
Japanese regional bank ALCO report: which statements identify causes of liquidity funding problems.

**Concept and theory**

GARP lists three causes of liquidity funding problems at a financial institution (Section 1.2):

1. **Liquidity stresses in the economy**, such as the flight to quality of 2007 to 2009. Investors then become reluctant to provide funding wherever there is any credit risk at all. This cause is market-wide and outside the institution’s control.
2. **Overly aggressive funding decisions.** GARP notes a tendency for all financial institutions to use short-term instruments to fund long-term needs, which creates a liquidity mismatch. GARP poses the question each institution must ask: how much of a mismatch is too much?
3. **Poor financial performance**, which leads to a lack of confidence. This can cause a loss of deposits and difficulty in rolling over funding.

GARP adds that, often, when a company experiences severe liquidity problems, all three occur at the same time. Northern Rock combined all of them: a market-wide flight from mortgage-exposed banks, a model built on short-term funding of long-term mortgages, and a collapse of confidence once its emergency borrowing became public.

Schweser condenses the same list into weak financial performance, liquidity stresses causing hesitant investors, and funding decisions that create short-for-long mismatches. The common thread is that funding risk lives on the liability side: it concerns whether funding is available and can be rolled over, not whether assets earn enough.

**Applying it to this question**

Check each statement against the list. Statement I is cause 1 almost verbatim. Statement II is cause 2. Statement III is cause 3. Statement IV reverses cause 2: funding long-term loans with long-term bonds and equity removes the short-for-long mismatch rather than creating it, so it cannot be a leading cause of funding problems. The bank’s loan figures (JPY 2.4 trillion, 70% beyond five years) are context only. They show why the mismatch question matters but do not change which statements are accurate.

**Fragile fact.** The mismatch runs short-term funding to long-term assets, not the reverse. All three causes often strike at the same time.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 66.b, verbatim):** Identify examples of liquidity funding risk, funding sources, and lessons learned from real cases: Northern Rock, Ashanti Goldfields, and Metallgesellschaft.

**GARP:** Chapter 1, Section 1.2, Liquidity Funding Risk (list of three causes). **GARP vs Schweser:** none; Schweser gives the same three causes in condensed form.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-1 b, where it is Q2 of 14.

a.reason: I, II and III match GARP’s three causes exactly; IV inverts the mismatch. Hence A.

b.reason: (Scope or condition error). B drops statement I, as if funding problems came only from firm-specific decisions or performance. GARP lists economy-wide liquidity stress (a flight to quality) as the first cause. B would be right only if the question asked for causes within management’s control.

c.reason: (Polarity flip (accepts IV)). Statement IV reverses the direction of the mismatch. The problem GARP describes is short-term funding of long-term needs; long-term funding of long-term assets is the conservative alternative. C would be right if IV read “financing long-term loans with short-term instruments”.

d.reason: (Polarity flip plus omission). D accepts the inverted statement IV and drops the genuine market-wide cause in statement I. It would be right only if IV described a short-for-long mismatch and I were not one of GARP’s causes.

questions.question: A treasury analyst at a Canadian bank is building a model that forecasts the bank’s cash needs over the next 90 days. The bank has CAD 1.5 billion of bonds outstanding, has granted CAD 4 billion of undrawn credit lines to corporate clients, holds CAD 22 billion of retail deposits, and has written guarantees and derivatives with downgrade triggers. Which of the following statements about the predictability of these cash needs is most accurate?

options.text: Retail deposit withdrawals are as predictable as bond coupons, because the bank serves many small depositors whose behaviour averages out.
Drawdowns on the credit lines are fully predictable, because the bank itself set the limits and the terms of each facility in advance.
As the bank’s instruments have grown more complex, its cash needs have become easier to forecast, since the triggers are written into contracts.
Coupons on the bank’s bonds are predictable, whereas downgrade triggers, guarantees, and derivative counterparty defaults can hit cash unexpectedly.

questions.solution:
Canadian bank 90-day cash-need model: which statement about the predictability of cash needs is most accurate.

**Concept and theory**

GARP states that the key to managing liquidity funding risk is predicting cash needs and ensuring that they can be met in adverse scenarios. Cash needs differ greatly in how predictable they are:

| Predictable | Less predictable |
|---|---|
| Coupons on bonds the bank has issued | Withdrawals of deposits by retail customers |
| (dates and amounts are known) | Drawdowns by corporations on credit lines the bank granted Downgrade triggers in contracts Guarantees provided by the institution Possible defaults by derivative counterparties |

GARP’s example of a predictable need is a bond issue: the bank knows when coupons will have to be paid. Deposit withdrawals and credit-line drawdowns depend on decisions by customers, made at times the bank does not control. GARP then adds a point that is easy to reverse: as the instruments entered into by financial institutions have become more complex, cash needs have become more difficult to predict. Downgrade triggers, guarantees, and possible counterparty defaults on derivatives can have an unexpected impact on cash resources.

This matters because sources of liquidity have to be sized against cash needs in stressed scenarios. A forecast that treats contingent outflows as if they were scheduled will understate what the bank needs to hold. GARP’s summary says cash needs depend on depositor withdrawals, credit-line drawdowns, guarantees, counterparty defaults, and so on, and should be forecast in both normal and stressed conditions so that they can be met with almost total certainty.

**Applying it to this question**

The four items in the stem map directly to the table. The bonds’ coupons are scheduled. The CAD 4 billion of undrawn lines and the CAD 22 billion of retail deposits are behavioural and uncertain in timing. The guarantees and downgrade triggers are contingent and can hit cash unexpectedly. The sizes of the balances do not change which category each falls into.

**Fragile fact.** Complexity makes cash needs harder, not easier, to predict. Coupons are the textbook predictable outflow.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 66.b, verbatim):** Identify examples of liquidity funding risk, funding sources, and lessons learned from real cases: Northern Rock, Ashanti Goldfields, and Metallgesellschaft.

**GARP:** Chapter 1, Section 1.2, Liquidity Funding Risk (predicting cash needs), and Summary. **GARP vs Schweser:** none. Schweser gives the coupon and withdrawal examples but omits the complexity point (downgrade triggers, guarantees, counterparty defaults), which comes from GARP.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-1 b, where it is Q3 of 14.

a.reason: (Sibling swap). A gives retail withdrawals the predictability of a scheduled coupon. GARP lists retail deposit withdrawals as an example of a less predictable cash need. A would be right only if deposits had fixed contractual withdrawal dates.

b.reason: (Scope or condition error). Knowing the limit of a credit line does not tell the bank when or how much will be drawn. GARP names credit-line drawdowns as less predictable. B would be right only if the lines were fully drawn on fixed dates.

c.reason: (Polarity flip). GARP says growing complexity has made cash needs more difficult to predict, not easier. C would be right if it said “harder to forecast”.

d.reason: D separates the predictable need (coupons) from the contingent ones (downgrade triggers, guarantees, counterparty defaults), exactly as GARP does.

questions.question: The treasurer of an Australian bank is presenting to the board on two of the bank’s sources of liquidity: its holdings of cash and Treasury securities (AUD 9 billion), and its ability to liquidate trading book positions (AUD 14 billion at mid-market value). Which of the following pairs of statements is most accurate?

options.text: Cash and Treasury securities are a cheap source of liquidity, so the bank should hold as much as it can; trading book liquidity should be assessed under stressed rather than normal market conditions.

Cash and Treasury securities are a relatively expensive source of liquidity, which limits how much the bank can hold; trading book liquidity should be assessed under normal market conditions, which prevail most of the time.

Australian bank treasurer: cash and Treasury securities versus trading book liquidation as liquidity sources.

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s Section 1.2.1 lists the main sources of liquidity for a financial institution: (1) holdings of cash and Treasury securities; (2) the ability to liquidate trading book positions; (3) the ability to borrow money at short notice; (4) the ability to offer favourable terms to attract retail and wholesale deposits at short notice; (5) the ability to securitize assets at short notice; (6) borrowings from the central bank. This question tests the first two.

**Cash and Treasury securities** are excellent sources of liquidity. Cash is always available, and Treasury securities issued by countries such as the United States and the United Kingdom can generally be converted into cash at short notice without any problem. But GARP calls them relatively expensive sources of liquidity. There is a trade-off between an asset’s liquidity and its return. To be profitable, an institution must invest in assets such as corporate loans that earn more than Treasuries, so there is a limit to how much cash and Treasury holdings can reasonably be held. The cost of this source is the return given up.

**Liquidating trading book positions** links funding risk to liquidity trading risk (Section 1.1). Selling part of the trading book is one way to meet funding needs, so the institution must quantify how liquid the book is. GARP insists that the analysis rest on stressed market conditions, when there is a general shortage of liquidity, not on normal conditions. That is why the stressed-market bid-offer measures matter.

**Applying it to this question**

Each option pairs a claim about cash and Treasuries with a claim about the trading book. The correct pair must call cash and Treasuries relatively expensive (with a limit on holdings) and require a stressed-market assessment of the trading book. The balance-sheet amounts (AUD 9 billion and AUD 14 billion) are context; they do not affect which statements are true.

**Fragile fact.** “Excellent” liquidity but “relatively expensive”: the cost is the return forgone. The trading book is assessed under stressed, not normal, conditions.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 66.b, verbatim):** Identify examples of liquidity funding risk, funding sources, and lessons learned from real cases: Northern Rock, Ashanti Goldfields, and Metallgesellschaft.

**GARP:** Chapter 1, Section 1.2.1, Sources of Liquidity (Cash and Treasury Securities; Liquidating Trading Book Positions). **GARP vs Schweser:** none. Schweser makes the same two points in condensed form.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-1 b, where it is Q4 of 14.

a.reason: (Polarity flip). A calls cash and Treasuries a cheap source of liquidity. GARP calls them relatively expensive, because their low return limits profitability. A would be right if the question concerned the cost of transacting in Treasuries, rather than the opportunity cost of holding them.

b.reason: B is the only option with both halves right: the trade-off between liquidity and return makes cash and Treasuries relatively expensive, which limits how much can be held, and the trading book must be assessed under stressed conditions.

c.reason: (Scope or condition error). C bases the trading-book assessment on normal conditions. GARP says the analysis should be based on stressed conditions, because funding is needed when liquidity is generally short. C would be right for measuring routine unwind costs, not for contingency funding.

d.reason: (Sibling swap). D cuts the link between the two risks. GARP says liquidity funding risk is related to liquidity trading risk precisely because liquidating the trading book is a source of funding. D would be right only for a book that is never used to raise cash.

questions.question: During a market-wide liquidity squeeze, the treasurer of a German bank proposes closing a EUR 3 billion funding gap within a month by offering deposit rates 50 basis points above those of competing banks, to attract both retail and wholesale deposits. The bank’s CET1 ratio is 14.2%. Which of the following assessments of the proposal is most accurate?

options.text: It is unreliable: liquidity problems tend to be market-wide, so other banks are likely to raise rates too, and wholesale deposits can vanish quickly in stress.
It is reliable for wholesale deposits, which are a more stable source of funding than retail deposits and are the last to leave in stressed conditions.
It is reliable for retail deposits, which are as stable as they have always been, because depositors rarely compare rates or move funds between banks.
It is reliable, because a bank that offers more attractive rates can always grow its deposit base at short notice, whatever other banks happen to be doing.

questions.solution:
German bank closing a EUR 3 billion gap with above-market deposit rates during a market-wide squeeze.

**Concept and theory**

Source (4) in GARP’s list is the ability to offer favourable terms to attract retail and wholesale deposits at short notice. GARP makes three separate points about it.

First, **wholesale deposits are a more volatile source of funding than retail deposits**, and they can disappear quickly in stressed market conditions. Wholesale funders are professional, rate-sensitive, and quick to withdraw when credit concerns appear. GARP’s chapter opens by noting that institutions relying on wholesale deposits ran into trouble in 2007 when investors lost confidence.

Second, **even retail deposits are not as stable as they used to be**. It is now very easy to compare the rates offered by different institutions and to move money over the Internet. Northern Rock showed how fast retail money can leave, including through Internet-only accounts.

Third, **liquidity problems tend to be market-wide** rather than confined to one or two institutions. When one institution tries to grow its deposit base by offering more attractive rates, others usually want to do the same thing. The extra funding is therefore likely to be hard to obtain at exactly the moment it is needed.

|  | Wholesale deposits | Retail deposits |
|---|---|---|
| Stability (GARP) | More volatile | More stable, but less than in the past |
| In stress | Can disappear quickly | Can still leave: rates easy to compare |
| Raising more in stress | Hard: competitors bid too | Hard: competitors bid too |

**Applying it to this question**

The stem names a market-wide squeeze, so GARP’s third point applies directly: other banks will match the higher rates, and the planned EUR 3 billion is unlikely to materialise. The plan also leans on wholesale deposits, the least stable component. The CET1 ratio of 14.2% is irrelevant: it measures capital adequacy (solvency), not the bank’s ability to raise deposits in a squeeze.

**Fragile fact.** Wholesale deposits are more volatile than retail. In a market-wide squeeze, higher deposit rates are matched by competitors.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 66.b, verbatim):** Identify examples of liquidity funding risk, funding sources, and lessons learned from real cases: Northern Rock, Ashanti Goldfields, and Metallgesellschaft.

**GARP:** Chapter 1, Section 1.2.1, Sources of Liquidity (Wholesale and Retail Deposits). **GARP vs** **Schweser:** Schweser says both wholesale and retail deposits “tend to be somewhat unstable” and does not rank them. GARP explicitly ranks wholesale as more volatile than retail; GARP is used here.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-1 b, where it is Q5 of 14.

a.reason: A states the market-wide point and the volatility of wholesale deposits, both from GARP’s discussion of wholesale and retail deposits.

b.reason: (Polarity flip). GARP says wholesale deposits are more volatile than retail deposits and can disappear quickly in stress. B reverses the ranking. B would be right if it said retail deposits are the more stable source.

c.reason: (Polarity flip). GARP says retail deposits are not as stable as they used to be, because comparing rates and moving funds online is easy. C reverses this. It would describe retail funding before online banking.

d.reason: (Absolute claim). D promises that higher rates always work “whatever other banks happen to be doing”. GARP says that when one institution bids for deposits, others usually do the same, so the extra funding is likely to be hard to get. D might hold for an isolated, idiosyncratic shortfall in a calm market, never with certainty in a market-wide squeeze.

questions.question: An internal auditor at a US mortgage originator is reviewing the assumptions in the firm’s funding plan about its ability to borrow. The firm holds USD 38 billion of mortgages awaiting sale and has a committed syndicated credit facility of USD 9 billion. Which of the following statements in the plan is least accurate?

options.text: When markets are unstressed, a creditworthy institution usually has no problem in borrowing money.
In stressed markets, heightened risk aversion leads to higher interest rates, shorter loan maturities, and in some cases a refusal to lend.
The committed facility costs nothing to maintain and removes the firm’s funding risk entirely, as Countrywide’s experience in 2007 demonstrated.
The firm should monitor the assets that it could pledge as collateral for loans at short notice.

questions.solution:
US mortgage originator’s funding plan: which statement about the ability to borrow is least accurate.

**Concept and theory**

The third source of liquidity in GARP’s list is the ability to borrow money at short notice. Its value depends heavily on the state of the market:

- **Unstressed markets:** a creditworthy bank usually has no problem borrowing money.
- **Stressed markets:** there is a heightened aversion to risk. GARP lists three consequences: higher interest rates, shorter maturities for loans, and in some cases a refusal to provide funds at all.

Two management responses follow. First, institutions should monitor the assets that can be pledged as collateral for loans at short notice, because secured borrowing may be available when unsecured borrowing is not. Second, an institution can, at a cost, mitigate its funding risks somewhat by arranging lines of credit. Both qualifiers matter: committed lines carry fees, and they reduce funding risk without removing it.

GARP’s example is Countrywide, a US mortgage originator, which had a syndicated loan facility of USD 11.5 billion that it was able to use during the 2007 credit crisis. The facility helped keep the company afloat, but Countrywide still experienced significant problems and was taken over by Bank of America in January 2008. The lesson is that a credit line buys time and helps; it is not a guarantee of survival. Because borrowing in stress becomes dearer, shorter and sometimes unavailable, GARP’s two remedies (monitoring pledgeable collateral and arranging lines of credit) have to be put in place before the stress arrives.

**Applying it to this question**

The question asks for the least accurate statement, so three statements must match GARP and one must not. A (easy borrowing in calm markets), B (higher rates, shorter maturities, refusal in stress) and D (monitor pledgeable collateral) all restate GARP. C claims the facility is costless and removes funding risk entirely, and cites Countrywide as proof. The USD 38 billion pipeline and USD 9 billion facility are context; they do not decide the answer.

**Fragile fact.** Credit lines work “at a cost” and only “somewhat”. Countrywide drew USD 11.5 billion and was still taken over (Bank of America, January 2008).

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 66.b, verbatim):** Identify examples of liquidity funding risk, funding sources, and lessons learned from real cases: Northern Rock, Ashanti Goldfields, and Metallgesellschaft.

**GARP:** Chapter 1, Section 1.2.1, Sources of Liquidity (Ability to Borrow; Countrywide example). **GARP vs Schweser:** none. Schweser covers higher rates, shorter maturities and lines of credit, but omits the Countrywide example and the collateral-monitoring point, which come from GARP.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-1 b, where it is Q6 of 14.

a.reason: (Qualifier misread: an accurate statement). GARP says that when markets are unstressed, a creditworthy bank usually has no problem borrowing. A would be the answer only if it claimed this held in stressed markets too, which would be a scope error.

b.reason: (Qualifier misread: an accurate statement). This lists GARP’s three consequences of stressed markets: higher rates, shorter maturities, and sometimes refusal. B would be the answer if it reversed one of them, for example “longer maturities”, which would be a polarity flip.

c.reason: C is the least accurate. GARP says credit lines mitigate funding risk only somewhat and at a cost, and Countrywide, despite drawing its facility, still had significant problems and was taken over.

d.reason: (Qualifier misread: an accurate statement). GARP advises monitoring the assets that can be pledged as collateral at short notice. D would be the answer only if it said collateral is irrelevant once a credit line exists, which would be an absolute claim.
