questions.question: A risk consultant is advising a Singapore bank that plans to fund SGD 5 billion of new loans through an originate-to-distribute model, using an asset-backed commercial paper (ABCP) conduit to warehouse the loans before securitization. The bank’s board asks what happened to this source of liquidity in 2007. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Securitization stayed a dependable source of liquidity after August 2007, because the senior tranches kept AAA ratings and investors kept buying them.
Securitization dried up almost overnight in August 2007, so banks had to fund their loans, and some had to buy unsold instruments under ABCP backstops.
Securitization dried up in August 2007, but banks were exposed only where legally obliged, since they never supported off-balance-sheet conduits voluntarily.
Securitization dried up in August 2007, and the ABCP backstops required the commercial paper investors, not the sponsoring banks, to buy unsold instruments.

questions.solution:
Singapore bank planning originate-to-distribute via an ABCP conduit: what happened to securitization funding in 2007.

**Concept and theory**

Source (5) in GARP’s list is the ability to securitize assets, such as loans, at short notice. Under the originate-to-distribute model, banks do not keep illiquid assets such as loans on their balance sheets: they pool them and sell the cash flows to investors as securities. Before August 2007 this was an important source of liquidity.

GARP describes three ways it failed in 2007:

1. **The market closed.** The source dried up almost overnight in August 2007, when investors decided securitized products were too risky. Originate-to-distribute was no longer viable, banks had to fund their loans themselves, and they became much less willing to lend.
2. **Liquidity backstops.** Banks had given liquidity backstop arrangements on asset-backed commercial paper (ABCP), which was used to fund debt instruments such as mortgages before securitization. When buyers could not be found, the banks had to buy the instruments themselves.
3. **Reputational support.** In some cases, to protect their reputations, banks provided financial support to conduits and other off-balance-sheet vehicles involved in securitization, even though they were not legally required to do so.

Points 2 and 3 show how a funding source turns into a funding need: a bank that planned to move assets off its balance sheet can find them coming back exactly when liquidity is tightest. GARP’s Section 1.1.1 adds the reason the market froze: the products lacked transparency, and when investors realised they did not understand them, liquidity disappeared.

**Applying it to this question**

The bank plans exactly the structure GARP describes: loans warehoused in an ABCP conduit before securitization. The board’s question is what happened to this source in 2007. Each option agrees or disagrees on three facts: whether the market dried up, who bore the backstop, and whether support went beyond legal obligation.

**Fragile fact.** Under the ABCP backstops the banks were the buyers of last resort. Banks also gave support beyond their legal obligations, to protect their reputations.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 66.b, verbatim):** Identify examples of liquidity funding risk, funding sources, and lessons learned from real cases: Northern Rock, Ashanti Goldfields, and Metallgesellschaft.

**GARP:** Chapter 1, Section 1.2.1, Sources of Liquidity (Securitization). **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser says the source “rapidly dissipated in late 2007”. GARP dates the collapse to August 2007, “almost overnight”. GARP is used. Schweser omits the ABCP backstop and reputational support points (GARP-only).

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-1 b, where it is Q7 of 14.

a.reason: (Polarity flip). A says the source stayed dependable. GARP says it dried up almost overnight in August 2007 as investors judged the products too risky. A describes the market before August 2007.

b.reason: B states that securitization dried up almost overnight in August 2007, that banks had to fund their own loans, and that some had to buy unsold instruments under their ABCP backstops. All three points are from GARP.

c.reason: (Scope or condition error). C limits bank exposure to legal obligations. GARP says some banks supported conduits and other off-balance-sheet vehicles to protect their reputations, even though they were not legally required to. C would be right only if reputational support had never been given.

d.reason: (Role misassignment). Under the backstops, it was the banks that had to buy the instruments when buyers could not be found, not the commercial paper investors. D would be right if the investors, rather than the sponsors, had written the liquidity facility.

questions.question:
A treasury analyst at a UK bank is drafting notes on central bank borrowing as a source of liquidity. The bank holds GBP 6 billion of eligible collateral. The draft contains the following statements:

I. The central bank requires collateral and typically applies a haircut, lending less than 100% of the collateral’s value, and may charge a relatively high rate of interest.

II. After August 2007, the European Central Bank applied higher haircuts than other central banks, so some British banks preferred to borrow from the Bank of England.

III. In March 2008, after the failure of Bear Stearns, the Federal Reserve extended its borrowing facility to investment banks as well as commercial banks.

IV. Banks try to keep central bank borrowing secret, because the market may read it as a sign of financial difficulty, causing other sources of liquidity to dry up.

Which of the statements are accurate?

options.text: I and IV only
I, II, and IV only
I, II, III, and IV
I, III, and IV only

questions.solution:
UK bank notes on central bank borrowing: which of four statements are accurate.

**Concept and theory**

Source (6) is borrowing from the central bank. Central banks such as the Federal Reserve, the Bank of England, and the European Central Bank are often called lenders of last resort: when commercial banks are in financial difficulty, they lend to maintain the health of the financial system. GARP sets out the terms and frictions:

- **Terms:** borrowers must post collateral. The central bank typically applies a haircut, meaning it lends less than 100% of the collateral’s value, and it may charge a relatively high rate of interest.
- **Widening access:** in March 2008, after the failure of Bear Stearns (taken over by JPMorgan Chase), the Federal Reserve extended its facility to investment banks as well as commercial banks, and later to Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac. GARP’s footnote explains why: investment banks trade so heavily with other banks that their failure could ripple through the system (systemic risk).
- **Different rules across central banks:** after August 2007 the ECB’s haircuts were lower than those of other central banks, so some British banks preferred to borrow from the ECB rather than the Bank of England. By September 2008 the ECB had lent EUR 467 billion and announced larger haircuts in future.
- **Stigma:** banks try to keep central bank borrowing secret, because the market may read it as a sign of financial difficulty, so that other sources of liquidity dry up. Northern Rock is the example: news of its emergency borrowing triggered an immediate run.

Schweser summarises the cost as the collateral, the relatively high rate, the haircut, and the negative signal.

**Applying it to this question**

Check each statement. I matches GARP on collateral, the haircut (lend less than 100%) and the rate. II reverses the haircut ranking: the ECB’s haircuts were lower, which is why British banks went to the ECB, not to the Bank of England. III matches GARP on the Fed and Bear Stearns. IV matches GARP’s stigma point. The accurate set is I, III and IV. The GBP 6 billion of collateral is context only.

**Fragile fact.** After August 2007 the ECB’s haircuts were lower, so British banks borrowed from the ECB. A haircut means lending less than the collateral’s value.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 66.b, verbatim):** Identify examples of liquidity funding risk, funding sources, and lessons learned from real cases: Northern Rock, Ashanti Goldfields, and Metallgesellschaft.

**GARP:** Chapter 1, Section 1.2.1, Sources of Liquidity (Central Bank Borrowing; footnote 4). **GARP vs Schweser:** none on substance. The ECB haircut comparison and the Fed extension to investment banks are GARP-only.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-1 b, where it is Q8 of 14.

a.reason: (Scope or condition error (rejects III)). A treats the Fed’s facility as limited to commercial banks. GARP says that in March 2008 it was extended to investment banks as well. A would be right for the period before March 2008.

b.reason: (Polarity flip (accepts II)). B accepts the reversed haircut ranking and rejects the true statement III. GARP says the ECB’s haircuts were lower, drawing British borrowers to the ECB. B would be right only if II read “lower haircuts . . . preferred the ECB” and III were false.

c.reason: (Polarity flip (accepts II)). C accepts all four statements, including the reversed haircut ranking in II. C would be right if II were corrected to say the ECB applied lower haircuts and British banks preferred the ECB.

d.reason: D lists exactly the three accurate statements and excludes the inverted statement II.

questions.question: A member of the risk committee of a Chinese joint-stock bank, which funds CNY 300 billion of long-term mortgages partly with short-term interbank borrowing, asks a risk consultant to summarise what went wrong at Northern Rock in 2007. Which of the following summaries is most accurate?

options.text: It relied on short-term debt to fund mortgages; after August 2007 it could not replace maturing debt, sought emergency funds, and news of that request set off a run, though the regulator judged it solvent.
It relied on short-term debt to fund mortgages; a run on its branches began first, and the resulting withdrawals then forced it to seek emergency funding from the Bank of England in September 2007.
It relied on short-term debt to fund mortgages, but it failed because the regulator found that its loan book was of poor quality and that its liabilities exceeded its assets.
It relied on short-term debt to fund mortgages, but its liquidity crisis came from margin calls on derivatives that hedged its mortgage book when interest rates moved sharply.

questions.solution:
Chinese bank risk committee: the most accurate summary of what went wrong at Northern Rock.

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s Business Snapshot 1.1 is the chapter’s main case of liquidity funding risk. The key facts, in order:

1. **Business model.** Northern Rock was a UK bank formed in 1997 when the Northern Rock Building Society floated its shares. By 2007 it was one of the top five UK mortgage lenders. Some mortgages were securitized through a Channel Islands subsidiary, Granite. It relied on selling short-term debt instruments for much of its funding.
2. **Trigger.** After the subprime crisis of August 2007, institutional investors became very nervous about lending to banks heavily involved in mortgages, and Northern Rock found it very difficult to replace maturing instruments.
3. **Solvent but illiquid.** Its assets covered its liabilities. The FSA judged it solvent, above its regulatory capital requirement, and holding a good-quality loan book. The problem was its inability to fund itself.
4. **Emergency borrowing, then the run.** It approached the Bank of England on 12 September 2007 and borrowed about GBP 3 billion from the Tripartite Authority (Bank of England, FSA, HM Treasury). On 13 September the BBC broke the news. On 14 September a run began, the first on a British bank in 150 years. About GBP 2 billion was withdrawn between 12 and 17 September.
5. **Aftermath.** A government and Bank of England guarantee of all deposits ended the queues. Emergency borrowing, at a penalty rate, reached GBP 25 billion by February 2008. The bank was nationalised and its management changed.

GARP’s lesson: the case shows how quickly liquidity problems can send a bank spiralling downward. With more conservative management and more attention to access to funding, it might have survived.

**Applying it to this question**

The stem’s bank resembles Northern Rock (long-term mortgages, short-term wholesale funding), but the question asks only for the accurate summary. The deciding facts are three: the funding source (short-term debt), the sequence (emergency borrowing first, then the news, then the run), and solvency (judged solvent).

**Fragile fact.** The sequence is: emergency borrowing on 12 September, BBC report on 13 September, run on 14 September. The FSA judged the bank solvent.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 66.b, verbatim):** Identify examples of liquidity funding risk, funding sources, and lessons learned from real cases: Northern Rock, Ashanti Goldfields, and Metallgesellschaft.

**GARP:** Chapter 1, Section 1.2 and Business Snapshot 1.1, Northern Rock. **GARP vs Schweser:** none on substance. Schweser says the GBP 2 billion left “over the next week” and that borrowing reached GBP 25 billion “within six months”; GARP gives 12 to 17 September and February 2008. These are consistent.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-1 b, where it is Q9 of 14.

a.reason: A gets all three right: short-term debt funding that could not be replaced after August 2007, emergency borrowing whose disclosure set off the run, and a regulator that judged the bank solvent.

b.reason: (Polarity flip (sequence reversed)). B gets the funding model right but reverses cause and effect. Northern Rock approached the Bank of England on 12 September; the run began on 14 September, after the BBC reported the emergency borrowing. The borrowing was not a response to an earlier run. B would describe a bank whose run came first and forced it to the central bank.

c.reason: (Sibling swap: insolvency for illiquidity). The FSA judged Northern Rock solvent, above its capital requirement, and holding a good-quality loan book. C turns a liquidity failure into a solvency failure. It would fit a bank that failed on credit losses.

d.reason: (Sibling swap: Ashanti/MG mechanism). Margin calls on hedges are the mechanism of Ashanti Goldfields and Metallgesellschaft, not of Northern Rock. D would be right for a hedging-driven cash drain.

questions.question:
A risk consultant is preparing a case review of the Northern Rock run for the board of a Singapore bank. One slide examines a depositor who joined the queue on 14 September 2007.

| Item | Amount (GBP) | Insured share (%) |
|---|---|---|
| Depositor’s balance at Northern Rock | 40,000 |  |
| Deposit insurance tier 1: the first | 2,000 | 100 |
| Deposit insurance tier 2: the next | 33,000 | 90 |
| Northern Rock share price earlier in 2007 | 12.00 |  |

Under the deposit insurance in force before the Chancellor’s announcement of 17 September 2007, how much of this depositor’s balance was not covered by insurance?
questions.solution:
Northern Rock depositor with GBP 40,000: uninsured amount under the pre-guarantee UK deposit insurance.

**Concept and theory**

In GARP’s account of Northern Rock, partial deposit insurance did not stop the run; the queues disappeared only after a guarantee of all deposits. GARP’s Business Snapshot 1.1 records that UK deposit insurance at the time guaranteed **100% of the first GBP 2,000** and **90% of the next** **GBP 33,000**. Under these terms every depositor with more than GBP 2,000 had something to lose, and anyone with more than GBP 35,000 also had an uninsured slice above the cap. The run began after the BBC reported the emergency borrowing on 13 September, even though the bank was solvent.

Late on 17 September 2007 the Chancellor, Alistair Darling, announced that the government and the Bank of England would guarantee all deposits at Northern Rock. After that announcement, and newspaper advertisements, the queues gradually disappeared. GARP’s wider lesson is that funding can be lost very quickly once confidence goes. News of central bank support can itself trigger a run, which is why banks try to keep such borrowing secret.

With balance B, tier-1 limit $\text{L}_{1} =$ 2,000 (covered 100%), tier-2 band $\text{L}_{2} =$ 33,000 (covered 90%): Insured $= \text{min}($B, $\text{L}_{1}) +$ 0.90 $\times\text{min}(\text{max}(\text{B} - \text{L}_{1}$, 0), $\text{L}_{2})$, Uninsured $= \text{B} -$ Insured.

The maximum insured amount is 2,000 + 0.9 × 33,000 = 31,700.

**Applying it to this question**

Formula first, then one step per line:

Tier 1 insured $= \text{min}($40,000, 2,000) = GBP 2,000

Balance above tier 1 = 40,000 − 2,000 = GBP 38,000

Amount in tier-2 band $= \text{min}($38,000, 33,000) = GBP 33,000

Tier 2 insured = 0.90 × 33,000 = GBP 29,700

Total insured = 2,000 + 29,700 = GBP 31,700

Uninsured = 40,000 − 31,700 = GBP 8,300

The uninsured GBP 8,300 is made of two parts: 10% of the tier-2 band (GBP 3,300) plus the whole GBP 5,000 above the GBP 35,000 cap. The GBP 12.00 share price is an irrelevant input: it relates to shareholders, not depositor protection. This exposure is why the depositor joined the queue, and why only the guarantee of all deposits ended the run.

**Fragile fact.** The scheme covered 100% of GBP 2,000 plus 90% of the next GBP 33,000 (at most GBP 31,700). The run ended only with the guarantee of all deposits on 17 September 2007.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 66.b, verbatim):** Identify examples of liquidity funding risk, funding sources, and lessons learned from real cases: Northern Rock, Ashanti Goldfields, and Metallgesellschaft.

**GARP:** Chapter 1, Business Snapshot 1.1, Northern Rock (deposit insurance terms; Chancellor’s guarantee). **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser mentions only “deposit guarantees by the British government and Bank of England”; the insurance tiers are GARP-only.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-1 b, where it is Q10 of 14.

questions.question: A portfolio manager at a Toronto-based resources fund is reviewing the 1999 Ashanti Goldfields episode before approving a position in a gold miner with a large hedge book. Which of the following statements about the Ashanti case is most accurate?

options.text: Ashanti had bought gold forward to lock in its costs; when European central banks announced larger gold sales, the price fell over 25% and it faced margin calls it could not meet.
Ashanti had sold gold forward to protect shareholders from falling prices; when the gold price jumped over 25%, it could not meet margin calls and had to sell a mine and dilute shareholders.
Ashanti had sold gold forward to protect shareholders from falling prices; when the gold price jumped over 25%, its forward losses were permanent, as its unmined gold did not rise in value.
Ashanti had sold gold forward to protect shareholders from falling prices; when the gold price jumped over 25%, it closed out all hedges and cancelled fixed-price supply contracts with customers.

questions.solution:
Toronto resources fund reviewing Ashanti Goldfields (1999): the most accurate description of the case.

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s section on hedging issues explains a liquidity funding problem that has nothing to do with deposits: liquidity problems are liable to arise when companies hedge illiquid assets with contracts that are subject to margin requirements. Gold miners often hedge by agreeing with financial institutions to sell gold forward for two or three years. The miner must post margin, recalculated every day to reflect the value of its forward agreements. If the gold price rises fast, the forward agreements lose money and the bank makes big margin calls. Those losses are offset by an increase in the value of the gold in the ground, but that gold is an illiquid asset. It cannot be used to pay a margin call next week.

Business Snapshot 1.2 applies this to Ashanti Goldfields, a West African gold miner based in Ghana:

- **Hedge:** to protect shareholders from declines in the gold price, it sold gold forward (a short forward position).
- **Trigger:** on 26 September 1999, 15 European central banks surprised the market by announcing they would limit their gold sales over the next five years. The gold price jumped by more than 25%.
- **Funding failure:** Ashanti could not meet the margin calls on its short forwards.
- **Outcome:** a major restructuring, including the sale of a mine, dilution of shareholders’ equity, and a restructuring of its hedge positions.

The economics were hedged; the cash flows were not. Gains on the asset arrived in an illiquid form, while losses on the hedge demanded cash immediately.

**Applying it to this question**

Each option describes Ashanti’s hedge direction, the price move, and the outcome. Check them in order. Direction: sold forward, to protect against falling prices. Price move: up more than 25%, after central banks announced limits on their sales. Outcome: unmet margin calls, then a restructuring with a mine sale and equity dilution. The investor’s interest in a gold miner with a large hedge book is context; nothing in the stem changes the facts of the case.

**Fragile fact.** Ashanti was short gold forwards and was hurt by a price rise after the central banks announced limits on their sales.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 66.b, verbatim):** Identify examples of liquidity funding risk, funding sources, and lessons learned from real cases: Northern Rock, Ashanti Goldfields, and Metallgesellschaft.

**GARP:** Chapter 1, Section 1.2.1 (Hedging Issues) and Business Snapshot 1.2, Ashanti Goldfields. **GARP vs Schweser:** none on substance. Schweser adds an interpretation (an expected supply reduction raised demand) that is not in GARP. GARP is used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-1 b, where it is Q11 of 14.

a.reason: (Polarity flip). A inverts the hedge: a long forward position, a central bank announcement of larger sales, and a falling price. Ashanti sold gold forward, and the announcement limited sales, sending the price up. A would describe a gold consumer hedging input costs.

b.reason: B has the right direction (short forwards to protect against declines), the right move (gold up more than 25%), and the right consequences (unmet margin calls, a mine sale, shareholder dilution). This matches Business Snapshot 1.2.

c.reason: (Scope or condition error). C denies the offset. GARP says the forward losses were offset by a rise in the value of the gold in the ground; the problem was that this gold was illiquid, not that the loss was permanent. C would be right only for an unhedged speculative short with no underlying gold.

d.reason: (Sibling swap: MG outcome). Closing out all hedges and cancelling fixed-price supply contracts with customers is Metallgesellschaft’s ending, not Ashanti’s. Ashanti restructured its hedge positions, sold a mine, and diluted shareholders. D would be right in a question about MG.

questions.question: A junior risk analyst at a Singapore commodity trading house is presenting the Metallgesellschaft (MG) case to newly hired analysts. Which of the following descriptions of the case is most accurate?

options.text: MG bought long-dated fixed-price oil supplies from producers and hedged with short positions in short-dated futures; rising oil prices then produced margin calls on the futures.
MG sold its own oil output forward to protect shareholders from falling prices; when oil prices then jumped sharply, the forwards produced margin calls it could not meet.
MG sold long-dated fixed-price supply contracts below market prices to win volume and hedged with long short-dated futures; the contracts themselves were loss-making.
MG sold long-dated fixed-price supply contracts above market prices and hedged with long short-dated futures; falling oil prices then produced margin calls on the futures.

questions.solution:
Singapore trading house briefing on Metallgesellschaft: the most accurate description of the case.

**Concept and theory**

GARP calls Metallgesellschaft (MG) “another extreme example” of a liquidity funding problem caused by hedging (Business Snapshot 1.3). The structure has two legs:

| Leg | Position | Effect of falling oil prices |
|---|---|---|
| Customer contracts | Sold 5- to 10-year fixed-price heating oil and gasoline supply, 6 to 8 cents above market | Gain (MG delivers at a price above market), realised slowly over years |
| Hedge | Long short-dated futures, rolled forward | Loss, paid in cash as margin calls |

In the early 1990s, MG sold a huge volume of these contracts. Selling fixed-price supply leaves MG short oil: it loses if oil prices rise. To hedge, it took long positions in short-dated futures and rolled them forward as they expired. Oil prices then fell. The long futures lost money and produced margin calls. Trading was made harder because MG’s trades were very large and were anticipated by other market participants.

The hedge’s designers argued that the short-term cash outflows would be offset by positive cash flows ultimately realised on the long-term contracts. Senior management and MG’s bankers, however, became concerned about the huge cash drain. MG closed out all the hedge positions and agreed with its customers to abandon the fixed-price contracts. The loss was USD 1.33 billion. GARP’s point is that the problem was a timing mismatch between immediate margin outflows and slow inflows from long-term contracts: a liquidity funding problem.

**Applying it to this question**

The four options differ in MG’s role (seller or buyer of supply), the hedge direction, the price move, and the pricing of the contracts. GARP’s facts: MG sold fixed-price supply above market, hedged with long short-dated futures, and oil fell. Only one option has all four.

**Fragile fact.** MG was long futures, hedging fixed-price contracts it had sold, and was hurt by falling oil prices. Ashanti is the mirror image: short forwards, hurt by rising prices.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 66.b, verbatim):** Identify examples of liquidity funding risk, funding sources, and lessons learned from real cases: Northern Rock, Ashanti Goldfields, and Metallgesellschaft.

**GARP:** Chapter 1, Section 1.2.1 (Hedging Issues) and Business Snapshot 1.3, Metallgesellschaft. **GARP vs Schweser:** none on substance. GARP gives the loss as USD 1.33 billion (the extracted text is garbled to “\$1.3 3 billion”); Schweser says “over \$1.3 billion”.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-1 b, where it is Q12 of 14.

a.reason: (Role misassignment). A makes MG the buyer of fixed-price supply, hedging with short futures and hurt by rising prices. In GARP, MG was the seller to its customers, so its hedge was long futures and it was hurt by falling prices. A would describe a fuel consumer locking in supply.

b.reason: (Sibling swap: Ashanti mechanism). Selling one’s own output forward to protect shareholders from falling prices, then being hit when prices jump, is Ashanti Goldfields’ story. MG had no oil output to sell; it supplied customers under fixed-price contracts. B would be right in a question about Ashanti.

c.reason: (Polarity flip). GARP says MG priced its contracts six to eight cents above market prices; GARP calls them profitable. C reverses this, making the contracts loss-making. It would be right only if the contracts had been priced below market.

d.reason: D matches Business Snapshot 1.3: long-dated fixed-price supply contracts sold above market, hedged with long short-dated futures, and falling oil prices causing margin calls on the futures.

questions.source: High quality paper LTR-1 b Q13
questions.question: The risk committee of a Brazilian gold producer is reviewing a programme to sell three years of expected output forward to banks. The banks recalculate the required margin daily. Planned hedge volume is 1.2 million ounces, and the producer’s annual operating cash flow is about BRL 2.5 billion. Which recommendation best reflects the lesson GARP draws from Ashanti Goldfields and Metallgesellschaft?

options.text: Keep the hedge if it suits the business, but secure access to funding large enough to meet the margin calls that an extreme price move could generate.
Abandon the forward programme altogether, since both cases show that hedging with forward and futures contracts tends to destroy value.
Keep the hedge, and plan to meet any margin calls from the rise in value of the gold in the ground, since that gain offsets the hedge losses.
Keep the hedge, but split it across many banks so that other traders cannot anticipate and trade against the producer’s large positions.

questions.solution:
Brazilian gold producer’s daily-margined forward programme: the recommendation that reflects GARP’s Ashanti and MG lesson.

**Concept and theory**

GARP draws one explicit lesson from the two hedging cases: the lesson from the Ashanti and Metallgesellschaft episodes is not that companies should not use forward and futures contracts for hedging, but rather that they should ensure that they have access to funding to handle the cash flow mismatches that might arise in extreme circumstances.

The reasoning follows from GARP’s description of hedging issues. When an illiquid asset or long-dated commitment is hedged with a margined contract, the two legs settle on different timetables:

|  | Ashanti Goldfields | Metallgesellschaft |
|---|---|---|
| Exposure | Gold in the ground (illiquid) | 5- to 10-year fixed-price supply contracts |
| Hedge | Short gold forwards, margined daily | Long short-dated futures, rolled |
| Adverse move | Gold price up more than 25% | Oil price down |
| Hedge cash flow | Immediate margin calls | Immediate margin calls |
| Offsetting gain | Value of gold in the ground | Gains on fixed-price contracts over years |
| Outcome | Restructuring, mine sold, dilution | Hedges closed, contracts abandoned, USD 1.33 bn loss |

In both cases the offsetting gain existed but could not be turned into cash in time. The hedge reduced economic risk but created liquidity funding risk. The remedy is on the funding side: committed access to cash sized for extreme moves. Abandoning hedging is not the remedy, and neither is relying on the illiquid gain.

**Applying it to this question**

The producer is in Ashanti’s position: selling future output forward to banks that recalculate margin daily, with the offsetting gain sitting in unmined gold. A sharp rise in gold prices would generate large margin calls. GARP’s lesson requires the producer to ensure funding can cover those calls in an extreme scenario. The hedge volume (1.2 million ounces) and operating cash flow (BRL 2.5 billion) are context; GARP’s lesson is qualitative and does not depend on them.

**Fragile fact.** GARP’s lesson is “ensure access to funding”. It is not “do not hedge with forwards and futures”.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 66.b, verbatim):** Identify examples of liquidity funding risk, funding sources, and lessons learned from real cases: Northern Rock, Ashanti Goldfields, and Metallgesellschaft.

**GARP:** Chapter 1, Section 1.2.1, Hedging Issues (lesson from Ashanti and Metallgesellschaft); Business Snapshots 1.2 and 1.3. **GARP vs Schweser:** none. Schweser frames the common lesson as margin outflows misaligned with inflows from illiquid positions, consistent with GARP.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-1 b, where it is Q13 of 14.

a.reason: A keeps the hedge and secures funding for margin calls under extreme moves. This is GARP’s lesson almost word for word.

b.reason: (Absolute claim). B draws the very conclusion GARP rejects. GARP says the lesson is not that companies should avoid forwards and futures for hedging. B would be right only if GARP had judged the hedges themselves economically harmful.

c.reason: (Scope or condition error). C drops the illiquidity condition. The gain on gold in the ground does offset the hedge loss, but it is illiquid and cannot meet a margin call. That is the core of Ashanti’s failure. C would work only if the offsetting asset could be sold or borrowed against at short notice.

d.reason: (Sibling swap: trading risk for funding risk). Large trades being anticipated by others made MG’s trading harder, and predatory trading is a liquidity trading risk issue (Section 1.1). It is not the funding lesson GARP draws. D would fit a question on reducing predatory trading when unwinding large positions.

questions.question:
The CRO of a Chinese bank is reviewing a training deck that pairs each case with a lesson. The deck contains the following statements:

I. Northern Rock: the run on its branches began before it approached the Bank of England, and the emergency borrowing was a response to those withdrawals.

II. Northern Rock: a bank judged solvent can still fail when it cannot roll over short-term funding; more conservative management might have saved it.

III. Ashanti Goldfields: hedging long-dated fixed-price supply commitments with long short-dated futures creates a cash drain when prices fall.

IV. Metallgesellschaft: the hedge’s designers argued that margin outflows would be offset by later gains on the long-term contracts, but the cash drain led management and its bankers to close out the hedge.

Which of the statements are accurate?

options.text: II only
II and IV only
I, II, and IV only
II, III, and IV only

questions.solution:
Chinese bank CRO auditing a training deck that pairs each case with a lesson.

**Concept and theory**

Each of the three cases teaches a distinct lesson about liquidity funding risk, and exam distractors often attach one case’s lesson to another case. A compact map:

| Case | What failed | Lesson (GARP) |
|---|---|---|
| Northern Rock (2007) | Short-term debt funding of mortgages could not be rolled; emergency borrowing became public; a run followed | A solvent bank can spiral down quickly; more conservative management and attention to funding access might have saved it |
| Ashanti Goldfields (1999) | Short gold forwards; gold up more than 25%; margin calls not met | Hedging illiquid assets with margined contracts needs funding for extreme moves |
| Metallgesellschaft (early 1990s) | Long short-dated futures hedging long-dated fixed-price sales; oil fell; cash drain | Same funding lesson; also, the designers’ offset argument did not stop management and bankers closing out |

For Northern Rock, the sequence is fragile and matters: the bank approached the Bank of England on 12 September 2007; the BBC reported it on 13 September; the run began on 14 September. The emergency borrowing came first, and its disclosure caused the run. GARP links this to central bank stigma: banks try to keep central bank borrowing secret because news of it can make other liquidity sources dry up.

For MG, GARP distinguishes the people who devised the hedge (who argued that margin outflows would be offset by cash flows ultimately realised on the long-term contracts) from senior management and the bankers (who, worried by the cash drain, closed out the hedges and abandoned the contracts).

**Applying it to this question**

Statement I reverses the Northern Rock sequence, so it is false. Statement II is GARP’s Northern Rock lesson, so it is true. Statement III attaches MG’s mechanism (long short-dated futures hedging fixed-price supply commitments, hurt by falling prices) to Ashanti, whose hedge was short forwards hurt by rising prices, so it is false. Statement IV is GARP’s MG account, so it is true. The accurate set is II and IV.

**Fragile fact.** Northern Rock: borrowing first, then the news, then the run. Ashanti: short, hurt by a price rise. MG: long, hurt by a price fall.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 66.b, verbatim):** Identify examples of liquidity funding risk, funding sources, and lessons learned from real cases: Northern Rock, Ashanti Goldfields, and Metallgesellschaft.

**GARP:** Chapter 1, Business Snapshots 1.1 (Northern Rock), 1.2 (Ashanti Goldfields), and 1.3 (Metallgesellschaft); Section 1.2.1 (Central Bank Borrowing; Hedging Issues). **GARP vs Schweser:** none on substance. Schweser’s case summaries agree with GARP.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-1 b, where it is Q14 of 14.

a.reason: (Role misassignment (rejects IV)). A rejects a true statement about MG, typically by mixing up who argued what: it was the hedge’s designers who claimed the outflows would be offset, and senior management and the bankers who closed out. A would be right only if IV attributed the close-out to the designers.

b.reason: B (II and IV only) contains both correctly paired lessons and excludes the reversed sequence (I) and the mislabelled hedge (III).

c.reason: (Polarity flip (accepts I)). C accepts the reversed Northern Rock sequence. The run followed the news of emergency borrowing; it did not cause it. C would be right if I said the run began after the BBC reported the request for Bank of England support.

d.reason: (Sibling swap (accepts III)). D accepts Metallgesellschaft’s lesson pinned on Ashanti Goldfields. Ashanti sold gold forward and lost when gold rose. D would be right if statement III were labelled Metallgesellschaft.

questions.loText: Explain liquidity black holes and identify the causes of positive feedback trading.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-1 d Q1
questions.question:
A junior risk analyst at a Tokyo-based bank is preparing slides for newly hired analysts on liquidity black holes in JPY markets. The draft slide contains the following statements:

I. A liquidity black hole is a situation in which liquidity has dried up in a market because almost everyone wants to sell and no one wants to buy, or vice versa; it is sometimes called a “crowded exit.”

II. Because average bid-offer spreads have declined as a result of technological developments, liquidity black holes have been occurring with decreasing frequency.

III. In a liquidity black hole, a price decline causes more participants to want to sell, driving the price well below the level at which it will eventually settle, so the asset can be sold only at a fire-sale price.

IV. A liquidity black hole can arise only when prices are falling, because rising prices always attract sellers who restore a balance in the market.

Which of the statements are accurate?

options.text: I only
I and II only
I and III only
I, III, and IV only

questions.solution:
Tokyo bank training slide: which statements about liquidity black holes are accurate.

**Concept and theory**

GARP opens Section 1.3 by challenging a popular view. It is sometimes argued that technology and other developments have improved the liquidity of financial markets, and it is true that bid-offer spreads have, on average, declined. However, GARP calls the conclusion questionable, because there has also been an increasing tendency for situations to develop in which almost everyone wants to do the same type of trade at the same time. The result is that “liquidity black holes” occur with increasing frequency.

A liquidity black hole describes a situation in which liquidity has dried up in a particular market because everyone wants to sell and no one wants to buy, or vice versa. It is also called a “crowded exit.” The key contrast is with a well-functioning market:

| Feature | Well-functioning market | Liquidity black hole |
|---|---|---|
| Reaction to news | Opinion of value changes, price adjusts | Price decline triggers more selling |
| Overreaction | No: if the fall is too great, traders buy | Yes: price driven well below its eventual level |
| Outcome | New equilibrium price | Liquidity dries up; only fire-sale prices |

A footnote in GARP adds that black holes tend to be associated with price decreases, but it is in theory also possible for them to occur when there are price increases (everyone wants to buy and no one wants to sell). The black hole is therefore defined by one-sidedness of the market, not by the direction of the move.

**Applying it to this question**

Statement I reproduces GARP’s definition, including the “or vice versa” and the “crowded exit” label: accurate. Statement II takes a true premise (average spreads have declined) and attaches the wrong conclusion; GARP says black holes occur with increasing frequency, which is exactly why the technology argument is called questionable: inaccurate. Statement III is GARP’s description of how a black hole is created: accurate. Statement IV turns a tendency into a rule: GARP says black holes are typically associated with falls but can in theory occur with rises: inaccurate. The accurate set is I and III.

**Fragile fact.** Direction words: black holes occur with increasing frequency even though average spreads have declined; and they are usually, not only, associated with falling prices.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 66.d, verbatim):** Explain liquidity black holes and identify the causes of positive feedback trading.

**GARP:** Chapter 1, Section 1.3 Liquidity Black Holes (introduction and footnote 8). **Schweser:** Module 66.3. **GARP vs Schweser:** no conflict; the technology and spreads argument and the price-increase footnote are in GARP only (Schweser condenses the definition to “everyone wanting to take the same side”).

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-1 d, where it is Q1 of 13.

a.reason: (Scope error, rejects a true statement). “I only” drops statement III, which is GARP’s own account of the overshoot to a fire-sale price. A would be correct only if statement III had instead said that the price adjusts to its new equilibrium without overreacting, which describes a well-functioning market rather than a black hole.

b.reason: (Polarity flip in statement II). Accepting II requires reading GARP’s frequency claim backwards: spreads have declined on average, yet black holes occur with increasing, not decreasing, frequency. B would be correct only if statement II had said that black holes have become more frequent despite narrower average spreads and statement III had been false.

c.reason: Option C is correct because it accepts the two statements that paraphrase GARP (the definition and the overshoot mechanism) and rejects the frequency statement, whose direction is reversed, and the “only when prices are falling” statement, which contradicts GARP’s footnote on price increases.

d.reason: (Absolute claim in statement IV). Including IV accepts “can arise only when prices are falling” and “always attract sellers.” GARP says black holes tend to be associated with price decreases but can in theory occur with price increases. D would be correct if IV had read “tend to be associated with price decreases, although they can in theory occur when prices rise.”

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Explain liquidity black holes and identify the causes of positive feedback trading.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-1 d Q2
questions.question: A portfolio manager at a Canadian pension fund is explaining to the fund’s trustees why the market for a CAD 2 billion block of provincial bonds remained orderly during a recent sell-off, while another market the fund trades in became one-sided. Which of the following statements best describes the trader behaviour that keeps a market liquid?

options.text: Negative feedback traders dominate liquid markets; they buy when prices fall and sell when prices rise, creating demand or supply that restores prices to a more reasonable level.
Positive feedback traders dominate liquid markets; they buy when prices fall and sell when prices rise, creating demand or supply that restores prices to a more reasonable level.
Negative feedback traders dominate liquid markets; they buy when prices rise and sell when prices fall, creating demand or supply that restores prices to a more reasonable level.
Negative feedback traders dominate liquid markets; since every trader can be classified as positive or negative feedback, their dominance guarantees that prices never overshoot.

questions.solution:
Canadian pension fund: which trader behaviour keeps a market liquid.

**Concept and theory**

GARP Section 1.3.1 explains that changes in the liquidity of financial markets are driven by the behaviour of traders, and divides them into two sorts:

| Trader type | After a price fall | After a price rise | Effect on the market |
|---|---|---|---|
| Negative feedback | Buys | Sells | Stabilising; restores reasonable prices |
| Positive feedback | Sells | Buys | Destabilising; one-sided, illiquid |

In liquid markets, negative feedback traders dominate. If the price of an asset gets unreasonably low, traders move in and buy, creating demand that restores the price to a more reasonable level. If the price gets unreasonably high, traders sell, creating supply that also restores the price. The result is a liquid market with reasonable prices and a good balance of buyers and sellers.

When positive feedback traders dominate, prices are liable to be unstable and the market may become one-sided and illiquid. A fall in price causes traders to sell, so prices fall further and there is more selling; a rise causes buying, so prices rise further and there is more buying. This self-reinforcing loop is the engine of a liquidity black hole.

GARP adds an important caveat in a footnote: the two-way classification is a simplification of reality to help understand market dynamics. Some traders follow complicated strategies that cannot be classified as either positive or negative feedback. The model therefore describes tendencies, not guarantees.

**Applying it to this question**

The question asks for the behaviour that keeps a market liquid. Three things must all be right: the label (negative feedback), the direction of trading (buy on falls, sell on rises), and the effect (restoring prices). Option A gets all three right. The CAD 2 billion size of the bond block is context only and does not affect the answer.

**Fragile fact.** Polarity: negative feedback traders buy on falls and sell on rises and dominate liquid markets; the word “negative” refers to trading against the move, not to a harmful effect.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 66.d, verbatim):** Explain liquidity black holes and identify the causes of positive feedback trading.

**GARP:** Chapter 1, Section 1.3.1 Positive and Negative Feedback Traders (including footnote 9). **Schweser:** Module 66.3. **GARP vs Schweser:** no conflict; the classification caveat (footnote 9) is in GARP only.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-1 d, where it is Q2 of 13.

a.reason: Option A is correct because it states GARP’s description of liquid markets: negative feedback traders dominate, they trade against the price move, and the resulting demand or supply restores the price to a more reasonable level.

b.reason: (Sibling swap (label)). B keeps the correct behaviour and effect but attaches them to positive feedback traders, who in GARP’s terms sell when prices fall and buy when prices rise. B would be correct only if the word “Positive” were replaced by “Negative.”

c.reason: (Polarity flip (trading direction)). C keeps the correct label but reverses the trading direction: buying on rises and selling on falls is positive feedback behaviour, which cannot restore prices. C’s direction would be correct in a statement describing positive feedback traders and concluding that they destabilise prices.

d.reason: (Absolute claim). D asserts that every trader can be classified and that prices “never” overshoot. GARP says the classification is a simplification because some strategies cannot be classified, and a liquid market avoids overreaction as a tendency, not a guarantee. D would be correct if it said that negative feedback dominance tends to keep prices from overreacting.

questions.source: High quality paper LTR-1 d Q3
questions.question:
A risk consultant engaged by a São Paulo asset manager is reviewing trading rules used across the firm’s BRL funds, to identify which of them are sources of positive feedback trading:

I. An equity fund buys a stock as soon as it moves above the top of its six-month trading range of BRL 18 to BRL 22, and sells it as soon as it moves below BRL 18.

II. A value fund buys a stock when its price falls well below the fund’s estimate of fair value and sells when the price rises well above it.

III. A credit fund automatically sells any bond whose price has fallen below a preset level, in order to limit losses.

IV. A derivatives desk dynamically hedges a large long position in call options on the Bovespa index that it bought from corporate clients.

Which of the rules are sources of positive feedback trading?

options.text: III only
I, III, and IV only
II and IV only
I and III only

questions.solution:
Sao Paulo asset manager: which trading rules are sources of positive feedback trading.

**Concept and theory**

GARP Section 1.3.1 lists the reasons why positive feedback trading exists. A positive feedback trader sells when prices fall and buys when prices rise, so any rule that trades with the price move is a source of positive feedback.

| Cause | Mechanism in GARP |
|---|---|
| Trend trading | Buy when the price appears to trend up, sell when it trends down |
| Breakout trading | Trade when the price moves outside an established range (buy above the top, sell below the bottom) |
| Stop-loss rules | Automatically sell an owned asset when its price falls below a level; always present in the market |
| Dynamic hedging | Hedging a short option position (call or put) buys after rises and sells after falls |
| Synthetic options | Creating a long option synthetically means trading as if hedging a short option |
| Margins | Unmet margin calls force close-outs that reinforce the move |
| Predatory trading | Others short an asset they know must be sold |
| LTCM | Leveraged relative value positions closed out under margin calls |

GARP’s breakout example is a stock that has traded between \$25 and \$30 for six months: traders buy as soon as it moves above \$30 and sell as soon as it moves below \$25. By contrast, buying when a price is unreasonably low and selling when it is unreasonably high is exactly how GARP describes negative feedback traders. Dynamic hedging of a long option position sells after a rise and buys after a decline, which GARP says is negative feedback trading that should not interfere with liquidity.

**Applying it to this question**

Rule I buys above BRL 22 and sells below BRL 18: breakout trading, positive feedback. Rule II buys on large falls and sells on large rises relative to fair value: negative feedback. Rule III is a stop-loss rule: positive feedback. Rule IV hedges a long call position (the desk bought the calls), which requires selling after rises and buying after falls: negative feedback. The positive feedback sources are I and III. The BRL range levels and the client type in rule IV are details; only the direction of trading relative to the price move matters.

**Fragile fact.** Actor and position: it is hedging a short option position that is positive feedback; hedging a long option position is negative feedback.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 66.d, verbatim):** Explain liquidity black holes and identify the causes of positive feedback trading.

**GARP:** Chapter 1, Section 1.3.1 Positive and Negative Feedback Traders, items 1 to 3. **Schweser:** Module 66.3, list of reasons for positive feedback trading. **GARP vs Schweser:** no conflict; GARP’s remark that stop-loss rules are “always present in the market” is in GARP only.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-1 d, where it is Q3 of 13.

a.reason: (Scope error, omits breakout trading). “III only” misses rule I. GARP explicitly treats breakout trading as a strategy related to trend trading and a source of positive feedback. A would be correct if rule I sold at the top of the range and bought at the bottom (range trading against the move), which is negative feedback.

b.reason: (Sibling swap (long versus short option hedging)). Including IV gives the hedging of a long option position the property of hedging a short one. B would be correct if the desk had written (sold) the Bovespa calls to clients, because hedging a short call buys after rises and sells after falls.

c.reason: (Polarity flip). II and IV are precisely the two negative feedback rules. C would be correct if the consultant had been asked to identify the rules that are sources of negative feedback trading, which support liquidity.

d.reason: Option D is correct because rules I and III are two of GARP’s named causes (breakout trading and stop-loss rules), while II and IV trade against the move.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Explain liquidity black holes and identify the causes of positive feedback trading.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-1 d Q4
questions.question:
A market surveillance officer at an Australian regulator is comparing two episodes on the local exchange. On both days the average quoted bid-offer spread across the index was 0.05% of mid price.

| Episode | Pre-news | News-day close | Intraday low | One month later |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| X: bank share (AUD) | 40.00 | 34.50 | 34.00 | 34.60 |
| Y: mining share (AUD) | 40.00 | 26.00 | 22.00 | 33.00 |

In X, buyers stepped in within an hour of the news. In Y, each fall triggered further selling and bids were scarce for most of the day. Which of the following best describes the two episodes?

options.text: Both are liquidity black holes, because in each case the share price fell by roughly 15% in response to the news, and neither recovered to its pre-news level within the month.
Only Y is consistent with a liquidity black hole, because the price decline caused more participants to sell, driving the price well below the level at which it later settled.
Only X is consistent with a liquidity black hole, because its price failed to recover after the news, showing that liquidity in the bank share did not return within the month.
Neither is a liquidity black hole, because a black hole requires that the asset cannot be sold at any price, whereas both shares continued to trade throughout the day.

questions.solution:
Australian regulator: which of two price falls is consistent with a liquidity black hole.

**Concept and theory**

A falling price is not, by itself, a liquidity black hole. GARP Section 1.3 distinguishes two situations. In a well-functioning market, the market may change its opinion about the price of an asset because of new information, but the price does not overreact: if a decrease is too great, traders quickly move in and buy, and a new equilibrium price is established. That is a repricing, and it can be large and permanent.

A liquidity black hole is created when a price decline causes more market participants to want to sell, driving prices well below where they will eventually settle. During the sell-off, liquidity dries up and the asset can be sold only at a fire-sale price. The diagnostic signs are therefore (i) one-sided order flow in which falls trigger more selling, (ii) scarce bids, and (iii) an overshoot: the trough lies well below the level at which the price later settles.

One useful way to measure the overshoot is the gap between the intraday low and the later settling price:

Overshoot $= \frac{\text{P}_{\text{settle}} - \text{P}_{\text{low}}}{\text{P}_{\text{settle}}}$

where $\text{P}_{\text{low}}$ is the lowest traded price during the episode and $\text{P}_{\text{settle}}$ is the price at which the asset eventually settles. A large overshoot together with one-sided selling is the signature of a black hole; a small overshoot with buyers stepping in is a well-functioning repricing.

**Applying it to this question**

Episode X: low AUD 34.00, settled near AUD 34.60, so the overshoot is (34.60 − 34.00)/34.60 ≈ 1.7%. Buyers stepped in within the hour: a new equilibrium on new information.

Episode Y: low AUD 22.00, settled near AUD 33.00, so the overshoot is (33.00 − 22.00)/33.00 ≈ 33%. Each fall triggered further selling and bids were scarce: a price decline that caused more selling, driving the price well below where it settled. Only Y fits.

Irrelevant input: the 0.05% average index spread. GARP warns that low average spreads coexist with increasingly frequent black holes, so a market-wide average says nothing about whether a particular market became one-sided.

**Fragile fact.** Convention: the test is overshoot relative to where the price eventually settles, not the size of the fall from the pre-news price.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 66.d, verbatim):** Explain liquidity black holes and identify the causes of positive feedback trading.

**GARP:** Chapter 1, Section 1.3 Liquidity Black Holes (well-functioning market versus black hole). **Schweser:** Module 66.3 (“only able to sell at prices far below the assets’ implicit values”). **GARP** **vs Schweser:** no conflict. The overshoot ratio is a teaching aid for reading the data; GARP states the idea in words (prices driven well below where they will eventually settle) and gives no formula.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-1 d, where it is Q4 of 13.

a.reason: (Scope error). A treats any large fall on news as a black hole and uses failure to regain the pre-news price as evidence. GARP allows a well-functioning market to reprice on new information. A would be correct if both episodes had shown a deep overshoot below the later settling price, with one-sided selling.

b.reason: Option B is correct because it applies GARP’s mechanism (price decline causing more selling, driving the price well below its eventual level) to the episode that shows it.

c.reason: (Sibling swap (repricing mistaken for a black hole)). C labels X’s lasting repricing as the black hole and ignores Y’s overshoot. C would be correct if X, rather than Y, had plunged well below its later settling level amid scarce bids.

d.reason: (Absolute claim). D requires that the asset cannot be sold at any price. GARP says that in a black hole the asset can be sold only at a fire-sale price; trading continues, but at distressed levels. D would be correct only under a definition requiring a complete absence of bids, which GARP does not use.
