questions.loText: Explain liquidity black holes and identify the causes of positive feedback trading.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-1 d Q5
questions.question: The CRO of a Frankfurt-based bank is reviewing two equity derivatives books on the same euro area index. Desk 1 has written (sold) EUR 6 billion notional of long-dated put options to retail structured-product buyers. Desk 2 has bought EUR 1 billion notional of call options from corporate clients. Both desks delta hedge daily in the underlying. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Hedging Desk 1’s short puts requires selling the underlying after a price decline and buying after a rise; this is positive feedback trading that could destabilise the market.
Hedging Desk 1’s short puts requires buying the underlying after a price decline and selling after a rise; this is negative feedback trading that should support market liquidity.
Hedging Desk 2’s long calls requires buying the underlying after a price rise and selling after a decline; this is positive feedback trading that adds to Desk 1’s hedging flow.
Neither desk’s hedging can reduce market liquidity, because delta hedging lowers the bank’s own exposure and a strategy that reduces risk cannot destabilise the market.

questions.solution:
Frankfurt bank: liquidity effect of delta hedging a short put book and a long call book.

**Concept and theory**

GARP Section 1.3.1, item 3, identifies dynamic hedging as a source of positive feedback trading, but only for one side of the option market. Hedging a short option position (call or put) involves buying the underlying after a price rise and selling after a price decline. That is positive feedback trading and has the potential to reduce liquidity. By contrast, dynamically hedging a long position in a call or put involves selling after a price rise and buying after a price decline; this is negative feedback trading and should not interfere with market liquidity.

The intuition comes from how the delta (sensitivity to the underlying) of each position moves when the price falls:

| Position | Effect of a price fall on the posi- tion’s delta | Hedge trade after a fall | Feedback |
|---|---|---|---|
| Short put | Position delta becomes more positive | Sell underlying | Positive |
| Short call | Short delta shrinks | Sell underlying (unwind hedge) | Positive |
| Long put | Position delta becomes more negative | Buy underlying | Negative |
| Long call | Long delta shrinks | Buy underlying (cover short hedge) | Negative |

GARP concludes that any situation in which banks have a large short option position has the potential to destabilise the market and cause illiquidity. Its example is banks that sold a huge volume of options on long-term interest rates to British insurance companies; as the banks hedged, the behaviour of long-term UK rates was dramatically affected.

**Applying it to this question**

Desk 1 is short EUR 6 billion of puts. After a decline the short puts’ delta exposure grows, so the hedge sells the underlying; after a rise it buys back. That is trading with the move: positive feedback, and at EUR 6 billion notional it is the kind of large short option position GARP flags. Desk 2 is long calls: its hedge sells after rises and buys after declines, which is negative feedback and partly offsets Desk 1. The notional sizes matter for impact, not for the direction of each desk’s hedge.

**Fragile fact.** Actor and sign: the destabilising hedger is the option writer (short calls or short puts); the option buyer’s hedge is negative feedback.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 66.d, verbatim):** Explain liquidity black holes and identify the causes of positive feedback trading.

**GARP:** Chapter 1, Section 1.3.1, item 3 Dynamic hedging. **Schweser:** Module 66.3 (“A short call (put) option position can be hedged by buying (selling) the underlying after a price increase (decrease)”). **GARP vs Schweser:** no conflict in substance. The delta table is a teaching aid that restates GARP’s buy-after-rise and sell-after-decline rule; GARP does not use the word delta in this section.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-1 d, where it is Q5 of 13.

a.reason: Option A is correct because it states GARP’s rule for short option hedging (buy after a rise, sell after a decline) and its consequence (positive feedback with the potential to destabilise).

b.reason: (Polarity flip). B reverses the hedge trades for a short put. Buying after declines and selling after rises is the hedge of a long option position. B would be correct if Desk 1 had bought, not written, the puts.

c.reason: (Sibling swap (long versus short option hedging)). C gives Desk 2’s long calls the hedging pattern of a short option position. Hedging long calls sells after rises and buys after declines (negative feedback). C would be correct if Desk 2 had written the calls to its clients.

d.reason: (Absolute claim). D assumes that a risk-reducing strategy cannot destabilise the market. GARP’s point is the opposite: hedging a large short option position is positive feedback trading, and the 1987 lesson is that it is dangerous to follow even a hedging strategy when many others do the same. D would be correct only if all the bank’s option positions were long.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Explain liquidity black holes and identify the causes of positive feedback trading.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-1 d Q6
questions.question: An internal auditor at a Singapore asset manager is reviewing a proposed protection overlay for an SGD 3 billion equity portfolio. A vendor’s program would synthetically create a put option on the portfolio by selling index futures after market declines and buying them back after market rises. The vendor notes that the same program is already used by many regional managers. Which lesson from a case in the reading is most directly relevant to the auditor’s review?

options.text: Assets whose nature is uncertain or poorly understood are unlikely to trade in a liquid market for long, so instruments that are not transparent should be avoided.
A bank that relies on short-term wholesale funding to finance long-term assets can fail through a lack of liquidity even when its assets exceed its liabilities.
It is dangerous to follow a particular trading strategy, even a hedging strategy, when many other market participants are following the same strategy at the same time.
A highly leveraged position that is long illiquid and short liquid instruments can suffer when a flight to quality widens the gap between their prices.

questions.solution:
Singapore asset manager: case lesson most relevant to a synthetic put overlay used by many managers.

**Concept and theory**

GARP Section 1.3.1, item 4, explains that hedging a short position in an option is equivalent to creating a long position in the same option synthetically. A financial institution can therefore create a long option position synthetically by doing the same sort of trading it would do to hedge a short option position. Because that trading buys after rises and sells after falls, creating options synthetically leads to positive feedback trading that can cause market instability and illiquidity.

The classic example is the stock market crash of October 1987 (Business Snapshot 1.4). In the period before the crash the market had done very well, and portfolios involving over \$60 billion of equity assets were managed with “portfolio insurance” trading rules designed to create synthetic put options. The rules sold equities (or index futures) when the market declined and bought when it rose.

| Fact | Detail in GARP |
|---|---|
| Wednesday 14 to Friday 16 October | Market fell about 10%, much of it on Friday afternoon |
| Sales dictated by the rules | At least \$12 billion; only \$4 billion executed |
| Monday 19 October | Dow Jones Industrial Average fell by more than 20% |
| Portfolio insurers’ share | Almost 10% of NYSE sales (three insurers); 21.3% of index futures sales |
| Aggravating factors | Others sold anticipating the insurers; systems overloaded |
| Aftermath | Market close to pre-crash level within four months |

The lesson GARP draws is that it is dangerous to follow a particular trading strategy, even a hedging strategy, when many other market participants are doing the same thing. A report on the crash described an “illusion of liquidity” that led similarly motivated investors to adopt strategies calling for liquidity far in excess of what the market could supply.

**Applying it to this question**

The proposed overlay sells index futures after declines and buys after rises in order to create a synthetic put: this is exactly the portfolio insurance mechanism. The decisive detail in the stem is that many regional managers already run the same program, so in a decline they would all be selling at once. That points directly to the 1987 lesson. The SGD 3 billion size is context and does not change which lesson applies.

**Fragile fact.** Direction: portfolio insurance sells after declines and buys after rises; creating a long option synthetically is the same trading as hedging a short option.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 66.d, verbatim):** Explain liquidity black holes and identify the causes of positive feedback trading.

**GARP:** Chapter 1, Section 1.3.1, item 4 Creating options synthetically, and Business Snapshot 1.4 The Crash of 1987. **Schweser:** Module 66.3 (1987 example: synthetic puts on portfolios over \$60 billion, \$12 billion dictated versus \$4 billion sold). **GARP vs Schweser:** no conflict; the 21.3% futures share, the overloaded systems and the four-month recovery are in GARP only.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-1 d, where it is Q6 of 13.

a.reason: (Sibling swap (lesson of the 2007 transparency problem)). A is the true lesson of Section 1.1.1: after August 2007, instruments that were not transparent became illiquid. The overlay trades plain index futures, so transparency is not the issue. A would be the answer if the auditor were reviewing an investment in ABS CDO-type instruments whose risks were poorly understood.

b.reason: (Sibling swap (lesson of Northern Rock)). B is the true lesson of Northern Rock, a solvent bank that failed for lack of funding liquidity. It concerns liability-side funding, not trading behaviour. B would be the answer if the auditor were reviewing a lender’s reliance on short-term wholesale funding.

c.reason: Option C is correct because it states the lesson GARP draws from the 1987 crash, and the overlay reproduces both features of that case: synthetic put creation (positive feedback) and many participants using the same rules.

d.reason: (Sibling swap (lesson of LTCM)). D is the true lesson of LTCM’s relative value trades after the 1998 Russian default. The overlay is not a leveraged long-illiquid, short-liquid position. D would be the answer if the review concerned a leveraged convergence trade financed with margin.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Explain liquidity black holes and identify the causes of positive feedback trading.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-1 d Q7
questions.question: The treasurer of a Shanghai-based bank must sell a CNY 40 billion holding of a thinly traded local bond over the coming weeks, and several dealers have learned that the sale is coming. Which of the following statements about the risk the treasurer faces is most accurate?

options.text: Dealers who expect the sale are likely to buy the bond ahead of the bank, so that they can resell it to other investors at the higher price that the bank’s sale will create.
Selling the entire holding as quickly as possible is the usual defence, because the dealers need several weeks to build up the short positions that would hurt the bank.
Predatory trading is a concern only in stressed markets; in normal markets the sale is absorbed at the quoted bid, so keeping the bank’s plans confidential adds little.
Dealers who expect the sale are likely to short the bond, reinforcing the decline; the bank should keep its position and plans confidential and unwind the holding slowly.

questions.solution:
Shanghai bank: predatory trading risk when selling a large, widely anticipated bond position.

**Concept and theory**

Predatory trading is introduced in GARP Section 1.1 and listed in Section 1.3.1 (item 6) as a cause of positive feedback trading. It occurs when a market participant has a large position and other participants guess that it will have to be unwound in the near future. The others try to profit by doing trades similar to those they expect from the forced seller. If a large sale of an asset is expected, they short the asset in anticipation of the price decline. This reinforces the decline, so the price falls further than it otherwise would, and it becomes harder for the seller to exit at competitive prices.

| Element | GARP |
|---|---|
| Trigger | Others know or guess that a large position must be unwound |
| Predators’ trade | Same direction as the forced trade (short ahead of a forced sale) |
| Effect | Reinforces the decline: positive feedback |
| Defences | Keep positions and future trading plans confidential; unwind large positions slowly |
| Examples | London Whale (2012); Metallgesellschaft; LTCM unwound slowly under Federal Reserve supervision |

Predatory trading is positive feedback because the predators sell into a falling market and push it lower. GARP’s two defences are confidentiality, so that predators do not know what is coming, and unwinding large positions slowly, so that the forced flow does not concentrate into a window that predators can trade ahead of.

**Applying it to this question**

The bank must sell a CNY 40 billion holding of a thinly traded bond, and dealers know the sale is coming. These are exactly GARP’s conditions for predatory trading: a large position, a forced unwind, and others who anticipate it. The dealers’ profitable trade is to short the bond ahead of the bank, which deepens the fall. GARP’s defences are confidentiality and a slow unwind, which is option D.

**Fragile fact.** Direction: predators trade with the forced seller (they short); the defence is to unwind slowly and keep plans confidential.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 66.d, verbatim):** Explain liquidity black holes and identify the causes of positive feedback trading.

**GARP:** Chapter 1, Section 1.1 Liquidity Trading Risk (predatory trading), and Section 1.3.1, item 6 Predatory trading. **Schweser:** Module 66.3 (“traders who become aware of large, upcoming sales of an asset take short positions”). **GARP vs Schweser:** no conflict; the defences (confidentiality, slow unwinding) are stated in GARP only.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-1 d, where it is Q7 of 13.

a.reason: (Polarity flip (predators’ direction)). Predators trade in the same direction as the forced seller; they short ahead of a forced sale and do not buy. A would be correct if the bank were known to need to buy a large amount, for example to close a large short position, because predators would then buy ahead of it.

b.reason: (Polarity flip (speed of unwind)). GARP says that to avoid predatory trading, large positions must usually be unwound slowly. A rushed sale concentrates the flow, which predators can trade ahead of, and also faces wider bid-offer spreads. B would be closer to correct only if no one knew of the sale and the sole concern were adverse moves in the mid-market price while the position is held.

c.reason: (Scope or condition error). GARP does not limit predatory trading to stressed markets; it arises whenever others guess that a large position must be unwound. Also, large trades are not absorbed at the quoted bid, because quotes are good only up to a certain size. C would be correct only for a small position, below the market maker’s size limit, whose sale nobody anticipated.

d.reason: Option D is correct because it identifies the predators’ trade (short the asset), its effect (reinforcing the decline), and both GARP defences (confidentiality and unwinding slowly).

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Explain liquidity black holes and identify the causes of positive feedback trading.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-1 d Q8
questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a New York hedge fund is stress testing a relative value fixed income trade, run at 25 times leverage:

| Leg | Instrument | Notional (USD billion) |
|---|---|---|
| Long | Off-the-run (illiquid) Treasury bond | 2.0 |
| Short | On-the-run (liquid) Treasury bond | 2.0 |

The scenario is a sovereign default elsewhere that triggers a flight to quality, after which the fund cannot meet its margin calls. Which of the following best describes the likely outcome?

options.text: Because the fund is both long and short, the sales and purchases needed to close out offset each other, so the forced close-out has no net effect on relative prices.
Illiquid bond prices fall relative to liquid ones; closing out means buying the liquid bonds and selling the illiquid bonds, which pushes the two prices further apart.
Illiquid bond prices fall relative to liquid ones; closing out means selling the liquid bonds and buying the illiquid bonds, which pulls the two prices closer together.
Illiquid bond prices fall relative to liquid ones; exchanges respond to higher volatility by reducing margin requirements, which eases pressure on leveraged funds.

questions.solution:
New York hedge fund: outcome of a leveraged long-illiquid, short-liquid bond trade after a flight to quality.

**Concept and theory**

GARP lists two linked causes of positive feedback trading in Section 1.3.1. Item 5 is margins: a big movement in market variables, particularly for highly leveraged traders, may lead to margin calls that cannot be met. This forces traders to close out their positions, which reinforces the underlying move. Volatility is likely to increase, and this may make things worse, because exchanges then increase their margin requirements.

Item 7 is LTCM. One of Long-Term Capital Management’s trades was “relative value fixed income”:

| Stage | What happened |
|---|---|
| Position | Short a liquid bond, long a similar illiquid bond; wait for prices to move close together |
| Shock | After the Russian default of 1998, illiquid instruments fell relative to similar liquid ones |
| Funding | LTCM and similar firms were highly leveraged and could not meet margin calls |
| Close-out | Buy the liquid bonds (cover the short), sell the illiquid bonds (exit the long) |
| Feedback | Reinforced the flight to quality; prices diverged even further |

The close-out is positive feedback because it trades with the move: the liquid bond was already rising relative to the illiquid one, and the forced trades buy more of the liquid bond and sell more of the illiquid one. GARP also notes in Section 1.1 that LTCM’s positions were eventually unwound slowly under Federal Reserve supervision to avoid predatory trading.

**Applying it to this question**

The fund’s trade is LTCM’s: long the illiquid off-the-run bond and short the liquid on-the-run bond. A flight to quality lowers illiquid prices relative to liquid ones, so the trade loses. If margin calls cannot be met, the fund must buy the on-the-run bond and sell the off-the-run bond, which widens the gap further. The 25 times leverage explains why margin calls cannot be met but does not change the direction of any trade; the equal USD 2 billion notionals are also not needed to reach the answer.

**Fragile fact.** Close-out direction: unwinding short liquid, long illiquid means buy liquid, sell illiquid; and exchanges raise margins when volatility rises.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 66.d, verbatim):** Explain liquidity black holes and identify the causes of positive feedback trading.

**GARP:** Chapter 1, Section 1.3.1, items 5 Margins and 7 LTCM; Section 1.1 (slow unwind of LTCM). **Schweser:** Module 66.3 (margin calls; LTCM). **GARP vs Schweser:** no conflict on the mechanism. Schweser adds that the failure led to a bailout by Wall Street banks, which GARP does not state and which is not used here. The rise in exchange margin requirements is in GARP only.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-1 d, where it is Q8 of 13.

a.reason: (Scope error (legs treated as offsetting)). A assumes that a hedged book’s close-out is neutral. The two legs are different instruments: buying the liquid bond pushes its price up while selling the illiquid bond pushes its price down, so both trades widen the gap. A would be correct only if the long and short legs were in the same instrument.

b.reason: Option B is correct because it gets right both the direction of the shock (illiquid down relative to liquid) and the close-out trades (buy liquid, sell illiquid), and it states GARP’s conclusion that the close-out drives the prices further apart.

c.reason: (Polarity flip (close-out direction)). C reverses the close-out trades. Exiting a short in the liquid bond requires buying it, and exiting a long in the illiquid bond requires selling it. C would be correct for a fund positioned the other way round, long liquid and short illiquid, whose close-out would narrow the gap.

d.reason: (Polarity flip (margin requirements)). GARP says that higher volatility may lead exchanges to increase margin requirements, which exacerbates the situation. D would be correct only if margins were cut as volatility rose, which is the opposite of GARP’s description.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Explain liquidity black holes and identify the causes of positive feedback trading.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-1 d Q9
questions.question:
A treasury analyst at a London hedge fund is modelling a deleveraging episode. Leverage is measured as total assets divided by equity. The prime broker has told the fund to cut leverage from 20 times to 5 times equity.

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Total assets (GBP million, market value) | 1,200 |
| Equity (GBP million) | 60 |
| Credit spread on the fund’s borrowing, before and after the call (bp) | 90 and 240 |

In round 1 the fund sells assets at current prices to reach 5 times. Sales by this and other funds then cause the market value of the assets it still holds to fall by 5%, with debt unchanged. In round 2 it sells again to restore 5 times. Which of the following is closest to total asset sales over the two rounds?

options.text: GBP 900 million
GBP 930 million
GBP 960 million
GBP 975 million

questions.solution:
London hedge fund: total asset sales when cutting leverage from 20 to 5 times with a price feedback round.

**Concept and theory**

GARP Section 1.3.2 (Figures 1.2 and 1.3) describes a leveraging and deleveraging cycle that turns credit conditions into positive feedback in asset prices.

| Leveraging | Deleveraging |
|---|---|
| Banks awash with liquidity (securitisation, high deposits) | Banks less liquid (e.g., less demand for securitised products) |
| Credit easily available; credit spreads fall | Banks reluctant to lend; credit spreads rise |
| Demand for assets rises; prices rise | Demand for assets falls; prices fall |
| Collateral values rise; more borrowing | Collateral values fall; lines of credit cut |
| More asset purchases; cycle repeats | Asset sales needed; prices fall further |

GARP notes that the period before 2007 was one of leveraging and that deleveraging started in mid-2007. Hedge funds are particularly affected. GARP’s example is a fund able to borrow 20 times its equity, which is told by its prime broker to cut leverage to 5 times. It can do this only by selling assets; asset prices fall because this and other funds are selling; the fund’s equity declines, and further sales are needed.

With leverage L defined, as in the stem, as total assets A divided by equity E, and debt D $= \text{A} -$ E:

L $= \frac{\text{A}}{\text{E}}$ , $\text{A}^{*} = \text{L}^{*} \times$ E, Sales $= \text{A} - \text{A}^{*}$

where $\text{L}^{*}$ is the target leverage and $\text{A}^{*}$ the asset level consistent with it. Sale proceeds repay debt, so sales at market value leave equity unchanged; a fall in the price of assets still held reduces equity one for one, because debt is fixed.

**Applying it to this question**

Round 1 target assets: $\text{A}^{*}_{1} =$ 5 × 60 = 300

Round 1 sales: $\text{S}_{1} =$ 1,200 − 300 = 900

Debt after round 1: $\text{D}_{1} = ($1,200 − 60) − 900 = 240

Assets after 5% fall: $\text{A}_{2} =$ 300 × 0.95 = 285

Equity after fall: $\text{E}_{2} =$ 285 − 240 = 45

Round 2 target assets: $\text{A}^{*}_{2} =$ 5 × 45 = 225

Round 2 sales: $\text{S}_{2} =$ 285 − 225 = 60

Total sales: $\text{S}_{1} + \text{S}_{2} =$ 900 + 60 = 960

Check: after round 2, 225/45 = 5 times. Meaning: a 5% fall in asset prices wiped out 25% of equity (GBP 15 million of GBP 60 million), because the fund was still leveraged 5 times, and forced GBP 60 million of further sales. This is the self-reinforcing loop in GARP’s example. The credit spreads (90 bp and 240 bp) are consistent with deleveraging but are irrelevant to the calculation.

**Fragile fact.** Convention and loop: leverage here is assets divided by equity; a price fall cuts equity by the full fall in asset value because debt is fixed, which forces more selling.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 66.d, verbatim):** Explain liquidity black holes and identify the causes of positive feedback trading.

**GARP:** Chapter 1, Section 1.3.2 Leveraging and Deleveraging (Figures 1.2 and 1.3, hedge fund example). **Schweser:** Module 66.3 (leveraging and deleveraging). **GARP vs Schweser:** no conflict. GARP’s hedge fund example says “borrow 20 times its equity” and does not define leverage precisely; the stem therefore fixes the convention (assets divided by equity). The two-round arithmetic is a stylised illustration of GARP’s verbal example.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-1 d, where it is Q9 of 13.

a.reason: (Intermediate result). GBP 900 million is round 1 only, 1,200 − 5 × 60. It ignores the price feedback, which is the point of the deleveraging cycle. A would be correct if the fund’s sales had no effect on the value of the assets it still held.

b.reason: (Wrong input twin (debt-to-equity used for assets-to-equity)). Reading “5 times” as debt of 5 times equity gives target assets of 6 × 60 = 360 and $\text{S}_{1} =$ 840, leaving debt of 300. Then $\text{A}_{2} =$ 342, $\text{E}_{2} =$ 42, target 6 × 42 = 252, $\text{S}_{2} =$ 90, so the total is 930. B would be correct if the stem had defined leverage as debt divided by equity.

c.reason: Option C, GBP 960 million, is correct: it is the total of the static deleveraging sale and the second-round sale forced by the price fall, with leverage measured as assets divided by equity, as the stem defines it.

d.reason: (Dropped term). Computing round 2 as 300 − 225 = 75 forgets that the 5% fall has already reduced the assets from 300 to 285, giving a total of 900 + 75 = 975. D would be correct only if the assets still had a market value of GBP 300 million after the fall, which contradicts the stem.

questions.loText: Explain liquidity black holes and identify the causes of positive feedback trading.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-1 d Q10
questions.question: The CCO of a Japanese bank is drafting a memo to the board after a desk built up a JPY 300 billion exposure to a single asset class over 18 months. The desk’s profits have been strong, and the bank’s risk managers have raised concerns that were not acted on. Which of the following statements in the memo is most accurate?

options.text: Most liquidity black holes can be traced to irrational exuberance, which is often self-reinforcing: when many institutions take a position, prices rise, the position looks profitable, and more is taken.
Senior management are generally quick to act on risk managers’ warnings in such episodes, because high profits on a crowded position are a well-recognised sign of an asset bubble.
Irrational exuberance is avoidable once risk managers are given veto power, because it arises from weak internal controls rather than being part of human nature.
Irrational exuberance describes the phase in which banks short of liquidity cut lending, and falling collateral values force borrowers to sell assets at lower prices.

questions.solution:
Japanese bank CCO memo: which statement about irrational exuberance is accurate.

**Concept and theory**

GARP Section 1.3.3 traces most liquidity black holes to irrational exuberance of one sort or another. The phrase comes from a December 1996 speech by Alan Greenspan, Federal Reserve Board chairman, who asked how we know when irrational exuberance has unduly escalated asset values.

The mechanism in GARP is as follows. Traders at many different institutions become irrationally exuberant about a particular asset class or market variable. Balance sheets become overextended through accumulating exposure. The process is often self-reinforcing: when many institutions take a position, prices increase, the position looks profitable, and this creates extra desire to take the position and yet more profits. Risk managers should (and probably will) complain, but senior management are likely to ignore the concerns because high profits are being made. Chuck Prince’s July 2007 remark (“as long as the music is playing, you’ve got to get up and dance”) captures the attitude.

At some stage the bubble bursts. Many traders try to exit at the same time, causing illiquid markets and huge losses. Volatility rises, and risk management procedures such as market VaR computed from historical data can cause many institutions to unwind a wide range of risky positions at once, leading to further losses and funding problems. GARP’s examples are the 2007 subprime crisis (the classic case), the 1987 crash, the 1994 bond market crash, the 1997 to 1998 Asian crisis and the 1998 LTCM failure. GARP calls irrational exuberance part of human nature and to some extent inevitable, and says it is exacerbated by year-end bonuses: a trader who expects the correction to be delayed until next year is motivated to keep building the position.

**Applying it to this question**

The stem has every feature of GARP’s description: a large exposure built up over time in one asset class, strong profits, and risk managers’ warnings not acted on. The only statement that reproduces GARP’s account is A: the link from irrational exuberance to black holes and the self-reinforcing price and profit loop. The JPY 300 billion size and the 18 months are context only.

**Fragile fact.** Actor: risk managers complain, but senior management tend to ignore them while profits are high; bonuses make traders keep building exuberant positions.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 66.d, verbatim):** Explain liquidity black holes and identify the causes of positive feedback trading.

**GARP:** Chapter 1, Section 1.3.3 Irrational Exuberance. **Schweser:** Module 66.3 (irrational exuberance, mid-1990s equities, mid-2000s housing). **GARP vs Schweser:** no conflict. Schweser’s housing example and GARP’s list of episodes differ only in illustration; the compensation and senior management points are in GARP only.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-1 d, where it is Q10 of 13.

a.reason: Option A is correct because it states GARP’s claim that most liquidity black holes can be traced to irrational exuberance and correctly describes the self-reinforcing process.

b.reason: (Polarity flip (management response)). GARP says senior management are likely to ignore risk managers’ concerns because high profits are being made. B would describe what should happen, not what GARP says usually happens; it would be correct if the stem asked what risk managers should do (complain about the risks).

c.reason: (Absolute claim). C says exuberance is fully avoidable through controls. GARP calls it part of human nature and to some extent inevitable, exacerbated by bonus structures. C would be correct if it said only that controls and compensation design can reduce, not remove, the problem.

d.reason: (Sibling swap (deleveraging)). D describes deleveraging from Section 1.3.2: banks short of liquidity cut lending and falling collateral values force asset sales. D would be correct if the memo’s term were “deleveraging” rather than “irrational exuberance.”

questions.source: High quality paper LTR-1 d Q11
questions.question: A member of the board risk committee of a Paris-based bank asks the CRO how a uniform global regulatory regime could contribute to liquidity black holes. Over the past month, measured volatilities and correlations in the bank’s EUR trading book have risen sharply, and market risk VaR has increased from EUR 50 million to EUR 80 million. Which of the following responses is most accurate?

options.text: Uniform rules reduce the risk of a black hole: as volatilities and correlations rise, VaR-based capital falls at all banks, leaving them free to buy assets that others are selling.
The Basel Committee has dealt with procyclical credit capital by requiring the probability of default to be a point-in-time estimate for the current stage of the cycle.
Uniform rules can contribute to black holes only in credit markets, because market risk capital does not change when volatilities and correlations rise or fall.
As volatilities and correlations rise, market risk VaR and capital rise at all banks; since banks hold similar positions, they try to do similar trades and a black hole can develop.

questions.solution:
Paris bank risk committee: how uniform regulation can contribute to liquidity black holes.

**Concept and theory**

GARP Section 1.3.4 accepts that uniform global regulation is in many ways a laudable goal. Before Basel I, capital requirements and their enforcement varied by country, and banks with low or weakly enforced requirements could take more risk and price more competitively. But a uniform regulatory environment comes with costs: all banks tend to respond in the same way to external events.

| Risk | Trigger | Common response |
|---|---|---|
| Market risk | Volatilities and correlations rise, so VaR and market risk capital rise | Banks reduce exposures; with similar positions they do similar trades; a black hole can develop |
| Credit risk | Low point of the cycle: PDs high, Basel II IRB capital high | Banks less willing to lend; at the high point, too willing |

For credit risk, GARP notes that the problem resembles the leveraging and deleveraging cycle of Figures 1.2 and 1.3. The Basel Committee dealt with it by asserting that the probability of default should be an average through the economic or credit cycle, rather than an estimate applicable to one particular point in time.

The thread linking both risks is the theme of Section 1.3.5: black holes are caused by a lack of independence among market participants. Uniform rules make banks’ responses more correlated, so their trades become more alike.

**Applying it to this question**

The bank’s VaR has risen from EUR 50 million to EUR 80 million because volatilities and correlations increased. Under uniform rules every bank sees a similar rise in VaR and capital; banks then try to cut exposures, and because they hold similar positions they try to do similar trades at the same time. That is GARP’s market risk route to a black hole, which is option D. The VaR figures illustrate the trigger but no calculation is required.

**Fragile fact.** Direction: rising volatilities and correlations raise VaR and capital at all banks at once; the Basel fix for credit is a through-the-cycle PD.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 66.d, verbatim):** Explain liquidity black holes and identify the causes of positive feedback trading.

**GARP:** Chapter 1, Section 1.3.4 The Impact of Regulation. **Schweser:** Module 66.3 (“liquidity black holes can develop as banks respond similarly to external events”). **GARP vs Schweser:** no conflict; the market risk VaR mechanism and the through-the-cycle PD are in GARP only.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-1 d, where it is Q11 of 13.

a.reason: (Polarity flip). VaR and market risk capital increase when volatilities and correlations increase; they do not fall. A would be correct only if capital fell as measured risk rose, which is the opposite of how VaR-based capital behaves.

b.reason: (Sibling swap (point-in-time versus through-the-cycle)). GARP says the Basel Committee responded by requiring the probability of default to be an average through the cycle, not a point-in-time estimate. B would be correct if “point-in-time estimate for the current stage of the cycle” were replaced by “average through the economic or credit cycle.”

c.reason: (Scope error). GARP’s main example of uniform regulation creating a black hole is market risk, where rising volatilities and correlations raise VaR and capital. Credit risk is a second, similar channel. C would be correct only if market risk capital were insensitive to volatility, which it is not.

d.reason: Option D is correct because it reproduces GARP’s chain: higher volatilities and correlations, higher VaR and capital, similar positions, similar trades, and a possible liquidity black hole.

questions.loText: Explain liquidity black holes and identify the causes of positive feedback trading.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-1 d Q12
questions.question:
A policy adviser at an Australian regulator is reviewing a proposal to apply bank-style liquidity and market risk rules, unchanged, to life insurers and superannuation (pension) funds holding AUD assets. The adviser lists the following arguments:

I. Life insurers and pension funds have longer time horizons than banks.

II. Life insurers and pension funds should not be penalised for investing in illiquid assets.

III. Life insurers and pension funds should be required to reduce exposures when volatilities and correlations increase, because these parameters tend to keep trending upward.

IV. Regulating life insurers and pension funds in the same way as banks is preferable, because a level playing field reduces the likelihood of liquidity black holes.

Which of the arguments are consistent with the reading’s view on the impact of regulation?

options.text: I only
I and II only
I, II, and III only
I, II, and IV only

questions.solution:
Australian regulator: arguments against regulating insurers and pension funds like banks.

**Concept and theory**

GARP Section 1.3.4 asks whether other financial institutions, such as life insurance companies and pension funds, should be regulated in the same way as banks. It is tempting to answer “yes,” so that no institution gains an advantage over others. GARP says the answer should be “no,” for three reasons:

| No. | Reason in GARP |
|---|---|
| 1 | These institutions have longer time horizons than banks. |
| 2 | They should not be penalised for investing in illiquid assets. |
| 3 | They should not be required to adjust their portfolios when volatilities and correlations increase, because these parameters tend to be mean reverting and eventually decrease again. |

The reasoning connects to Section 1.3.5, The Importance of Diversity. Black holes arise because participants do not act independently. One way of creating diversity is to recognise that different types of institutions have different risks and should be regulated differently. If insurers and pension funds were forced to sell whenever volatility rose, they would join banks on the same side of the market at the same time; if they are allowed to hold through such periods, they can act as patient, long-horizon participants who do not all trade together. A “level playing field” would therefore remove a source of diversity, the opposite of what is needed to avoid black holes.

**Applying it to this question**

Arguments I and II are GARP’s first two reasons. Argument III reverses the third: GARP says these institutions should not be required to adjust when volatilities and correlations rise, because those parameters are mean reverting, not persistently trending. Argument IV is the “tempting” level-playing-field answer that GARP rejects; uniform treatment reduces diversity and so raises, not lowers, black hole risk. The consistent set is I and II.

**Fragile fact.** Direction: insurers and pension funds should not be required to cut exposures when volatilities and correlations rise, because these parameters mean revert.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 66.d, verbatim):** Explain liquidity black holes and identify the causes of positive feedback trading.

**GARP:** Chapter 1, Section 1.3.4 The Impact of Regulation, and Section 1.3.5 The Importance of Diversity. **Schweser:** Module 66.3 (regulations should be applied differently; banks have different time horizons and risk profiles from pension funds and life insurers). **GARP vs** **Schweser:** no conflict; the illiquid-asset and mean reversion reasons are in GARP only.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-1 d, where it is Q12 of 13.

a.reason: (Scope error, rejects a true argument). “I only” leaves out II, which GARP states directly: these institutions should not be penalised for investing in illiquid assets. A would be correct only if argument II had said that insurers and pension funds should face penalties on illiquid holdings, which GARP does not say.

b.reason: Option B is correct because it accepts GARP’s two reasons stated in I and II and rejects III (reversed direction and wrong reason) and IV (the conclusion GARP rejects).

c.reason: (Polarity flip in argument III). Accepting III means accepting a mandatory adjustment when volatilities and correlations rise, justified by a persistent upward trend. GARP says the opposite: no requirement to adjust, because the parameters are mean reverting. C would be correct if III had said that these institutions should not be required to adjust because volatilities and correlations tend to mean revert.

d.reason: (Polarity flip in argument IV). IV adopts the level-playing-field answer that GARP calls tempting but wrong. Uniform regulation removes diversity, which is what is needed to avoid black holes. D would be correct if IV had argued that regulating these institutions differently from banks creates the diversity that reduces black hole risk.

questions.loText: Explain liquidity black holes and identify the causes of positive feedback trading.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-1 d Q13
questions.question: A risk committee member at a Singapore-based endowment, which invests USD assets with several hedge funds, asks the endowment’s senior risk analyst how market structure affects the risk of liquidity black holes. Which of the following responses is most accurate?

options.text: Black holes arise because participants do not act independently; hedge funds add some diversity, but being highly leveraged they may all have to unwind together when liquidity tightens.
Black holes are largely removed by hedge funds; because they are lightly regulated and can follow any strategy they like, they reliably supply liquidity whenever liquidity tightens.
A contrarian strategy has merit when markets overreact, and it is easiest to follow for institutions subject to short-term VaR-based risk management, since VaR highlights cheap assets.
Black holes arise mainly because complex products are not transparent, so the main remedy is better disclosure of asset quality rather than greater diversity of trading strategies.

questions.solution:
Singapore endowment: market structure, hedge funds, diversity and liquidity black holes.

**Concept and theory**

GARP Section 1.3.5 explains why diversity matters. Models in economics usually assume that market participants act independently. GARP argues that this is often not the case, and that it is this lack of independence that causes liquidity black holes: traders at financial institutions tend to want to do the same trades at the same time. The solution is more diversity in financial markets; one way of creating it is to regulate different types of institutions differently.

GARP’s view of hedge funds is two-sided:

| Adds diversity | Can amplify black holes |
|---|---|
| Much less regulated than banks or insurers | Tend to be highly leveraged |
| Can follow any trading strategy they like | When liquidity tightens (as in the second half of 2007), all have to unwind, accentuating the problem |

GARP also concludes that a contrarian strategy has some merit. If markets overreact for the reasons described, an investor can do well by buying when everyone else is selling and there is very little liquidity. But it can be quite difficult for a financial institution to follow such a strategy if it is subject to short-term VaR-based risk management. (Section 1.3.4 explains why: when volatilities and correlations rise, VaR rises and institutions take steps to reduce exposures, which is just when the contrarian would be buying.) GARP’s summary adds that traders with long-term objectives should avoid being influenced by the short-term overreaction of markets.

**Applying it to this question**

The committee member asks how market structure affects black hole risk, and the endowment invests with several hedge funds. Option A states both of GARP’s points: the root cause (lack of independence among participants) and the balanced verdict on hedge funds (some diversity, but leverage forces them to unwind together). The USD denomination and the endowment’s location are context only.

**Fragile fact.** Cause and remedy: black holes come from lack of independence; the remedy is diversity; contrarian buying is hard under short-term VaR limits.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 66.d, verbatim):** Explain liquidity black holes and identify the causes of positive feedback trading.

**GARP:** Chapter 1, Section 1.3.5 The Importance of Diversity, and the chapter Summary. **Schweser:** Module 66.3 (“Applying regulations differently creates diversity, which is needed to avoid liquidity black holes”). **GARP vs Schweser:** no conflict. The hedge fund and contrarian strategy points are in GARP only; Schweser does not cover them.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-1 d, where it is Q13 of 13.

a.reason: Option A is correct because it matches GARP’s diagnosis of the cause of black holes and its two-sided assessment of hedge funds’ contribution to liquidity.

b.reason: (Absolute claim). GARP says hedge funds add diversity “to some extent,” not that they reliably supply liquidity or remove black holes; being highly leveraged, they all have to unwind when liquidity tightens. B would be correct if it said that hedge funds add some diversity and liquidity in normal conditions.

c.reason: (Polarity flip). GARP says a contrarian strategy is difficult for an institution subject to short-term VaR-based risk management, because rising VaR pushes it to cut risk just when it should be buying. C would be correct if it said that such a strategy is easiest for investors with long horizons who are not constrained by short-term VaR.

d.reason: (Sibling swap (transparency lesson)). Transparency is the lesson of Section 1.1.1 about the 2007 crisis in complex products. The cause of black holes in Section 1.3.5 is lack of independence, and the remedy is diversity of trading strategies. D would be the answer to a question about why ABS CDO markets became illiquid after August 2007.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Calculate the expected transactions cost and the spread risk factor for a transaction and calculate the liquidity adjustment to VaR for a position to be liquidated over a number of trading days.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-2 f Q1
questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a UK asset manager is estimating the cost of exiting a mid-cap equity holding under normal market conditions. Spread changes are assumed to be normal with zero mean.

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Shares held | 2,400,000 |
| Bid price (GBP) | 12.46 |
| Ask price (GBP) | 12.54 |
| Sample standard deviation of the relative spread, $\sigma_{\text{s}}$ | 0.0011 |

The expected transactions cost of selling the entire holding is closest to:
questions.solution:
UK asset manager: expected transactions cost of selling 2.4 million shares quoted GBP 12.46 bid, GBP 12.54 ask.

**Concept and theory**

Transaction cost liquidity risk is the first of the two quantitative measures of transactions liquidity risk in GARP. It focuses on the risk of variation in transactions costs, and its starting point is a hypothesis about the distribution of the future bid-ask spread. Before measuring that risk, we need the expected cost itself.

A dealer buys at the bid and sells at the ask. The midprice P is the reference value of the asset, so a one-way trade gives up the distance from the mid to the side on which it executes. When you sell, you lose the mid-to-bid distance, which is half of the quoted spread. GARP calls the expected transactions cost “the half spread or mid-to-bid spread”. The spread is expressed in relative terms, as a fraction of the price:

s $= \frac{\text{ask} - \text{bid}}{\text{midprice}} =$ 2 $\frac{\text{ask} - \text{bid}}{\text{ask} + \text{bid}}$ , Expected transactions cost per unit $= \text{P} \times\frac{\bar{s}}{2}$ ,

where $\bar{\text{s}}$ is the expected (typical) relative spread, set equal to the latest observed s, and P is the midprice. The result is in currency per unit of the asset, so for a position of N units you multiply by N. Notice that P × s/2 is exactly the currency half-spread, $(\text{ask} - \text{bid})$/2.

| Measure | Formula (per unit) | Uses $\sigma_{\text{s}}$? |
|---|---|---|
| Expected transactions cost | P $\bar{\text{s}}$/2 | No |
| 99% transactions cost | $\bar{\text{P}}$ $\cdot\frac{1}{2} (\bar{\text{s}}$ + 2.33$\sigma_{\text{s}})$ | Yes |
| Round-trip cost (tightness) | P $\bar{\text{s}}$ | No |

**Applying it to this question**

Expected cost $= \text{N} \times\text{P} \times$ $\bar{\text{s}}$/2.

P = (12.46 + 12.54)/2 = 12.50

s = (12.54 − 12.46)/12.50 = 0.08/12.50 = 0.0064

Cost per share = 12.50 × 0.0064/2 = GBP 0.04

Cost of position = 0.04 × 2,400,000 = GBP 96,000

The spread volatility $\sigma_{\text{s}} =$ 0.0011 is an irrelevant input here: it enters only the 99% confidence bound, not the expected cost. Selling the whole holding is expected to cost GBP 96,000 relative to its mid valuation.

**Fragile fact.** A one-way trade costs half the spread, and $\sigma_{\text{s}}$ plays no part in the expected cost.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Calculate the expected transactions cost and the spread risk factor for a transaction and calculate the liquidity adjustment to VaR for a position to be liquidated over a number of trading days.

**GARP:** Chapter 2, Section 2.5 Liquidity Risk Measurement, Measuring Transactions Liquidity Risk: Transaction Cost Liquidity Risk. **Schweser:** Module 67.3, Transactions Cost. **GARP vs** **Schweser:** none. Both use the half-spread P$\bar{\text{s}}$/2 (Schweser example: USD 99.50 × 0.01005/2 ≈ USD 0.50).

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-2 f, where it is Q1 of 10.

a.reason: (Unit slip). GBP 7,680 = 0.0064/2 × 2,400,000. The relative half-spread is a fraction of price, so it must be multiplied by the midprice before being multiplied by the share count. This figure would be correct only if the stock’s midprice were GBP 1.00.

b.reason: GARP defines the expected transactions cost as the half spread, P$\bar{\text{s}}$/2. Applied to 2.4 million shares this is GBP 96,000, option B.

c.reason: (Scope error). GBP 134,445 = 12.50 $\times\frac{1}{2} ($0.0064 + 2.33 × 0.0011) × 2,400,000 = 12.50 × 0.0044815 × 2,400,000. This is the 99% transactions cost, which adds the spread risk term. It would be correct if the stem asked for the 99% confidence estimate of the cost rather than the expected cost.

d.reason: (Dropped term). GBP 192,000 = 12.50 × 0.0064 × 2,400,000 omits the one-half. That is the full quoted spread, the round-trip cost of buying at the ask and selling at the bid. It would be correct if the stem asked for the cost of a round trip in the whole position.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Calculate the expected transactions cost and the spread risk factor for a transaction and calculate the liquidity adjustment to VaR for a position to be liquidated over a number of trading days.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-2 f Q2
questions.question: A treasury analyst at a Singapore bank is computing transactions cost risk for a listed equity the bank holds as part of its liquidity buffer. The latest quotes are a bid of SGD 7.82 and an ask of SGD 7.90. Daily changes in the relative bid-ask spread are assumed normally distributed with zero mean, and the sample standard deviation of the relative spread is 0.0026. The 99% spread risk factor is closest to:
questions.solution:
Singapore bank: 99% spread risk factor with bid SGD 7.82, ask SGD 7.90 and $\sigma_{\text{s}} =$ 0.0026.

**Concept and theory**

The expected transactions cost uses today’s spread, but the spread you actually pay tomorrow may be wider. GARP models this by assuming that daily changes in the relative spread are normal with zero mean and a constant variance, estimated by the sample variance of the spread, $\sigma^{2}_{\text{s}}$. Under that assumption, the spread that will be exceeded on only 1% of days is $\bar{\text{s}}$ + 2.33$\sigma_{\text{s}}$, because 2.33 is the one-tailed 99% quantile of the standard normal. A one-way trade pays half of whatever spread prevails, so the half applies to the whole stressed spread:

99% spread risk factor $= \frac{1}{2} (\bar{\text{s}}$ + 2.33 $\sigma_{\text{s}})$ .

The factor is unit-free: it is a fraction of the price. Multiplying it by the estimated next-day midprice $\bar{\text{P}}$ converts it into currency per unit, the 99% transactions cost. Its two parts are worth keeping apart:

| Component | Expression | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| Expected relative half-spread | $\bar{\text{s}}$ | Cost you expect to pay |
| Spread risk add-on Spread risk factor | (2.33$\sigma_{\text{s}})$ $\frac{\frac{1\frac{1}{2}}{2}1}{2} (\bar{\text{s}}$ + 2.33$\sigma_{\text{s}})$ | Extra cost in a 1-in-100 day 99th percentile relative half-spread |

Only the relative spread is used, never a currency spread, so the factor can be compared across assets with very different price levels.

**Applying it to this question**

P = (7.82 + 7.90)/2 = 7.86

$\bar{\text{s}}$ $= \text{s} =$ 0.08/7.86 = 0.010178

2.33 $\sigma_{\text{s}} =$ 2.33 × 0.0026 = 0.006058

$\bar{\text{s}}$ + 2.33 $\sigma_{\text{s}} =$ 0.010178 + 0.006058 = 0.016236

Spread risk factor $= \frac{1}{2} \times$ 0.016236 = 0.008118

At 99% confidence, selling at tomorrow’s bid should cost no more than about 0.81% of the midprice.

**Fragile fact.** Use the one-tailed 2.33, not 1.645 or 2.58, and apply the one-half to both terms inside the bracket.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Calculate the expected transactions cost and the spread risk factor for a transaction and calculate the liquidity adjustment to VaR for a position to be liquidated over a number of trading days.

**GARP:** Chapter 2, Section 2.5, Transaction Cost Liquidity Risk. **Schweser:** Module 67.3, Transactions Cost, which names $\frac{1}{2} (\text{s} +$ 2.33$\sigma_{\text{s}})$ the 99% spread risk factor. **GARP vs Schweser:** none on content. Schweser writes s where GARP writes $\bar{\text{s}}$ for the expected spread.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-2 f, where it is Q2 of 10.

questions.question:
A portfolio manager at a Japanese pension fund wants a 99% confidence estimate of the bid-ask cost of selling a large equity position tomorrow. The fund uses the most recent observations as its estimates of the expected spread and the next-day midprice, and assumes zero-mean normal daily changes in the relative spread.

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Shares held | 500,000 |
| Bid price (JPY) | 2,985 |
| Ask price (JPY) | 3,015 |
| Volatility of the relative spread, $\sigma_{\text{s}}$ (basis points) | 35 |

The 99% transactions cost of selling the position is closest to:

options.text: JPY 7.50 million
JPY 11.82 million
JPY 13.62 million
JPY 27.23 million

questions.solution:
Japanese pension fund: 99% transactions cost of selling 500,000 shares, bid JPY 2,985, ask JPY 3,015, $\sigma_{\text{s}}$ = 35 bp.

**Concept and theory**

The spread risk factor is a proportion. To turn it into money, GARP multiplies it by $\bar{\text{P}}$, the estimate of the next-day midprice, because the position will be sold tomorrow at tomorrow’s prices:

99% transactions cost per unit = $\bar{\text{P}}$ $\times\frac{1}{2} (\bar{\text{s}}$ + 2.33 $\sigma_{\text{s}})$ , $\bar{\text{P}}$ = P, $\bar{\text{s}}$ = s.

GARP describes this as the 99 percent confidence interval on the transactions cost, in currency per unit of the asset. In practice $\bar{\text{P}}$ is set to the most recent midprice and $\bar{\text{s}}$ to the most recent relative spread, so the only extra input beyond the quote is the spread volatility $\sigma_{\text{s}}$. For a position of N units, multiply by N.

Two conventions trip candidates. First, every spread quantity is relative (a fraction of price), so $\sigma_{\text{s}}$ must be in the same decimal units as s. One basis point is 0.0001, so 35 bp is 0.0035, not 0.035 or 0.35. Second, the cost of a sale is half the stressed spread, so the bracket is halved. Leaving the half out gives the stressed round-trip cost, which overstates the cost of a single sale by a factor of two. The measure is a cost, so it is reported as a positive amount that the fund would give up relative to the mid valuation of the position.

**Applying it to this question**

P = (2,985 + 3,015)/2 = 3,000

s = 30/3,000 = 0.0100, $\sigma_{\text{s}} =$ 35 bp = 0.0035

2.33 $\sigma_{\text{s}} =$ 0.008155

Spread risk factor $= \frac{1}{2} ($0.0100 + 0.008155) = 0.0090775

Cost per share = 3,000 × 0.0090775 = JPY 27.2325

Cost of position = 27.2325 × 500,000 = JPY 13,616,250 ≈ JPY 13.62 million

With 99% confidence the sale should not cost more than about JPY 13.6 million relative to the mid valuation.

**Fragile fact.** 35 basis points is 0.0035, and the one-half applies to the whole bracket.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Calculate the expected transactions cost and the spread risk factor for a transaction and calculate the liquidity adjustment to VaR for a position to be liquidated over a number of trading days.

**GARP:** Chapter 2, Section 2.5, Transaction Cost Liquidity Risk. **Schweser:** Module 67.3, Transactions Cost. **GARP vs Schweser:** none. GARP says the interval is “in dollars per unit of the asset”; Schweser says “in dollars”. The formula images are missing from both text extracts, so the formula was rebuilt from the surviving text and Schweser’s worked example.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-2 f, where it is Q3 of 10.

b.reason: (Wrong percentile). JPY 11.82 million = 3,000 $\times\frac{1}{2} ($0.0100 + 1.645 × 0.0035) × 500,000 uses the 95% quantile. It would be correct for a 95% confidence estimate.

questions.question: An internal auditor at a Chinese commercial bank is validating the documentation of a model that measures transaction cost liquidity risk on the bank’s CNY equity book. The model follows the standard zero-mean normal approach to the bid-ask spread. Which of the following statements in the documentation is most accurate?

options.text: Daily changes in the relative spread are assumed to have a positive mean, since spreads tend to widen over time, so $\bar{\text{s}}$ is set above the latest observed spread.
The volatility $\sigma_{\text{s}}$ is estimated as the sample standard deviation of daily midprice returns of the asset, since price risk is what drives the spread.
The zero-mean assumption is justified because the relative spread of a liquid asset stays constant from one trading day to the next.
The expected relative spread $\bar{\text{s}}$ and the next-day midprice $\bar{\text{P}}$ are both typically set equal to their most recently observed values.

questions.solution:
Chinese bank audit: which statement about the zero-mean normal spread model is most accurate.

**Concept and theory**

The transaction cost measure rests on an explicit distributional hypothesis about the future bid-ask spread. GARP sets it out as follows:

- The variable modelled is the relative spread, the spread as a fraction of price.
- Its daily changes are assumed, as a starting point, to be normally distributed with a mean of zero and a constant variance, estimated by the sample variance of the spread, $\sigma^{2}_{\text{s}}$.
- The zero-mean assumption is described as unobjectionable because bid-ask spreads cannot rise indefinitely or shrink to zero. Spreads are bounded and fluctuate around a typical level, so there is no reason to forecast a systematic drift.
- Given a zero-mean change, today’s spread is the best estimate of tomorrow’s: GARP sets $\bar{\text{s}}$ = s, the most recent observation of the relative spread.
- The next-day midprice $\bar{\text{P}}$ is likewise typically set equal to P, the most recent observed price.

| Input | Estimate used | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Expected spread $\bar{\text{s}}$ Next-day midprice $\bar{\text{P}}$ | latest relative spread s latest midprice P | zero-mean daily changes typical convention |
| Spread volatility $\sigma_{\text{s}}$ | sample std. dev. of the relative spread | constant variance |

The zero mean refers to the changes in the spread, not to the spread level. The level stays positive.

**Applying it to this question**

The auditor checks each statement against these assumptions. A gives the changes a positive mean. B estimates $\sigma_{\text{s}}$ from price returns rather than from the spread. C justifies zero mean by claiming the spread never moves. D sets both $\bar{\text{s}}$ and $\bar{\text{P}}$ to their latest observations, which is what GARP prescribes.

**Fragile fact.** It is the changes in the relative spread that are zero-mean normal, and $\sigma_{\text{s}}$ is spread volatility, not price volatility.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Calculate the expected transactions cost and the spread risk factor for a transaction and calculate the liquidity adjustment to VaR for a position to be liquidated over a number of trading days.

**GARP:** Chapter 2, Section 2.5, Transaction Cost Liquidity Risk. **Schweser:** Module 67.3, Transactions Cost. **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser states only that “daily changes in the bid-ask spread are normally distributed” and that the current midprice estimates the next-day midprice. The relative-spread framing, constant variance, zero-mean justification and $\bar{\text{s}}$ = s come from GARP. This is a difference in depth, not a conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-2 f, where it is Q4 of 10.

a.reason: (Polarity flip). The model assumes zero-mean daily changes in the relative spread, so $\bar{\text{s}}$ equals the latest spread, not a higher value. The statement would be correct only for a model with an upward drift in spreads, which the standard approach rejects.

b.reason: (Sibling swap). $\sigma_{\text{s}}$ is the volatility of the relative bid-ask spread. Price-return volatility belongs to the one-day position VaR used in the liquidity adjustment to VaR. The statement would be correct if it described the input to the one-day position VaR.

c.reason: (Absolute claim). Spreads fluctuate; that is the whole source of transaction cost liquidity risk. If the spread were constant, the cost would be predictable and $\sigma_{\text{s}}$ would be zero. GARP justifies zero mean by boundedness: spreads cannot rise indefinitely or shrink to zero. The statement would be correct only if it said spread changes have no systematic drift.

d.reason: GARP sets $\bar{\text{s}}$ equal to s, the most recent observation of the relative spread, and typically sets $\bar{\text{P}}$ equal to P, the most recent observed price. Statement D reproduces both conventions.

questions.question: A member of the board risk committee of a US broker-dealer reads that the firm reports, for each equity position, the quantity $\bar{\text{P}}$ $\times\frac{1}{2} (\bar{\text{s}}$ + 2.33 $\sigma_{\text{s}})$ per share as its transaction cost liquidity risk measure. Which of the following best describes what this quantity measures?

options.text: The worst-case bid-ask cost, at 99% confidence, of changing the position, corresponding to the 99th percentile of proportional daily changes in the half-spread.
The worst-case loss, at 99% confidence, from the firm’s own sales moving the equilibrium price while the position is liquidated over several days.
The worst-case round-trip cost, at 99% confidence, of both buying the position at the ask and selling it at the bid on the same trading day.
The maximum bid-ask cost the firm can ever incur on the position, because under normality the spread cannot exceed $\bar{\text{s}}$ + 2.33 $\sigma_{\text{s}}$.

questions.solution:
US broker-dealer board: what $\bar{\text{P}}$ $\cdot\frac{1}{2} (\bar{\text{s}}$ + 2.33$\sigma_{\text{s}})$ per share measures.

**Concept and theory**

GARP distinguishes two quantitative measures of transactions liquidity risk, and they answer different questions.

Transaction cost liquidity risk concerns the bid-ask spread. The cost of changing a position is half the spread, and the spread itself varies. Under the zero-mean normal hypothesis, GARP measures the transactions cost risk at 99% confidence by the current value of the spread risk factor, $\frac{1}{2} (\bar{\text{s}}$ + 2.33$\sigma_{\text{s}})$. GARP equates this with the 99th percentile of the actual proportional daily changes in the half-spread over a historical period, say the past two years. In GARP’s words it represents the worst case, at a 99 percent confidence level, of the bid-ask spread cost of changing a position. Multiplied by $\bar{\text{P}}$, it is a currency amount per unit.

Adverse price impact is a different risk: the trader’s own selling moves the equilibrium price. Its tool is the liquidity-adjusted VaR, which scales the one-day position VaR for a liquidation spread over T days.

| Measure | Risk captured | Key input |
|---|---|---|
| $\bar{\text{P}}$ $\cdot\frac{1}{2} (\bar{\text{s}}$ + 2.33$\sigma_{\text{s}})$ | bid-ask cost of a one-way trade | spread volatility $\sigma_{\text{s}}$ |
| $\text{VaR}_{1}\sqrt{(1 + \text{T})(1 + \text{2T})\text{/}(\text{6T})}$ | price risk during liquidation | days to liquidate T |
| P $\bar{\text{s}}$ | round-trip cost (tightness) | quoted spread |

A confidence level is not a ceiling: on about 1% of days the half-spread cost exceeds the 99% figure.

**Applying it to this question**

The quantity in the stem contains $\sigma_{\text{s}}$ and the 2.33 quantile, is halved, and has no T and no position VaR. So it is a one-way, spread-based, 99% percentile measure. Only option A describes that.

**Fragile fact.** The spread risk factor is a one-way, 99% (not worst-ever) bid-ask cost measure. Adverse price impact belongs to LVaR.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Calculate the expected transactions cost and the spread risk factor for a transaction and calculate the liquidity adjustment to VaR for a position to be liquidated over a number of trading days.

**GARP:** Chapter 2, Section 2.5, Transaction Cost Liquidity Risk; Measuring the Risk of Adverse Price Impact. **Schweser:** Module 67.3, Transactions Cost; Adjusting VaR for Position Liquidity. **GARP vs Schweser:** the historical 99th-percentile reading and the “worst case of the bid-ask spread cost of changing a position” wording are GARP-only. Schweser gives the formula without the interpretation. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-2 f, where it is Q5 of 10.

a.reason: GARP says the spread risk factor is the 99th percentile of proportional daily changes in the half-spread and represents the worst case, at 99% confidence, of the bid-ask cost of changing a position. That is option A.

b.reason: (Sibling swap). Losses from the firm’s own sales moving the equilibrium price over a multi-day liquidation are adverse price impact, measured by the liquidity-adjusted VaR. This option would be correct if the stem’s quantity were $\text{VaR}_{1}\sqrt{(1 + \text{T})(1 + \text{2T})\text{/}(\text{6T})}$.

c.reason: (Scope error). The one-half makes the measure one-way: selling at the bid, or buying at the ask, relative to the mid. A round trip would use the full stressed spread, $\bar{\text{P}}$($\bar{\text{s}}$ + 2.33$\sigma_{\text{s}})$. This option would be correct if the formula had no one-half.

d.reason: (Absolute claim). A 99% normal quantile is a statistical bound, not a maximum. The normal distribution is unbounded, and the cost is exceeded on about 1% of days. This option would be correct if “maximum” were replaced by “99th percentile”.

questions.question:
A junior risk analyst at a Canadian pension plan is computing the liquidity-adjusted VaR of a concentrated equity position. Policy allows the plan to sell no more than 25% of the stock’s average daily trading volume per day, in equal daily amounts sold at each day’s close, to avoid adverse price impact.

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Shares held | 3,500,000 |
| Average daily trading volume (shares) | 2,000,000 |
| One-day 99% position VaR (CAD million) | 4.2 |
| Relative bid-ask spread | 0.0042 |

The liquidity-adjusted VaR of the position is closest to:

options.text: CAD 4.20 million
CAD 4.56 million
CAD 7.10 million
CAD 11.11 million

questions.solution:
Canadian pension plan: LVaR of 3.5 million shares sold at 25% of 2.0 million daily volume, one-day VaR CAD 4.2 million.

**Concept and theory**

Liquidity-adjusted VaR (LVaR) measures the risk of adverse price impact. A large position cannot be dumped in one day without moving the price, so the trader spreads the sale over T trading days. GARP’s first step is to estimate T. Estimates of the time to liquidate, or “time to escape”, are usually based on comparing the position size with the daily transactions volume. A participation limit such as “no more than 25% of daily volume” turns that comparison into a number of days.

If the position is sold in equal parts at the end of each day, the trader holds the whole position for one day, $(\text{T} -$ 1)/T of it for a second day, $(\text{T} -$ 2)/T for a third, and so on. Scaling the one-day VaR by $\sqrt{\text{T}}$ would assume the whole position is held for T days, which overstates the risk. Accounting for the shrinking position gives:

LVaR $= \text{VaR}_{1} \times\sqrt{\frac{(1 + \text{T})(1 + \text{2T})}{\text{6T}}}$,

where $\text{VaR}_{1}$ is the one-day position VaR and T is the number of trading days needed for an orderly liquidation. The multiplier depends only on T. The bid-ask spread does not enter, because LVaR measures price risk during the liquidation, not the dealer’s spread.

**Applying it to this question**

Maximum daily sale = 0.25 × 2,000,000 = 500,000 shares

T = 3,500,000/500,000 = 7 days

(1 $+ \text{T})($1 + 2T) = 8 × 15 = 120, 6T = 42

Ratio = 120/42 = 2.857143

Multiplier $= \sqrt{2.857143} =$ 1.690309

LVaR = 4.2 × 1.690309 = CAD 7.0993 million

The relative spread of 0.0042 is irrelevant: it feeds the transaction cost measure, not the liquidity adjustment to VaR. The LVaR of about CAD 7.10 million is 69% above the one-day VaR but well below the square-root-of-time figure.

**Fragile fact.** Derive T from the participation limit, not the full daily volume. The multiplier for T = 7 is 1.69, not $\sqrt{7} =$ 2.65.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Calculate the expected transactions cost and the spread risk factor for a transaction and calculate the liquidity adjustment to VaR for a position to be liquidated over a number of trading days.

**GARP:** Chapter 2, Section 2.5, Measuring the Risk of Adverse Price Impact. **Schweser:** Module 67.3, Adjusting VaR for Position Liquidity. **GARP vs Schweser:** estimating T from position size against daily transactions volume is GARP-only. Schweser says only that an estimate of the number of days is required. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-2 f, where it is Q6 of 10.

a.reason: (Intermediate result). CAD 4.20 million is the unadjusted one-day position VaR, the input to the calculation. It would be correct only if the position could be sold in one day (T = 1, multiplier 1).

b.reason: (Wrong input twin). CAD 4.56 million uses the full daily volume instead of the 25% limit: T = 3.5/2.0 = 1.75, multiplier $\sqrt{2.75 \times\text{4.5/10.5}} =$ 1.0856, and 4.2 × 1.0856 = 4.56. It would be correct if policy allowed selling 100% of daily volume each day.

c.reason: With T = 7 from the participation limit, GARP’s adjustment gives CAD 7.10 million, option C.

d.reason: (Time-conversion slip). CAD 11.11 million = 4.2 $\times\sqrt{7} =$ 4.2 × 2.6458 applies the square-root-of-time rule, which assumes the whole position is held for all seven days. It would be correct if no shares could be sold until the end of day 7.

questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a German insurer is presenting to newly hired analysts on adjusting VaR for a EUR position that will be liquidated in equal parts at the end of each of T > 1 trading days. The draft slide contains these statements:

I. The trader faces a one-day holding period on the entire position and a two-day holding period on a fraction $(\text{T} -$ 1)/T of the position.

II. Scaling the one-day position VaR by $\sqrt{\text{T}}$ understates the VaR of this position, because it ignores the extra days for which the unsold part is held.

III. The liquidity-adjusted VaR exceeds the one-day position VaR but is less than the one-day position VaR multiplied by $\sqrt{\text{T}}$.

IV. For a given T, the liquidity adjustment multiplier is larger for a position with a higher one-day VaR.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.text: I only
I, II and III
I, III and IV
I and III only

questions.solution:
German insurer training slide: four statements on the equal-parts liquidation schedule and LVaR bounds.

**Concept and theory**

GARP builds the liquidity adjustment from a simple liquidation schedule. The position is sold in equal parts at the end of each of T trading days, so the amount still held shrinks linearly:

| Day of exposure | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Fraction held (T = 4) | 1 | 3/4 | 1/2 | 1/4 |

So the trader has a one-day holding period on the entire position, a two-day holding period on $(\text{T} -$ 1)/T of it, a three-day holding period on $(\text{T} -$ 2)/T, and so on.

Suppose instead that the entire position were held for T days. The square-root-of-time rule gives $\text{VaR}_{1}\sqrt{\text{T}}$. GARP calls this an overstatement, because the trader actually holds the sequence 1, $\frac{\text{T}-1}{\text{T}}$ , $\frac{\text{T}-2}{\text{T}}$ , . . . , $\frac{1}{\text{T}}$ rather than 1, 1, . . . , 1. The true figure therefore lies strictly between two bounds:

$\text{VaR}_{1} < \text{LVaR} = \text{VaR}_{1}\sqrt{\frac{(1 + \text{T})(1 + \text{2T})}{\text{6T}}} < \text{VaR}_{1}\sqrt{\text{T}} (\text{T} >$ 1).

It exceeds the one-day VaR because part of the position is exposed for more than one day. It is below the square-root-of-time figure because the exposure shrinks. The multiplier contains only T, so the one-day VaR scales the result but never changes the percentage adjustment.

**Applying it to this question**

I matches GARP’s schedule: true. II reverses the direction: the square-root-of-time rule overstates the VaR. False. III restates GARP’s bounds: true. IV is false, because for fixed T the multiplier is the same for every position. The correct set is I and III.

**Fragile fact.** The square-root-of-time rule overstates VaR for a gradual liquidation, and the multiplier depends on T alone.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Calculate the expected transactions cost and the spread risk factor for a transaction and calculate the liquidity adjustment to VaR for a position to be liquidated over a number of trading days.

**GARP:** Chapter 2, Section 2.5, Measuring the Risk of Adverse Price Impact. **Schweser:** Module 67.3, Adjusting VaR for Position Liquidity (and the Professor’s Note on square-root-of-time overstatement). **GARP vs Schweser:** none.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-2 f, where it is Q7 of 10.

a.reason: (Condition error). “I only” rejects III, which is true. It would be correct only if the bounds failed, for instance at T = 1, where LVaR equals the one-day VaR and the inequality is not strict.

b.reason: (Polarity flip). This option accepts II, which says the square-root-of-time rule understates the VaR. GARP says it overstates, because it assumes the whole position is held for T days. It would be correct if II said “overstates”.

c.reason: (Scope error). This option accepts IV. The multiplier $\sqrt{(1 + \text{T})(1 + \text{2T})\text{/}(\text{6T})}$ depends only on T, so a riskier position has a larger LVaR in currency but the same multiplier. It would be correct if IV said “larger liquidity-adjusted VaR” rather than “larger multiplier”.

d.reason: GARP says the trader faces a one-day holding period on the entire position and a two-day holding period on $(\text{T} -$ 1)/T (I). It also says the VaR must lie above the one-day position VaR but below the one-day position VaR times $\sqrt{\text{T}}$ (III). So the answer is I and III only, option D.
