questions.question: A risk consultant validating the liquidity-adjusted VaR model of an Australian superannuation fund rebuilds the adjustment from first principles for one position. The position has a one-day 99% VaR of AUD 2.5 million and will be sold in three equal parts at the end of each of the next three trading days, so the fund holds position sizes of 1, $\frac{2}{3}$ and $\frac{1}{3}$ of the original over successive days. Daily returns are i.i.d. with the same variance. The liquidity-adjusted VaR is closest to:

options.text: AUD 3.12 million
AUD 3.54 million
AUD 3.89 million
AUD 4.33 million

questions.solution:
Australian superannuation fund: rebuild LVaR for T = 3 from position sizes 1, 2/3, 1/3 with one-day VaR AUD 2.5 million.

**Concept and theory**

GARP derives the liquidity adjustment from the shrinking sequence of position sizes. Let daily returns be i.i.d. with variance $\sigma^{2}$, and let the trader hold fraction $\text{w}_{\text{k}}$ of the original position on day k. The P&L over the liquidation is $\sum_{\text{k}} \text{w}_{\text{k}}\text{r}_{\text{k}}$. Since the daily returns are independent, variances add, and each day’s variance scales with the square of the position held:

Var $\left( \sum_{\text{k}} \text{w}_{\text{k}}\text{r}_{\text{k}}\right) = \sigma^{2} \sum_{\text{k}} \text{w}^{2}_{\text{k}}$.

VaR is proportional to the standard deviation, so the one-day VaR is scaled by the square root of the sum of squared position sizes. With equal daily sales, the sizes are 1, $\frac{\text{T}-1}{\text{T}}$ , . . . , $\frac{1}{\text{T}}$ , that is k/T for k = 1, . . . , T:

$\sum_{\text{k}=1}^{\text{T}} \left( \frac{\text{k}}{\text{T}} \right)^{2} = \frac{\text{T}(\text{T} + 1)(\text{2T} + 1)}{\text{6T}^{2}} = \frac{(1 + \text{T})(1 + \text{2T})}{\text{6T}}$ , LVaR $= \text{VaR}_{1}\sqrt{\frac{(1 + \text{T})(1 + \text{2T})}{\text{6T}}}$.

If every weight were 1 (whole position held for T days), the sum would be T and we would recover the square-root-of-time rule. The shrinking weights are why the LVaR multiplier is smaller than $\sqrt{\text{T}}$. Rebuilding the factor this way is a useful validation check because it tests the model’s two key assumptions: equal sales at each close, and independent returns with constant variance.

**Applying it to this question**

$\sum^{2}_{\text{w}_{\text{k}}} =^{2}_{1} +_{(} \frac{2}{3}^{2}_{)} +_{(} \frac{1}{3}^{2}_{)} =_{1} +_{0.4444} +_{0.1111} =_{1.5556}$

Check: $\frac{(1 + 3)(1 + 6)}{18} = \frac{28}{18} =$ 1.5556

Multiplier $= \sqrt{1.5556} =$ 1.2472

LVaR = 2.5 × 1.2472 = AUD 3.118 million

The first-principles sum and the closed form agree. A three-day equal liquidation raises VaR by about 25%.

**Fragile fact.** Variance scales with the square of the position held, and VaR scales with the square root of that sum.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Calculate the expected transactions cost and the spread risk factor for a transaction and calculate the liquidity adjustment to VaR for a position to be liquidated over a number of trading days.

**GARP:** Chapter 2, Section 2.5, Measuring the Risk of Adverse Price Impact. **Schweser:** Module 67.3, Adjusting VaR for Position Liquidity. **GARP vs Schweser:** GARP shows the sum over the position sequence (“all with the same variance”) simplifying to (1 $+ \text{T})($1 + 2T)/(6T). questions.source: High quality paper LTR-2 f Q9
questions.question:
The CRO of a Brazilian bank asks how much extra bid-ask cost, at 99% confidence, the bank should budget for above the expected transactions cost when selling a block of shares tomorrow. Daily changes in the relative spread are zero-mean normal.

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Shares to be sold | 1,500,000 |
| Bid price (BRL) | 24.80 |
| Ask price (BRL) | 25.20 |
| Sample standard deviation of the relative spread, $\sigma_{\text{s}}$ | 0.0040 |
| One-day 99% position VaR (BRL million) | 3.1 |

The amount by which the 99% transactions cost exceeds the expected transactions cost is closest to:
questions.solution:
Brazilian bank CRO: 99% transactions cost minus expected cost on 1.5 million shares, bid BRL 24.80, ask BRL 25.20, $\sigma_{\text{s}} =$ 0.0040.

**Concept and theory**

The 99% transactions cost splits into a predictable part and a risk part:

$$\underbrace{\bar{\text{P}} \cdot \tfrac{1}{2}(\bar{\text{s}} + 2.33\,\sigma_{\text{s}})}_{\text{99\% cost}} = \underbrace{\bar{\text{P}} \cdot \tfrac{1}{2}\,\bar{\text{s}}}_{\text{expected cost}} + \underbrace{\bar{\text{P}} \cdot \tfrac{1}{2}(2.33\,\sigma_{\text{s}})}_{\text{spread risk add-on}}, \qquad \bar{\text{P}} = \text{P}.$$

The expected cost is the half-spread the bank should plan to pay anyway. The add-on is the extra bid-ask cost that could arise if tomorrow’s spread widens to its 99th percentile under the zero-mean normal hypothesis for daily changes in the relative spread. This add-on is the transaction cost risk. It is what a budget for adverse spread moves needs to cover, beyond the expected cost. Because the one-half applies to the whole bracket, it applies to the add-on too: a one-way sale pays half of any widening in the spread. The add-on depends only on $\bar{\text{P}}$, $\sigma_{\text{s}}$ and the quantile, not on today’s spread level. A stock with a wide but stable spread can have a high expected cost and a small add-on.

The one-day position VaR is a separate measure of market and price-impact risk. It plays no part in the bid-ask spread calculation.

**Applying it to this question**

P = (24.80 + 25.20)/2 = 25.00, s = 0.40/25.00 = 0.0160

2.33 $\sigma_{\text{s}} =$ 2.33 × 0.0040 = 0.00932

Add-on per share = 25.00 $\times\frac{1}{2} \times$ 0.00932 = BRL 0.1165

Add-on for position = 0.1165 × 1,500,000 = BRL 174,750

Check: 99% cost $- \text{expected} =$ 474,750 − 300,000 = BRL 174,750

The one-day VaR of BRL 3.1 million is irrelevant: it is not an input to the transactions cost measure.

**Fragile fact.** The risk add-on is $\bar{\text{P}}$ $\cdot\frac{1}{2} \cdot$ 2.33$\sigma_{\text{s}}$: halved, and independent of the current spread level.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Calculate the expected transactions cost and the spread risk factor for a transaction and calculate the liquidity adjustment to VaR for a position to be liquidated over a number of trading days.

**GARP:** Chapter 2, Section 2.5, Transaction Cost Liquidity Risk. **Schweser:** Module 67.3, Transactions Cost. **GARP vs Schweser:** none.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-2 f, where it is Q9 of 10.

a.reason: (Wrong percentile). BRL 123,375 = 25.00 $\times\frac{1}{2} \times$ 1.645 × 0.0040 × 1,500,000 uses the 95% quantile. It would be correct for a 95% budget.

b.reason: The excess of $\bar{\text{P}}$ $\cdot\frac{1}{2} (\bar{\text{s}}$ + 2.33$\sigma_{\text{s}})$ over P$\bar{\text{s}}$/2 is $\bar{\text{P}}$ $\cdot\frac{1}{2} ($2.33$\sigma_{\text{s}})$ per share, BRL 174,750 for the block, option B.

c.reason: (Dropped term). BRL 349,500 = 25.00 × 2.33 × 0.0040 × 1,500,000 forgets to halve the add-on. It would be correct for the extra cost of a round trip, where the full widening is paid.

d.reason: (Intermediate result). BRL 474,750 = 25.00 $\times\frac{1}{2} ($0.0160 + 0.00932) × 1,500,000 is the full 99% transactions cost, which still includes the BRL 300,000 expected cost. It would be correct if the stem asked for the total 99% cost.

questions.question: A regulator reviewing the liquidity risk report of a USD hedge fund checks the fund’s description of its liquidity-adjusted VaR, which assumes each position is liquidated in equal parts at the end of each of T trading days. Which of the following statements in the report is NOT correct?

options.text: Because each slice is sold at the end of a trading day, the liquidity adjustments to VaR are typically small compared with the transaction cost liquidity risk measures.
The liquidation horizon T is usually estimated by comparing the size of the position with the daily transactions volume in the asset.
For a position that needs ten trading days to liquidate, the adjustment roughly doubles the overnight VaR of the position.
The adjustment multiplier depends only on T, so two positions with the same T receive the same percentage increase in VaR.

questions.solution:
USD hedge fund report: which statement about T and the size of the LVaR adjustment is NOT correct.

**Concept and theory**

Two practical points complete GARP’s treatment of the liquidity adjustment to VaR.

Where T comes from. The adjustment needs the number of trading days T required for an orderly liquidation. GARP notes that estimates of the time to liquidate, or “time to escape”, are usually based on comparing the position size with the daily transactions volume. A position that is large relative to daily volume needs more days.

How big the adjustment is. Because the multiplier $\sqrt{(1 + \text{T})(1 + \text{2T})\text{/}(\text{6T})}$ contains only T, it can be tabulated once and applied to any position:

| T | Multiplier | $\sqrt{\text{T}}$ | Increase in VaR |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | 1.1180 | 1.4142 | 12% |
| 4 | 1.3693 | 2.0000 | 37% |
| 5 | 1.4832 | 2.2361 | 48% |
| 10 | 1.9621 | 3.1623 | 96% (roughly doubles) |

GARP’s examples: for T = 5 the overnight VaR rises by 48%, and for T = 10 the adjustment doubles the overnight VaR. GARP then stresses that these adjustments are large by comparison with the transaction cost liquidity risk measures of the previous section. A spread risk factor is typically a fraction of 1% of the position value, whereas the LVaR adjustment adds tens of percent to VaR. For a large position, the risk of adverse price impact usually dominates the risk of spread variation.

**Applying it to this question**

B (time to escape from size against volume), C (T = 10 roughly doubles VaR) and D (the multiplier depends only on T) are all consistent with GARP. A says the adjustments are small relative to the transaction cost measures, the reverse of GARP’s comparison. Its stated reason (end-of-day sales) is simply the liquidation assumption, and it does not make the adjustment small.

**Fragile fact.** LVaR adjustments are large relative to transaction cost measures, and T comes from position size compared with daily volume.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Calculate the expected transactions cost and the spread risk factor for a transaction and calculate the liquidity adjustment to VaR for a position to be liquidated over a number of trading days.

**GARP:** Chapter 2, Section 2.5, Measuring the Risk of Adverse Price Impact. **Schweser:** Module 67.3, Adjusting VaR for Position Liquidity (worked example T = 4: 1.3693, an increase of 37%). **GARP vs Schweser:** the time-to-escape estimate, the T = 5 and T = 10 examples and the magnitude comparison are GARP-only. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-2 f, where it is Q10 of 10.

a.reason: GARP says the liquidity adjustments to VaR “are large by comparison with the transaction cost liquidity risk measures”. Statement A says the opposite, so it is the statement that is NOT correct: option A.

b.reason: (Qualifier misread: true statement). GARP says estimates of the time to liquidate are usually based on comparing the position size with the daily transactions volume. Choosing B would be right only if the report had said T is estimated from the volatility of the bid-ask spread, which is a sibling swap with $\sigma_{\text{s}}$.

c.reason: (Qualifier misread: true statement). For T = 10, $\sqrt{11 \times\text{21/60}} = \sqrt{3.85} =$ 1.9621, which GARP describes as doubling the overnight VaR. Choosing C would be right only if the report had used $\sqrt{10} =$ 3.16, the square-root-of-time figure.

d.reason: (Qualifier misread: true statement). The multiplier $\sqrt{(1 + \text{T})(1 + \text{2T})\text{/}(\text{6T})}$ has no other input, so equal T gives an equal percentage increase. Choosing D would be right only if the statement had said that equal T gives equal LVaR in currency, which also depends on each position’s one-day VaR.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Evaluate the characteristics of sound Early Warning Indicators (EWI) measures.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-3 a Q1
questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a Japanese regional bank is presenting the automobile dashboard analogy for early warning indicators (EWIs) to newly hired analysts. She uses three recent events at the bank:

I. The retail division launched a JPY deposit special to raise rate-sensitive liabilities.

II. The bank’s Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) dropped below a specified internal threshold.

III. Call centre volumes rose dramatically over two days, for reasons not yet known.

Which of the following correctly maps each event to the dashboard light it is analogous to?

options.text: I: turn signal; II: check engine light; III: low oil light
I: turn signal; II: low oil light; III: check engine light
I: low oil light; II: turn signal; III: check engine light
I: check engine light; II: low oil light; III: turn signal

questions.solution:
Dashboard analogy: map a deposit special, an LCR threshold breach and a call-centre spike to the three dashboard lights.

**Concept and theory**

GARP opens the chapter with an analogy: EWIs are like the warning lights on an automobile dashboard. A driver does not read the engine’s internals directly; a small set of lights tells the driver when something needs attention and how urgently. In liquidity risk management (LRM), EWIs play the same role for bank leadership, which is responsible for identifying and managing the underlying liquidity risk factors. GARP uses three lights, and each carries a distinct meaning:

| Light | What it tells the driver | LRM example in GARP |
|---|---|---|
| Turn signal (“blinker”) | An intentional, risky activity: a purposeful change of direction | Running a deposit special to raise rate-sensitive liabilities |
| Low engine oil | Direct action may be needed in the near future to prevent the engine seizing up | The bank’s LCR has dropped below a specified threshold |
| Check engine | Further investigation is warranted for a reason not yet determined | A dramatic rise in call centre volumes that may portend a shift in liquidity |

The analogy exists to show that EWIs differ in nature and urgency. Some flag a deliberate business decision that treasury should know about; some flag a measurable deterioration that calls for action soon; some flag an anomaly whose cause must be investigated before anyone knows whether action is needed. Schweser expresses the same idea as signals that can vary in severity and priority, giving three possibilities: an urgent problem needing action now, a potential problem that may need future action, and a prompt for further analysis.

**Applying it to this question**

Event I is a decision taken on purpose by the retail division: a JPY deposit special to attract rate-sensitive money. That is a purposeful directional change, so it is the turn signal. Event II is a measured metric, the LCR, crossing a specified threshold; that is the low oil light, where direct action may be needed soon. Event III is an unexplained spike in call centre volumes; nobody yet knows the reason, so it is the check engine light, which calls for further investigation. The mapping is I turn signal, II low oil, III check engine.

**Fragile fact.** The turn signal is the intentional activity (deposit special), not a deterioration; low oil is the LCR below a threshold; check engine is the unexplained call centre spike.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Evaluate the characteristics of sound Early Warning Indicators (EWI) measures. **GARP:** Chapter 3, Section 3.1, “Introduction: Dashboard and Beyond”, subsection “Dashboard”. **Schweser:** LO 68.a, “EWI Characteristics”. **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser’s three possibilities (urgent action now, potential future action, further analysis) do not map one-to-one onto GARP’s lights; GARP’s turn signal is an intentional activity, not an urgent problem. GARP followed.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-3 a, where it is Q1 of 12.

a.reason: (Sibling swap). It swaps the low oil and check engine lights for events II and III. A threshold breach on a known metric such as the LCR is not a mystery to be investigated; its meaning is known and action may be needed soon. The call centre spike, whose cause is unknown, is the one needing investigation. A would be correct only if the stem described the LCR move as unexplained and the call centre spike as a known, measured deterioration.

b.reason: Option B reproduces GARP’s mapping exactly: the deposit special is GARP’s own turn signal example, the LCR falling below a threshold is its low oil example, and the dramatic increase in call centre volumes is its check engine example.

c.reason: (Sibling swap). It swaps the turn signal and low oil lights for events I and II. The deposit special is a deliberate business action, not a deterioration; treating it as low oil confuses an intentional risky activity with a warning that action is needed. C would be correct only if the stem described the deposit campaign as an unplanned outflow and the LCR change as a planned strategy.

d.reason: (Sibling swap). It swaps the turn signal and check engine lights for events I and III. A deliberate campaign is not an unexplained anomaly, and an unexplained call centre spike is not a purposeful directional change. D would be correct only if the deposit special had been launched without treasury’s knowledge for unknown reasons and the call centre surge had been planned.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Evaluate the characteristics of sound Early Warning Indicators (EWI) measures.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-3 a Q2
questions.question:
An internal auditor at an Australian mutual bank is reviewing the bank’s policy on early warning indicators. The policy contains the following statements:

I. EWIs are changes in key metrics, which may be qualitative or quantitative, and the signals they give can vary in severity and priority.

II. The most important use of an EWI trigger is to initiate management discussions and actions, and these should be formally documented.

III. An EWI signal requires management discussion only once the underlying metric has breached a regulatory minimum, such as an LCR of 100%.

IV. A trigger that simply confirms treasury is aware of a business line’s AUD deposit campaign, so that it can increase its high-quality liquid asset buffer cost-efficiently, is a valid use of an EWI.

Which of the statements are consistent with the reading?

options.text: I and II only
II and IV only
I, II and III only
I, II and IV only

questions.solution:
Internal audit of an EWI policy: nature of EWIs and the main objective of EWI triggers.

**Concept and theory**

An early warning indicator is not a risk measure in the sense of a number that captures how much could be lost. It is a change in a key metric that could signal a pending liquidity problem. Schweser stresses two features of that definition. First, EWIs can be qualitative or quantitative: GARP’s examples range from the LCR (a ratio) to negative publicity and call centre volumes (much softer signals), and the BCBS list it reproduces explicitly contains both kinds. Second, EWI signals vary in severity and priority, which is why the dashboard analogy uses different lights.

Why do EWIs exist at all? GARP is explicit: “most importantly”, EWI triggers are used to initiate management discussions and actions, and these should be formally documented. Schweser restates this as the main objective: to get management to acknowledge the situation and to promote the necessary dialogue and actions, together with documentation. The response does not have to be dramatic. GARP’s example is simply treasury acknowledging that a business line is running a deposit campaign, so that it can orchestrate a corrective action such as increasing the high-quality liquid asset buffer in a cost-efficient manner while continuing to comply with LCR requirements.

The word “early” matters. An EWI that only prompts discussion after a regulatory minimum has been breached is no longer early; by then the bank is reacting to an event rather than preparing for it. GARP’s low oil example is the LCR falling below a specified threshold set by the bank, which sits well before any regulatory floor.

**Applying it to this question**

Test each statement. I restates the Schweser definition (qualitative or quantitative; varying severity and priority): correct. II restates GARP’s “most importantly” sentence, including formal documentation: correct. III ties discussion to a regulatory breach; this reverses the purpose of an early warning and contradicts the idea that some signals call for further analysis or future action: incorrect. IV is GARP’s own deposit campaign example, where a simple acknowledgment lets treasury raise the liquid asset buffer cost-efficiently: correct. The correct set is I, II and IV.

**Fragile fact.** EWIs may be qualitative or quantitative; the key output of a trigger is documented management discussion and action, which can be as modest as an acknowledgment.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Evaluate the characteristics of sound Early Warning Indicators (EWI) measures. **GARP:** Chapter 3, Section 3.1, “Introduction: Dashboard and Beyond”, subsection “Dashboard”; Table 3.1 (qualitative and quantitative BCBS indicators). **Schweser:** LO 68.a, “EWI Characteristics”. **GARP vs Schweser:** none.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-3 a, where it is Q2 of 12.

a.reason: (Scope or condition error). It omits IV, treating a mere acknowledgment of a deposit campaign as too slight to count as a valid EWI use. GARP states that the response “could be as simple as” that acknowledgment. A would be correct only if statement IV said the trigger was ignored with no follow-up or documentation.

b.reason: (Absolute claim). It omits I, implicitly treating EWIs as purely quantitative signals of uniform urgency. Both Schweser and GARP state that EWIs can be qualitative or quantitative and that signals vary in severity and priority. B would be correct only if statement I claimed that all EWIs must be quantitative and of equal priority.

c.reason: (Polarity flip). It includes III, which moves the trigger from before a problem to after a regulatory breach and drops IV. An EWI’s purpose is advance warning, so discussion is due when the signal fires, not when the minimum is breached. C would be correct only if III said that discussion should begin when an internal threshold set above the regulatory minimum is crossed, and IV were false.

d.reason: Option D contains exactly the three statements that match the source: the definition (I), the documented discussion and action objective (II), and GARP’s acknowledgment example (IV), while excluding the late-trigger statement (III).

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Evaluate the characteristics of sound Early Warning Indicators (EWI) measures.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-3 a Q3
questions.question: A supervisor at a U.K. regulator is reviewing the draft EWI measures of a GBP 40 billion retail bank. The draft contains only: the month-end LCR as reported, the month-end loan-to-deposit ratio, and month-end deposit balances by product. All three are calculated under business-as-usual conditions, and the bank has GBP 6 billion of undrawn committed credit facilities to corporate clients. Which feedback is most consistent with the hallmarks of sound EWI measures set out in BCBS Principle 5?

options.text: Add metrics that project cash flows and future liquidity positions, take account of off-balance sheet risks such as the committed facilities, and cover stressed as well as normal conditions over several horizons.
Replace the balance sheet structure metrics with projected cash flow metrics, because Principle 5 treats the structure of the balance sheet as backward looking and outside the scope of EWIs.
Add metrics derived only from external market prices, because Principle 5 defines a forward-looking metric as one that is implied by market prices rather than by the bank’s own data.
Add the off-balance sheet committed facilities, but keep a single month-end horizon for every measure, because a common horizon keeps the measures comparable across the balance sheet.

questions.solution:
Supervisory feedback on a month-end, business-as-usual EWI draft against BCBS Principle 5.

**Concept and theory**

Within the M.E.R.I.T. framework, “M” (measures) is the first building block. GARP grounds the hallmarks of sound measures in Principle 5 of the BCBS “Sound Principles” (2008). The principle says that, to obtain a forward-looking view of liquidity risk exposures, a bank should use metrics that assess:

(a) the structure of the balance sheet, as well as metrics that

(b) project cash flows and future liquidity positions, taking into account

(c) off-balance sheet risks.

GARP adds that these measures should span vulnerabilities across business-as-usual and stressed conditions over various time horizons. Schweser condenses the same points: a future-oriented perspective, both balance sheet and off-balance sheet items, normal and stressed states, several time periods, and an ultimate ability to forecast future cash flows and liquidity positions.

The logic is that liquidity crises are about future cash: whether the bank can meet outflows that have not happened yet. A snapshot of today’s ratios says something about the starting point, which is why balance sheet structure stays in the list, but it does not show how fast cash could leave. Off-balance sheet items matter because committed facilities, derivatives and similar contingent claims can turn into cash outflows precisely when stress arrives. Stressed conditions matter because the buffer has to be adequate in stress, not only in calm markets, and several horizons matter because the bank’s assets and liabilities run off at different speeds.

**Applying it to this question**

The draft has three month-end, business-as-usual metrics: all describe the current balance sheet structure. It lacks (b) projected cash flows and future liquidity positions, (c) off-balance sheet risks (the GBP 6 billion of undrawn committed facilities is exactly such a risk), stressed conditions and multiple horizons. Feedback A adds all four missing elements while keeping the structure metrics. The GBP 40 billion balance sheet size is context only; it does not change the assessment.

**Fragile fact.** Principle 5 has three parts: balance sheet structure and projected cash flows and off-balance sheet risks; GARP adds normal plus stressed conditions over various horizons.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Evaluate the characteristics of sound Early Warning Indicators (EWI) measures. **GARP:** Chapter 3, “Risk Identification and EWIs Framework Components: M.E.R.I.T.”, subsection “Measures” (quoting BCBS Principle 5). **Schweser:** LO 68.a, “Measures”. **GARP vs Schweser:** none; Schweser paraphrases Principle 5 without the (a) to (c) labels.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-3 a, where it is Q3 of 12.

a.reason: Option A asks for the elements that Principle 5 and GARP’s extension require: cash flow and future liquidity projections, off-balance sheet risks, and coverage of business-as-usual and stressed conditions over various horizons.

b.reason: (Scope or condition error). It drops element (a). Principle 5 explicitly includes metrics that assess the structure of the balance sheet alongside projected cash flows; it does not label them backward looking or exclude them. B would be correct only if the principle listed cash flow projections as the sole required metric.

c.reason: (Sibling swap). It confuses forward looking with market implied, borrowing a property of external measures. Principle 5’s forward-looking metrics are the bank’s own projections of cash flows and liquidity positions; GARP separately asks for a balance of internal and external measures. C would be correct only if the question asked how to add external measures to an internal-only suite.

d.reason: (Scope or condition error). It adds the off-balance sheet element but keeps a single month-end horizon and business-as-usual only. GARP requires the measures to span business-as-usual and stressed conditions over various time horizons. D would be correct only if the stem already contained stressed and multi-horizon measures and lacked only the committed facilities.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Evaluate the characteristics of sound Early Warning Indicators (EWI) measures.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-3 a Q4
questions.question:
A risk consultant is advising a Brazilian commercial bank on the balance between internal and external measures in its EWI suite. The bank currently funds itself in BRL through retail and wholesale deposits. The consultant drafts the following statements:

I. Internal measures are customised to the bank’s balance sheet and activities, while external measures signal systemic changes in the economy or the market.

II. Because liquidity events originate within the bank, external measures add little once the internal measures are sufficiently sharp.

III. An idiosyncratic deposit run may result either from the disclosure of poor performance or from a systemic failure.

IV. A sovereign default may cause liquidity dislocations in parts of the financial market and disrupt the funding of any institution exposed to those markets.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.text: I and III only
I, II and III only
I, III and IV only
III and IV only

questions.solution:
Advice to a Brazilian bank on balancing internal and external EWI measures.

**Concept and theory**

GARP states that a prudent suite of EWIs includes both internal and external metrics, and that banks should strike a balance between them. The two kinds differ in what they look at:

|  | Internal measures | External measures |
|---|---|---|
| Focus | Customised to the bank’s own balance sheet and activities | Signal systemic changes in the economy or market |
| Schweser wording | Focus on the bank’s balance sheet | Look at macroeconomic factors |
| Typical role | Catch idiosyncratic stress early, before it is public | Catch environment-driven stress that can hit any exposed bank |

The reason for needing both is that liquidity events can start either within the bank or be driven by the environment in which it operates. GARP gives an example that cuts across the two: an idiosyncratic deposit run may result from the disclosure of poor performance (an internal origin) or from a systemic failure (an external origin). It also gives a purely external example: a systemic crisis such as a sovereign default or a banking system crisis may trigger liquidity dislocations in parts of the financial market, disrupting the funding of any institution exposed to those markets. A bank that watched only its own metrics would see such a crisis only once it reached its balance sheet, by which time the warning is late. GARP’s figure on EWI dimensions makes the same point by placing indicators inside and outside the bank.

**Applying it to this question**

I is GARP’s definition of the two kinds of measure: correct. II argues that external measures can be dropped because events start inside the bank; GARP says events can start inside the bank or be influenced by external elements: incorrect. III is GARP’s deposit run example with its two possible causes: correct. IV is GARP’s systemic crisis example: correct. The correct set is I, III and IV.

**Fragile fact.** Liquidity events can start inside or outside the bank; that is why GARP wants a balance of internal and external measures, not a preference for either.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Evaluate the characteristics of sound Early Warning Indicators (EWI) measures. **GARP:** Chapter 3, “Measures”, subsection “Forward Looking Bias/View” (heading partly garbled in the extraction) and Figure 3.2 “Early warning indicator dimensions”. **Schweser:** LO 68.a, “Measures”. **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser describes external measures as macroeconomic; GARP’s wider wording is systemic changes in the economy or market. GARP followed.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-3 a, where it is Q4 of 12.

a.reason: (Scope or condition error). It omits IV, which is GARP’s own example of an externally driven event (sovereign default) disrupting funding. A would be correct only if IV claimed that a sovereign default affects only the sovereign’s own debt and never institutions’ funding.

b.reason: (Scope or condition error). It includes II, which narrows the origin of liquidity events to the bank itself, and omits IV. GARP stresses that events can start inside or outside the bank and that a balance of internal and external measures is required. B would be correct only if II said that internal measures should be sharp in addition to a set of external measures, and IV were false.

c.reason: Option C contains the definition of the two measure types (I) and both of GARP’s examples of how liquidity events can originate (III and IV), and excludes the claim that external measures add little (II).

d.reason: (Sibling swap). It omits I, rejecting the definitions of internal and external measures. The definitions are GARP’s: internal measures are tailored to the bank’s balance sheet and activities, external measures signal systemic changes. D would be correct only if statement I swapped the two definitions (for example, internal measures signal systemic changes).
