questions.question:
The CRO of a Chinese bank active in CNY large-value payment systems is reviewing a junior analyst’s summary of the BCBS (2012) guideline on intraday liquidity monitoring indicators. The summary states that the indicators include:

I. Daily maximum liquidity and available intraday liquidity.

II. The value of customer payments made on behalf of financial institution customers, and intraday credit lines extended to financial institution customers.

III. A decrease in the weighted average maturity of liabilities and increases in currency mismatches.

IV. The timing of intraday payments and intraday throughput.

Which parts of the summary are accurate?

options.text: I and II only
I, II, and IV only
II and III only
I, II, III, and IV

questions.solution:
CRO of a Chinese bank audits a junior analyst’s summary of the BCBS (2012) intraday indicators.

**Concept and theory**

BCBS (2012) gives supervisors and banks a common vocabulary for intraday liquidity. The logic follows the stages of a payment day:

(i) Need: how much liquidity the bank requires at the worst point of the day (daily maximum liquidity).

(ii) Resources: how much it can draw on within the day (available intraday liquidity).

(iii) Flows: total payments, the timing of intraday payments, and intraday throughput (how much of the day’s payments have settled by given times).

(iv) Obligations: time-specific and other critical obligations that cannot slip.

(v) Role as a provider to other banks: the value of customer payments made on behalf of financial institution customers, and intraday credit lines extended to financial institution customers.

Group (v) recognises that a bank serving other financial institutions is exposed to their payment flows and to the intraday credit it grants them.

These indicators are separate from the BCBS (2008) Sound Principles list. That list deals with structural vulnerabilities such as currency mismatches, concentrations, and the maturity profile of liabilities.

**Applying it to this question**

Statement I (daily maximum liquidity, available intraday liquidity) and Statement II (customer payments for FI customers, intraday credit lines to FI customers) are on the BCBS-2012 list.

Statement IV (timing of intraday payments, intraday throughput) is also on GARP’s BCBS-2012 list. Statement III (decreasing WAM of liabilities, rising currency mismatches) belongs to the BCBS (2008) list. The accurate parts are I, II and IV.

**Fragile fact.** Same committee, different years: structural items such as WAM and currency mismatches are 2008; daily maximum liquidity, throughput and timing are 2012 (intraday).

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 68.b, verbatim):** Identify EWI guidelines from banking regulators and supervisors (OCC, BCBS, Federal Reserve).

**GARP:** Chapter 3, “Key Supervisory Guidelines”, Table 3.2, BCBS-2012 column and source note 4 (“Monitoring Indicators for Intraday Liquidity”, 2012). **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser gives six items and omits intraday throughput; it merges timing into “total intraday payments, including their timing”. GARP is used here, so Statement IV rests partly on GARP-only content. Garbled-source caution: the BCBS-2012 column is interleaved in the extracted text; the reconstruction of “Timing of intraday payments” and “Intraday throughput” was checked against the column layout.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-3 b, where it is Q8 of 11.

a.reason: (Scope or condition error (incomplete list)). A rejects Statement IV. A reader who relies only on the condensed Schweser list might do this, since it has no throughput and folds timing into total payments. GARP’s Table 3.2 lists both timing of intraday payments and intraday throughput as BCBS (2012) indicators. A would be correct if Statement IV named items from another guideline, for example widening CDS spreads.

b.reason: B is correct because GARP’s Table 3.2 lists, under BCBS (2012), every item in Statements I, II and IV, while the items in Statement III are BCBS (2008) EWIs.

c.reason: (Sibling swap). C accepts Statement III, attaching the BCBS (2008) structural indicators (WAM of liabilities, currency mismatches) to the 2012 intraday document, and rejects the genuine Statements I and IV. C would be correct only if the question asked about BCBS (2008) and Statement I were false.

d.reason: (Sibling swap (overinclusion)). D accepts all four statements, including the BCBS (2008) items in Statement III. D would be correct if Statement III read “total payments and time-specific obligations”.

questions.source: High quality paper LTR-3 b Q9
questions.question: A Federal Reserve examiner is reviewing the liquidity policy of a U.S. bank holding company with USD 85 billion of assets against SR 10-6, the 2010 Interagency Policy Statement on Funding and Liquidity Risk Management. Which of the following best describes the EWI guidance in SR 10-6?

options.text: Management should monitor for potential liquidity stress events using EWIs and event triggers tailored to its specific liquidity risk profile; early recognition supports progressive states of readiness and communication inside and outside the institution.

Management should monitor for potential liquidity stress events using a common set of EWIs and event triggers prescribed for all institutions; early recognition lets supervisors compare readiness across institutions and communicate with outside parties.

Management should monitor for potential liquidity stress events using EWIs and event triggers tailored to its specific liquidity risk profile; early signals should be communicated only within the institution until the event has materialized.

Management should monitor for potential liquidity stress events using EWIs that signal whether embedded triggers in callable public debt and OTC derivatives are about to be breached, as the core requirement of the statement.

questions.solution:
Federal Reserve examiner checks a U.S. BHC’s policy against the EWI guidance in SR 10-6.

**Concept and theory**

SR 10-6 is the Federal Reserve’s issuance of the 2010 Interagency Policy Statement on Funding and Liquidity Risk Management, an interagency statement. Its EWI guidance in GARP’s Table 3.2 has four elements:

(i) Tools: institution management should monitor for potential liquidity stress events using early-warning indicators and event triggers.

(ii) Tailoring: the institution should tailor these indicators to its specific liquidity risk profile. Schweser says the EWIs should be consistent with the firm’s liquidity risk profile.

(iii) Readiness: early recognition of potential events lets the institution position itself into progressive states of readiness as the event evolves.

(iv) Communication: early recognition also provides a framework to report or communicate within the institution and to outside parties.

The idea of progressive readiness means that as signals worsen, the firm steps up its preparedness in stages rather than jumping from “normal” to “crisis”. The outside audience is named explicitly, so a framework limited to internal escalation falls short of the guidance. Tailoring matters because a standard indicator set misses the institution-specific vulnerabilities that supervisors increasingly scrutinise.

**Applying it to this question**

The examiner needs the option that keeps all four elements. Option A has EWIs and event triggers, tailoring to the specific profile, progressive states of readiness, and communication both within the institution and to outside parties. Each of the other options changes exactly one element: tailoring becomes standardisation, the outside audience is removed, or the OCC’s embedded-trigger provision is substituted. The holding company’s size (USD 85 billion) does not affect the answer.

**Fragile fact.** Actor and audience: SR 10-6 is institution-tailored EWIs plus event triggers, with communication inside and outside the firm.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 68.b, verbatim):** Identify EWI guidelines from banking regulators and supervisors (OCC, BCBS, Federal Reserve).

**GARP:** Chapter 3, “Key Supervisory Guidelines”, Table 3.2, SR 10-6 column and source note 5 (Interagency Policy Statement on Funding and Liquidity Risk Management, 2010). **GARP** **vs Schweser:** Schweser says “consistent to the firm’s liquidity risk profile” and “more time to prepare”; GARP says “tailor” and “progressive states of readiness”. Same substance; GARP’s wording is used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-3 b, where it is Q9 of 11.

a.reason: A is correct because it restates SR 10-6 as summarised in GARP’s Table 3.2: tailored EWIs and event triggers, progressive readiness, and a framework to communicate internally and to outside parties.

b.reason: (Scope or condition error). B replaces tailoring with a common set of indicators prescribed for all institutions and makes supervisors the users of the readiness signal. SR 10-6 says the institution should tailor indicators to its specific liquidity risk profile, and readiness belongs to the institution. B would describe a standardised supervisory metric such as a regulatory ratio, not SR 10-6 EWIs.

c.reason: (Scope or condition error). C keeps tailoring but drops the outside audience and delays communication until the event has materialized. SR 10-6 provides a framework to report or communicate within the institution and to outside parties, and the point is early recognition. C would be correct only if the guidance limited EWI reporting to internal escalation.

d.reason: (Sibling swap). D attributes the OCC (2012) embedded-trigger provision (callable public debt, OTC derivatives) to SR 10-6. D would be correct if the stem named the OCC’s Comptroller’s Handbook Liquidity booklet.

questions.source: High quality paper LTR-3 b Q10
questions.question:
A risk consultant is advising a Canadian bank (CAD 48 billion of assets) on the EWI list for its U.S. operations, which are expected to follow SR 10-6. The consultant’s draft list contains:

I. Negative publicity concerning an asset class owned by the institution.

II. Increased potential for deterioration in the institution’s financial condition.

III. Widening debt or credit default swap spreads.

IV. Daily maximum liquidity.

Which of the items appear among the early-warning signals listed in SR 10-6?

options.text: I and II only
I and IV only
II, III, and IV only
I, II, and III only

questions.solution:
Risk consultant screens a draft EWI list for a Canadian bank’s U.S. operations against SR 10-6.

**Concept and theory**

The SR 10-6 column in GARP’s Table 3.2 ends with a short, non-exhaustive list: early-warning signals “may include, but are not limited to”:

- negative publicity concerning an asset class owned by the institution;
- increased potential for deterioration in the institution’s financial condition;
- widening debt or credit default swap spreads;
- increased concerns over the funding of off-balance-sheet items.

The four items describe how a liquidity event spreads from perception to funding. Bad news about assets the firm holds raises questions about its solvency. Concern about its financial condition makes counterparties cautious. Wider spreads raise the cost of funding and limit access to it. Concerns over funding off-balance-sheet items point to commitments that may need on-balance-sheet funding just when funding is hardest to get. Schweser renders the first three as bad publicity about specific assets held, a possible worsening of the balance sheet (decreased assets, increased liabilities), and increasing spreads on fixed-income and swap products. It omits the off-balance-sheet item.

The SR 10-6 list contains no intraday payment metrics. Those belong to BCBS (2012).

**Applying it to this question**

Statement I matches the first SR 10-6 signal. Statement II matches the second. Statement III matches the third: widening debt or CDS spreads. Statement IV, daily maximum liquidity, is a BCBS (2012) intraday monitoring indicator, not an SR 10-6 early-warning signal. The bank’s Canadian parentage and its size (CAD 48 billion) are irrelevant inputs: the question is only about the contents of SR 10-6. The set that matches is I, II and III.

**Fragile fact.** Spread widening is shared by OCC (2012), SR 10-6 and the BCBS (2008) list; daily maximum liquidity belongs to BCBS (2012) alone.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 68.b, verbatim):** Identify EWI guidelines from banking regulators and supervisors (OCC, BCBS, Federal Reserve).

**GARP:** Chapter 3, “Key Supervisory Guidelines”, Table 3.2, SR 10-6 and BCBS-2012 columns. **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser paraphrases the SR 10-6 examples (“bad publicity surrounding specific assets held”, “possible worsening of the firm’s balance sheet”, “increasing spreads for fixed-income and swap products”) and omits the off-balance-sheet funding item; GARP wording used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-3 b, where it is Q10 of 11.

a.reason: (Scope or condition error (undercoverage)). A rejects Statement III, perhaps because spread widening is remembered as an OCC item. Spread widening appears in OCC (2012) and in SR 10-6 (“widening debt or credit default swap spreads”). A would be correct if Statement III read “reluctance of trust managers to place funds” (OCC only).

b.reason: (Sibling swap). B accepts the BCBS (2012) intraday indicator in Statement IV as an SR 10-6 signal and drops two genuine items. B would be correct only if the question asked for items drawn from SR 10-6 or BCBS (2012) and Statements II and III were false.

c.reason: (Sibling swap). C accepts Statement IV (BCBS 2012) and rejects Statement I, the first signal on the SR 10-6 list. C would be correct if Statement IV were replaced by “increased concerns over the funding of off-balance-sheet items” and Statement I were false.

d.reason: D is correct because Statements I, II and III each reproduce an early-warning signal listed under SR 10-6 in GARP’s Table 3.2, while Statement IV comes from the BCBS (2012) intraday list.

questions.question: The head of liquidity risk at a German bank with EUR 210 billion of assets is drafting the regulatory citations for the bank’s EWI framework. Which of the following attributions is most accurate?

options.text: FRB SR 12-7 states that, for a forward-looking view of liquidity risk, a bank should use metrics that assess balance sheet structure, project cash flows, and take account of off-balance sheet risks.
BCBS Principle 5 states that the liquidity risk management framework should be end-to-end and should sufficiently capture the banking organization’s exposures, activities, and risks.
BCBS Principle 5 calls for metrics on balance sheet structure, projected cash flows and future liquidity positions, and off-balance sheet risks, across both normal and stressed conditions.
BCBS Principle 5 calls for metrics on balance sheet structure, projected cash flows and future liquidity positions, and off-balance sheet risks, under business-as-usual conditions only.

questions.solution:
Head of liquidity risk at a German bank attributes two further regulatory statements cited in GARP’s EWI chapter.

**Concept and theory**

Besides Table 3.2, GARP’s chapter cites two other regulatory statements that shape how EWIs are built. They are easy to mix up because both concern the EWI framework.

**BCBS Principle 5** (from the 2008 Sound Principles) appears in the “Measures” section, where GARP says it articulates the hallmarks of EWIs. It states that to obtain a forward-looking view of liquidity risk exposures, a bank should use metrics that assess (a) the structure of the balance sheet, and metrics that (b) project cash flows and future liquidity positions, taking into account

(c) off-balance sheet risks. These measures should span vulnerabilities across business-as-usual and stressed conditions over various time horizons.

**FRB SR 12-7** is a Federal Reserve supervisory letter, cited in the section “Risk Identification and EWIs”. It requires the LRM framework to be end-to-end and to “sufficiently capture the banking organization’s exposures, activities, and risks”. GARP then describes the chain from risk identification to the liquidity risk inventory, risk assessment, and a measurement and monitoring framework made up of stress tests, EWIs, and limits with responses.

| Statement | Core idea |
|---|---|
| BCBS Principle 5 | What the metrics must cover: balance sheet structure, projected cash flows, off-balance sheet risks; normal and stressed; several horizons |
| FRB SR 12-7 | How the framework must be built: end to end, capturing all exposures, activities and risks |

**Applying it to this question**

Sort the options by the content they attribute. The “(a) balance sheet structure, (b) projected cash flows, (c) off-balance sheet risks” triad belongs to BCBS Principle 5. The “end-to-end, sufficiently capture exposures, activities and risks” wording belongs to FRB SR 12-7. Principle 5 also explicitly extends the measures to stressed conditions. Only Option C pairs the right content with the right source and keeps both conditions. The bank’s size (EUR 210 billion) is irrelevant.

**Fragile fact.** Who said what: the BCBS (Principle 5) specifies what metrics to use, and the Federal Reserve (SR 12-7) specifies an end-to-end framework.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 68.b, verbatim):** Identify EWI guidelines from banking regulators and supervisors (OCC, BCBS, Federal Reserve).

**GARP:** Chapter 3, “Risk Identification and EWIs” (FRB SR 12-7) and “Measures” (BCBS Principle 5, footnote to the BCBS 2008 Sound Principles). **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser does not cite Principle 5 or SR 12-7; it presents the same measure characteristics under LO 68.a without attribution. This target is GARP-only and was included as a boundary call, because the LO asks for EWI guidelines from the BCBS and Federal Reserve.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-3 b, where it is Q11 of 11.

a.reason: (Role misassignment). A gives the Principle 5 metric triad to the Federal Reserve’s SR 12-7. The content is right but the issuer is wrong. A would be correct if it began “BCBS Principle 5 states”.

b.reason: (Role misassignment). B gives SR 12-7’s end-to-end requirement to BCBS Principle 5. B would be correct if it began “FRB SR 12-7 states”.

c.reason: C is correct because GARP quotes BCBS Principle 5 as calling for metrics on balance sheet structure and on projected cash flows and future liquidity positions, taking off-balance sheet risks into account, spanning business-as-usual and stressed conditions over various time horizons.

d.reason: (Scope or condition error). D keeps the Principle 5 metrics but limits them to business-as-usual conditions. GARP’s quotation says the measures should span vulnerabilities across business-as-usual and stressed conditions over various time horizons. D would be correct if the stressed-conditions clause were absent from the principle.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Discuss the applications of EWIs in the context of the liquidity risk management process.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-3 c Q1
questions.question:
A member of the board risk committee at a Canadian bank is reviewing a draft policy that describes how the bank’s early warning indicators (EWIs) will be used within its CAD liquidity risk management framework. The draft contains the following statements:

I. The EWIs will have a tangible and favourable effect on liquidity risk governance only when they are linked to a clearly defined escalation plan.

II. The governance overseeing the escalation of EWI-triggered actions will be formalised and documented as part of the liquidity risk management framework and included in the contingency funding plan.

III. Because escalation criteria for EWIs are prescribed uniformly by banking supervisors, the bank will adopt the supervisory escalation criteria without modification.

IV. Because a sound set of measures is the first essential building block of the EWI framework, the measures deliver most of the framework’s value even before they are linked to escalation processes.

Which of the statements are accurate?

options.text: I only
I and III only
I and II only
I, II, and IV only

questions.solution:
Canadian bank board policy review: which statements about EWIs and escalation are accurate.

**Concept and theory**

GARP summarises the EWI framework with the acronym M.E.R.I.T.: Measures, Escalation, Reporting, Integrated systems, and Thresholds. The five components play different roles. Measures are the raw material: the indicators themselves, internal and external, leading and sharp. GARP calls an appropriate set of measures the first essential building block. It then warns that the framework becomes a “mere academic exercise” if it is not eventually linked to escalation processes. The other three components (timely reporting, integrated systems and data, and properly calibrated thresholds) are what make the move from measures to escalation possible.

The reason is the purpose of an EWI. GARP’s dashboard analogy says EWI triggers exist to start management discussions and actions, and those actions should be formally documented. A signal that reaches no one with authority to act changes nothing. Hence the governance statement in the Escalation section: EWIs have a tangible and favourable impact on LRM governance only when they are linked to a clearly defined escalation plan. The governance that oversees escalation of EWI-triggered actions must be formalised and documented as part of the LRM framework, and it must be included in the institution’s contingency funding plan (CFP). GARP also says escalation criteria are bespoke to a bank. What supervisors expect is an effective policy that sends limit breaches to the level of management with authority to take corrective action. They do not hand down a uniform rulebook.

| Component | Role in the framework |
|---|---|
| Measures | First building block; an academic exercise unless linked to escalation |
| Reporting, integrated systems, thresholds | Make the move from measures to escalation possible |
| Escalation | The link to action; bespoke criteria, documented, in the CFP |

**Applying it to this question**

Test each statement against the Escalation section and the M.E.R.I.T. introduction. Statement I restates the governance condition almost word for word, so it is true. Statement II restates the documentation requirement, including the link to the CFP, so it is true. Statement III claims that supervisors prescribe escalation criteria uniformly, but GARP says the criteria are bespoke to each bank, so it is false. Statement IV turns the “first building block” remark into a claim that measures deliver most of the value before they are linked to escalation. GARP says the opposite: without that link, the measures are an academic exercise. So it is false. The accurate set is I and II.

**Fragile fact.** The order of the framework matters: measures come first, but escalation is what gives them value. EWIs affect LRM governance only when linked to a clearly defined escalation plan.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 68.c, verbatim):** Discuss the applications of EWIs in the context of the liquidity risk management process.

**GARP:** Chapter 3, Section 3.1, “Framework Components: M.E.R.I.T.” (introduction and “Escalation”); “Introduction: Dashboard and Beyond”. **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser places the M.E.R.I.T. overview under LO 68.a and the escalation condition under LO 68.c. It condenses escalation to “only when included within a clear escalation plan” and omits the documentation and CFP requirement, which is GARP-only.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-3 c, where it is Q1 of 11.

a.reason: (Scope or condition error). Choosing “I only” means rejecting Statement II, as if documenting escalation governance and placing it in the CFP were optional or belonged outside the EWI framework. GARP states both requirements explicitly in the Escalation section. A would be correct only if Statement II had said the escalation governance should be kept separate from the CFP.

b.reason: (Role misassignment). B accepts Statement III, which gives supervisors the job of writing uniform escalation criteria. In GARP the criteria are bespoke to each bank. The supervisory expectation is only that breaches reach management with the authority to act. B would be correct only if Statement II were false and Statement III said that the bank sets its own escalation criteria.

c.reason: C (I and II only) matches the source. EWIs have a favourable impact on LRM governance only when linked to a clearly defined escalation plan, and the escalation governance must be formalised, documented in the LRM framework, and included in the CFP.

d.reason: (Polarity flip). D accepts Statement IV, which reverses GARP’s warning. Measures are the first building block, but without escalation they are a “mere academic exercise”. They do not deliver most of the value on their own. D would be correct only if IV said the measures deliver little value until they are linked to escalation.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Discuss the applications of EWIs in the context of the liquidity risk management process.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-3 c Q2
questions.question: The treasurer of a Japanese bank receives an EWI alert: projected drawdowns on committed credit facilities extended to corporate clients signal a potentially large JPY cash outflow over the next month. The bank is not in a crisis: its funding markets remain open, its rating is unchanged, and other EWIs are within normal bounds. The bank’s liquid asset buffer currently stands at JPY 1.4 trillion. Which of the following responses is most consistent with an effective EWI escalation policy?

options.text: The treasurer authorises a check on future asset growth directly, since all responses to EWI signals fall within the delegation of the corporate treasurer.
The signal is escalated to the asset-liability committee (ALCO), which may authorise a check on future asset growth.
Management initiates the contingency funding plan at once, since every EWI that signals a cash outflow requires the plan to be activated.
No escalation takes place until the outflow causes a regulatory limit to be breached, since the role of EWIs is to record breaches once they occur.

questions.solution:
Japanese bank: an EWI signals a potentially large cash outflow outside a crisis; who responds and how.

**Concept and theory**

Escalation answers a practical question: once an EWI fires, who acts, and with what tool? GARP’s starting point is that escalation criteria are bespoke to each bank. Whatever the criteria, an effective policy sends limit breaches to the level of management that has the authority to undertake the corrective action. GARP then gives three tiers, scaled to severity:

| Severity of signal | Who acts | Typical response |
|---|---|---|
| Modest | Corporate treasurer (own delegation) | Increase the liquid asset buffer |
| Potentially large cash outflow | ALCO | Authorise a check on future asset growth |
| Most extreme cases | Management | Initiate the contingency funding plan |

The logic is proportionality: the more far-reaching the response a signal calls for, the higher the authority that must take it. A modest top-up of the liquid asset buffer can usually stay within the treasurer’s existing delegation. A check on the bank’s future asset growth goes to the asset-liability committee (ALCO). Initiating the CFP, the bank’s contingency response, is reserved for the most extreme cases.

GARP’s dashboard analogy explains why this matters. EWI triggers exist to start management discussions and actions, and those actions should be formally documented. If a signal is escalated too little, it stays with someone who lacks the authority to make the decision it calls for. If it is escalated too far, the bank takes its most extreme response when a lesser one would do. In both cases the escalation plan has failed to match severity to authority.

**Applying it to this question**

The alert is a potentially large cash outflow, which is the middle tier in GARP’s description. The stem also rules out the extreme tier: markets are open, the rating is unchanged, and other EWIs are normal. So the signal belongs with ALCO, which may authorise a check on future asset growth. The JPY 1.4 trillion buffer is an irrelevant input. The question asks who has authority to respond to this type of signal, and GARP’s mapping from the type of signal to the authority does not depend on the size of the existing buffer.

**Fragile fact.** Three actors and three severities: treasurer for modest (buffer), ALCO for a potentially large outflow (asset growth), management for extreme cases (CFP).

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 68.c, verbatim):** Discuss the applications of EWIs in the context of the liquidity risk management process.

**GARP:** Chapter 3, Section 3.1, “Framework Components: M.E.R.I.T.”, “Escalation”. **GARP** **vs Schweser:** Schweser says only that EWIs help escalate an issue to relevant management and apply remedies “depending on the severity”. The treasurer, ALCO, and CFP tiers are GARP-only.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-3 c, where it is Q2 of 11.

a.reason: (Role misassignment). The right action is given to the wrong actor. GARP limits the treasurer’s delegation to modest responses such as increasing the liquid asset buffer. A check on asset growth in response to a large outflow is for ALCO. A would be correct if the signal were modest and the response were a buffer increase.

b.reason: B matches GARP’s statement that an EWI signalling a potentially large cash outflow may require ALCO to authorise a check on future asset growth.

c.reason: (Scope or condition error). C applies the CFP to every outflow signal. GARP keeps CFP activation for the most extreme cases, and the stem explicitly says this is not a crisis. C would be correct if the stem described an extreme case, such as a rating downgrade together with a run on wholesale funding.

d.reason: (Polarity flip). D reverses the timing purpose of EWIs. They are meant to give advance warning so that management can act before limits are breached, not to record breaches after the event. D would describe a lagging indicator, which GARP contrasts unfavourably with leading EWIs.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Discuss the applications of EWIs in the context of the liquidity risk management process.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-3 c Q3
questions.question: An internal auditor at a London broker-dealer with a significant trading focus is reviewing an incident. At 10:40 a.m. on a volatile day, initial margin calls on the firm’s cleared derivatives rose by GBP 640 million. The firm’s EWI dashboard is compiled once a day after the close, so treasury first saw the signal the following morning. The firm’s most recent reported LCR was 148%. Which of the following recommendations best describes good practice for EWI reporting at this firm?

options.text: Keep daily reporting: it is common practice, and intraday reporting is mainly adopted by retail-funded banks whose deposit balances can move within hours.
Move every indicator on the dashboard to intraday reporting, since supervisors require intraday reporting of all EWIs at firms with trading activity.
Keep daily reporting: any indicator that is refreshed at least once a month already satisfies the “early” aspect of an early warning indicator.
Daily reporting is common practice, but a firm with a significant trading focus should move toward intraday reporting of certain measures, given its greater exposure to external market conditions.

questions.solution:
London broker-dealer: margin calls spike intraday but the EWI dashboard is compiled once daily.

**Concept and theory**

Reporting is the R in M.E.R.I.T. An early warning indicator is only early if management sees it in time. GARP states the purpose directly: EWI reporting must be timely so that management has enough lead time to adjust before a potential crisis. It then describes industry practice in three steps:

- **Daily is the common baseline.** It is common practice to report the EWI dashboard daily, and most institutions do some daily liquidity reporting.
- **Leaders go further.** Leading institutions are moving toward intraday reporting of certain measures, not of every indicator.
- **Trading focus drives intraday use.** Firms with a significant trading focus are more likely to report intraday because they are more exposed to external market conditions.

GARP’s reason is exposure to external market conditions. A firm whose liquidity depends on market moves during the trading day can receive a dashboard compiled at the close too late to act on what happened that day.

A related point from the measures discussion (LO 68.a) sets the outer limit. An indicator that is not updated for more than a month is unlikely to satisfy the “early” aspect of an EWI. That is a minimum standard, not a sign that monthly or daily reporting is enough for every firm. Schweser adds the example that heavily trading banks may find hourly reporting even more effective.

**Applying it to this question**

The stem gives three facts that matter: the firm has a significant trading focus, the stress came from a market-driven source (margin calls on cleared derivatives), and a daily dashboard showed the signal almost a day late. Those facts match GARP’s case for intraday reporting of certain measures. The 148% LCR is irrelevant. A healthy regulatory ratio says nothing about whether the reporting cycle is fast enough to catch intraday stress.

**Fragile fact.** Who uses intraday reporting: firms with a significant trading focus, because of their exposure to external market conditions, and only for certain measures.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 68.c, verbatim):** Discuss the applications of EWIs in the context of the liquidity risk management process.

**GARP:** Chapter 3, Section 3.1, “Framework Components: M.E.R.I.T.”, “Reporting”; also “Spanning Various Time Horizons”. **GARP vs Schweser:** none of substance. Schweser gives “hourly” as an example of intraday reporting and says such reporting may be “even more effective” for heavily trading banks.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-3 c, where it is Q3 of 11.

a.reason: (Sibling swap). A gives the intraday driver to the wrong type of firm. GARP links intraday reporting to a significant trading focus and exposure to external market conditions, not to retail deposit funding. A would be correct only if the stem had named a firm with no significant trading focus, for which GARP’s common practice of daily reporting applies.

b.reason: (Absolute-claim trap). B demands intraday reporting for every indicator and invents a universal supervisory requirement. GARP says leading institutions move toward intraday reporting of certain measures, and that some EWIs are monitored intraday where business conditions warrant or regulators require it. B would be closer to correct if it limited intraday reporting to the market-sensitive measures.

c.reason: (Scope or condition error). C treats a minimum standard as if it were sufficient. GARP says an indicator not updated for more than a month is unlikely to be early. It does not say that monthly or daily updating is adequate for a firm with a significant trading focus.

d.reason: D reflects both parts of the GARP text. Daily reporting is common practice, and firms with a significant trading focus are more likely to report intraday because of their greater exposure to external market conditions. The word “certain” in D matches GARP’s “intraday reporting of certain measures”.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Discuss the applications of EWIs in the context of the liquidity risk management process.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-3 c Q4
questions.question: The CRO of an Australian bank is redesigning the daily EWI pack sent to senior management. The current pack runs to 14 pages and contains 160 indicators, and executives say they cannot tell which signals matter. The bank’s AUD wholesale funding totals AUD 38 billion. Which of the following design principles is most consistent with sound EWI reporting?

options.text: The pack should be broad enough to give wide coverage of the bank’s liquidity risks, yet specific enough to communicate only the key messages.
The pack should maximise coverage by giving every indicator equal prominence, since any filtering of the pack risks hiding a warning signal.
The pack should report only the indicators that have turned red, since indicators showing green or amber need no attention from management.
The pack should be limited to externally observable market indicators, since internal indicators cannot be calculated and reported consistently.

questions.solution:
Australian bank: redesigning a 160-indicator daily EWI pack that executives cannot read.

**Concept and theory**

Timeliness is not the only requirement for EWI reporting. A report that arrives on time but buries the signal fails just as badly as one that arrives late. GARP therefore adds a design requirement: reporting must strike a balance between being (a) broad enough to provide wide coverage, and (b) specific enough to communicate only the key messages. Schweser puts it the same way: broad enough to cover the full range of relevant matters, but focused enough to cover what is most important.

The two failure modes mirror each other.

| Design error | What happens | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| Too narrow | Some risk sources are not covered | A threat builds up unseen |
| Too broad | Every metric gets equal space | Key signals are lost in the noise |

The same idea appears in GARP’s discussion of measures. A “sharp” indicator is one that does not go unnoticed within the mass of data. Reporting has to protect that sharpness at the level of the whole pack. Breadth comes from tracking a full set of internal and external indicators across normal and stressed conditions. Focus comes from presenting them so that changes in status stand out. The stoplight system helps here, but amber items still need further investigation, so they cannot be dropped from the pack.

Integrated systems support good reporting: metrics are meaningful only if the bank can calculate them and report them consistently. Reporting design is therefore one of the components that carries the framework from measures to escalation.

**Applying it to this question**

The CRO’s problem is that the pack covers everything, but executives cannot tell which signals matter. That is the “too broad” failure. The fix is the balance GARP describes: keep wide coverage and make the key messages stand out. The AUD 38 billion of wholesale funding is irrelevant. It does not affect how the pack should be designed.

**Fragile fact.** Reporting has two jobs at once: broad for coverage and specific for key messages. Dropping either half is the trap.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 68.c, verbatim):** Discuss the applications of EWIs in the context of the liquidity risk management process.

**GARP:** Chapter 3, Section 3.1, “Framework Components: M.E.R.I.T.”, “Reporting” (also “Integrated Systems” and “Thresholds”). **GARP vs Schweser:** none; Schweser’s “sufficiently broad . . . sufficiently focused” matches GARP.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-3 c, where it is Q4 of 11.

a.reason: A states GARP’s balance between broad coverage and specific key messages almost word for word.

b.reason: (Scope or condition error). B keeps the first half of GARP’s balance (wide coverage) and drops the second half (communicate only key messages). Equal prominence for 160 indicators is exactly what produces the CRO’s problem. B would be correct only if the requirement were coverage alone.

c.reason: (Sibling swap). C treats amber as if it were green. In the stoplight system, amber means the measure should be investigated further, so it does need management attention. C would be correct only if the bank’s stoplight had just two states, normal and act now.

d.reason: (Polarity flip). D reverses the direction GARP describes. EWI frameworks are increasingly supplementing market-based metrics with a larger array of internal indicators, and integrated systems are what make internal metrics consistent. GARP also requires a balance between internal and external measures. D would be correct only if the bank had no way to calculate internal metrics, and GARP’s answer to that is to fix the systems, not to drop the metrics.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Discuss the applications of EWIs in the context of the liquidity risk management process.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-3 c Q5
questions.question: A risk consultant is reviewing the EWI framework of a Brazilian bank. The bank’s liquidity stress test takes retail deposit volumes from a month-end general ledger extract that is adjusted by hand, while its EWI for week-over-week declines in deposit funding uses a daily feed from the core banking system. At the last month-end the two deposit figures differed by BRL 2.4 billion. The bank plans to add 35 internal indicators, such as loan performance and operational losses, to its EWI list. Which of the following recommendations is most consistent with sound practice for integrated systems?

options.text: Replace the internal deposit EWI with market-based indicators such as the bank’s CDS spread, since market data avoid internal reconciliation problems.
Accept the difference, since stressed and non-stressed measures should be drawn from separate data sources to keep the stress test independent.
Derive the deposit volumes feeding the stress test from the same source system used for the week-over-week deposit EWI, so that the reported metrics are accurate and in sync.
Integrate the data systems first, after which the EWIs will reliably predict any liquidity crisis and the separate stress test can be retired.

questions.solution:
Brazilian bank: stress test and deposit EWI use different source systems that disagree by BRL 2.4 billion.

**Concept and theory**

Integrated systems are the I in M.E.R.I.T. GARP’s starting point is that metrics and reporting are feasible and meaningful only when they are backed by the bank’s ability to calculate the selected metrics and report them consistently. Integrated data and systems give liquidity managers two assurances about every reported metric: it is (a) accurate, and (b) in sync with the other metrics.

GARP’s example is specific. Deposit volumes that feed liquidity stress tests, and the stressed measures built from them, should come from the same source system used to produce non-stressed measures, such as week-over-week declines in deposit funding. If the two use different data, management may see a deposit EWI and a stress-test result that disagree. It then has to work out which figure is right before deciding whether to escalate, and that delay undermines the purpose of the framework.

GARP also explains why this matters more over time. This level of automation and integration is particularly important because EWI frameworks increasingly supplement traditional market-based metrics with a larger array of internal indicators, such as the loan performance and operational loss measures GARP mentions elsewhere in the chapter. The longer the internal list, the more the framework depends on integrated data.

Schweser’s condensed version says that an integrated data processing system gives more consistent and accurate reporting when data come from multiple sources. The resulting internal EWI information can then be used together with external measures. Integration is an enabler of good measurement, and it does not replace any of the other risk tools.

**Applying it to this question**

The stress test uses a hand-adjusted month-end ledger extract, while the deposit EWI uses the daily core banking feed. The resulting BRL 2.4 billion gap is the inconsistency GARP warns about. The bank also plans 35 new internal indicators, which raises the need for integration. The remedy is GARP’s own example: take the stress-test deposit volumes from the same source system as the week-over-week deposit EWI.

**Fragile fact.** Same source system for the stress-test inputs and the business-as-usual EWI. The need grows as internal indicators are added.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 68.c, verbatim):** Discuss the applications of EWIs in the context of the liquidity risk management process.

**GARP:** Chapter 3, Section 3.1, “Framework Components: M.E.R.I.T.”, “Integrated Systems”. **GARP vs Schweser:** none in substance. The same-source-system deposit example and the point about internal indicators are GARP-only.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-3 c, where it is Q5 of 11.

a.reason: (Sibling swap). A replaces an internal measure with an external one. GARP requires a balance of internal and external measures and notes that frameworks are adding internal indicators, not removing them. A would be correct only if the question asked how to add an external market signal alongside the internal ones.

b.reason: (Polarity flip). B reverses GARP’s recommendation. Stressed and non-stressed deposit measures should share a source system, not be kept apart. B would describe GARP’s view only if “separate” were replaced by “the same”.

c.reason: C repeats GARP’s example and its purpose: stressed and non-stressed deposit measures derived from the same source system, so that the metrics are accurate and in sync.

d.reason: (Absolute-claim trap). D promises that integration makes EWIs reliable predictors of any crisis and makes stress testing unnecessary. GARP treats integration as an enabler of accurate, in-sync metrics. Stress tests and EWIs are separate parts of the measuring and monitoring framework, and the stress-test deposit volumes are themselves what GARP wants integrated. D would be closer to correct if it said only that integration improves accuracy and consistency.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Discuss the applications of EWIs in the context of the liquidity risk management process.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-3 c Q6
questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a Singapore bank is reviewing the green-to-amber boundaries of two EWIs over the past 24 months. Both thresholds were calibrated on three years of SGD data.

| EWI | Times amber | Outcome |
|---|---|---|
| X: share of funding from overnight interbank borrowing | 46 | 1 investigation found a real issue |
| Y: share of deposits from the top 10 depositors | 0 | rose from 18% to 31% in the period |

Which of the following best describes the calibration of the two EWIs?

options.text: X’s boundary is too narrow, risking a “boy who cried wolf” effect that desensitises management; Y’s boundary is too wide, so its movements go undetected.
X’s boundary is too wide, so its movements go undetected; Y’s boundary is too narrow, risking a “boy who cried wolf” effect that desensitises management.
X’s boundary is well calibrated, because frequent amber signals ensure no emerging issue is missed; Y’s boundary is too wide, so its movements go undetected.
X’s boundary is too narrow, risking a “boy who cried wolf” effect that desensitises management; Y’s boundary is well calibrated, since it confirms a healthy environment.

questions.solution:
Singapore bank: one EWI turns amber 46 times with one real issue; another never leaves green while concentration rises.

**Concept and theory**

Most firms present EWIs with a stoplight. Green means the measure is within normal bounds. Amber means it should be investigated further. Red signals significant concern and may warrant an immediate response. GARP’s calibration discussion focuses on the boundary between green and amber, where the first warning is given.

GARP describes two opposite ways to get this boundary wrong.

| Boundary | Symptom | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| Too wide | Metric almost never leaves green | Movements go undetected; the dashboard keeps saying all is well |
| Too narrow | Metric keeps crossing into amber | Constant investigation desensitises management (“boy who cried wolf”) |

Both errors defeat the purpose of the framework. A boundary that is too wide misses emerging problems, so the indicator stops being an early warning. A boundary that is too narrow produces so many false alarms that management learns to ignore amber. When a real problem then appears, the signal that should prompt action is discounted. Schweser makes the same point: the shift from green to amber should be precisely calibrated to avoid both missing emerging issues and generating excessive false alarms.

The fix is calibration and back-testing. Historical data on the indicator’s volatility over a sufficiently long and recent period set the boundary, and back-testing checks whether it needs recalibration. Removing a level or ignoring signals does not fix a badly placed boundary.

**Applying it to this question**

EWI X crossed into amber 46 times in 24 months, and only one investigation found a real issue. That is the symptom of a boundary set too narrow. EWI Y never left green while depositor concentration rose from 18% to 31%. GARP itself lists growing concentration in liabilities as a warning sign. A metric that “constantly indicates” a healthy, unchanged environment while it is deteriorating is the symptom of a boundary set too wide. The detail that both thresholds were calibrated on three years of data is irrelevant to the diagnosis. The outcomes show the problem regardless of how long the window was.

**Fragile fact.** Narrow boundary means too many ambers and “boy who cried wolf”. Wide boundary means no ambers and missed deterioration. Do not swap them.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 68.c, verbatim):** Discuss the applications of EWIs in the context of the liquidity risk management process.

**GARP:** Chapter 3, Section 3.1, “Framework Components: M.E.R.I.T.”, “Thresholds”. **GARP vs** **Schweser:** none in substance. The “boy who cried wolf” wording and the “metric constantly indicates a healthy environment” symptom are GARP’s wording; Schweser condenses them to “missing emerging issues” and “excessive false alarms”.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-3 c, where it is Q6 of 11.

a.reason: A diagnoses both indicators correctly: X is too narrow (the “boy who cried wolf” problem) and Y is too wide (movements go undetected).

b.reason: (Polarity flip). B swaps the two diagnoses. Frequent amber signals point to a narrow boundary, not a wide one, and a metric that never changes colour points to a wide boundary. B would be correct only if X had never turned amber and Y had turned amber dozens of times.

c.reason: (Absolute-claim trap). C assumes that more amber signals are always better because nothing can be missed. GARP explicitly warns that boundaries set too narrow desensitise management. C would be correct only if most of X’s 46 investigations had found real issues.

d.reason: (Scope or condition error). D applies the calibration test to only one failure mode. It reads Y’s constant green as proof of health, but GARP describes that pattern as the symptom of a boundary set too wide. Y’s deteriorating concentration confirms it. D would be correct only if Y’s underlying concentration had stayed stable.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Discuss the applications of EWIs in the context of the liquidity risk management process.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-3 c Q7
questions.question:
A junior risk analyst at a German savings bank is calibrating thresholds for an EWI that tracks the weekly percentage change in EUR retail deposits. Bank policy sets the amber threshold at 1.5 standard deviations below the historical mean and the red threshold at 2.5 standard deviations below the mean. Four candidate calibration windows are available:

| Window | Period covered | Mean (%) | Std dev (%) |
|---|---|---|---|
| W1 | Last 8 months to last week; no stress episode | −0.10 | 0.60 |
| W2 | 5 years ending 2 years ago; includes a stress episode | −0.30 | 1.90 |
| W3 | Last 4 years to last week; includes a stress episode | −0.20 | 1.20 |
| W4 | Last 2 years to last week; no stress episode | −0.15 | 0.80 |

This week’s change is −2.60%. The bank’s current LCR is 141%. Using the most appropriate window, which of the following statements holds?

options.text: W1: amber at −1.00%, red at −1.60%; the EWI is red.
W2: amber at −3.15%, red at −5.05%; the EWI is green.
W4: amber at −1.35%, red at −2.15%; the EWI is red.
W3: amber at −2.00%, red at −3.20%; the EWI is amber.

questions.solution:
German savings bank: choose the calibration window, compute amber and red thresholds, classify a −2.60% reading.

**Concept and theory**

A threshold has to be anchored in how the indicator normally behaves, and GARP says historical data analysis is commonly used to estimate an EWI’s volatility and calibrate its thresholds. Schweser specifies that past data are used to compute the EWI’s standard deviation. Neither source prescribes a formula for the threshold itself, so the multiples used here (1.5 and 2.5 standard deviations) are bank policy given in the stem.

The source’s guidance is about which data to use. GARP sets three conditions on the calibration series:

(i) it must be **sufficiently long** to be significant, and when available a series of **at least one** **year** is used;

(ii) it must **capture recent events**, so that it represents the current operating environment;

(iii) **if possible**, it should **include a period of stress** (GARP’s example is 2007-08), so that the metric’s behaviour under stress is assessed accurately.

GARP gives a reason for each condition: length makes the estimate significant, recency makes the series represent the current operating environment, and a stress period lets the bank assess more accurately how the metric performs under stressed conditions. After calibration, thresholds are back-tested to see whether recalibration is needed.

With mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$ from the chosen window, the bank’s rule is

Amber threshold $= \mu-$ 1.5 $\sigma$, Red threshold $= \mu-$ 2.5 $\sigma$.

A reading below the amber threshold but not below the red threshold is amber; a reading below the red threshold is red.

**Applying it to this question**

Step 1: choose the window. W1 covers only 8 months, which fails condition (i). W2 ended two years ago, which fails condition (ii). W4 is long enough and recent but has no stress episode. Condition (iii) applies “if possible”, and W3 shows it is possible, so W4 is second best. W3 meets all three conditions.

Step 2: compute the thresholds from W3 ($\mu= -$0.20%, $\sigma=$ 1.20%):

Amber = −0.20 − 1.5 × 1.20 = −0.20 − 1.80 = −2.00%

Red = −0.20 − 2.5 × 1.20 = −0.20 − 3.00 = −3.20%

Step 3: classify the reading. Since −3.20% \< −2.60% \< −2.00%, the reading is past the amber threshold but not the red one, so the EWI is **amber**. Equivalently, z = (−2.60 + 0.20)/1.20 = −2.00, which lies between −1.5 and −2.5.

Meaning: amber means the deposit trend should be investigated further. An immediate response is not yet called for.

The LCR of 141% is irrelevant. The question concerns how this EWI is calibrated, and the bank’s regulatory ratio does not enter the threshold calculation.

**Fragile fact.** All three conditions must hold: at least one year, recent, and stress included where possible. The red threshold is further from the mean than amber (2.5$\sigma$ versus 1.5$\sigma$), so a reading between them is amber.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 68.c, verbatim):** Discuss the applications of EWIs in the context of the liquidity risk management process.

**GARP:** Chapter 3, Section 3.1, “Framework Components: M.E.R.I.T.”, “Thresholds”. **GARP vs** **Schweser:** Schweser gives “long enough (e.g., one year)” and “incorporate recent events”. The stress-period condition is GARP-only. The 1.5 and 2.5 standard-deviation multiples are stem assumptions, and neither source prescribes them.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-3 c, where it is Q7 of 11.

a.reason: (Wrong input twin (window too short)). Using W1: amber = −0.10 − 1.5(0.60) = −1.00%; red = −0.10 − 2.5(0.60) = −1.60%. Since −2.60% \< −1.60%, the status is red. The 8-month window fails GARP’s requirement of at least one year where available, and here its small $\sigma$ puts both thresholds close to the mean. A would be correct only if less than a year of data existed.

b.reason: (Wrong input twin (stale window)). Using W2: amber = −0.30 − 1.5(1.90) = −3.15%; red = −0.30 − 2.5(1.90) = −5.05%. Since −2.60% > −3.15%, the status is green. W2 includes stress but ends two years ago, so it does not represent the current environment. Its wide thresholds would let a real deterioration go undetected. B would be correct only if no recent data were available.

c.reason: (Wrong input twin (no stress period)). Using W4: amber = −0.15 − 1.5(0.80) = −1.35%; red = −0.15 − 2.5(0.80) = −2.15%. Since −2.60% \< −2.15%, the status is red. W4 is long and recent but leaves out stress, even though a window that includes stress (W3) is available. C would be correct only if no stress episode existed in the available history.

d.reason: D uses the only window that meets all three GARP conditions and applies the bank’s multiples correctly, giving amber at −2.00%, red at −3.20%, and an amber status.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Discuss the applications of EWIs in the context of the liquidity risk management process.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-3 c Q8
questions.question:
A banking regulator is reviewing the EWI log of a Chinese commercial bank, which uses a green, amber, and red stoplight system. Four entries from the CNY liquidity dashboard log read as follows:

I. Depositor concentration EWI moved to amber; the measure was referred to treasury for further investigation, with no remedial action yet taken.

II. Several EWIs turned red after a two-notch rating downgrade and a sustained run on wholesale funding; management initiated the contingency funding plan.

III. An EWI turned red, signalling a potentially large cash outflow; the treasurer handled it within his own delegation through a modest buffer increase, and ALCO was not informed.

IV. A funding concentration EWI moved from green to amber; management initiated the contingency funding plan immediately, as an amber status calls for an immediate response.

Which of the log entries are consistent with sound use of EWI thresholds and escalation?

options.text: I only
I and II only
I, II, and III only
I, II, and IV only

questions.solution:
Chinese bank EWI log: which recorded responses fit the stoplight status and escalation tiers.

**Concept and theory**

Thresholds and escalation work together. The threshold tells management how serious a signal is, and escalation tells it who acts and how. GARP’s stoplight definitions are:

| Status | GARP meaning | Fitting response |
|---|---|---|
| Green | Within normal bounds | No further action |
| Amber | Should be investigated further | Investigate and follow up |
| Red | Significant concern; may warrant immediate response | Escalate to the authority that fits the severity |

Schweser’s wording is close: green needs no further action, amber needs additional follow-up, and red needs immediate attention to remedy a serious problem.

The escalation tiers then decide who acts. The corporate treasurer can usually take modest steps, such as increasing the liquid asset buffer, within existing delegation. An EWI that signals a potentially large cash outflow may need ALCO to authorise a check on future asset growth. The most extreme cases may require management to initiate the contingency funding plan (CFP). GARP adds that an effective policy sends breaches to the level of management that has the authority to undertake corrective action, and that escalation governance must be documented and included in the CFP.

So a response has to pass two tests. It must fit the colour, and it must be taken by the right authority for the severity. Under-reacting to red, or leaving a large-outflow signal with the treasurer alone, breaks the escalation chain. Over-reacting to amber by activating the CFP treats a request for investigation as a crisis.

**Applying it to this question**

Entry I: amber, followed by further investigation and no remedy yet. This fits GARP’s definition of amber, so it is consistent. Entry II: several EWIs red after a downgrade and a sustained run, so this is an extreme case, and management initiated the CFP. That fits the top escalation tier, so it is consistent. Entry III: a red EWI signalling a potentially large outflow was kept within the treasurer’s delegation and ALCO was not informed. That misplaces the authority, so it is inconsistent. Entry IV: an amber status led to immediate CFP activation. Amber means investigate further, so this is inconsistent. The consistent entries are I and II.

**Fragile fact.** Amber means investigate further; red may warrant an immediate response; the CFP is for the most extreme cases, initiated by management.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 68.c, verbatim):** Discuss the applications of EWIs in the context of the liquidity risk management process.

**GARP:** Chapter 3, Section 3.1, “Framework Components: M.E.R.I.T.”, “Thresholds” and “Escalation”. **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser says red “requires” immediate attention, while GARP says red “may warrant” an immediate response. The treasurer, ALCO, and CFP tiers are GARP-only.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-3 c, where it is Q8 of 11.

a.reason: (Scope or condition error). A rejects Entry II, as if EWI escalation could never reach the CFP. GARP says the most extreme cases may require management to initiate the CFP, and the stem describes such a case. A would be correct only if Entry II had involved a single moderate signal.

b.reason: B (I and II only) is the only set in which every response fits both the stoplight meaning and the escalation tier GARP describes.

c.reason: (Role misassignment). C accepts Entry III, which leaves a large-outflow signal with the treasurer. GARP limits the treasurer to modest responses and assigns large-outflow signals to ALCO. C would be correct only if the signal in III had been modest.

d.reason: (Sibling swap). D accepts Entry IV, which gives amber the meaning of red, and treats the CFP as the response to it. Amber calls for further investigation. D would be correct only if the indicator had turned red in an extreme case.

questions.question: A treasury analyst at a US bank is reviewing the calibration of the bank’s EWI thresholds, including an EWI on the effective federal funds rate. The bank currently calibrates every threshold from the historical volatility of the indicator. Which of the following statements about threshold calibration is NOT accurate?

options.text: Historical data analysis is commonly used to estimate the volatility of an EWI and calibrate its thresholds, with a series of at least one year used when available.
Thresholds should be subjected to back-testing to determine whether recalibration is needed.
Because thresholds calibrated on historical volatility are objective, they should not be overridden by management, even when the FOMC specifies a target range for the rate.
If possible, the calibration series should include a period of stress, such as 2007-08, to assess more accurately how the metric performs under stressed conditions.

questions.solution:
US bank: which statement about calibrating thresholds, including an EWI on the fed funds rate, is NOT accurate.

**Concept and theory**

Calibration is not a one-off statistical exercise. GARP describes it as a cycle with three parts.

(i) **Historical estimation.** Historical data are commonly used to estimate an EWI’s volatility and calibrate its thresholds. The series should be long enough to be significant, capture recent events and, if possible, include a period of stress such as 2007-08. When available, at least one year of data is used.

(ii) **Back-testing.** The threshold should be subjected to back-testing to determine whether recalibration is needed.

(iii) **Management override.** The same review determines whether a management override, based on historical judgment, is warranted. GARP’s example is the Fed funds rate. Historical analysis of its volatility is informative, but triggers may be more appropriately set using the FOMC’s specified target range.

GARP does not spell out the reasoning behind the example, but its point is that historical volatility is an input to judgment, not a replacement for it. Where the FOMC specifies a target range for the rate, that range can be a more appropriate anchor for the trigger than past volatility alone. This fits GARP’s broader requirement that calibration should represent the current operating environment, which is also why the calibration series must capture recent events.

**Applying it to this question**

This is a NOT question, so look for the one statement that contradicts the source. A (historical volatility, at least one year), B (back-testing), and D (include a stress period if possible) each restate GARP. C says historical thresholds should never be overridden, even when the FOMC specifies a target range. That contradicts GARP’s own Fed funds example, so C is the statement that is not accurate.

**Fragile fact.** In GARP, a management override may be warranted. The Fed funds example anchors triggers on the FOMC target range rather than on historical volatility alone.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 68.c, verbatim):** Discuss the applications of EWIs in the context of the liquidity risk management process.

**GARP:** Chapter 3, Section 3.1, “Framework Components: M.E.R.I.T.”, “Thresholds”. **GARP** **vs Schweser:** Schweser mentions back-testing and recalibration but omits the management override and the FOMC example, which are GARP-only.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-3 c, where it is Q9 of 11.

a.reason: (True statement (qualifier misread)). A matches GARP: historical data are commonly used to estimate volatility and calibrate thresholds, with at least one year of data when available. A candidate who picks A has read “NOT accurate” as “accurate”. A would be the answer if the stem asked which statement is accurate about the data used for calibration.

b.reason: (True statement (qualifier misread)). B restates GARP’s back-testing requirement. It would be the answer to a question asking how a bank finds out whether a threshold needs recalibration.

c.reason: C is the inaccurate statement, and therefore the answer. GARP says back-testing helps determine whether a management override based on historical judgment is warranted, and gives the example that Fed funds triggers may be more appropriately set using the FOMC’s specified target range.

d.reason: (True statement (qualifier misread)). D restates GARP’s guidance that, if possible, the series should include a stress period such as 2007-08. It would be the answer to a question asking how to assess a metric’s behaviour under stressed conditions.

questions.question: The chief compliance officer of a Spanish bank is presenting to newly hired analysts on how EUR-reporting banks have developed their EWI dashboards since the 2007-08 crisis. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: The increased attention and resources devoted to EWI dashboards and their governance are largely attributable to supervisory demands such as matters requiring attention and exams, with some credit also due to leadership-initiated projects.

The increased attention and resources devoted to EWI dashboards and their governance are largely attributable to leadership-initiated projects, with supervisory demands such as matters requiring attention and exams playing a minor role.

The increased attention and resources devoted to EWI dashboards and their governance are largely attributable to a standard EWI list mandated by the BCBS, which has made dashboards uniform across banks.

The increased attention and resources devoted to EWI dashboards and their governance are largely attributable to credit rating agencies, which require an EWI dashboard as a condition of assigning a rating.

questions.solution:
Spanish bank briefing: what drove the growth of EWI dashboards and their governance.

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s “Industry Practices” section describes how EWIs have developed in practice. Over recent years banks have increased the attention and resources they devote to developing and maintaining EWI dashboards and the governance around them. GARP gives two drivers, in a clear order of importance:

1. **Mainly supervisory demands.** The extra emphasis is “largely attributed” to supervisory demands, in the form of matters requiring attention (MRAs), examinations, and similar actions.
2. **Partly leadership initiative.** In some cases credit should also go to bank leadership, which launched projects on its own initiative to strengthen liquidity management and risk reporting.

The background explains the order. After the 2007-08 crisis, the BCBS issued its Sound Principles in 2008, which include the use of EWIs, followed by standard metrics such as the LCR and NSFR. National regulators began benchmarking institutions against these principles, so supervisory expectations rose. GARP notes that the data needed for a modern LRM framework is an expensive investment. Some banks aim to minimise the cost of compliance, while others treat it as a strategic tool.

GARP also gives illustrative tables of the EWIs typically reported in the industry: market indicators (credit ratings, equity indices, money-market rates, FX, and economic data) and bank-specific indicators (credit risk, counterparty concentration, credit performance, funding need, liquidity metrics, market sentiment, maturity concentration, stress-testing results). It stresses that these lists are non-exhaustive. The BCBS list itself says EWIs “may include but are not limited to” the items shown. So there is no single mandated dashboard, and each bank tailors its own.

**Applying it to this question**

The CCO’s statement must get two things right: what the main driver was (supervisory demands) and what the secondary driver was (leadership initiative). Options B, C, and D each change who drove the change or how much.

**Fragile fact.** Largely supervisory (MRAs, exams), partly leadership self-initiative. EWI lists are illustrative and non-exhaustive.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 68.c, verbatim):** Discuss the applications of EWIs in the context of the liquidity risk management process.

**GARP:** Chapter 3, Section 3.1, “Industry Practices” (Tables 3.3 to 3.9); “Regulatory Emphasis in Recent Times”. **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser condenses the main driver to “to facilitate supervisory duties”, with part also “to improve risk reporting”. That is the same direction as GARP, but GARP names the mechanism (MRAs and exams) and credits leadership initiative.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-3 c, where it is Q10 of 11.

a.reason: A matches GARP: the increased emphasis is largely attributable to supervisory demands such as MRAs and exams, and in certain instances credit also goes to self-initiated projects by bank leadership.

b.reason: (Polarity flip). B reverses the weighting. GARP gives supervisory demands the main role and leadership initiative the secondary one. B would be correct only for a bank where GARP’s “certain instances” of self-initiative were the main story, which the general statement does not support.

c.reason: (Absolute-claim trap). C turns an illustrative BCBS list into a uniform mandate. GARP describes the BCBS EWIs as ones that “may include but are not limited to” the items listed, and says its own industry tables are non-exhaustive. C would be closer to correct if it said the BCBS gave example indicators that banks tailor to their own profile.

d.reason: (Role misassignment). D credits the change to rating agencies, which GARP does not mention as a driver. The demands came from supervisors, through MRAs and exams. D would be correct only if “credit rating agencies” were replaced by “supervisors”.

questions.source: High quality paper LTR-3 c Q11
questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a US regional bank is preparing a report on where EWIs sit within the bank’s USD liquidity risk management process. The draft includes the following statements:

I. A comprehensive framework begins by identifying the liquidity and funding risks inherent in the bank’s business activities; these are recorded in a liquidity risk inventory and assessed before stress tests, EWIs, and a limit and response framework are developed.

II. EWIs should be kept aligned with other core aspects of the framework, such as the risk inventory, stress testing assumptions, cash flow actuals and projections, business plans, and the contingency funding plan.

III. Because idiosyncratic EWIs are tailored to a single bank’s vulnerabilities, supervisors are expected to scrutinise them less closely than market-wide indicators.

IV. Using EWIs to build liquidity buffers ahead of stress can extend the survival horizon cost-effectively, and a strong position in stress can open opportunities such as gains in market share.

Which of the statements should the analyst retain?

options.text: I and II only
I, II, and III only
II and IV only
I, II, and IV only

questions.solution:
US regional bank report: where EWIs sit in the LRM process; which statements to retain.

**Concept and theory**

The LO asks how EWIs are applied in the context of the LRM process, so it helps to see the whole process. GARP describes it as a sequence:

1. **Identify** the liquidity and funding risks inherent in the institution’s business activities.
2. **Record** them in the firm’s liquidity risk inventory.
3. **Assess** them, in a process that involves the businesses, corporate treasury, independent risk management, and other stakeholders.
4. **Measure and monitor** them through a framework of stress tests, EWIs, and a limit and response framework.

GARP’s Figure 3.1 links risk identification to EWIs, limits and EWI thresholds, escalations and notifications, and the funding playbook (the figure is garbled in the source extraction, so its exact layout is not relied on here). GARP also says EWIs must align with, and be a natural extension of, the enterprise LRM framework.

The Conclusion turns this into governance. EWIs must be updated and kept aligned with the other core parts of the framework: the risk inventory, liquidity stress-testing assumptions, actual and projected cash flows, short- and long-term business plans, the contingency funding plan, and stakeholders (business lines, treasury, and risk as the second line of defence). Supervisors are likely to scrutinise idiosyncratic EWIs because they are more tailored to the bank’s specific vulnerabilities. GARP also says EWIs help only if the reporting mechanism is highly efficient, so data quality and timeliness matter.

Finally, GARP’s introduction (“Beyond”) gives a strategic use of EWIs. Holding liquid assets is a cost-benefit decision. Increasing buffers before times of stress can extend the survival horizon cost-effectively, and a strong balance sheet in stress opens opportunities such as gains in market share and acquisitions. GARP names the LRM EWI framework as the management tool that gives rise to this strategic advantage.

**Applying it to this question**

Statement I restates the GARP sequence (identify, inventory, assess, then measure and monitor through stress tests, EWIs, and limits), so retain it. Statement II restates the Conclusion’s alignment list, so retain it. Statement III reverses the supervisory focus: idiosyncratic EWIs attract more scrutiny because they are tailored to the bank’s vulnerabilities, so reject it. Statement IV restates the strategic benefit from “Beyond”, so retain it. The statements to retain are I, II, and IV.

**Fragile fact.** Supervisors look more closely at idiosyncratic EWIs. In GARP’s sequence, risk identification comes before EWIs.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 68.c, verbatim):** Discuss the applications of EWIs in the context of the liquidity risk management process.

**GARP:** Chapter 3, Section 3.1, “Risk Identification and EWIs” (Figure 3.1), “Introduction: Dashboard and Beyond” (“Beyond”), and “Conclusion”. **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser does not cover these passages under any LO 68 letter. They are GARP-only content, included here as the LRM-process context that the LO wording names; this is a boundary call.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-3 c, where it is Q11 of 11.

a.reason: (Scope or condition error). A rejects Statement IV, treating EWIs as purely defensive. GARP explicitly presents the EWI framework as the tool that lets a bank build buffers ahead of stress cost-effectively and take advantage of market disruption. A would be correct only if IV had claimed that EWIs remove the cost of holding liquid assets.

b.reason: (Polarity flip). B accepts Statement III, which reverses GARP’s direction. Supervisors are likely to scrutinise idiosyncratic EWIs more because they are tailored to the bank’s specific vulnerabilities. B would be correct only if III said that idiosyncratic EWIs attract closer supervisory scrutiny.

c.reason: (Scope or condition error). C rejects Statement I, as if EWIs could be designed before the bank had identified and assessed its liquidity risks. In GARP’s framework, risk identification, the risk inventory, and assessment come first, and EWIs follow as part of measurement and monitoring. C would be correct only if Statement I had put EWIs before risk identification.

d.reason: D (I, II, and IV only) keeps the three statements that GARP supports and drops the one that reverses the supervisory focus on idiosyncratic EWIs.
