questions.question: A junior risk analyst at a US savings institution is compiling notes on the principal sources of borrowed liquidity. Which of the following notes is most accurate?

options.text: Borrowing from the central bank’s discount window is usually available within minutes, provided the institution has collateral on hand and a signed borrowing authorization.
Repurchase agreements always carry a fixed interest rate and maturity, so a continuing-contract RP must be renegotiated with the lender every day.
Advances from the Federal Home Loan Bank system are available to any depository institution, regardless of whether it lends in the real-estate-backed loan market.
Eurocurrency deposits are issued at interest rates set by the central bank, rather than by the demand and supply for these short-term international deposits.

questions.solution:
Which note on the principal sources of borrowed liquidity is accurate?

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s box “Borrowing Liquidity: The Principal Options” describes six sources a bank can tap when a liquidity deficit arises. Their features matter when comparing how quickly, at what price and under what conditions purchased liquidity can be obtained.

| Source | Key features (GARP 5.4) |
|---|---|
| Federal funds borrowings | Reserves from other lenders that can be accessed immediately |
| Repurchase agreements | Sale of liquid, low-risk securities to institutions with temporary surpluses; generally fixed rate and maturity, but continuing-contract RPs stay in force until either party terminates |
| Jumbo negotiable CDs | USD 100,000 or more, issued to major corporations, governmental units and wealthy individuals for a few days to several months |
| Eurocurrency deposits | Issued to multinational banks and other corporations at rates set by the demand and supply for these short-term international deposits |
| FHLB advances | Loans from the Federal Home Loan Bank system to institutions lending in the real-estate-backed loan market; relatively low cost and more stable, with longer maturities than most deposits |
| Discount window | Usually available within minutes, provided the borrower has collateral on hand and a signed borrowing authorization |

The pattern is that the fastest sources (fed funds, discount window) are for immediate needs and carry conditions (collateral, authorization), while market-priced sources (CDs, Eurocurrency deposits) give volume control through the offer rate but expose the bank to market pricing of its risk.

**Applying it to this question**

Check each note against the box. A matches the discount-window description word for word in substance. B turns “generally” fixed rate and maturity into “always” and misdescribes continuing-contract RPs. C removes the condition that FHLB advances go to institutions lending in the real-estate-backed loan market. D gives the central bank a pricing role that GARP assigns to market demand and supply.

**Fragile fact.** The discount window is fast (minutes) but conditional: collateral on hand and a signed borrowing authorization.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** “Compare strategies that a bank can use to meet demands for additional liquidity.” **GARP:** Chapter 5, Section 5.4, box “Borrowing Liquidity: The Principal Options” and the FHLB factoid. **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser lists these sources by name only; all feature details are GARP-only.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-5 b, where it is Q10 of 12.

a.reason: A is correct: GARP states that discount window borrowing is usually available within a matter of minutes, provided the borrowing institution has collateral on hand and a signed borrowing authorization.

b.reason: (Absolute claim). GARP says RPs generally carry a fixed rate and maturity, and that continuing-contract RPs remain in force until either the borrower or the lender terminates the loan. B would be correct if it said most RPs have a fixed rate and maturity while continuing contracts run until terminated.

c.reason: (Scope error). It drops the stated condition: the FHLB system provides loans to institutions lending in the real-estate-backed loan market. C would be correct if restricted to such institutions.

d.reason: (Role misassignment). It assigns rate-setting to the central bank. GARP states that Eurocurrency deposit rates are determined by the demand and supply for these short-term international deposits. D would be correct as a description of a central bank’s own lending rate, not of Eurocurrency deposits.

questions.question:
A treasury analyst at a UK bank is comparing two funding plans for next week, when depositors are expected to withdraw GBP 300 million and the loan department wants to make GBP 450 million of new loans. The current balance sheet is shown below (GBP millions).

| Assets | GBP m | Liabilities and equity | GBP m |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cash | 120 | Deposits | 4,900 |
| Securities | 1,100 | Other borrowings | 600 |
| Loans | 4,500 | Equity | 500 |
| Premises and other | 280 |  |  |
| Total | 6,000 | Total | 6,000 |

Plan (i) raises all the funds needed by selling securities (asset conversion). Plan (ii) raises all the funds needed by issuing jumbo CDs and borrowing federal funds (liability management). Cash is unchanged in both plans. Which of the following correctly states total assets after next week under each plan?

options.text: (i) GBP 5,700 million; (ii) GBP 6,000 million
(i) GBP 6,000 million; (ii) GBP 6,450 million
(i) GBP 5,250 million; (ii) GBP 6,450 million
(i) GBP 5,700 million; (ii) GBP 6,450 million

questions.solution:
Total assets under full asset conversion vs full liability management for a GBP 300 million withdrawal plus GBP 450 million of new loans.

**Concept and theory**

The two pure strategies affect the size of the balance sheet differently, and the effect depends on whether the liquidity demand comes from the liability side or the asset side.

- **Liability-derived demand (deposit withdrawal).** Asset conversion: assets sold and cash paid out, so assets and deposits both fall and the firm shrinks (GARP states this directly). Liability management: borrowings replace deposits, so assets are unchanged.
- **Asset-side demand (new loans).** Asset conversion: securities are sold to fund loans, one asset replaces another, so size is unchanged. Liability management: new borrowings fund new loans, so both sides grow.

With withdrawal W and new loans N, the total need is W + N:

Asset conversion: $\Delta\text{TA} = -(\text{W} + \text{N}) + \text{N} = -$W

Liability management: $\Delta\text{TA} = +$N

This captures GARP’s comparison: asset conversion keeps (or shrinks) the bank’s size and changes the composition of its assets, while borrowing leaves the existing asset portfolio unchanged and lets the balance sheet grow with lending. The loan-demand case is derived from the same balance-sheet logic and appears as GARP end-of-chapter Problem 7.

**Applying it to this question**

Working, in GBP millions:

Funds needed = 300 + 450 = 750

(i) Securities sold = 750 (1,100 → 350); loans 4,500 → 4,950

(i) Total assets = 6,000 − 750 + 450 = 5,700

(i) Check = (4,900 − 300) + 600 + 500 = 5,700

(ii) Borrowed = 750; loans 4,500 → 4,950; securities unchanged

(ii) Total assets = 6,000 + 450 = 6,450

(ii) Check = (4,900 − 300) + (600 + 750) + 500 = 6,450

Under asset conversion the bank shrinks by the withdrawal (GBP 300 million); under liability management it grows by the new loans (GBP 450 million).

**Fragile fact.** Deposit drain: asset conversion shrinks, borrowing keeps size. Loan demand: asset conversion keeps size, borrowing grows. The direction flips with the source of demand.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** “Compare strategies that a bank can use to meet demands for additional liquidity.” **GARP:** Chapter 5, Section 5.4, Borrowed Liquidity (Liability) Management Strategies; end-of-chapter Problems 6 and 7. **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser does not discuss balance-sheet size; the loan-demand result is an accounting derivation consistent with GARP Problem 7.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-5 b, where it is Q11 of 12.

a.reason: (Scope error). Plan (ii) at GBP 6,000 million applies the deposit-drain rule (“borrowing leaves size unchanged”) to the whole need, ignoring that borrowing to fund new loans enlarges the balance sheet. It would be correct if the GBP 750 million were all deposit withdrawals.

b.reason: (Scope error). Plan (i) at GBP 6,000 million applies the loan-funding rule (asset swap, size unchanged) to the whole need, ignoring that selling securities to pay departing depositors shrinks the bank. It would be correct if the GBP 750 million were all new loan demand.

c.reason: (Dropped term). Plan (i) at GBP 5,250 million = 6,000 − 750 deducts the securities sold but drops the GBP 450 million of new loans that the proceeds buy. It would be correct if the whole GBP 750 million had been paid out to depositors.

d.reason: D is correct: asset conversion yields GBP 5,700 million and liability management GBP 6,450 million, consistent with GARP’s statement that asset sales for deposit withdrawals shrink the firm while borrowing leaves the asset portfolio intact.

questions.question: A risk consultant is preparing a comparison of liquidity strategies for the board of a mid-sized French banking group. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Asset conversion is used mainly by the largest institutions, since they hold the biggest securities portfolios available for sale.
Asset conversion is used mainly by smaller institutions as the less risky approach; borrowing is the riskiest but has the highest expected return.
Liability management is the least risky approach, because funds are borrowed only when actually needed and no storehouse of assets is held.
Most financial firms rely on pure liability management, because the largest banks borrow close to 100 percent of their liquidity needs.

questions.solution:
Comparison of strategies by typical user, risk and expected return.

**Concept and theory**

The core of this LO is a comparison. GARP’s Section 5.4 provides the dimensions on which the three strategies differ:

|  | Asset conversion | Liability management | Balanced |
|---|---|---|---|
| Typical user | Mainly smaller institutions | Largest banks, often borrowing close to 100% of needs | Most financial firms (compromise) |
| Risk | Less risky than relying on borrowing | Most risky approach | Not ranked separately |
| Expected return | Lowest: liquid assets carry the lowest returns | Highest expected return | Not ranked separately |
| Main cost or risk | Opportunity cost, commissions, falling markets, weaker balance-sheet appearance | Rate volatility, credit availability, uncertain cost, troubled-firm problem | Both, in part |
| Balance sheet | Shrinks for deposit withdrawals | Asset portfolio unchanged | Depends on the mix |

The pattern is a risk-return trade-off. Storing liquidity in assets is safe but expensive in forgone earnings; borrowing frees the bank from holding low-yielding assets and so raises expected return, but exposes it to the market’s pricing and willingness to lend at exactly the moments of stress. GARP notes that the largest banks use liability management most extensively, while smaller institutions use asset conversion because they find it less risky than relying on borrowings. Because neither extreme is attractive for most firms, GARP observes that most compromise by using both, which is the balanced strategy.

**Applying it to this question**

The board needs a statement that gets user, risk and return right. B states that smaller institutions use asset conversion as the less risky approach and that borrowing is the riskiest approach with the highest expected return, matching GARP on all three. A misassigns the user; C reverses the risk ranking; D overgeneralizes the largest banks’ practice to most firms.

**Fragile fact.** Smaller banks: asset conversion (safer, lower return). Largest banks: liability management (riskiest, highest expected return). Most firms: balanced.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** “Compare strategies that a bank can use to meet demands for additional liquidity.” **GARP:** Chapter 5, Section 5.4 (asset conversion, borrowed liquidity and balanced strategies). **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser says borrowing “is a risky strategy” but omits GARP’s “highest expected return”; that part is GARP-only.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-5 b, where it is Q12 of 12.

a.reason: (Role misassignment). It assigns asset conversion to the largest institutions. GARP says it is used mainly by smaller institutions, while the largest institutions rely most on liability management. A would be correct with “smaller” in place of “largest”.

b.reason: B is correct because GARP says asset conversion is used mainly by smaller institutions that find it less risky than borrowing, and that borrowing liquidity is the most risky approach but also carries the highest expected return.

c.reason: (Polarity flip). It ranks liability management as least risky; GARP ranks it most risky. The reason given (borrow only when needed, no storehouse) is a true advantage, but it concerns return, not risk. questions.question:
A treasury analyst at a Canadian commercial bank is applying the sources and uses of funds approach to the following month-end forecasts (CAD million). January is the base month. The bank also expects fee income of CAD 14 million in each month.

| Forecast | Jan | Feb | Mar | Apr | May | Jun |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Demand deposits | 340 | 325 | 350 | 310 | 330 | 315 |
| Time and savings deposits | 860 | 850 | 905 | 880 | 845 | 870 |
| Commercial loans | 690 | 735 | 700 | 760 | 745 | 720 |
| Consumer loans | 310 | 320 | 335 | 330 | 300 | 325 |

Which month is projected to show the largest liquidity deficit, and how large is it?

options.text: March, a deficit of CAD 100 million
April, a deficit of CAD 120 million
April, a deficit of CAD 95 million
May, a deficit of CAD 60 million

questions.solution:
Largest monthly liquidity deficit from deposit and loan forecasts (CAD).

**Concept and theory**

The sources and uses of funds approach (GARP 5.5) starts from two simple facts: a bank’s liquidity rises when deposits increase and loans decrease, and falls when deposits decrease and loans increase. Deposit growth and loan run-off are sources of liquidity; deposit run-off and loan growth are uses. Whenever sources and uses do not match there is a liquidity gap. When sources exceed uses the gap is positive (a surplus that must be invested quickly); when uses exceed sources the gap is negative (a deficit that must be funded from the cheapest and most timely sources).

GARP lists three steps: (1) forecast loans and deposits for the planning period; (2) calculate the estimated change in loans and deposits over that period; (3) estimate the net liquid funds surplus or deficit by comparing the two changes. The working equation (GARP Eq. 5.4) is

Liquidity surplus(+) or deficit(−) = ∆Deposits − ∆Loans,

where each ∆ is the forecast change from the previous period (here, the previous month-end), and total deposits and total loans are the sums of their components. The approach works on changes, not on levels: a bank with far more deposits than loans can still face a deficit in a month when deposits fall and loans grow. GARP’s Table 5.2 applies exactly this weekly: it flags the weeks needing new funds and the week whose surplus must be invested.

**Applying it to this question**

Total deposits (demand plus time and savings): Jan 1,200; Feb 1,175; Mar 1,255; Apr 1,190; May 1,175; Jun 1,185. Total loans (commercial plus consumer): Jan 1,000; Feb 1,055; Mar 1,035; Apr 1,090; May 1,045; Jun 1,045.

Feb : (−25) − (+55) = −80

Mar : (+80) − (−20) = +100

Apr : (−65) − (+55) = −120

May : (−15) − (−45) = +30

Jun : (+10) − (0) = +10

The largest deficit is April, CAD 120 million: deposits fall by 65 while loans rise by 55, so both move the wrong way. The fee income of CAD 14 million is irrelevant: the approach as set out in GARP compares forecast changes in deposits and loans only, and the fee figure is the same every month.

**Fragile fact.** Surplus = ∆Deposits − ∆Loans: a loan decrease is a source, a deposit decrease is a use.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** “Estimate a bank’s liquidity needs through three methods (sources and uses of funds, structure of funds, and liquidity indicators).” **GARP:** Chapter 5, Section 5.5 Estimating Liquidity Needs, “The Sources and Uses of Funds Approach”, Eq. 5.4 and Table 5.2. **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser’s sentence describes the surplus as the change in deposits “subtracted from” the change in loans, which read literally reverses the sign; GARP Eq. 5.4 and Table 5.2 (−100 − 50 = −150) use ∆D − ∆L, which is used here.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-5 c, where it is Q1 of 12.

a.reason: (Sign error). Computing ∆L − ∆D reverses every gap: March becomes −20 − 80 = −100, the largest “deficit”. In fact March is the largest surplus (deposits up 80, loans down 20). A would be right only if the question asked for the largest surplus (and then the answer would say surplus, not deficit).

b.reason: B is correct because it applies GARP’s Eq. 5.4 to the change in total deposits and total loans each month. April is the only month in which a deposit outflow and loan growth combine to a 120 gap.

c.reason: (Dropped term). Using only demand deposits as the source series gives April (310 − 350) − 55 = −95. Time and savings deposits are deposits too and fell by 25 in April. C would be right only if time deposits were held constant.

d.reason: (Polarity flip). Treating loan growth as a source (∆D + ∆L) gives May −15 + (−45) = −60 as the worst month. Loan growth uses liquidity, so its sign must be subtracted. D would be right only if loans were funding sources, which they are not.

questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a Japanese regional bank forecasts deposits and loans by splitting each into trend, seasonal and cyclical elements (JPY billion). The bank’s legal reserve requirement on transaction deposits is 3%.

| Item | Trend element | Seasonal element | Cyclical element |
|---|---|---|---|
| Deposits, week 1 | 2,410 | −35 | 15 |
| Deposits, week 2 | 2,414 | −120 | −24 |
| Loans, week 1 | 1,605 | 10 | −5 |
| Loans, week 2 | 1,607 | 88 | 25 |

Using the sources and uses of funds approach, the estimated liquidity position for week 2 is closest to:

options.text: a deficit of JPY 161 billion.
a deficit of JPY 10 billion.
a surplus of JPY 230 billion.
a deficit of JPY 230 billion.

questions.solution:
Week 2 liquidity gap from trend, seasonal and cyclical elements (JPY).

**Concept and theory**

GARP offers a “somewhat simpler” way to forecast deposits (or other funds sources) and loans (or other funds uses) inside the sources and uses approach: split the forecast into three components and add them.

| Component | What it measures (GARP 5.5) |
|---|---|
| Trend | A constant-growth line fitted to year-end, quarterly or monthly totals over at least the last 10 years. |
| Seasonal | How deposits and loans behave in a given week or month because of seasonal factors, relative to the most recent year-end level. |
| Cyclical | Positive or negative deviation from expected levels (trend plus seasonal), depending on the strength or weakness of the economy. |

Estimated total $= \text{trend} + \text{seasonal} +$ cyclical, for deposits and for loans separately (GARP Table 5.1, column 4). The totals are then fed into the gap equation (Table 5.2):

$\text{Gap}_{\text{t}} = (\text{D}_{\text{t}} - \text{D}_{\text{t}-1}) - (\text{L}_{\text{t}} - \text{L}_{\text{t}-1})$.

The decomposition only produces the levels; the liquidity decision still rests on the change in deposits minus the change in loans. GARP’s illustration shows deficits when deposits fall and loans rise in the same week, and a surplus when the reverse happens.

**Applying it to this question**

$\text{D}_{1} =$ 2410 − 35 + 15 = 2390, $\text{D}_{2} =$ 2414 − 120 − 24 = 2270

$\text{L}_{1} =$ 1605 + 10 − 5 = 1610, $\text{L}_{2} =$ 1607 + 88 + 25 = 1720

$\Delta\text{D} =$ 2270 − 2390 = −120, $\Delta\text{L} =$ 1720 − 1610 = +110

$\text{Gap}_{2} = -$120 − 110 = −230

The bank should plan to raise about JPY 230 billion in week 2. The 3% legal reserve requirement is irrelevant: legal reserves enter the structure of funds approach, not the sources and uses gap.

**Fragile fact.** The cyclical element is a deviation from trend plus seasonal; it must be added to both series before taking changes.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** “Estimate a bank’s liquidity needs through three methods (sources and uses of funds, structure of funds, and liquidity indicators).” **GARP:** Chapter 5, Section 5.5, “The Sources and Uses of Funds Approach” (three-component forecast; Tables 5.1 and 5.2). **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser describes the trend as “10-plus-year”; GARP says at least the last 10 years. Same meaning. GARP’s Table 5.1 loan rows are partly garbled in the source extract; this question relies only on the component definitions.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-5 c, where it is Q2 of 12.

a.reason: (Intermediate result (dropped term)). Omitting the cyclical element gives D: 2375 to 2294 (−81) and L: 1615 to 1695 (+80), so −161. This is the trend-plus-seasonal “expected” level only. A would be right only if the economy were assumed neutral (all cyclical elements zero).

b.reason: (Polarity flip). Adding the loan change as if it were a source, −120 + 110 = −10. Loan growth uses liquidity. B would be right only if loans had fallen by 110.

c.reason: (Sign error). Computing ∆L $- \Delta\text{D} =$ 110 − (−120) = +230 reports the right magnitude with the wrong sign. C would be right if deposits rose by 120 and loans fell by 110.

d.reason: D is correct: all three components are summed for each series, and the gap is the deposit change minus the loan change, giving a deficit of JPY 230 billion.

questions.question:
An internal auditor at a German savings bank is reviewing the bank’s sources and uses of funds methodology document, which contains the following statements:

I. The estimated change in total loans is modelled as a function of projected economic growth, quarterly corporate earnings, money supply growth, the prime rate minus the commercial paper or CD rate, and expected inflation.

II. The seasonal component captures positive or negative deviations from expected deposits and loans that depend on the strength or weakness of the economy in the current year.

III. The estimated liquidity surplus or deficit for the coming period equals the estimated change in deposits minus the estimated change in loans.

IV. The trend component should be fitted to no more than the last two to three years of data so that it reflects current conditions.

Which of the statements are accurate?

options.text: I and III only
I, II and III only
III and IV only
I, III and IV only

questions.solution:
Auditing a sources and uses methodology: drivers, components, sign.

**Concept and theory**

In the sources and uses approach, banks forecast deposits and loans with statistical models plus management judgment (GARP Eqs. 5.2 and 5.3). The drivers are deliberately different for the two series:

| Series | Drivers named in GARP |
|---|---|
| Change in total loans | Projected growth in the economy (GDP or business sales), quarterly corporate earnings, current growth of the money supply, the prime loan rate minus the commercial paper or CD rate, estimated inflation |
| Change in total deposits | Projected growth in personal income, increase in retail sales, current growth of the money supply, projected yield on money market deposits, estimated inflation |

The loan equation contains the prime-minus-CP spread because that spread governs whether corporate borrowers turn to banks or to the paper market. The deposit equation contains household income, retail sales and money market deposit yields because these drive what customers place with the bank. The forecasts feed Eq. 5.4, surplus = ∆D − ∆L. A simpler alternative splits each forecast into a trend component (a constant-growth line over at least ten years), a seasonal component (behaviour in a given week or month relative to the latest year-end) and a cyclical component (deviations that depend on the strength or weakness of the economy).

**Applying it to this question**

Statement I matches GARP’s loan equation: true. Statement II describes the cyclical component, not the seasonal one: false. Statement III is Eq. 5.4: true. Statement IV contradicts GARP’s “at least the last 10 years” base period: false. Accurate set: I and III only.

**Fragile fact.** The prime-minus-CP spread drives loans; money market deposit yields drive deposits. Economy strength defines the cyclical element.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** “Estimate a bank’s liquidity needs through three methods (sources and uses of funds, structure of funds, and liquidity indicators).” **GARP:** Chapter 5, Section 5.5, “The Sources and Uses of Funds Approach”, Eqs. 5.2 to 5.4. **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser’s surplus sentence reads as ∆L − ∆D; GARP’s ∆D − ∆L is used (see Q1). Equations 5.2 and 5.3 are garbled in the source extract; the driver lists were reconstructed and match Schweser’s lists.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-5 c, where it is Q3 of 12.

a.reason: A is correct because only I and III restate GARP accurately: the loan forecasting drivers and the ∆D − ∆L surplus convention.

b.reason: (Sibling swap (in statement II)). B adds statement II, which gives the seasonal component the cyclical component’s definition. Seasonal compares a week or month with the year-end level. B would be right if statement II read “cyclical component”.

c.reason: (Scope error (in statement IV) plus omission). C includes IV, which shortens GARP’s base period of at least ten years to two or three years, and it leaves out the true statement I. C would be right only if statement IV said “at least the last ten years” and statement I were false.

d.reason: (Scope error (in statement IV)). D adds IV, which shortens the trend base period. A trend estimated over two or three years would be dominated by the cycle. D would be right if IV said “at least the last ten years”.

questions.question: A member of the board risk committee of an Australian bank asks the CRO how the bank sizes its liquidity reserves on top of the estimates produced by its liquidity estimation models. Which response by the CRO best describes the two components of liquidity reserves?

options.text: The protective component is the reserve called for by the latest forecast, and the planned component is an extra margin set by management’s risk attitude.
The protective component is fixed by the central bank’s legal reserve rules, so it is identical across all banks holding the same deposits.
The planned component is the reserve called for by the latest forecast, and the protective component is an extra margin set by management’s risk attitude.
Once forecasts have been refined, the estimation methods give exact requirements, so the protective component can safely be set to zero.

questions.solution:
Planned versus protective components of liquidity reserves (AUD bank).

**Concept and theory**

GARP opens Section 5.5 by noting that each estimation method (sources and uses, structure of funds, liquidity indicators, market signals) “rests on specific assumptions” and yields only an approximation of actual liquidity requirements. That is why a liquidity manager must keep fine-tuning estimates as new information arrives, and why most financial firms build their liquidity reserves in two layers:

| Component | Definition (GARP 5.5) |
|---|---|
| Planned | The reserves called for by the latest forecast |
| Protective | An extra margin of liquid reserves above those dictated by the most recent forecast |

The protective layer may be large or small, depending on management’s philosophy and attitude toward risk: in GARP’s words, how much chance of running a “cash-out” management is willing to accept. It is a management choice, not a regulatory rule. Legal reserves are a separate concept handled by the money position manager (LO 70.d). The two-layer design follows from the fact that forecasts are approximations. The planned layer covers the forecast; the protective layer covers forecast error.

**Applying it to this question**

The committee member asks how reserves are sized on top of the model estimates. The deciding fact is which layer is tied to the forecast (planned) and which is the discretionary cushion (protective), and who sets the cushion (management, by its risk appetite).

**Fragile fact.** Planned = forecast; protective = cushion above forecast, sized by management’s risk attitude.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** “Estimate a bank’s liquidity needs through three methods (sources and uses of funds, structure of funds, and liquidity indicators).” **GARP:** Chapter 5, Section 5.5 Estimating Liquidity Needs (introduction). **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser says the protective component is “based on recent forecasted liquidity needs”, which blurs it with the planned component. GARP defines it as a margin over the forecast; GARP is used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-5 c, where it is Q4 of 12.

a.reason: (Sibling swap). A swaps the two labels. The forecast-driven amount is the planned component. A would be right if the labels “planned” and “protective” were exchanged.

b.reason: (Role misassignment). B makes the central bank set the cushion. GARP makes it management’s choice, varying with risk appetite, so it differs across banks. B would describe legal reserve requirements, not the protective component.

c.reason: C matches GARP exactly: planned = latest forecast requirement; protective = extra margin whose size reflects management’s attitude toward risk.

d.reason: (Absolute claim). GARP stresses that every method yields only an approximation, so forecast error never disappears. D would be right only if forecasts were certain.

questions.question:
A junior risk analyst at a Singapore bank is setting up the structure of funds approach. She has identified three funding items:

I. SGD 40 million of overnight interbank borrowings that management is sure will run off this period.

II. SGD 120 million of large corporate deposits, of which roughly a quarter is expected to leave this period.

III. SGD 600 million of small retail savings balances that rarely move.

Which of the following statements about how she should apply the approach is most accurate?

options.text: Item I is hot money, and management’s operating rule sets a high liquid reserve percentage on it, net of legal reserves held.
Item II is hot money because part of it will leave, so it should carry a liquid reserve percentage close to 100%.
Item III is core funding and needs the highest liquid reserve percentage because it is the largest balance.
The reserve percentages for all three categories are prescribed by the central bank, so the analyst simply applies them.

questions.solution:
Classifying funds and setting operating rules under the structure of funds approach (SGD).

**Concept and theory**

The structure of funds approach (GARP 5.5) has two steps. First, deposits and other funds sources are divided into categories according to their estimated probability of being withdrawn and therefore lost to the bank:

| Category | GARP description | Illustrative reserve |
|---|---|---|
| Hot money (volatile) | Deposits and borrowed funds (e.g. federal funds borrowings) that are very interest sensitive or that management is sure will be withdrawn this period | 95% |
| Vulnerable funds | Customer deposits of which a substantial portion, perhaps 25 to 30%, will probably be withdrawn this period | 30% |
| Stable (core) funds | Unlikely to be removed except for a minor percentage | 15% or less |

Second, the liquidity manager sets aside liquid funds according to a desired operating rule for each category, applied net of the legal reserves already held behind those funds (GARP Eq. 5.5). The percentages are management’s subjective choices, relying on judgment, experience and attitude toward risk. GARP’s and Schweser’s examples use different figures (95/30/15 versus 90/25/10), and Schweser notes the exam will provide them. The reserve can be held as immediately spendable correspondent deposits, Treasury bills and repurchase agreements.

**Applying it to this question**

Item I is borrowed funds that management is sure will leave: hot money. Item II has about a quarter at risk: vulnerable. Item III is stable core funding. The highest percentage goes on the category most likely to leave, net of legal reserves held, and the percentages are set by management.

**Fragile fact.** Category is set by probability of withdrawal; the percentage is management’s rule, applied net of legal reserves.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** “Estimate a bank’s liquidity needs through three methods (sources and uses of funds, structure of funds, and liquidity indicators).” **GARP:** Chapter 5, Section 5.5, “The Structure of Funds Approach”, Eq. 5.5. **GARP vs Schweser:** illustrative percentages differ (GARP 95/30/15, Schweser 90/25/10); no conceptual conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-5 c, where it is Q5 of 12.

a.reason: A is correct: item I fits GARP’s hot money definition, and the reserve percentage comes from management’s operating rule applied net of legal reserves.

b.reason: (Sibling swap). Deposits with roughly a quarter likely to leave are GARP’s vulnerable funds, which carry about 25 to 30%, not close to 100%. B would be right if management were sure the whole balance would leave.

c.reason: (Polarity flip). Core funds carry the lowest percentage (15% or less) because withdrawal is unlikely. Size does not drive the percentage; the probability of withdrawal does. C would be right if “highest” read “lowest”.

d.reason: (Role misassignment). The central bank sets legal reserve requirements, which are only deducted. The liquidity percentages are management’s operating rules. D would be right only for the legal reserve deduction itself.

| Category | Amount | Desired reserve (%) |
|---|---|---|
| Hot money funds | 60 | 90 |
| Vulnerable funds | 140 | 30 |
| Stable (core) funds | 480 | 12 |

Loans outstanding are GBP 900 million, recently peaked at GBP 930 million and grow at a trend rate of 5% a year. The liability liquidity reserve is closest to:

Vulnerable: 0.30 (140 − 0.04 × 140) = 0.30 × 134.4 = 40.32

Core: 0.12 (480 − 0.04 × 480) = 0.12 × 460.8 = 55.296

Liability reserve = 51.84 + 40.32 + 55.296 = 147.456 ≈ 147.5

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** “Estimate a bank’s liquidity needs through three methods (sources and uses of funds, structure of funds, and liquidity indicators).” **GARP:** Chapter 5, Section 5.5, “The Structure of Funds Approach”, Eq. 5.5 and Table 5.3. **GARP vs Schweser:** none in method; illustrative figures differ.

| Category | Amount | Desired reserve (%) |
|---|---|---|
| Hot money funds | 30 | 95 |
| Vulnerable funds | 75 | 25 |
| Stable (core) funds | 250 | 10 |

$\text{L}^{\text{max}} =$ 425 × 1.08 = 459.0

Loan requirement = 459.0 − 410 = 49.0

TLR = 70.805 + 49.0 = 119.805 ≈ 119.8

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-5 c, where it is Q7 of 12.

a.reason: (Intermediate result). 70.8 is the liability liquidity reserve alone. A would be right if the bank did not aim to meet all good loan demand, or if the question asked for the liability reserve.

b.reason: (Dropped term). Using only peak minus actual loans, 425 − 410 = 15, ignores trend growth: 70.805 + 15 = 85.8. B would be right if the trend growth rate were zero.

c.reason: (Wrong input twin). Growing current loans instead of the peak: 410 × 0.08 = 32.8, so 70.805 + 32.8 = 103.6. C would be right only if the bank had no recent peak above current loans, so that potential loans were simply current loans grown at trend.

d.reason: D is correct: it adds the full gap between potential loans (the recent peak grown at trend) and actual loans to the liability reserve, as GARP Table 5.3 does.

questions.question: The chief credit officer of a eurozone bank questions why the structure of funds approach adds a loan liquidity requirement equal to 100% of the gap between maximum potential loans and actual loans outstanding. Which explanation is most accurate?

options.text: Borrowers usually leave loan proceeds on deposit at the lender, so only about 30% of the potential new loans needs to be covered by liquid reserves.
Liquidity takes priority over lending, so the bank should turn down good loan requests whenever its liquid reserves fall below the estimated requirement.
Borrowers spend loan proceeds at once, yet good loan customers bring deposits and fee business, so the full gap is held in liquid assets or borrowing capacity.
The full gap must be held as liquid assets on the balance sheet, because unused borrowing capacity cannot count toward a liquidity requirement.

questions.solution:
Why the loan liquidity requirement is 100% of potential minus actual loans (EUR).

**Concept and theory**

The loan side of the structure of funds approach reflects GARP’s view of the lending relationship. A lending institution must be ready at all times to make good loans, meaning loans to customers who meet its quality standards and have legitimate credit needs. It needs liquid reserves for them because, once a loan is made, the borrower spends the proceeds immediately and the funds flow out to other institutions. Yet the lender does not want to turn down any good loan: loan customers bring in new deposits and are normally the principal source of interest and fee earnings. Under relationship banking, once a customer takes a loan the lender can sell other services, building a multidimensional relationship that adds fee income and loyalty.

GARP adds that a substantial body of current thinking says a lender should make all good loans, counting on its ability to borrow liquid funds if needed. Management therefore estimates the maximum possible total loans and holds, in liquid reserves or borrowing capacity, the full (100%) difference between that maximum and actual loans outstanding. GARP also notes that liquidity management has been relegated to a supporting role relative to the top priority of making loans and supplying fee-generating services to qualified customers.

**Applying it to this question**

The CCO’s question is about the 100% weight. The deciding facts are: proceeds leave immediately (so cover is needed), good customers are valuable (so do not turn them away), and cover can be liquid assets or borrowing capacity.

**Fragile fact.** Proceeds leave immediately; the gap is covered at 100%, by liquid assets or borrowing capacity.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** “Estimate a bank’s liquidity needs through three methods (sources and uses of funds, structure of funds, and liquidity indicators).” **GARP:** Chapter 5, Section 5.5, “The Structure of Funds Approach” (loan liquidity requirement); Section 5.4, “Guidelines for Liquidity Managers” (priorities). **GARP vs Schweser:** none; Schweser condenses the rationale to “loans often lead to other forms of business”.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-5 c, where it is Q8 of 12.

a.reason: (Polarity flip). GARP says borrowers spend proceeds immediately and the funds flow out, the opposite of leaving them on deposit. The 30% figure belongs to vulnerable deposits. A would be right only if loan proceeds stayed in the bank.

b.reason: (Polarity flip). GARP says the lender does not want to turn down any good loan, and today lending ranks above liquidity, which plays a supporting role. B describes the older view in which liquidity got top priority.

c.reason: C restates GARP’s rationale: immediate spending of proceeds, the relationship value of good loan customers, and holding the full gap in liquid assets or borrowing capacity.

d.reason: (Scope error). GARP explicitly counts borrowing capacity: the requirement is held “in liquid reserves or borrowing capacity”. D would be right only for a bank with no access to borrowed funds.

questions.question:
The treasurer of a Brazilian bank refines the structure of funds approach by assigning probabilities to possible outcomes for next week (BRL million):

| Outcome | Average deposits | Average loans | Probability (%) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Best (maximum deposits, minimum loans) | 880 | 610 | 20 |
| Most likely | 820 | 700 | 50 |
| Adverse | 760 | 790 | 20 |
| Worst (minimum deposits, maximum loans) | 700 | 900 | 10 |

The bank’s expected liquidity requirement for next week is closest to:

options.text: a surplus of BRL 40 million.
a surplus of BRL 120 million.
a surplus of BRL 114 million.
a surplus of BRL 88 million.

questions.solution:
Probability-weighted expected liquidity requirement (BRL).

**Concept and theory**

GARP presents the use of probabilities as a refinement of the structure of funds approach. The manager defines the worst possible liquidity position (deposit growth below expectations at the bottom of its historical track, loan demand above the top of its track: maximum pressure and a sizeable deficit) and the best possible position (deposits at the top of their track, loans along their minimum path: likely a surplus). The most likely outcome lies in between. For each outcome, the estimated surplus or deficit is average deposits minus average loans, and

E\[Liquidity requirement$] = \sum_{\text{s}} \pi_{\text{s}} \times($surplus or deficit$)_{\text{s}}$, $\sum_{\text{s}} \pi_{\text{s}} =$ 1.

In GARP’s example: 0.15(+60) + 0.60(+10) + 0.25(−20) = +10, so management plans for a USD 10 million surplus, reviews investment options, and keeps a contingency plan for the worst case. The expected value is the planning figure; the worst case drives the contingency plan.

**Applying it to this question**

Best: 880 − 610 = +270 × 0.20 = +54

Most likely: 820 − 700 = +120 × 0.50 = +60

Adverse: 760 − 790 = −30 × 0.20 = −6

Worst: 700 − 900 = −200 × 0.10 = −20

E = 54 + 60 − 6 − 20 = +88

The bank should plan to invest an expected BRL 88 million surplus and keep a contingency plan for the BRL 200 million worst-case deficit. The probabilities sum to 100%.

**Fragile fact.** Best = maximum deposits, minimum loans; each outcome’s position is deposits minus loans, weighted by probability.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** “Estimate a bank’s liquidity needs through three methods (sources and uses of funds, structure of funds, and liquidity indicators).” **GARP:** Chapter 5, Section 5.5, probability refinement of “The Structure of Funds Approach”, Eq. 5.7. **GARP vs** **Schweser:** none.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-5 c, where it is Q9 of 12.

a.reason: (Wrong input (equal weights)). Simple average: (270 + 120 − 30 − 200)/4 = 40. A would be right only if all four outcomes had 25% probability.

b.reason: (Intermediate result). Using the most likely outcome alone, +120, ignores the other outcomes. B would be right if the most likely outcome had 100% probability.

c.reason: (Dropped term). Weighting only the surplus outcomes, 54 + 60 = 114, drops the −6 and −20 deficit terms. C would be right if the adverse and worst outcomes had zero probability.

d.reason: D is correct: each outcome’s surplus or deficit is weighted by its probability, as in GARP Eq. 5.7.

questions.loText: Estimate a bank’s liquidity needs through three methods (sources and uses of funds, structure of funds, and liquidity indicators).
questions.reading: LTR-5: Liquidity and Reserves Management: Strategies and Policies
questions.topic: Liquidity and Reserves Management: Strategies and Policies
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-5 c Q10
questions.question:
A bank examiner at a US regulator is computing liquidity indicators for a mid-sized bank from the following balance sheet items (USD million):

| Asset item | Amount | Liability item | Amount |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cash and due from depository inst. | 220 | Large CDs (over USD 100,000) | 350 |
| Short-term securities | 180 | Eurocurrency deposits | 120 |
| Federal funds sold | 90 | Federal funds purchased | 80 |
| Reverse repurchase agreements | 60 | Repurchase agreements | 100 |
| Long-term government bonds | 400 | Brokered deposits | 70 |
| Total assets | 4,000 | Core deposits | 2,100 |

The bank’s hot money ratio is closest to:
questions.solution:
Hot money ratio from a balance sheet with excess data (USD).

**Concept and theory**

The liquidity indicator approach estimates liquidity needs from experience and industry averages, using balance sheet ratios. GARP defines the hot money ratio as

Hot money ratio $= \frac{\text{Money market (short-term) assets}}{\text{Volatile liabilities}}$ ,

where money market assets = cash and due from depository institutions + holdings of short-term securities + federal funds loans (sold) + reverse repurchase agreements, and volatile liabilities $= \text{large CDs} + \text{Eurocurrency deposits} +$ federal funds borrowings (purchased) + repurchase agreements. The ratio shows whether the bank has roughly balanced the volatile liabilities it has issued with money market assets it could sell quickly to cover them. A higher value means more liquidity, a positive indicator, even though “hot money” sounds risky. Related indicators use other denominators: cash position (cash and due from banks over total assets), liquid securities (government securities over total assets), core deposit ratio (deposits under USD 100,000 over total assets), and deposit brokerage index (brokered over total deposits).

**Applying it to this question**

Money market assets = 220 + 180 + 90 + 60 = 550

Volatile liabilities = 350 + 120 + 80 + 100 = 650

Hot money ratio = 550/650 = 0.846 = 84.6%

Long-term government bonds, brokered deposits, core deposits and total assets are irrelevant: they belong to other indicators. A ratio below 100% means volatile funding is not fully covered by money market assets.

**Fragile fact.** Hot money ratio = money market assets over volatile liabilities; higher means more liquid.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** “Estimate a bank’s liquidity needs through three methods (sources and uses of funds, structure of funds, and liquidity indicators).” **GARP:** Chapter 5, Section 5.5, “Liquidity Indicator Approach”, indicator 6. **GARP vs Schweser:** none.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-5 c, where it is Q10 of 12.

a.reason: A is correct: it uses exactly GARP’s four money market asset items over the four volatile liability items.

b.reason: (Scope error). Adding brokered deposits to volatile liabilities: 550/720 = 76.4%. Brokered deposits feed the deposit brokerage index, not the hot money ratio. B would be right if brokered deposits were in GARP’s volatile liability list.

c.reason: (Inverted ratio). 650/550 = 118.2% puts volatile liabilities over money market assets. C would be the reciprocal, where higher means less liquidity.

d.reason: (Scope error). Including long-term government bonds in the numerator: 950/650 = 146.2%. Only short-term securities qualify. D would be right if the bonds matured within the money market horizon.

questions.loText: Estimate a bank’s liquidity needs through three methods (sources and uses of funds, structure of funds, and liquidity indicators).

questions.question:
A portfolio manager at an asset manager holding a bank’s senior debt compares the bank’s liquidity indicators over two years:

| Indicator (%) | Prior year | Current year |
|---|---|---|
| Deposit composition ratio | 55.0 | 48.0 |
| Net federal funds and repurchase agreements position | −3.1 | −1.4 |
| Deposit brokerage index | 2.0 | 4.5 |
| Hot money ratio | 70.0 | 92.0 |
| Capacity ratio | 61.0 | 61.0 |

Which change most clearly signals a deterioration in the bank’s liquidity?

options.text: The fall in the deposit composition ratio
The rise in the net federal funds and repurchase agreements position
The rise in the deposit brokerage index
The rise in the hot money ratio

questions.solution:
Which indicator trend signals deteriorating liquidity.

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s liquidity indicators split by the direction of their signal:

| Higher value = more liquidity | Higher value = less liquidity |
|---|---|
| Cash position indicator; liquid securities indicator; net federal funds and repurchase agreements position; hot money ratio; core deposit ratio | Capacity ratio (net loans and leases / total assets); pledged securities ratio; deposit composition ratio (demand / time deposits); loan commitments ratio; deposit brokerage index (brokered / total deposits) |

The reasons matter more than the lists. Brokered deposits are packages of funds, usually USD 100,000 or less for deposit insurance, placed by brokers with institutions paying the highest yields. They are interest sensitive and may be withdrawn quickly, so “the more a depository institution holds, the greater the chance of a liquidity crisis”. Demand deposits can be withdrawn at once, while time deposits carry penalties for early withdrawal, so a decline in demand-to-time deposits means greater stability. A rising net federal funds position means overnight lending is growing relative to overnight borrowing. GARP also stresses that managers watch the change in each indicator.

**Applying it to this question**

Deposit composition fell (more stable funding): an improvement. Net federal funds position rose from −3.1% to −1.4%: an improvement. Deposit brokerage index more than doubled: a deterioration. Hot money ratio rose: better coverage of volatile liabilities. The unchanged capacity ratio is irrelevant.

**Fragile fact.** Deposit composition and brokerage index are negative indicators; the hot money ratio is positive.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** “Estimate a bank’s liquidity needs through three methods (sources and uses of funds, structure of funds, and liquidity indicators).” **GARP:** Chapter 5, Section 5.5, “Liquidity Indicator Approach”, indicators 1 to 10. **GARP vs Schweser:** none.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-5 c, where it is Q11 of 12.

a.reason: (Polarity flip). Treats the deposit composition ratio as positive. GARP says a decline suggests greater deposit stability and a smaller need for liquidity. A would be right if the ratio had risen.

b.reason: (Polarity flip). A rising net federal funds and repo position shows a shift toward net overnight lending; GARP says liquidity tends to increase as it rises. B would be right if the position had fallen.

c.reason: C is correct: the deposit brokerage index is a negative indicator, and its rise means more reliance on rate-sensitive, quickly withdrawn brokered funds.

d.reason: (Sibling confusion). Confuses the hot money ratio with hot money liabilities. The ratio has money market assets in the numerator, so a rise is favourable. D would be right if the ratio had fallen.

questions.question: A senior risk analyst at a bank is presenting the liquidity indicator approach to newly hired analysts. Which statement in her presentation is most accurate?

options.text: Indicators based on stored liquidity tend to rise during boom periods of strong loan demand and to fall when business activity is sluggish.
Indicators based on purchased liquidity tend to rise quickly when credit demand is heavy, and managers focus on changes in indicators judged against similar peers.
Industrywide averages are the preferred benchmark for each indicator because they remove differences in bank size and local market conditions.
A rise in the loan commitments ratio implies smaller future liquidity needs, because unused commitments are not yet on the balance sheet.

questions.solution:
Stored versus purchased liquidity indicators, peers and changes.

**Concept and theory**

GARP notes that about half the liquidity indicators focus on liquid assets, which it calls stored liquidity. The other half focus on liabilities or future lending commitments, mainly purchased liquidity. The two groups behave differently over the season and the business cycle:

| Group | Boom (heavy loan demand) | Sluggish economy |
|---|---|---|
| Stored liquidity (asset-based) | Often decline, as liquid assets are run down to fund loans | Rise again |
| Purchased liquidity (liability-based) | Increase quickly as borrowing grows | Begin falling |

GARP then gives two rules for interpretation. First, using industrywide averages can be misleading: each institution’s liquidity must be judged against peer institutions of similar size in similar markets. Second, managers usually focus on changes in their indicators rather than levels: they want to know whether liquidity is rising or falling, and why. GARP’s Table 5.4 shows how far indicators move over time; for example, the loan commitments ratio rose to 70.9% in 2003 before falling to 45.2% in 2010 as commitments evaporated in the recession. A rise in the loan commitments ratio signals greater future liquidity needs, because commitments can be taken down at uncertain times and amounts.

**Applying it to this question**

The deciding facts are the cyclical direction of each group, the peer benchmark, and the focus on changes. Only one option states all of them correctly.

**Fragile fact.** Stored liquidity falls in booms; purchased liquidity rises in booms. Benchmark against peers, and watch changes.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** “Estimate a bank’s liquidity needs through three methods (sources and uses of funds, structure of funds, and liquidity indicators).” **GARP:** Chapter 5, Section 5.5, “Liquidity Indicator Approach” (stored versus purchased liquidity; peer comparison; Table 5.4). **GARP vs Schweser:** none; Schweser omits the peer-group point (GARP used).

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-5 c, where it is Q12 of 12.

a.reason: (Polarity flip). Stored-liquidity indicators fall in booms (liquid assets are run down to make loans) and rise in sluggish periods. A would be right if “stored” read “purchased”.

b.reason: B is correct: purchased-liquidity indicators rise quickly when credit demand is heavy, and managers focus on changes judged against similar peers, both as stated in GARP.

c.reason: (Role misassignment (wrong benchmark)). GARP warns that industrywide averages can mislead and that the right benchmark is peers of similar size in similar markets. C would be right only if every bank were alike in size and market.

d.reason: (Polarity flip). GARP says a rise in the loan commitments ratio implies greater future liquidity needs: being off the balance sheet is exactly what makes takedown timing uncertain. D would be right if the ratio had fallen.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Identify and explain the uses and sources of intraday liquidity.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-6 a Q1
questions.question: A risk consultant is presenting to newly hired analysts at a Canadian bank. One analyst points out that the domestic banking system starts and ends each business day with very large deposits at the central bank, and asks why individual banks still run daylight overdrafts in the middle of the day. Which of the following explanations is most consistent with the reading?

options.text: Daylight overdrafts arise only when the system as a whole opens the day short of reserves, so ample opening deposits at the central bank should remove them.
Borrowed interbank funds are usually returned first thing the next morning while new borrowing covers afternoon shortfalls, and banks let clients make payments before covering funds arrive.
A bank expecting a large end-of-day credit from a clearinghouse usually borrows early to avoid any intraday deficit, preferring to carry the uninvested proceeds overnight.
Banks grant daylight overdraft lines to clients mainly because each line earns a direct fee, so client overdrafts are a priced and fully compensated exposure.

questions.solution:
Why banks run daylight overdrafts although the system opens and closes the day with ample central bank deposits.

**Concept and theory**

GARP opens Section 6.2 with a puzzle. The US banking system starts and ends each day with plenty of cash at the Federal Reserve (nearly USD 1.5 trillion at end-2012), and reserve requirements even mandate some deposits. So why do individual banks run short during the day? GARP gives a two-part answer.

First, market conventions and behaviours that have been ingrained over decades institutionalise intraday overdrafts:

- Fed funds can be borrowed at any time of the business day with almost immediate delivery, but the borrowed funds are typically returned as a first-order item the next morning. The typical pattern is to borrow to cover afternoon shortfalls and repay at the next opening, so a net borrower may overdraw its Fed account in mid-day after repaying yesterday’s borrowing.
- Many (not all) FMUs settle in one window, typically at the end of the day. A bank expecting a large end-of-day credit (for example from selling a large block of securities) could not invest it on receipt, so rather than hold a large uninvested balance overnight it prefers to run a deficit until the credit arrives.

Second, banks provide intraday credit to clients. Corporate and institutional clients are allowed to deploy cash before funds arrive (payroll paid in the morning ahead of an afternoon incoming wire; a custody client buying an asset before a maturing asset is credited). Banks set up daylight overdraft lines for this and typically receive no direct compensation.

These two drivers explain why the uses of intraday liquidity run ahead of the sources during the day even when the system is flush at the open and close.

**Applying it to this question**

The analyst’s premise (ample system-wide deposits at the open and close) is exactly GARP’s starting point, so any answer that blames a system-wide shortage is ruled out. The deciding facts are the two drivers: the timing convention of overnight funds (delivered at once, repaid first thing next morning) and intraday credit given to clients. Option B states both. The Canadian setting is irrelevant: the mechanism is generic.

**Fragile fact.** Direction: fed funds are delivered almost immediately but repaid first thing the next morning; the mid-day overdraft follows the repayment.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser 71.a, verbatim):** “Identify and explain the uses and sources of intraday liquidity.”

**GARP:** Chapter 6, Intraday Liquidity Risk Management, Section 6.2, Uses and Sources of Intraday Liquidity (introductory discussion).

**GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser’s LO 71.a summary does not reproduce this explanation of why overdrafts arise; the content is GARP-only and sits inside the GARP section mapped to this LO.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-6 a, where it is Q1 of 13.

a.reason: (Scope or condition error). It makes a system-wide reserve shortage a necessary condition. GARP stresses that the system starts and ends the day with plenty of cash, yet individual banks still overdraw because of timing conventions and client credit. A would only be right in a stem asking about end-of-day (overnight) reserve shortfalls in a system that is short of reserves.

b.reason: B paraphrases GARP’s two drivers: borrowed fed funds are returned “as a first order item” the next morning while new borrowing covers afternoon shortfalls, and banks let clients pay before covering funds arrive, through daylight overdraft lines.

c.reason: (Polarity flip). GARP says the bank prefers to keep its account in deficit until the clearinghouse credit arrives, rather than carry a large uninvested balance overnight. C reverses that preference. It would be right only if the bank could invest the late credit on receipt, which GARP says it typically cannot.

d.reason: (Polarity flip). GARP states that banks typically do not receive direct compensation for client daylight overdraft lines. D would be right only in a regime where banks charge clients for intraday credit; GARP notes (in the monitoring discussion) only that banks with real-time client data could pass central bank charges on “if the industry moves in that direction”.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Identify and explain the uses and sources of intraday liquidity.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-6 a Q2
questions.question:
A senior treasury analyst at a Japanese bank is validating a draft procedures memo on outgoing wire transfers, which the bank sends in JPY over the domestic large value payment system. The memo contains the following statements:

I. Outgoing wires, sent for clients and for the bank’s own account, are typically the largest use of intraday liquidity.

II. Outgoing payment activity is concentrated in a single late-afternoon window, which makes its timing hard to predict.

III. When the daylight overdraft approaches the debit cap, a large bank may throttle outgoing payments while closely monitoring incoming credits.

IV. The bank’s own payments can usually be forecast with one to two days’ notice, whereas client payment activity is harder to predict.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.text: I and III only
II and IV only
I, II and III only
I, III and IV only

questions.solution:
Four-statement audit of a memo on outgoing wire transfers as a use of intraday liquidity.

**Concept and theory**

GARP Table 6.2 lists five common uses of intraday liquidity: outgoing wire transfers, settlements at PCS systems, funding of nostro accounts, collateral pledging, and asset purchases/funding. Outgoing wires are singled out as typically the largest use (Schweser: the most significant use).

Key features from GARP:

- **Who:** payments on large value payment systems (LVPSs) such as Fedwire and CHIPS, made on behalf of clients or for the bank’s own account. Both client and bank activity drive them.
- **When:** activity runs the entire business day and follows a fairly predictable pattern (Schweser: “a steady pattern”).
- **Control:** as the daylight overdraft approaches the debit cap, large banks “throttle” outgoing payments and closely monitor incoming credits so the cap is not exceeded. Most LVPSs and some PCS systems have hard controls that stop participants from exceeding intraday credit limits.
- **Forecasting:** bank activity can usually be forecast with 1 to 2 days’ notice; client payment activity is more difficult to predict (Schweser: client wires are “often unpredictable”).

Contrast this with PCS settlements, which GARP describes as mostly a single settlement per day, many in the late afternoon. Mixing the two profiles is the classic trap.

**Applying it to this question**

I: true, the “largest use” statement. II: false, it attaches the PCS profile (one late-afternoon settlement) to wires, which actually flow all day in a fairly predictable pattern. III: true, throttling near the debit cap plus monitoring incoming credits. IV: true, bank payments 1 to 2 days’ notice versus less predictable client payments. Correct set: I, III and IV.

**Fragile fact.** Wires: all day, fairly predictable, the largest use; the single late-afternoon window belongs to PCS settlement.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser 71.a, verbatim):** “Identify and explain the uses and sources of intraday liquidity.”

**GARP:** Chapter 6, Intraday Liquidity Risk Management, Section 6.2, Table 6.2 (Uses of Intraday Credit) and “Outgoing wire transfers”.

**GARP vs Schweser:** none of substance. Schweser adds that controls “often exist that do not allow any exceptions” and that payments “can be slightly delayed”, which is consistent with GARP’s throttling and hard controls.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-6 a, where it is Q2 of 13.

a.reason: (Scope or condition error). A rejects IV, treating client and bank payments as equally forecastable. GARP draws the distinction explicitly. A would be right only if IV claimed client wires were the more predictable component.

b.reason: (Sibling swap). B accepts II, which gives wires the PCS profile (one late-afternoon window), and drops the true statements I and III. It would fit a memo about settlements at PCS systems, not wires.

c.reason: (Sibling swap). C contains I and III but also accepts the sibling-swapped II, and leaves out the true IV. Again the late-afternoon single window belongs to PCS settlement.

d.reason: D matches GARP’s description of outgoing wires on all three true points and rejects the one sibling-swapped statement.
