questions.loText: Identify and explain the uses and sources of intraday liquidity.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-6 a Q3
questions.question: A treasury analyst at a Brazilian bank reviews the bank’s participation in a domestic clearinghouse that settles once per business day in the late afternoon. On Monday the bank received a net credit of BRL 310 million at settlement; on Tuesday it paid a net debit of BRL 185 million. Which of the following best describes how this activity fits into the bank’s intraday liquidity framework?

options.text: It acted as a source of funds on Monday and a use on Tuesday, and the amounts are easier to forecast for securities with multi-day settlement than for same-day settlement activity.
It is always a use of funds, because settlements at PCS systems are listed among the uses of intraday liquidity whatever the participant’s net position.
It acted as a source of funds on Monday and a use on Tuesday, and the amounts are easier to forecast for same-day settlement activity than for securities with multi-day settlement.
Like outgoing wire transfers, it runs throughout the business day in a fairly predictable pattern, so it can be managed by throttling individual payments.

questions.solution:
Classifying a once-daily clearinghouse net settlement and its forecastability.

**Concept and theory**

Settlements at payment, clearing and settlement (PCS) systems are the second use in GARP Table 6.2. A PCS (or FMU such as a clearinghouse) nets the many transactions of each participant during the day and settles the net amount by transferring funds to or from the clearinghouse accounts, which may be held at another bank or at the central bank.

Key features:

- **Timing:** most PCS systems have one settlement per day, many in the late afternoon (Schweser: once daily, near the end of the business day).
- **Direction:** because the settlement is net, it may be a source or a use of funds depending on the participant’s net position that day. It sits in the uses table but is two-directional.
- **Initiation:** not directly initiated by clients, though it includes client activity; the position is monitored by operations groups.
- **Forecasting:** it can be forecast for securities with multi-day settlement cycles (GARP’s example: T+3), because the trades are known days ahead; same-day settlement activity is more difficult.

The once-a-day net settlement is also one of the market conventions GARP cites as institutionalising daylight overdrafts: a bank due a large credit at the end of the day may run a deficit until it arrives.

**Applying it to this question**

On Monday the bank was a net receiver (BRL 310 million in): a source. On Tuesday it was a net payer (BRL 185 million out): a use. The amounts themselves are irrelevant except for their sign. On forecasting, multi-day settlement cycles give advance notice; same-day activity does not. A states both facts correctly.

**Fragile fact.** PCS settlement sits in the uses table yet can be a source; multi-day settlement = easier to forecast, same-day = harder.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser 71.a, verbatim):** “Identify and explain the uses and sources of intraday liquidity.”

**GARP:** Chapter 6, Intraday Liquidity Risk Management, Section 6.2, Table 6.2 and “Settlements at PCS systems”.

**GARP vs Schweser:** none. Schweser says forecasting is “challenging for same-day settlements but is easier for multi-day settlements”, consistent with GARP.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-6 a, where it is Q3 of 13.

a.reason: A reflects GARP’s statement that PCS settlement “may serve as either a source or use of funds depending on the net position”, and Table 6.2’s forecastability column (forecastable for multi-day settlements, harder for same-day).

b.reason: (Absolute claim). B turns “listed among the uses” into “always a use”. GARP says PCS settlement can be a source or a use. B would be right only for a participant that was a net payer every day by construction.

c.reason: (Polarity flip). C gets the source/use classification right but reverses the forecasting direction. Multi-day settlement cycles are easier to forecast; same-day activity is harder. C would be right only if the question asked which activity is harder to forecast and named the multi-day one as easier.

d.reason: (Sibling swap). D gives PCS settlement the profile of outgoing wires (all day, fairly predictable, managed by throttling). The stem itself states a once-daily late-afternoon settlement. D would be right for a stem about outgoing wire transfers.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Identify and explain the uses and sources of intraday liquidity.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-6 a Q4
questions.question: An internal auditor at an Australian bank is reviewing the treasury’s management of an SGD nostro account that the bank holds with a correspondent bank in Singapore. Which of the following statements regarding the funding of nostro accounts is most accurate?

options.text: Nostro funding is directly initiated by the bank’s clients, so the treasury forecasts it in the same way as client wire instructions.
Nostro funding is always a use of intraday liquidity, because cash only ever flows from the bank to the correspondent.
The balance is managed to a target average monthly level as compensation for the correspondent’s services, and on a given day the account may act as a source or a use of funds.
The bank runs the account down to zero every day, because correspondents are compensated only through explicit per-item fees and idle balances serve no purpose.

questions.solution:
Funding of a nostro account held with a correspondent bank abroad.

**Concept and theory**

A nostro account (GARP glossary) is a cash account a bank maintains outside its home market at a correspondent bank, to support payments and securities transactions in that market. An Australian bank needing to pay and receive SGD keeps a nostro with a Singapore correspondent.

Funding of nostro accounts is the third use in GARP Table 6.2:

- **Why balances are held:** banks manage the cash in correspondent accounts to a target average monthly balance, as part of the compensation they provide the correspondent for its banking services. The balance is an economic payment for services, not idle cash.
- **Direction:** on any given day the account funding position may act as a source or a use of funds, depending on the net activity flowing through the account. Balances are replenished or drawn down daily.
- **Initiation:** not directly initiated by clients, though client activity flows through the account; the position is monitored by operations groups.
- **Forecasting:** securities settlements are generally predictable; client payment activity flowing through correspondents is less predictable.

Schweser summarises the same points more briefly: net inflow or outflow depending on the day’s activity, easier to forecast for securities settlements than for client activity. Schweser does not mention the target average balance.

**Applying it to this question**

The auditor’s question is about the economics and direction of the account. The deciding facts are (i) the target average monthly balance as compensation for services and (ii) the two-directional nature of daily funding. C states both. The SGD and AUD detail is context only.

**Fragile fact.** The nostro balance is itself part of the correspondent’s compensation (target average monthly balance); the account can be a source or a use on a given day.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser 71.a, verbatim):** “Identify and explain the uses and sources of intraday liquidity.”

**GARP:** Chapter 6, Intraday Liquidity Risk Management, Section 6.2, Table 6.2 and “Funding of nostro accounts”; Glossary, “Nostro Account”.

**GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser omits the target average monthly balance and compensation point (GARP-only detail); otherwise consistent.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-6 a, where it is Q4 of 13.

a.reason: (Role misassignment). GARP’s table says nostro funding is not directly initiated by clients (client activity flows through it, but the bank manages the funding, monitored by operations). A gives the initiating role to clients. It would describe outgoing client wire transfers, where clients do provide the instructions.

b.reason: (Absolute claim). B says nostro funding is “always” a use. GARP says the position may be a source or a use on any given day. B would be right only for a pure replenishment transfer viewed in isolation.

c.reason: C paraphrases GARP: balances are managed “to a target average monthly balance as part of the compensation” for the correspondent, and the position “may act as a source or use of funds”.

d.reason: (Polarity flip). GARP says the bank holds a target average balance precisely as compensation for the correspondent’s services. D reverses this into a zero-balance, fee-only arrangement. D would be right only under a pure explicit-fee compensation arrangement, which is not the model GARP describes.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Identify and explain the uses and sources of intraday liquidity.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-6 a Q5
questions.question: The CRO of a UK bank is briefed at 07:30. Overnight, GBP swap rates moved sharply against the bank’s over-the-counter derivatives book, and the bank also holds a large deposit of public funds from a local authority that must be secured. Which of the following statements about the intraday liquidity implications is most accurate?

options.text: Acquiring the additional collateral required by the mark-to-market margin call is a use of intraday funding; collateral positions are adjusted daily and needs are generally known about one day in advance.
Pledging collateral is a source of intraday liquidity, because the securities posted to counterparties can be repoed by the bank to raise cash during the day.
Collateral for the public funds deposit is set by the depositor, so it falls outside the bank’s intraday liquidity management and can be ignored by treasury.
Because margin calls are driven by price changes, collateral needs cannot be forecast in any way and must always be met from central bank intraday credit.

questions.solution:
Intraday liquidity effect of an overnight margin call and a secured public funds deposit.

**Concept and theory**

Collateral pledging is the fourth use in GARP Table 6.2. Some activities require a bank to earmark and set aside collateral for an outside beneficiary:

- **Drivers:** GARP names over-the-counter capital markets trading and deposits of certain public funds. Clients may require collateral for bank trading liabilities or deposits; banks must post collateral for margin at FMUs or with other trading counterparties.
- **Why it uses liquidity:** acquiring additional collateral to support an increasing liability, or because of a mark-to-market induced margin call, is a frequent use of intraday funding. Getting the collateral consumes cash.
- **Frequency:** collateral positions are adjusted on a daily basis.
- **Forecasting:** dependent on trading volumes and asset price changes, but generally known one day in advance (Schweser: forecasting relies on trading volume and daily price change data).

The link to the treasurer’s wider challenge is direct: GARP lists “market forces” (daily asset price volatility causing unanticipated margin calls) as one of the factors that make intraday management hard. Collateral pledging is the use through which that factor bites.

**Applying it to this question**

The rate move overnight creates a mark-to-market margin call on the OTC book: the bank must acquire collateral, which is a cash outflow, a use. Because it arose from yesterday’s price move, the requirement is known before the open (the CRO is briefed at 07:30), consistent with “generally known one day in advance”. The public funds deposit is GARP’s second named driver of collateral needs and is also within treasury’s scope.

**Fragile fact.** Collateral pledging is a use (it absorbs cash), driven by OTC trading and public funds deposits, and is generally known one day ahead.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser 71.a, verbatim):** “Identify and explain the uses and sources of intraday liquidity.”

**GARP:** Chapter 6, Intraday Liquidity Risk Management, Section 6.2, Table 6.2 and “Collateral pledging”.

**GARP vs Schweser:** none of substance; Schweser gives margin trading as the example and omits public funds deposits (GARP-only detail).

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-6 a, where it is Q5 of 13.

a.reason: A combines GARP’s three points: acquiring collateral for a mark-to-market margin call is a frequent use of intraday funding, collateral positions are adjusted daily, and needs are generally known one day in advance.

b.reason: (Sibling swap). B gives collateral pledging the property of the liquid asset buffer (assets that can be repoed for cash, a source). Securities posted as collateral are encumbered and set aside for the beneficiary; pledging consumes liquidity. B would describe unencumbered liquid assets.

c.reason: (Scope or condition error). GARP names “deposits of certain public funds” as a driver of collateral pledging, which is a use of intraday liquidity. C wrongly excludes it from scope. C would be right only for a deposit that requires no collateral.

d.reason: (Absolute claim). D says needs cannot be forecast “in any way” and must “always” be met from central bank credit. GARP says they are generally known one day in advance, and any source can fund them. D would be closer for a truly unanticipated intraday margin call.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Identify and explain the uses and sources of intraday liquidity.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-6 a Q6
questions.question: A treasury analyst at a Canadian bank is building the intraday forecast for the use category “asset purchases/funding”. Next week’s pipeline (in CAD) includes: a CAD 45 million purchase of a new operations centre, CAD 120 million of investment portfolio bond purchases, and CAD 200 million of undrawn client credit lines and letters of credit. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Client draws on credit lines are the most predictable component, because the line amounts are contractually fixed in advance.
The fixed asset purchase should be known in advance, the bond purchases may settle on the same day, and client draws on lines and letters of credit are the hardest component to predict.
This use is initiated only by the bank’s own treasury and investment desks, so client activity cannot affect the forecast for this category.
The operations centre purchase counts as an intraday use only if it is financed with term funding; otherwise it falls outside intraday liquidity planning.

questions.solution:
Forecasting the components of the use “asset purchases/funding”.

**Concept and theory**

Asset purchases/funding is the fifth use in GARP Table 6.2: the exchange of bank cash for another asset. GARP lists three components, each with a different forecasting profile:

| Component | Forecastability (GARP Table 6.2) |
|---|---|
| Fixed asset purchases | Should be known in advance |
| Investment portfolio securities | Purchases may be same-day settlement |
| Client loans (draws on lines of credit or letters of credit) | More difficult to predict |

Both clients and the bank drive this use: clients draw on lines of credit or letters of credit, while the bank buys securities for its investment portfolio or fixed assets. Schweser compresses the forecasting into “securities and fixed asset purchases are easier to forecast, but the client loans are more challenging”. GARP’s finer point is that securities purchases may settle the same day, so they can still surprise the intraday position even if they are planned.

The reason client draws are hard to forecast is the same theme that runs through the whole of Table 6.2: activity the bank controls (its own payments, its own purchases) is forecastable; activity clients control (client payments, client drawdowns) is not.

**Applying it to this question**

The CAD 45 million operations centre is a fixed asset purchase: known in advance. The CAD 120 million bond purchases are investment portfolio securities: may settle same day. The CAD 200 million undrawn lines and letters of credit are client loans: hardest to predict, since the client chooses when to draw. The amounts are not needed; the question tests the profile of each component. B lists all three correctly.

**Fragile fact.** Fixed assets = known in advance; securities = may settle same day; client draws = hardest to predict.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser 71.a, verbatim):** “Identify and explain the uses and sources of intraday liquidity.”

**GARP:** Chapter 6, Intraday Liquidity Risk Management, Section 6.2, Table 6.2 and “Asset purchases/funding”.

**GARP vs Schweser:** none. Schweser groups securities with fixed assets as “easier to forecast”; GARP adds the same-day settlement caveat for securities.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-6 a, where it is Q6 of 13.

a.reason: (Polarity flip). A makes client draws the most predictable component. GARP says client loans are more difficult to predict; a fixed line amount caps the exposure but does not fix the timing or size of draws. A would be right if the question were about the bank’s fixed asset purchases.

b.reason: B reproduces Table 6.2’s forecastability column for asset purchases/funding.

c.reason: (Role misassignment). GARP’s table answers “Yes” to client impact: clients can draw down on lines of credit or letters of credit. C removes clients’ role. C would be right only for a bank with no client lending.

d.reason: (Scope or condition error). D adds a condition that GARP does not have. A fixed asset purchase is a use of intraday liquidity because it pays cash; how it is financed does not change its classification. D would be relevant only to a question about the choice of funding source.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Identify and explain the uses and sources of intraday liquidity.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-6 a Q7
questions.question: A senior risk analyst at a Singapore bank is preparing a briefing for the asset-liability committee on the sources of intraday liquidity for its SGD accounts. Which of the following statements should she include?

options.text: Starting cash balances are the largest source of intraday funding in normal markets, because they are available from the opening of business.
All incoming funds flows are credited in real time, so the treasury can treat every expected inflow as immediately available on arrival.
Client payment activity directly determines the bank’s closing and start-of-day cash balances, so treasury has no control over their level.
Incoming payments and FMU settlements are the largest source in normal markets; LVPS payments arrive in real time, while net clearinghouse settlements are batch-oriented.

questions.solution:
Cash balances versus incoming funds flow as sources of intraday liquidity.

**Concept and theory**

GARP Table 6.3 lists six common sources of intraday liquidity: cash balances, incoming funds flow, intraday credit, liquid assets, overnight borrowings and other term funding. Each contributes differently from day to day, but each matters to the overall funding picture.

**Cash balances** are the most obvious source: the starting cash on the balance sheet at the beginning of the day, comprising deposits at the central bank and at correspondent (nostro) accounts. GARP’s table says clients do not directly impact closing or start-of-day cash balances; bank treasury determines their level.

**Incoming funds flow** comprises incoming payments and FMU settlement credits to the bank’s accounts at the central bank and correspondents. GARP calls it the largest source of intraday funding in periods of normal market function. Timing differs by channel:

- real-time: for example LVPS payments;
- batch-oriented: net settlements with clearinghouses, retail payment systems and similar.

Schweser says the same: inflows may occur instantaneously or in batches. Forecastability mirrors the uses: bank activity can usually be forecast with 1 to 2 days’ notice, client payments are harder, and FMU credits are forecastable for multi-day settlements but harder for same-day activity.

Note the parallel: outgoing wires are the largest use; incoming payments and FMU settlements are the largest source.

**Applying it to this question**

The briefing must state the largest source correctly and describe inflow timing correctly. D does both: payments and FMU settlements are the largest source in normal markets, and some inflows are real-time (LVPS) while others are batch (clearinghouse net settlements).

**Fragile fact.** Largest source = incoming funds flow (normal markets); most obvious source = cash balances.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser 71.a, verbatim):** “Identify and explain the uses and sources of intraday liquidity.”

**GARP:** Chapter 6, Intraday Liquidity Risk Management, Section 6.2, Table 6.3 (Sources of Intraday Credit), “Cash balances” and “Incoming funds flow”.

**GARP vs Schweser:** framing difference: Schweser says cash balances impacted by bank operations are easier to forecast than those impacted by client activities; GARP’s table says clients do not directly impact closing/start-of-day balances, which treasury determines. Resolved from GARP; it does not change the answer.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-6 a, where it is Q7 of 13.

a.reason: (Sibling swap). A gives cash balances the “largest source” attribute that belongs to incoming funds flow. Cash balances are the most obvious source, not the largest. A would be right if it said “the most obvious source”.

b.reason: (Absolute claim). B says “all” inflows are real-time. GARP says some (LVPS payments) are real-time, while others are batch-oriented. B would be right only for a bank whose inflows came solely through an RTGS system.

c.reason: (Role misassignment). C gives clients control over closing and start-of-day balances. GARP’s table says clients do not directly impact them; bank treasury determines their level. (Schweser notes client-driven balances are harder to forecast, but does not remove treasury’s control.)

d.reason: D paraphrases GARP’s description of incoming funds flow: “the largest source of intraday funding in periods of normal market function”, with real-time LVPS inflows and batch-oriented clearinghouse and retail settlements.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Identify and explain the uses and sources of intraday liquidity.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-6 a Q8
questions.question: A member of the board risk committee of a global bank with branches in New York and London asks the treasurer to compare the intraday credit terms offered by the two central banks. Which of the following comparisons is accurate?

options.text: Federal Reserve: overdrafts collateralised by the highest-quality government securities, no interest charged. Bank of England: unsecured committed line, interest charged.
Federal Reserve: unsecured committed line, no interest charged. Bank of England: overdrafts collateralised by the highest-quality government securities, interest charged.
Federal Reserve: unsecured committed line, interest charged. Bank of England: overdrafts collateralised by the highest-quality government securities, no interest charged.
Federal Reserve: unsecured uncommitted line, interest charged. Bank of England: overdrafts collateralised by the highest-quality government securities, no interest charged.

questions.solution:
Comparing Federal Reserve and Bank of England intraday credit terms.

**Concept and theory**

Intraday credit is a credit line or overdraft permitted during business hours and covered by the close of business (GARP Table 6.3). Its defining feature is that it does not survive the day: the overdraft must be gone by the end of business. Central banks are a large source of intraday credit for the banking system, but GARP stresses that their terms vary across jurisdictions. It gives two contrasting models:

|  | Federal Reserve | Bank of England |  |  |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Form | Unsecured, committed line (Net Debit Cap programme) | Intraday overdrafts collateralised highest-quality government securities | by | the |
| Price | Charges interest for tapping the line | Does not charge interest |  |  |

So the cost of central bank intraday credit takes one of two forms: an explicit interest charge on unsecured usage (Fed), or an implicit cost of tying up top-quality collateral (BoE). Schweser condenses this to “in some cases, interest is explicitly charged, and in other cases, very high-quality collateral must be pledged”.

Two related facts help eliminate traps. The net debit cap is a disclosed, committed facility (GARP Table 6.3 cites the FRB net debit cap as a facility “disclosed and well known to a bank”). Interbank daylight overdraft lines, by contrast, are generally uncommitted and free. Section 6.1 adds the history: the Fed’s fee on unsecured overdrafts rose over time while fully collateralised overdrafts carry a zero fee, consistent with the “unsecured line, interest charged” description.

**Applying it to this question**

Each option pairs a form (secured or unsecured, committed or not) and a price for each central bank. The correct pairing is Fed: unsecured, committed, interest charged; BoE: highest-quality government collateral, no interest. Only C matches on every attribute.

**Fragile fact.** Fed = unsecured, committed, interest; BoE = top-quality collateral, no interest.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser 71.a, verbatim):** “Identify and explain the uses and sources of intraday liquidity.”

**GARP:** Chapter 6, Intraday Liquidity Risk Management, Section 6.2, “Intraday credit” and Table 6.3.

**GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser does not name the central banks; it states the two pricing models generically (Schweser-consistent, GARP gives the attribution).

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-6 a, where it is Q8 of 13.

a.reason: (Role misassignment). A swaps the two central banks: each description is correct for the other institution. A would be right if the labels “Federal Reserve” and “Bank of England” were exchanged.

b.reason: (Polarity flip). B gets the form right but reverses the pricing for both: the Fed charges interest and the BoE does not. B would be right only under a pricing regime opposite to the one GARP describes.

c.reason: C reproduces GARP: the Fed provides “an unsecured committed line of credit” and “charges interest”, while the BoE requires collateral of the highest-quality government securities but “does not charge interest”.

d.reason: (Sibling swap). D makes the Fed line “uncommitted”, which is the attribute of interbank daylight overdraft lines. The Fed’s Net Debit Cap programme is a committed, disclosed line. D would be right if it described a commercial bank’s daylight line (which, however, is generally free).

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Identify and explain the uses and sources of intraday liquidity.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-6 a Q9
questions.question:
A risk consultant reviewing the intraday credit sources of a mid-sized EUR-denominated bank lists the following observations:

I. FMUs extend daylight credit by allowing a participant to enter transactions during the day while it builds up a settlement position that must be met at the end of the day.

II. Counterparties often adjust the intraday credit they extend to a bank to reflect its business with them in other areas, such as OTC trading.

III. Interbank daylight overdraft lines are generally committed and carry an explicit interest charge.

IV. Some intraday credit facilities, such as a central bank net debit cap, are disclosed, while others are undisclosed but can often be inferred from historical data.

Which of the observations are correct?

options.text: I and II only
II and III only
I, III and IV only
I, II and IV only

questions.solution:
Audit of statements on intraday credit from FMUs, counterparties and other banks.

**Concept and theory**

Central banks are not the only providers of intraday credit. GARP’s description of the source “intraday credit” continues:

- **Other banks:** interbank daylight overdraft lines are generally uncommitted and free, although there are some signs of change, especially in Europe. GARP’s Table 6.3 description says lines are often uncommitted and provided without interest charges.
- **FMUs:** FMUs extend daylight credit by allowing a participant to enter trades or transactions during the day while potentially accumulating a large settlement position that must be met at end of day. The participant is in effect borrowing until the settlement window.
- **Counterparty behaviour:** client activity does not directly affect the amount of intraday credit extended to a bank, but counterparties often adjust their intraday credit extensions to reflect business activity from other areas of the bank (GARP’s example: OTC trading). Credit is relationship-driven.
- **Disclosure and forecasting:** some facilities are disclosed and well known (the FRB net debit cap); others are not disclosed but can often be inferred from historical data.

Because much interbank and FMU credit is uncommitted and undisclosed, the amount available often cannot simply be read from a contract; GARP says it can often be inferred from historical data instead.

**Applying it to this question**

I: true (FMU daylight credit via an accumulating settlement position). II: true (counterparties adjust credit for other business such as OTC trading). III: false, it reverses “generally uncommitted and free”. IV: true (disclosed versus inferred facilities). Correct set: I, II and IV.

**Fragile fact.** Interbank daylight lines: generally uncommitted and free; FMU daylight credit = the settlement position built up until end of day.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser 71.a, verbatim):** “Identify and explain the uses and sources of intraday liquidity.”

**GARP:** Chapter 6, Intraday Liquidity Risk Management, Section 6.2, “Intraday credit” and Table 6.3.

**GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser covers only central bank credit; the FMU, interbank and disclosure points are GARP-only detail.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-6 a, where it is Q9 of 13.

a.reason: (Scope or condition error). A rejects IV, implying that all intraday credit facilities are disclosed (or none can be inferred). GARP explicitly contrasts disclosed facilities such as the net debit cap with undisclosed ones inferred from history. A would be right only if IV had claimed that no facility is ever disclosed.

b.reason: (Polarity flip). B accepts III, which flips “uncommitted and free” to “committed and carry an explicit interest charge”, and drops the true I and IV. B would be right only in the market change GARP hints at (“signs of change, especially in Europe”) having fully happened, which the reading does not claim.

c.reason: (Polarity flip). C accepts the flipped III and drops the true II. Counterparties do adjust intraday credit to reflect the bank’s business with them in other areas.

d.reason: D accepts the three statements that paraphrase GARP and rejects the one with the reversed attributes.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Identify and explain the uses and sources of intraday liquidity.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-6 a Q10
questions.question: A portfolio manager at a Chinese bank manages a CNY buffer of money market instruments, time deposits, banker’s acceptances and short-term government bills, held to meet intraday needs. Which of the following statements about this source of intraday liquidity is most accurate?

options.text: The buffer tends to have low volatility and is therefore predictable, although the bank’s trading and investment activity can change the amount of liquid assets available.
Long-dated government bonds belong in the buffer as well, because high government credit quality means they can always be converted to cash at par within hours.
Because the assets are owned outright, client activity plays no part in converting them to cash, so clients can never be a source of liquidity for this category.
Liquid asset balances are highly volatile from day to day, making this the least predictable of the sources of intraday liquidity.

questions.solution:
Characteristics of the liquid asset buffer as a source of intraday liquidity.

**Concept and theory**

Liquid assets are the fourth source in GARP Table 6.3. Banks typically carry a buffer of highly liquid, near-cash investments that can be liquidated for cash within short order.

- **Composition (GARP):** money market instruments, time deposits, banker’s acceptances, and high-quality, short-term government debt (Table 6.3: e.g., T-bills). Schweser: money market instruments, time deposits, and government securities with maturities of one year or less.
- **Role of clients and the bank:** clients may be sources of liquidity in converting liquid assets to cash (for example as the counterparty to a repo); the bank’s trading and investment portfolio activity can change the amount of liquid assets available.
- **Forecastability:** liquid assets held in the investment portfolio and other money market investments tend to have low volatility and, as a result, are predictable.

The logic is that the buffer is the bank’s own stock of near-cash: its size changes only when the bank chooses to buy, sell or encumber assets, so it does not jump around with client flows the way incoming and outgoing payments do. The emphasis on short-term instruments matters: what qualifies is debt that can be turned into cash quickly with little price risk, not merely debt of a high-quality issuer.

**Applying it to this question**

The CNY buffer described in the stem matches GARP’s list. The question asks which statement is accurate. A states the low volatility and predictability of the buffer and the fact that bank trading and investment activity can change the amount available, both from Table 6.3.

**Fragile fact.** Liquid assets: short-term near-cash, low volatility, predictable; clients can be the repo counterparty.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser 71.a, verbatim):** “Identify and explain the uses and sources of intraday liquidity.”

**GARP:** Chapter 6, Intraday Liquidity Risk Management, Section 6.2, “Liquid assets” and Table 6.3.

**GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser defines the government component as maturities of one year or less and omits banker’s acceptances in its body text (it mentions them in its quiz answer); GARP says high-quality, short-term government debt. No conflict for this question.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-6 a, where it is Q10 of 13.

a.reason: A paraphrases Table 6.3: liquid assets “tend to have low volatility and as a result are predictable”, and “bank trading and investment portfolio activity can impact the amount of liquid assets available”.

b.reason: (Scope or condition error). B drops the “short-term” condition. GARP lists high-quality, short-term government debt (Schweser: one year or less). Long-dated bonds carry price risk and are not convertible “at par” with certainty. B would be right if it referred to T-bills.

c.reason: (Role misassignment). C denies clients any role. GARP’s table says clients may be sources of liquidity in converting liquid assets to cash, for example as the counterparty in a repo. C would be right only for a bank that could liquidate solely through outright sales on an exchange.

d.reason: (Polarity flip). D reverses “low volatility and predictable” into “highly volatile, least predictable”. D would better describe client-driven payment flows.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Identify and explain the uses and sources of intraday liquidity.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-6 a Q11
questions.question: At 14:00 the treasurer of a US bank sees that the bank’s Federal Reserve account is likely to approach its daylight overdraft limit later in the afternoon, and considers borrowing USD 750 million of fed funds overnight. Which of the following best describes the trade-off the treasurer should weigh, according to the reading?

options.text: There is no balance sheet trade-off, because overnight borrowings are repaid before the close of business and do not remain on the balance sheet.
The bank should instead rely on one-week and one-month term funding as its routine daily source, because term funding is the usual source of intraday liquidity.
The cost of carrying excess liquidity at the end of the day against the risk of not completing the day’s business, or of reputational harm from delayed transactions, after a breach of the limit.
Fed funds borrowed in the afternoon are delivered only the next morning, so the borrowing cannot help with the afternoon shortfall and should be declined.

questions.solution:
Overnight borrowing to cover an afternoon shortfall: the treasurer’s trade-off.

**Concept and theory**

GARP distinguishes three borrowed sources of intraday liquidity by when they are repaid:

| Source | Repayment | Role in intraday funding |
|---|---|---|
| Intraday credit | Covered by close of business | Temporary overdraft or line during the day |
| Overnight borrowings | Next day; stay on the balance sheet overnight | Quick intraday liquidity (fed funds, LIBOR, Eurodollar deposits) |
| Other term funding | One week, one month, etc. | Incremental, not a consistent source |

**Overnight borrowings** provide quick intraday liquidity (delivery of fed funds is almost immediate), but because they are not repaid the same day they remain on the borrower’s balance sheet overnight. In deciding whether and how much to borrow, treasury must weigh the potential cost of having excess liquidity at the end of the day against the risk of not being able to complete the current day’s business, or facing reputational risk from delayed transactions, because a daylight overdraft limit is breached. Schweser frames this as a cost-benefit decision between too much and too little liquidity.

**Other term funding** (for example FHLB borrowings, term repos) extends the same idea further out the maturity curve, if lenders can deliver at a useful time of day, and only if the bank has an appetite for longer-term funding. GARP calls it an incremental factor in a given day’s liquidity positioning rather than a consistent source.

**Applying it to this question**

At 14:00 the treasurer foresees the Fed account nearing its daylight limit. Borrowing USD 750 million overnight would deliver funds at once and avoid the breach, but leaves the bank holding the borrowed cash overnight, possibly as excess liquidity. That is precisely GARP’s trade-off, stated in C. The amount of USD 750 million is irrelevant to the classification.

**Fragile fact.** Overnight borrowings: delivered now, repaid next day, so they sit on the balance sheet overnight; intraday credit is gone by close of business.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser 71.a, verbatim):** “Identify and explain the uses and sources of intraday liquidity.”

**GARP:** Chapter 6, Intraday Liquidity Risk Management, Section 6.2, “Overnight borrowings” and “Other term funding”; Table 6.3.

**GARP vs Schweser:** none of substance; GARP adds the reputational-risk dimension of delayed transactions.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-6 a, where it is Q11 of 13.

a.reason: (Sibling swap). A gives overnight borrowings the defining attribute of intraday credit (repaid by close of business). Overnight borrowings remain on the balance sheet overnight, which is what creates the trade-off. A would describe intraday credit.

b.reason: (Absolute claim). B makes term funding the routine daily source. GARP says other term funding is an incremental factor rather than a consistent source, used only when the bank has appetite for longer-term funding. B would be right if it said term funding is an occasional supplement.

c.reason: C paraphrases GARP’s description of the overnight borrowing decision: excess end-of-day liquidity versus failing to complete the day’s business, or reputational risk from delayed transactions, after breaching the daylight overdraft limit.

d.reason: (Polarity flip). D reverses the timing of fed funds. GARP says borrowed fed funds are delivered almost immediately; it is the repayment that happens the next morning. D would be right if it described the repayment leg.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Identify and explain the uses and sources of intraday liquidity.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-6 a Q12
questions.question: A member of the risk committee of a eurozone bank asks the CRO why staying within daylight credit limits is so hard for the treasury. Which of the following responses is most accurate?

options.text: Because most activities generate consistent inflows and outflows, day-to-day volatility is low and large cash requirements are usually known well in advance.
The objective is to end every business day with a zero balance in all accounts, which is difficult because of the volume of transactions.
The data problem lies mainly in central bank accounts, which cannot be monitored in real time, while line-of-business systems give a consolidated real-time view.
Daily asset price volatility can produce unanticipated margin calls, and central bank money desks implementing monetary policy can influence the liquidity available to the bank.

questions.solution:
Factors that make it hard for treasury to stay within daylight credit limits.

**Concept and theory**

After listing uses and sources, GARP states the bank treasurer’s challenge: to manage the “cacophony” of high-volume incoming and outgoing transactions, originated all over the bank, so that the bank stays within the limits of its daylight credit resources and ends the day with the appropriate target balances in its accounts. GARP then names three factors that exacerbate this challenge:

1. **Variability of cash flow patterns.** Many activities generate consistent patterns over time, but there can be high day-to-day volatility with little advance notice of large cash requirements or sources.
2. **Market forces.** Daily volatility in asset prices can cause unanticipated margin calls that require additional cash. Central bank money desks that implement monetary policy directly may influence liquidity available in the market, affecting the bank’s ability to source or deploy intraday funds. (Schweser calls these macroeconomic factors.)
3. **Lack of real-time data.** Most treasurers do not have a comprehensive, single source of real-time balances and expected flows, which complicates determining and forecasting cash through the day.

GARP also notes earlier that banks can monitor central bank accounts (and often correspondent accounts) in real time through online reporting tools, while other data sits in systems run by lines of business and operations. The data gap is therefore in consolidation, not in the central bank account.

**Applying it to this question**

The committee member asks why staying within limits is hard. D states the market-forces factor accurately (margin calls from price volatility; monetary policy operations affecting available liquidity). Each other option misstates the objective or one of the factors.

**Fragile fact.** Three factors: cash flow variability, market forces (margin calls; monetary policy operations), lack of real-time data. Central bank accounts are the visible part.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser 71.a, verbatim):** “Identify and explain the uses and sources of intraday liquidity.”

**GARP:** Chapter 6, Intraday Liquidity Risk Management, Section 6.2, closing discussion of the treasurer’s challenge.

**GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser presents the same three problems in its LO 71.a summary, calling the second “macroeconomic factors”; consistent.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-6 a, where it is Q12 of 13.

a.reason: (Polarity flip). A reverses the first factor. GARP says that despite consistent patterns there can be high day-to-day volatility with little advance notice. A would be right only for the long-run average pattern, not the day-to-day behaviour.

b.reason: (Scope or condition error). GARP’s objective is to stay within daylight credit limits and end the day with the appropriate target balances, not a zero balance. (Nostro accounts, for example, are run to a target average balance.) B would be right only if the target balance happened to be zero.

c.reason: (Role misassignment). C swaps which systems are visible. GARP says banks can monitor central bank accounts in real time; the gap is that other data sits in line-of-business and operations systems with no single real-time source. C would be right with the two locations reversed.

d.reason: D paraphrases GARP’s second factor: daily asset price volatility can lead to unanticipated margin calls, and central bank money desks implementing monetary policy may influence available liquidity.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Identify and explain the uses and sources of intraday liquidity.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-6 a Q13
questions.question:
A treasury analyst at a European bank reconstructs one day’s movements in the bank’s EUR account at the central bank. All amounts are in EUR millions; each item settles in the account at the time shown.

| Time | Item | Amount |
|---|---|---|
| 07:00 | Opening balance | 450 |
| 09:00 | Outgoing client and own-account wires | 700 |
| 10:00 | Incoming LVPS payments | 250 |
| 11:00 | Cash used to acquire collateral for a margin call | 180 |
| 12:00 | Transfer to replenish a nostro account | 120 |
| 13:00 | Proceeds of overnight interbank borrowing | 400 |
| 15:00 | Outgoing client wires | 350 |
| 16:30 | Clearinghouse settlement (bank is net receiver) | 520 |
| Memo | Central bank intraday credit limit | 750 |
| Memo | Client loan approved, to be funded next week | 300 |

Which of the following is closest to the bank’s largest daylight overdraft during the day?

options.text: EUR 250 million
EUR 300 million
EUR 650 million
EUR 770 million

questions.solution:
Reconstructing a central bank account through the day and finding the largest daylight overdraft.

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s glossary defines a daylight (intraday) overdraft as a negative cash position during the business day, which arises when cumulative debits posted to the account exceed the opening balance plus posted credits. To reconstruct the position, each item must be classified using Tables 6.2 and 6.3:

- **Uses (debits):** outgoing wires; cash to acquire collateral (collateral pledging); a transfer to replenish a nostro account; a PCS settlement when the bank is a net payer.
- **Sources (credits):** opening cash balance; incoming LVPS payments (incoming funds flow); proceeds of overnight borrowing, delivered almost immediately; a PCS settlement when the bank is a net receiver.

Two items need care. A PCS settlement can be a source or a use depending on the net position, and overnight borrowing is a source available today even though it is repaid tomorrow. Items that do not settle in the account today (a loan to be funded next week) and limits (a credit line) are not flows and do not move the balance.

$\text{B}_{\text{t}} = \text{B}_{0} + \sum_{\text{s}\le\text{t}} \text{Credits}_{\text{s}} - \sum_{\text{s}\le\text{t}} \text{Debits}_{\text{s}}$, Largest overdraft $= - \text{m}_{\text{t}}\text{in B}_{\text{t}}$ (if negative)

where $\text{B}_{0}$ is the opening balance and $\text{B}_{\text{t}}$ the balance after the items at time t. The ratio of this figure to the credit line is a monitoring metric under LO 71.c and is not asked here.

**Applying it to this question**

Classify and accumulate (EUR millions):

$\text{B}_{\text{07:00}} =$ 450

$\text{B}_{\text{09:00}} =$ 450 − 700 = −250 (wires, use)

$\text{B}_{\text{10:00}} = -$250 + 250 = 0 (incoming LVPS, source)

$\text{B}_{\text{11:00}} =$ 0 − 180 = −180 (collateral, use)

$\text{B}_{\text{12:00}} = -$180 − 120 = −300 (nostro replenishment, use)

$\text{B}_{\text{13:00}} = -$300 + 400 = 100 (overnight borrowing, source)

$\text{B}_{\text{15:00}} =$ 100 − 350 = −250 (wires, use)

$\text{B}_{\text{16:30}} = -$250 + 520 = 270 (PCS, net receiver, source)

The most negative balance is −300 at 12:00, so the largest daylight overdraft is EUR 300 million. Irrelevant inputs: the EUR 750 million intraday credit limit (a limit, not a flow) and the EUR 300 million loan to be funded next week (not settled today). The bank ends the day with EUR 270 million.

**Fragile fact.** PCS settlement direction follows the net position (here a credit), and overnight borrowing is a source today, repaid tomorrow.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser 71.a, verbatim):** “Identify and explain the uses and sources of intraday liquidity.”

**GARP:** Chapter 6, Intraday Liquidity Risk Management, Section 6.2, Tables 6.2 and 6.3; Glossary, “Daylight Overdraft”.

**GARP vs Schweser:** none. The ratio of the peak overdraft to the credit line (daily maximum intraday liquidity usage) belongs to LO 71.c and is deliberately excluded.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-6 a, where it is Q13 of 13.

a.reason: (Intermediate result). EUR 250 million is the balance after the 09:00 wires (and again after the 15:00 wires): 450 − 700 = −250. Stopping at the first overdraft, or reading the last negative point, misses the deeper 12:00 trough. A would be right if the question asked for the overdraft after the morning wires.

b.reason: B is the most negative point of the correctly classified running balance, matching GARP’s definition of a daylight overdraft.

c.reason: (Dropped term). EUR 650 million results from ignoring the overnight borrowing as if it were not available until tomorrow: −300 − 350 = −650 at 15:00. Overnight funds are delivered almost immediately and are a same-day source. C would be right if the borrowing settled the next morning.

d.reason: (Sign error). EUR 770 million treats the clearinghouse settlement as a use: −250 − 520 = −770 at 16:30. The stem says the bank is a net receiver, so the settlement is a source that day. D would be right if the bank were a net payer of EUR 520 million.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Differentiate between methods for tracking intraday flows and monitoring risk levels.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-6 c Q1
questions.question:
The head of liquidity risk at a Brazilian bank is designing a dashboard of ratios against which the board will set BRL intraday limits and thresholds. She wants to include only measures from the set that the framework presents for quantifying and monitoring intraday risk levels, and to leave out measures whose purpose is to understand the profile of the bank’s intraday flows. The candidate measures are:

I. The percentage of the day’s outgoing payment activity released by each of several time markers.

II. The average and peak usage of the intraday lines the bank extends to each client and counterparty, with the ability to model activity at client and portfolio levels.

III. The day’s largest net negative balance in a cash account relative to the size of that account’s credit line.

IV. The amount of intraday credit the bank relies on in business-as-usual conditions compared with the maximum it can draw down across its committed and uncommitted lines.

Which of the candidate measures belong on the dashboard?

options.text: I and IV only
II and III only
I and III only
I, III, and IV only

questions.solution:
Brazilian bank dashboard: which of four candidate measures are risk-level measures.

**Concept and theory**

GARP Section 6.3 (“Measurement of Intraday Liquidity”) draws on the BCBS paper Monitoring Tools for Intraday Liquidity Management (April 2013) and splits the commonly used measures into two sets with different jobs. The **first set** is “helpful for understanding the profile of the institution’s intraday flows”: it describes what moves through the accounts, when, and against which credit lines. The **second set** “provides ratios for monitoring risk levels”, and GARP adds that institutions may set limits or thresholds and monitor against these measures. The distinction is therefore functional: flow measures are descriptive inventories (payments, positions, deadlines, credit lines), while risk-level measures are ratios that scale a usage or exposure against a capacity (a credit line, Tier 1 capital, time of day).

| Measures for understanding intraday flows | Measures for quantifying and monitoring risk levels |
|---|---|
| Total payments | Daily maximum intraday liquidity usage |
| Other cash transactions | Intraday credit relative to Tier 1 capital |
| Settlement positions | Client intraday credit usage |
| Time-sensitive obligations | Payment throughput |
| Total intraday credit lines to clients and counterparties |  |
| Total bank intraday credit lines available and usage |  |

The trap is that three of the six flow measures talk about intraday credit, which sounds like risk. Credit-line inventories (to clients, or available to the bank) are still flow measures; only the ratios built from them sit in the second set.

**Applying it to this question**

Statement I describes the percentage of outgoing payment activity by time of day: this is payment throughput, a risk-level measure. Statement II describes the size of lines extended to clients and counterparties with average and peak usage and client or portfolio modelling: this is total intraday credit lines to clients and counterparties, a flow measure. Statement III is the day’s largest net negative balance relative to the credit line: daily maximum intraday liquidity usage, a risk-level measure. Statement IV is the intraday credit the bank relies on in business-as-usual conditions versus the maximum it can draw: total bank intraday credit lines available and usage, a flow measure. So I and III belong on the dashboard.

**Fragile fact.** “Intraday credit” in a measure’s name does not make it a risk-level measure: the two credit-line inventories are flow measures; the three ratios plus throughput are risk-level measures.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** “Differentiate between methods for tracking intraday flows and monitoring risk levels.” **GARP:** Chapter 6, Section 6.3, “Measurement of Intraday Liquidity”, subsections “Measures for Understanding Intraday Flows” and “Measures for Quantifying and Monitoring Risk Levels”. **GARP vs Schweser:** none (same classification).

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-6 c, where it is Q1 of 13.

a.reason: (Sibling swap). Including IV treats total bank intraday credit lines available and usage as a risk ratio because it concerns systemic risk. GARP places it among flow measures. The option would be right if IV were reworded as “available unsecured intraday credit relative to Tier 1 capital”, which is a risk-level measure.

b.reason: (Sibling swap). Including II confuses total intraday credit lines to clients and counterparties (flow) with client intraday credit usage (risk-level). It also drops I. The option would be right if II described each client’s peak daily overdraft relative to its line and I were a flow item.

c.reason: Only I and III appear under GARP’s heading “Measures for Quantifying and Monitoring Risk Levels”; II and IV are listed under “Measures for Understanding Intraday Flows”. Schweser’s key concepts list the same split.

d.reason: (Sibling swap). It correctly includes I and III but adds IV, again misplacing the bank’s own credit-lines inventory into the risk-level set. It would be right only if IV were the Tier 1 ratio.

questions.source: High quality paper LTR-6 c Q2
questions.question:
A junior risk analyst at a Japanese bank is specifying a data warehouse for the “total payments” measure, which will cover the bank’s JPY payment activity. Her manager asks her to state what is stored and what it is used for.

Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: For every payment on every electronic payment system in which the bank participates, the bank stores the amount, timing, processing steps, routing, payer, payee, system used and any suspensions, so it can derive its net settlement-account position at any time of day, in aggregate and by payment type.

For every payment on every electronic payment system in which the bank participates, the bank stores the amount, timing, processing steps, routing, payer, payee, system used and any suspensions, so it can derive its net settlement-account position at the close of business only.

For every payment on the central bank’s large value payment system only, the bank stores the amount, timing, processing steps, routing, payer, payee, system used and any suspensions, so it can derive its net settlement-account position at any time of day, in aggregate and by payment type.

For every payment on every electronic payment system in which the bank participates, the bank stores the amount, timing, processing steps, routing, payer, payee, system used and any suspensions, so it can compute each client’s peak daily overdraft relative to its credit line.

questions.solution:
Japanese bank: what the total payments measure stores and what it is used for.

**Concept and theory**

Total payments is the first and most granular flow-tracking measure. GARP says a bank and its intraday risk teams “should maintain statistics concerning the amount of payments it makes on all electronic payments systems in which it participates”. For every payment the bank stores in a data warehouse the critical information needed for analysis: payment amount, time received or originated, times for each processing step in the payment workflow, routing information, payer and payee, payment system used, and any suspensions of the payment. The motivation is that most banks lack a single real-time source of balances (one of the three challenges in Section 6.2); a payment-level warehouse lets the bank rebuild its position after the fact and study patterns. Compiling the data supports summaries such as:

- total payments sent and received for non-financial institution clients, for financial institution clients, and for bank activity;
- net position in the settlement account at any time of day in aggregate, and filtered by payment type;
- trend in payment volumes over time, for correlation analysis.

Schweser condenses this to amount, time, payer and payee, with metrics of total payments sent and received, net position in the settlement account, and volume trends. Total payments is descriptive: it is the raw material for later ratios but is not itself a ratio of usage to capacity.

**Applying it to this question**

The stem asks what is stored and what it is used for. Three of the options store the right fields; the discriminator is the coverage (all systems versus one) and the purpose (intraday position at any time versus close of business, or a client ratio). Option A keeps both the full coverage and the “at any time of day, in aggregate and by payment type” purpose.

**Fragile fact.** Total payments covers all electronic payment systems and supports the net settlement-account position at any time of day, not just at close.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** “Differentiate between methods for tracking intraday flows and monitoring risk levels.” **GARP:** Chapter 6, Section 6.3, “Measures for Understanding Intraday Flows”, “Total Payments”. **GARP vs Schweser:** none in substance; Schweser lists fewer stored fields and summaries.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-6 c, where it is Q2 of 13.

a.reason: A matches GARP word for word in substance: all electronic payment systems in which the bank participates, the listed per-payment fields, and the net settlement-account position at any time of day, both aggregate and filtered by payment type.

b.reason: (Scope or condition error). Restricting the use to the close-of-business position throws away the point of storing time stamps and processing-step times. GARP’s summary is the net position “at any time of day”. B would be right for an end-of-day reconciliation report, not for total payments.

c.reason: (Scope or condition error). GARP covers payments on all electronic payment systems in which the bank participates, not only the central bank LVPS. C would be right if the bank participated in only one system.

d.reason: (Sibling swap). Peak daily overdraft relative to the client’s line is client intraday credit usage, a risk-level measure. D would be right if the stem had asked about client intraday credit usage.

questions.source: High quality paper LTR-6 c Q3
questions.question:
An internal auditor at a mid-sized Canadian bank finds that the bank’s systems cannot reconstruct its CAD account positions at every point of the business day. The bank participates in a large value payment system, a retail clearinghouse and a securities settlement network that uses a central counterparty.

Which of the following is the most appropriate minimum recommendation for tracking intraday flows?

options.text: Capture snapshots of account and collateral positions at one-minute intervals at every securities settlement network, since this interval is the stated minimum for all participants.
Suspend tracking of FMU positions until complete real-time position data are available, since partial data would give a misleading picture of intraday flows.
Maintain data on the settlement position at the single FMU through which the largest payment of the day settles, and monitor its pattern over time.
Maintain data on its settlement positions with all of its FMUs, monitor their patterns, and correlate them with external market factors to anticipate needs earlier in the day.

questions.solution:
Canadian bank cannot reconstruct positions at every point in the day: minimum flow-tracking recommendation.

**Concept and theory**

Two neighbouring flow measures deal with FMUs, and the LO expects the candidate to tell them apart.

| Measure | What GARP says |
|---|---|
| Other cash transactions | Track intraday and end-of-day settlement positions at all FMUs in which the bank participates; maximise transaction-level detail captured and stored. Securities settlement networks (SSNs), especially CCP-based ones, manage exposure through collateralisation, so a participant should capture snapshots of its account and collateral positions through the trading day (example: the Federal Reserve tracks collateral positions at one-minute intervals). |
| Settlement positions | “If complete data to reconstruct account positions at any time of day is not available, at a minimum” maintain data on settlement positions with all FMUs. These deadline-specific, often large payments are critical to managing intraday liquidity and systemic risk. Monitor patterns and correlate them with external market factors to predict liquidity requirements earlier in the day. |

So other cash transactions is the full-detail ideal, and settlement positions is the explicit minimum standard when full reconstruction is not possible. The reason the minimum focuses on FMU settlement positions is that they have hard deadlines and large amounts, so missing them threatens both the bank’s liquidity and the system. Schweser links the trend analysis to “macroeconomic factors”; GARP says “external market factors”.

**Applying it to this question**

The decisive fact in the stem is that the bank cannot reconstruct positions at every point of the day. That is exactly the condition GARP attaches to the settlement-positions fallback. The list of three FMUs is there to test the “all its FMUs” scope; the CCP-based SSN is there to tempt the candidate towards the collateral-snapshot practice of other cash transactions.

**Fragile fact.** The fallback trigger is “complete data to reconstruct positions is not available”; the fallback covers all FMUs.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** “Differentiate between methods for tracking intraday flows and monitoring risk levels.” **GARP:** Chapter 6, Section 6.3, “Other Cash Transactions” and “Settlement Positions”. **GARP vs Schweser:** wording only (GARP “external market factors”, Schweser “macroeconomic factors”).

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-6 c, where it is Q3 of 13.

a.reason: (Scope or condition error). One-minute collateral tracking is GARP’s example of Federal Reserve practice, offered within other cash transactions, not a minimum for all participants; and it presupposes the very data the bank lacks. A would be right if asked for an example of how a central bank tracks collateral positions.

b.reason: (Polarity flip). GARP’s response to incomplete data is to fall back to a minimum dataset, not to stop tracking. B would be right only if the rule were “no data until complete data”.

c.reason: (Scope or condition error). The minimum covers settlement positions with all FMUs, not the single largest one. C would be right if the bank participated in only one FMU.

d.reason: D restates the GARP minimum: settlement positions with all FMUs, monitoring of patterns, and correlation with external market factors to anticipate needs earlier in the day.

questions.question:
A treasury analyst at a US bank is presenting to newly hired analysts. She describes one of the bank’s tracking processes as follows: “For each payment that must be completed at a specific time of day, such as the return of borrowed funds, a margin payment, or the funds a client needs to close a corporate acquisition, we record the USD amount and the deadline time, and we monitor the volume and settlement pattern of these payments.”

Which of the following best describes the measure she has described?

options.text: Payment throughput; a measure for monitoring risk levels; late completion of these payments can result in a financial penalty or other negative consequences.
Time-sensitive obligations; a measure for understanding intraday flows; late completion of these payments can result in a financial penalty or other negative consequences.
Time-sensitive obligations; a ratio for monitoring risk levels against which limits are set; late completion of these payments can result in a financial penalty or other negative consequences.
Time-sensitive obligations; a measure for understanding intraday flows; late completion carries no penalty provided the payment settles before the end of the same business day.

questions.solution:
US bank: identify the measure that logs amounts and deadlines of time-critical payments.

**Concept and theory**

Time-sensitive obligations are flow measures closely related to settlement positions: “similar to settlement positions, these transactions require completion at a specific time during the day”. GARP’s examples are transactions concerning market activities (such as the return of borrowings), margin payments, and other payments critical to the bank’s business or reputation (for example, a client closing on a corporate acquisition). Failure to settle “could result in a financial penalty or other negative consequences”. The tracking method is descriptive: the bank should monitor the volume and settlement patterns of these obligations by recording the amounts and deadline times. Schweser adds that late settlement, even on the same day, may result in penalties and potentially worse outcomes, so deadlines must be monitored carefully. The glossary entry “time critical payment” gives the same idea: a payment due at a specific time, such as a clearinghouse deadline or a client payment needed to close a mortgage or an acquisition.

How it differs from its nearest risk-level sibling: payment throughput measures the percentage of outgoing payment activity completed by time of day, a ratio used for monitoring. Time-sensitive obligations is an inventory of amounts and deadlines, not a ratio, and it sits in the flow set.

**Applying it to this question**

The stem gives three cues: payments “that must be completed at a specific time”, the three GARP examples, and recording “amount and deadline time” and monitoring “volume and settlement pattern”. Each points to time-sensitive obligations; the recording of amounts (not a percentage) places it in the flow set.

**Fragile fact.** The deadline is a specific time of day; same-day but late still counts as late.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** “Differentiate between methods for tracking intraday flows and monitoring risk levels.” **GARP:** Chapter 6, Section 6.3, “Time Sensitive Obligations”; Glossary, “Time Critical Payment”. **GARP vs Schweser:** none; the “even on the same day” wording is Schweser’s.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-6 c, where it is Q4 of 13.

a.reason: (Sibling swap). Payment throughput is the risk-level ratio of outgoing payments by time of day, not a log of amounts and deadlines. A would be right if the stem had described the share of payments sent by each time marker.

b.reason: B names the measure correctly, places it in the flow set, and states the GARP consequence of failure.

c.reason: (Sibling swap (category)). Correct name, wrong set: time-sensitive obligations is a flow measure, not one of the ratios for monitoring risk levels. C would be right for payment throughput or daily maximum usage.

d.reason: (Scope or condition error). The deadline is a time of day, not end of day; Schweser states that late settlement even on the same day may bring penalties. D would be right only for an obligation whose deadline was the close of business.

questions.question:
A risk consultant reviewing the intraday liquidity reporting of a UK bank finds two GBP reports:

- **Report X:** for each client and counterparty, the size of the intraday line extended, whether it is committed and disclosed, and its average and peak usage.
- **Report Y:** each client’s peak daily intraday overdraft compared with its committed or uncommitted line, also aggregated across clients, with averages, volatility and correlation to money market indicators.

Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Report X is total intraday credit lines to clients and counterparties, a flow measure; Report Y is client intraday credit usage, a risk-level measure whose aggregate indicates the liquidity needed to support clients’ business.

Report X is total intraday credit lines to clients and counterparties, a flow measure in which most lines are committed and disclosed to clients; Report Y is client intraday credit usage, a risk-level measure.

Report X is total intraday credit lines to clients and counterparties, a flow measure; Report Y is daily maximum intraday liquidity usage, a risk-level measure whose aggregate indicates the liquidity needed to support clients.

Report X is client intraday credit usage, a risk-level measure; Report Y is total intraday credit lines to clients and counterparties, a flow measure whose aggregate indicates the liquidity needed to support clients.

questions.solution:
UK bank: classify a client credit-line inventory and a client peak-overdraft ratio.

**Concept and theory**

Both measures concern the bank as a provider of intraday credit, which is why candidates confuse them.

**Total intraday credit lines to clients and counterparties** (flow measure). A risk manager looking after the bank’s own intraday liquidity needs to understand the potential and actual amounts of intraday credit extended to clients and counterparties. Some lines are committed and disclosed, “but most are uncommitted and undisclosed”. Beyond the lines, the bank should have data on average and peak usage and the ability to model activity at client and portfolio levels. Schweser: awareness of actual versus potential credit is important in determining maximum exposure; keep statistics on normal and high-use times and levels.

**Client intraday credit usage** (risk-level measure). Derived by comparing a client’s peak daily intraday overdraft to the established (committed or uncommitted) credit line:

Client $\text{usage}_{\text{i}} = \frac{\text{Peak daily intraday overdraft}_{\text{i}}}{\text{Credit line}_{\text{i}}}$

Tracked in aggregate, it indicates the liquidity the bank needs to support its clients’ business activities; monitoring averages, volatility and correlation with money market indicators shows how client activity affects the bank’s own intraday liquidity management.

The difference is between an inventory (lines, commitment status, usage statistics) and a ratio (peak overdraft over line) designed for monitoring.

**Applying it to this question**

Report X lists line size, commitment and disclosure, and average and peak usage: an inventory, hence total intraday credit lines to clients and counterparties. Report Y divides each client’s peak daily overdraft by its line and aggregates with averages, volatility and correlation to money market indicators: client intraday credit usage. Only A pairs these correctly and attaches the right aggregate interpretation.

**Fragile fact.** Client lines: most are uncommitted and undisclosed. Client usage is the client’s peak overdraft over its line; daily maximum usage is the bank’s own.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** “Differentiate between methods for tracking intraday flows and monitoring risk levels.” **GARP:** Chapter 6, Section 6.3, “Total Intraday Credit Lines to Clients and Counterparties” and “Client Intraday Credit Usage”. **GARP vs Schweser:** none; the committed or undisclosed detail is GARP-only.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-6 c, where it is Q5 of 13.

a.reason: A matches GARP: X is the flow inventory, Y is the risk-level ratio, and the aggregate of Y indicates the liquidity required to support clients’ business.

b.reason: (Polarity flip). GARP says most client intraday lines are uncommitted and undisclosed, not committed and disclosed. B would be right if the word “most” were attached to “uncommitted and undisclosed”.

c.reason: (Sibling swap). Daily maximum intraday liquidity usage uses the bank’s own largest net negative balance in its cash account relative to its credit line, not clients’ overdrafts. C would be right if Report Y measured the bank’s own account at the central bank.

d.reason: (Sibling swap (reversal)). It swaps the two labels. D would be right only if Report X held the ratio and Report Y the inventory.

questions.question:
A member of the board risk committee of a UK bank asks why the bank tracks “total bank intraday credit lines available and usage” across its GBP and EUR cash and settlement accounts.

Which of the following responses is most accurate?

options.text: It records the potential and actual intraday credit the bank extends to clients and counterparties, so that the bank knows the maximum exposure it could face if clients drew their lines in full.
It is the ratio of available unsecured intraday credit to Tier 1 capital, which gives a rough measure of the inadvertent systemic risk the bank poses to the financial system.

Regulators, as resolution planning shows, expect banks to understand the systemic risk they pose; the measure captures the intraday credit relied on in normal conditions and the maximum that can be drawn, committed and uncommitted.

Regulators, as resolution planning shows, expect banks to understand the systemic risk they pose; the measure captures the intraday credit relied on in normal conditions and the maximum that can be drawn, counting committed lines only.

questions.solution:
UK bank board: why track total bank intraday credit lines available and usage.

**Concept and theory**

This flow measure looks at the bank as a user of intraday credit. GARP motivates it through regulation: “as demonstrated through the requirements for preparing resolution plans, regulators increasingly expect financial institutions to understand and manage the amount of systemic risk they pose to the overall financial system” (in addition to risks to taxpayers and industry-funded insurance plans). A key component of that analysis is:

- the amount of intraday credit the bank relies on in business-as-usual conditions; and
- the maximum amount of intraday borrowing it can draw down.

The data capture committed and uncommitted intraday credit and its usage, ideally across all cash and settlement accounts. Schweser: compute how much intraday credit the bank uses in normal circumstances and compare it with the maximum available (committed and uncommitted), so the bank can determine and control the systemic risk it contributes.

Two neighbours sit close by. Total intraday credit lines to clients and counterparties is the mirror image (credit the bank extends). Intraday credit relative to Tier 1 capital is the risk-level ratio that scales available unsecured credit by capital. The measure in this question is an inventory, not a ratio, and it belongs to the flow set even though its motivation is systemic risk.

**Applying it to this question**

The committee member asks about the bank’s own lines “available and usage”. The answer needs the regulatory motivation (resolution planning, systemic risk), the two quantities (normal reliance and maximum drawable), and the scope (committed and uncommitted). Only C has all three.

**Fragile fact.** Bank lines available and usage: bank as borrower, committed and uncommitted, BAU versus maximum; it is a flow measure.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** “Differentiate between methods for tracking intraday flows and monitoring risk levels.” **GARP:** Chapter 6, Section 6.3, “Total Bank Intraday Credit Lines Available and Usage”. **GARP vs Schweser:** none.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-6 c, where it is Q6 of 13.

a.reason: (Role misassignment). Credit the bank extends to clients is the subject of total intraday credit lines to clients and counterparties. The bank here is the borrower, not the lender. A would be right for that sibling measure.

b.reason: (Sibling swap). The ratio of available unsecured credit to Tier 1 is the risk-level measure intraday credit relative to Tier 1 capital. B would be right if the committee had asked about that measure.

c.reason: C paraphrases GARP’s paragraph: regulatory expectation shown by resolution planning, BAU reliance versus maximum drawdown, committed and uncommitted lines.

d.reason: (Scope or condition error). GARP explicitly includes uncommitted as well as committed intraday credit. D would be right only if the policy deliberately excluded uncommitted lines, which the source does not do.
