questions.question:
A treasury analyst at a Singapore bank reconstructs, after the close, the day’s movements in the bank’s SGD settlement account at the central bank, which carries an uncommitted intraday credit line of SGD 950 million. The bank’s Tier 1 capital is SGD 2,400 million.

| Item | SGD million |
|---|---|
| Opening balance at 08:00 | 120 |
| Net flow 08:00 to 09:00 | −180 |
| Net flow 09:00 to 10:00 | −260 |
| Net flow 10:00 to 11:00 | 90 |
| Net flow 11:00 to 12:00 | −150 |
| Net flow 12:00 to 13:00 | 210 |
| Net flow 13:00 to 14:00 | −120 |
| Net flow 14:00 to 15:00 | 260 |
| Net flow 15:00 to 16:00 | 40 |
| Net flow 16:00 to 17:00 | 70 |

Assuming balances move only at the hourly marks shown, which of the following is closest to the account’s daily maximum intraday liquidity usage?
questions.solution:
Singapore bank: daily maximum intraday liquidity usage from opening balance and hourly net flows.

**Concept and theory**

Daily maximum intraday liquidity usage is the first risk-level measure. GARP calls it “a measure of the bank’s usage of an intraday credit extension”. It is the ratio of the day’s largest net negative balance to the size of the committed or uncommitted credit line:

Daily max usage $= \frac{|\text{min}_{\text{t}} \text{B}_{\text{t}}|}{\text{L}}$ , $\text{B}_{\text{t}} = \text{B}_{0} + \sum_{\text{s}\le\text{t}} \text{F}_{\text{s}}$

where $\text{B}_{0}$ is the opening balance, $\text{F}_{\text{s}}$ the net flow in interval s, $\text{B}_{\text{t}}$ the cumulative balance at time t, and L the credit line. Only negative values of $\text{B}_{\text{t}}$ matter, because a negative balance is the use of intraday credit. Real-time monitoring is not required, provided the bank can recreate all of a day’s positions ex post. The peak and average of the daily ratio are typically tracked over a period such as a month. The measure exists because end-of-day balances can be flat or positive while the account was deeply overdrawn mid-day; the intraday extreme is what consumes the line.

**Applying it to this question**

Formula first: usage $= | \text{min}_{\text{t}} \text{B}_{\text{t}}|$/L with $\text{B}_{0} =$ 120 and L = 950 (SGD million).

$\text{B}_{09} =$ 120 − 180 = −60

$\text{B}_{10} = -$60 − 260 = −320

$\text{B}_{11} = -$320 + 90 = −230

$\text{B}_{12} = -$230 − 150 = −380

$\text{B}_{13} = -$380 + 210 = −170

$\text{B}_{14} = -$170 − 120 = −290

$\text{B}_{15} = -$290 + 260 = −30

$\text{B}_{16} = -$30 + 40 = 10, $\text{B}_{17} =$ 10 + 70 = 80

Largest net negative balance = 380

Daily max usage = 380/950 = 0.400 = 40.0%

The bank used 40% of its intraday line at the worst point of the day (12:00), even though it closed with a positive balance of SGD 80 million. Tier 1 capital (SGD 2,400 million) is an irrelevant input: it belongs to the intraday credit relative to Tier 1 measure.

**Fragile fact.** Use the cumulative balance path and its single most negative point, divided by the credit line, not Tier 1 capital.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** “Differentiate between methods for tracking intraday flows and monitoring risk levels.” **GARP:** Chapter 6, Section 6.3, “Measures for Quantifying and Monitoring Risk Levels”, “Daily Maximum Intraday Liquidity Usage”. **GARP vs Schweser:** none on the formula.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-6 c, where it is Q7 of 13.

a.reason: (Wrong input twin). 380/2,400 = 15.8% divides by Tier 1 capital instead of the credit line. A would be right if the question had asked for peak intraday credit used relative to Tier 1 capital.

b.reason: (Wrong statistic (intermediate result)). Averaging the seven negative balances gives (60 + 320 + 230 + 380 + 170 + 290 + 30)/7 = 1,480/7 = 211.4, and 211.4/950 = 22.3%. The measure uses the single largest negative balance; averaging is done across days, not within a day. B would be right for an average intraday overdraft ratio, which is not this measure.

c.reason: (Wrong input twin). 260/950 = 27.4% uses the largest single hourly net outflow instead of the cumulative balance. C would be right only if the account had started each hour at zero.

d.reason: D is the largest cumulative negative balance divided by the account’s credit line, exactly GARP’s definition.

questions.question:
A banking regulator is validating a Chinese bank’s methodology for daily maximum intraday liquidity usage across its CNY and USD accounts at the central bank, two FMUs and three correspondent banks.

Which of the following statements in the methodology is most accurate?

options.text: Because the measure uses the day’s largest net negative balance, it can be computed only for accounts that support real-time reporting of positions.
At a minimum, the measure is tracked for every cash account held at the central bank, FMUs and correspondent banks, with its peak and average tracked over a period such as a month.
The consolidated measure should combine all of the bank’s accounts across currencies and jurisdictions, whether or not cash and collateral can be moved between them intraday.
The measure compares the day’s largest net negative balance in each account with the bank’s Tier 1 capital, and its peak and average are tracked over a period such as a month.

questions.solution:
Chinese bank methodology for daily maximum intraday liquidity usage: data, coverage and consolidation.

**Concept and theory**

GARP adds three implementation rules to the definition (largest net negative balance relative to the committed or uncommitted line).

- **Data:** many accounts allow real-time reporting, but “this calculation does not require real-time monitoring” provided the bank can recreate all of a day’s positions ex post.
- **Coverage:** “at a minimum” the measure should be tracked for every cash account held at the central bank, FMUs and correspondent banks; typically its peak and average are tracked over a period such as a month.
- **Consolidation:** ideally the bank also monitors its consolidated position “across all accounts between which liquidity can be readily transferred intraday without restrictions”, to get a true picture. This is logically done for accounts in the same currency connected to a common payment system, but can extend to multiple currencies and jurisdictions if cash and collateral can be freely transferred between them intraday.

The logic of the consolidation condition: a surplus in one account offsets a deficit in another only if funds can actually move between them during the day. Summing accounts that cannot be connected intraday would understate true usage. Schweser condenses this to “calculated for all the bank’s cash accounts and viewed on a combined basis” and omits the transferability condition; GARP’s condition governs.

**Applying it to this question**

The regulator is checking four claims. The real-time claim, the consolidation claim and the Tier 1 claim each conflict with a GARP rule. B states the coverage minimum and the monthly peak and average, both directly from GARP.

**Fragile fact.** Consolidate only across accounts between which liquidity can move intraday without restrictions; real-time data are not required.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** “Differentiate between methods for tracking intraday flows and monitoring risk levels.” **GARP:** Chapter 6, Section 6.3, “Daily Maximum Intraday Liquidity Usage”. **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser says “viewed on a combined basis” without GARP’s free-transferability condition; resolved from GARP (a condensation, not a content conflict).

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-6 c, where it is Q8 of 13.

a.reason: (Polarity flip). GARP says the calculation does not require real-time monitoring if positions can be recreated ex post. A would be right only for a bank unable to reconstruct positions after the fact.

b.reason: B reproduces GARP’s minimum coverage (central bank, FMUs, correspondents) and the typical tracking of peak and average over a period.

c.reason: (Scope or condition error). It drops GARP’s condition that cash and collateral be freely transferable intraday between the accounts being combined. C would be right if every account were connected and unrestricted.

d.reason: (Sibling swap). The denominator is the account’s credit line; Tier 1 capital belongs to intraday credit relative to Tier 1 capital. D would be right for that measure.

questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a eurozone bank is computing the “intraday credit relative to Tier 1 capital” measure. Data for the review date (EUR billion):

| Item | EUR billion |
|---|---|
| Total intraday credit available (committed and uncommitted) | 18.0 |
| of which secured by posted collateral | 7.5 |
| Total intraday credit used at the daily peak | 9.6 |
| of which secured by posted collateral | 4.1 |
| Tier 1 capital | 6.0 |
| Total regulatory capital (Tier 1 plus Tier 2) | 7.8 |

Which of the following is closest to the version of the measure that serves as a rough indicator of the inadvertent systemic risk the bank poses to the financial system?
questions.solution:
Eurozone bank: available unsecured intraday credit relative to Tier 1 capital.

**Concept and theory**

Intraday credit relative to Tier 1 capital is “a broad representation of the intraday settlement risk posed by a bank”. GARP says it should be tracked in four versions: total and unsecured intraday credit, each available and used. The reason for separating unsecured credit is the theory that posting high-quality collateral mitigates intraday settlement risk. The reason for looking at available (not just used) credit is that the full drawable amount is what the bank could draw on the system. One version is singled out:

Indicator $= \frac{\text{Available credit} - \text{Available secured credit}}{\text{Tier 1 capital}} = \frac{\text{Available unsecured credit}}{\text{Tier 1 capital}}$

GARP calls this “a rough measure of the inadvertent systemic risk that the institution poses to the financial system”. “Inadvertent” because intraday exposures arise as a cost of doing business rather than as deliberate, compensated credit extensions. Viewed as a time series and against other institutions, the measure shows the relative systemic risk of the bank’s business model and changes in its risk profile.

**Applying it to this question**

Formula first, then the steps (EUR billion):

Available unsecured = 18.0 − 7.5 = 10.5

Indicator = 10.5/6.0 = 1.750 = 175.0%

The bank’s undrawn-plus-drawn unsecured intraday capacity is 1.75 times its Tier 1 capital. The “used” rows and total regulatory capital are not needed: used credit belongs to the other versions of the ratio, and the denominator is Tier 1 only.

**Fragile fact.** Systemic-risk version: available, unsecured, over Tier 1. Each of the three words has a twin that gives a wrong number.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** “Differentiate between methods for tracking intraday flows and monitoring risk levels.” **GARP:** Chapter 6, Section 6.3, “Intraday Credit Relative to Tier 1 Capital”. **GARP vs Schweser:** none; Schweser states the same ratio (unsecured and available, as opposed to used).

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-6 c, where it is Q9 of 13.

a.reason: (Wrong input twin (used for available)). (9.6 − 4.1)/6.0 = 5.5/6.0 = 91.7% is used unsecured credit over Tier 1. A would be right if asked for the used, unsecured version.

b.reason: (Wrong input twin (total capital for Tier 1)). 10.5/7.8 = 134.6% divides by Tier 1 plus Tier 2. B would be right only if the denominator were total regulatory capital, which GARP does not use.

c.reason: (Wrong input twin and dropped term). 9.6/6.0 = 160.0% uses total used credit, with no deduction for collateral. C would be right if asked for total used intraday credit relative to Tier 1.

d.reason: D uses available (not used), unsecured (not total) credit over Tier 1 capital, which is the GARP version identified as the rough systemic-risk measure.

questions.question:
The CRO of an Australian bank is preparing a statement for the risk committee on how the bank will use the measure “intraday credit relative to Tier 1 capital” for its AUD operations.

Which of the following statements should the CRO include?

options.text: The measure is tracked for total and unsecured intraday credit, available and used, because posting high-quality collateral mitigates intraday settlement risk; it is most informative as a time series and against peer institutions.

The measure is tracked for total and unsecured intraday credit, available and used, because posting high-quality collateral increases intraday settlement risk; it is most informative as a time series and against peer institutions.

The measure is tracked for total and unsecured intraday credit, available and used; because it is scaled by Tier 1 capital, it gives a precise measure of the systemic risk the bank poses to the financial system.

The measure is tracked for total and unsecured intraday credit that is used only, because available but undrawn intraday credit poses no settlement risk; it is most informative as a time series and against peers.

questions.solution:
Australian bank CRO: how to use intraday credit relative to Tier 1 capital.

**Concept and theory**

The measure scales intraday credit by the bank’s loss-absorbing capital, giving a broad view of the intraday settlement risk the bank poses. GARP’s design choices:

| Design choice | Reason in GARP |
|---|---|
| Total and unsecured credit | Posting high-quality collateral mitigates intraday settlement risk, so the unsecured portion isolates the uncovered exposure. |
| Available and used credit | Used credit shows today’s reliance; available credit shows what could be drawn. Available unsecured over Tier 1 is the rough measure of inadvertent systemic risk. |
| Time series and horizontal view | Viewed over time and against other institutions, the measure shows the relative systemic risk of the business model and changes in the risk profile. |

GARP’s language is deliberately cautious: “broad representation” and “rough measure”. The ratio is a monitoring indicator against which thresholds can be set, not a precise quantification of systemic risk. It is a risk-level measure, in contrast with total bank intraday credit lines available and usage, which is the flow inventory that supplies its numerator.

**Applying it to this question**

All four options start from total and unsecured credit; they differ in the theory behind the collateral split, the precision claimed, and whether available credit is included. Option A keeps the correct direction (collateral mitigates risk), includes available and used, and gives the time-series and peer use.

**Fragile fact.** Direction: collateral reduces intraday settlement risk; the ratio is rough, and available credit counts.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** “Differentiate between methods for tracking intraday flows and monitoring risk levels.” **GARP:** Chapter 6, Section 6.3, “Intraday Credit Relative to Tier 1 Capital”. **GARP vs Schweser:** none; time-series and peer comparison detail is GARP-only.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-6 c, where it is Q10 of 13.

a.reason: A paraphrases GARP’s design rules and interpretation exactly.

b.reason: (Polarity flip). GARP says collateral mitigates intraday settlement risk; that is why unsecured credit is separated. B would be right only if collateral increased risk, the opposite of the source.

c.reason: (Absolute claim). GARP calls the measure a “rough” measure and a “broad representation”; it is not precise. C would be right without the word “precise”.

d.reason: (Scope or condition error). GARP tracks available as well as used credit, and singles out available unsecured credit as the systemic-risk gauge. D would be right only if undrawn credit could never be drawn.

questions.question:
The chief credit officer of a US bank receives a monthly report on client intraday credit usage, computed client by client and in aggregate, for the bank’s USD corporate and institutional clients.

Which of the following is least likely to be an appropriate use of this measure?

options.text: Pinpointing clients that run frequent overdrafts and deciding whether they must change their practices or the bank must raise its charges for the credit.
Monitoring the averages, volatility and correlation of aggregate usage with money market indicators to see how client activity affects the bank’s own intraday liquidity.
Gauging the inadvertent systemic risk the bank poses to the financial system by comparing clients’ peak overdrafts with the bank’s Tier 1 capital.
Informing the bank’s policies on the provision and size of intraday credit lines relative to industry cohorts and client risk levels.

questions.solution:
US bank: least appropriate use of client intraday credit usage.

**Concept and theory**

Client intraday credit usage compares each client’s peak daily intraday overdraft with its established (committed or uncommitted) line. GARP describes uses at two levels.

- **Aggregate:** tracking aggregate exposures indicates the liquidity the bank needs to support clients’ business. Monitoring averages, volatility and correlation with other money market indicators shows how client activity affects the bank’s ability to manage its own intraday liquidity.
- **Individual client:** pinpoint clients that run frequent overdrafts and decide whether they need to change their practices or the bank needs to increase its charges; monitor over time whether initiatives to modify client behaviour reduce reliance on intraday credit.
- **Policy:** inform policies on the provision and size of intraday lines relative to industry cohorts and client risk levels.

The motivation, from Section 6.2, is that client intraday credit is one of the two behaviours that generate daylight overdrafts, and banks usually receive no direct compensation for it. The measure tells the bank how much of its own intraday liquidity its clients consume, and it is distinct from the systemic-risk gauge, which compares the bank’s available unsecured intraday credit with Tier 1 capital.

**Applying it to this question**

The qualifier is “least likely”. Options A, B and D each reproduce a GARP use. Option C borrows the Tier 1 denominator and the systemic-risk purpose from a different measure.

**Fragile fact.** Client usage tells you how much liquidity clients consume; the systemic-risk gauge is the bank’s available unsecured credit over Tier 1.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** “Differentiate between methods for tracking intraday flows and monitoring risk levels.” **GARP:** Chapter 6, Section 6.3, “Client Intraday Credit Usage”. **GARP vs Schweser:** none; the policy use is GARP-only.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-6 c, where it is Q11 of 13.

a.reason: (Not an error: stated individual-level use). GARP says client-level tracking pinpoints frequent-overdraft clients and decides whether they change practice or the bank raises charges. Choosing A misreads the “least likely” qualifier.

b.reason: (Not an error: stated aggregate use). GARP lists averages, volatility and correlation with money market indicators. Choosing it misreads the qualifier.

c.reason: C is the least appropriate use: systemic risk relative to Tier 1 is gauged by available unsecured intraday credit over Tier 1 capital, not by clients’ overdrafts. The error is a sibling swap.

d.reason: (Not an error: stated policy use). GARP says the data can inform policies on the provision and size of lines relative to industry cohorts and client risk levels. Choosing it misreads the qualifier.

questions.question:
The treasurer of a German bank that is a direct participant in a EUR large value payment system notes that the system requires participants to submit a target percentage of their payments by a midday deadline. She asks the liquidity team to explain the payment throughput measure.

Which of the following explanations is most accurate?

options.text: Payment throughput records the amount and deadline time of each payment that must be completed at a specific time, which places it among the measures for understanding intraday flows.

Payment throughput tracks outgoing payment activity relative to time of day, helping the bank process the day’s payments in time, meet FMU deadline targets, and relate its peak periods to liquidity on hand and credit usage.

Payment throughput tracks incoming payment activity relative to time of day, helping the bank process the day’s payments in time, meet FMU deadline targets, and relate its peak periods to liquidity on hand and credit usage.

Payment throughput tracks outgoing payment activity relative to time of day and is relevant chiefly to indirect participants, which rely on a direct member to route their payments to the clearing system.

questions.solution:
German bank, direct LVPS participant: what payment throughput measures and why.

**Concept and theory**

Payment throughput measures “track the percentage of outgoing payment activity relative to time of day”. GARP says that for banks that are direct participants in FMUs it is useful to measure and monitor outgoing payments relative to total payments or time markers for three reasons:

1. to track volume patterns and help ensure all of the day’s payments are processed in time;
2. in some cases, to meet FMU requirements for submitting a target percentage of payments by a deadline;
3. to identify and monitor peak periods over time and their correlation with intraday liquidity on hand and intraday credit usage.

In symbols, at time marker t:

$\text{Throughput}_{\text{t}} = \frac{\text{Outgoing payments released by t}}{\text{Total outgoing payments for the day}}$

Why it matters: Section 6.2 notes that banks near their debit cap “throttle” outgoing payments while waiting for incoming credits; a throughput rule sets a minimum pace of submission, and the measure lets the bank see whether it keeps that pace. GARP also links throughput to liquidity savings mechanisms (FMU throughput requirements). It is a risk-level measure, unlike time-sensitive obligations, which record amounts and deadlines.

**Applying it to this question**

The stem sets up a direct participant facing an FMU target-percentage rule. The correct explanation must say outgoing, by time of day, and list the GARP reasons. B does this; the others swap the measure, the direction of flow, or the type of participant.

**Fragile fact.** Throughput is outgoing payments by time of day, for direct participants.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** “Differentiate between methods for tracking intraday flows and monitoring risk levels.” **GARP:** Chapter 6, Section 6.3, “Payment Throughput”. **GARP vs** **Schweser:** none.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-6 c, where it is Q12 of 13.

a.reason: (Sibling swap). Recording amounts and deadline times is time-sensitive obligations, a flow measure. A would be right if the stem had asked about time-sensitive obligations.

b.reason: B restates GARP’s definition and all three reasons.

c.reason: (Polarity flip). Throughput tracks outgoing payments; the FMU target concerns payments the bank submits. C would be right only if the rule concerned receipts.

d.reason: (Role misassignment). GARP frames the measure for banks that are direct participants in FMUs; indirect participants route through a direct member. D would be right if “indirect” were replaced by “direct”.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Differentiate between methods for tracking intraday flows and monitoring risk levels.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-6 c Q13
questions.question:
A treasury analyst at a Canadian bank compares the bank’s CAD activity at two FMUs on a representative day:

| Item | FMU P | FMU Q |
|---|---|---|
| Value of the bank’s transactions (CAD billion) | 48.00 | 30.00 |
| Bank’s peak credit usage (CAD billion) | 1.92 | 0.66 |
| Bank’s average credit usage (CAD billion) | 0.77 | 0.27 |
| Direct participants (number) | 22 | 140 |

Using the indicator of the efficiency of each FMU’s usage of daylight credit, which of the following is most accurate?

options.text: P 4.0%, Q 2.2%; FMU P uses daylight credit more efficiently, because a higher ratio shows fuller use of the credit extended.
P 1.6%, Q 0.9%; FMU Q uses daylight credit more efficiently, and the bank could redirect payment flows towards it if operationally able.
P 4.0%, Q 2.2%; FMU Q uses daylight credit more efficiently, and the bank could redirect payment flows towards it if operationally able.
P 25.0 times, Q 45.5 times; FMU P uses daylight credit more efficiently, because its indicator is the lower of the two.

questions.solution:
Canadian bank at two FMUs: peak intraday credit usage relative to total volumes as an efficiency indicator.

**Concept and theory**

Within payment throughput, GARP adds a second indicator: a bank “can track its peak intraday credit usage relative to total volumes with an FMU to provide an indicator of the efficiency of the FMU’s usage of daylight credit”. FMUs have different system rules and operating models (for example netting, settlement windows, liquidity savings mechanisms), so they differ in how much intraday liquidity they need to settle a given value of transactions. Understanding these differences can enable a bank to redirect payment flows as a tool to manage its intraday liquidity needs, “assuming it has the requisite operational capabilities”.

$\text{E}_{\text{k}} = \frac{\text{Peak intraday credit usage at FMU k}}{\text{Total transaction value at FMU k}}$

A lower $\text{E}_{\text{k}}$ means less daylight credit is consumed per unit of value settled, so the FMU uses credit more efficiently. Schweser states the same idea (maximum intraday credit use as a percentage of total transaction amounts with an FMU).

**Applying it to this question**

Formula first, then (CAD billion):

$\text{E}_{\text{P}} =$ 1.92/48.00 = 0.040 = 4.0%

$\text{E}_{\text{Q}} =$ 0.66/30.00 = 0.022 = 2.2%

$\text{E}_{\text{Q}} < \text{E}_{\text{P}} \Rightarrow$ FMU Q uses daylight credit more efficiently

The bank consumes CAD 2.2 of peak credit per CAD 100 settled through Q against CAD 4.0 through P, so shifting suitable flows to Q could reduce its need for daylight credit, if operationally feasible. Average credit usage and the number of participants are irrelevant inputs: the indicator uses peak usage and total volume only.

**Fragile fact.** Peak credit over volume: lower is more efficient; redirecting flows is subject to operational capability.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** “Differentiate between methods for tracking intraday flows and monitoring risk levels.” **GARP:** Chapter 6, Section 6.3, “Payment Throughput” (final paragraph). **GARP vs Schweser:** none.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-6 c, where it is Q13 of 13.

a.reason: (Polarity flip). Correct ratios, wrong reading: a higher ratio means more credit per unit settled, i.e. less efficient. A would be right if the indicator were volume per unit of credit.

b.reason: (Wrong input twin (average for peak)). 0.77/48.00 = 1.6% and 0.27/30.00 = 0.9% use average rather than peak usage. The conclusion happens to match, but the numbers do not follow GARP’s definition. B would be right if the indicator were based on average usage.

c.reason: C has both correct ratios, the correct direction (lower is more efficient), and GARP’s operational-capability condition.

d.reason: (Inverted ratio). 48.00/1.92 = 25.0 and 30.00/0.66 = 45.5 compute volume per unit of credit, then apply the “lower is better” rule meant for credit per unit of volume. D would be right only if the ratio were defined as credit over volume.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Differentiate between deterministic and stochastic cash flows and provide examples of each.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-7 a Q1
questions.question:
A junior risk analyst at a Japanese trust bank is preparing an introductory session for newly hired analysts on how the bank classifies future cash flows for liquidity monitoring. The draft slides contain the following statements:

I. Cash flows are classified along two dimensions, time and amount; a cash flow is deterministic in time if it will occur at a future instant that is known with certainty at the reference time.

II. The category of a cash flow is a permanent property of the contract, so it does not change when the point of view is shifted from today to some later reference date.

III. Cash flows whose amount is deterministic are labelled “fixed” in the taxonomy.

IV. A cash flow whose amount is stochastic must also be stochastic in time, since the uncertainty that affects its size also affects its date.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.text: I and II only
I, III and IV only
I and III only
II and IV only

questions.solution:
Japanese trust bank slides: which statements about the two dimensions and the deterministic/stochastic labels are correct.

**Concept and theory**

GARP opens Chapter 7 by arguing that a clear taxonomy of the cash flows a bank’s business generates is the starting point for any tool that monitors and manages liquidity risk. The taxonomy it proposes uses two dimensions. The first is time: a cash flow is deterministic in time if it will occur at a future instant known with certainty at the reference time (for example, today), and stochastic in time if it can occur at some random future instant. The second is amount: a cash flow is deterministic in amount if its size is known with certainty at the reference time, and stochastic in amount if its size cannot be fully determined. Every cash flow therefore sits in one cell of a two-way grid.

Two refinements matter. First, when the amount is deterministic the taxonomy simply labels the cash flow fixed, since a contract has set it that way; when the amount is stochastic it is broken into four subcategories (credit related, indexed/contingent, behavioural, new business). Second, the classification is relative to a reference point: GARP stresses that it depends on the point of view, and that a cash flow can change category when the point of view is shifted to some other future date. A floating coupon whose rate has already been fixed, for instance, is uncertain in amount before the fixing date but known afterwards.

The two dimensions are independent. Knowing the date says nothing about the size, and vice versa, which is why all four combinations (fixed/deterministic, fixed/stochastic, stochastic/deterministic, stochastic/stochastic) contain real examples.

**Applying it to this question**

Statement I restates GARP’s two dimensions and its definition of deterministic time: correct.

Statement II contradicts GARP’s explicit remark that cash flows can change category when the point of view shifts: wrong. Statement III matches GARP’s label “fixed” for deterministic-amount cash flows: correct. Statement IV is refuted by any indexed/contingent cash flow at a known date, such as a floating-rate coupon or a European option payout: wrong. Hence I and III only.

**Fragile fact.** Category is relative to the reference time; time and amount are independent dimensions, so “stochastic amount” never implies “stochastic time”.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Differentiate between deterministic and stochastic cash flows and provide examples of each.

**GARP:** Chapter 7, Section 7.1 “A Taxonomy of Cash Flows” and Figure 7.1. **Schweser:** Module 72.1, “Deterministic and Stochastic Cash Flows”. **GARP vs Schweser:** none; the reference-point remark is GARP-only (Schweser does not mention it).

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-7 a, where it is Q1 of 12.

a.reason: (Absolute-claim trap). It accepts Statement II, which turns a classification that GARP says depends on the point of view into a permanent property of the contract. It would be right only if the stem fixed the reference date for good and asked about classification at that single date.

b.reason: (Scope or condition error). It accepts Statement IV, which ties stochastic amount to stochastic time. GARP’s indexed/contingent cash flows (floating coupons, European option payouts) are stochastic in amount but occur at known dates. Statement IV would hold only if the stem restricted attention to, say, credit-related cash flows, where the uncertain default time drives both dimensions.

c.reason: C accepts exactly the two true statements. GARP defines both dimensions, labels deterministic-amount cash flows “fixed”, and notes that categories can change when the reference date moves.

d.reason: (Polarity flip). It reverses the verdicts on all four statements, accepting the two false ones and rejecting the two true ones. It would be right only if the question asked which statements are incorrect.

questions.loText: Differentiate between deterministic and stochastic cash flows and provide examples of each.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-7 a Q2
questions.question:
The treasurer of an Australian commercial bank is deciding which of the following expected cash flows can be placed in the fixed amount, deterministic time cell of the bank’s cash flow taxonomy:

I. Semi-annual coupons the bank will pay on AUD fixed-rate senior bonds it has issued.

II. Scheduled capital instalments on fixed-rate amortising mortgages granted to retail borrowers with material default risk.

III. Coupons on fixed-rate Australian government bonds held in the bank’s assets, the issuer being treated as default-risk free.

IV. Coupons on government floating-rate notes, the issuer being treated as default-risk free, reset quarterly to the 3-month BBSW fixing.

Which items belong in that cell?

options.text: I and III only
III only
I, II and III only
I, III and IV only

questions.solution:
Australian bank: which items belong in the fixed amount, deterministic time cell.

**Concept and theory**

The fixed amount, deterministic time cell is the simplest cell of GARP’s taxonomy: both the date and the size of the cash flow are known at the reference time. GARP says these cash flows typically come from financial contracts such as fixed-rate bonds and fixed-rate mortgages or loans, and are produced by periodic interest payments (for example every six months) and, where the asset amortises, periodic repayment of capital instalments. Figure 7.1 lists “risk-free fixed rate bonds coupons” and “capital amortisation of risk-free fixed rate mortgage”.

GARP adds two points that make this cell trickier than it looks. First, the category is not limited to assets: bonds issued by the bank and loans received by the bank, held among its liabilities, generate the same kind of cash flows. Second, on the asset side the classification “can only be ensured” if the obligor or the bond’s issuer is risk free, so that credit events cannot alter the contractual schedule. If the borrower can default, the schedule can be disrupted and part of the flow moves into the credit-related subcategory (missing cash flows, recovery). A coupon whose size is reset to a market fixing, however safe the issuer, is not fixed at all: it is indexed/contingent.

| Feature | In the cell? | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Fixed coupon, risk-free issuer | Yes | Contract fixes date and size |
| Fixed coupon paid on own bonds | Yes | Liability side counts too |
| Fixed instalments, risky borrower | Not ensured | Credit events can alter schedule |
| Floating coupon, risk-free issuer | No | Amount indexed to market fixing |

**Applying it to this question**

Item I: the bank’s own fixed-rate bond coupons are liability cash flows with contractual dates and sizes, so they qualify. Item II: the instalments are contractual, but the retail borrowers carry material default risk, so GARP’s risk-free condition fails. Item III: fixed-rate government coupons with a risk-free issuer are GARP’s textbook example. Item IV: the coupon is reset to BBSW, so the amount is stochastic (indexed/contingent) even though the dates are known. Hence I and III only.

**Fragile fact.** Liabilities count; risky assets do not qualify; a known date never makes an indexed amount “fixed”.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Differentiate between deterministic and stochastic cash flows and provide examples of each.

**GARP:** Chapter 7, Section 7.1, paragraph on deterministic amount/deterministic time cash flows; Figure 7.1. **GARP vs Schweser:** none; the liability-side and risk-free points are GARP-only (Schweser’s figure was not machine-readable).

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-7 a, where it is Q2 of 12.

a.reason: GARP extends the fixed/deterministic category to bonds issued and loans received by the bank, and confines it on the asset side to risk-free obligors. Only items I and III satisfy both requirements.

b.reason: (Scope or condition error). It restricts the category to assets, dropping item I. GARP explicitly says bonds issued and loans received by the bank also produce such cash flows. B would be right only if the question asked which asset cash flows qualify.

c.reason: (Scope or condition error). It drops the risk-free condition and admits item II. The contractual schedule of a loan to a risky borrower is not assured, because a default changes it. C would be right only if the stem said the mortgage borrowers were treated as default-risk free.

d.reason: (Sibling swap). It puts the floating-rate coupon (item IV), which belongs to the indexed/contingent subcategory, into the fixed row. D would be right only if the notes paid a fixed coupon.

questions.source: High quality paper LTR-7 a Q3
questions.question: A portfolio manager at a Singapore private bank reviews a structured trade in which the bank has sold a client a one-touch option with an 18-month expiry. If the underlying exchange rate breaches a barrier level at any time before expiry, the bank pays the client SGD 2 million; otherwise nothing is paid. The counterparty is treated as default-risk free. From today’s point of view, which of the following best describes how the possible payout is classified?

options.text: Deterministic in time and stochastic in amount, as an indexed/contingent cash flow whose size depends on the underlying’s level.
Stochastic in both time and amount, as an indexed/contingent cash flow in the same cell as an American option payout.
Deterministic in both time and amount, since both the payout and the expiry date are fixed by the terms of the contract.
Deterministic in amount and stochastic in time, since the sum is set by the contract but the time the barrier is hit is unknown.

questions.solution:
Singapore private bank: classifying the payout of a one-touch option it sold.

**Concept and theory**

Fixed amounts do not always fall on known dates. GARP gives two reasons why a deterministic amount can occur at a stochastic time: either the contract provides for a given sum to be paid or received, but at a time that depends on some event, or the amount depends on a choice the bank itself makes (Question 6 treats the second case). Its example of the first case is the one-touch option. The buyer receives a given amount of money when the underlying breaches a barrier level, from below or from above. Seen from the reference instant, the time of that breach is unknown; the amount, however, “can easily be deducted” from the contract’s terms.

Compare the option payouts in the taxonomy:

| Payout | Amount | Time |
|---|---|---|
| One-touch option | Fixed (contract sum) | Stochastic (barrier hit) |
| European option | Stochastic (indexed) | Deterministic (expiry) |
| American option | Stochastic (indexed) | Stochastic (early exercise) |

The one-touch is the mirror image of the European option: the European pays a market-dependent amount on a known date, while the one-touch pays a contract-fixed amount on an unknown date. What makes a payout “indexed/contingent” is that its size depends on market variables; for a one-touch the market only determines when (and whether) the fixed sum is paid.

**Applying it to this question**

The payout is SGD 2 million, set by the contract, so the amount is deterministic (fixed). The payment is triggered when the barrier is breached, which can happen at any time before expiry, so the time is stochastic. The 18-month expiry is only the latest possible date, not the payment date, and the counterparty’s risk-free status removes any credit-related element.

**Fragile fact.** One-touch: the amount is fixed and the time is stochastic, the reverse of a European option.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Differentiate between deterministic and stochastic cash flows and provide examples of each.

**GARP:** Chapter 7, Section 7.1, paragraph “Deterministic amount cash flows can also occur at stochastic times”; Figure 7.1. **GARP vs Schweser:** none (Schweser’s Figure 72.1 is not readable in the text extraction; GARP used).

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-7 a, where it is Q3 of 12.

a.reason: (Sibling swap). It gives the one-touch the European option’s cell (known date, market-dependent size). A would be right if the option were a European digital paying at expiry an amount linked to the underlying’s level.

b.reason: (Sibling swap). It puts the one-touch with the American option payout. The American payout is stochastic in amount because its size depends on the underlying at exercise; the one-touch pays a contractual sum. B would be right for an American call or put.

c.reason: (Scope or condition error). It treats the expiry date as the payment date. The payment occurs when the barrier is hit, not at expiry. C would be right for a contract paying SGD 2 million on a fixed date with certainty.

d.reason: D reproduces GARP’s classification of the one-touch payout: given sum from the contract, unknown time from the reference instant.

questions.question:
An internal auditor at a Brazilian bank is validating how the treasury’s cash flow manual assigns stochastic amount cash flows to subcategories. The manual lists four items:

I. Early redemption of fixed-term deposits by retail clients.

II. The recovery received on a defaulted corporate loan.

III. New loans the bank plans to originate to replace exactly the loans that mature over the next two years.

IV. Coupons on a bond issued by a default-risk-free issuer that are linked to an interbank rate fixing.

Which assignment of subcategories is consistent with the reading?

options.text: I new business; II credit related; III behavioural; IV indexed/contingent
I behavioural; II credit related; III new business; IV indexed/contingent
I behavioural; II indexed/contingent; III new business; IV credit related
I credit related; II behavioural; III new business; IV indexed/contingent

questions.solution:
Brazilian bank auditor: assigning four stochastic-amount items to subcategories.

**Concept and theory**

When the amount of a cash flow cannot be fully determined at the reference time, GARP asks why it is uncertain, and the answer gives four subcategories:

| Subcategory | Source of amount uncertainty (GARP) |
|---|---|
| Credit related | Credit events, such as the default of one or more of the bank’s clients |
| Indexed/contingent | Market variables, such as rate fixings or the level of an option’s underlying |
| Behavioural | Decisions of the bank’s clients or counterparties, only loosely predictable from rational behaviour based on market variables, and sometimes based on information the bank does not have |
| New business | New contracts dealt in the future and more or less planned by the bank, including the replacement of expiring contracts |

The test is the driver of the uncertainty, not the product. Deposits appear in two places, for example: withdrawals and prepayments of existing deposits are behavioural (clients decide), while new deposits are new business (contracts not yet dealt). Likewise, a loan is fixed while performing and risk free, credit related once default is in question, and new business when it is a planned replacement loan.

Each subcategory needs its own model: interest rate models for indexed flows, credit models (including default correlation) for credit-related flows, behavioural models for liquidity options such as deposit withdrawals and prepayments, and business-planning models for new business, which GARP calls quite difficult to model and manage.

**Applying it to this question**

Item I: early redemption of term deposits is a client decision; GARP’s figure lists “prepayment of deposits” under behavioural. Item II: a recovery after default exists only because of a credit event; GARP inserts recovery value in the credit-related category. Item III: replacing expiring loans with planned new loans is GARP’s own new business example. Item IV: a coupon linked to an interbank fixing, with a risk-free issuer, is indexed/contingent. Mapping: I behavioural, II credit related, III new business, IV indexed/contingent.

**Fragile fact.** Classify by the driver of uncertainty: default, market variable, client decision, or future contract.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Differentiate between deterministic and stochastic cash flows and provide examples of each.

**GARP:** Chapter 7, Section 7.1, paragraph “When the amount is stochastic, it is possible to recognize four possible subcategories”; Figure 7.1. **Schweser:** Module 72.1 lists the same four subcategories. **GARP vs Schweser:** none.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-7 a, where it is Q4 of 12.

a.reason: (Sibling swap). It swaps behavioural and new business for items I and III. Replacement loans depend partly on whether clients want them, but GARP places replacement of expiring contracts under new business, and early redemption of existing deposits under behavioural. A would be right if item I were new deposits to be raised and item III were early repayments of existing loans.

b.reason: B assigns each item according to the source of its amount uncertainty exactly as GARP’s figure and text do.

c.reason: (Sibling swap). It swaps credit related and indexed/contingent for items II and IV. A recovery is driven by a credit event, not by a market fixing, and a coupon of a risk-free issuer cannot be credit related. C would be right if item II were a fixing-linked coupon and item IV a post-default recovery.

d.reason: (Sibling swap). It swaps credit related and behavioural for items I and II. The depositor’s early redemption involves no default, and a recovery is not a client’s liquidity decision. D would be right if item I were the shortfall on a defaulted deposit-funded loan and item II a client prepayment.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Differentiate between deterministic and stochastic cash flows and provide examples of each.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-7 a Q5
questions.question: A senior risk analyst at a German bank is mapping two positions into the cash flow taxonomy. The first is a EUR floating-rate note issued by a sovereign treated as default-risk free, paying coupons reset to 6-month Euribor on fixed semi-annual dates. The second is a European put option bought from a default-risk-free counterparty, exercisable only on its expiry date next March. Which of the following statements best describes the classification of the two cash flows?

options.text: Both are indexed/contingent cash flows that are deterministic in time and stochastic in amount.
Both are fixed cash flows at deterministic times, since the payment dates and payment formulas are set by the contracts.
The coupons are deterministic in time and stochastic in amount, but the option payout is stochastic in both time and amount.
Both are stochastic in time and in amount, since each payment depends on market variables observed on the payment date.

questions.solution:
German bank: classifying floating coupons and a European option payout.

**Concept and theory**

Indexed/contingent cash flows are stochastic in amount because their size depends on market variables. GARP’s examples are floating-rate coupons linked to market fixings such as Libor (Euribor here) and the payout of European options, whose value depends on the level of the underlying at expiry. For both, GARP stresses that the time of occurrence is known: the coupon payment date and the exercise date are fixed by contract. Hence they sit in the deterministic time column.

GARP then notes that indexed/contingent cash flows can also occur at stochastic times, giving American options as the example (Question 8). It also makes clear that, for these examples, the counterparty is assumed default-risk free; otherwise a credit-related element would be added.

Why does the distinction matter for liquidity monitoring? The expected cash flow for an indexed item at a known date can be computed with an interest rate or option model, and placed in the term structure of expected cash flows on that date. An item with stochastic timing also needs a model of when it will occur, which is harder. Practically, a floating coupon whose fixing has not yet been observed contributes uncertainty to the size of the bar in the maturity ladder but not to its position.

A useful contrast:

| Cash flow | Amount | Time |
|---|---|---|
| Fixed-rate coupon, risk-free | Fixed | Deterministic |
| Floating coupon, risk-free | Indexed | Deterministic |
| European option payout | Indexed | Deterministic |
| American option payout | Indexed | Stochastic |

**Applying it to this question**

The FRN pays on fixed semi-annual dates but at a rate set by 6-month Euribor: known date, unknown size. The European put can be exercised only on its expiry date: known date, with a payoff depending on the underlying at expiry. Both counterparties are risk free, so neither is credit related. Both are indexed/contingent, deterministic in time and stochastic in amount.

**Fragile fact.** European payout and floating coupons: indexed amount, deterministic time.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Differentiate between deterministic and stochastic cash flows and provide examples of each.

**GARP:** Chapter 7, Section 7.1, paragraph “Stochastic amount cash flows can also be indexed/contingent”; Figure 7.1. **Schweser:** Module 72.1 defines indexed/contingent as “market variables drive cash flow amounts”. **GARP vs Schweser:** none.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-7 a, where it is Q5 of 12.

a.reason: A matches GARP’s statement that for floating coupons and European options “the time of the occurrence of cash flows is known”, while the amount depends on market variables.

b.reason: (Scope or condition error). It treats a known payment formula as a known amount. The formula is fixed, but its inputs (the Euribor fixing, the underlying price) are not known at the reference time. B would be right for a fixed-rate coupon and a contract paying a stated sum on a fixed date.

c.reason: (Sibling swap). It gives the European option the American option’s stochastic timing. A European option can be exercised only at expiry. C would be right if the second position were an American put.

d.reason: (Scope or condition error). It extends amount uncertainty to the time dimension. Market variables observed on the payment date determine the size, not the date. D would describe American option payouts, whose exercise time depends on future market conditions.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Differentiate between deterministic and stochastic cash flows and provide examples of each.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-7 a Q6
questions.question: The CRO of a Canadian bank asks the liquidity team how two credit-line cash flows are classified. Flow 1 is the bank’s own drawdowns on a CAD 500 million committed line it has received from a syndicate of other banks, to be drawn when a liquidity need arises. Flow 2 is drawdowns by corporate clients on committed lines that the bank has granted to them. Which of the following best describes the classification?

options.text: Both are behavioural cash flows, stochastic in time and in amount, since in each case a line is drawn at an uncertain date.
Flow 1 is behavioural and stochastic in time and amount; Flow 2 is deterministic in amount and stochastic in time.
Flow 1 is deterministic in amount and stochastic in time; Flow 2 is behavioural and stochastic in time and amount.
Flow 1 is deterministic in time and in amount; Flow 2 is behavioural and stochastic in time and amount.

questions.solution:
Canadian bank: classifying the bank’s own drawdowns on a line received versus client drawdowns on lines granted.

**Concept and theory**

Credit lines appear in two different cells of GARP’s taxonomy, and the difference is who decides. **Lines received by the bank.** GARP’s second reason why a deterministic amount can occur at a stochastic time is that the amount depends on a choice made by the bank. Its example is the positive cash flow from withdrawals of credit lines received by the bank: the amount “can safely be assumed” to be some level between zero and the limit of the line, chosen by the bank according to its needs, but it can occur at any time until the line expires, since liquidity needs may arise at a stochastic time. Figure 7.1 puts “withdrawals by the bank from credit lines received” in the fixed row, stochastic time column.

**Lines granted by the bank.** When the bank has opened lines to clients, the clients decide. GARP describes these as behavioural cash flows at stochastic times: withdrawals may occur at any time until the expiry of the contract and in an uncertain amount, within the limits of the line. They are liquidity options sold by the bank (LO 72.b), and their amounts must be estimated with behavioural models.

| Credit line | Decision maker | Amount | Time |
|---|---|---|---|
| Received by bank | The bank | Fixed (bank’s choice) | Stochastic |
| Granted to clients | The client | Stochastic (behavioural) | Stochastic |

The logic is that the bank can plan how much it will draw, but cannot know when a need will arise; it can know neither the size nor the date of what its clients will do.

**Applying it to this question**

Flow 1 is the bank drawing on a line received from a syndicate when a need arises: the bank chooses the amount, but the time depends on when the need arises, so it is deterministic in amount and stochastic in time. Flow 2 is clients drawing on lines the bank has granted: behavioural, stochastic in both dimensions. The CAD 500 million limit caps Flow 1 but does not make its timing known.

**Fragile fact.** Lines received by the bank: fixed amount, stochastic time. Lines granted to clients: behavioural, both stochastic.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Differentiate between deterministic and stochastic cash flows and provide examples of each.

**GARP:** Chapter 7, Section 7.1, paragraphs on deterministic amount at stochastic times and “Other behavioural cash flows”; Figure 7.1. **GARP vs Schweser:** none; the lines-received example is GARP-only (Schweser’s figure not readable).

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-7 a, where it is Q6 of 12.

a.reason: (Scope or condition error). It ignores who chooses the amount and treats every drawdown as behavioural. GARP classifies the bank’s own drawdowns as deterministic in amount because the bank chooses them. A would be right if the question concerned two sets of client lines.

b.reason: (Role misassignment). It swaps the actors: the bank’s own drawdowns become behavioural, and the clients’ drawdowns get the deterministic amount. B would be right only if Flow 1 were the clients’ drawdowns and Flow 2 the bank’s.

c.reason: C reproduces GARP’s distinction: bank-chosen amount at a stochastic time for lines received, behavioural and fully stochastic for lines granted to clients.

d.reason: (Polarity flip). It flips the time dimension of Flow 1 to deterministic. The bank chooses how much, but the need, and therefore the drawdown, arises at a stochastic time. D would be right for a drawdown scheduled on a fixed date for a fixed sum.

questions.source: High quality paper LTR-7 a Q7
questions.question: A risk consultant is advising a Chinese bank that holds a CNY fixed-rate amortising loan to a corporate borrower. The bank wants to classify the cash flows that would arise if the borrower defaulted: the scheduled interest and capital instalments that would no longer be received, and the recovery that would be collected after default. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Only the recovery is a credit-related cash flow; the instalments that would not be received are not cash flows and are excluded from the taxonomy.
Both are credit-related cash flows, stochastic in time because the default time is unknown, although their amount can be implied once that time is fixed.
Both are credit-related and stochastic in amount, but deterministic in time, since they can fall only on the loan’s scheduled payment dates.
The recovery is credit related, but the instalments that would not be received are behavioural, since they stem from the borrower’s decision to stop paying.

questions.solution:
Chinese bank: classifying missing instalments and recovery on a defaulting fixed-rate loan.

**Concept and theory**

The first stochastic-amount subcategory is credit related: cash flows whose amount is uncertain because of credit events, typically the default of one or more of the bank’s clients. GARP explains its structure precisely. Once the default time is fixed, the amount of these cash flows “can be implied”; but the default time is obviously not known at the reference time, so the time at which these cash flows occur is stochastic. Figure 7.1 places them only in the stochastic time column.

GARP gives two examples. The first is the missing cash flows after default: the contractual stream of fixed interest and capital repayments that will not be received. GARP says a missing cash flow may be considered a negative cash flow that alters a given schedule; for a fixed-rate amortising loan the result is a modified schedule of interest and capital at the contract dates. The second is the recovery value after default, also inserted in this category.

This is why the fixed amount, deterministic time cell is reserved for risk-free obligors (Question 2): any risky contract carries a credit-related component, and the treasury’s term structure of expected cash flows must be adjusted with credit models that consider defaults on an aggregate basis, including correlation between counterparties. Note that the taxonomy still records the missing flows; they are not removed from the analysis, they are reclassified and modelled.

**Applying it to this question**

Both items exist only because of a default. The default date is unknown today, so both are stochastic in time; given a default date, the lost instalments follow from the contract schedule and the recovery can be implied. Neither is a client liquidity decision, so neither is behavioural.

**Fragile fact.** Credit related: time stochastic (default date unknown); amount implied once that date is fixed.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Differentiate between deterministic and stochastic cash flows and provide examples of each.

**GARP:** Chapter 7, Section 7.1, paragraph “Shifting the analysis to the stochastic amount category”; Figure 7.1. **Schweser:** Module 72.1, “credit related (uncertainty due to credit events)”; Module Quiz 72.1 treats a recovery on default as stochastic in time and amount. **GARP vs** **Schweser:** none.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-7 a, where it is Q7 of 12.

a.reason: (Scope or condition error). It removes missing cash flows from the taxonomy. GARP explicitly treats a missing cash flow as a negative cash flow that alters the schedule. A would be right only if the question asked which items are actual receipts of cash.

b.reason: B states GARP’s two defining features of credit-related cash flows: stochastic time, because default time is unknown, and amount implied once default time is fixed, covering both missing cash flows and recovery.

c.reason: (Polarity flip). It flips the time dimension to deterministic. The default time is unknown at the reference date, which is precisely why GARP puts credit-related flows in the stochastic time column. C would be right only if default could occur solely on a known date.

d.reason: (Sibling swap). It reclassifies the missing instalments as behavioural. Behavioural cash flows come from clients exercising choices such as prepayment or withdrawal; non-payment due to default is a credit event. D would be right if the borrower had instead chosen to prepay the loan.

questions.question:
A banking supervisor is reviewing a U.K. bank’s liquidity documentation, which makes the following statements about option-related cash flows (all amounts in GBP):

I. The payout of an American option the bank has bought is indexed/contingent and stochastic in time, because early exercise depends on future market conditions.

II. The payout of an American option the bank has written is stochastic in time only when the bank is long; when the bank is short, exercise is assumed at expiry, so the payout is deterministic in time.

III. The payout of a European option is indexed/contingent but deterministic in time.

IV. In these classifications the option counterparty is assumed to be default-risk free.

Which of the statements are consistent with the reading?

options.text: I and III only
I, II and III only
III and IV only
I, III and IV only

questions.solution:
U.K. supervisor: statements on American and European option payouts and the counterparty assumption.

**Concept and theory**

Within the indexed/contingent subcategory GARP separates option payouts by the time dimension. European option payouts occur at the exercise date, which is known: indexed amount, deterministic time. American option payouts can occur at any time up to expiry, because the holder may exercise early. GARP is explicit that this applies “both when the bank is long or short” the option, since the exercise time is stochastic and depends on future market conditions that determine whether early exercise is optimal. Being short does not make the date any more knowable: the bank simply does not control it.

GARP then adds a qualification: in these examples it is referring to contracts whose counterparty to the bank is default risk free. This is the same logic as for fixed-rate bonds (Question 2). If the counterparty could default, a credit-related element would be layered on top of the indexed/contingent one.

| Payout | Time | Applies when |
|---|---|---|
| European option | Deterministic | Bank long or short |
| American option | Stochastic | Bank long or short |
| Either | Indexed amount | Counterparty default-risk free |

For liquidity management, the American option’s stochastic timing means the bank must model both the expected payoff and the probability that exercise occurs in each period, which is harder than placing a single expected amount on a known expiry date.

**Applying it to this question**

Statement I matches GARP for a long American option: correct. Statement II invents a long/short distinction that GARP explicitly denies: wrong. Statement III matches GARP for the European payout: correct. Statement IV restates GARP’s assumption of a default-risk-free counterparty: correct. Hence I, III and IV.

**Fragile fact.** American payout: stochastic time whether the bank is long or short; counterparty assumed risk free.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Differentiate between deterministic and stochastic cash flows and provide examples of each.

**GARP:** Chapter 7, Section 7.1, indexed/contingent paragraph (“Examples are the payout of American options, both when the bank is long or short them”); Figure 7.1. **Schweser:** Module Quiz 72.1 treats an American option payout as stochastic in time and amount. **GARP vs** **Schweser:** none.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-7 a, where it is Q8 of 12.

a.reason: (Scope or condition error). It rejects Statement IV, dropping the default-risk-free counterparty condition that GARP attaches to these examples. A would be right if Statement IV claimed that counterparty default is included in the indexed/contingent classification.

b.reason: (Scope or condition error). It accepts Statement II, which limits stochastic timing to long positions. GARP says the American payout is stochastic in time whether the bank is long or short. B would be right only if the written option were European.

c.reason: (Polarity flip). It rejects Statement I, treating the American payout as deterministic in time. Early exercise makes the time stochastic. C would be right only if Statement I described a European option.

d.reason: D accepts exactly the three statements supported by GARP: American payouts are stochastic in time whether the bank is long or short, European payouts are deterministic in time, and the counterparty is assumed risk free.

questions.loText: Differentiate between deterministic and stochastic cash flows and provide examples of each.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-7 a Q9
questions.question: A treasury analyst at a U.S. mortgage lender is documenting how prepayments on the lender’s USD fixed-rate amortising mortgages are treated in its cash flow taxonomy. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Prepayments are deterministic in time, since the contract lists the dates on which prepayment is permitted, but stochastic in amount.
Prepayments are new-business cash flows, since the borrower usually refinances by entering a new contract at current market rates.
Prepayments are behavioural and occur at stochastic times; once a prepayment occurs, the prepaid amount and the modified schedule can be computed.
Prepayments are behavioural, but since they are driven by interest rates, their timing can be predicted with certainty and they are deterministic in time.

questions.solution:
U.S. mortgage lender: how prepayments on fixed-rate amortising mortgages are classified.

**Concept and theory**

Behavioural cash flows are stochastic in amount because they depend on decisions made by the bank’s clients or counterparties. GARP stresses that these decisions “can only be loosely predicted” according to rational behaviour based on market variables, and sometimes rest on information the bank does not have. The leading example is prepayment: clients decide to repay the outstanding amount of their loans or mortgages early.

GARP describes the mechanics in some detail. The prepayment time cannot be predicted with certainty, so the cash flow is stochastic in time. Once prepayment happens, however, the bank can compute the prepaid amount it receives, and the missing cash flows relative to the contract schedule can be determined; for a fixed-rate amortising mortgage this yields a modified schedule of interest and capital at the contract dates. Other behavioural cash flows at stochastic times include client withdrawals from credit lines and withdrawals from sight or savings deposits.

Prepayment is also a liquidity option sold by the bank (LO 72.b): it is often triggered by falling rates, but also by life events such as divorce or retirement. The rate link explains why behavioural models use market variables, but it does not make the timing certain. In the bank’s monitoring, prepayments are handled by adjusting the term structure of expected cash flows with behavioural models.

| Before prepayment | After prepayment |
|---|---|
| Time unknown | Prepaid amount computable |
| Size unknown | Modified schedule determinable |

**Applying it to this question**

The mortgages are fixed-rate amortising, so their scheduled instalments would be fixed and deterministic if no prepayment option existed. The borrowers’ right to prepay introduces a client decision, which makes the cash flow behavioural; its timing is uncertain; and once it happens the amount and the revised schedule follow, exactly as option C states.

**Fragile fact.** Prepayment: behavioural, time stochastic; amount computable only once prepayment occurs.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Differentiate between deterministic and stochastic cash flows and provide examples of each.

**GARP:** Chapter 7, Section 7.1, paragraph “Another type of stochastic amount cash flow is behavioural”; Figure 7.1. **Schweser:** Module Quiz 72.1 treats mortgage prepayments as stochastic in time and amount. **GARP vs Schweser:** none.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-7 a, where it is Q9 of 12.

a.reason: (Polarity flip). It flips the time dimension to deterministic. GARP says the prepayment time cannot be predicted with certainty. A would be right only for a contract obliging repayment of an uncertain sum on a fixed date.

b.reason: (Sibling swap). It assigns prepayments to new business. The prepayment is the client’s exercise of a right on an existing contract; any new loan the borrower takes elsewhere is not the bank’s cash flow from this mortgage. B would be right if the question concerned new mortgages the lender plans to originate.

c.reason: C restates GARP: prepayments are behavioural, occur at stochastic times, and once they occur the bank can compute the prepaid amount and the modified schedule.

d.reason: (Absolute-claim trap). It turns a loose, rate-influenced prediction into certainty. GARP says behavioural decisions can only be loosely predicted and may depend on information the bank lacks. D would be right only if the bank knew every borrower’s decision in advance.

questions.question:
A member of the board risk committee at a Japanese bank is reviewing the treasury’s projections of new-business cash flows over the next two years:

I. Replacing the JPY loans that expire over the next two years with new loans for the same planned amount.

II. A JPY senior bond issuance planned for a set date next year.

III. Inflows from new retail deposits the bank expects to gather through a digital campaign.

IV. New mortgages from a planned expansion into a new region.

Which items are deterministic in time but stochastic in amount?

options.text: I and II only
II only
I, II and III only
II and IV only

questions.solution:
Japanese bank board review: which new-business items are deterministic in time but stochastic in amount.

**Concept and theory**

New business is the fourth stochastic-amount subcategory: cash flows from contracts that will be dealt in the future and are more or less planned by the bank. Their amount is stochastic because the plan may not be met. GARP then splits them by the time dimension:

| Item | Time | GARP’s reasoning |
|---|---|---|
| Renewal of expiring contracts | Deterministic | Old contracts expire at a known maturity, so the replacement cash flows are known in time |
| New debt issuance by the bank | Deterministic | Well defined in time, but the amount may not be in line with plans |
| New deposits, new loans, new assets | Stochastic | Completely new contracts may not follow the business plan, so both time and amount are stochastic |

GARP illustrates the renewal case with a bank planning new loans to replace exactly the loans expiring in the next two years. The amount is stochastic because it is unsure whether clients will want or need such contracts, but the replacement dates are anchored to the known maturities. New retail deposits, new mortgages and new assets in general can only be partially predicted in both dimensions. GARP concludes that new business and rollover flows are quite difficult to model and manage, yet they must enter the term structure of expected cash flows, which includes all activities that can reasonably be expected, not only existing contracts.

**Applying it to this question**

Item I is a renewal of expiring contracts: deterministic time, stochastic amount. Item II is a planned bond issuance on a set date: deterministic time, stochastic amount. Item III (new retail deposits from a campaign) and Item IV (new mortgages from expansion) are completely new contracts: stochastic in both. Hence I and II only.

**Fragile fact.** New business is time-deterministic only for renewals and planned issuance; brand-new contracts are stochastic in both.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Differentiate between deterministic and stochastic cash flows and provide examples of each.

**GARP:** Chapter 7, Section 7.1, paragraph “Finally, we have stochastic amount cash flows related to the replacement of expiring contracts and to new business activity”; Figure 7.1. **Schweser:** Module Quiz 72.1 treats new debt issued as time deterministic and amount stochastic. **GARP** **vs Schweser:** none.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-7 a, where it is Q10 of 12.

a.reason: A selects GARP’s two new-business examples in the deterministic time column, renewals of expiring contracts and new debt issuance.

b.reason: (Polarity flip). It treats the renewal of expiring loans as stochastic in time. GARP says the replacement is anchored to known maturities, so its time is known. B would be right if item I were loans to entirely new clients with no planned timing.

c.reason: (Scope or condition error). It extends deterministic timing to new deposits. Completely new contracts are stochastic in both time and amount. C would be right if the deposits were renewals of term deposits maturing on known dates.

d.reason: (Sibling swap). It swaps the renewal (item I) for the new mortgages (item IV). Both are lending, but only the renewal is tied to known expiry dates. D would be right if the mortgages were planned for a fixed launch date and the replacement loans were not tied to maturities.

questions.source: High quality paper LTR-7 a Q11
questions.question:
A junior risk analyst at a Brazilian bank is classifying expected cash flows for next quarter (positive = inflow, negative = outflow). All counterparties and issuers are treated as default-risk free.

| Item | Expected amount (BRL m) |
|---|---|
| Coupons on fixed-rate government bonds held | 40 |
| Coupons on government floating-rate notes linked to the CDI rate | 25 |
| Payout of a European option bought, expiring in the quarter | 6 |
| Payout of an American option written by the bank | −9 |
| Proceeds of a bond issuance planned for a set date in the quarter | 120 |
| Drawdowns by clients on credit lines granted by the bank | −35 |
| Bank’s own drawdown on a credit line received, if a need arises | 50 |
| Withdrawals from sight deposits | −60 |

The bank also holds a liquidity buffer of BRL 300 million. What is the net expected amount of the cash flows that are deterministic in time but stochastic in amount?

options.text: BRL 31 million
BRL 142 million
BRL 145 million
BRL 151 million

questions.solution:
Brazilian bank: net expected amount of the deterministic time, stochastic amount cell.

**Concept and theory**

The taxonomy is not only descriptive: when a treasury builds the term structure of expected cash flows, each item has to be modelled according to its cell. Items with deterministic time can be placed on known dates, with the modelling effort spent on the amount; items with stochastic time also need a model for when they occur. The deterministic time, stochastic amount cell in GARP’s Figure 7.1 contains three kinds of example:

- indexed/contingent flows on known dates: risk-free floating-rate coupons, European option payouts;
- new business on known dates: new debt issuance by the bank, renewal of expiring contracts;
- (no credit-related or behavioural examples: those subcategories sit in the stochastic time column).

Items outside the cell: fixed/deterministic (fixed risk-free coupons), fixed amount at stochastic time (one-touch payouts, the bank’s own drawdowns on lines received), and fully stochastic (American option payouts, client credit-line drawdowns, deposit withdrawals, credit-related flows, new contracts).

Because the stochastic-amount items enter at their expected values, the cell total is a sum of expectations. A liquidity buffer is a stock of assets that generates liquidity capacity, not a cash flow from the business, so it does not enter the classification at all.

**Applying it to this question**

Classify each line, then sum the target cell:

Fixed gov coupons : fixed, deterministic time ⇒ excluded

CDI floating notes : indexed, deterministic time ⇒ +25

European option bought : indexed, deterministic time ⇒ +6

American option written : indexed, stochastic time ⇒ excluded

Planned bond issuance : new business, deterministic time ⇒ +120

Client drawdowns : behavioural, stochastic time ⇒ excluded

Bank’s own drawdown : fixed, stochastic time ⇒ excluded

Sight deposit withdrawals : behavioural, stochastic time ⇒ excluded

Cell total = 25 + 6 + 120 = BRL 151 million

The BRL 300 million liquidity buffer is irrelevant: it is a source of liquidity, not a cash flow to be classified. The result means that BRL 151 million of next quarter’s expected net inflow falls on known dates but with uncertain size, so it needs amount models (rates, options, issuance plans) but no timing model.

**Fragile fact.** Short American payouts stay in the stochastic time column; planned issuance and European payouts are deterministic in time.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Differentiate between deterministic and stochastic cash flows and provide examples of each.

**GARP:** Chapter 7, Section 7.1 and Figure 7.1. **GARP vs Schweser:** none. Working in calc.py.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-7 a, where it is Q11 of 12.

a.reason: (Dropped term). BRL 31 million = 25 + 6 omits the planned issuance, treating new debt as stochastic in time. GARP says new bond issuance is well defined in time. A would be right if the issuance date were not yet fixed.

b.reason: (Sibling swap). BRL 142 million = 151 − 9 adds the written American option, giving it the European option’s deterministic time. GARP says American payouts are stochastic in time whether the bank is long or short. B would be right if the written option were European.

c.reason: (Sibling swap). BRL 145 million = 151 − 6 drops the European option, giving it the American option’s stochastic time. A European option is exercised only at expiry. C would be right if the bought option were American.

d.reason: D is the sum of exactly the three items GARP places in the deterministic time, stochastic amount cell.
