questions.question:
The head of treasury at a U.K. bank asks for the net amount of next year’s cash flows that are deterministic in both time and amount (positive = inflow, negative = outflow).

| Item | Amount (GBP m) |
|---|---|
| Coupons on fixed-rate gilts held (issuer default-risk free) | 18 |
| Capital amortisation on a fixed-rate loan to a default-risk-free public body | 30 |
| Coupons the bank pays on its own fixed-rate bonds | −22 |
| Scheduled instalments on fixed-rate loans to BB-rated corporates | 45 |
| Coupons on floating-rate gilts linked to SONIA (expected) | 12 |
| Planned drawdown of a received credit line, date not yet known | 40 |
| Fixed-rate term deposits maturing, with no early withdrawal right | −35 |

Which of the following is closest to that net amount?

options.text: GBP −39 million
GBP −9 million
GBP 36 million
GBP 48 million

questions.solution:
U.K. bank: net amount of next year’s cash flows that are deterministic in both time and amount.

**Concept and theory**

The fixed amount, deterministic time cell is the only one in which both dimensions are known at the reference time. GARP lists its members and its condition:

- periodic interest on fixed-rate bonds, mortgages and loans, and periodic capital instalments where the asset amortises;
- the same flows on the liability side: bonds issued and loans received by the bank;
- on the asset side, only if the obligor or issuer is risk free, since otherwise credit events can affect the contractual schedule.

Liabilities enter with a negative sign, since the bank pays them. GARP’s balance sheet example in Section 7.4 makes the same point for deposits: deposit cash flows are deterministic in time and amount only under the assumption that no liquidity options are embedded in them. Without that assumption, deposit withdrawals and prepayments are behavioural.

Items that look similar but fail one test: a fixed-rate loan to a risky borrower (credit-related component), a floating coupon (indexed amount), and the bank’s own drawdown on a received line (fixed amount, but stochastic time).

**Applying it to this question**

Classify and sum:

Gilt coupons (risk-free, fixed) = +18

Amortisation, risk-free public body = +30

Coupons on own fixed-rate bonds = −22

Term deposits, no early withdrawal = −35

BB-rated corporate instalments : not risk free ⇒ excluded

SONIA-linked gilt coupons : indexed amount ⇒ excluded

Planned drawdown, date unknown : stochastic time ⇒ excluded

Net = 18 + 30 − 22 − 35 $= \text{GBP} -$9 million

The fixed contractual flows are a small net outflow of GBP 9 million: the bank’s contractually certain payments on its liabilities slightly exceed its contractually certain receipts from risk-free assets.

**Fragile fact.** The cell includes liabilities (negative sign) and excludes risky assets, floating coupons and drawdowns with unknown dates.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Differentiate between deterministic and stochastic cash flows and provide examples of each.

**GARP:** Chapter 7, Section 7.1 (fixed amount/deterministic time paragraph) and Figure 7.1; deposit assumption from Example 7.4.1. **GARP vs Schweser:** none. Working in calc.py.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-7 a, where it is Q12 of 12.

a.reason: (Dropped term). GBP −39 million = −9 − 30 omits the capital amortisation, treating only coupons as fixed. GARP lists capital amortisation of a risk-free fixed-rate mortgage in this cell. A would be right if the public-body loan were a bullet loan with no instalment this year.

b.reason: B includes all four items that are fixed in amount and date, on both sides of the balance sheet, and excludes the three that fail the risk-free, fixed-amount or known-date tests.

c.reason: (Scope or condition error). GBP 36 million = −9 + 45 adds the BB-rated instalments, dropping the risk-free condition. A would-be fixed schedule on a risky loan is not ensured. C would be right if the corporates were treated as default-risk free.

d.reason: (Scope or condition error). GBP 48 million = 18 + 30 counts assets only, leaving out the bank’s own bond coupons and term deposits. GARP extends the category to bonds issued and loans received by the bank. D would be right if the question asked only for fixed contractual inflows.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Describe and identify examples of liquidity options and explain the impact of liquidity options on a bank’s liquidity position and its liquidity management process.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-7 b Q1
questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a German cooperative bank is presenting to newly hired analysts on the options embedded in the bank’s retail and corporate products. Her draft slide contains the following statements:

I. A liquidity option is the right of a holder to receive cash from, or to give cash to, the bank at predefined times and terms.

II. Because exercise is triggered by the holder’s need for, or surplus of, liquidity, exercising a liquidity option never has any financial effect on the bank.

III. Exercising a liquidity option does not directly entail a profit or a loss in financial terms; it is a result of the holder’s need for, or surplus of, liquidity.

IV. A liquidity option exists only where the holder can receive cash from the bank; a client’s right to repay funds to the bank before maturity is not a liquidity option.

Which of the statements should remain on the slide?

options.text: I only
I and II only
I and III only
I, III and IV only

questions.solution:
Slide for new analysts: which statements on the definition of a liquidity option are correct.

**Concept and theory**

GARP opens Section 7.2 by noting that some of the cash flow categories in the taxonomy of Section 7.1 (withdrawals from deposits, usage of credit lines, prepayments) are connected with the exercise of so-called liquidity options. These options are conceptually no different from other options, but the decision to exercise them depends on their particular nature.

The definition has four parts, each a testable element:

| Element | GARP’s content |
|---|---|
| Holder | A counterparty of the bank (a client or another institution) holds the right. |
| Direction | The holder may receive cash from the bank (draw a line, withdraw a deposit) or give cash to the bank (repay a loan or mortgage early). |
| Terms | Exercise is at predefined times and terms set by the contract. |
| Trigger | Exercise does not directly entail a financial profit or loss; it results from the holder’s need for, or surplus of, liquidity. |

GARP immediately qualifies the last element: the definition does not exclude a link between exercise and financial effects; on the contrary, the link is sometimes quite strong (a borrower whose spread has widened draws on a fixed-spread line; a mortgagor refinances when rates fall). The point is that the driver of exercise is liquidity, while the consequences may still be financial. This is why GARP later says the exercise has a two-fold effect on the bank, one of liquidity and one financial.

**Applying it to this question**

Statement I is the definition itself. Statement III restates GARP’s characterisation of the trigger (no direct profit or loss; need for or surplus of liquidity). Statement II turns “does not directly entail a profit or a loss” into “never has any financial effect”, which GARP explicitly rejects.

Statement IV drops the “give cash to the bank” half of the definition; GARP says exercise “can also work the other way round”, with the client repaying funds before the contract ends. So I and III only.

**Fragile fact.** Direction is two-way: receive cash from the bank (draw, withdraw) or give cash to the bank (prepay). The holder is the client, not the bank.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Describe and identify examples of liquidity options and explain the impact of liquidity options on a bank’s liquidity position and its liquidity management process.

**GARP:** Chapter 7, Section 7.2 “Liquidity Options”, opening paragraphs.

**GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser says “the need for a surplus of liquidity drives the exercise”, compressing GARP’s “a need for or a surplus of liquidity”; GARP’s wording is used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-7 b, where it is Q1 of 13.

a.reason: (Scope or condition error). Rejecting III treats “no direct profit or loss” as if it were the absolute claim in II. III is hedged by the word “directly” and is GARP’s own description. A would be correct only if the stem had replaced III with a statement that liquidity options are exercised when profitable.

b.reason: (Absolute-claim trap). Accepting II. GARP says the definition does not exclude financial effects and that the link is sometimes quite strong; every exercise also has a positive or negative financial impact. II would be true only if it said “exercise is not driven by a financial profit”.

c.reason: C keeps exactly the two statements that match GARP: the holder’s right to receive cash from, or give cash to, the bank at predefined times and terms, and exercise driven by a need for or surplus of liquidity rather than by a direct profit or loss.

d.reason: (Scope or condition error). Accepting IV. Early repayment of a loan or mortgage is a liquidity option in which the holder gives cash to the bank. IV would be correct only if the definition covered drawings and withdrawals alone.

questions.source: High quality paper LTR-7 b Q2
questions.question: A risk consultant is explaining to the asset-liability committee of a Canadian credit union how the liquidity options in its deposit and lending book differ from the options that its investment portfolio trades on exchanges. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: A financial option is exercised when there is a profit, independently of the cash flows after exercise; a liquidity option is exercised because of the cash flows after exercise, even when exercise is not financially convenient.
A financial option is exercised because of the cash flows produced after exercise; a liquidity option is exercised when there is a profit, independently of the cash flows that follow exercise.
Both types of option are exercised only when they are in the money for the holder; they differ only in that liquidity options are written on deposits and loans rather than on securities.

A financial option is exercised when there is a profit, and the cash flows after its exercise are always positive for the holder; a liquidity option is exercised because of the cash flows after exercise.

questions.solution:
Credit union ALCO: how liquidity options differ from exchange-traded financial options.

**Concept and theory**

GARP contrasts liquidity options with the standard options traded in financial markets along one axis: what drives the exercise decision, and how that decision relates to the cash flows that follow.

|  | Standard financial option | Liquidity option |
|---|---|---|
| Why exercised | When there is a profit | Because of the cash flows produced after exercise |
| Link to post-exercise cash flows | Independent of them, although they are typically positive | They are the reason for exercise |
| Financial convenience | Necessary | Not necessary: may be exercised even when not financially convenient |
| Typical example | European call on a stock | Committed credit line, sight deposit, prepayable mortgage |

The logic is that a financial option holder compares strike and market price; whether the holder then sells the stock (net inflow) or keeps it (pure outflow) is a separate decision, so the exercise is “independent of the cash flows following exercise”. A liquidity option holder, by contrast, exercises because it needs the cash (or has surplus cash to return). The financial profitability of that exercise can be positive, zero or negative. This is the root of the behavioural nature of these cash flows and the reason they must be modelled statistically rather than with a pure optimal-exercise rule.

**Applying it to this question**

The stem asks for the contrast in general terms. Only one option states both halves the right way round: financial options are exercised on profit, independently of post-exercise cash flows; liquidity options are exercised because of post-exercise cash flows, even if not financially convenient.

**Fragile fact.** Financial option: profit drives exercise, cash flows are incidental. Liquidity option: cash flows drive exercise, profit is incidental.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Describe and identify examples of liquidity options and explain the impact of liquidity options on a bank’s liquidity position and its liquidity management process.

**GARP:** Chapter 7, Section 7.2 “Liquidity Options”, comparison with standard options.

**GARP vs Schweser:** none in substance; Schweser condenses the comparison to “exercised when profitable” versus “based on cash flows produced after exercise”.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-7 b, where it is Q2 of 13.

a.reason: A paraphrases GARP’s comparison: the major difference is that financial options are exercised when there is a profit independently of the following cash flows (typically positive), whereas a liquidity option is exercised because of the cash flows produced after exercise, even if sometimes not convenient financially.

b.reason: (Sibling swap). B attributes each option type’s exercise rule to the other. It would be correct only if the labels “financial option” and “liquidity option” were exchanged.

c.reason: (Scope or condition error). Extends the in-the-money rule to liquidity options. GARP stresses that a credit line can be drawn even when the borrower’s spread has shrunk and new market funding is cheaper. C would be correct only for two financial options.

d.reason: (Absolute-claim trap). GARP says post-exercise cash flows of a financial option are typically positive, and gives the counterexample of exercising and keeping the stock, which yields only a negative cash flow. D would be correct with “typically” in place of “always”.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Describe and identify examples of liquidity options and explain the impact of liquidity options on a bank’s liquidity position and its liquidity management process.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-7 b Q3
questions.question:
A junior analyst at a Japanese trust bank is comparing financial options with liquidity options. The bank’s equity desk holds a European call option on a listed stock:

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Strike price (JPY per share) | 2,400 |
| Stock price at expiry (JPY per share) | 2,750 |
| Shares covered by the option | 1,000 |

At expiry the desk exercises the option and keeps the shares in its portfolio rather than selling them. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Because exercising and keeping the shares produces only a cash outflow of JPY 2,400 per share, the option behaved like a liquidity option, since the decision was driven by the post-exercise cash flow.
The desk should not have exercised, because a financial option is exercised only when the net cash flow following exercise is positive for the holder.
Exercise produces a positive net cash flow of JPY 350 per share whether the shares are kept or sold, because the profit on a financial option is fixed at the moment of exercise.

Exercise is convenient because buying at the strike is cheaper than buying at market; keeping the shares produces only an outflow of JPY 2,400 per share, so the decision is independent of the post-exercise cash flows.

questions.solution:
Equity desk exercises a European call and keeps the shares: what this shows.

**Concept and theory**

GARP uses a European call on a stock to show why a financial option’s exercise decision is independent of the cash flows after exercise. At expiry the holder exercises if the strike is below the market price. Two paths follow:

| Path after exercise | Cash flows to the holder |
|---|---|
| Exercise and sell | Pay the strike, receive the market price: positive net cash flow equal to market price less strike |
| Exercise and keep | Pay the strike only: a pure negative cash flow |

In the second path the holder exercises because it is cheaper to buy the stock at the strike than at the prevailing market price, for example because it wants to hold the stock. The exercise is equally rational on both paths; the cash flow sign depends on a separate decision. Hence GARP’s conclusion that “the convenience to exercise is then independent of the cash flows after exercise”.

A liquidity option is the mirror image. Its holder exercises because of the cash flows after exercise (it needs to draw cash, or wants to return surplus cash), even when the financial terms are unattractive. The European call is therefore the benchmark against which the liquidity option is defined, not an example of one.

**Applying it to this question**

Data check: profit per share if sold is

2,750 − 2,400 = JPY 350 per share (only if the shares are sold)

Cash flow if kept = −JPY 2,400 per share

The desk kept the shares, so its only cash flow is the outflow of the strike. Exercise was still worthwhile because the shares are acquired JPY 350 below market. The number of shares (1,000) is irrelevant to the conceptual question.

**Fragile fact.** Exercise-and-keep yields a negative cash flow yet is rational: that is what “independent of the cash flows after exercise” means.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Describe and identify examples of liquidity options and explain the impact of liquidity options on a bank’s liquidity position and its liquidity management process.

**GARP:** Chapter 7, Section 7.2 “Liquidity Options”, European stock option example.

**GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser omits the exercise-and-keep example and says only that post-exercise cash flows “are often positive”; GARP used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-7 b, where it is Q3 of 13.

a.reason: (Sibling swap). Treats the financial option as a liquidity option. The decision was driven by the strike being below market (profit), not by the cash flow. A would be correct only if the desk had exercised to obtain or place cash.

b.reason: (Polarity flip). Reverses the rule: financial options are exercised on profit, independently of the sign of post-exercise cash flows. B would be correct only for a liquidity option.

c.reason: (Scope or condition error). The positive JPY 350 per share arises only on the “exercise and sell” path. C would be correct if the desk had sold the shares immediately.

d.reason: D states both of GARP’s points: exercise is convenient because buying at the strike beats buying at market, and keeping the stock produces only a negative cash flow, so convenience is independent of post-exercise cash flows.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Describe and identify examples of liquidity options and explain the impact of liquidity options on a bank’s liquidity position and its liquidity management process.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-7 b Q4
questions.question: The CRO of a Canadian commercial bank is reviewing a drawdown. Three years ago the bank granted a manufacturing client a committed credit line of CAD 250 million at a 3-month floating reference rate plus 140 bp, with the spread fixed until expiry. The client’s credit standing has since improved, and it could now raise new funds in the market at the reference rate plus 95 bp. The client nonetheless draws CAD 60 million on the line to settle a supplier payment at short notice. Which of the following statements best describes this event?

options.text: The drawdown is irrational, because a committed line is a liquidity option that the client will draw only after its credit spread has widened above the contract spread.
The client is exercising a liquidity option sold to it by the bank; the line can be drawn for reasons other than financial convenience even though new market funding is cheaper.
The client is exercising a liquidity option that it sold to the bank; because the bank is long the option, the drawdown adds CAD 60 million to the bank’s liquidity position.
Because the client’s spread has narrowed, the drawdown produces a financial loss for the bank of 45 bp a year applied to the CAD 60 million drawn on the line.

questions.solution:
Client draws on a committed line although its market spread has narrowed.

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s first example of a liquidity option is the committed credit line, which the bank sells to a customer. The obligor has the right to withdraw any amount up to the notional of the line whenever it wants, on contract terms fixed until expiry, typically a floating rate (GARP’s example is 3-month Libor) plus a spread that reflects the obligor’s default risk at origination.

GARP describes two exercise situations:

| Situation | Reasoning |
|---|---|
| Spread has widened | Drawing also makes financial sense: funds come at the old, lower contract spread, a clear saving versus opening a new line. |
| Spread has shrunk | New market funding would be cheaper, yet the obligor may still draw on the line for reasons other than financial convenience. |

The second case is what makes it a liquidity option: the exercise is driven by the need for cash, not by profitability. Whatever the reason, the bank’s balance sheet absorbs the amount drawn (the liquidity impact), and a financial impact arises from the gap between the contract spread and the market spread at exercise, applied to the drawn amount. When the borrower’s market spread is below the contract spread, that gap favours the bank, not the borrower.

**Applying it to this question**

The bank sold the option; the client holds it. The client draws CAD 60 million although it could borrow at reference plus 95 bp in the market, against 140 bp on the line: a non-financial (convenience, short notice) exercise. The bank pays out CAD 60 million. The CAD 250 million line size is irrelevant to the identification.

**Fragile fact.** Spread widening favours the borrower (and hurts the bank); spread narrowing favours the bank. The bank is short the line.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Describe and identify examples of liquidity options and explain the impact of liquidity options on a bank’s liquidity position and its liquidity management process.

**GARP:** Chapter 7, Section 7.2 “Liquidity Options”, committed credit line example.

**GARP vs Schweser:** none; Schweser calls drawing despite a narrower spread “convenience”.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-7 b, where it is Q4 of 13.

a.reason: (Absolute-claim trap). Spread widening is one reason to draw, not the only one. A would be correct only for a standard financial option exercised solely when profitable.

b.reason: B correctly assigns the option (sold by the bank, held by the client) and matches GARP’s point that the line can be used even if the credit spread shrinks, for reasons other than financial convenience.

c.reason: (Role misassignment). The bank sold the line; it is short, and the drawing is a cash outflow for the bank. C would describe a committed line the bank received from another institution.

d.reason: (Polarity flip). With the contract spread (140 bp) above the borrower’s market spread (95 bp), the bank lends above market: the financial impact for the bank is positive, about 60 × 0.45% = CAD 0.27 million a year. D would be correct if the spread had widened by 45 bp.

questions.loText: Describe and identify examples of liquidity options and explain the impact of liquidity options on a bank’s liquidity position and its liquidity management process.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-7 b Q5
questions.question: The treasurer of a Brazilian retail bank is drafting the section of the liquidity policy that explains why the bank’s BRL 4.2 billion of sight and savings deposits embed liquidity options. Which of the following statements should the treasurer include?

options.text: Withdrawals are driven solely by the spread between the deposit rate and market yields, so they can be predicted exactly from the bank’s interest rate scenarios.
Only savings deposits with a contractual notice period embed a liquidity option; sight deposits, being payable on demand, contain no option for the depositor.
The bank, not the depositor, holds the liquidity option, because the bank decides when to repay the balances held in sight and savings accounts.
Clients can usually withdraw all or part of their balances with no or short notice, for yield or transaction reasons or for reasons that can at best be forecast statistically.

questions.solution:
Liquidity policy text on why sight and savings deposits embed liquidity options.

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s second example is sight and savings deposits. The bank’s clients can typically withdraw all or part of the deposited amount with no or short notice. The client is the holder; the bank is short the option (Schweser: a liquidity option “offered by the bank”).

GARP gives three families of reasons for withdrawal:

- the possibility of investing in assets with higher yields that more than compensate for higher risk (a financial rationale);
- the need for liquidity for transaction purposes;
- many other reasons that are hardly predictable, or that can only be forecast on a statistical basis.

So even here a financial rationale may exist, but it is not the only driver, which is why deposits are a liquidity option rather than a financial one. In the cash flow taxonomy of Section 7.1, withdrawals from sight or savings deposits are behavioural cash flows, stochastic in amount and occurring at stochastic times. This has a direct consequence for monitoring: contractual maturity (overnight) is not a usable description of when the money leaves, and behavioural models must be used to forecast it (Section 7.4.1).

**Applying it to this question**

The treasurer needs a statement that names the holder correctly (the depositor), covers both sight and savings deposits, and captures the mixed, partly unpredictable reasons for withdrawal. The BRL 4.2 billion figure plays no role.

**Fragile fact.** Holder = depositor; bank = short. Withdrawals are forecast statistically, not predicted exactly.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Describe and identify examples of liquidity options and explain the impact of liquidity options on a bank’s liquidity position and its liquidity management process.

**GARP:** Chapter 7, Section 7.2 “Liquidity Options”, sight and savings deposit example; Section 7.1 taxonomy (behavioural cash flows).

**GARP vs Schweser:** none.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-7 b, where it is Q5 of 13.

a.reason: (Absolute-claim trap). “Solely” and “exactly” contradict GARP: a financial rationale may exist but withdrawals can be triggered by many other reasons. A would be correct only for a pure rate-driven financial option.

b.reason: (Scope or condition error). Sight deposits, withdrawable on demand, are the clearest case of the option. B would be correct only if the policy covered term deposits that cannot be withdrawn before maturity.

c.reason: (Role misassignment). The depositor holds the right to withdraw; the bank is short. C would describe a callable liability the bank had issued.

d.reason: D reproduces GARP’s description: withdrawal of all or part of the balance with no or short notice, for yield or transaction reasons, or for reasons hardly predictable that can be forecast only statistically.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Describe and identify examples of liquidity options and explain the impact of liquidity options on a bank’s liquidity position and its liquidity management process.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-7 b Q6
questions.question:
An internal auditor at a U.K. building society is reviewing treasury’s note on two prepayments of fixed-rate mortgages during the quarter:

| Client | Reason for prepayment | Amount (GBP m) | Contract rate (%) | Market rate now (%) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| X | Retirement | 1.1 | 5.2 | 6.0 |
| Y | Refinancing | 0.9 | 5.2 | 4.1 |

Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Both prepayments increase the society’s liquidity; X causes no loss and the funds can even be re-lent at better rates, whereas Y causes a loss because replacement lending is at rates below the old contract rate.
Both prepayments increase the society’s liquidity and both cause a financial loss, because the economic effects of a prepayment are always negative for the lender whatever the level of market rates.
Both prepayments increase the society’s liquidity; X causes a loss because it was triggered by an exogenous life event, whereas Y causes no loss because it was triggered by a financial incentive.
Both prepayments reduce the society’s liquidity, because the mortgage assets leave its balance sheet; of the two, only Y has a financial impact because only Y was driven by the level of rates.

questions.solution:
Building society: retirement prepayment versus refinancing prepayment.

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s third example shows the option working “the other way round”: the client has the right to repay funds before the contract ends. Prepayment of fixed-rate mortgages or loans is the standard case.

The bank always benefits on the liquidity side, because it receives cash earlier than expected. The economic effect, however, is usually negative. GARP separates two causes:

| Cause | Market rates | Financial effect on the bank |
|---|---|---|
| Exogenous (divorce, retirement) | Rose or unchanged | No loss; the bank may even reinvest the funds at better conditions |
| Financial incentive (refinance) | Fell | Loss: the replacement mortgage, or early closure of the loan, is at rates below the old contract rate |

GARP adds that the second cause is the more frequent one: prepayment is more often triggered by the incentive to close the contract and reopen it under current conditions when rates fall. Hence the generalisation that prepayment economics are usually, but not always, adverse for the lender. The financial impact is measured as the gap between the contract rate and the market rate at exercise, applied to the repaid amount; the liquidity impact is the repaid amount itself.

**Applying it to this question**

X prepays on retirement while market rates (6.0%) are above the contract rate (5.2%): no loss, and the GBP 1.1 million can be re-lent at a better rate. Y refinances after rates fell to 4.1%: the GBP 0.9 million must be re-lent below 5.2%, a loss. Both prepayments bring cash in.

**Fragile fact.** Prepayment: liquidity always up; financial result depends on rates (loss when rates fall, none or a gain when they rise).

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Describe and identify examples of liquidity options and explain the impact of liquidity options on a bank’s liquidity position and its liquidity management process.

**GARP:** Chapter 7, Section 7.2 “Liquidity Options”, prepayment example.

**GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser says prepayment is “typically” due to falling rates and omits the exogenous case; GARP’s fuller treatment is used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-7 b, where it is Q6 of 13.

a.reason: A matches GARP on both dimensions: a liquidity gain in both cases, no loss (even a reinvestment gain) in the exogenous case with rising rates, and a loss in the rate-driven case.

b.reason: (Absolute-claim trap). GARP says economic effects are usually negative, not always; X shows the exception. B would be correct if rates had fallen in both cases.

c.reason: (Sibling swap). Swaps the financial consequence between the two causes. C would be correct only if the rate movements in the table were exchanged.

d.reason: (Polarity flip). A prepayment is a cash inflow that increases the bank’s liquidity; it is the bank that “would benefit from the greater amount of liquidity”. X also has a (positive) financial impact. D would be correct for a client drawing funds, not repaying them.
