questions.loText: Describe and identify examples of liquidity options and explain the impact of liquidity options on a bank’s liquidity position and its liquidity management process.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-7 b Q7
questions.question:
A treasury analyst at a Dutch bank is preparing a report on a corporate borrower that has just prepaid a fixed-rate loan after a fall in market rates. The analyst measures the financial impact as the difference between the contract rate and the rate at which the bank can now re-lend the funds at the same risk, applied to the repaid amount.

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Original loan amount (EUR m) | 50.00 |
| Outstanding amount prepaid (EUR m) | 36.00 |
| Contract rate (%) | 4.60 |
| Current re-lending rate, same risk (%) | 3.15 |
| Remaining contract life (years) | 4.00 |

Which of the following best describes the two impacts of the prepayment on the bank?

options.text: Annual financial loss of EUR 0.725 million; liquidity inflow of EUR 50 million
Annual financial gain of EUR 0.522 million; liquidity inflow of EUR 36 million
Annual financial loss of EUR 0.522 million; liquidity inflow of EUR 36 million
Annual financial loss of EUR 1.656 million; liquidity inflow of EUR 36 million

questions.solution:
Dutch bank: liquidity and financial impact of a rate-driven loan prepayment.

**Concept and theory**

GARP concludes Section 7.2 by stating that, whatever triggers it, the exercise of a liquidity option affects the bank in two ways:

1. a **liquidity impact** on the balance sheet, given by the amount withdrawn or repaid;
2. a **financial impact**, positive or negative, given by the difference between the contract’s interest rate and credit spread and the market level of the same variables at the time of exercise, applied to the withdrawn or repaid amount.

For a prepaid fixed-rate loan, write Q for the repaid amount, $\text{r}_{\text{c}}$ for the contract rate and $\text{r}_{\text{m}}$ for the rate at which the funds can be re-lent at the same risk. The stem fixes the convention as an annual figure:

Liquidity impact = +Q, Annual financial impact $= - \text{Q} (\text{r}_{\text{c}} - \text{r}_{\text{m}})$.

When rates have fallen $\text{(r}_{\text{m}} < \text{r}_{\text{c}}$) the bank loses the margin $\text{r}_{\text{c}} - \text{r}_{\text{m}}$ on the funds it gets back: the classic rate-driven prepayment loss. When rates have risen the sign reverses. Note that the financial impact is applied to the amount actually repaid, not to the original size of the loan.

**Applying it to this question**

Formula first, then one step per line:

Liquidity impact = +EUR 36 million (inflow)

$\text{r}_{\text{c}} - \text{r}_{\text{m}} =$ 4.60% − 3.15% = 1.45%

Annual financial impact = −36 × 1.45% = −EUR 0.522 million

The bank receives EUR 36 million now but loses EUR 0.522 million a year of margin. The original loan amount (EUR 50 million) has already partly amortised and is irrelevant; the remaining life (4 years) is irrelevant because the question asks for the annual figure.

**Fragile fact.** Financial impact is applied to the repaid amount and is a loss when rates have fallen.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Describe and identify examples of liquidity options and explain the impact of liquidity options on a bank’s liquidity position and its liquidity management process.

**GARP:** Chapter 7, Section 7.2 “Liquidity Options”, two-fold effect of exercise and prepayment example.

**GARP vs Schweser:** none. GARP gives no horizon convention for the financial impact; the stem fixes it as annual.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-7 b, where it is Q7 of 13.

a.reason: (Wrong input twin). Uses the original loan amount: 50 × 1.45% = 0.725 and an inflow of 50. Correct only if the full original amount were outstanding and prepaid.

b.reason: (Sign error). Right magnitude, wrong sign. Re-lending at 3.15% instead of earning 4.60% is a loss. Correct only if market rates had risen by 1.45 points.

c.reason: C pairs the inflow equal to the repaid amount with the annual margin loss computed on that amount, exactly GARP’s two-fold impact under the stem’s convention.

d.reason: (Dropped term). 36 × 4.60% = 1.656 treats the whole contract interest as lost, ignoring that the funds are re-lent at 3.15%. Correct only if the cash could not be reinvested at all.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Describe and identify examples of liquidity options and explain the impact of liquidity options on a bank’s liquidity position and its liquidity management process.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-7 b Q8
questions.question:
A bank supervisor is reviewing the inventory of liquidity options reported by a Chinese commercial bank. The bank lists the following items:

I. Committed credit lines of CNY 8 billion granted to corporate clients.

II. Sight and savings deposits of CNY 30 billion.

III. Fixed-rate mortgages of CNY 12 billion that borrowers may prepay at any time.

IV. A committed credit line of CNY 5 billion received by the bank from another financial institution.

V. European call options on equities bought by the bank’s trading desk.

Which of the items are liquidity options sold by the bank, that is, short liquidity option positions?

options.text: I and II only
I, II and III only
I, II, III and IV only
I, II, III and V only

questions.solution:
Supervisor’s review: which items are liquidity options sold by the bank.

**Concept and theory**

To identify a liquidity option, ask two questions: (1) does someone hold a right to receive cash from, or give cash to, the bank at predefined terms, with exercise driven by liquidity needs rather than profit; and (2) who holds the right?

| Item | Holder of the right | Bank’s position |
|---|---|---|
| Committed line granted to a client | Client (draws cash from the bank) | Short (GARP: “sells”) |
| Sight and savings deposits | Depositor (withdraws cash) | Short |
| Prepayable fixed-rate mortgage | Borrower (gives cash back early) | Short |
| Committed line received from another institution | Bank (draws cash) | Long |
| European call on equities | Bank, but a financial option | Not a liquidity option |

GARP states explicitly that easy access to credit lines is “a long position in liquidity options for the bank”, and that this is one of the tools for managing the liquidity impact of the short options sold to clients. The European call is GARP’s own benchmark example of a standard financial option, exercised when profitable, independently of the cash flows after exercise. Both long and short liquidity options need pricing models, which is why the inventory must separate them.

**Applying it to this question**

Items I, II and III are rights held by clients over the bank’s cash: short liquidity options. Item IV is a right the bank holds: long. Item V is a financial option. Hence I, II and III only.

**Fragile fact.** Credit lines granted = short; credit lines received = long.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Describe and identify examples of liquidity options and explain the impact of liquidity options on a bank’s liquidity position and its liquidity management process.

**GARP:** Chapter 7, Section 7.2 “Liquidity Options” (examples; “long position in liquidity options for the bank”).

**GARP vs Schweser:** none; Schweser does not use the long and short labels, so the classification is from GARP.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-7 b, where it is Q8 of 13.

a.reason: (Scope or condition error). Omits the prepayment option, the “other way round” case in which the client gives cash to the bank. Correct only if liquidity options were limited to withdrawals.

b.reason: B lists exactly the three client-held liquidity options GARP describes (credit line, deposits, prepayment).

c.reason: (Role misassignment). Includes the line the bank received, in which the bank is the holder (long). Correct if the question asked for all liquidity options, long or short.

d.reason: (Sibling swap). Includes a standard financial option. Correct only if exercise of the call depended on the desk’s need for cash rather than on profit.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Describe and identify examples of liquidity options and explain the impact of liquidity options on a bank’s liquidity position and its liquidity management process.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-7 b Q9
questions.question:
A risk consultant at an Australian bank is calculating the effect of a drawdown on a committed credit line after the borrower was downgraded. The consultant measures the financial impact as the difference between the contract spread and the borrower’s current market spread, applied to the amount drawn.

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Committed line notional (AUD m) | 450.00 |
| Amount drawn today (AUD m) | 280.00 |
| Contract spread over 3-month BBSW (%) | 1.20 |
| Borrower’s current market spread over BBSW (%) | 3.05 |
| Current 3-month BBSW (%) | 4.10 |
| Remaining life of the line (years) | 3.00 |

Which of the following best describes the impacts of the drawdown on the bank?

options.text: Liquidity outflow of AUD 280 million; annual financial gain of AUD 5.18 million
Liquidity outflow of AUD 450 million; annual financial loss of AUD 8.325 million
Liquidity outflow of AUD 280 million; annual financial loss of AUD 8.54 million
Liquidity outflow of AUD 280 million; annual financial loss of AUD 5.18 million

questions.solution:
Australian bank: liquidity and financial impact of a drawdown after the borrower’s downgrade.

**Concept and theory**

The committed credit line is the liquidity option GARP uses to show that financial effects can be strongly linked to exercise. The contract fixes the spread over a floating reference rate until expiry. If the obligor’s credit standing worsens, its market spread widens, and drawing on the line gives it funds below market cost. The bank bears the mirror image.

Applying GARP’s two-fold impact, with D the amount drawn, $\text{s}_{\text{c}}$ the contract spread and $\text{s}_{\text{m}}$ the borrower’s current market spread:

Liquidity impact = −D, Annual financial impact for the bank $= \text{D} (\text{s}_{\text{c}} - \text{s}_{\text{m}})$.

Because the line pays a floating reference rate plus a spread, the reference rate appears on both the contract and the market side and cancels: only the spread difference matters. The impact is applied to the amount drawn, not to the notional of the commitment. When $\text{s}_{\text{m}} > \text{s}_{\text{c}}$ the bank is lending below the price the market would charge: a financial loss to the bank and a saving to the borrower.

**Applying it to this question**

Formula first, then one step per line:

Liquidity impact = −AUD 280 million (outflow)

$\text{s}_{\text{c}} - \text{s}_{\text{m}} =$ 1.20% − 3.05% = −1.85%

Annual financial impact = 280 × (−1.85%) = −AUD 5.18 million

Irrelevant inputs: BBSW at 4.10% cancels between contract and market; the 3-year remaining life does not enter an annual figure; the AUD 450 million notional is the undrawn commitment, not the exercised amount.

**Fragile fact.** Spread widening after origination: borrower gains, bank loses; apply it to the drawn amount, not the notional.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Describe and identify examples of liquidity options and explain the impact of liquidity options on a bank’s liquidity position and its liquidity management process.

**GARP:** Chapter 7, Section 7.2 “Liquidity Options”, credit line example and two-fold effect.

**GARP vs Schweser:** none. The annual convention is fixed in the stem.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-7 b, where it is Q9 of 13.

a.reason: (Sign error). The spread gap favours the borrower, not the bank. Correct only if the borrower’s market spread had fallen to 1.20% − 1.85%, below the contract spread.

b.reason: (Wrong input twin). Uses the notional: 450 × 1.85% = 8.325 and an outflow of 450. Correct only if the whole line had been drawn.

c.reason: (Dropped term). 280 × 3.05% = 8.54 ignores the 1.20% contract spread the bank still earns. Correct only if the line carried no spread at all.

d.reason: D gives the outflow equal to the amount drawn and the annual loss of 1.85% on that amount, as GARP’s definition requires.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Describe and identify examples of liquidity options and explain the impact of liquidity options on a bank’s liquidity position and its liquidity management process.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-7 b Q10
questions.question: A member of the board risk committee of a Singapore bank asks how to assess the closure of a large savings account. A private banking client has withdrawn and closed a savings account of SGD 650 million that paid 1.20% a year. The bank had invested the balance in risk-free assets yielding 2.95% a year, which it now sells to fund the withdrawal. Which of the following statements best describes the impacts on the bank?

options.text: Liquidity outflow of SGD 650 million; financial gain of SGD 7.8 million a year, because the bank no longer pays the deposit rate on the closed balance.
The liquidity impact is negligible because the funds sat in risk-free assets that can be sold; only the financial loss of SGD 11.375 million a year matters.
Liquidity outflow of SGD 650 million, which can be substantial; financial loss of about SGD 11.375 million a year, which is small by comparison.
Liquidity outflow of SGD 650 million; financial loss of SGD 19.175 million a year, being the yield the bank gives up on the risk-free assets it sells.

questions.solution:
Singapore bank: impacts of the closure of a large savings account.

**Concept and theory**

GARP singles out the savings account as the case where the two impacts of exercise are most unequal. When a client closes a savings account:

- the **financial impact** is often quite small: it is the missing margin between the contract deposit rate and the rate the bank earns on reinvesting the received amounts (usually risk-free assets), or alternatively the cost of replacing the deposit with a new one at a higher rate;
- the **liquidity impact** can be quite substantial if the deposit has a big notional, because the full balance leaves the bank.

With Q the balance, $\text{r}_{\text{d}}$ the deposit rate and $\text{r}_{\text{f}}$ the reinvestment (risk-free) rate:

Liquidity impact = −Q, Annual financial impact $= - \text{Q} (\text{r}_{\text{f}} - \text{r}_{\text{d}})$.

The lesson for management is that the financial side can be hedged, at least partially, while the liquidity side needs dedicated tools: cash reserves, liquid assets or access to credit lines. Holding the deposit in liquid assets is one of those tools; it does not make the liquidity impact disappear, it is how the bank meets it.

**Applying it to this question**

Formula first, then one step per line:

Liquidity impact = −SGD 650 million

$\text{r}_{\text{f}} - \text{r}_{\text{d}} =$ 2.95% − 1.20% = 1.75%

Annual financial impact = −650 × 1.75% = −SGD 11.375 million

SGD 11.375 million a year is under 2% of the SGD 650 million that leaves the balance sheet.

**Fragile fact.** Savings account closure: the financial impact is a margin (small); the liquidity impact is the whole balance (large).

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Describe and identify examples of liquidity options and explain the impact of liquidity options on a bank’s liquidity position and its liquidity management process.

**GARP:** Chapter 7, Section 7.2 “Liquidity Options”, savings account example.

**GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser omits the savings account example; GARP used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-7 b, where it is Q10 of 13.

a.reason: (Dropped term). 650 × 1.20% = 7.8 counts the deposit interest saved but drops the 2.95% the bank no longer earns. Correct only if the funds had been held as non-earning cash.

b.reason: (Scope or condition error). Confuses the tool (liquid assets) with the absence of an impact: the bank still loses SGD 650 million of funding and must sell assets. Correct only for a deposit replaced at once by an identical one.

c.reason: C pairs the full SGD 650 million outflow, which can be substantial, with the lost margin of 1.75% on the balance, small by comparison, matching GARP’s savings account example.

d.reason: (Dropped term). 650 × 2.95% = 19.175 counts the lost yield but drops the 1.20% the bank stops paying. Correct only for a zero-rate deposit.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Describe and identify examples of liquidity options and explain the impact of liquidity options on a bank’s liquidity position and its liquidity management process.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-7 b Q11
questions.question:
A member of the board risk committee of a U.S. bank is reviewing the following statements in the bank’s draft policy on managing liquidity options (credit lines, deposits and prepayable loans):

I. The financial effects of liquidity options can be hedged directly, although only partially, by a mixture of standard and statistical techniques.

II. The liquidity impact of liquidity options can be managed only by holding cash reserves, by constraining the allocation of assets towards liquid assets, or by easy access to credit lines.

III. Easy access to committed credit lines from other financial institutions amounts to a short position in liquidity options for the bank.

IV. Because the liquidity impact can be hedged with interest rate derivatives, a bank with a hedging programme does not need to hold liquidity reserves.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.text: I and II only
I, II and III only
I, II and IV only
II only

questions.solution:
U.S. board review: how the financial and liquidity impacts of liquidity options are managed.

**Concept and theory**

Having split the effect of exercise into a liquidity impact and a financial impact, GARP assigns each a different management approach:

| Impact | How it is managed |
|---|---|
| Financial | Can be hedged directly, although only partially, by a mixture of standard and statistical techniques |
| Liquidity | Can only be managed by the liquidity tools analysed in the rest of the chapter: cash reserves, a constrained allocation of assets in liquid assets, or easy access to credit lines |

GARP labels easy access to credit lines “a long position in liquidity options for the bank”: the bank buys liquidity options to offset the short ones it sells to clients. All of these tools are costly (low-yielding reserves, a constrained asset mix, fees and spreads on received lines), which feeds into pricing (see Q12). The rest of the chapter turns these tools into measurement: received committed lines and unencumbered liquid assets enter the liquidity generation capacity that offsets negative cumulated expected cash flows.

The key asymmetry is that derivatives and statistical hedging can address the profit and loss consequences of exercise, but cannot produce cash on the day a depositor withdraws or a borrower draws.

**Applying it to this question**

I and II restate GARP. III reverses the bank’s position on received lines (long, not short). IV transfers the financial-hedging toolkit to the liquidity impact, which GARP says can only be handled with reserves, liquid assets or credit lines.

**Fragile fact.** Financial effects: hedged partially. Liquidity impact: reserves, liquid assets, received credit lines only. Received line = long.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Describe and identify examples of liquidity options and explain the impact of liquidity options on a bank’s liquidity position and its liquidity management process.

**GARP:** Chapter 7, Section 7.2 “Liquidity Options”, closing paragraph.

**GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser says the tools “needed to hedge liquidity impacts” are cash reserves, liquid assets and credit lines, and omits the partial hedging of financial effects; GARP used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-7 b, where it is Q11 of 13.

a.reason: A accepts exactly the two accurate statements: partial hedging of financial effects, and reserves, liquid assets and access to credit lines as the only means of managing the liquidity impact.

b.reason: (Polarity flip). Accepts III. A received committed line is a right the bank holds: long. Correct only for credit lines the bank grants to clients.

c.reason: (Sibling swap). Accepts IV, giving the liquidity impact the hedge that belongs to the financial impact. Correct only if IV referred to the financial effects.

d.reason: (Absolute-claim trap). Rejecting I amounts to claiming financial effects cannot be hedged at all. GARP says they can be hedged directly, although only partially. Correct only if I claimed a complete hedge.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Describe and identify examples of liquidity options and explain the impact of liquidity options on a bank’s liquidity position and its liquidity management process.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-7 b Q12
questions.question: A senior risk analyst at a Japanese regional bank is validating the bank’s client pricing model and recommending improvements. The model charges clients for interest rate risk and credit risk, but assigns zero cost to the cash reserves, the liquid-asset buffer and the received credit lines that the bank holds against deposit withdrawals and credit line drawdowns. Which recommendation is most consistent with the reading?

options.text: No change is needed, because liquidity options are exercised for liquidity reasons and therefore carry no financial value that needs to be priced into client contracts.
Include the costs of these tools when pricing client contracts, using models that price both long and short liquidity options and jointly consider liquidity and financial aspects.
Price the liquidity options sold to clients with a standard option model capturing only the financial effect, since the liquidity impact is managed separately by treasury.
Charge the buffer cost only to borrowers that draw on credit lines, because depositors give cash to the bank and therefore do not hold any liquidity option.

questions.solution:
Validating a client pricing model that ignores the cost of liquidity tools.

**Concept and theory**

GARP closes Section 7.2 with the consequences of liquidity options for the bank’s management process and pricing. The tools that manage the liquidity impact (cash reserves, a constrained allocation of assets towards liquid assets, easy access to credit lines) all imply costs. These costs “have to be properly accounted for” when pricing the contracts dealt with clients. Three implications follow:

1. Client products that embed short liquidity options (deposits, credit lines, prepayable loans) must carry a charge for the liquidity tools they require.
2. Models are needed to price both short liquidity options (sold to clients) and long liquidity options (such as received credit lines).
3. Because exercise produces financial profits or losses as well as liquidity effects, liquidity options can in some respects be seen as financial options too, so models must jointly consider liquidity and financial aspects.

In other words, liquidity options are not free: each one sold to a client consumes buffer capacity, which has a cost. A pricing framework that charges only for interest rate and credit risk will underprice deposit and credit line products and over-grant liquidity options.

**Applying it to this question**

The model under review omits the cost of reserves, buffer and received lines. GARP’s recommendation is to include these costs in client pricing, through models that value both long and short liquidity options and combine the liquidity and financial dimensions.

**Fragile fact.** Long and short liquidity options both need pricing; models must be joint (liquidity plus financial).

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Describe and identify examples of liquidity options and explain the impact of liquidity options on a bank’s liquidity position and its liquidity management process.

**GARP:** Chapter 7, Section 7.2 “Liquidity Options”, closing paragraph.

**GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser omits the pricing implication entirely; GARP-only content.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-7 b, where it is Q12 of 13.

a.reason: (Polarity flip). GARP says liquidity options also produce financial profits or losses and that the tools’ costs must be priced. A would be correct only if exercise had no financial effect and the tools were costless.

b.reason: B states all three of GARP’s prescriptions: account for the tools’ costs in pricing, price long and short liquidity options, and model liquidity and financial aspects jointly.

c.reason: (Scope or condition error). Drops the liquidity dimension; GARP requires joint modelling. Correct only for a standard financial option.

d.reason: (Role misassignment). Depositors do hold a liquidity option (the right to withdraw). Correct only for term deposits with no early withdrawal.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Describe and identify examples of liquidity options and explain the impact of liquidity options on a bank’s liquidity position and its liquidity management process.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-7 b Q13
questions.question: A junior risk analyst at an Italian bank is building the term structure of expected cash flows (TSECF). She has slotted EUR 2.4 billion of sight deposits at their contractual (overnight) maturity, committed credit lines granted to clients at zero usage, and fixed-rate mortgages at their contractual amortisation schedule, noting that the textbook TSECF example assumes that no liquidity options are embedded in deposits. Her manager asks how liquidity options should be reflected. Which response is most accurate?

options.text: Liquidity options should be left out of the TSECF and handled only in the term structure of liquidity generation capacity, since they are sources rather than causes of liquidity risk.
Since cash flows arising from liquidity options are stochastic, they cannot enter a term structure of expected cash flows and should be ignored until the options are exercised.
Cash flows should be adjusted for liquidity options with behavioural models for products such as sight deposits, credit line usage and mortgage prepayment, as these flows are stochastic.
Only the deposits need a behavioural adjustment; credit line usage and mortgage prepayments are fixed by contract, so their cash flows remain deterministic in time and amount.

questions.solution:
Building the TSECF: how liquidity options should be reflected.

**Concept and theory**

The LO asks for the impact of liquidity options on the bank’s liquidity management process. In monitoring, the main tool is the term structure of expected cash flows (TSECF) and its cumulated version (TSECCF), built from the causes of liquidity: existing and forecast contracts from ordinary business.

GARP’s textbook example deliberately assumes that no liquidity options are embedded in deposits, so that every flow is deterministic in time and amount. In a real balance sheet GARP lists the adjustments the TSECF needs, including: “cash flows are adjusted to account for liquidity options: behavioural models are used for typical banking products such as sight deposits, credit line usage and prepayment of mortgages”.

Why behavioural models? In the Section 7.1 taxonomy, the cash flows produced by liquidity options (withdrawals from deposits, drawings of credit lines granted to clients, prepayments) are behavioural: stochastic in amount and occurring at stochastic times, depending on client decisions that can be only loosely predicted. The TSECF records expected values of such flows, which is precisely what a behavioural model supplies. Leaving them at contractual terms (overnight for sight deposits, zero usage for lines, the contractual schedule for mortgages) misstates when cash actually leaves or arrives.

**Applying it to this question**

The analyst used contractual terms, which is valid only under the textbook’s no-option assumption. The manager’s correct response is to adjust all three products with behavioural models.

**Fragile fact.** Liquidity options sold to clients are causes (TSECF); received lines and assets are sources (LGC).

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Describe and identify examples of liquidity options and explain the impact of liquidity options on a bank’s liquidity position and its liquidity management process.

**GARP:** Chapter 7, Section 7.4.1 “The Term Structure of Expected Cash Flows and the Term Structure of Expected Cumulated Cash Flows”; Section 7.1 taxonomy; Section 7.2.

**GARP vs Schweser:** none. Boundary note: this question borrows the TSECF setting of LO 72.d but tests only the liquidity-option adjustment.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-7 b, where it is Q13 of 13.

a.reason: (Sibling swap). The options sold to clients generate flows from ordinary business and are causes of liquidity risk; sources (LGC) are the bank’s tools such as asset sales, repo and received lines. Correct only for a credit line the bank has received.

b.reason: (Scope or condition error). The TSECF is built on expected values precisely so that stochastic flows can be included. Correct only for a purely contractual (deterministic) ladder.

c.reason: C repeats GARP’s TSECF requirement: adjust cash flows for liquidity options with behavioural models for sight deposits, credit line usage and mortgage prepayment, because these flows are stochastic.

d.reason: (Scope or condition error). Credit line usage and prepayments are behavioural, at stochastic times and in uncertain amounts. Correct only if those products carried no client option.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Interpret the term structure of expected cash flows and cumulative cash flows.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-7 d Q1
questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a Canadian bank is validating the documentation of the bank’s liquidity monitoring engine, which uses the following notation for a set of contracts and securities $\{\text{d}_{1}$, . . . , $\text{d}_{\text{N}} \}$ viewed from the reference time $\text{t}_{0}$:

c $\text{f}^{+}_{\text{e}}(\text{t}_{0}$, $\text{t}_{\text{i}}) = \text{E}[ \sum_{\text{j}=1}^{\text{N}} \text{c f}^{+}(\text{t}_{0}$, $\text{t}_{\text{i}}$; $\text{d}_{\text{j}})]$, CF$(\text{t}_{0}$, $\text{t}_{\text{a}}$, $\text{t}_{\text{b}}) = \sum_{\text{i}=\text{a}}^{\text{b}} (\text{c f}^{+}_{\text{e}}(\text{t}_{0}$, $\text{t}_{\text{i}}) + \text{c f}^{-}_{\text{e}}(\text{t}_{0}$, $\text{t}_{\text{i}}))$

where c $\text{f}^{-}_{\text{e}}(\text{t}_{0}$, $\text{t}_{\text{i}})$ is defined analogously for negative cash flows. The analyst reviews four statements in the documentation:

I. c $\text{f}^{+}_{\text{e}}(\text{t}_{0}$, $\text{t}_{\text{i}})$ is the expected value, assessed at $\text{t}_{0}$, of the sum of the positive cash flows that all contracts and securities generate at date $\text{t}_{\text{i}}$.

II. Because expected negative cash flows enter with their own negative sign, CF$(\text{t}_{0}$, $\text{t}_{\text{a}}$, $\text{t}_{\text{b}})$ is the algebraic sum of all expected inflows and outflows from $\text{t}_{\text{a}}$ up to $\text{t}_{\text{b}}$.

III. Once the expected values have been computed, the distribution of cash flows at each date carries no further information that is useful for liquidity management.

IV. CF$(\text{t}_{0}$, $\text{t}_{\text{a}}$, $\text{t}_{\text{b}})$ measures the net expected cash flow falling on date $\text{t}_{\text{b}}$ alone, so the collection of these values for successive $\text{t}_{\text{b}}$ is the TSECF.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.text: I and IV only
I and II only
I, II and III only
II, III and IV only

questions.solution:
Canadian bank: auditing four statements on the notation c $\text{f}^{+}_{\text{e}}$, c $\text{f}^{-}_{\text{e}}$ and CF$(\text{t}_{0}$, $\text{t}_{\text{a}}$, $\text{t}_{\text{b}})$.

**Concept and theory**

Before a bank can draw any term structure, it must say precisely what number sits in each date bucket. GARP sets the notation at the start of Section 7.4. Viewed from a reference time $\text{t}_{0}$, the bank looks at a set of contracts and securities $\{\text{d}_{1}$, . . . , $\text{d}_{\text{N}} \}$ and, for each future date $\text{t}_{\text{i}}$, defines two quantities:

c $\text{f}^{+}_{\text{e}}(\text{t}_{0}$, $\text{t}_{\text{i}}) = \text{E}[ \sum_{\text{j}=1}^{\text{N}} \text{c f}^{+}(\text{t}_{0}$, $\text{t}_{\text{i}}$; $\text{d}_{\text{j}})]$, c $\text{f}^{-}_{\text{e}}(\text{t}_{0}$, $\text{t}_{\text{i}}) = \text{E}[ \sum_{\text{j}=1}^{\text{N}} \text{c f}^{-}(\text{t}_{0}$, $\text{t}_{\text{i}}$; $\text{d}_{\text{j}})]$

Here c $\text{f}^{+}(\text{t}_{0}$, $\text{t}_{\text{i}}$; $\text{d}_{\text{j}})$ is the positive cash flow that contract $\text{d}_{\text{j}}$ produces at $\text{t}_{\text{i}}$, c $\text{f}^{-}$ the negative one, and E\[·\] the expectation taken at $\text{t}_{0}$. The expectation is there because, as the taxonomy of Section 7.1 shows, many cash flows are stochastic in amount, in time or in both; the bank can only enter their expected value. GARP adds that, precisely because these are expectations, the distribution at each date should also be determined so as to recover measures other than the average, which increases the effectiveness of liquidity management (this is later developed into cash flow at risk under LO 72.c).

The cumulated quantity is

CF$(\text{t}_{0}$, $\text{t}_{\text{a}}$, $\text{t}_{\text{b}}) = \sum_{\text{i}=\text{a}}^{\text{b}} (\text{c f}^{+}_{\text{e}}(\text{t}_{0}$, $\text{t}_{\text{i}}) + \text{c f}^{-}_{\text{e}}(\text{t}_{0}$, $\text{t}_{\text{i}}))$

the cumulative amount of all expected cash flows from date $\text{t}_{\text{a}}$ up to $\text{t}_{\text{b}}$. The plus sign between c $\text{f}^{+}_{\text{e}}$ and c $\text{f}^{-}_{\text{e}}$ only makes sense because negative flows carry a negative sign: the sum is algebraic, inflows minus outflows.

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $\text{t}_{0}$ c $\text{f}^{+}_{\text{e}}(\text{t}_{0}$, $\text{t}_{\text{i}})$, c $\text{f}^{-}_{\text{e}}(\text{t}_{0}$, $\text{t}_{\text{i}})$ | reference time from which everything is viewed expected positive / negative flows on the single date $\text{t}_{\text{i}}$ |
| CF$(\text{t}_{0}$, $\text{t}_{\text{a}}$, $\text{t}_{\text{b}})$ | cumulated expected net flows over all dates from $\text{t}_{\text{a}} \text{to t}_{\text{b}}$ |
| TSECF | date-ordered collection of the single-date c $\text{f}^{+}_{\text{e}}$ and c $\text{f}^{-}_{\text{e}}$ |
| TSECCF | date-ordered collection of the cumulated CF values |

**Applying it to this question**

Statement I restates eq (7.1) exactly: an expectation, taken at $\text{t}_{0}$, of the sum across all contracts of the positive flows at $\text{t}_{\text{i}}$. Correct. Statement II is the reading of eq (7.3): because c $\text{f}^{-}_{\text{e}}$ is negative, adding it to c $\text{f}^{+}_{\text{e}}$ nets outflows against inflows, and the summation runs over every date from $\text{t}_{\text{a}}$ to $\text{t}_{\text{b}}$. Correct. Statement III contradicts GARP, which says the distribution at each time should be determined to recover measures other than the expected amount. Statement IV collapses a cumulated quantity into a single-date one: CF sums over i = a, . . . , b, so it is not the net flow on $\text{t}_{\text{b}}$, and its collection over dates is the TSECCF, not the TSECF. Only I and II survive.

**Fragile fact.** CF$(\text{t}_{0}$, $\text{t}_{\text{a}}$, $\text{t}_{\text{b}})$ is a sum over dates (cumulative, feeds the TSECCF); c $\text{f}^{+}_{\text{e}}$ and c $\text{f}^{-}_{\text{e}}$ are single-date (feed the TSECF); c $\text{f}^{-}_{\text{e}}$ is negative, so the sum is algebraic.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Interpret the term structure of expected cash flows and cumulative cash flows.

**GARP:** Chapter 7, Section 7.4 “Quantitative Liquidity Risk Measures”, eqs (7.1) to (7.3). **GARP vs** **Schweser:** none on content; Schweser LO 72.d states the same formulas (images not reproduced in the notes extraction) and omits GARP’s remark that the distribution at each date should also be determined.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-7 d, where it is Q1 of 12.

a.reason: (Sibling swap). It accepts IV, which swaps the cumulated measure for its sibling, the single-date net flow. CF$(\text{t}_{0}$, $\text{t}_{\text{a}}$, $\text{t}_{\text{b}})$ adds up every date in the interval; the single-date pair c $\text{f}^{+}_{\text{e}}(\text{t}_{0}$, $\text{t}_{\text{b}})$, c $\text{f}^{-}_{\text{e}}(\text{t}_{0}$, $\text{t}_{\text{b}})$ is what enters the TSECF. A would be right only if IV defined c $\text{f}^{+}_{\text{e}}(\text{t}_{0}$, $\text{t}_{\text{b}}) + \text{c f}^{-}_{\text{e}}(\text{t}_{0}$, $\text{t}_{\text{b}})$ rather than CF$(\text{t}_{0}$, $\text{t}_{\text{a}}$, $\text{t}_{\text{b}})$.

b.reason: B is correct because I and II are faithful readings of eqs (7.1) and (7.3): expected values at the reference time, summed across contracts, with negative flows entering with their sign and cumulated from $\text{t}_{\text{a}} \text{to t}_{\text{b}}$.

c.reason: (Absolute claim). It accepts III, which claims the expected value exhausts all useful information. GARP says the opposite: since the flows are only expected, their distribution at each date should be determined to recover other measures. C would need III to say that the distribution is still needed beyond the expected value.

d.reason: (Sibling swap and absolute claim). It drops the correct statement I and accepts both false statements, combining the cumulated-versus-single-date confusion in IV with the absolute claim in III. It would be right only if I were false and III and IV were true, which contradicts eqs (7.1) and (7.3).

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Interpret the term structure of expected cash flows and cumulative cash flows.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-7 d Q2
questions.question:
A treasury analyst at a Singapore bank is drafting the glossary for the asset and liability committee (ALCO) pack. The draft contains the following entries on the term structure of expected cash flows (TSECF):

I. The TSECF is the collection, ordered by date, of positive and negative expected cash flows up to the expiry of the contract with the longest maturity.

II. In the last bucket of the TSECF, whose indefinite expiry corresponds to the end of business activity, the bank records the reimbursement of equity to stockholders.

III. In the reading’s terminology, the name maturity ladder is reserved for the initial part of the TSECF, up to a one-year maturity.

IV. Standard practice labels the part of the TSECF up to one year as structural liquidity and the part beyond one year as short-term liquidity.

Which of the entries are consistent with the reading?

options.text: I and II only
II and IV only
I, III and IV only
I, II and III only

questions.solution:
Singapore bank ALCO glossary: four entries on the TSECF, equity bucket and maturity ladder.

**Concept and theory**

The term structure of expected cash flows (TSECF) is the first monitoring tool GARP builds in Section 7.4.1. Formally,

TSECF$(\text{t}_{0}$, $\text{t}_{\text{b}}) = \{\text{c f}^{+}_{\text{e}}(\text{t}_{0}$, $\text{t}_{0})$, c $\text{f}^{-}_{\text{e}}(\text{t}_{0}$, $\text{t}_{0})$, c $\text{f}^{+}_{\text{e}}(\text{t}_{0}$, $\text{t}_{1})$, c $\text{f}^{-}_{\text{e}}(\text{t}_{0}$, $\text{t}_{1})$, . . . , c $\text{f}^{+}_{\text{e}}(\text{t}_{0}$, $\text{t}_{\text{b}})$, c $\text{f}^{-}_{\text{e}}(\text{t}_{0}$, $\text{t}_{\text{b}})\}$

that is, the collection, ordered by date, of positive and negative expected cash flows, running up to the expiry of the contract with the longest maturity, $\text{t}_{\text{b}}$. Positive and negative flows are kept separately in each bucket, which is why the charts in the reading show bars above and below the axis.

Three conventions surround this definition. First, a balance sheet contains equity, which has no contractual expiry. GARP closes the TSECF with a bucket of indefinite expiry corresponding to the end of business activity, in which the equity is reimbursed to stockholders; in Example 7.4.1 this is the “> 10” bucket. Second, GARP is careful with names: the TSECF “is often referred to as the maturity ladder”, but the authors reserve that name for the initial part of the TSECF, up to one-year maturity. Third, standard practice splits the horizon in two:

| Horizon | Label in the reading |
|---|---|
| Up to one year | short-term liquidity (the maturity ladder segment) |
| Beyond one year | structural liquidity |

The purpose of these conventions is practical: short-term liquidity is where an immediate cash gap can arise, while structural liquidity describes the longer mismatch of the balance sheet.

**Applying it to this question**

Entry I reproduces the definition: date order, both signs, up to the longest-maturity contract. Entry II reproduces the end-of-business bucket with the reimbursement of equity. Entry III reproduces GARP’s own restriction of the name maturity ladder to the first year. Entry IV reverses the two labels: up to one year is short-term liquidity, beyond one year is structural. Hence I, II and III are consistent and IV is not.

**Fragile fact.** Up to one year is short-term liquidity (GARP’s maturity ladder); beyond one year is structural; equity sits in the final, indefinite bucket.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Interpret the term structure of expected cash flows and cumulative cash flows.

**GARP:** Chapter 7, Section 7.4.1 “The Term Structure of Expected Cash Flows and the Term Structure of Expected Cumulated Cash Flows”, eq (7.4) and following paragraph. **GARP vs** **Schweser:** Schweser says the TSECF is “also known as the maturity ladder”; GARP reserves that name for the part up to one year. GARP used. Schweser also omits the equity bucket and the short-term vs structural split.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-7 d, where it is Q2 of 12.

a.reason: (Scope or condition error). It omits III, as if the name maturity ladder applied to the whole TSECF without restriction. That is the looser usage GARP mentions (and Schweser adopts), but the reading explicitly reserves the name for the first year. A would be correct if the question asked which entries are consistent with Schweser’s wording, where the TSECF as a whole is called the maturity ladder.

b.reason: (Polarity flip). It accepts IV, which flips the two horizon labels: short-term liquidity is the part up to one year and structural liquidity the part beyond one year. B would require IV to read “short-term up to one year, structural beyond”; even then it would wrongly omit I.

c.reason: (Polarity flip). It accepts the flipped labels in IV and drops II, the end-of-business bucket in which equity is reimbursed. C would be right only if equity had no place in the TSECF and the horizon labels were reversed, neither of which matches Section 7.4.1.

d.reason: D is correct because entries I to III match GARP’s definition of the TSECF, the reimbursement of equity at the end of business activity, and the reservation of the name maturity ladder for the initial part up to one year, while IV inverts the short-term and structural labels.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Interpret the term structure of expected cash flows and cumulative cash flows.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-7 d Q3
questions.question:
A junior risk analyst at an Australian bank is building the TSECF and the term structure of expected cumulated cash flows (TSECCF) for a simplified balance sheet (AUD million): assets are bonds 60 and loans 140; liabilities are deposits 90, bonds issued 80 and equity 30. Assets bear no default risk, no liquidity options are embedded in the deposits, and interest is ignored. The TSECF runs to the end of business activity (the bucket beyond 10 years).

| Item | Amount (AUD m) | Contractual maturity profile |
|---|---|---|
| Bonds held | 60 | 25 in year 1; 35 in year 3 |
| Loans | 140 | 40 in year 2; 40 in year 4; 60 in year 8 |
| Deposits | 90 | 40 in year 1; 50 in year 2 |
| Bonds issued | 80 | 30 in year 3; 50 in year 6 |
| Equity | 30 | no contractual expiry |
| Undrawn committed line received | 25 | available until year 5 (off balance sheet) |

Which of the following is closest to the TSECCF at year 6 and in the bucket beyond 10 years?

options.text: AUD −30 million at year 6; AUD 0 million beyond 10 years
AUD −50 million at year 6; AUD −30 million beyond 10 years
AUD −30 million at year 6; AUD 30 million beyond 10 years
AUD 20 million at year 6; AUD 0 million beyond 10 years

questions.solution:
Australian bank: TSECCF at year 6 and beyond 10 years for a simplified balance sheet, no interest.

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s Example 7.4.1 shows how a TSECF is built from a balance sheet in the simplest setting. Two assumptions make every flow deterministic in time and amount: the assets bear no default risk, and no liquidity options are embedded in the deposits. Under those assumptions:

1. Order all assets and liabilities by maturity, disregarding which kind of contract they are.
2. When assets expire, the bank receives positive cash flows equal to their notional; when liabilities expire, it pays negative cash flows equal to their notional.
3. Equity has no contractual expiry, so it is reimbursed to stockholders in the final bucket, corresponding to the end of business activity.
4. Cumulate the net flows from the initial date to each date using eq (7.3) to obtain the TSECCF.

The TSECF records each date’s net flow; the TSECCF is the running total:

TSECCF$(\text{t}_{\text{i}}) = \sum_{\text{k}\le\text{i}} \left(\text{assets maturing}_{\text{k}} - \text{liabilities maturing}_{\text{k}}\right)$

Because the balance sheet balances (assets equal liabilities plus equity), the final TSECCF in a no-interest example returns to zero once equity is repaid: every unit funded is eventually paid back. Off-balance-sheet sources of liquidity, such as a committed line the bank has received, are not causes of cash flows. GARP states that the TSECF and the TSECCF do not include flows produced by the sources of liquidity; those belong to the liquidity generation capacity under LO 72.c.

**Applying it to this question**

Net flows by bucket (AUD million):

Year 1 : 25 − 40 = −15 $\text{TSECCF}_{1} = -$15

Year 2 : 40 − 50 = −10 $\text{TSECCF}_{2} = -$15 − 10 = −25

Year 3 : 35 − 30 = +5 $\text{TSECCF}_{3} = -$25 + 5 = −20

Year 4 : 40 − 0 = +40 $\text{TSECCF}_{4} = -$20 + 40 = +20

Year 6 : 0 − 50 = −50 $\text{TSECCF}_{6} = +$20 − 50 = −30

Year 8 : 60 − 0 = +60 $\text{TSECCF}_{8} = -$30 + 60 = +30

Beyond 10 : 0 − 30 = −30 TSECCF$>_{10} = +$30 − 30 = 0

The TSECCF is AUD −30 million at year 6 and AUD 0 at the end of business activity. The undrawn committed line of AUD 25 million is an irrelevant input: it is a source of liquidity, not a contractual flow, and is excluded from the TSECF and the TSECCF. Reading the result: the profile is negative in years 1 to 3 and again from year 6 until the loans mature in year 8, which is exactly the situation in which the bank must turn to its liquidity generation capacity.

**Fragile fact.** Expiring assets are inflows and expiring liabilities are outflows; equity is repaid in the final bucket; a received credit line is a source of liquidity and stays out.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Interpret the term structure of expected cash flows and cumulative cash flows.

**GARP:** Chapter 7, Section 7.4.1, Example 7.4.1 (Table 7.1, Figure 7.4). **GARP vs Schweser:** none on method; Schweser does not mention the equity bucket. Numbers are original.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-7 d, where it is Q3 of 12.

a.reason: A is correct: cumulating the date-ordered net flows from expiring assets and liabilities gives −30 at year 6, and repaying equity in the last bucket brings the balanced balance sheet back to zero.

b.reason: (Sibling swap). It reports the TSECF (single-date net flows) instead of the TSECCF: 0 − 50 = −50 at year 6 and 0 − 30 = −30 beyond 10 years. B would be correct if the question asked for the net expected cash flow in each bucket.

c.reason: (Dropped term). It gets year 6 right but omits the reimbursement of equity in the final bucket, so the cumulation stops at the year-8 value: −30 + 60 = +30. C would be correct only if the TSECF ended at the longest contractual maturity and equity were left out.

d.reason: (Intermediate result). It stops cumulating at year 4 (+20), the last positive value before the bonds issued mature in year 6, and so misses the −50 outflow. D would be correct if the question asked for the TSECCF at year 4 (and at the end of business activity).

questions.loText: Interpret the term structure of expected cash flows and cumulative cash flows.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-7 d Q4
questions.question:
The CRO of a Japanese regional bank presents the following extract of the bank’s expected cash flow profile to the board (JPY billion):

| Month | TSECF (net) | TSECCF |
|---|---|---|
| 6 | 18 | 65 |
| 7 | −40 | 25 |

A board member asks how the month-7 figures should be interpreted. Which of the following answers is most accurate?

options.text: The bank faces an expected cash shortfall of JPY 40 billion in month 7 that must be funded with new liabilities, because the net balance of that date is negative.
The bank faces an expected cash shortfall of JPY 15 billion in month 7, the amount by which the month-7 net outflow exceeds the month-7 TSECCF.
On an expected basis, the month-7 net outflow is netted against the cash position built up by earlier inflows, leaving a cumulative position of JPY 25 billion and no expected shortfall at that date.
The positive month-7 TSECCF guarantees that the bank will not face a liquidity shortfall in month 7, since the earlier inflows are certain to be available to cover the outflow.

questions.solution:
Japanese bank: interpreting a negative month-7 TSECF alongside a positive month-7 TSECCF.

**Concept and theory**

Why does a bank need two term structures rather than one? GARP’s answer in Section 7.4.1 is that banks are interested not only in monitoring the net balance of cash flows on a given date, but also in how the past dynamic evolution of net cash flows affects the total cash position on that date. Cash flows on their own are not enough to monitor liquidity, since what matters in the end is the cash available up to a given time, and that is given by the cumulated cash flows.

The two tools therefore answer different questions:

| Tool | Content | Question it answers |
|---|---|---|
| TSECF | net expected flow on each date | What comes in and goes out on this date? |
| TSECCF | running total of expected flows | How much cash is available up to this date? |

The key interpretive rule follows directly. If on a given date the balance of inflows and outflows is net negative, this position can be netted against a positive cash position originated by past inflows. A negative TSECF entry is therefore not, by itself, a cash shortfall: the shortfall exists only if the TSECCF is negative. A useful analogy is a current account: a large payment on one day does not overdraw the account if earlier deposits have built up a balance larger than the payment.

Finally, every entry is an expected value. A positive TSECCF says that on average the bank has enough cash; it does not say the bank cannot face a shortfall, since the flows behind it are stochastic.

**Applying it to this question**

Month 7 shows a net expected outflow of JPY 40 billion. The TSECCF at month 7 is JPY 25 billion, which already includes the month-7 outflow: 65 − 40 = 25. The earlier inflows built a cumulative position of JPY 65 billion by month 6, and the month-7 outflow is netted against it. On an expected basis there is no shortfall at month 7; the cumulative position remains positive at JPY 25 billion. The month-6 net figure of 18 is context only; it is already inside the 65.

**Fragile fact.** A negative TSECF entry is not a shortfall; only a negative TSECCF signals one, and even a positive TSECCF is an expectation, not a guarantee.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Interpret the term structure of expected cash flows and cumulative cash flows.

**GARP:** Chapter 7, Section 7.4.1, paragraph explaining why the TSECCF is useful and the text after Table 7.1. **GARP vs Schweser:** none; Schweser LO 72.d gives the same netting rule (the key measure is “the cumulative amount of cash it has available”).

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-7 d, where it is Q4 of 12.

a.reason: (Sibling swap). It reads the single-date TSECF entry as if it were the cash position. The JPY 40 billion outflow is netted against the cash accumulated from earlier inflows, so it does not have to be funded. A would be correct if the month-7 TSECCF were −40, for example if month 7 were the first date of the profile with no earlier inflows.

b.reason: (Double counting). It subtracts the month-7 TSECCF from the month-7 net outflow, 40 − 25 = 15, treating the outflow as if it were not yet in the cumulated figure. The TSECCF of 25 already includes the month-7 outflow. B would be correct only if 25 were the cumulative position at month 6 and the question asked for the shortfall after the month-7 outflow on a different profile.

c.reason: C is correct because it applies GARP’s rule that a net negative balance on a date can be netted out with a positive cash position originated by past inflows, and it keeps the expected-value qualification (“on an expected basis”).

d.reason: (Absolute claim). It turns an expected value into a guarantee. GARP stresses that the TSECF forecasts only the expected value of a distribution, so a TSECCF that is positive on average can still have negative outcomes with some probability. D would be acceptable only if all flows were deterministic in time and amount.

questions.source: High quality paper LTR-7 d Q5
questions.question:
A treasury analyst at a UK bank is extending a simplified TSECCF to include interest. Interest is paid annually at each year-end on every contract outstanding during that year, including the year in which the contract expires. Assets bear no default risk and no liquidity options are embedded in the deposits.

| Item | Side | Notional (GBP m) | Rate (%) | Expiry (years) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Interbank loan | Asset | 30 | 4.0 | 1 |
| Corporate bonds held | Asset | 50 | 5.0 | 3 |
| Mortgages | Asset | 80 | 6.0 | 5 |
| Term deposits | Liability | 60 | 3.0 | 2 |
| Senior bonds issued | Liability | 70 | 4.5 | 4 |

The bank also has equity of GBP 30 million, on which shareholders require a return of 11%. Which of the following is closest to the TSECCF at the end of year 4?

options.text: GBP −38.30 million
GBP −50.00 million
GBP −68.35 million
GBP −35.80 million

questions.solution:
UK bank: TSECCF at the end of year 4 including annual interest on outstanding contracts.

**Concept and theory**

GARP makes Example 7.4.1 more realistic by adding the interest payments that assets and liabilities yield, assuming a yearly coupon period. Each bucket of the TSECF then has four components:

$$\text{TSECF}_{\text{t}} = \underbrace{\text{N}^{+}_{\text{t}}}_{\text{assets expiring}} + \underbrace{\text{I}^{+}_{\text{t}}}_{\text{interest received}} - \underbrace{\text{N}^{-}_{\text{t}}}_{\text{liabilities expiring}} - \underbrace{\text{I}^{-}_{\text{t}}}_{\text{interest paid}}, \qquad \text{TSECCF}_{\text{t}} = \sum_{\text{k} \le \text{t}} \text{TSECF}_{\text{k}}$$

where interest in year t is earned or paid on every contract still outstanding during that year:

$$\text{I}^{+}_{\text{t}} = \sum_{\text{assets with expiry} \,\ge\, \text{t}} \text{N}_{\text{j}}\,\text{y}_{\text{j}}, \qquad \text{I}^{-}_{\text{t}} = \sum_{\text{liabilities with expiry} \,\ge\, \text{t}} \text{N}_{\text{j}}\,\text{y}_{\text{j}}$$

with $\text{N}_{\text{j}}$ the notional and $\text{y}_{\text{j}}$ the annual rate of contract j. Two features matter. First, interest income and expense shrink step by step as contracts mature: once a contract has expired it no longer pays or receives interest. Second, the interest in the expiry year is still paid, together with the notional (in GARP’s Table 7.3, year 1 includes interest on the year-1 assets). The effect on interpretation is that interest can shift the TSECCF materially: in GARP’s example the notional-only profile and the profile with interest differ, and the negative window around years 7 to 8 is shaped by the interest flows. Equity earns no contractual interest in this framework and is repaid only in the final bucket.

**Applying it to this question**

Interest by year (GBP million):

$\text{I}^{+}_{1} =$ 30(0.04) + 50(0.05) + 80(0.06) = 1.20 + 2.50 + 4.80 = 8.50

$\text{I}^{-}_{1} =$ 60(0.03) + 70(0.045) = 1.80 + 3.15 = 4.95

$\text{I}^{+}_{2} = \text{I}^{+}_{3} =$ 2.50 + 4.80 = 7.30, $\text{I}^{-}_{2} =$ 4.95, $\text{I}^{-}_{3} = \text{I}^{-}_{4} =$ 3.15, $\text{I}^{+}_{4} =$ 4.80

Net flows and cumulation:

$\text{TSECF}_{1} =$ 30 + 8.50 − 0 − 4.95 = 33.55 $\text{TSECCF}_{1} =$ 33.55

$\text{TSECF}_{2} =$ 0 + 7.30 − 60 − 4.95 = −57.65 $\text{TSECCF}_{2} =$ 33.55 − 57.65 = −24.10

$\text{TSECF}_{3} =$ 50 + 7.30 − 0 − 3.15 = 54.15 $\text{TSECCF}_{3} = -$24.10 + 54.15 = 30.05

$\text{TSECF}_{4} =$ 0 + 4.80 − 70 − 3.15 = −68.35 $\text{TSECCF}_{4} =$ 30.05 − 68.35 = −38.30

The TSECCF at the end of year 4 is GBP −38.30 million: on an expected basis the bank is short of cash at that date and must rely on its liquidity generation capacity. The equity of GBP 30 million and the 11% required return are irrelevant: equity has no contractual interest flow in the TSECF and is repaid only in the end-of-business bucket.

**Fragile fact.** Interest is earned or paid only on contracts still outstanding, including in their expiry year; the answer is the running total, not the year-4 net flow.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Interpret the term structure of expected cash flows and cumulative cash flows.

**GARP:** Chapter 7, Section 7.4.1, Example 7.4.1 continued (Tables 7.2 and 7.3, Figure 7.5). **GARP** **vs Schweser:** none on method (Schweser’s King Bank example uses the same approach). Caution: in the extracted GARP Table 7.3 the positive interest in years 8 to 10 is printed as 1.69, whereas 30 at 6.50% gives 1.95; the numbers here are original and do not rely on that table.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-7 d, where it is Q5 of 12.

a.reason: A is correct: it cumulates notional and interest flows, earning and paying interest only on contracts still outstanding in each year, exactly as in GARP’s Table 7.3.

b.reason: (Dropped term). It ignores interest altogether and cumulates notionals only: 30 − 60 + 50 − 70 = −50.00. B would be correct in the simpler version of Example 7.4.1 where interest payments are not considered.

c.reason: (Sibling swap). It reports the year-4 TSECF instead of the TSECCF: 0 + 4.80 − 70 − 3.15 = −68.35. C would be correct if the question asked for the net expected cash flow in year 4.

d.reason: (Stale balance (dropped maturity)). It keeps charging and earning interest on contracts after they have matured, using year-1 interest (8.50 received, 4.95 paid) in every year: 33.55 − 56.45 + 53.55 − 66.45 = −35.80. D would be correct only if matured contracts were replaced by identical new ones (a rollover assumption that the stem does not make).

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Interpret the term structure of expected cash flows and cumulative cash flows.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-7 d Q6
questions.question:
An internal auditor at a Brazilian bank is reviewing the scope of the bank’s TSECF engine, which projects BRL cash flows for its full balance sheet. The engine’s methodology note states that the TSECF:

I. Includes the expected cash flows of all existing contracts on both sides of the balance sheet, including bonds issued and loans received by the bank.

II. Includes the cash flows of new loans the bank can reasonably expect to originate, even though these contracts do not exist at the reference time.

III. Includes the expected rollover of maturing liabilities and the new bond issuance planned to fund the increase in assets.

IV. Treats the cash flows of planned new mortgage origination as deterministic in both amount and time, because the business plan fixes the volumes and the origination dates.

Which of the statements in the methodology note are consistent with the reading?

options.text: I and II only
I, II and III only
I, III and IV only
I, II, III and IV

questions.solution:
Brazilian bank: auditing the scope of a TSECF engine for a real balance sheet.

**Concept and theory**

Example 7.4.1 is deliberately artificial: a handful of deterministic contracts that exist at the reference date. GARP then explains what a TSECF must contain for a real balance sheet. The number and type of contracts is much greater, and the analysis is not limited to contracts existing at the reference time but also covers all new activities that can reasonably be expected, most of them in the new business category of the taxonomy. In detail, the TSECF:

- includes the cash flows of all existing contracts on the asset and liability side; many are stochastic because they are linked to market indices, so interest rate models are needed;
- adjusts cash flows for credit risk and for liquidity options (with credit and behavioural models);
- includes cash flows from new business that increases the assets; these are typically stochastic in both amount and time and are handled with models that consider all the related risks;
- includes the rollover of maturing liabilities, by similar or different contracts, and new bond issuance to fund the increase in assets.

The rationale is that the TSECF is meant to capture all flows produced by the causes of liquidity risk, which GARP defines as all factors referring to existing and forecast future contracts originated by ordinary business activity. A plan does not make new business deterministic: whether clients will want or need to close such contracts is uncertain, so the related flows are stochastic in amount and, for completely new contracts, in time as well. The risks related to this stochastic nature must be measured, which leads to liquidity buffers.

**Applying it to this question**

Statement I matches the first bullet: all existing contracts, assets and liabilities alike (GARP even stresses that bonds issued and loans received generate contractual flows). Statement II matches the inclusion of new activities reasonably expected to be operated. Statement III matches the rollover and new issuance bullet. Statement IV treats planned new mortgages as deterministic in both amount and time, whereas GARP says new business flows are typically stochastic in both dimensions. So I, II and III are consistent; IV is not.

**Fragile fact.** New business and rollovers are inside the TSECF, and they are stochastic; a business plan does not make them deterministic.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Interpret the term structure of expected cash flows and cumulative cash flows.

**GARP:** Chapter 7, Section 7.4.1, list following Example 7.4.1 (“In greater detail, the cash flows of the TSECF are those produced by all the causes of cash flows”); Section 7.4, Definition 7.4.1. **GARP vs Schweser:** none; Schweser gives a shorter version of the same list.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-7 d, where it is Q6 of 12.

a.reason: (Scope or condition error). It drops III, as if the TSECF stopped at contractual and new-asset flows and left funding rollovers out. GARP lists the rollover of maturing liabilities and new bond issuance to fund asset growth as items that have to be taken into account. A would be correct only if III described exceptional funding raised to cover a gap, which belongs to the liquidity generation capacity instead.

b.reason: B is correct because the TSECF covers existing contracts, reasonably expected new business, and the rollover and new issuance that fund ordinary business, and because it must treat new business as stochastic, which rules out IV.

c.reason: (Scope or condition error). It drops II (new business that does not yet exist) and accepts IV (new business as deterministic). Both errors misstate the condition attached to new business: it is included, and it is stochastic. C would require GARP to restrict the TSECF to existing contracts while treating plans as certain, which it does not.

d.reason: (Scope or condition error). It accepts IV, which overextends a business plan into certainty. GARP says new business cash flows are typically stochastic in both amount and time and need models that consider the related risks. D would be correct only if IV said the planned flows are included as stochastic.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Interpret the term structure of expected cash flows and cumulative cash flows.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-7 d Q7
questions.question:
The treasurer of a US bank is reviewing a draft of the month-4 bucket of the TSECF prepared by a junior analyst. The analyst has entered three positive amounts:

I. USD 300 million from the planned rollover of certificates of deposit maturing that month, in line with the funding plan for ordinary business.

II. USD 500 million the treasury could raise by drawing a committed credit line received from another bank, should a cash gap appear.

III. USD 200 million the treasury could raise by selling unencumbered Treasury bonds, should a cash gap appear.

Which of the following treatments is most consistent with the reading?

options.text: Keep all three amounts, since each is a positive cash flow the bank expects to be able to obtain in month 4.
Keep II and III only, since rollovers belong to the new business category and are modelled outside the TSECF.
Keep I and II only, since unsecured funding always enters the TSECF, whereas asset sales belong to the liquidity generation capacity.
Keep I only, since II and III are sources of liquidity that feed the liquidity generation capacity and are kept out of the TSECF and the TSECCF.

questions.solution:
US bank: which of three positive amounts belong in the month-4 TSECF bucket.

**Concept and theory**

GARP organises liquidity risk measurement around two classes of factors. The causes of liquidity risk (Definition 7.4.1) are all factors referring to existing and forecast future contracts originated by the ordinary business activity of the institution; their flows can be positive or negative. The sources of liquidity (Definition 7.4.2) are all factors capable of generating positive cash flows to manage and hedge liquidity risk that can be disposed of promptly by the bank; they determine the liquidity generation capacity (LGC).

Section 7.4.1 draws the boundary explicitly: the TSECF, and hence the TSECCF, do not include the flows produced by the sources of cash flows, which are tools to manage the liquidity risk originated by the causes. The logic is that the TSECCF must show the problem before any remedy is applied; if remedies were mixed in, a structural gap could be hidden by funding that might not be available.

| Inside the TSECF / TSECCF (causes) | Outside, in the LGC (sources) |
|---|---|
| existing contracts, new business | asset sales (balance sheet shrinkage) |
| planned rollover of maturing liabilities planned new issuance funding asset growth | repo and secured funding on available assets exceptional unsecured funding, drawing received lines |

GARP adds a precision that is easy to miss: new debt raised as LGC is not the same as debt planned to roll over existing contracts or to fund new business. The planned kind is part of ordinary business and its flows are included in the TSECF and the TSECCF. Likewise, the unsecured funding in the LGC is not the unsecured funding inserted in the TSECF; it refers to shorter-term exceptional funding.

**Applying it to this question**

Item I is a planned rollover of maturing liabilities in line with the funding plan for ordinary business: a cause, included. Item II is a drawing on a committed line the bank has received, made only if a gap appears: a source of liquidity (unsecured funding in the LGC), excluded. Item III is the sale of unencumbered bonds if a gap appears: balance sheet shrinkage, a source of liquidity, excluded. The bucket should keep I only.

**Fragile fact.** The test is cause versus source, not positive versus negative: planned rollovers are in; lines drawn or assets sold to fill a gap are out.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Interpret the term structure of expected cash flows and cumulative cash flows.

**GARP:** Chapter 7, Section 7.4, Definitions 7.4.1 and 7.4.2; Section 7.4.1 (sources of cash flows excluded from the TSECF and TSECCF); the clarification on new debt at the start of Section 7.4.2. **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser defines causes and sources under LO 72.d but does not state the exclusion rule explicitly. Boundary: LGC mechanics belong to LO 72.c; only the exclusion is tested here.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-7 d, where it is Q7 of 12.

a.reason: (Scope or condition error). It extends the TSECF to every positive flow the bank could obtain. Being positive is not the test; being produced by ordinary business (a cause) is. A would be correct only if the question asked what enters the term structure of expected liquidity, which combines the TSECCF with the cumulated LGC (LO 72.c).

b.reason: (Sibling swap). It swaps the two categories: it places the planned rollover outside and the LGC sources inside. GARP explicitly includes rollovers of maturing liabilities in the TSECF and excludes sources. B would describe the composition of the LGC with the rollover removed, not the TSECF.

c.reason: (Absolute claim). It claims that unsecured funding “always” enters the TSECF. GARP distinguishes the planned unsecured funding of ordinary business (in the TSECF) from the exceptional unsecured funding of the LGC, such as drawing received credit lines (excluded). C would be correct only if item II were a planned, ordinary-business funding flow rather than a contingency drawing.

d.reason: D is correct because GARP states that the TSECF and TSECCF exclude flows produced by the sources of liquidity, while planned rollovers of maturing liabilities are explicitly included.

questions.source: High quality paper LTR-7 d Q8
questions.question:
A risk consultant at a Canadian bank is interpreting the bank’s TSECF, shown below in CAD million (positive flows with a plus sign, negative flows with a minus sign). The bank also holds CAD 18 million of unencumbered government bonds that it could sell if needed.

| Year | Notional (+) | Interest (+) | Notional (−) | Interest (−) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 10 | 6.0 | 0 | −4.0 |
| 2 | 0 | 5.5 | −15 | −4.0 |
| 3 | 25 | 5.5 | 0 | −3.4 |
| 4 | 0 | 4.0 | −40 | −3.4 |
| 5 | 0 | 4.0 | 0 | −1.6 |
| 6 | 30 | 4.0 | 0 | −1.6 |

Which of the following best describes the bank’s TSECCF over the six years?

options.text: Negative in years 2 and 4 only; deepest point CAD −39.4 million in year 4.
Negative in year 2 and years 4 to 5; deepest point CAD −20.0 million in years 4 and 5.
Negative in year 2 and years 4 to 5; deepest point CAD −13.8 million in year 4.
Positive in every year; lowest point CAD 1.0 million in year 4.

questions.solution:
Canadian bank: reading a six-year TSECF table to locate negative TSECCF windows.

**Concept and theory**

Interpreting a TSECF table means converting date-by-date flows into the cumulated profile and reading its sign over time. GARP’s Table 7.3 is laid out with four columns, notional and interest for positive flows and notional and interest for negative flows, and a TSECCF column that cumulates their sum:

$\text{TSECF}_{\text{t}} = \text{N}^{+}_{\text{t}} + \text{I}^{+}_{\text{t}} + \text{N}^{-}_{\text{t}} + \text{I}^{-}_{\text{t}}$, $\text{TSECCF}_{\text{t}} = \text{TSECCF}_{\text{t}}-_{1} + \text{TSECF}_{\text{t}}$

with negative flows carrying a minus sign. The interpretive questions are then: on which dates is the TSECCF negative, how deep is the negative position, and how long does it last? GARP explains that the temporal distribution of the maturities of assets and liabilities can produce periods of negative cumulated cash flows; such periods may be accepted if they are short and can be managed effectively with the available tools. In GARP’s own example the TSECCF is positive for six years, falls to −3.20 in year 7 when large liabilities expire, stays negative in year 8 and turns positive again in year 9 as interest accumulates and assets mature.

Two cautions apply. First, interest flows on both sides belong in the profile; dropping them can create or hide negative windows. Second, the TSECCF is built from the causes of liquidity only. Sources such as unencumbered bonds that could be sold are not in the TSECCF; they are what the bank uses to cover a negative window, under the liquidity generation capacity.

**Applying it to this question**

Net flow and cumulation (CAD million):

Year 1 : 10 + 6.0 − 0 − 4.0 = 12.0 $\text{TSECCF}_{1} =$ 12.0

Year 2 : 0 + 5.5 − 15 − 4.0 = −13.5 $\text{TSECCF}_{2} =$ 12.0 − 13.5 = −1.5

Year 3 : 25 + 5.5 − 0 − 3.4 = 27.1 $\text{TSECCF}_{3} = -$1.5 + 27.1 = 25.6

Year 4 : 0 + 4.0 − 40 − 3.4 = −39.4 $\text{TSECCF}_{4} =$ 25.6 − 39.4 = −13.8

Year 5 : 0 + 4.0 − 0 − 1.6 = 2.4 $\text{TSECCF}_{5} = -$13.8 + 2.4 = −11.4

Year 6 : 30 + 4.0 − 0 − 1.6 = 32.4 $\text{TSECCF}_{6} = -$11.4 + 32.4 = 21.0

The TSECCF is negative in year 2 and in years 4 to 5, with the deepest point at CAD −13.8 million in year 4; the small positive net flow in year 5 does not restore a positive position, which only returns in year 6. The CAD 18 million of unencumbered bonds is irrelevant to the TSECCF: it is a source of liquidity that could be used to cover these windows, not a contractual flow.

**Fragile fact.** Cumulate every component with its sign; a negative net flow is not a negative cumulated position, and a small positive flow does not end a negative window.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Interpret the term structure of expected cash flows and cumulative cash flows.

**GARP:** Chapter 7, Section 7.4.1, Table 7.3 and Figure 7.5; the paragraph on the temporal distribution of maturities producing periods of negative cumulated cash flows. **GARP vs** **Schweser:** none; Schweser repeats that timing of maturities can create periods of negative cumulated cash flows.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-7 d, where it is Q8 of 12.

a.reason: (Sibling swap). It reads the TSECF net flows as if they were cumulated: years 2 and 4 have negative net flows (−13.5 and −39.4), and −39.4 is the year-4 net flow. A would be correct if the question asked in which years the net expected cash flow is negative and what the largest net outflow is.

b.reason: (Dropped term). It cumulates notionals only, ignoring interest: 10, −5, 20, −20, −20, 10. This gives the same negative years but a deepest point of −20.0 in years 4 and 5. B would be correct in a version of the table without interest payments.

c.reason: C is correct because cumulating all four flow components gives negative values exactly in years 2, 4 and 5, and the minimum is −13.8 in year 4.

d.reason: (Dropped term). It drops the negative interest column, cumulating $\text{N}^{+} + \text{I}^{+} + \text{N}^{-}$ only: 16.0, 6.5, 37.0, 1.0, 5.0, 39.0, which never turns negative and bottoms at 1.0 in year 4. D would be correct only if the bank paid no interest on its liabilities.
