questions.question:
A senior treasury analyst at a Singapore bank reviews the expected profile below (SGD million). The month-3 short cash position has been covered with short-term interbank borrowing.

| Month | TSECF (net) | TSECCF |
|---|---|---|
| 3 | −170 | −120 |
| 4 | 150 | 30 |

A colleague proposes to lend the whole month-4 inflow to corporate clients for one year. Which of the following statements is NOT correct?

options.text: The month-4 inflow first offsets the short cash position created by earlier outflows, so the cumulative position at month 4 is SGD 30 million.
The full SGD 150 million month-4 inflow can be treated as free surplus, since liquidity monitoring only needs the net balance of cash flows on a given date.
Because the month-3 short position had to be financed in any case, typically with new liabilities, SGD 120 million of the month-4 inflow goes to repaying those debts.
Netting in the TSECCF works in both directions: earlier inflows can cover a later net outflow, and a later net inflow can cover a short position left by earlier outflows.

questions.solution:
Singapore bank: interpreting a month-4 inflow that follows a negative month-3 TSECCF.

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s netting argument for the TSECCF works in both directions. The familiar direction: if on a given date the balance of inflows and outflows is net negative, it can be netted against a positive cash position originated by past inflows. The reverse direction is equally true: the bank can use a net positive inflow on a given date to cover a short cash position deriving from past outflows.

GARP attaches a condition to the reverse case. A short cash position does not simply wait to be filled; it must be financed in any case, typically with new liabilities. When the later inflow arrives, it is used to pay back these debts. So a later inflow is not free cash: part of it is already committed to repaying the funding that covered the earlier shortfall.

The practical consequence for interpretation is that the TSECCF, not the date’s TSECF entry, tells the bank how much cash is truly available. A large positive TSECF entry following a negative TSECCF is mostly absorbed by repayments; the surplus available for new uses is the cumulative position after netting.

| Direction | What nets against what | Condition |
|---|---|---|
| Forward | date outflow vs earlier accumulated cash | none |
| Reverse | date inflow vs earlier short position | short position financed, then repaid |

**Applying it to this question**

At month 3 the TSECCF is SGD −120 million, financed with short-term interbank borrowing. At month 4 the TSECF is +150, so the TSECCF becomes −120 + 150 = +30. Of the 150 inflow, 120 repays the debt raised to fund the earlier short position; only 30 is cumulative surplus. Statements A, C and D describe this correctly. Statement B treats all 150 as free surplus on the grounds that only the date’s net balance matters, which is precisely the view GARP rejects when explaining why the TSECCF is needed. B is the statement that is NOT correct.

**Fragile fact.** Later inflows can cover earlier short positions, but those positions were funded with debt, so the inflow repays debt first; the free amount is the TSECCF.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Interpret the term structure of expected cash flows and cumulative cash flows.

**GARP:** Chapter 7, Section 7.4.1, paragraph explaining why the TSECCF is useful (“Obviously the reverse can also be true”). **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser gives only the forward direction (earlier inflows reduce a later net negative position) and omits the financing and repayment condition. GARP used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-7 d, where it is Q9 of 12.

a.reason: (Accurate statement, so not the answer). It is accurate: the month-4 inflow first offsets the short position from earlier outflows, leaving a cumulative position of −120 + 150 = 30. It would be the answer only if it misstated the cumulation, for example by reporting 150 or −120.

b.reason: B is the required answer because it contradicts GARP: banks monitor not only the net balance on a given date but how the past evolution of net cash flows affects the total cash position, and the earlier short position must be financed and then repaid from the later inflow.

c.reason: (Accurate statement, so not the answer). It is accurate and is GARP’s own condition: short cash positions must be financed in any case, typically with new liabilities, so positive inflows are used to pay back these debts. It would be the answer only if it claimed the short position needed no financing.

d.reason: (Accurate statement, so not the answer). It is accurate: GARP states the forward case and then that “the reverse can also be true”. It would be the answer only if it said netting worked in one direction only.

questions.question: A risk consultant is advising a Chinese bank on how to move from a contractual CNY cash flow ladder to a TSECF for its real balance sheet. The bank’s books include floating-rate loans indexed to a market fixing, a large corporate loan book exposed to default, and retail products such as sight deposits, credit lines granted to clients and prepayable mortgages. Which of the following best describes the adjustments the consultant should recommend?

options.text: Interest rate models for index-linked flows; credit models applied on an aggregated basis that reflects correlation among counterparties for defaults; behavioural models for sight deposits, credit line usage and mortgage prepayment.

Behavioural models for index-linked flows; credit models applied on an aggregated basis that reflects correlation among counterparties for defaults; interest rate models for sight deposits, credit line usage and mortgage prepayment.

Interest rate models for index-linked flows; credit models applied loan by loan, assuming independent defaults across counterparties; behavioural models for sight deposits, credit line usage and mortgage prepayment.

Interest rate models for index-linked flows; credit models applied on an aggregated basis that reflects correlation among counterparties for defaults; sight deposits, credit lines and prepayable mortgages left at contractual flows and covered by buffers.

questions.solution:
Chinese bank: mapping index-linked, credit and liquidity-option flows to the right model adjustments.

**Concept and theory**

A contractual ladder lists what contracts say will happen; a TSECF lists what the bank expects to happen. Turning the first into the second requires three distinct model families, each aimed at a different source of uncertainty identified in the cash flow taxonomy (Section 7.1):

| Uncertainty (taxonomy) | Typical flows | Model family in the TSECF |
|---|---|---|
| Indexed / contingent | coupons linked to Libor or Euribor fixings | interest rate models |
| Credit related | missed flows and recoveries after default | credit models, aggregated, with correlation |
| Behavioural (liquidity options) | sight deposits, credit line usage, prepayments | behavioural models |

GARP is specific about each. Cash flows from existing contracts are often stochastic because they are linked to market indices, so interest rate models are needed to compute expected flows. Cash flows are adjusted for credit risk using credit models that take defaults into account on an aggregated basis, also considering the correlation existing among the bank’s counterparties; a contract-by-contract view under independence would understate clustered defaults. Cash flows are adjusted for liquidity options using behavioural models for typical banking products such as sight deposits, credit line usage and mortgage prepayments. These products embed options whose exercise is driven by clients’ needs, not by the contract schedule, so leaving them at contractual values would misstate both amount and timing.

**Applying it to this question**

The bank has three features: index-linked loans (indexed/contingent), a default-exposed corporate book (credit related) and retail products with embedded options (behavioural). The consultant must recommend interest rate models, aggregated credit models with correlation, and behavioural models respectively. Only option A pairs every feature with the right model and the right condition.

**Fragile fact.** Market fixings need interest rate models, defaults need aggregated credit models with correlation, liquidity options need behavioural models; do not swap them.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Interpret the term structure of expected cash flows and cumulative cash flows.

**GARP:** Chapter 7, Section 7.4.1, list following Example 7.4.1; Section 7.1 taxonomy for the categories. **GARP vs Schweser:** none; Schweser lists the same three adjustments more briefly.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-7 d, where it is Q10 of 12.

a.reason: A is correct because it reproduces GARP’s three adjustments: interest rate models for index-linked flows, credit models on an aggregated basis with counterparty correlation, and behavioural models for liquidity options in sight deposits, credit lines and prepayable mortgages.

b.reason: (Sibling swap). It swaps the interest rate and behavioural models: behavioural models are for client decisions (liquidity options), interest rate models for index-linked flows. B would be correct only if the index-linked flows depended on client behaviour and the retail products on market fixings, which is the reverse of the taxonomy.

c.reason: (Scope or condition error). It drops the condition that credit models work on an aggregated basis that considers correlation among counterparties, replacing it with loan-by-loan independence. C would be correct only if defaults across counterparties were genuinely independent, which GARP does not assume.

d.reason: (Scope or condition error). It leaves products with liquidity options at contractual flows and relies on buffers alone. GARP requires the TSECF itself to be adjusted with behavioural models; buffers address the residual risk of stochastic flows, not the expected flows. D would be correct only if the deposits and mortgages carried no embedded options.

questions.source: High quality paper LTR-7 d Q11
questions.question:
A member of the risk committee of an Indian bank is reviewing a memo from the treasury on how to read the TSECCF. The memo makes four statements:

I. The perfect condition is a TSECCF that is positive at all times, meaning that positive cash flows from usual business activity are able to cover negative ones.

II. The temporal distribution of asset and liability maturities can produce periods of negative cumulated cash flows, which may be accepted if they are short and can be managed effectively with the available tools.

III. When the TSECCF shows negative values on an expected basis, the bank may become insolvent and eventually go bankrupt.

IV. Because the TSECCF is cumulative, once it turns negative at one date it must remain negative at all later dates unless the bank raises new funding.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.text: I and IV only
II, III and IV only
I, II and III only
I, II, III and IV

questions.solution:
Indian bank: four statements on the treasury objective and on negative TSECCF values.

**Concept and theory**

GARP assigns the Treasury Department a clear task: monitor the TSECF and the TSECCF. The perfect condition is reached if the TSECCF is positive at all times, which means that positive cash flows are able to cover negative ones, both generated by usual business activity. GARP immediately qualifies this: although this is the ideal, it cannot be verified, for two reasons.

1. Many cash flows are stochastic in amount and/or time, so the TSECF forecasts only the expected value of a distribution, and the TSECCF contains only expected values. A TSECCF positive on average can still have negative outcomes with some probability.
2. The temporal distribution of the maturities of assets and liabilities could produce periods of negative cumulated cash flows. These periods may be accepted if they are short and can be managed effectively with the tools introduced next (the liquidity generation capacity).

GARP then states what a negative value means: when the TSECCF shows negative values on an expected basis, the bank may become insolvent and eventually go bankrupt; this is why the treasurer’s main task is to ensure that the future TSECCF is always positive, and why tools are needed for the case in which it is not.

Note what the cumulative nature does and does not imply. A negative TSECCF is a running total; later net inflows add to it and can bring it back above zero without any action by the bank. In GARP’s Example 7.4.1 the TSECCF is −3.20 in year 7 and −1.51 in year 8, and turns positive to 0.18 in year 9 purely through interest received, then to 31.87 in year 10 when assets mature.

**Applying it to this question**

Statement I is GARP’s definition of the perfect condition. Statement II is GARP’s second reason, including the acceptance condition (short and manageable). Statement III is GARP’s reading of negative expected values. Statement IV claims that a negative TSECCF stays negative until new funding is raised; GARP’s own example contradicts it, since contractual inflows restore the profile. Hence I, II and III are correct.

**Fragile fact.** A negative TSECCF can reverse through later contractual inflows; negative windows are tolerable only if short and manageable; on an expected basis they signal possible insolvency.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Interpret the term structure of expected cash flows and cumulative cash flows.

**GARP:** Chapter 7, Section 7.4.1, closing paragraphs (Treasury task, the two reasons, negative values and insolvency) and Table 7.3. **GARP vs Schweser:** none of substance; Schweser compresses the same points (“a precursor to insolvency and bankruptcy”).

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-7 d, where it is Q11 of 12.

a.reason: (Absolute claim). It accepts IV, which claims a negative cumulated position must persist at all later dates. Contractual inflows from ordinary business add to the running total and can restore it, as in GARP’s years 8 to 9. A would also wrongly omit II and III. IV would be true only if all later net flows were zero or negative.

b.reason: (Absolute claim). It accepts IV and drops I, the definition of the perfect condition. B would be correct only if the treasury objective were something other than a TSECCF positive at all times and if negative cumulated positions could never reverse on their own.

c.reason: C is correct because statements I to III paraphrase GARP’s treasury objective, its acceptance of short and manageable negative windows, and its insolvency warning, while IV is refuted by the reading’s example.

d.reason: (Absolute claim). It accepts all four, including IV. D would be correct only if IV were reworded to say that a negative TSECCF persists until later net inflows from ordinary business or the bank’s liquidity tools cover it.

questions.source: High quality paper LTR-7 d Q12
questions.question: The CFO of a euro area bank shows the board a base-case TSECCF that is positive at every date over the next 10 years, with a minimum of EUR 1.2 billion at month 18. The TSECF behind it includes existing contracts, behavioural adjustments, new business and planned rollovers. A board member proposes that the bank stop holding liquidity buffers against these flows. Which of the following responses is most accurate?

options.text: Agree, because a TSECCF that is positive at every date shows that positive cash flows cover negative ones, so the treasurer’s objective is met and buffers are redundant.
Agree for the first year only, because flows beyond one year are structural and cannot create a cash shortfall that a buffer would need to cover.
Disagree, because the TSECCF omits new business and rollover flows, and adding them could turn the cumulated profile negative at some dates.
Disagree, because the TSECCF holds only expected values: with stochastic flows, cumulated flows can still turn negative with some probability, which calls for buffers.

questions.solution:
Euro area bank: whether a positive base-case TSECCF makes liquidity buffers unnecessary.

**Concept and theory**

Every entry in the TSECF is an expectation: c $\text{f}^{+}_{\text{e}}(\text{t}_{0}$, $\text{t}_{\text{i}}) = \text{E}[\cdot]$ and c $\text{f}^{-}_{\text{e}}(\text{t}_{0}$, $\text{t}_{\text{i}}) = \text{E}[\cdot]$. The reason is the taxonomy of Section 7.1: most cash flows are stochastic in amount, in time or both (index-linked coupons, defaults, behavioural flows such as deposit withdrawals and prepayments, new business and rollovers). The TSECCF, built by cumulating these expectations, therefore contains only expected values too.

GARP draws the consequence directly. The ideal of a TSECCF positive at all times cannot be verified, first because the TSECF forecasts just the expected value of a distribution of flows; if the TSECCF is positive on average, the distribution of cumulated cash flows at a given time can still envisage negative outcomes with an assigned probability. Second, in describing what the TSECF must include for a real balance sheet, GARP notes that the risks related to the stochastic nature of these flows have to be properly measured as well, resulting in a need to set up proper liquidity buffers.

So a positive base-case profile answers the question “is the bank liquid on average?”, not “is the bank liquid in adverse outcomes?”. The second question is addressed by measuring the dispersion of flows (developed as cash flow at risk and liquidity at risk under LO 72.c) and by holding buffers. A helpful analogy: a household whose expected monthly income exceeds expected spending still keeps an emergency fund, because income and spending are uncertain.

**Applying it to this question**

The CFO’s TSECCF is positive at every date and already includes behavioural adjustments, new business and planned rollovers, so the inputs are complete. The board member infers from a positive expected profile that no buffer is needed. That inference ignores that the profile is an expectation over stochastic flows. Since cumulated flows at a date can still be negative with some probability, the risk of those flows must be measured and covered with buffers. The minimum of EUR 1.2 billion is informative about the expected cushion, not about adverse outcomes.

**Fragile fact.** Positive on expectation is not positive in every outcome; the stochastic nature of the flows is what creates the need for liquidity buffers.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Interpret the term structure of expected cash flows and cumulative cash flows.

**GARP:** Chapter 7, Section 7.4.1, the list of TSECF contents (final bullet on measuring risks and liquidity buffers) and the first of the two reasons the ideal cannot be verified. **GARP vs** **Schweser:** Schweser states that the TSECCF captures only expected values but does not mention liquidity buffers under this LO. GARP used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-7 d, where it is Q12 of 12.

a.reason: (Absolute claim). It treats a positive expected TSECCF as proof that positive flows will cover negative ones in every outcome. GARP says this ideal cannot be verified because the profile is an expectation. A would be correct only if every flow were deterministic in time and amount, as in the stylised version of Example 7.4.1.

b.reason: (Scope or condition error). It restricts the risk to the first year and claims structural flows cannot create shortfalls. The short-term versus structural split is a labelling convention for horizons, not a statement that flows beyond one year are risk free; GARP’s own example has its negative window in years 7 and 8. B would be correct only if all flows beyond one year were deterministic.

c.reason: (Sibling swap). It attributes to the TSECCF the omission of new business and rollovers, which GARP explicitly includes (and the stem confirms). The flows that are excluded are those of the sources of liquidity. C would be correct only if the profile had been built from existing contracts alone.

d.reason: D is correct because it states GARP’s point that the TSECCF contains only expected values, that the distribution of cumulated flows can include negative outcomes, and that measuring the risk of stochastic flows results in a need for liquidity buffers.

questions.source: High quality paper LTR-7 e Q1
questions.question:
A risk consultant is presenting to newly hired analysts in the treasury of a Dutch savings bank on the term structure of available assets (TSAA). Her draft slide contains the following statements:

I. For each date from the reference time to a terminal date, the TSAA of an asset records the quantity of that asset in the possession of the bank, regardless of who owns it.

II. Because the TSAA records the quantity available on each date, the full notional shown in the TSAA can be converted into liquidity on that date, so no price or haircut model is needed.

III. For a stock held by the bank, the only contract cash flows entering the TSECF and the TSECCF are the initial purchase outflow and the periodic dividends received, and the stock can still be the underlying of repo, sell/buyback or lending transactions.

IV. When a bond held by the bank reaches its expiry, the TSAA is unaffected because the face value reimbursed by the issuer is recorded in the TSCLGC.

Which of the statements should remain on the slide?

options.text: I only
I and II only
I and III only
I, III and IV only

questions.solution:
Slide for new analysts: which statements about the term structure of available assets (TSAA) are correct.

**Concept and theory**

GARP introduces the TSAA in Section 7.4.3 as a monitoring tool for the part of liquidity generation capacity (LGC) that is hardest to track: unencumbered assets, mostly bonds available for sale. The problem it solves is bookkeeping. A bank can extract balance sheet liquidity (BSL) from an asset either by selling it or by repoing it (or pledging it in a collateralised loan), and the same bond cannot be used twice. Once a bond has been sold, repoed or lent, it cannot be counted again as a source of liquidity for the same period. The TSAA keeps that inventory, date by date.

Formally, for an asset $\text{A}^{1}$ the TSAA is the collection, from the reference time $\text{t}_{0}$ to a terminal date $\text{t}_{\text{b}}$, of the quantity of the asset in the bank’s possession:

$\text{TSAA}^{1}(\text{t}_{0}$, $\text{t}_{\text{b}}) = \{\text{A}^{1}(\text{t}_{0})$, $\text{A}^{1}(\text{t}_{1})$, . . . , $\text{A}^{1}(\text{t}_{\text{b}})\}$, TSAA$(\text{t}_{0}$, $\text{t}_{\text{b}}) = \sum_{\text{m}=1}^{\text{M}} \text{TSAA}^{\text{m}}(\text{t}_{0}$, $\text{t}_{\text{b}})$,

where $\text{A}^{1}(\text{t}_{\text{i}})$ is the quantity of asset 1 in the bank’s possession at $\text{t}_{\text{i}}$ and the second expression aggregates over a set of M securities. The key word is possession: what matters for availability is possession of the asset rather than its ownership, because only an asset the bank physically holds can be sold or delivered as collateral.

Three further points from GARP complete the picture:

- The TSAA only shows how many securities are available for inclusion in LGC. It does not imply that the notional can be fully converted into liquidity: depending on whether the bank sells or repos, the price and/or the haircut determine the actual liquidity, so models are needed to forecast expected (or stressed) prices and haircuts.
- A purchase raises the TSAA by the quantity bought; at expiry the TSAA records a reduction to zero, since the asset no longer exists. Coupons and the face value received at expiry are contract cash flows, entered in the TSECF and the TSECCF.
- Non-maturing assets such as stocks generate only two kinds of contract cash flow in the TSECF and the TSECCF: the initial purchase outflow and the periodic dividends. They can still be the underlying of repos, buy/sellbacks, sell/buybacks and security lending or borrowing, with the same analysis as for bonds.

**Applying it to this question**

Test each statement against those points. Statement I is the GARP definition almost word for word: the quantity in possession, regardless of ownership. Statement II turns “available” into “convertible”: GARP explicitly warns that availability does not imply full conversion and that price and haircut models are needed, so II is false. Statement III repeats GARP’s treatment of stocks and its remark that non-maturing assets can underlie repo-type contracts, so it is true.

Statement IV misplaces the expiry: the TSAA drops to zero at expiry, and the face value is a contract inflow in the TSECF, not an LGC entry. Only I and III survive.

**Fragile fact.** Possession, not ownership, drives the TSAA, and the TSAA counts quantity available, not cash obtainable: price and haircut still sit between the two.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Discuss the impact of available asset transactions on cash flows and liquidity generation capacity. **GARP:** Chapter 7, Section 7.4.3 “The Term Structure of Available Assets”, equations (7.8) and (7.9) and the paragraph on non-maturing assets. **GARP** **vs Schweser:** none on these points; Schweser omits the warning that availability does not mean full conversion (GARP used).

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-7 e, where it is Q1 of 13.

a.reason: (Scope error). Keeping only I discards III, a correct statement of how non-maturing assets enter the TSECF and the TSAA analysis. A would be correct only if the slide’s statement on stocks had claimed that stocks cannot be repoed or lent.

b.reason: (Absolute claim). Statement II promises that every unit in the TSAA converts fully into liquidity. GARP says the TSAA “does not imply” this, because the sale price or the repo haircut cuts the cash actually raised. II would be true only in a world with no haircuts and sale at par, which GARP does not assume.

c.reason: C is correct. GARP defines the TSAA as the quantity of the asset in the bank’s possession on each date “regardless of its ownership” (I), and states that for stocks the contract cash flows in the TSECF and the TSECCF are just the purchase outflow and the dividends, with such assets still usable in repo, sell/buyback and lending transactions (III).

d.reason: (Sibling swap). Statement IV gives the reimbursement of face value to the TSCLGC (an LGC measure) and leaves the TSAA unchanged. In GARP the face value is a contract cash flow in the TSECF/TSECCF, and the TSAA falls to zero at expiry. IV would describe a sale before maturity (TSCLGC inflow), not an expiry, and even then the TSAA falls.

A junior risk analyst at a Japanese trust bank is mapping the bank’s securities financing book onto its liquidity reports. The book contains the following live contracts, each written on a bond:

I. A reverse repo in which the bank paid cash and received the bond.

II. A buy/sellback in which the bank paid cash and received the bond.

III. A security borrowing in which the bank received the bond and paid no cash.

IV. A repo in which the bank received cash and delivered the bond.

V. A security lending in which the bank delivered the bond and received no cash.

Which of the contracts increase the bank’s TSAA while leaving ownership of the bond with the counterparty?

options.text: I and III only
I, II and III only
II and III only
I and IV only

questions.solution:
Securities financing book: which contracts raise the TSAA while ownership stays with the counterparty.

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s Table 7.4 classifies every contract written on an asset by two legal attributes, who owns the asset during the contract and who possesses it, and then reads off the effect on each term structure. The logic is simple. Ownership decides who is entitled to the payments the asset makes (coupons, dividends), so it drives the TSECF/TSECCF. Possession decides who can sell or pledge the asset, so it drives the TSAA.

| Contract | Owner during contract | Possessor | TSAA |
|---|---|---|---|
| Buy | Bank | Bank | Up |
| Sell | Counterparty | Counterparty | Down |
| Repo | Bank | Counterparty | Down |
| Reverse repo | Counterparty | Bank | Up |
| Sell/buyback | Counterparty | Counterparty | Down |
| Buy/sellback | Bank | Bank | Up |
| Security lending | Bank | Counterparty | Down |
| Security borrowing | Counterparty | Bank | Up |

Three pairs mirror each other. In a repo the bank keeps ownership but hands over possession; the reverse repo is the opposite. In a sell/buyback both ownership and possession leave the bank; in a buy/sellback both arrive. Security lending moves only possession (no cash at the start); security borrowing brings in only possession. The TSAA therefore rises in exactly the three “mirror” contracts in which the bank receives possession: reverse repo, buy/sellback and security borrowing. Within those three, the buy/sellback is the odd one out because the bank also becomes the legal owner for the life of the contract.

**Applying it to this question**

The question has two filters: (1) TSAA increases, and (2) ownership stays with the counterparty. Filter 1 keeps I (reverse repo), II (buy/sellback) and III (security borrowing) and removes IV (repo) and V (security lending), both of which cut the TSAA. Filter 2 then removes II, because in a buy/sellback ownership passes to the bank at the start together with possession. What remains is I and III.

**Fragile fact.** The TSAA follows possession: up for reverse repo, buy/sellback and borrowing; but only the buy/sellback also transfers ownership to the bank.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Discuss the impact of available asset transactions on cash flows and liquidity generation capacity. **GARP:** Chapter 7, Section 7.4.3, bullet list of contract types and Table 7.4 “Types of Contracts Involving Assets and Effects on the TSECF/TSECCF, TSAA and TSLGC”. **GARP vs Schweser:** none; Schweser lists the same increases and decreases in the TSAA.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-7 e, where it is Q2 of 13.

a.reason: A is correct. GARP: in a reverse repo the asset “is owned by the counterparty, but it is now in the possession of the bank”, and the TSAA rises by the notional; in a security borrowing “possession passes to the bank” while payments on the asset belong to the counterparty (its owner), and the TSAA rises by the notional.

b.reason: (Scope error). Adding II drops the second condition in the stem. A buy/sellback does raise the TSAA, but GARP stresses that ownership passes to the bank together with possession, which is exactly why its coupons enter the bank’s TSECF. B would be correct if the question asked only which contracts increase the TSAA.

c.reason: (Sibling swap). C swaps the reverse repo for its sibling, the buy/sellback. It keeps III correctly but includes II, where the bank is owner, and omits I, the textbook case of possession without ownership. C would answer a different question: which TSAA-raising contracts are not reverse repos.

d.reason: (Polarity flip). IV is a repo, in which possession moves away from the bank, so the TSAA falls by the notional. Treating it as an increase reverses the direction. D would answer a different question: which of the listed contracts are repo agreements (one in each direction).

questions.question:
A treasury analyst at an Australian regional bank is assessing a planned purchase of a 2-year fixed-coupon bond. The purchase settles on a coupon date, so the dirty price equals the clean price.

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Face value bought | AUD 30 million |
| Purchase price (per 100 of face) | 98.40 |
| Coupon rate (paid semiannually) | 6.0% p.a. |
| Repo haircut the bank’s dealers apply to this bond | 12% |

Ignoring default risk, which of the following correctly describes the cumulative effect of the purchase on the TSECCF and the level of the TSAA for this bond, both measured 13 months after settlement?

options.text: TSECCF: minus AUD 28.62 million; TSAA: AUD 30.00 million
TSECCF: minus AUD 28.20 million; TSAA: AUD 30.00 million
TSECCF: minus AUD 27.72 million; TSAA: AUD 29.52 million
TSECCF: minus AUD 27.72 million; TSAA: AUD 30.00 million

questions.solution:
Purchase of AUD 30 million face of a 6% semiannual bond at 98.40: TSECCF and TSAA after 13 months.

**Concept and theory**

GARP starts Section 7.4.3 with the simplest asset transaction, an outright purchase, because every other contract is analysed as a modification of it. When a bond is bought, three things happen to the term structures:

- **TSECF/TSECCF.** An outflow equal to the notional times the (dirty) price is recorded on the settlement date. Each coupon is then an inflow on its payment date, and at expiry the face value is reimbursed. All of these are contract-related cash flows, so they belong in the TSECF and, cumulated, in the TSECCF, after allowing for the probability that the issuer defaults.
- **TSAA.** The quantity available rises by the amount bought (the notional, not its market value) and stays there until expiry, when it is reset to zero.
- **TSLGC.** A purchase does not itself generate liquidity, so the TSLGC is not affected; Table 7.4 marks it “No/Possible” because the bond could later be sold or repoed.

In GARP’s Example 7.4.2 the bank buys 1,000,000 notional on a coupon date, so the dirty and clean prices coincide; the TSECCF starts negative and climbs by each coupon until the final coupon plus reimbursement turns it positive.

The cumulative cash flow at a horizon t is

TSECCF$(\text{t}) = -\text{F} \cdot\text{P}_{\text{dirty}} + \sum_{\text{t}_{\text{k}} \le\text{t}}$ F $\cdot\frac{\text{c}}{2}$ ,

where F is face value, $\text{P}_{\text{dirty}}$ the price per unit of face, c the annual coupon rate and $\text{t}_{\text{k}}$ the coupon dates up to t.

**Applying it to this question**

Working, one step per line:

Purchase outflow = −30 × 0.9840 = −AUD 29.52 million

Coupon per period = 30 × 0.060/2 = AUD 0.90 million

Coupons paid by month 13 = 2 (months 6 and 12) ⇒ 2 × 0.90 = 1.80

TSECCF at month 13 = −29.52 + 1.80 = −AUD 27.72 million

TSAA at month 13 $= \text{face held} =$ AUD 30.00 million

The bond does not mature until month 24, so the TSAA has not yet dropped to zero. The 12% repo haircut is irrelevant: no repo is executed, and in any case haircuts affect the cash a repo would raise, not the quantity recorded in the TSAA.

**Fragile fact.** Cash flows use the price (outflow F × P), but the TSAA uses the notional quantity; the haircut appears in neither for an outright purchase.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Discuss the impact of available asset transactions on cash flows and liquidity generation capacity. **GARP:** Chapter 7, Section 7.4.3, opening paragraphs on purchases and Example 7.4.2 (Table 7.5, “Purchase of a Bond: Effects on Term Structures”). **GARP vs Schweser:** none.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-7 e, where it is Q3 of 13.

a.reason: (Dropped term (intermediate result)). −29.52 + 0.90 = −28.62 counts only the month 6 coupon and drops the month 12 coupon, which falls inside the 13-month horizon. A would be correct at a horizon between 6 and 12 months.

b.reason: (Wrong input twin). −30.00 + 1.80 = −28.20 uses the face value instead of the price paid for the outflow. B would be correct only if the bond had been bought at par (price 100.00).

c.reason: (Wrong input twin). The TSECCF is right, but the TSAA is shown as 30 × 0.984 = 29.52, i.e., market value instead of quantity. GARP’s TSAA records the quantity (notional) in possession. C would be right only if the TSAA were defined in market value terms, which it is not.

d.reason: D is correct. Consistent with GARP Example 7.4.2 and Table 7.5, the purchase enters the TSECF at notional times price, the coupons received are added cumulatively, and the TSAA rises by the quantity bought until expiry.

questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a UK building society is recording a sale in the liquidity reports. The society holds GBP 4,000,000 notional of a bond that pays a 5.4% coupon once a year. It bought the bond 4 months after the last coupon date and now, 5 months after the purchase, sells GBP 1,500,000 notional to generate liquidity.

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Purchase clean price (per 100) | 99.10 |
| Sale clean price (per 100) | 99.60 |
| Repo haircut on the bond | 10% |

What inflow is recorded in the TSCLGC on the sale date?
questions.solution:
Sale of GBP 1.5 million notional of a 5.4% annual-coupon bond 9 months after its last coupon: TSCLGC inflow.

**Concept and theory**

Selling an asset is the purest form of balance sheet shrinkage: the bank gives up the asset (and its future cash flows) in exchange for cash now. GARP treats a sale dealt to generate liquidity as an LGC event, not as an ordinary contract flow. In Example 7.4.2 the bank sells 500,000 notional of the bond after 9 months and “the TSCLGC records an inflow equal to the amount times the price, including the accrued interests”:

TSCLGC inflow $= \text{N}_{\text{sold}} \times(\text{P}_{\text{clean}} + \text{c} \cdot\tau)$ ,

where $\text{N}_{\text{sold}}$ is the notional sold, $\text{P}_{\text{clean}}$ the clean price per unit, c the annual coupon rate and $\tau$ the time in years since the last coupon date (so c$\tau$ is the accrued interest per unit).

The other term structures move as follows. The TSECF and TSECCF are modified to show the reduced coupons and the smaller principal reimbursement on the scheduled dates (the bank no longer owns the part sold). The TSAA records a cut equal to the notional sold, from the sale date until expiry, when the remaining position drops to zero. A sale is never subject to a haircut: the haircut is the lender’s protection in a repo or collateralised loan, where the bank must buy the asset back.

**Applying it to this question**

Working, one step per line:

$\tau=$ 4 + 5 = 9 months since the last coupon = 0.75 years

Accrued interest per unit = 0.054 × 0.75 = 0.0405

Dirty price per unit = 0.9960 + 0.0405 = 1.0365

TSCLGC inflow = 1,500,000 × 1.0365 = GBP 1,554,750

Two inputs are irrelevant: the purchase clean price (99.10) has already been recorded in the TSECF at purchase and does not affect sale proceeds, and the 10% repo haircut applies only to repo-type financing, not to an outright sale. The GBP 1,554,750 is the liquidity the sale generates on that date.

**Fragile fact.** Sale proceeds into the TSCLGC are notional times (clean price plus accrued interest since the last coupon), with no haircut.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Discuss the impact of available asset transactions on cash flows and liquidity generation capacity. **GARP:** Chapter 7, Section 7.4.3, Example 7.4.2 (sale of 500,000 after 0.75 years; Table 7.6 “Selling of a Bond: Effects on Term Structures”). **GARP vs** **Schweser:** none. Caution: in the extracted Table 7.6 the TSCLGC shows 512,000, then 512,250 and 512,500 at later dates; these later figures are not explained in the text and are not used here.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-7 e, where it is Q4 of 13.

a.reason: (Dropped term). 1,500,000 × 0.9960 = 1,494,000 omits accrued interest and uses the clean price. A would be correct only if the sale settled on a coupon date (accrued interest zero).

b.reason: B is correct. It follows GARP’s rule that the sale inflow equals the amount times the price including accrued interest, with accrual measured from the last coupon date (here 9 months), not from the purchase date.

c.reason: (Time-conversion slip). 1,500,000 × (0.9960 + 0.054 × 5/12) = 1,527,750 accrues interest only over the 5 months since purchase. Accrued interest runs from the last coupon date, regardless of when the seller bought. C would be correct if the bank had bought on the coupon date.

d.reason: (Sibling swap). 1,554,750 × 0.90 = 1,399,275 applies the repo haircut to an outright sale. A haircut belongs to a repo, where the counterparty lends less than the market value. D would be the cash raised if the bank had repoed (not sold) the same notional at a 10% haircut.

questions.source: High quality paper LTR-7 e Q5
questions.question:
A treasurer at a Singapore bank repos a bond it owns to cover a negative entry in its TSECCF. The repo starts 2 months after the bond’s last coupon date and runs for 3 months.

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Notional repoed | SGD 25 million |
| Clean price (per 100) | 101.20 |
| Coupon rate (paid semiannually) | 4.8% p.a. |
| Haircut | 6% |
| Repo rate | 3.5% p.a. |

Which of the following best describes the effect at the start of the repo?

options.text: TSCLGC rises by SGD 23.78 million; TSAA falls by SGD 25.00 million
TSCLGC rises by SGD 25.50 million; TSAA falls by SGD 25.00 million
TSCLGC rises by SGD 23.97 million; TSAA falls by SGD 25.00 million
TSCLGC rises by SGD 23.97 million; TSAA falls by SGD 23.97 million

questions.solution:
Repo of SGD 25 million notional at 101.20 clean, 2 months of accrued coupon, 6% haircut: TSCLGC and TSAA at the start.

**Concept and theory**

A repo lets the bank extract balance sheet liquidity from a bond without selling it. At the start of the agreement the bank receives cash equal to the price of the asset reduced by the haircut and delivers the asset to the counterparty; at the end it pays the cash back with repo interest and gets the asset back. GARP describes the repo as a collateralised loan to the bank: because the lender holds the bond, liquidity is easier and cheaper to obtain than unsecured funding.

The haircut is the cut in the bond’s market value that tells the bank how much the counterparty is willing to lend against it; GARP links its size to the price volatility of the collateral and the default probability of the issuer. Since the bond changes hands mid-coupon, the price used is the dirty price, so the start cash is

$\text{Cash}_{0} = \text{N} \times(\text{P}_{\text{clean}} + \text{c} \cdot\tau) \times($1 $- \text{h})$,

with N the notional repoed, c the annual coupon rate, $\tau$ the years since the last coupon and h the haircut. In GARP’s Example 7.4.2: 500,000 × (99.85% + 10% × 0.25) × (1 − 15%) = 434,988.

Effects on the term structures. The cash received at the start (and the repayment at the end) is entered in the TSLGC, so the TSCLGC rises at inception and falls back to zero when the repo ends. The TSAA falls by the notional of the repo for the life of the contract, because possession passes to the counterparty and the bond becomes encumbered. Coupons stay with the bank, which still owns the bond, so the TSECF is not affected by them.

**Applying it to this question**

Working, one step per line:

Accrued interest per unit = 0.048 × 2/12 = 0.0080

Dirty price per unit = 1.0120 + 0.0080 = 1.0200

Market value delivered = 25 × 1.0200 = SGD 25.50 million

Cash received = 25.50 × (1 − 0.06) = SGD 23.97 million

TSAA change $= -\text{notional} = -$SGD 25.00 million

The repo rate (3.5%) and the 3-month term matter only for the repayment at the end, 23.97 × (1 + 0.035 × 0.25) = 24.18 million; they are irrelevant at inception.

**Fragile fact.** Cash in the TSCLGC is net of the haircut and includes accrued interest; the TSAA falls by the full notional, not by the cash.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Discuss the impact of available asset transactions on cash flows and liquidity generation capacity. **GARP:** Chapter 7, Section 7.4.2 (haircut) and Section 7.4.3 (repo bullet; Example 7.4.2, Table 7.7 “Repo and Reverse Repo of a Bond: Effects on Term Structures”). **GARP vs Schweser:** none. Caution: the extracted Table 7.7 shows 424,469 in the TSCLGC while the text computes 434,988; the formula in the text is used here.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-7 e, where it is Q5 of 13.

a.reason: (Dropped term). 25 × 1.012 × 0.94 = 23.78 uses the clean price and omits the 2 months of accrued coupon. GARP’s example explicitly adds accrued interest. A would be correct if the repo started on a coupon date.

b.reason: (Dropped term). 25 × 1.02 = 25.50 omits the haircut, treating the repo as if it were a sale. B would be the TSCLGC inflow from an outright sale of the same notional, or from a repo with a zero haircut.

c.reason: C is correct. GARP: the bank “receives cash for an amount equal to the price of the asset reduced by the haircut”, this cash is entered in the TSLGC, and the TSAA “is reduced by an amount equal to the notional of the repo agreement”.

d.reason: (Wrong input twin). The cash amount is right, but the TSAA is cut by the cash received instead of the notional. The TSAA counts quantity in possession, and the whole SGD 25 million notional has been delivered. D would be correct only if the TSAA were measured in cash raised.

questions.question: The CRO of a Canadian bank is reviewing a liquidity report on a 3-month repo the bank has executed on CAD 40 million notional of a government bond that it owns. A coupon on the bond falls due halfway through the repo. Which of the following statements in the report is most accurate?

options.text: The coupon stays in the bank’s TSECF because the bank still owns the bond; the TSAA falls by CAD 40 million, and the cash received at the start enters the TSCLGC.
The coupon is removed from the bank’s TSECF because the counterparty has possession of the bond; the TSAA falls by CAD 40 million, and the cash received enters the TSCLGC.
The coupon stays in the bank’s TSECF because the bank still owns the bond; the TSAA is unchanged for the same reason, and only the TSCLGC rises.
The coupon stays in the bank’s TSECF because the bank still owns the bond; the TSAA falls by CAD 40 million, and the cash received enters the TSECF as a contract flow.

questions.solution:
CAD 40 million repo on an owned government bond with a coupon during the contract: effects on TSECF, TSAA and TSCLGC.

**Concept and theory**

The repo is the transaction that most clearly shows why GARP separates ownership from possession. In a repo:

- **Ownership stays with the bank.** The bank sold the bond only temporarily under a repurchase agreement, so it remains the owner. Payments made by the asset during the repo belong to the bank, and GARP says the TSECF and the TSECCF “are not affected in any way” by them. Table 7.4 marks the repo “No” under TSECF/TSECCF.
- **Possession passes to the counterparty.** The bond becomes encumbered: the bank can neither sell it nor use it as collateral until it is returned. The TSAA is therefore reduced by the notional of the repo until the end of the agreement.
- **The cash is LGC.** The cash received at the start and the cash paid at the end are both entered in the TSLGC, because the repo is dealt precisely to generate balance sheet liquidity. The TSCLGC rises at the start and goes back to zero at the end.
- **Balance sheet.** The repo produces a liability, since it can be seen as a collateralised debt of the bank.

In GARP’s Example 7.4.2, the 0.5-year coupon of 50,000 on the full 1,000,000 notional is still recorded in the TSECF while 500,000 is out on repo, which confirms that the coupon follows ownership. (GARP’s worked example also enters the repo interest, the difference between repayment and initial cash, as a contract flow in the TSECF at the end; that detail is not needed here.)

**Applying it to this question**

The report must get three things right: where the coupon goes (TSECF stays intact, bank is owner), what happens to availability (TSAA down by CAD 40 million, possession has passed) and where the initial cash goes (TSCLGC). Option A is the only one that gets all three right. Each wrong option corrupts exactly one of the three.

**Fragile fact.** Repo: owner = bank (coupons stay in the TSECF), possessor = counterparty (TSAA down), cash = TSCLGC.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Discuss the impact of available asset transactions on cash flows and liquidity generation capacity. **GARP:** Chapter 7, Section 7.4.3, repo bullet, Table 7.4 and Example 7.4.2 (Table 7.7). **GARP vs Schweser:** none in substance. Schweser’s summary says all transactions except repos affect the TSECF; GARP’s worked example nonetheless books the repo interest in the TSECF at expiry, so this question does not test the interest leg.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-7 e, where it is Q6 of 13.

a.reason: A is correct. It matches GARP’s repo bullet: payments by the asset “belong to the bank since it is the owner”, the TSAA is reduced by the notional, and the cash received at the start is entered in the TSLGC.

b.reason: (Sibling swap). Removing the coupon from the TSECF is the treatment GARP gives the sell/buyback, where ownership passes to the counterparty. In a repo only possession passes. B would be correct for a traditional sell/buyback of the same bond.

c.reason: (Scope error). C lets ownership drive the TSAA as well as the coupons. GARP is explicit that availability depends on possession rather than ownership, so the TSAA falls even though the bank still owns the bond. C would be right only if the TSAA tracked owned quantities.

d.reason: (Sibling swap). Booking the start cash in the TSECF as a contract flow is GARP’s treatment of a reverse repo (or buy/sellback), where the bank pays cash. The repo cash is raised to generate liquidity and goes to the TSLGC. D would describe the cash leg of a reverse repo.

questions.source: High quality paper LTR-7 e Q7
questions.question:
A portfolio manager at a Brazilian bank’s treasury enters a 4-month reverse repo, receiving a bond as collateral. The contract starts 3 months after the bond’s last coupon date, so one coupon is paid by the issuer while the contract is live. Under the contract, the coupon is not passed through to the bank.

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Notional of the bond received | BRL 50 million |
| Clean price (per 100) | 97.60 |
| Coupon rate (paid semiannually) | 9.0% p.a. |
| Haircut | 10% |
| Reverse repo rate | 12.0% p.a. |

What cash flow is recorded in the bank’s TSECF when the reverse repo ends?

options.text: An inflow of BRL 1.80 million
An inflow of BRL 48.98 million
An inflow of BRL 51.92 million
An inflow of BRL 46.73 million

questions.solution:
BRL 50 million 4-month reverse repo at 97.60 clean, 3 months accrued, 10% haircut, 12% rate: TSECF entry at expiry.

**Concept and theory**

In a reverse repo the bank is the cash lender. At the start it pays cash equal to the price of the asset reduced by the haircut and receives the asset; at the end it gets the cash back with interest and returns the asset. GARP treats the contract as a collateralised loan to the counterparty and records it as an asset in the balance sheet.

The term structure effects follow from who owns and who holds the bond:

- **Ownership stays with the counterparty**, so payments by the asset during the contract (coupons) belong to the counterparty and do not enter the bank’s TSECF or TSECCF.
- **The cash legs are contract flows.** GARP includes the cash paid at the start and the cash received at the end in the TSECF, and hence in the TSECCF.
- **Possession passes to the bank**, so the TSAA rises by the notional; the TSLGC is not affected, although it may be if the bank repoes the bond.

With simple money-market interest, the cash amounts are

$\text{Cash}_{0} = \text{N} (\text{P}_{\text{clean}} + \text{c}\tau) ($1 $- \text{h})$, $\text{Cash}_{\text{T}} = \text{Cash}_{0} ($1 $+ \text{r T})$,

where r is the reverse repo rate and T the contract term in years. GARP’s example: 500,000 × (99.90% + 10% × 0.25) × (1 − 15%) = 435,200 paid, and 435,200 × (1 + 11% × 0.5) = 459,136 received.

**Applying it to this question**

Working, one step per line:

Accrued interest per unit = 0.09 × 0.25 = 0.0225

Dirty price per unit = 0.9760 + 0.0225 = 0.9985

Cash paid at start = 50 × 0.9985 × (1 − 0.10) = BRL 44.9325 million

Interest for 4 months = 44.9325 × 0.12 × 4/12 = BRL 1.7973 million

Cash received at end = 44.9325 × 1.04 = BRL 46.7298 ≈ 46.73 million

The coupon paid during the contract (50 × 4.5% = 2.25 million) belongs to the counterparty, the owner, and the stem confirms it is not passed through, so it is not part of the bank’s TSECF.

**Fragile fact.** Reverse repo: both cash legs go to the TSECF, the end leg is principal plus interest, and the coupon belongs to the counterparty.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Discuss the impact of available asset transactions on cash flows and liquidity generation capacity. **GARP:** Chapter 7, Section 7.4.3, reverse repo bullet and Example 7.4.2 (reverse repo at 1.25 years). **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser says only that the end inflow “reflects interest earned”; GARP records principal plus interest (GARP used). Caution: the extracted Table 7.7 shows −424,681 and 471,396 for the reverse repo legs, inconsistent with the 435,200 and 459,136 computed in GARP’s text; the text’s formula is used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-7 e, where it is Q7 of 13.

a.reason: (Intermediate result). BRL 1.80 million is only the interest earned, an intermediate step. GARP’s example enters the full 459,136 (principal plus interest), not just the interest. A would be correct if the question asked for the net income from the reverse repo. Schweser’s condensed wording (“a cash inflow reflecting interest earned”) invites this error.

b.reason: (Role misassignment). 46.73 + 2.25 = 48.98 credits the coupon to the bank. In a reverse repo the counterparty owns the bond, so its payments belong to the counterparty. B would fit a buy/sellback under the traditional convention, where the bank is the owner and the coupon enters its TSECF.

c.reason: (Dropped term). 50 × 0.9985 × 1.04 = 51.92 omits the haircut, so the bank is assumed to lend the full market value. C would be correct only if the reverse repo were dealt with a zero haircut.

d.reason: D is correct. GARP records the cash paid at the start and the cash received at the end of a reverse repo in the TSECF, and the end amount is the initial cash grown at the repo rate for the contract term.

questions.source: High quality paper LTR-7 e Q8
questions.question: A member of the risk committee of a US bank asks how a 6-month reverse repo on USD 75 million notional of a Treasury note, executed today, affects the bank’s liquidity generation capacity. Which of the following answers is most accurate?

options.text: The TSCLGC rises at inception by the cash the bank pays, since a reverse repo is one of the transactions dealt to generate balance sheet liquidity.
The TSLGC is not changed by the reverse repo itself, but the note received can be repoed until the contract ends, so the TSLGC may be altered up to that date.
The TSLGC cannot be altered at any point during the contract, because the counterparty, not the bank, owns the note received.
The TSLGC rises at inception by USD 75 million, since every change in the TSAA produces an equal change in the TSLGC on the same date.

questions.solution:
Risk committee question: effect of a USD 75 million reverse repo on liquidity generation capacity.

**Concept and theory**

Liquidity generation capacity (LGC) is the bank’s ability to generate positive cash flows, beyond contractual ones, from the sources of liquidity available at a given date. Its term structure, the TSLGC, collects the liquidity that can be generated at each date by asset sales (AS), repo and secured funding (RP) and unsecured funding (USF); the TSCLGC cumulates it. Whether an asset transaction affects the TSLGC depends on why it is dealt.

GARP’s Table 7.4 gives three answers for the TSLGC column:

- **Yes** for sale, repo and sell/buyback: these are dealt to generate BSL, so the cash raised enters the TSCLGC.
- **No/Possible** for buy, reverse repo, buy/sellback and security borrowing: the transaction itself generates no liquidity (often the bank pays cash), but it brings an asset into the bank’s possession that could later be sold or repoed, so the LGC is potentially increased over the contract’s life.
- **No** for security lending: the asset leaves the bank and cannot produce any liquidity until the contract ends.

For the reverse repo specifically, GARP says: “The TSLGC is not affected but the asset can be repoed until the end, so that it can be altered until this date.” The cash the bank pays at the start is a contract flow in the TSECF, not an LGC entry, and the TSAA rises by the notional.

**Applying it to this question**

The member asks about LGC, so the decisive fact is the “No/Possible” entry. The reverse repo does not itself put anything into the TSLGC; what it does is enlarge the TSAA, and that extra availability is potential LGC if the bank repoes the note before the contract ends. Option B says exactly this.

**Fragile fact.** Reverse repo: TSAA up, TSECF hit by the cash paid, TSLGC “No/Possible”, not “Yes”.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Discuss the impact of available asset transactions on cash flows and liquidity generation capacity. **GARP:** Chapter 7, Section 7.4.2 (definition of LGC, TSLGC, TSCLGC) and Section 7.4.3 (reverse repo bullet; Table 7.4). **GARP vs Schweser:** none; Schweser states the TSLGC is not impacted “unless the asset is repoed”.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-7 e, where it is Q8 of 13.

a.reason: (Polarity flip). In a reverse repo the bank pays cash; that outflow is a TSECF contract flow. Treating it as an LGC increase reverses the direction and confuses the reverse repo with the repo, which is the transaction dealt to generate BSL. A would describe a repo.

b.reason: B is correct. It restates GARP’s reverse repo bullet: the TSLGC is not affected, but because the asset can be repoed until the end of the agreement, the TSLGC can be altered up to that date.

c.reason: (Absolute claim). C rules out any effect on the TSLGC at any point because the bank is not the owner. But availability for liquidity depends on possession, and the bank holds the note and may repo it during the contract. C would be closer to correct for security lending, where the asset leaves the bank and cannot produce liquidity until the end.

d.reason: (Absolute claim). D assumes the TSAA and the TSLGC always move together. They do not: the TSAA counts quantity available, while the TSLGC counts liquidity actually generated (and even then net of price and haircut). D would be right only if every unit of available asset were automatically converted into cash at notional.

questions.question: A treasury analyst at a Chinese joint-stock bank compares two 6-month contracts on the same CNY 200 million notional of a bond, during each of which one coupon is paid. Trade X is a reverse repo; trade Y is a buy/sellback. Assume the traditional convention that GARP uses, under which coupons paid during a buy/sellback are not passed back to the original seller. Which of the following statements best describes how the two trades differ?

options.text: Only trade X increases the TSAA, because under trade Y the bank must sell the bond back and so cannot treat it as available.
Trade Y records the cash paid at the start in the TSCLGC, while trade X records the cash paid at the start in the TSECF.
The coupon enters the bank’s TSECF under trade Y but not under trade X, because only under trade Y does ownership pass to the bank.
The coupon enters the bank’s TSECF under trade X but not under trade Y, because under a reverse repo the bank holds the bond.

questions.solution:
Reverse repo versus buy/sellback on CNY 200 million of the same bond, with a coupon during the contract.

**Concept and theory**

A buy/sellback looks economically like a reverse repo: the bank pays cash, receives a bond and commits to return it at a fixed (forward) price. GARP’s point is that the legal form differs, and the term structures follow the legal form.

|  | Reverse repo | Buy/sellback (traditional) |
|---|---|---|
| Ownership | Stays with counterparty | Passes to the bank |
| Possession | Passes to the bank | Passes to the bank |
| Coupons during contract | Belong to counterparty; not in bank’s TSECF | Belong to the bank; in bank’s TSECF |
| Start and end cash | TSECF | TSECF |
| TSAA | Up by notional | Up by notional |
| TSLGC | No/Possible | No/Possible |
| Balance sheet | Asset (collateralised loan) | Asset for the contract period |

In GARP’s Example 7.4.2 the bank buys 400,000 extra bonds through a buy/sellback and the next coupon in its TSECF is 70,000, i.e., 5% on 1,400,000, which shows that it collects the coupon on the bonds it bought temporarily. By contrast, under the reverse repo the bank’s coupon stays at 50,000 on its own 1,000,000.

GARP adds a caveat (footnotes 4 and 5): since an annex was added to the standard GMRA, sell/buybacks and buy/sellbacks are treated much like repos, with payments returned to the seller at the end of the contract, so under recent conventions the TSECF effects would be the same as in the repo case, while the TSAA effects stay the same. The stem therefore fixes the traditional convention.

**Applying it to this question**

Both trades raise the TSAA by CNY 200 million, both put the start and end cash legs into the TSECF, and neither changes the TSLGC at inception. The only difference the stem can expose is the coupon paid during the contract: the bank collects it under Y (owner) but not under X (counterparty is owner). That is option C.

**Fragile fact.** Coupons follow ownership, the TSAA follows possession: the buy/sellback gives the bank both, the reverse repo only possession.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Discuss the impact of available asset transactions on cash flows and liquidity generation capacity. **GARP:** Chapter 7, Section 7.4.3, buy/sellback and reverse repo bullets, footnotes 4 and 5, Example 7.4.2 (Table 7.8 “Buy/sellback and Sell/buyback of a Bond: Effects on Term Structures”). **GARP vs Schweser:** none; Schweser omits the GMRA footnote (GARP-only caveat).

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-7 e, where it is Q9 of 13.

a.reason: (Scope error). The obligation to sell back does not cancel availability: GARP increases the TSAA by the notional of the buy/sellback for the contract period, exactly as for the reverse repo (the bond can be repoed until the end). A would be true only if a forward commitment made an asset unavailable, which GARP does not say.

b.reason: (Sibling swap). Booking the start cash in the TSCLGC is the treatment of the sell/buyback (dealt to raise BSL). In a buy/sellback the bank pays cash, which GARP enters in the TSECF, and the TSCLGC “is not modified”. B would describe a sell/buyback compared with a repo.

c.reason: C is correct. GARP: in a buy/sellback ownership passes to the bank together with possession, so “the payments received for the asset before the sellback belong to the bank” and enter the TSECF; in a reverse repo “the payments by the asset during the repo agreement belong to the counterparty”.

d.reason: (Role misassignment). D gives the coupon to the party with possession. Coupons follow ownership, so under the reverse repo they go to the counterparty. D would be correct only if payments followed possession, which in GARP they never do.

questions.question:
An internal auditor at a French bank is reviewing the treasury’s documentation comparing a repo with a sell/buyback, each on EUR 120 million notional of a bond the bank owns. The documentation states:

I. In both transactions the TSAA of the bond falls by EUR 120 million at the start of the contract.

II. Under a repo, coupons paid during the contract stay in the bank’s TSECF; under a traditional sell/buyback, they belong to the counterparty and are taken out of the bank’s TSECF.

III. The cash received at the start of a sell/buyback is recorded in the TSECF as a contract flow, whereas the cash received at the start of a repo is recorded in the TSCLGC.

IV. Under the annex now incorporated in the standard GMRA, payments on the bond during a sell/buyback are returned to the seller on each payment date, exactly as in a repo.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.text: I only
I and III only
II and IV only
I and II only

questions.solution:
Audit of documentation comparing a repo with a sell/buyback on EUR 120 million of an owned bond.

**Concept and theory**

Repo and sell/buyback are the two ways a bank can temporarily give up a bond it owns to raise cash. Economically they are close substitutes; GARP separates them by the legal transfer involved.

|  | Repo | Sell/buyback (traditional) |
|---|---|---|
| Ownership during contract | Bank | Counterparty (buyer) |
| Possession | Counterparty | Counterparty |
| Coupons during contract | Bank’s; TSECF not affected | Counterparty’s; taken out of bank’s TSECF |
| Cash at start and end | TSLGC (TSCLGC up, then back) | TSLGC, “in the same way as in the repo” |
| TSAA | Down by notional | Down by notional |
| Balance sheet | Liability (collateralised debt) | Commitment for the bank at the end |

GARP’s Example 7.4.2 shows the coupon effect numerically: during a 300,000 sell/buyback the bank’s coupon falls to 35,000, i.e., 5% on the 700,000 it still owns, while the 307,200 received and the 314,726 paid at the buyback are booked in the TSCLGC. During a repo, by contrast, the full 50,000 coupon stays in the TSECF.

The convention caveat (footnote 4): the traditional treatment was generally true until an annex was incorporated in the standard GMRA. Now sell/buybacks are treated very similarly to repos, so that all payments are returned to the seller, “although only at the end of the contract and not on each payment date as in the repo case”. Under that convention the effects on the term structures are similar to those of a repo.

**Applying it to this question**

Statement I: both transactions hand possession to the counterparty, so the TSAA falls by the notional in each case. True. Statement II: this is the core GARP distinction between the two (coupons follow ownership). True. Statement III: wrong placement; both cash legs of a sell/buyback go to the TSLGC, as for a repo, since both are ways to generate BSL. False. Statement IV: under the GMRA annex the payments are returned to the seller only at the end of the contract, not on each payment date. False. Hence I and II only.

**Fragile fact.** In a sell/buyback ownership leaves the bank (coupons out of the TSECF), but the cash still goes to the TSCLGC, just as in a repo.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Discuss the impact of available asset transactions on cash flows and liquidity generation capacity. **GARP:** Chapter 7, Section 7.4.3, repo and sell/buyback bullets, footnote 4, Example 7.4.2 (Table 7.8). **GARP vs Schweser:** none in substance; the GMRA convention is GARP-only (Schweser omits it).

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-7 e, where it is Q10 of 13.

a.reason: (Scope error). Keeping only I rejects II, which is the defining difference between the two contracts in GARP. A would be correct only if II had misattributed the coupons (for example, given repo coupons to the counterparty).

b.reason: (Sibling swap). III treats the sell/buyback cash like the cash of its mirror, the buy/sellback (whose legs are TSECF contract flows). GARP books the sell/buyback cash in the TSCLGC because the trade is a way to extract BSL. B would need III to describe a buy/sellback versus a reverse repo, where the TSECF treatment is correct for both.

c.reason: (Scope or condition error). IV overextends the GMRA annex: payments are returned to the seller at the end of the contract only, not on each payment date as in a repo. C also drops the true statement I. IV would be correct if it said “at the end of the contract”.

d.reason: D is correct. Statements I and II reproduce GARP’s sell/buyback and repo bullets: the TSAA decreases by the notional in both, coupons during a repo belong to the bank (owner) and stay in the TSECF, and in a sell/buyback they belong to the counterparty and are taken from the TSECF.

questions.source: High quality paper LTR-7 e Q11
questions.question: A senior risk analyst at a Japanese regional bank is projecting cash flows for a security lending trade. The bank owns JPY 6.0 billion notional of a bond paying a 1.8% coupon semiannually. Two months after a coupon date, it lends JPY 2.5 billion notional of the bond for 6 months at a lending fee of 0.40% p.a., receiving no cash at the start. One coupon is paid during the contract. What is the total inflow from this bond that enters the bank’s TSECF over the life of the lending contract, including the amount received at its end?

options.text: JPY 59.0 million
JPY 36.5 million
JPY 64.0 million
JPY 54.0 million

questions.solution:
Security lending of JPY 2.5 billion out of a JPY 6.0 billion holding for 6 months at 0.40% p.a.: TSECF inflows over the contract.

**Concept and theory**

Security lending resembles a sell/buyback in that the asset leaves the bank, but two features differ: no cash is paid by the counterparty to the bank (apart from a periodic fee as service remuneration), and only possession passes. GARP’s consequences:

- **TSECF/TSECCF.** Because the bank remains the owner, the payments received on the asset before the end of the contract (coupons) belong to the bank and enter its TSECF. The fee, or interest, paid by the counterparty at expiry when it returns the asset also enters the TSECF. Nothing is recorded at inception.
- **TSAA.** The TSAA decreases by the notional lent, since the bank cannot use the asset as collateral or sell it, and returns to its previous level when the asset comes back.
- **TSLGC.** Not affected, and the asset cannot produce any liquidity until the end of the contract. GARP calls security lending the only contract that does not increase the TSLGC, since it actually decreases the LGC related to BSL.
- **Balance sheet.** Security lending represents an asset of the bank for the contract period.

The fee is computed as simple interest on the notional lent:

Fee $= \text{N}_{\text{lent}} \times\text{f} \times$ T,

with f the annual fee rate and T the term in years. GARP’s example: 500,000 × (3% × 0.5) = 7,500, while the coupon on the full 1,000,000 (50,000) is still recorded during the lending.

**Applying it to this question**

Working, one step per line:

Coupon per period (full holding) = 6.0 bn × 0.018/2 = JPY 54.0 million

Fee at expiry = 2.5 bn × 0.0040 × 0.5 = JPY 5.0 million

Total TSECF inflow over the contract = 54.0 + 5.0 = JPY 59.0 million

The coupon is computed on the full JPY 6.0 billion because the bank still owns the JPY 2.5 billion it has lent. Over the same period the TSAA shows only JPY 3.5 billion available.

**Fragile fact.** Lending: the bank keeps the coupons (still owner) and adds the fee at expiry, while the TSAA is down by the notional lent.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Discuss the impact of available asset transactions on cash flows and liquidity generation capacity. **GARP:** Chapter 7, Section 7.4.3, security lending bullet and Example 7.4.2 (Table 7.9 “Lending and Borrowing of a Bond: Effects on Term Structures”). **GARP vs Schweser:** none; Schweser’s phrase “fee received by the borrower” should read “fee received from the borrower”.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-7 e, where it is Q11 of 13.

a.reason: A is correct. GARP: payments received for the asset before the end of a lending contract “belong to the bank and they enter the TSECF and the TSECCF, as does the interest paid by the counterparty at expiry”.

b.reason: (Sibling swap). 3.5 bn × 0.9% + 5.0 = 31.5 + 5.0 = 36.5 removes the coupon on the lent bonds, which is the sell/buyback treatment (ownership passes). In security lending only possession passes. B would be the total only if ownership of the lent bonds had passed to the counterparty, as in a traditional sell/buyback.

c.reason: (Time-conversion slip). 54.0 + 2.5 bn × 0.40% = 54.0 + 10.0 = 64.0 charges a full year of fee for a 6-month contract. C would be correct for a 12-month lending (if the coupon count were unchanged).

d.reason: (Dropped term). JPY 54.0 million is the coupon alone; it omits the fee received at expiry, which GARP records in the TSECF (7,500 in its example). D would be correct only for a fee-free lending.

questions.question: An internal auditor at a UK bank is reviewing the treasury’s treatment of a 6-month security borrowing of GBP 15 million notional of a gilt, for which the bank pays a fee of 0.5% p.a. at expiry and pays no cash at the start. One coupon on the gilt is paid during the contract. Which of the following statements in the treasury’s memo is NOT correct?

options.text: The TSAA rises by GBP 15 million for the life of the contract, since the bank can use the gilt as collateral provided it returns it at expiry.
The coupon paid on the gilt during the contract enters the bank’s TSECF, since the bank has possession of the gilt.
The only entry in the bank’s TSECF from this contract is the fee of GBP 37,500 paid at expiry.
The borrowing represents a liability of the bank; the TSLGC is not affected, but the gilt can produce liquidity until the contract ends.

questions.solution:
Audit of the treasury memo on a 6-month GBP 15 million security borrowing of a gilt at 0.5% p.a.: which statement is not correct.

**Concept and theory**

Security borrowing is the mirror image of security lending and resembles a buy/sellback in the movement of the asset, but with two differences: the bank pays no cash to the counterparty (apart from a periodic fee) and only possession passes to the bank. GARP’s consequences:

- **TSECF/TSECCF.** Payments received for the asset before the end of the contract belong to the counterparty, which remains the owner. The bank’s TSECF and TSECCF are not affected apart from the interest (fee) paid by the bank at the expiry of the borrowing.
- **TSAA.** The TSAA increases by the notional of the borrowing, since the bank can use the asset as collateral, provided it returns it to the counterparty at expiry.
- **TSLGC.** Not affected, but the asset can produce liquidity until the end of the contract (Table 7.4: “No/Possible”).
- **Balance sheet.** Security borrowing represents a liability of the bank.

In GARP’s Example 7.4.2 the bank borrows 300,000 of the bond for 6 months: the TSAA changes only at the start and end, the TSECF records only the fee of 300,000 × 3% × 0.5 = 4,500, and the coupon paid during the contract remains 50,000, i.e., on the bank’s own 1,000,000 only.

**Applying it to this question**

Check each statement. A: TSAA up by the notional because the bank can use the gilt as collateral, provided it returns it. True. B: the coupon is credited to the party in possession. False, because payments follow ownership and the owner is the counterparty. C: fee = 15,000,000 × 0.005 × 0.5 = GBP 37,500, and it is the only TSECF entry. True. D: liability; TSLGC not affected but the gilt can produce liquidity until the end. True (GARP’s wording). The statement that is NOT correct is B.

**Fragile fact.** Borrowing: possession in (TSAA up), ownership not (coupons to the counterparty); the only TSECF entry is the fee paid at the end.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Discuss the impact of available asset transactions on cash flows and liquidity generation capacity. **GARP:** Chapter 7, Section 7.4.3, security borrowing bullet, Table 7.4 and Example 7.4.2 (Table 7.9). **GARP vs Schweser:** none.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-7 e, where it is Q12 of 13.

a.reason: (Accurate statement (not the exception)). A restates GARP: the TSAA rises by the notional because the bank can use the asset as collateral provided it returns it at expiry. A would be the answer only if it said the TSAA is unchanged because the bank does not own the gilt (an ownership error).

b.reason: B is the required answer because it is false. GARP: in a security borrowing, “the payments received for the asset before the end of the contract belong to the counterparty”, and the TSECF and TSECCF are not affected apart from the interest paid by the bank at expiry.

c.reason: (Accurate statement (not the exception)). The fee is 15,000,000 × 0.5% × 0.5 = 37,500 and is the only TSECF entry. C would be the answer if it used a full year (GBP 75,000) or added the coupon.

d.reason: (Accurate statement (not the exception)). D matches GARP’s statement that security borrowing is a liability of the bank and that the TSLGC is not affected, although the asset can produce liquidity until the contract ends. D would be the answer if it called the borrowing an asset (that is security lending) or said the TSLGC rises at inception.
