questions.question:
A portfolio manager in the treasury investment team of a U.K. bank is preparing the GBP stress test estimate. Treasury policy permits strategic liquidity held in highly liquid assets to be redirected to contingent needs under stress. The secured borrowing collateralized by the pledged gilts is assumed to roll over and is not among the outflows.

| Item | GBP million |
|---|---|
| Liquid asset buffer reported by treasury (contingent liquidity) | 1,050 |
| Cash held to ensure orderly clearing of payments | 140 |
| Gilts pledged as collateral for a wholesale borrowing | 230 |
| Strategic liquidity held in U.K. Treasury bills (for a planned acquisition) | 160 |
| Strategic liquidity held as a stake in an unlisted fintech | 240 |
| Stressed outflows | 1,320 |
| Stressed inflows | 290 |

Which of the following is closest to the bank’s stressed liquid asset buffer?

options.text: GBP 180 million
GBP 20 million
GBP 420 million
GBP 320 million

questions.solution:
U.K. bank: which liquidity pools count toward the stressed buffer.

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s liquidity taxonomy (Section 9.1, Figure 9.1) decides which pools of liquidity may be counted when contingent liquidity is estimated. The test is simple: is the liquidity available to meet general financial obligations under a stress scenario?

| Pool | GARP treatment under the stress test | Counts? |
|---|---|---|
| Contingent (buffer) | Available to meet general obligations under stress | Yes |
| Operational | Must be maintained to ensure operations; unavailable | No |
| Restricted | Unavailable for general obligations; applied only to the outflows it supports | No |
| Strategic, highly liquid part | May be redirected to contingent needs; high quality portion contributes | Yes, if redirected |
| Strategic, illiquid part | Redirection not feasible without highly liquid assets | No |

The strategic row is where precision matters. GARP says strategic liquidity is not primarily aimed at supporting the bank in stress, but it may be redirected to meet contingent liquidity needs, and as a pragmatic matter this is feasible only if the liquidity is held in highly liquid assets. Figure 9.1 accordingly says the high quality asset portion of strategic liquidity contributes to contingent funding. Restricted liquidity is excluded from general obligations; GARP’s rider that it “should be applied to any assumed outflows which they support” matters only when the supported outflow is in the scenario, which the stem rules out here.

**Applying it to this question**

Exclude the operational cash (GBP 140 million), the pledged gilts (GBP 230 million) and the unlisted fintech stake (GBP 240 million); count the buffer and the redirected Treasury bills.

Contingent liquidity available = 1,050 $(\text{buffer}) +$ 160 $(\text{strategic T-bills}) =$ GBP 1,210 m

Stressed LAB = 1,210 − 1,320 + 290 = GBP 180 m

Without the redirected Treasury bills the buffer would leave only GBP 20 million; the strategic portion is material.

**Fragile fact.** Only the highly liquid part of strategic liquidity can be redirected; operational and restricted liquidity never count toward general obligations.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** LO 74.b: “Estimate contingent liquidity via the liquid asset buffer.”

**GARP:** Chapter 9, Section 9.1 “Measuring Contingent Liquidity Requirements” and Figure 9.1 “Liquidity taxonomy”; Section 9.2. **GARP vs Schweser:** none of substance; Schweser says the most liquid strategic funds may be reallocated to contingent obligations if required. **Boundary** **note:** the definitions of the four types belong to LO 74.a; here they are used only as inputs to the buffer estimate.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-9 b, where it is Q10 of 11.

a.reason: A counts the buffer plus the highly liquid portion of strategic liquidity (which treasury policy permits to be redirected, as GARP allows), excludes operational, restricted and illiquid strategic holdings, and applies the formula.

b.reason: (Scope or condition error). Excluding all strategic liquidity: 1,050 − 1,320 + 290 = 20. GARP allows the highly liquid portion of strategic liquidity to be redirected to contingent needs, and the stem confirms policy permits it. B would be correct if treasury policy barred redirection of strategic holdings.

c.reason: (Scope or condition error). Counting all strategic liquidity, including the unlisted fintech stake: 180 + 240 = 420. Redirection is feasible only via highly liquid assets; an unlisted stake fails that condition. C would be correct only if the GBP 240 million were also held in highly liquid assets.

d.reason: (Sibling swap). Counting the operational cash: 180 + 140 = 320. Operational liquidity ensures the orderly clearing of payments and is unavailable to meet obligations under a stress test. D would be correct if the GBP 140 million were surplus cash beyond operational needs and under central treasury control.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Estimate contingent liquidity via the liquid asset buffer.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-9 b Q11
questions.question:
An internal auditor at an Australian bank is reviewing the model documentation for the four components of the liquidity stress testing model. The documentation contains the following statements:

I. The normal liquid asset buffer is the contingent liquidity that is currently in place.

II. Stressed outflows are a mixture of contractual and contingent outflows that can produce a liquidity gap extending from the short term to the long term.

III. Stressed inflows are assumed to fully offset stressed outflows, so the model needs to measure only the larger of the two flows.

IV. The stressed liquid asset buffer is total contingent liquidity reduced by net cash outflows, and it indicates the adequacy of the normal buffer given the scenario assumptions.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.text: I and II only
I, II and IV only
I, III and IV only
II and IV only

questions.solution:
Australian bank internal audit: statements on the four components of the stress testing model.

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s Section 9.2 says that if the objective of the liquidity stress test is to measure required contingent liquidity, the institution must build a cash flow model that accurately and precisely measures four components. Figure 9.2 depicts them as a waterfall:

| Component | GARP description |
|---|---|
| Normal liquid asset buffer | Contingent liquidity currently in place; a well diversified portfolio of actively traded assets with ease and certainty of valuation |
| (Less) stressed cash outflow | Mixture of contractual and contingent outflows assumed under stress, e.g. premature non-contractual settlement and inability to roll over funding, resulting in a short to long-term liquidity gap |
| (Plus) stressed cash inflows | Inflows assumed to partially offset stressed outflows; may be limited by market conditions or a regulatory cap |
| (Yields) stressed liquid asset buffer | Total contingent liquidity reduced by net cash outflows; indicates the adequacy of the normal buffer given the scenario |

Each component must be modeled in its own right. Outflows and inflows are separate projections with different drivers (customer and counterparty behavior on the liability side; repayments, maturities and facility access on the asset side), and the model’s output depends on their difference, not on whichever is larger. The words “partially offset” are deliberate: an institution that assumes inflows cancel outflows has assumed away the stress it is testing. The stressed buffer is then read as a test of adequacy of the buffer currently in place, conditional on the scenario.

**Applying it to this question**

I matches GARP’s description of the normal buffer: correct. II matches Figure 9.2’s description of stressed outflows (mixture of contractual and contingent; short to long-term liquidity gap): correct. III claims a full offset and that only the larger flow needs measuring: incorrect, since GARP says inflows partially offset outflows and both must be modeled. IV matches Figure 9.2’s description of the stressed buffer: correct. Hence I, II and IV only.

**Fragile fact.** Inflows partially offset outflows; the normal buffer is what is in place now, the stressed buffer is what is left after the scenario.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** LO 74.b: “Estimate contingent liquidity via the liquid asset buffer.”

**GARP:** Chapter 9, Section 9.2 “Overview of the Model” and Figure 9.2 “Components of the liquidity stress testing model”. **GARP vs Schweser:** none of substance; Schweser gives the same formula with the label “(normal) liquidity asset buffer”.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-9 b, where it is Q11 of 11.

a.reason: (Scope or condition error). Choosing I and II only rejects statement IV, which is GARP’s own description of the stressed buffer (total contingent liquidity reduced by net cash outflows, indicating adequacy given the scenario). A would be correct if IV had been corrupted, for example to say the stressed buffer measures adequacy under all possible scenarios.

b.reason: B is the only combination that accepts the three statements matching Figure 9.2 and rejects the absolute-claim statement III.

c.reason: (Absolute claim). Choosing I, III and IV accepts III’s claim that inflows fully offset outflows, and rejects the true statement II. GARP says inflows only partially offset outflows. C would be correct only if III said inflows “partially offset” outflows and II were false.

d.reason: (Sibling swap). Choosing II and IV only rejects statement I, perhaps by confusing the normal buffer (contingent liquidity currently in place) with the stressed buffer (the buffer net of flows). Statement I is GARP’s definition. D would be correct only if I had described the normal buffer as the liquidity remaining after the scenario.

questions.question:
A junior risk analyst at a German commercial bank is presenting the bank’s deposit tracker report to newly hired analysts. The report shows month-end actual loan-to-deposit (LTD) ratios of 87.4%, 86.9% and 86.2% for the last three months against a board-approved LTD limit of 85%, with forecasts that fall steadily to 82.8% by year-end. The analyst’s slides contain the following statements:

I. The report is tracked weekly and monthly because it gives an idea of the LTD ratio in the immediate short term.

II. The forecast months are generated mechanically from contractual maturities, so the views of relationship managers play no part in them.

III. The bank is currently outside its limit even though the year-end forecast is within it, because the board limit is a ceiling on the LTD ratio.

IV. Because the tracker reports only customer deposits, the LTD ratio has to be taken from the daily liquidity report rather than from the tracker.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.text: I only
I, II and III only
I and III only
I, III and IV only

questions.solution:
Deposit tracker shown to new analysts: which statements about purpose, limit and forecasts are correct.

**Concept and theory**

The deposit tracker is the simplest of the benchmark liquidity reports in GARP Section 10.1. It records the current size of customer deposits and a forecast of where deposits are expected to go. GARP explains why it is tracked weekly and monthly: it gives an idea of the loan-to-deposit (LTD) ratio in the immediate short term, and the LTD is a key management liquidity ratio,

LTD $= \frac{\text{Total customer loans}}{\text{Total customer deposits}}$ .

A higher LTD means each unit of deposits is supporting more lending, so the board sets a maximum (a ceiling). GARP’s Table 10.1A, for a medium-sized commercial bank, reports:

- month-end actual deposits by customer type;
- the change from each month-end;
- aggregate customer assets (loans) and hence the LTD ratio;
- a forecast of the month-end position for each month to the end of the year.

In GARP’s example the bank must meet a board-approved LTD limit of 85%, “which it is just exceeding” at the report date, while the year-end forecast is within the limit. The forecasts are a matter of judgement: the historical trend helps, but otherwise the bank makes the best estimate it can with inputs from the relationship managers who look after the customer accounts. A second section (Table 10.1B) shows how much liabilities must increase, or assets reduce, to meet a given LTD, and Figure 10.1 presents the same information graphically.

**Applying it to this question**

Statement I paraphrases GARP’s reason for weekly and monthly tracking: true. Statement II says the forecasts are mechanical and ignore relationship managers; GARP says the opposite: false. Statement III: the latest actual LTD (86.2%) is above the 85% ceiling, so the bank is outside its limit now, whatever the forecast says, exactly as in GARP’s example: true. Statement IV is false because the tracker itself reports aggregate customer loans and the LTD ratio. Correct set: I and III.

**Fragile fact.** Direction: the LTD board limit is a ceiling (above 85% is a breach), and the tracker itself computes the LTD from loans over deposits.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Compare and interpret different types of liquidity risk reports.

**GARP:** Chapter 10, Section 10.1, “Deposit Tracker Report” (Table 10.1A, Table 10.1B, Figure 10.1).

**GARP vs Schweser:** none of substance. Schweser says the limit was exceeded “in two of the last three months” in its version of the figure; GARP’s Table 10.1A shows the LTD above 85% in every actual month to May 2009 (86.08% in May).

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-10 b, where it is Q1 of 14.

a.reason: (Polarity flip). Rejecting III treats the limit as satisfied by a favourable forecast or as a floor rather than a ceiling. A would be correct only if the stem said the board limit was a minimum LTD, or that compliance is judged on the year-end forecast.

b.reason: (Sibling swap). Accepting II gives the tracker the contractual, bucket-by-bucket method of the mismatch report. GARP says the tracker’s forecast rests on judgement, the historical trend and relationship managers’ inputs. B would be correct only for a report built purely from contractual maturities.

c.reason: C matches GARP: the tracker exists to show the short-term LTD position (I), and a bank above a board LTD ceiling is in excess today even when the forecast shows a return within it (III).

d.reason: (Scope error). Accepting IV understates the tracker’s content: Table 10.1A carries total customer loans and the LTD row. D would be correct only if the stem described a deposits-only report with no customer assets.

questions.question:
A treasury analyst at a Spanish bank is preparing the section of the deposit tracker that shows the cash flow changes required to meet a target LTD ratio. The board’s target is 85%. Extract (EUR thousands):

| Item | 31 May (actual) | 30 Sep (forecast) |
|---|---|---|
| Of which: retail bank deposits | 1,402,300 | 1,455,900 |
| Total customer deposits | 3,051,200 | 3,184,600 |
| Total customer loans | 2,768,400 | 2,846,300 |

All else being equal, which of the following correctly states, for the 30 September forecast, the increase in customer deposits alone, or alternatively the reduction in customer loans alone, needed to meet the target?

options.text: Increase deposits by EUR 164.0 million, or reduce loans by EUR 139.4 million
Increase deposits by EUR 139.4 million, or reduce loans by EUR 164.0 million
Increase deposits by EUR 205.7 million, or reduce loans by EUR 174.9 million
Increase deposits by EUR 139.4 million, or reduce loans by EUR 139.4 million

questions.solution:
Deposit increase or loan reduction needed to bring a 30 September forecast LTD down to 85%.

**Concept and theory**

The second section of GARP’s deposit tracker (Table 10.1B) turns the LTD ratio into an action plan. For each target LTD (85%, 84%, . . . , 80%) and each month it shows how much liabilities would need to increase, or alternatively how much assets would need to reduce, all else being equal, for the bank to meet that target. With L = total customer loans, D = total customer deposits and k = the target LTD:

Required deposits = L/k, $\Delta\text{D} =$ L/k − D (deposits only),

Required loans = k D, $\Delta\text{L} = \text{L} -$ k D (loans only).

The two answers differ because the target is a ratio: each extra unit of deposits supports only k extra units of loans, so $\Delta\text{D} = \Delta$L/k. One can check the formulas against GARP’s own table. For January 2009, L = 2,266,004 and D = 2,387,036 (thousands), so L/0.85 $- \text{D} =$ 278,851 and 0.85D $- \text{L} = -$237,023, exactly the “Liabilities increase” and “Assets reduce” entries in the 85% rows (a negative “Assets reduce” figure means assets must fall). When the LTD is already below the target the signs reverse: liabilities could fall, or assets could grow, and the bank would still meet the target (GARP’s September to December columns).

**Applying it to this question**

Use the 30 September column; the May column and the retail sub-total are irrelevant (the retail figure is already inside total deposits).

$\text{LTD}_{\text{Sep}} =$ 2,846,300/3,184,600 = 89.38% (> 85%)

Required deposits = 2,846,300/0.85 = 3,348,588

$\Delta\text{D} =$ 3,348,588 − 3,184,600 = 163,988 ≈ EUR 164.0 million

Required loans = 0.85 × 3,184,600 = 2,706,910

$\Delta\text{L} =$ 2,846,300 − 2,706,910 = 139,390 ≈ EUR 139.4 million

Check: ∆L/0.85 = 139,390/0.85 = 163,988 = ∆D

Either deposits rise by about EUR 164.0 million with loans unchanged, or loans fall by about EUR 139.4 million with deposits unchanged.

**Fragile fact.** Convention: the deposit-side change is always the larger one ($\Delta\text{D} = \Delta$L/k), and the target is applied to deposits for the loan route but divides loans for the deposit route.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Compare and interpret different types of liquidity risk reports.

**GARP:** Chapter 10, Section 10.1, “Deposit Tracker Report” (Table 10.1B, “Deposit Tracker, LTD Ratio Required Cash Flow Changes”).

**GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser’s worked example quotes an asset increase of 189,400 for November from its own version of the figure; GARP’s Table 10.1B shows 89,973 for the 85% row in November. The formulas above reproduce GARP’s table exactly.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-10 b, where it is Q2 of 14.

a.reason: A applies the Table 10.1B logic to the right column: required deposits are loans divided by the target, required loans are the target times deposits.

b.reason: (Sibling swap). The two figures are attached to the wrong lever: 139.4 is the loan reduction and 164.0 is the deposit increase. B would be correct only if the target were defined as deposits divided by loans.

c.reason: (Wrong input twin). These are the May (actual) figures: 2,768,400/0.85 − 3,051,200 = 205,741 and 2,768,400 − 0.85 × 3,051,200 = 174,880. C would be correct if the question asked about 31 May.

d.reason: (Dropped term). D assumes a one-for-one adjustment, taking the loan gap L $- \text{kD} =$ 139,390 as the deposit increase too and dropping the division by k. D would be correct only if the target were a difference (loans minus deposits) rather than a ratio.

questions.question:
A treasury analyst at a Japanese commercial bank reviews the deposit type and tenor section of the deposit tracker (JPY billions):

| Division | Current | Rolling | Up to 1m | 1m to 6m | Over 6m |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Retail banking | 118.4 | 1,046.2 | 8.1 | 96.7 | 11.6 |
| Correspondent banks | 21.9 | 0.0 | 312.5 | 207.3 | 0.0 |
| Local authorities | 0.0 | 0.0 | 101.4 | 198.6 | 30.2 |
| Private banking | 14.2 | 97.8 | 0.0 | 0.0 | 0.0 |

Which of the following conclusions and actions is most consistent with the reading?

options.text: Retail balances are mostly held in fixed-term deposits, so the bank’s regulatory liquidity metrics already benefit from them and no action is needed.
Because retail current and rolling balances have been stable, the bank may report them as long-term funds without showing the regulator that they behave as such.
The bank should encourage correspondent banks to move their fixed-term deposits into current accounts, as current accounts count as long-term funds for regulatory purposes.
Most retail balances sit in current and rolling accounts, which count as short-term liabilities; moving customers into fixed-term or notice accounts would improve the metrics.

questions.solution:
Deposit type and tenor report: retail balances concentrated in current and rolling accounts.

**Concept and theory**

Alongside the LTD figures, GARP’s deposit tracker includes charts of customer deposits by account type and tenor (Figure 10.2A) and of the deposits’ maturity profile (Figure 10.2B). Their purpose is to help the Treasury department gauge the trend of deposit balances over time and, crucially, the regulatory quality of that funding.

GARP’s reading of its example: a large percentage of the retail bank’s deposits are current accounts and rolling deposits, with very little in fixed-term deposits. For regulatory purposes these funds are treated as short-term liabilities and do not assist the bank’s regulatory liquidity metrics, which emphasise long-term funds. The local regulator may allow overnight balances to be treated as longer term, but only if the bank can show that they act as such in behavioural terms. GARP therefore suggests a marketing exercise to find out whether customers would move into fixed-term or notice accounts: any increase in those balances improves the firm’s liquidity metrics.

| Account type | Regulatory treatment (GARP) |
|---|---|
| Current and rolling (on demand) | Short-term liabilities; no help to regulatory metrics unless behaviour is demonstrated |
| Fixed-term and notice | Longer-term funds; growth improves liquidity metrics |

This connects to the LO 75.a rule that callable and demand deposits are generally treated as 1-day money.

**Applying it to this question**

Retail banking holds 118.4 + 1,046.2 = 1,164.6 of 1,281.0 (JPY billions), about 91%, in current and rolling accounts; private banking is entirely current and rolling. Correspondent banks and local authorities are mostly fixed-term. The deciding facts are GARP’s treatment of current and rolling balances as short-term liabilities and its recommended remedy of moving customers into fixed-term or notice accounts.

**Fragile fact.** Direction: current and rolling balances count as short-term liabilities; the fix is to move customers into fixed-term or notice accounts, not the reverse.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Compare and interpret different types of liquidity risk reports.

**GARP:** Chapter 10, Section 10.1, “Deposit Tracker Report” (Figures 10.2A and 10.2B and accompanying text).

**GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser’s worked answer speaks of moving private banking customers into longer-term fixed accounts, while GARP’s text discusses retail bank deposits. Both divisions are mostly current and rolling in GARP’s figure; the remedy is the same.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-10 b, where it is Q3 of 14.

a.reason: (Sibling swap). A gives retail the fixed-term profile that actually belongs to correspondent banks and local authorities. A would be correct only if the large retail figure sat in the fixed-term columns.

b.reason: (Scope or condition error). B drops GARP’s condition: overnight balances may be treated as longer term only if the regulator allows it and the bank shows they behave that way. B would be correct only if the stem said the regulator had accepted behavioural evidence of stability.

c.reason: (Polarity flip). C reverses the desired direction: current accounts are short-term liabilities, so moving fixed-term funds into them would worsen the metrics. C would be correct only if the move were from current accounts into fixed-term deposits.

d.reason: D states both halves of GARP’s interpretation: the concentration in current and rolling accounts weakens the regulatory metrics, and migration to fixed-term or notice products improves them.

questions.question: The chief compliance officer at a Chinese commercial bank with several subsidiaries asks an internal auditor to explain how the daily liquidity report differs from the funding maturity gap (mismatch) report. Which of the following comparisons is most accurate?

options.text: The daily liquidity report is completed once for the whole group and never by subsidiaries, whereas the mismatch report must be completed separately by each subsidiary.

The daily liquidity report gives an end-of-day view of liquid and marketable assets and of liabilities by tenor; the mismatch report shows the gap per time bucket for all assets and liabilities, adjusted for liquid securities.
The mismatch report shows the gap per time bucket for all assets and liabilities but makes no adjustment for liquid securities, which enter only the daily liquidity report.
The daily liquidity report gives an end-of-day view of liquid assets and liabilities by tenor, and it is this report, not the mismatch report, that generates the survival horizon report.

questions.solution:
Comparing the daily liquidity report with the funding maturity gap (mismatch) report.

**Concept and theory**

GARP describes two closely related cash flow reports.

**Daily liquidity report.** A straightforward spreadsheet detailing the bank’s liquid and marketable assets, together with liabilities, up to 1-year maturity and beyond. It gives an end-of-day picture of the bank’s liquidity position for the Treasury and Finance departments. Each branch and subsidiary completes one, although a bank with only a branch structure (no subsidiaries) may aggregate the report. It takes inputs from the balance sheet accounting system and contains: a summary of liquid securities (government bonds, central bank eligible and non-eligible bank CDs), where the value of securities deemed instantly liquid feeds the liquidity ratio; a summary of assets and liabilities by tenor (Table 10.2A); and the cumulative liquidity report with the liquidity risk factor (Table 10.2B).

**Funding maturity gap (mismatch) report.** It shows the maturity gap, also called the maturity mismatch, per time bucket for all assets and liabilities, with an adjustment for liquid securities. It includes the cumulative liquidity cash flow of the daily report, and the two reports can be combined. Figure 10.4 shows the mismatch graphically by product, and the same report is used to generate the cash flow survival horizon report (Figure 10.5).

| Feature | Daily liquidity report | Mismatch report |
|---|---|---|
| Core content | Liquid assets, liabilities by tenor, cumulative liquidity | Gap per bucket, all assets and liabilities |
| Liquid securities | Listed; instantly liquid value feeds the ratio | Adjustment to the gap |
| Who prepares | Each branch and subsidiary | Bank level (can be combined) |
| Feeds | Liquidity ratio, LRF | Cash flow survival horizon report |

**Applying it to this question**

The question asks for the most accurate comparison. Only B describes both reports as GARP does. The other options each contain one misstatement about who prepares a report, whether the liquid-securities adjustment exists, or which report feeds the survival horizon.

**Fragile fact.** Source of the survival horizon: it is generated from the mismatch (maturity gap) report, which already carries the adjustment for liquid securities.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Compare and interpret different types of liquidity risk reports.

**GARP:** Chapter 10, Section 10.1, “Daily Liquidity Report” (Figure 10.3, Tables 10.2A and 10.2B) and “Funding Maturity Gap (‘Mismatch’) Report” (Table 10.3, Figures 10.4 and 10.5).

**GARP vs Schweser:** none of substance. The branch and subsidiary point is GARP-only content.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-10 b, where it is Q4 of 14.

a.reason: (Scope or condition error). GARP’s aggregation option applies only to a bank with a branch structure and no subsidiaries; otherwise each branch and subsidiary completes a daily report. A would be correct only for a branch-only bank, and even then it misstates the mismatch report.

b.reason: B pairs GARP’s description of the daily report (end-of-day view of liquid and marketable assets and of liabilities by tenor) with its description of the mismatch report (gap per time bucket for all assets and liabilities, with an adjustment for liquid securities).

c.reason: (Scope error). C drops the adjustment for liquid securities that GARP builds into the mismatch report (“with an adjustment for liquid securities”). C would be correct only for a raw contractual gap report such as the unadjusted rows of Table 10.3.

d.reason: (Sibling swap). GARP states that the mismatch report is the one used to generate the cash flow survival horizon report. D would be correct only if the stem had defined a bank that builds its survival chart from the daily liquidity report.

questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a Canadian bank reviews the cumulative liquidity section of the daily liquidity report. The cumulative cash gap is shown as cumulative inflows less outflows (a negative figure is a shortfall), and counterbalancing capacity is shown as a positive amount. Total liabilities are CAD 4,120 million. Extract (CAD thousands):

| Bucket | 1 day | 2 days | 1 week | 2 weeks | 1 month | 2 months |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cumulative cash gap | −42,500 | −58,900 | −210,400 | −305,700 | −388,200 | −512,600 |
| Counterbalancing capacity | 15,000 | 15,000 | 260,000 | 330,000 | 395,000 | 420,000 |

Which of the following correctly states the liquidity gap for the 1-month bucket and its interpretation?

options.text: Negative CAD 783.2 million: counting securities makes the 1-month shortfall larger than the cash gap
Negative CAD 388.2 million: liquid securities do not change the 1-month position
Positive CAD 6.8 million: available securities just cover the cumulative cash shortfall to 1 month
Positive CAD 312.5 million: securities comfortably cover the outflows falling in the 1-month bucket

questions.solution:
Liquidity gap for the 1-month bucket from the cumulative cash gap and counterbalancing capacity.

**Concept and theory**

The cumulative liquidity report (GARP Table 10.2B) is the summary section of the daily liquidity report. Its rows, for buckets from 1 day to 1 year, are: cumulative net cash balance, other forecast inflows and outflows, the **cumulative cash gap**, the **counterbalancing capacity**, the **liquidity** **gap**, a limit and the variance against it, followed by liquidity metrics (1-week and 1-month ratios) and the liquidity risk factor.

The cumulative cash gap is cumulative inflows less outflows to the end of each bucket, so a negative number is a funding shortfall. Counterbalancing capacity is “the sum of available securities to cover for sudden cash outflows”, a positive resource. The liquidity gap nets the two:

Liquidity $\text{gap}_{\text{t}} =$ Cumulative cash $\text{gap}_{\text{t}} +$ Counterbalancing $\text{capacity}_{\text{t}}$.

GARP’s own figures confirm the addition: at 1 day, −111,734 + 8,676 = −103,058; at 1 week, −301,843 + 797,674 = 495,831. A positive liquidity gap means available securities cover the cumulative shortfall to that horizon; a negative one means they do not. Because both inputs are cumulative, the liquidity gap is a running position, not a bucket-by-bucket flow.

**Applying it to this question**

Formula first, then the 1-month bucket:

Liquidity $\text{gap}_{\text{1m}} =$ Cumulative cash $\text{gap}_{\text{1m}} + \text{CBC}_{\text{1m}}$

= −388,200 + 395,000

= +6,800 thousand = CAD 6.8 million

The bank’s securities only just cover its cumulative shortfall at one month; at two months the gap turns negative (−512,600 + 420,000 = −92,600). Total liabilities of CAD 4,120 million are irrelevant to the gap itself.

**Fragile fact.** Sign: with the cash gap negative and capacity positive, the liquidity gap is their sum; both inputs are cumulative.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Compare and interpret different types of liquidity risk reports.

**GARP:** Chapter 10, Section 10.1, “Daily Liquidity Report” (Table 10.2B, cumulative liquidity report).

**GARP vs Schweser:** conflict on wording. Schweser says the liquidity gap is the cumulative cash gap “less” the counterbalancing capacity; GARP’s table shows it as the sum when capacity is positive. Resolved from GARP’s figures; Schweser’s phrasing probably measures the gap as a shortfall magnitude.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-10 b, where it is Q5 of 14.

a.reason: (Sign error). A subtracts the capacity: −388,200 − 395,000 = −783,200, treating liquid securities as a further outflow. This is the trap in a literal reading of Schweser’s wording (“cumulative cash gap . . . less the counterbalancing capacity”). A would be correct only if capacity were recorded as a negative number under a sign convention where shortfalls are positive.

b.reason: (Dropped term). B reports the cumulative cash gap and ignores the counterbalancing capacity. B would be correct only if the question asked for the cash gap rather than the liquidity gap.

c.reason: C adds the positive counterbalancing capacity to the negative cumulative cash gap, the construction that reproduces every column of GARP’s Table 10.2B.

d.reason: (Wrong input twin). D uses the bucket flow instead of the cumulative gap: (−388,200) − (−305,700) = −82,500, then −82,500 + 395,000 = 312,500. D would be correct only if the stem had given non-cumulative bucket flows and asked about the 1-month bucket alone.

questions.question:
A risk consultant is validating the liquidity risk factor (LRF) in a GBP-reporting bank’s daily liquidity report. The LRF relates the average remaining term of the bank’s assets to that of its liabilities, using the same inputs as the reading’s report. The bank’s data are:

| Item (months unless stated) | Value |
|---|---|
| Average remaining term of assets, excluding marketable securities | 52.40 |
| Average remaining term of assets, adjusted for marketable securities | 41.26 |
| Average remaining term of liabilities, with no call stickiness | 6.85 |
| Average remaining term of liabilities, excluding call deposits | 7.31 |
| Combined average remaining term of liabilities | 8.42 |
| 1-week liquidity ratio (%) | 9.60 |

Which of the following is closest to the LRF the report should show?
questions.solution:
Liquidity risk factor: which asset and liability term inputs the daily liquidity report uses.

**Concept and theory**

The liquidity risk factor (LRF) appears at the foot of GARP’s cumulative liquidity report (Table 10.2B), which forms part of the daily liquidity report. It compares how long the bank’s assets take to run off with how long its liabilities stay. GARP’s table lists the inputs:

| GARP Table 10.2B item (months) | Value |
|---|---|
| Average remaining term of assets (excluding marketable securities) | 44.5900 |
| Adjusted for marketable securities | 34.8776 |
| Average remaining term of liabilities (with no call stickiness) | 7.7200 |
| Excluding call deposits | 8.0046 |
| Average tenor of call deposits | 37.55 |
| Combined average remaining term of liabilities | 9.0593 |
| LRF | 3.8499 |

GARP gives no formula in the prose, but the table pins it down: 34.8776/9.0593 = 3.8499, whereas the unadjusted pair gives 44.59/7.72 = 5.78. So

LRF $= \frac{\text{Average remaining term of assets, adjusted for marketable securities}}{\text{Combined average remaining term of liabilities}}$ .

The asset term is adjusted because marketable securities can be turned into cash before their legal maturity (the daily report counts instantly liquid securities in the liquidity ratio). The liability term is the combined figure, which brings call deposits back in at a behavioural tenor rather than assuming no call stickiness. An LRF of 3.85 says the adjusted asset term is about 3.85 times the liability term. This formula is inferred from GARP’s table; Schweser only mentions that the LRF is summarised in the daily report.

**Applying it to this question**

Formula first, then the bank’s inputs:

LRF $= \frac{\text{Assets, adjusted for marketable securities}}{\text{Combined liabilities term}} = \frac{41.26}{8.42} =$ 4.90

The unadjusted asset term (52.40), the two partial liability terms (6.85 and 7.31) and the 1-week liquidity ratio (9.6%) are not inputs. The result means the bank’s adjusted asset term is about 4.9 times its combined liability term.

**Fragile fact.** Inputs: adjusted asset term over combined liability term (GARP: 34.8776/9.0593 = 3.8499); the unadjusted pair gives a higher, wrong figure.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Compare and interpret different types of liquidity risk reports.

**GARP:** Chapter 10, Section 10.1, “Daily Liquidity Report” (Table 10.2B, liquidity risk factor block).

**GARP vs Schweser:** no conflict; Schweser gives no LRF formula. The formula is inferred from GARP’s table figures, not stated in GARP’s prose.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-10 b, where it is Q6 of 14.

a.reason: A uses the same pair of inputs that reproduces GARP’s reported LRF of 3.8499.

b.reason: (Wrong input twin). 41.26/7.31 = 5.64 uses the liability term excluding call deposits. B would be correct only if the report defined the LRF on non-call liabilities.

c.reason: (Wrong input twin). 41.26/6.85 = 6.02 uses the liability term with no call stickiness. C would be correct only if call deposits were treated as 1-day money in the LRF.

d.reason: (Wrong input twin). 52.40/8.42 = 6.22 uses the asset term excluding marketable securities. D would be correct only if marketable securities were held to legal maturity in the calculation.

questions.question:
The CRO of a Brazilian bank reviews the cash flow survival report generated from the bank’s maturity mismatch report. The cumulative net cash flow (contractual, no adjustments) is shown below. The cash flow value of liquid securities and other adjustments is BRL 880 million, and the bank’s LTD ratio is 88%.

| Day | 1 | 5 | 8 | 15 | 22 | 29 | 36 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cumulative net cash flow (BRL m) | 210 | 95 | −40 | −380 | −690 | −905 | −1,150 |

Which of the following interpretations is most accurate?

options.text: Once liquid securities are included, cumulative cash flow stays positive through day 36, so the bank meets the Basel III survival requirement.
The horizon ends between days 5 and 8 unadjusted and between days 22 and 29 adjusted; the bank meets Basel III as it survives beyond three weeks.
The bank fails the Basel III requirement because the unadjusted horizon ends between days 5 and 8; the adjusted figures play no part in that assessment.
The horizon ends between days 5 and 8 unadjusted and between days 22 and 29 adjusted; the bank is still short of Basel III and needs to take action.

questions.solution:
Reading unadjusted and adjusted survival horizons from a mismatch-based report against Basel III.

**Concept and theory**

GARP explains that the funding maturity gap (mismatch) report is used to generate the cash flow survival horizon report (Figure 10.5). The chart shows daily inflows and outflows and two lines: the cumulative cash flow on contractual flows, and the adjusted cumulative cash flow, which adds the cash flow value of liquid securities and other adjustments. The survival horizon is the point at which the cumulative line turns negative, the day the bank would run out of cash.

GARP’s example: the horizon is only seven days under normal circumstances; including liquid securities and other adjustments extends it to 27 days. “This is still below the Basel III requirement” (Schweser: a 30-day survival horizon), so on the strength of the report the bank must act to address the liquidity shortage. Two points follow: compliance is judged on the adjusted horizon (the word “still”), and the target is 30 days.

The adjustment is a stock of liquidity applied once, not a flow added in each bucket. GARP’s mismatch table repeats the same “total adjustments” figure in every column, but its cumulative mismatch uses it once: at Sight-8 days, −14,262,374 + 209,277,716 − 1,256,876,281 = −1,061,860,939.

Adjusted cumulative $\text{CF}_{\text{t}} = \text{Cumulative CF}_{\text{t}} +$ Liquid securities and other adjustments.

**Applying it to this question**

Unadjusted: +95 on day 5, −40 on day 8, so the horizon ends between days 5 and 8.

$\text{Adjusted}_{22} = -$690 + 880 = +190

$\text{Adjusted}_{29} = -$905 + 880 = −25

So the adjusted horizon ends between days 22 and 29, below 30 days: the bank is short of the Basel III requirement and must act. The 88% LTD ratio is irrelevant to the survival horizon.

**Fragile fact.** Benchmark and basis: Basel III requires survival for 30 days, assessed on the adjusted horizon; liquid securities are added once, not in every bucket.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Compare and interpret different types of liquidity risk reports.

**GARP:** Chapter 10, Section 10.1, “Funding Maturity Gap (‘Mismatch’) Report” (Table 10.3, Figure 10.5).

**GARP vs Schweser:** GARP’s text gives 7 days unadjusted and 27 days adjusted; Schweser’s example says 8 and 27 days and its Module Quiz answer says 8 and 21 days (figure-reading differences). The 30-day figure is from Schweser; GARP says only “the Basel III requirement”. Stress-scenario survival reports (BAU versus mitigating actions) belong to LO 75.c.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-10 b, where it is Q7 of 14.

a.reason: (Calculation slip (adjustment counted in every bucket)). A adds BRL 880 million again in each bucket, as if the repeated adjustment row were a flow: at day 36, −1,150 + 7 × 880 = 5,010. A would be correct only if the bank received a fresh BRL 880 million of liquidity in every bucket.

b.reason: (Scope or condition error). B reads the horizons correctly but replaces the 30-day requirement with “three weeks”. B would be correct only if the requirement were a 21-day survival period.

c.reason: (Scope error). C reaches the right verdict for the wrong reason: GARP judges the bank on the horizon after liquid securities and adjustments (27 days, “still below”). C would be correct only if the stem had stated that the regulator assesses the unadjusted contractual horizon.

d.reason: D reads both horizons correctly and, like GARP’s example (7 and 27 days), concludes that the adjusted horizon is still below the requirement, so action is needed.

questions.question:
The treasurer of a Singapore banking group reviews the large depositor concentration report. The group treats depositors of USD 50 million or more as large, and ALCO also treats any deposit above 5% of total liabilities as large. The internal single-source concentration limit is 10% of total liabilities.

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Total liabilities (SGD m) | 8,450.0 |
| Deposits from Corporate X (SGD m) | 1,180.0 |
| Corporate X share of its country’s external funding (%) | 21.3 |

Corporate X is a close relationship, so the treasurer prefers not to ask it to remove funds. Holding Corporate X’s deposits constant, by how much must the group’s total liabilities increase to bring Corporate X within the limit?

options.text: SGD 372.2 million
SGD 3,350.0 million
SGD 11,800.0 million
SGD 15,150.0 million

questions.solution:
Increase in total liabilities needed to bring a large depositor down to a 10% single-source limit.

**Concept and theory**

Funding source concentration reports are key MI for senior Treasury and relationship managers. GARP’s reason is a central principle of liquidity management, funding diversity: a bank should not become over-reliant on a single source, or sector, of funds, and this includes reliance on intra-group funds. GARP’s Table 10.4 is a Large Depositor Concentration Report for a banking group. “Large” is defined there as a depositor of USD 50 million or more, but a bank may instead define it as a percentage of total liabilities; generally a deposit of 5% of total liabilities should be treated as large by ALCO. Separately, the group sets an internal single-source concentration limit, 10% in GARP’s example.

In GARP’s illustration the largest depositor (“CBS”, 16.5% of funding) exceeds the 10% limit by a considerable margin. If the relationship is close, the bank will need to increase its liabilities base to bring the share down to the limit, or otherwise risk damaging the relationship by asking the depositor to remove some funds. Holding the deposit D fixed, with total liabilities L and limit k:

s $= \frac{\text{D}}{\text{L}}$ , $\text{L}^{*} = \frac{\text{D}}{\text{k}}$ , $\Delta\text{L} = \frac{\text{D}}{\text{k}} -$ L.

Keep the two thresholds apart: the 5% (or USD 50 million) figure decides who appears on the report as large; the single-source limit decides who is in breach.

**Applying it to this question**

Share first, then the required base and the increase:

s = 1,180/8,450 = 13.96% (> 10%)

$\text{L}^{*} =$ 1,180/0.10 = 11,800

$\Delta\text{L} =$ 11,800 − 8,450 = SGD 3,350.0 million

The USD 50 million and 5% definitions only confirm that Corporate X is a large depositor; the 21.3% country share is a different denominator. None of them enters the calculation.

**Fragile fact.** Two thresholds: 5% of liabilities (or USD 50 million) defines “large”; the 10% single-source limit defines a breach.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Compare and interpret different types of liquidity risk reports.

**GARP:** Chapter 10, Section 10.1, “Funding Concentration Report” (Table 10.4).

**GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser’s example names customer “ABC” exceeding the 10% limit by 1.1%; GARP’s table names “CBS” at 16.5%, “a considerable margin”. Same lesson; GARP followed.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-10 b, where it is Q8 of 14.

a.reason: (Sibling swap). A computes the other remedy, the withdrawal that would restore the limit: $(\text{D} - \text{kL})$/(1 $- \text{k}) = ($1,180 − 845)/0.9 = 372.2. A would be correct only if the question asked how much Corporate X must remove.

b.reason: B applies GARP’s preferred remedy for a close relationship, growing the liabilities base, against the 10% single-source limit.

c.reason: (Intermediate result). SGD 11,800 million is the required total liability base D/k, not the increase. C would be correct only if the question asked for the new total.

d.reason: (Wrong input twin). D uses the 5% large-depositor threshold as if it were the limit: 1,180/0.05 − 8,450 = 15,150. D would be correct only if the single-source limit were 5%.

questions.question:
A member of the board risk committee at an Australian bank is reviewing a briefing paper on the funding concentration report. The paper makes the following statements:

I. Funding source concentration reports are key MI for senior Treasury and relationship managers, because a central principle of liquidity management is funding diversity.

II. A large depositor may be defined by an absolute amount or as a percentage of total liabilities; generally, a deposit of 5% of total liabilities should be treated as large by ALCO.

III. Reliance on intra-group funds is not a funding diversity concern, because such funds remain within the banking group.

IV. When a close-relationship depositor breaches the single-source limit, the bank must always require it to withdraw the excess at once.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.text: I and II only
I, II and IV only
I only
I, II and III only

questions.solution:
Risk committee briefing: which statements about the funding concentration report are correct.

**Concept and theory**

The funding concentration report answers one question: is the bank too dependent on any one provider, or type, of funds? GARP calls funding source concentration reports key MI for senior Treasury and relationship managers, because funding diversity is a central principle of liquidity management. A bank should not become over-reliant on a single source, or sector, of funds, and GARP adds explicitly that this includes reliance on intra-group funds.

Building the report requires a definition of “large”. GARP’s Table 10.4 uses deposits of USD 50 million or more, but a bank may define large in terms of a percentage of total liabilities, and generally a deposit of 5% of total liabilities should be treated as large by ALCO. The report then shows each large depositor’s amount and its share of country and group external funding, and compares the biggest against the internal single-source limit (10% in GARP).

When a depositor breaches the limit GARP gives two routes and a judgement between them:

| Remedy | GARP’s comment |
|---|---|
| Increase the liabilities base | Preferred where the relationship is close |
| Ask the depositor to remove funds | Risks damaging the relationship |

**Applying it to this question**

Statement I is GARP’s rationale: true. Statement II is GARP’s definition of large: true. Statement III contradicts GARP’s explicit inclusion of intra-group funds in the diversity principle: false.

Statement IV turns one of two options into an absolute requirement, while GARP prefers to grow liabilities for a close relationship: false. Correct set: I and II.

**Fragile fact.** Scope: funding diversity explicitly includes intra-group funds; “large” is about 5% of total liabilities (or an absolute amount such as USD 50 million), not the 10% limit.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Compare and interpret different types of liquidity risk reports.

**GARP:** Chapter 10, Section 10.1, “Funding Concentration Report” (Table 10.4).

**GARP vs Schweser:** none; Schweser attributes the 5% guide to UK regulators, GARP to ALCO practice (“generally speaking”).

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-10 b, where it is Q9 of 14.

a.reason: A matches GARP’s purpose (diversity) and definition (absolute amount or about 5% of total liabilities) and rejects both distortions.

b.reason: (Absolute claim). Accepting IV makes withdrawal mandatory and immediate. GARP presents it as a fallback that risks the relationship, after growing the liabilities base. B would be correct only if the stem said the bank’s policy required immediate repayment of any excess.

c.reason: (Scope error). Choosing “I only” rejects II, as if large could be defined only in absolute terms. GARP allows a percentage-of-liabilities definition and gives the 5% guide. C would be correct only if II had stated the threshold as 5% of total assets or as the single-source limit.

d.reason: (Polarity flip). Accepting III reverses GARP: reliance on intra-group funds is part of the concentration concern. D would be correct only if the stem restricted the question to external funding percentages, as in the columns of Table 10.4.

questions.question:
The chief compliance officer of a U.S. bank holding company reviews the undrawn commitment report (USD millions):

| Quarter-end | Q1 | Q2 | Q3 | Q4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Head office undrawn commitments | 2,140 | 2,310 | 2,585 | 2,790 |
| Subsidiary undrawn commitments | 610 | 640 | 705 | 760 |
| Total undrawn commitments | 2,750 | 2,950 | 3,290 | 3,550 |
| Aggregate limit | 3,800 | 3,800 | 3,800 | 3,800 |
| Drawn committed facilities | 4,900 | 4,950 | 4,880 | 4,910 |

Which of the following interpretations is most accurate?

options.text: The rising undrawn total improves liquidity, because unused facilities cause no cash outflow until drawn and are therefore left out of the liquidity metrics.
Only the stable drawn balances matter for liquidity; the undrawn lines become relevant to the liquidity metrics only once the aggregate limit is breached.
The undrawn total is rising toward its limit; such lines tend to be drawn in a stress just when funding is short, so they are included in the metrics and reported separately.
Subsidiary undrawn commitments belong in the funding concentration report, so the undrawn commitment report should be confined to the head office total.

questions.solution:
Undrawn commitment report: a rising undrawn total approaching its aggregate limit.

**Concept and theory**

Off-balance sheet products such as liquidity lines, revolving credit facilities, letters of credit and guarantees are, in GARP’s words, potential stress points for a bank’s funding requirement. The mechanism is behavioural and pro-cyclical: in a stress situation a bank can expect un-utilised liquidity and funding lines to be drawn down, because its customers face funding difficulties of their own. Undrawn commitments therefore “exacerbate funding shortages at exactly the wrong time”. GARP draws two consequences:

- liquidity metrics include undrawn commitments (their regulatory outflow treatment is LO 75.a);
- the same risk is a reason to report them separately, in an undrawn commitment report.

GARP shows two forms: Figure 10.6A tracks the undrawn commitment trend over time (head office and subsidiary totals), and Figure 10.6B shows the trend for both drawn and undrawn committed facilities against an aggregate limit. These are aggregate-level reports; the bank also produces detailed breakdowns per customer. Schweser adds that such reports are useful for measuring the trend over time.

**Applying it to this question**

Total undrawn commitments rose from USD 2,750 million to USD 3,550 million over four quarters (+29.1%), and now stand at 3,550/3,800 = 93.4% of the aggregate limit. Each extra dollar is a potential outflow that would most likely be drawn in a stress. The stable drawn balances (about USD 4.9 billion) are not the point of the report and do not change the interpretation.

**Fragile fact.** Direction and timing: undrawn lines are drawn in a stress, when funding is already scarce, so they count against liquidity and are also reported separately.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Compare and interpret different types of liquidity risk reports.

**GARP:** Chapter 10, Section 10.1, “Undrawn Commitment Report” (Figures 10.6A and 10.6B).

**GARP vs Schweser:** none. GARP’s figures are partly garbled in the source extraction; the content above relies on the text.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-10 b, where it is Q10 of 14.

a.reason: (Polarity flip). A reverses GARP: undrawn lines are included in liquidity metrics precisely because they can become outflows in stress, so a rising total weakens the position. A would be correct only for commitments the bank could cancel at will before any drawing.

b.reason: (Scope or condition error). B adds a condition GARP does not have: undrawn lines matter for liquidity whether or not the aggregate limit is breached. B would be correct only if the question concerned compliance with the internal aggregate limit, not liquidity risk.

c.reason: C states the trend, GARP’s reason it matters (drawdowns arrive just when funding is short) and both consequences (inclusion in liquidity metrics and separate reporting).

d.reason: (Sibling swap). Subsidiary undrawns are part of the undrawn commitment report (GARP shows head office and subsidiary totals); the concentration report covers large depositors. D would be correct only if the stem were about subsidiaries’ deposits.

questions.question:
A senior analyst at an Australian prudential regulator compares the firm-specific wholesale funding yield curve of Bank K with the peer group average (spreads over benchmark, bps). Bank K’s own cash flow liquidity ratios are within their limits.

| Tenor | 1m to 3m | 3m to 6m | 6m to 1y | 1y to 2y | 2y to 5y |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bank K | 18 | 27 | 46 | 78 | 115 |
| Peer average | 16 | 22 | 29 | 41 | 58 |

Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Bank K’s curve sitting above the peer average mainly reflects strong investor demand for its paper, so the regulator would read it as a sign of liquidity strength.
Because Bank K’s cash flow liquidity ratios are within their limits, the comparison of its funding costs with peers adds no information about its liquidity position.
To perform the comparison, Bank K’s management should obtain each peer bank’s individual funding yield curve directly from the competitor banks themselves.
Bank K’s curve rising materially above its peers’ is an early warning of funding stress; its management should compare its funding level with the peer average at least quarterly.

questions.solution:
Regulator comparing a bank’s firm-specific wholesale funding yield curve with its peer group.

**Concept and theory**

GARP opens this section with a warning: a bank’s liquidity position is not illustrated solely by its cash flow liquidity metrics. An indication of liquidity strength can also be gleaned from two further sources: the bank’s funding costs, and the composition of its funding by product. Funding cost in particular is valuable market intelligence, and the bank regulator will also be compiling it.

The regulator’s use is comparative. It can obtain an early warning that a particular bank is experiencing funding stress if that bank’s funding yield curve is rising materially above its peer group’s. Individual bank management finds it difficult to get this information about other banks, but should be able to get an idea of the peer group average from the regulator. Comparing one’s own funding level with that average is worthwhile and should be done on at least a quarterly basis. GARP’s Figure 10.8 shows a firm-specific yield curve for a UK bank by product (cash deposits, primary issuance, covered bonds, ABCP and ABS), and Figure 10.9 shows the same bank’s wholesale funding by volume, product type and tenor bucket.

| Actor | Role in GARP |
|---|---|
| Regulator | Compiles funding cost data across banks; early warning from a curve rising above peers |
| Bank management | Obtains the peer average from the regulator; compares at least quarterly |

**Applying it to this question**

Bank K’s spread over the peer average is +2, +5, +17, +37, +57 bps from the shortest to the longest bucket; at 2 to 5 years it pays roughly double the peer spread (115 versus 58). That is a curve rising materially above the peer group, GARP’s early-warning pattern. The fact that Bank K’s cash flow ratios are within limits does not cancel the signal, because GARP says cash flow metrics alone do not show the whole position.

**Fragile fact.** Actor and direction: the regulator holds the peer data and reads a curve rising above peers as stress; bank management gets only the peer average, and compares at least quarterly.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Compare and interpret different types of liquidity risk reports.

**GARP:** Chapter 10, Section 10.1, “Wholesale Pricing and Volume” (Figures 10.8 and 10.9).

**GARP vs Schweser:** minor. Schweser says these reports are typically run quarterly unless the regulator asks for more; GARP says the comparison should be made on at least a quarterly basis.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-10 b, where it is Q11 of 14.

a.reason: (Polarity flip). A reverses the signal: paying more than peers to borrow points to funding stress, not strength. A would be correct only if Bank K’s curve sat below the peer average.

b.reason: (Absolute claim). B treats cash flow metrics as a complete picture, contrary to GARP’s opening statement that liquidity is not shown solely by cash flow metrics. B would be correct only if funding costs carried no information, which GARP denies.

c.reason: (Role misassignment). GARP says it is difficult for a bank to obtain other banks’ funding data; the peer average comes from the regulator, which compiles it. C would be correct only if the actor were the regulator rather than Bank K’s management.

d.reason: D combines GARP’s interpretation (a curve materially above peers signals funding stress) with its guidance for bank management (compare against the peer average at least quarterly).

questions.question:
An internal auditor at a CNY-reporting commercial bank reviews the liability profile included in the bank’s liquidity MI:

| Liability type | Share of total liabilities (%) |
|---|---|
| Customers: individuals | 58 |
| Customers: large enterprises | 17 |
| Repo (highly liquid securities) | 8 |
| Repo (high-quality securities) | 5 |
| Asset-backed securities | 4 |
| Unsecured: other wholesale | 4 |
| Repo (other assets) | 2 |
| Conditional liabilities | 2 |

Which of the following statements about this report is most accurate?

options.text: Because individual customers make up 58% of liabilities, the report shows that the bank breaches a 10% single-source concentration limit.
The report shows each liability type’s share of the total, led by individual customers; its format can be set to the user’s choice and extended to other funding types.
The report shows the remaining maturity of each type of liability, so it can be used directly to generate the bank’s cash flow survival horizon.
The categories in the report are fixed, so the bank cannot add funding types such as covered bonds, client free cash or structured deposit products.

questions.solution:
Interpreting a liability profile and distinguishing it from the concentration and mismatch reports.

**Concept and theory**

The liability profile is, in GARP’s words, a simple breakdown of the share of each type of liability at the bank (Figure 10.7). In GARP’s example total liabilities are split into: customers (individuals); customers (large enterprises); repo of highly liquid securities; repo of high-quality securities; asset-backed securities; unsecured other wholesale; repo of other assets; and conditional liabilities. Schweser reads the figure as individuals at 65% and large enterprises at 15% (GARP’s chart labels are garbled in the source).

GARP stresses flexibility. Other funding types by product may be included, for example covered bonds, client free cash, structured deposit products, unsecured funding from credit institutions, from governments and central banks or from non-bank financials, SME customers, group funding, net derivatives margin, undated and dated capital, and primary issuance. “The report format can be set to the user’s desired choice.”

The profile answers “what kinds of funding do we have?”. It does not show maturities (the mismatch report does that) or individual counterparties against a limit (the funding concentration report does that).

**Applying it to this question**

The table is a share-by-type breakdown summing to 100%, led by individual customers (58%) and large enterprises (17%). The deciding facts are what the report contains (shares by liability type) and GARP’s statement that its format is the user’s choice and can include further product types.

**Fragile fact.** Content: the liability profile is shares by type of liability, with a flexible format; maturities belong to the mismatch report and named depositors to the concentration report.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Compare and interpret different types of liquidity risk reports.

**GARP:** Chapter 10, Section 10.1, “Liability Profile” (Figure 10.7).

**GARP vs Schweser:** none on content. The 65% and 15% shares are Schweser-only (condensed source); GARP’s chart percentages are illegible in the extraction.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-10 b, where it is Q12 of 14.

a.reason: (Scope or condition error). A applies a single-source limit, which tests individual depositors, to a whole category made up of many customers. A would be correct only if the 58% came from one depositor in the funding concentration report.

b.reason: B describes the report’s content and reading correctly and reflects GARP’s point that the format is flexible and can be extended to other funding types.

c.reason: (Sibling swap). C gives the liability profile the content of the mismatch report, which shows gaps by time bucket and generates the survival horizon. C would be correct only if the stem described the funding maturity gap report.

d.reason: (Absolute claim). D says the categories are fixed; GARP lists further funding types and says the format can be set to the user’s choice. D would be correct only for a prescribed regulatory template, which the liability profile is not.

questions.question:
The head of Group Treasury at a French banking group that operates across several countries through multiple subsidiaries is redesigning the group’s liquidity MI. A consultant proposes the following:

I. Liquidity MI for senior management should be a one-page summary of key metrics, since keeping it to one side of A4 raises the chance that it is actually read.

II. A qualitative report should be completed for Head Office Group Treasury on a monthly basis, to help the group understand the liquidity position in each country.

III. The summary should be distributed at a frequency set by the regulator’s supervisors, who alone may increase it during a stress period.

IV. The qualitative template replaces quantitative commentary, so branches need not explain changes in their 1-week and 1-month liquidity ratios.

Which of the proposals are consistent with the reading?

options.text: I only
I, II and III only
I, II and IV only
I and II only

questions.solution:
Designing senior management summary MI and a group qualitative liquidity report.

**Concept and theory**

GARP closes its tour of liquidity MI with two reports aimed at decision-makers rather than analysts.

**One-page summary for senior management.** Liquidity MI for senior management should be a 1-page summary of the key liquidity metrics. It can be distributed monthly or as directed by ALCO, and the frequency may be increased during a stress period. Keeping it to one side of A4 increases the chance that it will actually be read and noted at senior management level. GARP’s Figure 10.10, a monthly liquidity snapshot, carries the cumulative liquidity report, the liquidity ratios over a three-month view, the liquidity risk factor, the LTD ratio and net inter-group lending, with current month, previous month and change.

**Qualitative report.** For banking groups operating across country jurisdictions with multiple subsidiaries, a qualitative report should be completed for Head Office Group Treasury on a monthly basis, to help the group understand the liquidity position in each country. GARP’s template (Figure 10.11) asks branches and subsidiaries to:

- explain significant changes in the 1-week and 1-month liquidity ratios, in the cash and liquidity gaps, and in the liquidity risk factor;
- explain growth or shrinkage of asset books and changes in the inter-group position;
- report changes in corporate deposits (with confidence of roll-over) and in retail deposits, and the average daily opening cash position.

The qualitative report explains the numbers; it does not replace them.

**Applying it to this question**

Proposal I is GARP’s one-page rule and its rationale: consistent. Proposal II matches GARP’s qualitative report for multi-country groups: consistent. Proposal III gives ALCO’s role to the regulator’s supervisors: inconsistent. Proposal IV contradicts the template’s first item, which asks precisely for explanations of changes in the 1-week and 1-month ratios: inconsistent. Correct set: I and II.

**Fragile fact.** Actor and length: ALCO sets the summary’s frequency (more often in stress), and the report stays at one page.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Compare and interpret different types of liquidity risk reports.

**GARP:** Chapter 10, Section 10.1, “Summary and Qualitative Reports” (Figures 10.10 and 10.11). **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser covers the one-page summary but omits the qualitative report (GARP-only content). GARP’s text says the qualitative report is monthly, while its template header refers to a fixed date each week; the text is followed.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-10 b, where it is Q13 of 14.

a.reason: (Scope error). “I only” rejects II, as if a qualitative report had no place in liquidity MI. GARP prescribes it for groups operating across countries with multiple subsidiaries, which is exactly this group. A would be correct only for a single-entity domestic bank.

b.reason: (Role misassignment). Accepting III gives the regulator’s supervisors the power over distribution frequency; GARP says monthly or as directed by ALCO, increased in stress. B would be correct only if the actor named were ALCO.

c.reason: (Polarity flip). Accepting IV reverses the template, whose first point asks branches to explain significant changes in their 1-week and 1-month liquidity ratios. C would be correct only if the template omitted ratio commentary.

d.reason: D keeps the two proposals that restate GARP: the one-page senior management summary, and the monthly qualitative report for Head Office Group Treasury in a multi-country group.

questions.question:
A newly appointed CRO at a U.S. regional bank wants to know which liquidity report to consult for each of the following questions:

(1) Will the LTD ratio be back within the board limit by year-end?

(2) Is any single depositor above the 10% single-source limit?

(3) After counting liquid securities, how many days pass before cumulative cash flow turns negative?

(4) Is the bank paying more than its peers for wholesale funding of similar tenor?

Which of the following correctly matches the questions, in order (1) to (4), to the reports?

options.text: Deposit tracker; funding concentration; mismatch (survival horizon); wholesale pricing and volume
Deposit tracker; liability profile; mismatch (survival horizon); wholesale pricing and volume
Daily liquidity report; funding concentration; mismatch (survival horizon); wholesale pricing and volume
Deposit tracker; funding concentration; undrawn commitment report; wholesale pricing and volume

questions.solution:
Matching four management questions to the liquidity report that answers each.

**Concept and theory**

To “compare” the reports, the most useful lens is the question each one answers. Drawing on GARP Section 10.1:

| Report | Question it answers and key content |
|---|---|
| Deposit tracker | Where are deposits and the LTD ratio now and by year-end? Actuals and forecasts by customer type, loans, LTD versus board limit, changes needed to hit a target LTD |
| Daily liquidity report | What is today’s liquid asset and liability position? Liquid securities, assets and liabilities by tenor, cumulative cash gap, counterbalancing capacity, liquidity gap, LRF |
| Mismatch report | How large is the gap per time bucket, and how long can we survive? Gap for all assets and liabilities with liquid-securities adjustment; generates the survival horizon |
| Funding concentration | Are we over-reliant on one source or sector? Large depositors against the single-source limit |
| Undrawn commitments | How much could customers draw on us in a stress? Trend of undrawn facilities, head office and subsidiaries |
| Liability profile | What types of funding do we have? Share of each liability type |
| Wholesale pricing and volume | What do we pay for wholesale funding, in what products? Firm-specific yield curve versus peers; volume by product and tenor |

Several reports share data (the mismatch report includes the cumulative liquidity cash flow of the daily report), but each has a distinct purpose, and the senior management summary pulls the headline metrics together.

**Applying it to this question**

(1) LTD ratio to year-end: the deposit tracker, which reports actual and forecast LTD against the board limit. (2) A single depositor against the 10% limit: the funding concentration report. (3) Days until cumulative cash flow turns negative after liquid securities: the survival horizon generated from the mismatch report. (4) Funding cost against peers: wholesale pricing and volume.

**Fragile fact.** Pairings: LTD with the deposit tracker, single depositors with the concentration report, survival days with the mismatch report, peer funding cost with wholesale pricing and volume.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Compare and interpret different types of liquidity risk reports.

**GARP:** Chapter 10, Section 10.1, “Liquidity Risk Reporting” (all report subsections).

**GARP vs Schweser:** none. Reporting frequencies (Table 10.5) belong to LO 75.a and are not tested here.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-10 b, where it is Q14 of 14.

a.reason: A assigns each question to the report whose purpose GARP defines around it.

b.reason: (Sibling swap). B sends question (2) to the liability profile, which shows shares by liability type, not individual depositors against a limit. B would be correct only if question (2) asked which type of liability is the largest share of funding.

c.reason: (Sibling swap). C sends question (1) to the daily liquidity report; the LTD ratio and its year-end forecast sit in the deposit tracker. C would be correct only if question (1) asked about today’s cumulative liquidity gap.

d.reason: (Sibling swap). D sends question (3) to the undrawn commitment report, which tracks one source of contingent outflow, not the cumulative survival horizon. D would be correct only if question (3) asked how much customers could draw on committed lines.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Discuss the relationship between contingency funding planning and liquidity stress testing.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-11 a Q1
questions.question:
A risk consultant is preparing a briefing for the board risk committee of an Australian regional bank on how the bank’s contingency funding plan (CFP) relates to its liquidity stress testing framework. The draft contains the following statements:

I. Stress test results and other related information are inputs to the CFP’s governance, its menu of contingent liquidity actions and its decision framework.

II. The CFP’s menu of contingent actions is the primary input from which the stress testing framework derives its scenarios, so the CFP sits upstream of the stress test.

III. Once the stress test has been run, its results are the sole input that the CFP’s decision framework requires; no other information is needed.

IV. The CFP serves as a logical connection to its companion framework, the liquidity stress testing framework.

Which of the statements should remain in the briefing?

options.text: I only
II and IV only
I and IV only
I, III and IV only

questions.solution:
Board briefing on the direction of the link between the CFP and the liquidity stress testing framework.

**Concept and theory**

GARP opens Chapter 11 by describing the CFP as a logical connection to its companion, the liquidity stress testing framework. The two tools answer different questions. The stress testing framework asks: if the stresses in its scenarios materialise, what would their effects on the liquidity profile be? The CFP asks: given that answer, who decides, what can be done, and in what order? The bridge between them is a flow of information in one direction: the stress test results, together with other related information, are fed as inputs into three parts of the CFP:

| CFP element fed by the stress test | What the input does there |
|---|---|
| Governance | tells the decision makers how severe the position could become |
| Menu of contingent liquidity actions | sizes and times the actions that may be needed |
| Decision framework | informs when to invoke the plan and how far to escalate |

Two features of this sentence are fragile. First, the direction: the stress test is upstream and the CFP is downstream. Stress results flow into the CFP, not the reverse. Second, the qualifier: the inputs are stress test results and other related information. Elsewhere in the chapter GARP gives examples of that other information, such as the review of markets, industry and institution-specific conditions that the treasurer considers before invoking the plan, and the EWIs built from BAU measures. Schweser compresses the same idea to: CFPs use the results of liquidity stress testing and other relevant data as inputs within the context of governance, available contingent liquidity actions and decision-making.

**Applying it to this question**

Audit each statement against the source sentence. Statement I repeats the GARP sentence almost word for word: true. Statement II reverses the direction of the flow, putting the CFP upstream of the stress test: false. Statement III takes the true idea (stress results are inputs) and turns it into a sole-input claim, deleting “other related information”: false. Statement IV is GARP’s own characterisation of the CFP as the logical connection to its companion framework: true. The surviving set is I and IV.

**Fragile fact.** Direction: stress test results flow into the CFP (governance, contingent action menu, decision framework), and they are not the only input.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Discuss the relationship between contingency funding planning and liquidity stress testing. **GARP:** Chapter 11, Section 11.1 “Actions in a Liquidity Crisis”. **Schweser:** LO 76.a. **GARP vs Schweser:** none of substance; Schweser paraphrases “menu of contingent liquidity actions” as “available contingent liquidity actions”.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-11 a, where it is Q1 of 11.

a.reason: (Scope error). Keeping only I drops statement IV, which is a true statement taken from the same opening sentence of Section 11.1. This would be correct only if the stem asked which single statement describes what flows from the stress test into the CFP.

b.reason: (Polarity flip). It keeps statement II, which reverses the direction of the link: the stress test feeds the CFP, not the other way round. It also discards the true statement I. B would be correct only in a framework where the stress test scenarios were reverse-engineered from the contingent actions, which is not the GARP design.

c.reason: Option C keeps exactly the two statements that match the source: GARP describes the CFP as the logical connection to the stress testing framework, linking the stress test results and other related information as inputs to the CFP governance, menu of contingent liquidity actions and decision framework.

d.reason: (Absolute claim). It keeps statement III, which turns “stress test results and other related information” into “the sole input”. D would be correct only if the source said the CFP decision framework relies exclusively on the stress test, which it does not.
