questions.loText: Discuss the relationship between contingency funding planning and liquidity stress testing.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-11 a Q2
questions.question:
A treasury analyst at a Singapore commercial bank is mapping possible liquidity events to the framework that should primarily address them. Her list is:

I. Routine daily swings in retail deposit balances around month-end salary payments, small relative to the bank’s liquid assets.

II. A sudden multi-notch downgrade of the bank that coincides with lenders refusing to roll over its wholesale funding.

III. A predictable quarter-end rise in corporate drawdowns on credit lines, of a size the bank absorbs every quarter.

IV. A market-wide freeze in which repo funding is withdrawn across the banking industry.

Which of the events are high-impact, low-probability contingent liquidity events that the bank should address primarily through its CFP rather than through business-as-usual (BAU) funding and liquidity risk management?

options.text: II and IV only
I and III only
I, II, III and IV
II only

questions.solution:
Mapping four liquidity events to the CFP or to BAU liquidity risk management.

**Concept and theory**

GARP classifies contingent liquidity events along two dimensions: their estimated adverse impact and their probability. The two ends of this spectrum are handled by different machinery.

| End of spectrum | Typical example | Managed through |
|---|---|---|
| Low impact, high probability | routine deposit and drawdown swings | BAU funding and liquidity risk management |
| High impact, low probability | severe idiosyncratic or systemic stress | the CFP |

The logic is one of proportionality. Frequent, small events are absorbed within BAU funding and liquidity risk management. Rare but severe events are different: GARP notes that in a crisis the ability to convene management and start to develop contingent strategies and a plan of action would likely prove highly challenging without prior planning, and the actions they may require (large asset sales, business divestitures) are of a different order from BAU activity. The CFP exists to give a structured approach for developing and implementing the institution’s financial and operational strategies for exactly these events, during periods of severe market and financial stress.

This is where the stress test comes in. The stress test is the tool that quantifies the high-impact, low-probability end of the spectrum, and its results are inputs to the CFP. Note that the CFP’s high-impact end includes both institution-specific (idiosyncratic) and market-wide (systemic) stress: GARP’s stress scenarios cover both, and the availability of contingent actions depends on the systemic and/or idiosyncratic nature of the event. Schweser uses the vocabulary of “severity” and “frequency” instead of “impact” and “probability”; the meaning is the same.

**Applying it to this question**

Classify each event on both dimensions. Event I (month-end deposit swings, small relative to liquid assets) is high probability and low impact: BAU. Event III (quarter-end drawdowns of a size absorbed every quarter) is also high probability and low impact: BAU. Event II (multi-notch downgrade with wholesale lenders refusing to roll) is high impact and low probability, idiosyncratic: CFP. Event IV (industry-wide repo freeze) is high impact and low probability, systemic: CFP. The CFP set is II and IV.

**Fragile fact.** Impact high, probability low: CFP. Impact low, probability high: BAU. Systemic events are not excluded from the CFP.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Discuss the relationship between contingency funding planning and liquidity stress testing. **GARP:** Chapter 11, Section 11.1 “Actions in a Liquidity Crisis”; Section 11.4 “Scenarios and Liquidity Gap Analysis”. **Schweser:** LO 76.a. **GARP vs** **Schweser:** terminology only: GARP says “impact” and “probability”, Schweser says “severity” and “frequency”.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-11 a, where it is Q2 of 11.

a.reason: Option A selects exactly the two high-impact, low-probability events. GARP states that institutions manage the low-impact, high-probability end of the spectrum as part of BAU funding and liquidity risk management, and use CFPs for the high-impact, low-probability end.

b.reason: (Polarity flip). It assigns the low-impact, high-probability events (I and III) to the CFP, reversing the spectrum. B would be correct if the stem asked which events are handled through BAU funding and liquidity risk management.

c.reason: (Scope error). It extends the CFP to every liquidity event, including routine ones. The source splits the spectrum: only the high-impact, low-probability end goes to the CFP. C would be correct only if the stem asked which events the stress test or the bank’s overall liquidity risk management framework must be aware of.

d.reason: (Scope error). It keeps the idiosyncratic downgrade but drops the systemic repo freeze, as if the CFP covered only institution-specific events. GARP’s scenarios cover systemic and idiosyncratic risks, and contingent actions depend on the systemic and/or idiosyncratic nature of the stress. D would be correct only if the stem asked which events are idiosyncratic and severe.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Discuss the relationship between contingency funding planning and liquidity stress testing.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-11 a Q3
questions.question: An internal auditor at a Canadian bank is reviewing the opening section of the bank’s CFP policy, which is meant to position the CFP relative to BAU liquidity risk management and the liquidity stress testing framework. Which of the following statements best describes the position that the policy should take?

options.text: The CFP is the main tool for managing low-impact, high-probability liquidity events, while the rarer high-impact events are left to the liquidity stress testing framework to manage directly.
The CFP provides a structured approach for managing contingent liquidity events in normal market conditions, so that the stress testing framework can be reserved for periods of severe stress.
The CFP addresses contingent liquidity events of high impact and high probability, since these are the events that business-as-usual liquidity risk management is not designed to absorb.
The CFP provides a structured approach for managing high-impact, low-probability events during severe market and financial stress, while low-impact, high-probability events are handled in BAU.

questions.solution:
Opening section of a CFP policy: positioning the CFP against BAU and the stress test.

**Concept and theory**

A CFP policy must explain why the plan exists alongside the institution’s other liquidity tools. GARP gives the answer in three linked ideas. First, contingent liquidity events lie on a spectrum of impact and probability. Second, the low-impact, high-probability end is managed through BAU funding and liquidity risk management, while CFPs address the high-impact, low-probability end. Third, the CFP provides a structured approach for developing and implementing the institution’s financial and operational strategies for managing such events during periods of severe market and financial stress. Schweser summarises: CFPs provide a way to control for contingent liquidity events in times of extreme stress.

It helps to keep three tools apart:

| Tool | Role |
|---|---|
| BAU liquidity risk management | absorbs low-impact, high-probability events; its measures are the baseline for EWIs |
| Liquidity stress testing framework | measures and monitors the effects of severe systemic and idiosyncratic stresses on the liquidity profile; its results are inputs to the CFP |
| CFP | structured approach to act in severe stress: governance, contingent actions, escalation |

The stress test does not itself “manage” severe events: it quantifies them. The CFP is the plan of action. A policy that confused these roles, or that placed the CFP in normal conditions, would be misdirected from the first page. Schweser’s module quiz tests the same traps by flipping “low-frequency” to “high-frequency” and “extreme stress” to “normal times”.

**Applying it to this question**

The stem asks for the position the policy should take. Test each option on three attributes: which events the CFP covers (impact and probability), in which conditions it operates (severe stress), and what the other tools do. Only D gets all three right: high impact, low probability; severe market and financial stress; low-impact, high-probability events left to BAU.

**Fragile fact.** Two words to hold: “low probability” (not high) and “severe stress” (not normal times).

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Discuss the relationship between contingency funding planning and liquidity stress testing. **GARP:** Chapter 11, Section 11.1 “Actions in a Liquidity Crisis”; Section 11.4 “Scenarios and Liquidity Gap Analysis” (roles of the stress test and CFP). **Schweser:** LO 76.a. **GARP vs Schweser:** none; Schweser uses “severity/frequency” and “extreme stress” for GARP’s “impact/probability” and “severe market and financial stress”.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-11 a, where it is Q3 of 11.

a.reason: (Role misassignment). It hands the CFP’s role to BAU-type events and makes the stress testing framework the manager of severe events. In GARP the stress test measures severe events and feeds the CFP, which manages them. A would be correct for a description of BAU liquidity risk management, not of the CFP.

b.reason: (Scope or condition error). It places the CFP in normal market conditions. The CFP operates during periods of severe market and financial stress (Schweser: “times of extreme stress”). B would be correct only for a description of BAU liquidity risk management.

c.reason: (Polarity flip). It flips one dimension: the CFP addresses high-impact, low-probability events, not high-probability ones. C would be correct only if “high probability” were replaced by “low probability”.

d.reason: D restates the source: the CFP is a structured approach for developing and implementing financial and operational strategies to manage high-impact, low-probability contingent liquidity events during periods of severe market and financial stress, with the low-impact, high-probability end handled in BAU.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Discuss the relationship between contingency funding planning and liquidity stress testing.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-11 a Q4
questions.question: The CRO of a Brazilian universal bank is reviewing a validation report. The validators found that the CFP and the liquidity stress test are documented in separate manuals owned by different teams, and that nothing in either manual states what a stress test result means for the CFP. They recommend one change to create the explicit link between the two frameworks that is expected of a sound CFP. Which of the following recommendations is most appropriate?

options.text: Link the CFP to the stress test through a shared communication plan, so that the stress testing team and the crisis team issue messages to external stakeholders from one central script.
Link the CFP to the stress test through its limit structure and escalation levels, so that stress test results measured against limits map to defined CFP escalation levels.
Link the CFP to the business continuity and crisis management framework, so that key operational and communication protocols are reinforced during times of crisis.
Link the CFP to the capital plan through a single capital ratio trigger, so that the CFP is invoked only when the bank’s minimum capital requirement is breached.

questions.solution:
Validation finding: separate CFP and stress test manuals; which change creates the explicit link.

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s second design consideration says that the CFP is not a stand-alone tool but an integrated part of the institution’s liquidity risk management and firm-wide risk management frameworks, including enterprise risk management, capital management, and business continuity and crisis management. Within that integration, one link is singled out as explicit: the CFP should be explicitly linked to the liquidity risk measurement framework and the liquidity stress test, in particular through its limit structure and escalation levels. Schweser places the same idea under LO 76.a: the relationship between CFPs and liquidity stress testing is further established in terms of limits and escalation levels.

Why limits and escalation levels? A stress test measures the effects of stress on the liquidity profile, but a measurement on its own does not tell anyone what to do. Limits (and the risk appetite targets behind them) turn the measurement into a judgement, and escalation levels turn that judgement into graduated responses. GARP’s escalation section shows the chain at work: Level 1 could be triggered by stress test results indicating a greater decline in liquidity than the risk appetite targets, and it brings elevated monitoring and the convening of the liquidity crisis team. This is the mechanism by which a stress result moves the CFP.

| Linkage named in GARP | What it connects the CFP to |
|---|---|
| Limit structure and escalation levels | the liquidity risk measurement framework and the liquidity stress test |
| BAU liquidity risk measures as EWI foundation | BAU liquidity risk management |
| Operational and communication protocols | business continuity and crisis management |

The other linkages are real but connect the CFP to different frameworks.

**Applying it to this question**

The finding is that nothing tells the reader what a stress result means for the CFP. The required fix is the explicit stress-test link. Match each option to the framework it connects: A connects two teams through communications, C connects the CFP to business continuity, D connects it to capital. Only B connects the CFP to the stress test, and it does so through the mechanism GARP names.

**Fragile fact.** The explicit link is “limit structure and escalation levels”; communication and business continuity are links to other frameworks.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Discuss the relationship between contingency funding planning and liquidity stress testing. **GARP:** Chapter 11, Section 11.3 “Design Considerations”, II “Integrate with Broader Risk Management Frameworks”. **Schweser:** LO 76.a. **GARP vs** **Schweser:** none on content; GARP places the sentence under design consideration II, while Schweser places it under LO 76.a.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-11 a, where it is Q4 of 11.

a.reason: (Sibling swap). A communication plan is a separate CFP design consideration (consideration V) and a component of governance; it is not the mechanism that links the CFP to the stress test. A would be correct if the stem asked how to coordinate internal and external messaging in a crisis.

b.reason: B is GARP’s sentence: the CFP should be explicitly linked to the liquidity risk measurement framework and the liquidity stress test, in particular through its limit structure and escalation levels.

c.reason: (Sibling swap). The link to business continuity and crisis management is genuinely in GARP, but it reinforces operational and communication protocols; it does not connect the CFP to the stress test. C would be correct if the validators had found that the CFP was disconnected from the business continuity plan.

d.reason: (Scope or condition error). It replaces the liquidity link with a single capital trigger and restricts invocation to a capital breach. The CFP is triggered through liquidity limits and escalation levels informed by stress results; GARP integrates capital management with the CFP but does not make a capital breach the sole trigger. D would be correct only for a recovery plan keyed to capital ratios.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Discuss the relationship between contingency funding planning and liquidity stress testing.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-11 a Q5
questions.question: A senior risk analyst at a UK building society is designing the early warning indicators (EWIs) in the society’s CFP. A colleague argues that, because the CFP is used only in severe stress, each EWI should be calibrated from the values that the corresponding measure takes in the most severe stress scenario. Which of the following statements best describes the approach consistent with the relationship between the CFP and the society’s liquidity risk measurement and stress testing frameworks?

options.text: The liquidity risk measures used in BAU risk management serve as the foundation from which the CFP defines its EWIs, so that deterioration from the normal baseline is signalled early.
The EWIs should be defined from the values that liquidity measures take under stressed conditions, because the CFP is reserved for high-impact, low-probability events.
The EWIs should be defined from the capital adequacy measures used in BAU capital management, since liquidity measures only become informative once a crisis is underway.
The EWIs should be defined from BAU liquidity measures, but since the CFP is linked to the stress test only through scenarios, they need not connect to any limit or escalation level.

questions.solution:
Calibrating CFP early warning indicators: BAU baseline or stressed values.

**Concept and theory**

Early warning indicators (EWIs) are the CFP’s sensors. GARP describes them as a set of key risk indicators, made up of market and business measures and liquidity health measures, that provide advance signalling of potential liquidity problems on the horizon, so that management can take measured steps as the crisis escalates. GARP adds that such EWIs are generally most useful before or at the onset of a liquidity crisis and during the early stages of the CFP escalation levels.

Where do they come from? In the design consideration on integration, GARP gives the answer as an example of the CFP’s link to the liquidity risk measurement framework and the stress test: the liquidity risk measures used in the institution’s BAU risk management activities serve as a foundation from which the CFP defines its EWIs. Schweser: liquidity risk measures used during normal circumstances are a baseline for developing EWIs.

The logic is that an early warning is a deviation from normal. If the indicator were calibrated to the values seen in the most severe scenario, it would fire only once that scenario had largely arrived, which defeats the purpose of early warning. Building on BAU measures also means the CFP uses metrics that are already produced, understood and controlled, and GARP gives this as its example of the explicit link through the limit structure and escalation levels, so EWIs feed the escalation framework.

| Element | Source of calibration |
|---|---|
| EWI baseline | BAU (normal-times) liquidity risk measures |
| Escalation link | limit structure and escalation levels tied to the stress test |

**Applying it to this question**

The colleague’s argument infers from “the CFP is used in severe stress” that its indicators must be calibrated from stressed values. That inference is the trap. The source anchors EWIs in BAU measures and ties them to limits and escalation levels. A states this; the other three options each break one element.

**Fragile fact.** EWI baseline = normal-times (BAU) measures, not stressed values; the link runs through limits and escalation levels.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Discuss the relationship between contingency funding planning and liquidity stress testing. **GARP:** Chapter 11, Section 11.3, II “Integrate with Broader Risk Management Frameworks”; Section 11.4 “Monitoring and Escalation” (Early Warning Indicators). **Schweser:** LO 76.a. **GARP vs Schweser:** none; GARP says “BAU risk management activities”, Schweser says “normal circumstances”.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-11 a, where it is Q5 of 11.

a.reason: A matches GARP: the liquidity risk measures used in BAU risk management serve as the foundation from which the CFP defines its EWIs; the early-signal purpose follows from GARP’s description of EWIs as advance signalling, most useful before or at the onset of a crisis.

b.reason: (Polarity flip). It swaps normal for stressed conditions as the EWI baseline. B would be correct if the stem asked how the stress test calibrates the severity of its scenarios, not how the CFP defines its EWIs.

c.reason: (Sibling swap). It replaces BAU liquidity measures with capital adequacy measures. Capital is integrated with the CFP elsewhere, but the EWI foundation in GARP is liquidity risk measures. C would be correct only for a capital recovery plan.

d.reason: (Scope or condition error). It keeps the correct BAU foundation but drops the condition that the link to the stress test runs through the limit structure and escalation levels. D would be correct only if GARP said that scenarios were the sole connection, which it does not.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Discuss the relationship between contingency funding planning and liquidity stress testing.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-11 a Q6
questions.question: An internal auditor at a Chinese joint-stock bank finds that the stress scenarios in the bank’s CFP were written by treasury two years ago and now differ materially from the scenarios in the liquidity stress testing framework, which risk management refreshed this year. The CFP scenarios do, however, reference the bank’s recovery and resolution plan. Which of the following recommendations is most appropriate?

options.text: Keep the CFP scenarios as they are, because the CFP should be designed independently of the stress test so that it gives a second view of liquidity risk.
Align the CFP scenarios to the stress testing framework but drop the link to the recovery and resolution plan, because that plan addresses capital rather than liquidity.
Align the CFP scenarios to those in the stress testing framework and to other frameworks such as the recovery and resolution plan, while allowing the CFP to keep additional scenarios.
Replace the stress testing framework’s scenarios with the CFP’s scenarios, so that the stress test inherits the scenario set already used in the bank’s contingency planning.

questions.solution:
Audit finding: CFP scenarios out of line with the refreshed stress testing scenarios.

**Concept and theory**

The scenarios are where the CFP and the stress test meet most concretely. GARP’s guidance, under the component “Scenarios and Liquidity Gap Analysis”, is that institutions should align their CFP stress scenarios to those in the liquidity stress testing framework, as well as to other frameworks such as the recovery and resolution plans. Schweser: there should be consistency between the CFP stress scenarios and the liquidity stress testing ones, and the CFP stress scenarios should link to the recovery provisions.

Why align? If the CFP prepared for one set of crises while the stress test quantified another, the stress results (which are inputs to the CFP) would not map to any CFP response, and the limit and escalation link would break. Alignment means a stress result can be read straight across into a CFP scenario, an escalation level and a set of contingent actions. The link to recovery and resolution plans exists because liquidity is often a key driver of potential failure; GARP describes the CFP as a bridge between BAU liquidity risk management and recovery and resolution planning.

Alignment is not identity. GARP adds that, in addition to incorporating the outcomes of stress testing, the CFP itself may contain additional liquidity-related stress scenarios.

| CFP scenarios should | Source |
|---|---|
| be aligned to the stress testing scenarios | GARP 11.4; Schweser 76.c |
| also be aligned to recovery and resolution plans may add CFP-specific scenarios | GARP 11.4; Schweser “recovery provisions” GARP 11.4 |

**Applying it to this question**

The finding has two parts: the CFP scenarios have drifted from the stress test (a defect), and they reference the recovery and resolution plan (correct practice). The right recommendation fixes the first and keeps the second. C does both and preserves the freedom to hold additional scenarios.

**Fragile fact.** Align CFP scenarios to the stress test (and to recovery and resolution plans), not the other way round; alignment still allows extra CFP scenarios.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Discuss the relationship between contingency funding planning and liquidity stress testing. **GARP:** Chapter 11, Section 11.4 “Framework and Building Blocks”, “Scenarios and Liquidity Gap Analysis”; Section 11.2 (CFP as bridge to recovery and resolution planning). **Schweser:** LO 76.c (scenario section), applied here as part of the 76.a relationship. **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser says “recovery provisions”; GARP says “recovery and resolution plans”.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-11 a, where it is Q6 of 11.

a.reason: (Polarity flip). It recommends independence where GARP requires alignment. A would be correct only for an independent challenger model used in validation, which is not what the CFP scenarios are.

b.reason: (Scope error). It keeps the stress-test alignment but drops the alignment to the recovery and resolution plan, which GARP names explicitly. B would be correct only if the stem asked for the minimum alignment to the stress test alone.

c.reason: C restates GARP: align CFP stress scenarios to those in the liquidity stress testing framework and to other frameworks such as recovery and resolution plans; the CFP may also contain additional scenarios.

d.reason: (Polarity flip (direction)). It reverses the direction of the flow: stress test scenarios and results feed the CFP, not the reverse. D would be correct only if the stress testing framework were defined as a by-product of the CFP.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Discuss the relationship between contingency funding planning and liquidity stress testing.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-11 a Q7
questions.question: The head of treasury at a German Landesbank is presenting to newly hired analysts on how responsibilities are divided between the liquidity stress testing framework and the CFP once the CFP scenarios have been aligned to the stress test. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: The stress testing framework provides the tactical mechanism for escalating a developing crisis to management, while the CFP ensures that the effects of stress on the liquidity profile are measured and monitored.

The stress testing framework ensures that the effects of stress on the liquidity profile are measured and monitored, while the CFP provides a tactical mechanism for escalating a developing crisis and ensuring actionable responses.
Both frameworks measure and monitor the effects of stress on the liquidity profile, while escalating a developing crisis to management is left to the board of directors outside both frameworks.

The stress testing framework ensures that the effects of stress on the liquidity profile are measured and monitored, while the CFP guarantees that the institution survives every scenario the stress test measures.

questions.solution:
Who does what once scenarios are aligned: stress testing framework versus CFP.

**Concept and theory**

After requiring alignment of scenarios, GARP describes a division of labour between the two frameworks. The liquidity stress testing scenarios cover systemic and idiosyncratic risks, market (asset) and funding liquidity, and short-term and prolonged periods. Then:

| Framework | Role (GARP 11.4) |
|---|---|
| Liquidity stress testing framework | ensure that the effects of these stresses on the institution’s liquidity profile are appropriately measured and monitored |
| CFP | provide a tactical mechanism for escalating a developing crisis to management’s attention and ensuring actionable responses are available |

Schweser condenses the CFP side as: the CFP’s role is to make management aware of an upcoming crisis along with feasible methods of remedying the situation.

The split mirrors the input relationship in Section 11.1. The stress test is analytical: it quantifies how stress would affect cash flows, buffers and survival. The CFP is operational: it turns those signals into escalation (through EWIs, limits and escalation levels) and into a menu of actions with governance around them. Neither replaces the other. A stress test without a CFP produces numbers nobody is organised to act on; a CFP without a stress test has no quantified view of what it must respond to.

A further point: the CFP does not promise success. GARP stresses that the CFP cannot anticipate all possible situations and must leave room for management judgement; it ensures that actionable responses are available, not that survival is guaranteed.

**Applying it to this question**

The presenter needs the statement that assigns measurement and monitoring to the stress test and escalation and actionable responses to the CFP. B does exactly that; A swaps the two; C removes escalation from the CFP; D overstates the CFP’s role.

**Fragile fact.** Stress test: measure and monitor. CFP: escalate and respond. Swapping these is the classic role trap.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Discuss the relationship between contingency funding planning and liquidity stress testing. **GARP:** Chapter 11, Section 11.4 “Scenarios and Liquidity Gap Analysis”; Section 11.3, III (cannot anticipate all situations). **Schweser:** LO 76.c (scenario section). **GARP vs Schweser:** none; Schweser condenses the CFP role as making management aware of an upcoming crisis with feasible remedies.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-11 a, where it is Q7 of 11.

a.reason: (Role misassignment). It swaps the roles of the two frameworks. A would be correct if the framework labels were exchanged.

b.reason: B paraphrases GARP: the stress testing framework should ensure that the effects of stresses on the liquidity profile are appropriately measured and monitored, and the CFP in turn should provide a tactical mechanism for escalating a developing crisis to management’s attention and ensuring actionable responses are available.

c.reason: (Role misassignment). It strips escalation out of the CFP and hands it to the board outside both frameworks. Escalation is the CFP’s tactical role; the board is an advisor within the CFP governance. C would be correct only if the stem described a bank with no CFP.

d.reason: (Absolute claim). It turns “ensuring actionable responses are available” into a guarantee of survival in every scenario. D would be correct only if “guarantees that the institution survives” were replaced by “ensures that actionable responses are available”.

questions.loText: Discuss the relationship between contingency funding planning and liquidity stress testing.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-11 a Q8
questions.question: A senior risk analyst at a US bank holding company proposes three scenarios for the CFP: the bank’s intraday debit cap with Fedwire is exceeded; a specific clearing counterparty fails; and Federal Home Loan Bank advances become unavailable. The stress testing team objects that none of the three is in the liquidity stress test or covered by its limit structure. Which of the following responses to the objection is most accurate?

options.text: The objection is valid, because CFP scenarios must be identical to the stress testing scenarios; the three scenarios should be removed from the CFP.
The scenarios may stay in the CFP only after each has been added to the liquidity stress test and assigned a limit within its limit structure.
The scenarios belong in the CFP because they are more likely than the stress testing scenarios, so they require contingency plans more urgently.
The CFP may contain additional liquidity-related scenarios outside the stress test’s monitoring and limit structure, to ensure effective contingency plans exist for such events.

questions.solution:
Three proposed CFP scenarios that sit outside the stress test and its limit structure.

**Concept and theory**

Alignment of scenarios (Q6) does not make the CFP a copy of the stress test. GARP adds a second, complementary idea: in addition to incorporating the outcomes of the institution’s liquidity stress testing, the CFP itself may contain additional liquidity-related stress scenarios. These scenarios sit outside the institution’s broader liquidity risk monitoring and limit structure (as contained within the liquidity stress test), and their purpose is to ensure effective contingency plans are in place for certain events that could potentially impact liquidity. GARP’s examples are a breach of the intraday debit cap with Fedwire, the failure of specific counterparties, and Federal Home Loan Bank funding becoming unavailable.

Why would a CFP need scenarios that the stress test does not carry? The stress test’s scenarios sit within the institution’s broader liquidity risk monitoring and limit structure. GARP’s examples are specific events (a payment-system cap, a named counterparty, a particular funding source) for which the institution still needs an effective contingency plan. The CFP is the playbook, so GARP allows it to plan for them even though they sit outside the stress test’s monitoring and limit structure.

| Scenario type | Where it lives |
|---|---|
| Stress testing scenarios | stress test, monitored against limits; outcomes incorporated in the CFP |
| Additional CFP scenarios | CFP only; outside the stress test’s monitoring and limit structure |

Schweser adds a gloss that these extra scenarios help strengthen contingency plans for possible (but perhaps less likely) events beyond the firm’s normal scope of analysis. GARP itself does not rank their likelihood; it justifies them by the need for contingency plans for specific events.

**Applying it to this question**

The stress testing team’s objection rests on the premise that a CFP scenario must be part of the stress test and its limit structure. The source rejects that premise. The three proposed scenarios are GARP’s own examples of CFP-only scenarios, so they may stay. Only D gives the correct reason.

**Fragile fact.** CFP-only scenarios sit outside the stress test’s monitoring and limit structure; Schweser calls them “perhaps less likely”, never more likely.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Discuss the relationship between contingency funding planning and liquidity stress testing. **GARP:** Chapter 11, Section 11.4 “Scenarios and Liquidity Gap Analysis”. **Schweser:** LO 76.c (scenario section). **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser adds “possible (but perhaps less likely)”; GARP does not characterise likelihood and instead says the scenarios are outside the stress test’s monitoring and limit structure. GARP used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-11 a, where it is Q8 of 11.

a.reason: (Scope or condition error). It turns “aligned to” into “identical to” and so forbids any extra scenario. A would be correct only if the stem asked whether the CFP may omit the stress testing scenarios, for which alignment is required.

b.reason: (Scope or condition error). It adds a precondition that GARP does not impose: that each CFP scenario first be built into the stress test with a limit. GARP explicitly says these scenarios are outside the stress test’s limit structure. B would be correct only for a scenario intended to drive limit-based escalation.

c.reason: (Polarity flip). It justifies the scenarios by claiming they are more likely than the stress test scenarios. GARP justifies them by the need for contingency plans for specific events, and Schweser describes them as possible but perhaps less likely. C would be correct only if “more likely” were replaced by a reason based on the need for event-specific contingency plans.

d.reason: D restates GARP: the CFP may contain additional liquidity-related stress scenarios that, while outside the broader liquidity risk monitoring and limit structure of the stress test, ensure effective contingency plans are in place for events that could impact liquidity.

questions.loText: Discuss the relationship between contingency funding planning and liquidity stress testing.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-11 a Q9
questions.question:
The CRO of an Australian mutual bank reviews the latest monthly liquidity stress test. The bank’s CFP uses three escalation levels. No market or institution-specific event has yet affected the bank’s business, and its credit spreads are unchanged.

| Measure | Risk appetite target | Stress test result |
|---|---|---|
| Survival horizon, combined scenario (days, minimum) | 90 | 72 |
| Stressed liquidity surplus (AUD billion, minimum) | 2.0 | 1.4 |
| CET1 capital ratio (%, minimum) | 10.5 | 11.8 |

Which of the following responses is most consistent with the link between the stress test and the CFP?

options.text: No CFP response is needed, because stress test results only size the liquidity buffer and the CFP is triggered only by actual outflows.
Move directly to Level 3 and begin selling business units, because the stressed surplus is below the risk appetite target.
Treat the results as a potential Level 1 trigger: elevated monitoring of market conditions and business impact, with the liquidity crisis team convened.
Treat the results as a Level 2 trigger, because a stress test shortfall means market events are already adversely impacting the business.

questions.solution:
Monthly stress test shows shortfalls against risk appetite; which CFP response follows.

**Concept and theory**

The explicit link between the stress test and the CFP runs through limits and escalation levels (Q4). The escalation section of the chapter shows how that link operates in practice. GARP notes that there are no specific guidelines on the number of escalation levels (three to five are common) and illustrates three:

| Level | GARP description |
|---|---|
| Level 1 | initial level: elevated monitoring of market conditions and the impact on business segments and performance; could be triggered by stress test results indicating a greater decline in liquidity than the institution’s risk appetite targets and/or a shift in market perception; the liquidity crisis team (LCT) is convened |
| Level 2 | noticeable market and/or idiosyncratic events are adversely impacting the business and liquidity profile; closer monitoring of causes of deterioration |
| Level 3 | later stages: dramatic steps such as significant curtailing of businesses or sales of businesses; focus on survival |

So a stress test result measured against risk appetite is a named trigger for the initial escalation level. This is the operational meaning of “stress test results are inputs to the CFP decision framework”. At Level 1, GARP says the convening of the LCT prompts closer internal coordination and a communication plan to keep external stakeholders informed, with monitoring focused on forward-looking measures of liquidity health and market perception. Movement between levels, up or down, is explicitly considered and approved by the LCT, and management’s expert judgement remains important. Schweser gives the same trigger as stress test results suggesting a greater than desirable reduction in liquidity.

**Applying it to this question**

Read the table against the targets:

Survival horizon shortfall = 90 − 72 = 18 days below the minimum

Stressed surplus shortfall = 2.0 − 1.4 = AUD 0.6 billion below the minimum

CET1 headroom = 11.8 − 10.5 = 1.3 percentage points above the minimum

Both liquidity stress measures show a greater decline in liquidity than the risk appetite targets. The stem also says that no event has yet affected the business and spreads are unchanged, so the conditions for Level 2 (events already adversely impacting the business) and Level 3 (late-stage survival actions) are absent. The CET1 ratio is an irrelevant input: it is a capital measure, comfortably above its minimum, and does not alter the liquidity escalation reading. The fitting response is a Level 1 trigger with the LCT convened.

**Fragile fact.** A stress result worse than risk appetite is a Level 1 trigger (elevated monitoring, LCT convened), not an automatic jump to drastic actions; the capital ratio is a distractor.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Discuss the relationship between contingency funding planning and liquidity stress testing. **GARP:** Chapter 11, Section 11.4 “Monitoring and Escalation”, “Escalation Levels”; Section 11.3, II (link through escalation levels). **Schweser:** LO 76.a (limits and escalation levels) and LO 76.c (escalation levels). **GARP vs Schweser:** GARP’s trigger is “greater decline in liquidity than the institution’s risk appetite targets”; Schweser says “greater than desirable reduction in liquidity”. Survival horizon and stressed surplus labels are illustrative stem metrics; the chapter defines the trigger in general terms.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-11 a, where it is Q9 of 11.

a.reason: (Scope or condition error). It narrows the use of stress results to buffer sizing and requires actual outflows before the CFP responds. GARP names stress results as an input to the CFP and as a Level 1 trigger. A would be correct only if both stress measures were within their risk appetite targets.

b.reason: (Scope or condition error). It jumps to the late-stage Level 3 actions on the strength of a stress result alone. Level 3 belongs to the later stages of a crisis that is already under way. B would be correct only if the stem described a crisis in its later stages with survival at stake.

c.reason: C matches GARP: Level 1 represents elevated monitoring over market conditions and the impact on business segments and performance, and could be triggered by stress test results indicating a greater decline in liquidity than the risk appetite targets; the LCT is convened.

d.reason: (Sibling swap). It attaches the Level 2 description (events already adversely impacting the business and liquidity profile) to a stress result. Here no event has yet hit the business. D would be correct if the stem reported noticeable market or idiosyncratic events already damaging the bank’s business and liquidity.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Discuss the relationship between contingency funding planning and liquidity stress testing.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-11 a Q10
questions.question: A member of the risk committee of a Japanese trust bank notes that the bank’s capital and liquidity management practices have historically been run in separate silos, and asks what an integrated approach to liquidity and capital would add to the relationship between the CFP and stress testing. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: It brings a common set of EWIs and a more comprehensive view of the impact of liquidity stress test results and proposed response actions on capital positions, and vice versa.
It allows the capital stress test to replace the liquidity stress test as the CFP’s input, because a capital shortfall always arises before any liquidity shortfall does.
It brings a view of the impact of capital stress test results on liquidity positions, while liquidity stress results and response actions stay outside capital planning.
It brings separate sets of EWIs for capital and for liquidity, so that each framework keeps fully independent triggers for its own contingency actions.

questions.solution:
What an integrated liquidity and capital approach adds to the CFP and stress testing relationship.

**Concept and theory**

In Section 11.5 (“Liquidity and Capital”) GARP observes that capital and liquidity management practices have historically been highly siloed, and that institutions have recently started to bring a more integrated approach and view to these areas. GARP lists what this integration brings:

- a common set of EWIs;
- a more comprehensive view of the impact of liquidity-specific stress test results and proposed response actions on capital positions, and vice versa;
- stronger alignment of the integrated liquidity and capital stress testing and contingency plans to other enterprise-wide applications, including recovery and resolution plans, capital management and ERM.

This extends the CFP and stress testing relationship in two ways. First, it widens the set of consequences considered: a liquidity stress result is no longer read only for its cash impact but also for its effect on capital, and a contingent action (for example, a fire sale of assets or a business divestiture) is assessed for both liquidity relief and capital cost. Second, it is two-directional: capital stress results and capital actions are likewise read for their liquidity consequences. The earlier design consideration on integration points the same way: the CFP is an integrated part of firm-wide frameworks including capital management. Elsewhere GARP also asks that escalation trigger events be analysed for their association to capital adequacy.

Schweser does not cover Section 11.5 under LO 76.a; this question draws on GARP only.

**Applying it to this question**

The committee member asks what integration adds. Check each option for three features in GARP’s list: common EWIs, impact of liquidity stress results and response actions on capital, and the “vice versa” direction. A contains all three. The other options either replace one framework with the other, keep only one direction, or split the EWIs.

**Fragile fact.** Integration means common EWIs and impacts read both ways (liquidity on capital and capital on liquidity).

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Discuss the relationship between contingency funding planning and liquidity stress testing. **GARP:** Chapter 11, Section 11.5 “Additional Considerations”, “Liquidity and Capital”; Section 11.3, II. **Schweser:** not covered under LO 76.a. **GARP vs** **Schweser:** GARP-only content; no conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-11 a, where it is Q10 of 11.

a.reason: A is GARP’s sentence: the integrated approach will help bring a common set of EWIs and a more comprehensive view of the impact of liquidity-specific stress test results and proposed response actions on capital positions, and vice versa.

b.reason: (Absolute claim). It asserts that a capital shortfall always precedes any liquidity shortfall and lets the capital stress test replace the liquidity stress test. GARP integrates the two; it does not rank them or substitute one for the other. B would be correct only if “replace” were “complement”.

c.reason: (Scope error). It keeps only one direction (capital to liquidity) and leaves liquidity results and response actions outside capital planning. GARP’s integrated view runs both ways (“and vice versa”). C would be correct only for the siloed, pre-integration practice GARP describes as historical.

d.reason: (Polarity flip). It replaces “a common set of EWIs” with separate sets and independent triggers, which is the siloed practice that integration removes. D would be correct if the stem asked about the historical, siloed approach.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Discuss the relationship between contingency funding planning and liquidity stress testing.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-11 a Q11
questions.question:
A risk consultant is validating the liquidity stress testing scenario set of a Canadian deposit-taking institution, to which the institution’s CFP stress scenarios are aligned. The institution’s liquidity coverage ratio is currently 128%.

| Scenario | Source of stress | Liquidity type | Horizon (days) |
|---|---|---|---|
| S1: Name-specific rating downgrade | Idiosyncratic | Funding | 30 |
| S2: Market-wide repo freeze | Systemic | Funding | 30 |
| S3: Fire sale in bond markets | Systemic | Market (asset) | 30 |
| S4: Deposit run after a fraud event | Idiosyncratic | Funding | 30 |

Which of the following conclusions is most appropriate?

options.text: The set is deficient because it contains systemic scenarios; market-wide stress belongs in the central bank’s stress test rather than in the institution’s own scenarios.
The set is deficient because every scenario uses a short-term horizon; the scenarios should also address prolonged stress periods.
The set is deficient because it contains a market (asset) liquidity scenario; scenarios aligned to a contingency funding plan should address funding liquidity only.
The set is complete, because it covers both systemic and idiosyncratic risks and both market (asset) liquidity and funding liquidity.

questions.solution:
Validating the coverage of a stress scenario set to which the CFP scenarios are aligned.

**Concept and theory**

Because CFP stress scenarios are aligned to the liquidity stress testing scenarios (Q6), the quality of the CFP depends on the coverage of the stress test. GARP specifies that coverage on three dimensions, in the same paragraph that sets out the alignment and the division of labour:

| Dimension | Both ends must be covered |
|---|---|
| Source of stress | systemic (general market) and idiosyncratic (institution-specific) |
| Type of liquidity | market (asset) liquidity and funding liquidity |
| Time | short-term and prolonged stress periods |

The stress testing framework must then ensure that the effects of these stresses on the liquidity profile are appropriately measured and monitored, and the CFP turns them into escalation and actionable responses. A gap on any dimension passes straight into the CFP: if no prolonged scenario is tested, the CFP receives no stress result for a crisis that persists beyond the short term, and its contingent actions may be sized and timed only for a short shock. GARP’s emphasis on timing in the contingent actions component (the timing and pattern of the expected shortfall) shows why the horizon matters.

Schweser summarises the same list: liquidity stress testing encompasses systemic and idiosyncratic risks, together with market liquidity and funding liquidity, for stress periods in both the short and long term. A GARP practice-exam item tests the “solely institution-specific” version of this trap; this question tests the time dimension.

**Applying it to this question**

Score the set on each dimension. Source of stress: S1 and S4 are idiosyncratic, S2 and S3 are systemic, so both are covered. Type of liquidity: S1, S2 and S4 are funding, S3 is market (asset), so both are covered. Time: every scenario has a 30-day horizon, so prolonged stress is missing. The deficiency is the horizon. The liquidity coverage ratio of 128% is an irrelevant input: it describes the current position, not the coverage of the scenario set.

**Fragile fact.** Three pairs, not two: systemic and idiosyncratic, market and funding, short-term and prolonged.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Discuss the relationship between contingency funding planning and liquidity stress testing. **GARP:** Chapter 11, Section 11.4 “Scenarios and Liquidity Gap Analysis”. **Schweser:** LO 76.c (scenario section). **GARP vs Schweser:** none; Schweser says “short and long term” for GARP’s “short-term and prolonged”.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-11 a, where it is Q11 of 11.

a.reason: (Role misassignment). It assigns systemic stress to the central bank’s stress test rather than the institution’s own. GARP requires the institution’s scenarios to cover systemic (general market) risk. A would be correct only in reverse: a set with no systemic scenario at all would be deficient.

b.reason: B identifies the missing dimension. GARP states that the stress testing scenarios cover systemic and idiosyncratic risks and address market and funding liquidity over short-term and prolonged stress periods.

c.reason: (Sibling swap). It confines the scenarios to funding liquidity, swapping the CFP’s focus on funding for the stress test’s required coverage of both market (asset) and funding liquidity. C would be correct only if GARP restricted the scenarios to funding liquidity, which it does not.

d.reason: (Scope or condition error). It checks two of the three dimensions and drops the time condition. D would be correct if at least one scenario covered a prolonged stress period.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Describe best practices in the design of a sound contingency funding plan.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-11 b Q1
questions.question:
A risk consultant engaged by a Spanish savings bank is presenting a short briefing to the bank’s newly hired treasury analysts on how a sound contingency funding plan (CFP) should be designed. The briefing contains the following statements:

I. Because no universal CFP can cover all types of institutions and situations, a set of key design considerations should guide the bank when it designs or refreshes its own plan.

II. A sound CFP is best built as a stand-alone treasury tool, kept apart from enterprise risk management and capital management so that it is not slowed by their controls in a crisis.

III. Involving appropriate stakeholder groups helps capture the right elements of the CFP in its design and supports successful coordination when the plan is executed.

IV. Because rumours can spread quickly, the communication plan should concentrate on internal coordination, with counterparties, clients and regulators informed only once the crisis has passed.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.text: I, II and III only
I, III and IV only
I and III only
III only

questions.solution:
Briefing to new treasury analysts: which statements about sound CFP design are correct.

**Concept and theory**

A contingency funding plan (CFP) is the institution’s playbook for high-impact, low-probability liquidity events: it sets out how the firm will recognise a developing liquidity crisis and which financial and operational actions it will take. GARP notes that formal CFPs have gained importance as market disruptions became more common, yet institutions still differ widely in coverage and detail. Supervisors expect each CFP to be tailored to the institution’s own business and risk profile.

Because of that diversity, GARP does not prescribe one model. It states that no universal CFP exists that can cover all types of institutions and situations, and instead lists five key design considerations that firms should keep in mind when designing or refreshing their plans:

| Design consideration | Core idea |
|---|---|
| I. Aligned to business and risk profiles | Cover the firm’s actual activities, products, geographies, FX and legal entities; tie the RAS to the CFP through quantifiable EWIs, limits, escalation levels; refresh as the profile changes |
| II. Integrated with broader risk management frameworks | Not a stand-alone tool: part of liquidity risk management, ERM, capital management, business continuity and crisis management |
| III. Operational and actionable, but flexible playbook | Menu of actions by scenario and graduated severity; balance between specified actions and management discretion |
| IV. Inclusive of appropriate stakeholder groups | Committees, business units, finance, treasury, risk, operations and technology, for design and for execution |
| V. Supported by a communication plan | Coordinated, timely internal and external communication to sustain confidence |

These five are the whole of LO 76.b in Schweser; the components (governance roles, gap analysis, contingent actions, escalation, reporting) belong to LO 76.c.

**Applying it to this question**

Statement I restates GARP’s preamble to Section 11.3: no universal CFP, so design considerations guide each firm’s design or refresh. True. Statement II contradicts consideration II: the CFP is explicitly “not a stand-alone tool”. False. Statement III paraphrases consideration IV, which says stakeholder involvement captures the appropriate elements of the CFP in design and ensures coordination in execution. True. Statement IV contradicts consideration V, which calls for timely external communication to clients, analysts, counterparties and regulators during the crisis. False. Only I and III survive.

**Fragile fact.** “Not a stand-alone tool” (integration) and “timely external communication during the crisis” are the two directions most often reversed in distractors.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Describe best practices in the design of a sound contingency funding plan.

**GARP:** Chapter 11, Section 11.3 “Design Considerations” (preamble and I to V); context from 11.1 and 11.2. Schweser LO 76.b.

**GARP vs Schweser:** none on content; Schweser lists the five considerations without GARP’s “no universal CFP” preamble.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-11 b, where it is Q1 of 12.

a.reason: (Polarity flip). Accepting Statement II flips GARP’s statement that the CFP is not a stand-alone tool but an integrated part of liquidity risk management, ERM and capital management. Integration is meant to let the CFP use established controls, not to avoid them. A would be correct only if the stem asked about a firm with no other risk frameworks to integrate with, which no sound design assumes.

b.reason: (Scope or condition error). Accepting Statement IV narrows the communication plan to internal coordination and moves external communication to after the crisis. GARP says external communication with timely and accurate information is critical during the crisis, to reinforce confidence and stop rumours from spreading. B would be correct only if the statement said internal coordination must accompany, not replace, external communication.

c.reason: C is correct because Statements I and III are faithful restatements of GARP Section 11.3 (the preamble and consideration IV), while II and IV each reverse or narrow a design consideration.

d.reason: (Absolute claim). Rejecting Statement I implies that a single universal CFP could serve every institution, so design considerations would be unnecessary. GARP states the opposite. D would be correct only if the stem asked which statement concerns stakeholder groups alone.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Describe best practices in the design of a sound contingency funding plan.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-11 b Q2
questions.question: A senior risk analyst at a Singapore banking group is reviewing the group’s contingency funding plan (CFP). The parent bank is funded mainly with SGD retail deposits, but the group also owns a separately incorporated subsidiary in Hong Kong, raises USD wholesale funding through its London branch, and has just launched a structured deposit product. The current CFP covers only the parent’s SGD retail deposit base. Which recommendation best reflects best practice in aligning the CFP to the group’s business and risk profiles?

options.text: Extend the CFP to cover the group’s full scope of business activities, products and asset classes, geographic and FX coverage, and legal entity structures.
Keep the CFP focused on the SGD deposit base, because integration with the group’s capital management framework already covers the subsidiary and the USD funding.
Replace the CFP with the standard template issued by the supervisor, because a single CFP design that suits all institutions ensures comparability across banks.
Extend the CFP to the subsidiary and the USD funding only after a stress event has revealed liquidity gaps in those parts of the group’s business.

questions.solution:
Singapore group whose CFP covers only the parent’s SGD deposit base: how to align it.

**Concept and theory**

The first design consideration is that the CFP must be aligned to the institution’s specific business and risk profiles. The motivation is simple: a liquidity crisis attacks wherever the firm is actually exposed. A plan that covers only one funding source or one legal entity leaves the rest of the group without pre-planned triggers or actions, even though a run on a subsidiary, a freeze in a foreign currency market, or the behaviour of a new product can drain the group’s liquidity.

GARP (Section 11.3, I) lists the dimensions the CFP should reflect:

| Dimension | Example of what the CFP must reflect |
|---|---|
| Scope of business activities | Retail, wholesale, trading, payments |
| Products and asset classes | New deposit products, structured products, loans, securities |
| Geographic and FX coverage | Branches and markets abroad; currencies in which the firm funds itself |
| Legal entity structures | Separately incorporated subsidiaries with their own liquidity |

The same idea recurs in the supervisory guidance summarised in Section 11.1: a CFP, or a collective set of CFPs, should be tailored to the institution’s businesses, subsidiaries, legal entities, products, asset classes and geographic and FX coverage. Schweser’s condensed list names business activities, products, asset classes, geographic coverage and foreign exchange, but omits legal entity structures; GARP includes them, and GARP governs content.

**Applying it to this question**

The stem describes four exposures outside the current plan: a separately incorporated Hong Kong subsidiary (legal entity), USD wholesale funding through London (geographic and FX coverage), a new structured deposit (product), and the group’s broader activities. The plan covers only the parent’s SGD retail deposits. The design consideration requires the CFP to reflect all of these dimensions, so the fix is to extend coverage to the group’s full business and risk profile.

**Fragile fact.** Four dimensions, and GARP’s list includes legal entity structures (Schweser’s list does not): a subsidiary is a reason to extend the CFP.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Describe best practices in the design of a sound contingency funding plan.

**GARP:** Chapter 11, Section 11.3 “I. Align to Business and Risk Profiles”; Section 11.1 supervisory guidance. Schweser LO 76.b, “Alignment with business and risk profiles”.

**GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser omits legal entity structures from the list; GARP followed.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-11 b, where it is Q2 of 12.

a.reason: A restates GARP’s alignment consideration: the CFP should be considered in the context of the firm’s scope of business activities, products and asset classes, geographic and FX coverage, and legal entity structures.

b.reason: (Sibling swap). B borrows consideration II (integration with capital management) and treats it as a substitute for consideration I (coverage of the business profile). Integration lets the CFP reference established controls; it does not give the CFP liquidity triggers or actions for an uncovered subsidiary or currency. B would be correct only if the stem asked how to make the CFP consistent with existing controls, and even then it would not justify leaving exposures uncovered.

c.reason: (Absolute claim). C assumes one CFP design suits every institution. GARP states that no universal CFP exists and that each plan must be tailored to the firm’s own profile. C would be correct only if the stem asked how to make reporting to the supervisor comparable, not how to design the plan.

d.reason: (Scope or condition error). D makes coverage conditional on a stress event first exposing the gap. The CFP is meant to be in place before the crisis, so alignment is an ex ante design requirement. D would be correct only if the stem asked when lessons from an actual event should be fed into the next refresh.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Describe best practices in the design of a sound contingency funding plan.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-11 b Q3
questions.question:
An internal auditor at an Australian commercial bank with total assets of AUD 64 billion is testing whether the bank’s contingency funding plan (CFP) is consistent with its board-approved risk appetite statement (RAS). Extracts from the two documents are shown below.

| Element | RAS (board-approved) | CFP (current wording) |
|---|---|---|
| Funding concentration | No single provider above 8% of total funding | Early warning indicator: “watch for heavy reliance on any one funder” |
| Liquid assets to volatile liabilities | At least 110% | Limit: “maintain an adequate cushion” |
| Escalation | Report to the board if either metric breaches its limit | “Escalate when management considers that conditions have deteriorated” |

Which recommendation is most consistent with best practice in the design of a sound CFP?

options.text: Retain the CFP’s qualitative wording, because a CFP must be a flexible playbook and fixed numbers would remove the discretion that management needs in a crisis.
Ask the board to restate the RAS in the same qualitative terms as the CFP, so that the two documents use consistent language and cannot conflict.
Quantify the CFP’s limits in line with the RAS, but keep its early warning indicators and escalation levels descriptive, since these are set in BAU monitoring.
Restate the CFP’s early warning indicators, limits and escalation levels in quantifiable terms that tie back to the metrics in the board-approved RAS.

questions.solution:
Auditor finds that a CFP uses qualitative EWIs, limits and escalation wording against a quantified RAS.

**Concept and theory**

The risk appetite statement (RAS) is the board’s statement of how much risk the institution is willing to accept, including liquidity risk, usually expressed through metrics and limits. A CFP that is to act on that appetite must speak the same language. GARP’s first design consideration says institutions should ensure consistency by aligning their RAS to the CFP framework through quantifiable early warning indicators (EWIs), limits and escalation levels. Schweser condenses this as EWIs, limits and escalation levels that are quantitative in nature.

Why quantifiable? Three reasons follow from the role of each tool:

| Tool | What quantification achieves |
|---|---|
| Early warning indicators | An objective signal that conditions are moving toward the appetite boundary |
| Limits | A clear line whose breach is unambiguous and can be audited |
| Escalation levels | A defined point at which the plan moves to the next stage, so the move is not left to mood |

Without numbers, the board cannot tell whether the CFP will activate at the boundary it approved, and two managers could read the same wording differently. Quantification does not conflict with flexibility: in consideration III the flexibility concerns which contingency actions management chooses as a crisis evolves, not whether the indicators that signal the crisis can be measured.

**Applying it to this question**

Each RAS row is a number (8% concentration cap, 110% minimum liquid assets to volatile liabilities, a breach-based board report). Each CFP row is a phrase (“heavy reliance”, “adequate cushion”, “when management considers”). All three tools named in the design consideration (EWI, limit, escalation) are qualitative, so the fix is to quantify all three and tie them to the RAS metrics. The total assets of AUD 64 billion are irrelevant: the design requirement applies whatever the bank’s size.

**Fragile fact.** All three tools, EWIs, limits and escalation levels, are to be quantifiable; flexibility belongs to actions, not to indicators.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Describe best practices in the design of a sound contingency funding plan.

**GARP:** Chapter 11, Section 11.3 “I. Align to Business and Risk Profiles”. Schweser LO 76.b, “Alignment with business and risk profiles”.

**GARP vs Schweser:** none; GARP says “quantifiable”, Schweser “quantitative in nature”.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-11 b, where it is Q3 of 12.

a.reason: (Sibling swap). A takes the flexibility of consideration III (discretion over contingency actions) and applies it to the indicators and limits of consideration I. GARP’s flexibility is about choosing actions as the crisis evolves; the triggers themselves are to be quantifiable. A would be correct only if the stem asked whether the plan should fix in advance every action to be taken at each trigger.

b.reason: (Polarity flip). B reverses the direction of alignment by degrading the RAS to qualitative terms. Consistency is supposed to come from quantifying the CFP, not from removing numbers from the board’s appetite. B would be correct only if the RAS were the document lacking metrics and the CFP were already quantified.

c.reason: (Scope or condition error). C quantifies only one of the three tools GARP names. EWIs and escalation levels must also be quantifiable. That BAU measures are the foundation for EWIs (a point Schweser places in LO 76.a) does not make the CFP’s EWIs descriptive. C would be correct only if the stem had asked about limits alone.

d.reason: D applies GARP’s requirement in full: the RAS is aligned to the CFP through quantifiable EWIs, limits and escalation levels.

questions.loText: Describe best practices in the design of a sound contingency funding plan.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-11 b Q4
questions.question:
The treasurer of a mid-sized Brazilian bank notes that its contingency funding plan (CFP) was last refreshed three years ago under a fixed review cycle. Since then the bank has launched a BRL digital deposit account and entered payroll lending, while the central bank’s policy rate and market volatility have risen sharply. The board is about to begin its annual strategic planning exercise. The treasurer considers four proposals:

I. Refresh the CFP now to reflect the new deposit product and the new lending business.

II. Refresh the CFP to reflect the changed macroeconomic and market environment.

III. Develop the next CFP refresh as part of, or in parallel with, the strategic planning exercise.

IV. Avoid changes to the CFP between scheduled reviews, so that the plan stays identical to the version last approved.

Which proposals are consistent with best practice?

options.text: I and II only
I, II and III only
I, II, III and IV
II and III only

questions.solution:
Brazilian bank’s stale CFP: which refresh proposals are consistent with best practice.

**Concept and theory**

A CFP aligned to the business and risk profile at one date will drift out of alignment as that profile changes. GARP’s first design consideration therefore adds that the CFP should be refreshed accordingly as the profile changes over time, and it names two sources of change:

| Source of change | Examples given by GARP |
|---|---|
| Internal | Corporate and business strategies change; new products and services are introduced |
| External | The macroeconomic and market environments evolve |

GARP then describes a leading practice that goes beyond periodic updates. Leading institutions take a more proactive stance by incorporating the CFP as part of, or in parallel with, their strategic planning exercises. The effect is to position the CFP to be more forward-looking and flexible: the plan anticipates the liquidity consequences of the strategy before the strategy is executed, rather than catching up after the event. Schweser condenses this as adding the CFP to the firm’s strategic planning process so that it is more future-oriented and adaptable.

The conclusion of the chapter repeats the idea: the CFP is a playbook and therefore requires updating on a regular basis. Regular updating is not the same as freezing the plan between scheduled reviews; a material change in the profile is itself a reason to refresh.

**Applying it to this question**

The bank has had internal change (new BRL digital deposit account, entry into payroll lending), so Proposal I is required. It has had external change (higher policy rate, higher market volatility), so Proposal II is required. A strategic planning exercise is about to begin, which is exactly the leading practice of Proposal III. Proposal IV would keep the plan unchanged despite both kinds of change, contradicting the requirement to refresh as the profile changes. So I, II and III only.

**Fragile fact.** Both directions count: internal (strategy, products) and external (macro, markets); strategic planning integration is the “leading institutions” practice.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Describe best practices in the design of a sound contingency funding plan.

**GARP:** Chapter 11, Section 11.3 “I. Align to Business and Risk Profiles”; Conclusion. Schweser LO 76.b, “Alignment with business and risk profiles”.

**GARP vs Schweser:** none of substance; GARP frames strategic planning integration as a practice of leading institutions (“part of, or in parallel with”), Schweser as a general recommendation.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-11 b, where it is Q4 of 12.

a.reason: (Scope or condition error). A stops at reactive refreshes and omits the forward-looking practice of incorporating the CFP in strategic planning. A would be correct only if the stem asked which events require a refresh, rather than which proposals are consistent with best practice.

b.reason: B combines both triggers for refreshing the CFP (internal and external change) with GARP’s leading practice of building the CFP as part of, or in parallel with, strategic planning.

c.reason: (Polarity flip). C accepts Proposal IV, which reverses GARP’s instruction that the CFP be refreshed as the profile changes. A plan frozen between scheduled reviews cannot remain aligned. C would be correct only if no internal or external change had occurred since the last approval.

d.reason: (Scope or condition error). D drops Proposal I and so treats only external change as a reason to refresh. GARP names internal changes (new strategies, products and services) as well. D would be correct only if the bank’s business mix had been unchanged since the last refresh.
