questions.loText: Describe best practices in the design of a sound contingency funding plan.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-11 b Q5
questions.question: The chief compliance officer of a Japanese trust bank is reviewing a proposal from the CRO to integrate the bank’s contingency funding plan (CFP), currently a treasury document, with the bank’s enterprise risk management (ERM), capital management, and business continuity and crisis management frameworks. The bank holds JPY 2.1 trillion of high-quality liquid assets. Which of the following best describes the benefit that this integration is expected to deliver?

options.text: It increases the CFP’s effectiveness and consistency by enabling it to leverage and reference controls and processes already established in those frameworks.
It guarantees that the CFP will anticipate every liquidity crisis scenario, so that management no longer needs to exercise any discretion during a crisis.
It transfers ownership of the CFP from corporate treasury to the ERM function, which then becomes responsible for activating the plan in a crisis.
It allows the CFP’s controls to be designed independently of the other frameworks, so that the plan does not depend on processes that may fail in a crisis.

questions.solution:
Japanese bank CCO: the benefit of integrating the CFP with ERM, capital and business continuity frameworks.

**Concept and theory**

The second design consideration is that the CFP is not a stand-alone tool. GARP describes it as an integrated part of the institution’s liquidity risk management and firm-wide risk management frameworks, naming three firm-wide frameworks in particular: enterprise risk management (ERM), capital management, and business continuity and crisis management.

What does integration buy? GARP gives a precise answer: integrating the CFP with the other components of the ERM disciplines increases the CFP’s effectiveness and consistency by enabling it to leverage and reference established controls and processes. A stand-alone CFP would have to build its own controls, approvals and data flows, which may never have been exercised and which may contradict those used elsewhere. An integrated CFP inherits processes that already work and are already governed. Schweser phrases the same benefit as making the CFP more effective because it can work within the firm’s internal control system.

Two further linkages appear in the same subsection. First, the CFP should be explicitly linked to the liquidity risk measurement framework and the liquidity stress test through its limit structure and escalation levels, with BAU liquidity risk measures serving as the foundation for the CFP’s EWIs (Schweser treats this relationship under LO 76.a). Second, linkages to the business continuity and crisis management frameworks reinforce key operational and communication protocols during a crisis.

Integration does not change who owns or activates the plan, and it does not remove the need for judgment; those are separate matters.

**Applying it to this question**

The CCO is asked what the integration is expected to deliver. GARP’s answer is greater effectiveness and consistency through leveraging and referencing established controls and processes. The JPY 2.1 trillion of HQLA is irrelevant: the benefit of integration does not depend on the size of the liquidity buffer.

**Fragile fact.** The benefit is “effectiveness and consistency” via leveraging and referencing established controls and processes, not independence from them.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Describe best practices in the design of a sound contingency funding plan.

**GARP:** Chapter 11, Section 11.3 “II. Integrate with Broader Risk Management Frameworks”. Schweser LO 76.b, “Integration with broader risk management frameworks”.

**GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser says “work within the firm’s internal control system”, a compression of GARP’s “leverage and reference established controls and processes”; no conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-11 b, where it is Q5 of 12.

a.reason: A states GARP’s stated benefit almost exactly: effectiveness and consistency, achieved by leveraging and referencing established controls and processes.

b.reason: (Absolute claim). B promises that integration lets the CFP anticipate every scenario and removes discretion. GARP says the opposite elsewhere in the design considerations: the CFP cannot anticipate all situations, so it must leave management flexibility and discretion. B would be correct only if the stem asked what a CFP can never achieve.

c.reason: (Role misassignment). C turns integration into a transfer of ownership and activation to the ERM function. Integration concerns using shared controls and processes, not reallocating roles; GARP’s governance material (LO 76.c) has the treasurer, in consultation with the CFO and others, invoking the CFP. C would be correct only if the stem asked about a reorganisation of governance, which is outside this design consideration.

d.reason: (Polarity flip). D reverses the benefit: GARP values integration precisely because the CFP can rely on established controls and processes, not because it is insulated from them. D would be correct only if the stem described the stand-alone design that GARP rejects.

questions.loText: Describe best practices in the design of a sound contingency funding plan.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-11 b Q6
questions.question:
A junior risk analyst at a Canadian bank is preparing slides for newly hired analysts on the design consideration that a contingency funding plan (CFP) should be integrated with broader risk management frameworks. The draft contains the following statements:

I. The CFP is an integrated part of the bank’s liquidity risk management and firm-wide risk management frameworks, including ERM, capital management, and business continuity and crisis management.

II. Once the CFP is integrated with ERM, a separate linkage to capital management is unnecessary, so it can be dropped from the design.

III. Because the CFP operates in severe stress, it should rely on controls and processes built specifically for it rather than on those established in other risk disciplines.

IV. The main purpose of linking the CFP to the business continuity and crisis management frameworks is to provide the foundation from which the CFP defines its early warning indicators.

Which of the statements should the analyst keep?

options.text: I and II only
I and III only
I only
I and IV only

questions.solution:
Canadian bank training slides on integration: which statements to keep.

**Concept and theory**

Consideration II has three layers, and distractors usually corrupt one of them.

**Which frameworks.** The CFP is an integrated part of the institution’s liquidity risk management framework and of its firm-wide risk management frameworks, explicitly ERM, capital management, and business continuity and crisis management. Each is named separately; none is said to absorb another.

**Why integrate.** Integration with the other ERM disciplines increases the CFP’s effectiveness and consistency because the CFP can leverage and reference established controls and processes.

**What each specific linkage does.** GARP attaches a distinct purpose to two linkages:

| Linkage | Purpose stated by GARP |
|---|---|
| Liquidity risk measurement framework and stress test | Explicit link through the limit structure and escalation levels; BAU liquidity risk measures are the foundation from which the CFP defines its EWIs (Schweser: LO 76.a) |
| Business continuity and crisis management | Reinforces key operational and communication protocols during times of crisis |

Keeping these purposes separate matters. The EWI foundation comes from the measures the firm already uses in BAU liquidity risk management; the business continuity linkage is about operations and communication when the crisis hits. Schweser’s version of the second point is that inclusion in business continuity and crisis management strengthens important operating and communicating procedures needed in a crisis.

**Applying it to this question**

Statement I lists the frameworks exactly as GARP does: keep. Statement II drops capital management on the theory that ERM covers it, but GARP names capital management in its own right: remove. Statement III reverses the rationale for integration, which is to use established controls and processes: remove. Statement IV gives the business continuity linkage the purpose that GARP gives to BAU liquidity risk measures (the EWI foundation): remove. Only Statement I should stay.

**Fragile fact.** Business continuity linkage reinforces operational and communication protocols; the EWI foundation is the BAU liquidity risk measures.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Describe best practices in the design of a sound contingency funding plan.

**GARP:** Chapter 11, Section 11.3 “II. Integrate with Broader Risk Management Frameworks”. Schweser LO 76.b, “Integration with broader risk management frameworks”; LO 76.a for the stress test link.

**GARP vs Schweser:** GARP places the limit structure, escalation level and EWI linkage inside consideration II; Schweser moves it to LO 76.a. Used here only to identify the false attribution in Statement IV.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-11 b, where it is Q6 of 12.

a.reason: (Scope or condition error). Keeping Statement II drops one of the frameworks GARP names explicitly. A would be correct only if the bank had no separate capital management framework and ERM formally contained it, a condition the source does not make.

b.reason: (Polarity flip). Keeping Statement III reverses GARP’s reason for integration: the CFP gains effectiveness and consistency by leveraging established controls, not by building separate ones. B would be correct only if the stem asked which design GARP warns against.

c.reason: C is correct because Statement I is the only faithful restatement of GARP’s integration consideration; II, III and IV each corrupt a distinct layer of it.

d.reason: (Sibling swap). Keeping Statement IV attributes to the business continuity linkage the role of the liquidity risk measurement linkage. EWIs are built from BAU liquidity risk measures; business continuity linkages reinforce operational and communication protocols. D would be correct only if Statement IV named BAU liquidity risk measures as the EWI foundation.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Describe best practices in the design of a sound contingency funding plan.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-11 b Q7
questions.question: The CRO of a UK building society is reviewing its contingency funding plan (CFP). The plan lists 14 possible contingency actions, such as raising GBP retail deposit rates and drawing on committed facilities, in a single list with no reference to stress scenarios or severity. It states that the asset-liability committee will “develop a response at the time” if a liquidity crisis occurs. Which recommendation is most appropriate?

options.text: Retain the single list, since convening management to develop contingent strategies once a crisis begins produces the response best tailored to that crisis.
Replace the list with one action plan for the most severe scenario, since actions designed for the worst case will be adequate at every less severe stage.
Organize the actions by graduated severity levels tied to the society’s regulatory capital ratios, rather than to early warning indicators and triggers.
Organize the actions by stress scenario and graduated severity levels aligned to early warning indicators and triggers, so they can be calibrated to each crisis stage.

questions.solution:
UK building society: an undifferentiated list of 14 actions and “develop a response at the time”.

**Concept and theory**

The third design consideration is that the CFP must be an operational and actionable, but flexible, playbook. This solution covers the “operational and actionable” half.

GARP’s starting point is that a playbook’s effectiveness lies in its operational readiness. In a crisis, convening management and only then starting to develop contingent strategies and a plan of action would likely be highly challenging without prior planning: time is short, information is incomplete and the people involved are under pressure. The CFP must therefore do the thinking in advance.

GARP specifies what that advance thinking should contain:

| Design element | What GARP requires |
|---|---|
| Menu of contingency actions | Possible actions management can undertake |
| Organised by stress scenario | Different actions for different kinds of stress |
| At graduated levels of severity | Actions scaled to how bad the stress is |
| Alignment | Graduated stress levels aligned to EWIs, triggers and contingency actions |

The result, in GARP’s words, is a structured roadmap outlining potential liquidity risks and associated management actions that can be calibrated for different stages of the liquidity crisis. Schweser condenses this as presenting numerous stress scenarios, each with potential contingency actions that vary with severity levels, and tying the severity levels to EWIs, triggers and contingency actions.

**Applying it to this question**

The building society’s plan has a menu of actions but fails on every organising element: no scenarios, no severity levels, no link to EWIs or triggers. Its statement that ALCO will “develop a response at the time” is exactly what GARP says would prove highly challenging without prior planning. The recommendation must add the scenario and severity structure and tie it to EWIs and triggers so actions can be calibrated to the stage of the crisis. The number of actions (14) and the examples given are irrelevant to the decision.

**Fragile fact.** The graduated severity levels are aligned to EWIs, triggers and contingency actions, not to capital ratios, and they exist before the crisis.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Describe best practices in the design of a sound contingency funding plan.

**GARP:** Chapter 11, Section 11.3 “III. Operational, Actionable, but Flexible Playbook”. Schweser LO 76.b, “Operational, actionable, and flexible playbook”.

**GARP vs Schweser:** none.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-11 b, where it is Q7 of 12.

a.reason: (Polarity flip). A reverses GARP’s reasoning: developing strategies only once the crisis begins is what GARP says would likely be highly challenging without prior planning. A would be correct only if the stem asked which weakness of the current plan the CRO should report.

b.reason: (Scope or condition error). B collapses graduated severity levels into a single worst-case plan. GARP requires actions at graduated levels so they can be calibrated to each stage; worst-case actions taken early could be excessive or send damaging signals. B would be correct only if the stem asked how to plan for the most severe level alone.

c.reason: (Sibling swap). C ties severity levels to regulatory capital ratios, a capital management measure, instead of the liquidity EWIs and triggers GARP names. C would be correct only if the stem were about a capital contingency or recovery plan.

d.reason: D reproduces GARP’s design: actions by stress scenario and graduated severity, aligned to EWIs and triggers, giving a roadmap calibrated to the stages of the crisis.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Describe best practices in the design of a sound contingency funding plan.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-11 b Q8
questions.question: A member of the board risk committee of a Chinese joint-stock bank with CNY 1.8 trillion of deposits is reviewing a draft contingency funding plan (CFP). One director argues that every contingency action should be pre-specified and executed automatically when its trigger is hit. Another argues that the plan should contain only general principles, because no plan can foresee the next crisis. Which approach best reflects best practice in designing the CFP as a playbook?

options.text: Pre-specify every action and execute it automatically when triggered, since the value of a playbook lies in removing judgment from crisis decisions.
Specify recommended contingency actions while leaving management sufficient flexibility and discretion to make informed decisions as the crisis evolves.
Include only general principles and no specified actions, since a plan that cannot anticipate every situation gains nothing from a menu of actions.
Specify recommended actions, but reserve all discretion to depart from them for the board, with management executing the specified actions as written.

questions.solution:
Chinese bank board debate: fully automatic actions versus principles only.

**Concept and theory**

The same third consideration has a second half: the playbook must be flexible. GARP’s reasoning starts from a limitation. The CFP cannot anticipate all possible situations that may lead to a liquidity crisis; the next crisis will differ in cause, speed and the reaction of markets. A plan that tried to dictate every response would fail on contact with an unforeseen situation.

GARP therefore describes effective CFPs as striking a balance between two things:

| Side of the balance | Why it is needed |
|---|---|
| Specifying recommended contingency actions | Operational readiness: management is not inventing strategy under pressure (the “actionable” half) |
| Sufficient flexibility and discretion for management | Informed decisions as the crisis evolves over time, since not every situation can be foreseen |

Schweser’s version: the CFP should prescribe stated contingency actions while allowing room for sudden but logical decisions throughout the crisis. The theme recurs in GARP’s escalation material (LO 76.c), which stresses that management’s expert judgment in assembling the “mosaic” of challenges should not be understated. Note who holds the discretion: GARP refers to management. The board is engaged as adviser and counsel, but the flexibility is designed for the people running the response.

**Applying it to this question**

The two directors stake out the two extremes. The first removes discretion entirely; the second removes the specified actions entirely. GARP rejects both, because the CFP must be actionable (so actions are specified) and flexible (so management retains discretion). The CNY 1.8 trillion deposit base is irrelevant to the design principle.

**Fragile fact.** Balance, not either extreme; and the discretion belongs to management.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Describe best practices in the design of a sound contingency funding plan.

**GARP:** Chapter 11, Section 11.3 “III. Operational, Actionable, but Flexible Playbook”. Schweser LO 76.b, “Operational, actionable, and flexible playbook”.

**GARP vs Schweser:** none; Schweser’s “sudden but logical decisions” paraphrases GARP’s “informed decisions as the crisis evolves”.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-11 b, where it is Q8 of 12.

a.reason: (Absolute claim). A assumes the plan can foresee every trigger and the right response to it, removing judgment altogether. GARP’s premise is that the CFP cannot anticipate all situations. A would be correct only if crises were fully predictable, which the source denies.

b.reason: B is GARP’s balance: specify recommended contingency actions while enabling management sufficient flexibility and discretion to make informed decisions as the crisis evolves.

c.reason: (Scope or condition error). C overextends the flexibility point until it eliminates the menu of actions, contradicting the “operational and actionable” half of the same consideration. C would be correct only if the question asked about a high-level liquidity policy rather than the CFP playbook.

d.reason: (Role misassignment). D moves discretion from management to the board. GARP gives the flexibility to management, with the board as an engaged adviser. D would be correct only if the stem asked who should be consulted on strategic actions such as large asset or subsidiary sales as the position worsens.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Describe best practices in the design of a sound contingency funding plan.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-11 b Q9
questions.question: A treasury analyst at a U.S. bank holding company is summarizing lessons from a liquidity crisis simulation. The contingency funding plan (CFP) had been designed by corporate treasury and the risk function alone. During the exercise, the operations team could not execute the planned collateral movements within the assumed timeframe, and business unit heads objected to client-facing actions they had never seen. Which recommendation is most consistent with best practice in the design of a sound CFP?

options.text: Add the board and the bank’s shareholder groups to the design team, since the owners must approve each contingency action before it is placed in the plan.
Keep the design within treasury and risk to protect confidentiality, and brief operations and the business units on their roles once a crisis is formally declared.
Involve management committees, business units, finance, treasury, risk, and operations and technology in the design, to capture its elements and coordinate execution.
Involve every employee of the bank in designing the CFP, so that no operational detail of any contingency action can be overlooked when a crisis arrives.

questions.solution:
U.S. BHC simulation exposes a CFP designed by treasury and risk alone.

**Concept and theory**

The fourth design consideration is that the CFP must include appropriate stakeholder groups. GARP’s reasoning: developing operational readiness requires a thorough understanding of both the strategic and the tactical aspects of the institution. No single function holds all of that knowledge. Treasury knows funding; operations knows how collateral and cash actually move; business units know how clients will react to actions that touch them.

GARP lists the groups whose involvement is needed:

| Stakeholder group | Examples or contribution |
|---|---|
| Management committees | ALCO, risk and capital committee, investment committee |
| Business units | How their businesses behave under stress; client impact of actions |
| Finance, corporate treasury | Funding and liquidity profile management |
| Risk | Liquidity risk measurement and limits |
| Operations and technology | Execution: collateral, cash management, systems |

GARP states two purposes for involving them: to capture the appropriate elements of the CFP as part of the design, and to ensure successful coordination from an execution standpoint. Schweser’s list is shorter (management committees, business units, corporate treasury, risk management and technology) and its purpose is to ensure the CFP is operationally ready. GARP’s fuller list governs.

Note what is not on the list: shareholders as such. Schweser’s own quiz uses “all shareholder groups” as a distractor for “appropriate stakeholder groups”.

**Applying it to this question**

The simulation failed in exactly the two places GARP’s stakeholder consideration protects: operations could not execute collateral movements (an execution and design gap from excluding operations), and business units rejected client-facing actions they had not helped design (a design gap from excluding business units). The fix is to bring the full set of appropriate groups into the design so that the plan’s elements are captured and execution is coordinated.

**Fragile fact.** Appropriate stakeholder groups (not all shareholders), involved in design and execution; operations and technology are on the list.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Describe best practices in the design of a sound contingency funding plan.

**GARP:** Chapter 11, Section 11.3 “IV. Inclusive of Appropriate Stakeholder Groups”. Schweser LO 76.b, “Inclusive of appropriate stakeholder groups”.

**GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser’s LO text omits finance and operations (it names technology only, though its quiz answer mentions operations); GARP followed.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-11 b, where it is Q9 of 12.

a.reason: (Role misassignment). A gives a design and approval role to shareholders, confusing “stakeholder” with “shareholder”. The CFP is designed by the firm’s committees and functions; shareholders do not approve contingency actions. A would be correct only if the question concerned a shareholder vote on a capital raise, which is not CFP design.

b.reason: (Scope or condition error). B limits operations and business units to a post-declaration briefing, dropping the design-stage involvement GARP requires. The simulation shows why: execution failed because these groups were absent from design. B would be correct only if the stem asked how roles are communicated once the CFP is invoked.

c.reason: C names GARP’s stakeholder groups and both of GARP’s purposes: capturing the appropriate elements in design and ensuring coordination in execution.

d.reason: (Absolute claim). D replaces “appropriate” stakeholder groups with every employee and promises that nothing can be overlooked. GARP calls for appropriate groups, not universal participation, and no design can guarantee completeness. D would be correct only if the consideration read “inclusive of all staff”.

questions.question:
A supervisor at the French banking regulator is assessing whether a bank has built operational readiness into the design of its contingency funding plan (CFP) through the involvement of appropriate stakeholder groups. She notes the following statements from the bank’s CFP methodology document:

I. Developing operational readiness in the CFP requires a thorough understanding of both the strategic and the tactical aspects of the bank.

II. The readiness assessment is complete once scenario design, contingency planning and communication strategies have been agreed; execution lies outside its scope.

III. Involving the various stakeholder groups provides a strong forum in which potential issues or challenges with the plan can be openly discussed and addressed.

IV. During execution, maintaining the confidence of external stakeholders is the supervisor’s responsibility rather than that of the bank’s own coordinated stakeholder groups.

Which statements are consistent with best practice?

options.text: I and III only
I, II and III only
I, III and IV only
I only

questions.solution:
French supervisor reviews statements on operational readiness and stakeholder involvement.

**Concept and theory**

Consideration IV is fundamentally about operational readiness, and GARP describes readiness as a process with a beginning and a continuation:

| Stage | What GARP says |
|---|---|
| Prerequisite | A thorough understanding of both strategic and tactical aspects of the institution |
| Begins with | Scenario design, contingency planning and communication strategies |
| Continues through | Execution, where timely coordination and communication are critical to keeping internal and external stakeholders confident in the institution’s financial strength |

“For these reasons”, GARP continues, the involvement of appropriate stakeholder groups is needed. The final benefit GARP names is practical: in practice, involving the various stakeholder groups provides a strong forum in which potential issues or challenges can be openly discussed and addressed. Schweser says the same: a range of stakeholder groups gives a good opportunity for open discussion of potential problems with the CFP, which can then be remedied.

Two points are easy to corrupt. First, readiness does not stop at the design documents; it extends into execution. Second, keeping stakeholders confident during execution, both internal and external, is achieved by the institution’s own timely coordination and communication. External parties such as regulators, counterparties and rating agencies are the audience of that effort, not its owners.

**Applying it to this question**

Statement I restates GARP’s prerequisite: true. Statement II cuts the process off before execution, whereas GARP says it continues through execution: false. Statement III restates the open-forum benefit: true. Statement IV assigns the institution’s job of sustaining external confidence to the supervisor: false. So I and III only.

**Fragile fact.** Readiness runs from design through execution; the forum benefit is that issues are openly discussed and addressed.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Describe best practices in the design of a sound contingency funding plan.

**GARP:** Chapter 11, Section 11.3 “IV. Inclusive of Appropriate Stakeholder Groups”. Schweser LO 76.b, “Inclusive of appropriate stakeholder groups”.

**GARP vs Schweser:** none; Schweser omits the strategic and tactical prerequisite and the design-to-execution sequence (GARP-only content used in I and II).

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-11 b, where it is Q10 of 12.

a.reason: A is correct because Statements I and III are faithful restatements of GARP’s stakeholder consideration, while II and IV each corrupt it.

b.reason:
(Scope or condition error). Accepting Statement II drops the execution stage from the readiness assessment, whereas GARP says it begins with scenario design, contingency planning and communication strategies and continues through execution. B would be correct only if

Statement II said the assessment begins with those three steps.

c.reason: (Role misassignment). Accepting Statement IV gives the supervisor responsibility for the confidence of external stakeholders. GARP places that on the institution’s own timely coordination and communication. C would be correct only if the stem concerned the supervisor’s own public statements, which are outside the bank’s CFP.

d.reason: (Polarity flip). Rejecting Statement III treats broad stakeholder involvement as a hindrance rather than as the strong forum for open discussion of issues that GARP describes. D would be correct only if the question asked which statement concerns the understanding needed for readiness.

questions.question: A senior treasury analyst at an Irish retail bank is drafting the communication plan section of the bank’s contingency funding plan (CFP), after false social media rumours about a peer’s solvency drove EUR 900 million of deposit outflows from that peer in two days. Which of the following statements about the communication plan is NOT consistent with best practice?

options.text: Coordinated and timely communication of information to stakeholders is critical, a key lesson that resurfaced in the recent financial crisis.
In addition to coordinating internally, the bank must communicate externally with clients, analysts, counterparties and regulators.
Timely and accurate external information helps reinforce confidence and mitigate the risk that rumours and fears further harm the bank.
Because accuracy matters more than speed, external communication should wait until the crisis is resolved and all of the facts are established.

questions.solution:
Irish bank drafting its CFP communication plan after a rumour-driven run at a peer: the statement that is NOT best practice.

**Concept and theory**

The fifth design consideration is that the CFP is supported by a communication plan. GARP grounds it in experience: in any crisis, coordinated and timely communication of information to stakeholders is critical, a key lesson that resurfaced in the recent financial crisis.

The communication plan has two directions:

| Direction | What GARP requires |
|---|---|
| Internal | The institution must be internally coordinated |
| External | Communication to clients, analysts, counterparties and regulators with timely and accurate information |

Why does external communication matter so much? Liquidity is a confidence business. GARP explains that timely and accurate external communication helps reinforce confidence in the institution and mitigate the risk that rumours and fears further precipitate and adversely impact it. A silence while rumours circulate lets the market fill the gap with the worst interpretation, which can itself trigger withdrawals, collateral calls and refusals to roll over funding. Schweser’s version adds the reputational framing: communication, especially to external stakeholders, helps maintain the firm’s reputation and works as damage control to contain negative financial impact. GARP’s requirement is “timely and accurate”. These are joint conditions, not a trade-off in which one is sacrificed for the other. (Central management of messaging and the mapping of who speaks to which stakeholder belong to the communication and coordination component in LO 76.c.)

**Applying it to this question**

The question asks for the statement that is NOT consistent with best practice. A, B and C each restate GARP’s consideration V. D makes timeliness subordinate to accuracy and postpones external communication until the crisis is over, which is precisely when it can no longer stop rumours from spreading. The EUR 900 million outflow at the peer is context only; it does not change the principle.

**Fragile fact.** “Timely and accurate”, during the crisis, internally and externally; delaying until the facts are settled is the polarity trap.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Describe best practices in the design of a sound contingency funding plan.

**GARP:** Chapter 11, Section 11.3 “V. Supported by a Communication Plan”. Schweser LO 76.b, “Supported by a communication plan”.

**GARP vs Schweser:** none; Schweser adds the “damage control” and reputation framing, GARP emphasises confidence and rumours.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-11 b, where it is Q11 of 12.

a.reason: (True statement (qualifier misread)). A paraphrases GARP’s opening of consideration V: coordinated and timely communication is critical, a lesson that resurfaced in the financial crisis. A would be the answer only if the stem asked which statement is consistent with best practice.

b.reason: (True statement (qualifier misread)). B restates GARP’s two directions of communication: internal coordination plus external communication to clients, analysts, counterparties and regulators. B would be the answer only if it confined communication to one of those directions.

c.reason: (True statement (qualifier misread)). C restates GARP’s reason for the communication plan: timely, accurate information reinforces confidence and mitigates the risk that rumours and fears precipitate further harm. C would be the answer only if it claimed communication can always prevent rumours.

d.reason: D is the inconsistent statement: GARP requires external communication that is timely and accurate during the crisis, to reinforce confidence and contain rumours.

questions.question: An internal auditor at a German universal bank is mapping practices found in the bank’s contingency funding plan (CFP) to the five key design considerations for a sound CFP. Which of the following correctly pairs a design consideration with a practice that belongs to it?

options.text: Aligned to business and risk profiles: linking the CFP to business continuity and crisis management frameworks to reinforce operational and communication protocols.
Operational and actionable, but flexible playbook: a menu of contingency actions for different stress scenarios at graduated levels of severity.
Inclusive of appropriate stakeholder groups: aligning the risk appetite statement to the CFP through quantifiable early warning indicators, limits and escalation levels.
Supported by a communication plan: incorporating the CFP into the strategic planning exercise so that the plan becomes more forward-looking and flexible.

questions.solution:
German bank auditor maps CFP practices to the five design considerations.

**Concept and theory**

The five design considerations are easy to recall as headings and easy to confuse in detail, because several practices sound as if they could belong anywhere. Exam distractors exploit this by attaching a true practice to the wrong heading. The map below places each practice where GARP puts it:

| Consideration | Practices GARP places under it |
|---|---|
| I. Aligned to business and risk profiles | Coverage of activities, products and asset classes, geographic and FX coverage, legal entities; RAS aligned through quantifiable EWIs, limits and escalation levels; refresh for internal and external change; part of, or parallel with, strategic planning |
| II. Integrated with broader frameworks | Part of liquidity risk management, ERM, capital management, business continuity and crisis management; leverage established controls; business continuity linkage reinforces operational and communication protocols |
| III. Operational and actionable, but flexible playbook | Menu of contingency actions for different stress scenarios at graduated levels of severity, aligned to EWIs, triggers and actions; balance between specified actions and management discretion |
| IV. Inclusive of appropriate stakeholder groups | Committees, business units, finance, treasury, risk, operations and technology; design and execution; forum for open discussion |
| V. Supported by a communication plan | Coordinated, timely, internal and external communication to sustain confidence and contain rumours |

A useful test: ask what problem the practice solves. Coverage and calibration problems belong to I; reliance on other firm-wide processes to II; “what do we actually do, and when” to III; “who must be in the room” to IV; “what do we tell people” to V.

**Applying it to this question**

Check each pairing against the map. A puts the business continuity linkage under alignment, but it belongs to integration (II). B puts the menu of actions by scenario and graduated severity under the playbook (III), which is where GARP places it. C puts RAS alignment through quantifiable EWIs, limits and escalation levels under stakeholders, but it belongs to alignment (I). D puts strategic planning integration under the communication plan, but it belongs to alignment (I). Only B is correctly paired.

**Fragile fact.** Strategic planning and the RAS sit under alignment (I); the business continuity linkage sits under integration (II).

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Describe best practices in the design of a sound contingency funding plan.

**GARP:** Chapter 11, Section 11.3 “Design Considerations”, I to V. Schweser LO 76.b (all five considerations).

**GARP vs Schweser:** none on attribution; both place each practice under the same heading.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-11 b, where it is Q12 of 12.

a.reason: (Sibling swap). A attaches a consideration II practice (business continuity and crisis management linkage reinforcing operational and communication protocols) to consideration I. A would be correct if the heading were “Integrated with broader risk management frameworks”.

b.reason: B matches GARP’s consideration III, which requires a menu of possible contingency actions that management can undertake in different stress scenarios and at graduated levels of severity.

c.reason: (Sibling swap). C attaches a consideration I practice (aligning the RAS through quantifiable EWIs, limits and escalation levels) to consideration IV. C would be correct if the heading were “Aligned to business and risk profiles”.

d.reason: (Sibling swap). D attaches a consideration I practice (incorporating the CFP into strategic planning to make it more forward-looking and flexible) to consideration V. D would be correct if the heading were “Aligned to business and risk profiles”.

questions.question: A risk consultant at a Canadian bank is reviewing the governance section of the bank’s draft contingency funding plan (CFP). The draft names four groups with CFP roles: corporate treasury, the liquidity crisis team (LCT), the management committee and the board of directors. Which of the following role assignments in the draft is most consistent with sound CFP governance?

options.text: The board of directors provides direct oversight of the LCT during a crisis and reviews the LCT’s specific recommendations for CFP actions.
The treasurer, in consultation with the CFO and others, may invoke the CFP and convene the LCT after reviewing market, industry and institution-specific conditions and stress test results.
The management committee designs the CFP and submits it to the LCT, which reviews and approves the plan before it is adopted.
The LCT serves as advisor and counsel to the management committee, particularly when large asset or subsidiary sales are being evaluated.

questions.solution:
Canadian bank, draft CFP governance section: which role assignment among treasury, LCT, management committee and board is correct?

**Concept and theory**

A contingency funding plan (CFP) is the playbook a firm uses for high-impact, low-probability liquidity events. GARP stresses that a playbook is only as good as the people who run it, so the first component of the CFP framework, governance and oversight, starts with well-defined roles and responsibilities, backed by a communication strategy, written policies and periodic testing. GARP names four groups that play a pivotal role in CFP design and implementation, while noting that institutions should tailor the roles to their own structure:

| Group | Role in GARP Chapter 11 |
|---|---|
| Corporate treasury | In business as usual (BAU), monitors the ongoing business, risk, funding and liquidity profile. The treasurer, in consultation with the CFO and others, may invoke the CFP and convene the LCT, based on markets, industry, institution-specific conditions and stress testing results. |
| Liquidity crisis team (LCT) | Central point of contact; continuously monitors the liquidity profile; recommends CFP actions working with treasury and the management committee; coordinates and communicates internally and externally; designs the CFP and submits it to senior management for review and approval. |
| Management committee | During a crisis, senior management oversees the LCT, consults with the board, monitors the liquidity risk profile, and reviews specific recommendations for (and coordination of) CFP actions. |
| Board of directors | Actively engaged during the crisis as advisor and counsel to the management committee and LCT; especially involved if liquidity keeps worsening and strategic actions (large asset or subsidiary sales) are needed. |

The logic is a chain: treasury sees trouble first and pulls the trigger; the LCT runs the response day to day; senior management supervises the LCT; the board advises from above. Most exam traps simply move one verb (invoke, design, oversee, advise) to the wrong group.

**Applying it to this question**

Each option pairs a group with a responsibility, so the task is to test each pairing against the table. Option B gives corporate treasury (the treasurer with the CFO) the power to invoke the CFP and convene the LCT, and lists exactly the four inputs GARP names: markets, industry, institution-specific conditions and liquidity stress testing results. Every other option takes a real responsibility and hands it to the wrong group.

**Fragile fact.** Treasurer (with CFO) invokes; LCT designs and coordinates; management committee oversees the LCT; board advises. Note that Schweser says the board “provides leadership” to the LCT and management committee; GARP’s wording is “advisor and counsel”.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Assess the key components of a contingency funding plan (governance and oversight, scenarios and liquidity gap analysis, contingent actions, monitoring and escalation, and data and reporting). **GARP:** Chapter 11, Section 11.4 Framework and Building Blocks, Governance and Oversight, “Stakeholder Involvement, Roles, and Responsibilities”. **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser describes the board as providing “leadership” to the LCT and management committee and the management committee as “managing” the LCT; GARP uses “advisor and counsel” and “provides oversight”. GARP wording followed; the conflict does not affect the key.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-11 c, where it is Q1 of 15.

a.reason: (Role misassignment). Providing oversight of the LCT and reviewing its specific recommendations for CFP actions is the management committee’s role during a crisis. The board serves as advisor and counsel, not as the LCT’s direct supervisor. The option would be correct if “board of directors” were replaced by “management committee”.

b.reason: GARP states that the treasurer, in consultation with the CFO and others, may invoke the CFP and convene the LCT based on a review of markets, industry and institution-specific conditions and stress testing results. Option B restates this without alteration, so it is the only consistent assignment.

c.reason: (Role misassignment (reversed direction)). GARP gives design to the LCT, which submits the CFP to the senior management group for review and approval. The option reverses designer and approver. It would be correct if it read: “The LCT designs the CFP and submits it to the management committee for review and approval.”

d.reason: (Role misassignment). Serving as advisor and counsel, particularly when large asset or subsidiary sales are on the table, is the board’s role. The LCT is the operational centre (monitoring, coordination, recommendations), not an advisor to the committee that oversees it. The option would be correct if the actor were the board of directors.

questions.question:
A member of the board risk committee at a Japanese banking group with several business segments, geographies and legal entities is reviewing the following statements drafted for the governance and oversight section of the group’s CFP:

I. The LCT should be composed of senior members of the business and supporting functions, including C-level executives and the heads of business segments, geographies and legal entities.

II. During a crisis, corporate treasury provides oversight of the LCT and consults with the board of directors on specific recommendations for CFP actions.

III. Board engagement in evaluating CFP actions becomes particularly important if the liquidity position continues to worsen and strategic actions, such as large asset or subsidiary sales, need to be taken.

IV. Because the group is complex, the CFP organizational structure should be defined at the parent level only, leaving each operating subsidiary to set its own chain of command.

Which of the statements are accurate?

options.text: I and II only
II and IV only
I, III and IV only
I and III only

questions.solution:
Japanese banking group, four governance statements on LCT composition, LCT oversight, board engagement and chain of command.

**Concept and theory**

Governance in a CFP is about who decides, who executes and who supervises when liquidity deteriorates quickly. GARP adds three details beyond the basic role list. First, composition: the LCT should be made up of senior members of the institution’s business and supporting functions, including C-level executives and the heads of business segments, geographies and legal entities. Seniority matters because the LCT must coordinate across the whole organization and recommend actions that cut across businesses. Second, escalation of board involvement: the board should be actively engaged with the management committee and LCT during the crisis, and a strong understanding of the CFP’s contents allows board members to help evaluate CFP actions, particularly if the liquidity position continues to worsen and strategic actions such as large asset or subsidiary sales must be taken. Third, structure in complex groups: where an institution has multiple segments, geographies or legal entities, the organizational structure should be well defined both at the parent level and at the operating subsidiaries, so that there is a proper chain of command and decisions are coordinated and aligned across the institution as a whole.

The underlying principle is that in a crisis there is no time to negotiate authority. Every legal entity must know who acts, and the parent must know that its subsidiaries will act consistently. Oversight of the LCT during a crisis sits with the management committee (senior management), not with corporate treasury.

**Applying it to this question**

Test each statement against the source. Statement I reproduces GARP’s composition guidance: true. Statement II gives oversight of the LCT and consultation with the board to corporate treasury; GARP gives both to the management committee: false. Statement III reproduces GARP’s description of when board engagement matters most: true. Statement IV keeps the parent-level definition but drops the requirement that the structure also be well defined at the operating subsidiaries: false. The accurate set is I and III only.

**Fragile fact.** Who oversees the LCT in a crisis: the management committee (senior management), not treasury and not the board. In complex groups, structure is defined at parent and subsidiary level.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Assess the key components of a contingency funding plan (governance and oversight, scenarios and liquidity gap analysis, contingent actions, monitoring and escalation, and data and reporting). **GARP:** Chapter 11, Section 11.4, Governance and Oversight, “Stakeholder Involvement, Roles, and Responsibilities”. **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser lists LCT members as “executives, business unit leaders, and other senior management” and omits the parent and subsidiary chain-of-command point; Statement IV is therefore GARP-only content.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-11 c, where it is Q2 of 15.

a.reason: (Role misassignment (Statement II accepted)). Option A accepts Statement II, which moves the management committee’s crisis role (oversight of the LCT, consulting the board) to corporate treasury. It also omits the true Statement III. Statement II would be true if “corporate treasury” read “the management committee”.

b.reason: (Role misassignment and scope error). Option B accepts both false statements and rejects both true ones. Statement II has the wrong actor, and Statement IV drops the subsidiary half of GARP’s requirement. Option B would be right only if the treasury were the LCT’s overseer and the group’s subsidiaries were free to define their own command chains, neither of which GARP supports.

c.reason:
(Scope or condition error (Statement IV accepted)). Option C includes Statement

IV. GARP requires the organizational structure to be well defined at the parent level and the operating subsidiaries to ensure a proper chain of command. Statement IV would be true if it read “defined at both the parent level and each operating subsidiary”.

d.reason: Option D (I and III only) is the only option that includes both true statements and excludes both false ones. GARP’s text on LCT composition and on board engagement during a worsening liquidity position supports I and III directly.

questions.question: The chief compliance officer of a Singapore bank is finalizing the communication and coordination section of the bank’s CFP. The bank already has a business continuity communication plan, and its investor relations, legal and compliance, corporate treasury and business unit teams each hold established external relationships. Which of the following arrangements is most consistent with sound CFP practice?

options.text: Messaging and content are centrally managed, while bidirectional communication with rating agencies and clearing banks resides with corporate treasury.
Messaging and content are centrally managed, and all bidirectional communication with external stakeholders is routed through the LCT alone.
Messaging and content are centrally managed, while bidirectional communication with regulators and supervisors resides with investor relations.
Messaging and content are centrally managed, and the CFP plan is built separately from existing communication plans to avoid conflicting protocols.

questions.solution:
Singapore bank, communication and coordination section of the CFP: central messaging plus relationship-based coordination points.

**Concept and theory**

GARP treats communication as part of governance because confidence is the scarcest resource in a liquidity crisis. Clear and timely communication shows that management understands the challenges and has a plan, which matters to employees, clients, counterparties, shareholders, rating agencies and regulators alike; loss of confidence can spiral quickly once rumours dominate headlines, whether or not they are grounded in reality. The CFP should therefore include a communications strategy that ensures proper notification, coordination, issue reporting and escalation, with groups across the institution relying on each other so that information is available on time for decisions.

GARP then separates two things. Messaging and content should be centrally managed, so everyone works off the same page. Bidirectional communication and coordination with each stakeholder should reside with the executive and management teams that already have working relationships with that stakeholder. GARP’s illustrative mapping is:

| Internal team | External stakeholders |
|---|---|
| Business units | Clients, counterparties |
| Corporate treasury | Regulators and supervisors, rating agencies, clearing banks |
| Investor relations | Investors, analyst community, public media |
| Legal and compliance | Regulators and supervisors |

GARP adds that these points may differ with size, complexity and structure, and that institutions should leverage communication plans they already have (BAU and business continuity) and enhance them where appropriate, rather than starting from nothing.

**Applying it to this question**

All four options share the correct first half (central management of messaging and content), so the decision rests on the second half. The stem tells you the bank has a business continuity communication plan and that several teams hold established relationships: both facts point to GARP’s guidance to use existing relationships and leverage existing plans. Option A assigns rating agencies and clearing banks to corporate treasury, exactly as in GARP’s mapping.

**Fragile fact.** Content is central; dialogue is decentralized to relationship owners. Treasury talks to regulators, rating agencies and clearing banks; investor relations to investors, analysts and media.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Assess the key components of a contingency funding plan (governance and oversight, scenarios and liquidity gap analysis, contingent actions, monitoring and escalation, and data and reporting). **GARP:** Chapter 11, Section 11.4, Governance and Oversight, “Communication and Coordination”. **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser says central management ensures “absolute consistency” but that some groups (investor relations, legal, compliance) should keep the dialogue with their established contacts; it omits GARP’s detailed mapping and the instruction to leverage existing plans. No conflict on the key.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-11 c, where it is Q3 of 15.

a.reason: GARP says communication content should be centrally managed while bidirectional coordination resides with teams that have existing working relationships, and it lists corporate treasury as the point of contact for regulators and supervisors, rating agencies and clearing banks. Option A matches both parts.

b.reason: (Absolute claim). Routing all bidirectional communication through the LCT alone overextends central management from content to every conversation. GARP keeps the content central but leaves the two-way dialogue with the teams that hold the relationships. The option would be correct if it said messaging and content were routed through a single central function, with dialogue left to relationship owners.

c.reason: (Role misassignment). GARP’s illustrative coordination points pair regulators and supervisors with corporate treasury and with legal and compliance; investor relations covers investors, the analyst community and public media. The option would be correct if the stakeholders named were investors and analysts.

d.reason: (Polarity flip). GARP tells institutions to leverage existing communication plans (BAU and business continuity) in the CFP design and enhance them where appropriate. Building a separate plan reverses that direction. The option would be correct if it said the CFP plan should build on the existing business continuity communication plan.

questions.question: An internal auditor at an Australian bank is comparing the table of contents of the bank’s draft CFP policy with the illustrative CFP policy outline described in the FRM reading. The outline has five headings: Introduction; Governance; Stress testing and scenarios overview; Monitoring and escalation; and Reporting. Which of the following placements in the draft matches the illustrative outline?

options.text: Key assumptions and model validation are placed under Governance.
Liquidity gap analysis and contingent actions are placed under Stress testing and scenarios overview.
Liquidity gap analysis and contingent actions are placed under Monitoring and escalation.
Periodic review of the CFP is placed under Introduction.

questions.solution:
Australian bank, CFP policy document: which placement matches the illustrative CFP policy outline?

**Concept and theory**

Policies and procedures are the written backbone of CFP governance. GARP says institutions should document their CFPs and align the documentation with other risk management, business continuity and recovery planning policies. The documentation should cover all aspects of the CFP: governance structure, processes, data and reporting. The policy should be applied consistently, whether the firm has one CFP or several, and reviewed and updated periodically so it stays aligned with current and forecast business activities and risk exposures. GARP’s illustrative outline is:

| Heading | Sub-items |
|---|---|

questions.question: A treasury analyst at a U.S. bank holding company is drafting the annual testing and readiness assessment plan for the bank’s CFP. The CFP’s menu of contingent actions includes debt issuance, brokered deposit issuance, sales of investment portfolio securities, Federal Reserve borrowing, large asset sales and business divestitures. Which of the following proposals for the plan is most appropriate?

options.text: Assess only the menu of contingent actions, because governance, escalation, communication and reporting are already validated through the annual policy approval.
Execute a debt issuance, a brokered deposit issuance and a limited sale of investment portfolio securities to test that these channels can generate liquidity.
Restrict the assessment to a desk review of the CFP document, because simulated crisis exercises rarely uncover gaps beyond those found during design.
Test every contingent action in the menu, including large asset sales and a business divestiture, so that each is proven executable before a crisis.

questions.solution:
U.S. bank holding company, annual CFP testing and readiness plan: which proposal is most appropriate?

**Concept and theory**

A CFP that has never been exercised is, in GARP’s phrase, left “purely as a theoretical design exercise”. Testing and readiness assessment is therefore part of the governance component. GARP sets out two strands.

Testing targeted elements. On a periodic basis, institutions should evaluate their CFP’s operational readiness and test targeted elements to make sure they remain relevant and executable under stress, given changing market dynamics and the firm’s business and risk profile. Not everything can be tested. Business divestitures, large asset sales and use of Federal Reserve borrowing may be impractical or unavailable for testing. Some market activities can be tested: debt issuances, brokered deposit issuances and limited sales of securities from the investment portfolio to generate liquidity.

Evaluating operational effectiveness. Institutions should also evaluate the CFP’s governance, escalation process, communication, coordination and reporting. Leading institutions run frequent exercises that best simulate the potential crisis environment; this improves operational effectiveness and response times, which are critical in a crisis, and can reveal gaps and improvement opportunities that would otherwise go undetected.

| Can be tested (GARP) | Likely impractical or unavailable to test |
|---|---|
| Debt issuance | Business divestitures |
| Brokered deposit issuance | Large asset sales |
| Limited sale of investment portfolio securities | Federal Reserve borrowing |

**Applying it to this question**

The stem’s action menu mixes both columns of the table. A sound plan tests the channels that can realistically be exercised in small size (debt issuance, brokered deposits, limited securities sales) and separately evaluates the operational machinery through simulation. Option B proposes exactly GARP’s testable activities.

**Fragile fact.** Testable: debt issuance, brokered deposits, limited securities sales. Not practical to test: divestitures, large asset sales, Fed borrowing. Effectiveness review covers governance, escalation, communication, coordination and reporting.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Assess the key components of a contingency funding plan (governance and oversight, scenarios and liquidity gap analysis, contingent actions, monitoring and escalation, and data and reporting). **GARP:** Chapter 11, Section 11.4, Governance and Oversight, “Testing and Readiness Assessment”. **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser gives debt issuance and investment portfolio sales as testable examples and omits brokered deposits and the list of impractical activities; GARP followed.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-11 c, where it is Q5 of 15.

a.reason: (Scope or condition error (dropped element)). GARP says the operational effectiveness evaluation should cover governance, the escalation process, communication, coordination and reporting, not only the action menu. Annual policy approval is not a substitute for testing. The option would be correct if it proposed assessing the action menu together with governance, escalation, communication, coordination and reporting.

b.reason: GARP names debt issuances, brokered deposit issuances and limited securities sales from the investment portfolio as market activities that may be appropriate to test. Option B limits the live tests to these three channels, so it is consistent with the source.

c.reason: (Polarity flip). GARP says simulation exercises may identify gaps and improvement opportunities that would otherwise go undetected, and that frequent realistic exercises improve response times. The option reverses this. It would be correct if it said simulated exercises often uncover gaps that a desk review would miss.

d.reason: (Absolute claim). GARP explicitly notes that business divestitures, large asset sales and Federal Reserve borrowing may be impractical or unavailable for testing. Promising that every action will be proven executable overstates what testing can do. The option would be correct if limited to actions that can be exercised in small size.

questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a German bank presents the scenarios and liquidity gap analysis section of the bank’s CFP to the risk committee. The section contains the following statements:

I. The CFP stress scenarios should be aligned to those in the liquidity stress testing framework and to other frameworks, such as the recovery and resolution plans.

II. The liquidity stress testing scenarios that feed the CFP need to cover only idiosyncratic risks, because systemic stress is addressed through central bank facilities.

III. The CFP may contain additional liquidity-related scenarios, such as the failure of specific counterparties, that sit outside the bank’s broader liquidity risk monitoring and limit structure.

IV. The liquidity stress testing framework, rather than the CFP, provides the tactical mechanism for escalating a developing crisis to management’s attention.

Which of the statements are accurate?

options.text: I and III only
I, II and III only
III and IV only
I, III and IV only

questions.solution:
German bank, four statements on CFP scenarios and liquidity gap analysis: alignment, coverage, additional scenarios, tactical role.

**Concept and theory**

The second component, scenarios and liquidity gap analysis, is where the CFP connects to the stress testing framework. GARP makes four points.

Alignment. Institutions should align their CFP stress scenarios to those in the liquidity stress testing framework and to other frameworks such as recovery and resolution plans. One set of scenarios, used consistently, means the triggers, actions and recovery plans are all sized for the same events.

Coverage of the stress testing scenarios. The stress testing scenarios cover both systemic (general market) and idiosyncratic (institution-specific) risks, address both market (asset) liquidity and funding liquidity, and run over short-term and prolonged stress periods. The stress testing framework measures and monitors the effect of these stresses on the liquidity profile.

Division of labour. The CFP in turn provides a tactical mechanism for escalating a developing crisis to management’s attention and ensuring actionable responses are available. Stress testing measures; the CFP escalates and acts.

Additional scenarios. Beyond the stress test outcomes, the CFP may contain additional liquidity-related scenarios that sit outside the broader liquidity risk monitoring and limit structure, to make sure contingency plans exist for specific events. GARP’s examples: the intraday debit cap with Fedwire is exceeded, specific counterparties fail, or Federal Home Loan Bank funding becomes unavailable.

These scenario results drive the liquidity gap analysis, which in turn is the basis for choosing contingent actions (the third component).

**Applying it to this question**

Statement I matches GARP’s alignment guidance: true. Statement II restricts coverage to idiosyncratic risk; GARP requires both systemic and idiosyncratic: false. Statement III matches GARP’s description of additional scenarios outside the limit structure, with one of GARP’s own examples: true. Statement IV gives the tactical escalation role to the stress testing framework; GARP gives it to the CFP: false. So I and III only.

**Fragile fact.** Stress testing measures; the CFP escalates and acts. Coverage is systemic and idiosyncratic, asset and funding liquidity, short and prolonged. Extra CFP scenarios may sit outside the limit structure.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Assess the key components of a contingency funding plan (governance and oversight, scenarios and liquidity gap analysis, contingent actions, monitoring and escalation, and data and reporting). **GARP:** Chapter 11, Section 11.4, “Scenarios and Liquidity Gap Analysis”. **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser says CFP scenarios should “link to the recovery provisions” and that the CFP may examine scenarios “beyond the firm’s normal scope of analysis”; GARP is more specific (recovery and resolution plans; outside the monitoring and limit structure; Fedwire, counterparty failure, FHLB examples). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-11 c, where it is Q6 of 15.

a.reason: Option A selects exactly the two statements that restate GARP: alignment with the stress testing framework and recovery and resolution plans (I), and additional CFP scenarios outside the broader monitoring and limit structure (III).

b.reason: (Scope or condition error (Statement II accepted)). Statement II drops systemic risk from the required coverage. GARP’s stress testing scenarios cover both systemic and idiosyncratic risks; the availability of central bank facilities does not remove systemic scenarios. Option B would be correct only if Statement II said “both systemic and idiosyncratic risks”.

c.reason: (Role misassignment (Statement IV accepted) and omission of I). Option C accepts Statement IV, which hands the CFP’s tactical escalation role to the stress testing framework, and it drops the true Statement I. Statement IV would be true if it read “the CFP, rather than the stress testing framework, provides the tactical mechanism”.

d.reason: (Role misassignment (Statement IV accepted)). Option D includes the two true statements but adds Statement IV, in which the actor is swapped. In GARP, stress testing measures and monitors the effects of stress, while the CFP escalates a developing crisis and keeps responses actionable.

questions.question:
The CRO of an Australian bank has received the results of the bank’s liquidity gap analysis under a severe combined stress scenario, together with three candidate contingent actions.

| Projected cumulative liquidity shortfall | AUD billion |
|---|---|
| Within 1 week | 0.4 |
| Within 1 month | 1.6 |
| Within 3 months | 3.1 |

| Candidate action | Estimated relief (AUD billion) | Time to execute |
|---|---|---|
| Sale of liquid investment securities | 1.2 | 2 days |
| Securitization of a mortgage pool | 2.5 | 10 weeks |
| Sale of an insurance subsidiary | 4.0 | 9 months |

The bank’s current liquidity coverage ratio is 131%. Which of the following approaches to selecting contingent actions is most appropriate?

options.text: Prioritize the subsidiary sale, because its estimated relief alone exceeds the largest cumulative shortfall in the analysis.
Compare each action’s relief only with the 3-month cumulative shortfall, because that single figure captures the full liquidity need.
Rank the actions by their cost of funding, because contingent actions are intended to protect profitability through the stress period.
Match each action’s relief and execution timing to the size, timing and pattern of the shortfall, and to the bank’s ability to execute it.

questions.solution:
Australian bank, liquidity gap analysis with three candidate contingent actions: how should actions be selected?

**Concept and theory**

Contingent actions are the third component of the CFP, and GARP ties them directly to the liquidity gap analysis. Based on that analysis, institutions develop contingent actions, which GARP also calls capital recovery actions: business scoping activities, pricing initiatives, disposition actions and expense controls that strengthen the liquidity position. GARP then gives the test for whether an action is applicable and appropriate. It should be considered in the context of:

(1) the nature and severity (amount) of the shortfall;

(2) the associated timing and pattern of the expected shortfall;

(3) the estimated relief from the contingent action; and

(4) the institution’s ability to execute the internal or external market activities the action requires.

The reason is simple: a gap analysis produces a profile through time, not one number. An action that releases a large amount but only after nine months does nothing for a gap that opens next week, and an action that depends on a market the firm cannot access under stress is not really available. The CFP therefore needs a sequence of actions whose relief, timing and feasibility line up with the shape of the projected shortfall. GARP’s later section on availability adds that the systemic or idiosyncratic nature and the severity of the stress determine which actions remain available.

**Applying it to this question**

The gap grows from AUD 0.4 billion (1 week) to AUD 1.6 billion (1 month) to AUD 3.1 billion (3 months). The securities sale (AUD 1.2 billion in 2 days) addresses the early part of the profile; the securitization (AUD 2.5 billion in 10 weeks) arrives within the 3-month horizon; the subsidiary sale (AUD 4.0 billion in 9 months) arrives after the whole analysed horizon. Only an approach that weighs amount, timing, pattern, relief and execution capability can handle this profile, which is option D. The liquidity coverage ratio of 131% is irrelevant: it is a regulatory ratio, not one of GARP’s selection criteria for contingent actions, and it does not change the shape of the gap.

**Fragile fact.** Four selection factors: amount (nature and severity), timing and pattern, estimated relief, ability to execute. Schweser’s condensed list has only the first three.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Assess the key components of a contingency funding plan (governance and oversight, scenarios and liquidity gap analysis, contingent actions, monitoring and escalation, and data and reporting). **GARP:** Chapter 11, Section 11.4, “Contingent Actions”. **GARP** **vs Schweser:** Schweser lists amount of the shortfall, when it occurs and the inflow from the action, omitting the institution’s ability to execute; GARP’s fuller list followed. Both sources describe the shortfall as a “capital” shortfall in this passage; it is read here as the liquidity shortfall identified by the gap analysis.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-11 c, where it is Q7 of 15.

a.reason: (Scope or condition error (dropped timing and execution conditions)). The subsidiary sale’s AUD 4.0 billion does exceed the AUD 3.1 billion peak gap, but it takes 9 months, well after the 1-week and 1-month gaps arise, and a divestiture depends on the bank’s ability to execute it in stressed markets. The option would be correct if the sale could be completed within the 1-week horizon.

b.reason: (Scope or condition error (dropped timing and pattern)). Using only the 3-month cumulative figure throws away the timing and pattern of the shortfall, which GARP lists as a separate consideration. The option would be correct only if the whole shortfall arose at a single date, so that one figure did describe the full need.

c.reason: (Sibling swap (profitability objective substituted for liquidity objective)). Contingent actions are chosen to strengthen the liquidity position against the projected shortfall, not to protect profitability. Funding cost matters only after an action can close the gap in time. The option would describe a BAU funding optimization exercise, not CFP action selection.

d.reason: GARP says the applicability of contingent actions should be considered in light of the nature and severity of the shortfall, its timing and pattern, the estimated relief from the action, and the institution’s ability to execute. Option D lists these factors and applies them to the bank’s actual profile.
