questions.source: High quality paper LTR-12 c Q1
questions.question:
A junior risk analyst at a US regional bank owned by a Japanese banking group is drafting the “relative cost” paragraph of the bank’s funding policy. Her draft contains the following statements about short-term borrowing rates:

I. Among the cheapest short-term borrowed funds is usually the prevailing effective interest rate on Federal funds loaned overnight to borrowing institutions.

II. The primary credit rate on loans from the Federal Reserve banks is generally among the lowest short-term borrowing rates, because the central bank does not lend for profit.

III. Commercial paper may normally be issued at interest rates slightly above the Federal funds and CD rates, depending upon maturity and time of issue.

IV. The effective Federal funds rate is usually the absolute lowest rate in the money market, below even the rate on the shortest-term US Treasury bills.

Which of the statements are accurate?

options.text: I and II only
I, III and IV only
I and III only
II and III only

questions.solution:
Funding policy draft: four statements on the relative cost of short-term borrowing sources.

**Concept and theory**

The first of GARP’s five factors in choosing among nondeposit sources is the relative cost of raising funds from each source. Managers practising liability management must constantly track the going market rates on each source; major lenders post daily rates at which they will commit funds to institutions needing reserves. In general managers prefer to borrow from the cheapest source, although the other four factors (risk, maturity, size, regulation) also play a role, which is why cost alone never settles the choice.

GARP gives a typical ordering of short-term borrowing rates (illustrated by Table 13.9):

| Source | Typical position (GARP Section 13.4, Relative Costs) |
|---|---|
| Overnight Fed funds | Among the cheapest short-term borrowed funds (effective rate) |
| Domestic CDs, Eurocurrency deposits | In most cases slightly higher than the Fed funds rate |
| Commercial paper | Normally slightly above Fed funds and CD rates, depending on maturity and time of issue |
| Primary credit (discount window) | Today generally among the highest short-term rates, because it is priced above the central bank’s target Fed funds rate |
| Shortest-term Treasury bills | Often slightly lower than the Fed funds rate (GARP Factoid) |

Two subtleties matter. First, the primary credit rate’s position is a policy choice: before 2003 the Fed’s discount rate was frequently the lowest money market rate and often below the Fed funds rate, which tempted banks to borrow at the window and relend in the Fed funds market. Since then primary credit has been set above the target (initially 100 basis points, later around 50 basis points above). Second, “among the cheapest” is not “the cheapest”: GARP’s Factoid explicitly says the Fed funds rate is not usually the absolute lowest, because short Treasury bill rates often sit slightly below it.

**Applying it to this question**

Audit each statement against the ordering. Statement I repeats GARP’s claim that the effective overnight Fed funds rate is usually among the cheapest sources: accurate. Statement II reverses the position of primary credit and gives an invented reason; GARP says the primary credit rate is generally among the highest short-term rates because it is priced above the Fed funds target: inaccurate. Statement III matches GARP on commercial paper, including the qualifier “depending upon maturity and time of issue”: accurate. Statement IV upgrades “among the cheapest” to “the absolute lowest” and contradicts the Factoid that the shortest Treasury bills often yield slightly less: inaccurate. Only I and III survive.

**Fragile fact.** Direction: today primary credit sits above the Fed funds target (among the highest short-term rates); Fed funds are among the cheapest borrowed funds but not below short Treasury bills.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Discuss factors affecting the choice of nondeposit funding sources. **GARP:** Chapter 13, Section 13.4 Choosing among Alternative Nondeposit Sources, “Relative Costs”, Table 13.9 and the Factoids box; the pre-2003 discount rate point is from the “Real Banks, Real Decisions” box on the Lombard rate (Section 13.3). **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser gives the same ordering for Fed funds, CDs, Eurocurrency deposits and commercial paper but omits the primary credit rate and the Treasury bill Factoid (GARP used).

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-12 c, where it is Q1 of 11.

a.reason: (Polarity flip). Including statement II accepts that primary credit is among the lowest rates. GARP places it among the highest because it is priced above the target Fed funds rate. The option would be correct only for the pre-2003 regime, when the discount rate was often below the Fed funds rate (for example, Table 13.9 shows 3.76% versus 4.47% in 1994).

b.reason: (Absolute claim). Including statement IV turns “among the cheapest” into “the absolute lowest in the money market”. GARP’s Factoid says the shortest-term Treasury bill rate is often slightly lower than the Fed funds rate. B would be correct only if IV had said Fed funds are among the cheapest borrowed funds for depository institutions.

c.reason: C is correct because statements I and III paraphrase GARP’s Relative Costs subsection (Fed funds among the cheapest; commercial paper slightly above Fed funds and CD rates depending on maturity and time of issue), while II and IV each contain a single error.

d.reason: (Polarity flip). D keeps the true statement III but swaps statement I for the false statement II, placing primary credit at the cheap end instead of the expensive end. It would be correct only if the stem described the Fed’s discount window before 2003.

questions.source: High quality paper LTR-12 c Q2
questions.question: The treasurer of a mid-sized US commercial bank is presenting to newly hired treasury analysts on how Federal funds compare with negotiable CDs and commercial paper as nondeposit funding sources. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: The key advantage of Fed funds is ready availability, with maturities from a few hours to several months; CD and commercial paper rates are usually somewhat more stable and slightly above the Fed funds rate, reflecting longer average maturity and marketing costs.

The key advantage of Fed funds is ready availability, with maturities from a few hours to several months; CD and commercial paper rates are usually somewhat more stable and slightly below the Fed funds rate, reflecting longer average maturity and marketing costs.

The key advantage of Fed funds is a stable market rate that tracks the central bank’s target closely, even on reserve settlement days; CD and commercial paper rates are usually slightly above the Fed funds rate, reflecting longer average maturity and marketing costs.

The key advantage of Fed funds is ready availability, with maturities from a few hours to several months; CDs and commercial paper are usually more popular than Fed funds in the short run, when a depository institution needs money right away.

questions.solution:
Treasurer’s induction talk: Fed funds versus negotiable CDs and commercial paper.

**Concept and theory**

Within the relative cost factor GARP contrasts the cheapest short-term source, Federal funds, with the next tier, negotiable CDs and commercial paper. The comparison is a trade-off rather than a ranking on price alone.

| Feature | Fed funds | Negotiable CDs and commercial paper |
|---|---|---|
| Level of rate | Among the lowest borrowing rates | Close to and slightly above Fed funds |
| Stability of rate | Volatile around the target; wide swings, especially on reserve settlement day | Usually somewhat more stable |
| Why | Overnight market priced by supply and demand | Longer average maturity; marketing costs of finding buyers |
| Availability | Key advantage: ready availability by phone or online request; maturities from a few hours to several months | Less popular in the short run when money is needed right away |
| Best use | Immediate, short-term needs | Longer-term needs stretching over several days or weeks |

GARP names the “key advantage” of Fed funds as ready availability with flexible maturities, and the “key disadvantage” as the volatile market rate, whose often wide fluctuations (especially on the settlement day when institutions are meeting legal reserve requirements) make planning difficult. CD and commercial paper rates hover slightly above Fed funds for two stated reasons: their longer average maturity and the marketing costs spent finding buyers. In the short run, when a depository institution needs money right away, Fed funds and the discount window are the popular choices, and CDs and commercial paper are better suited to needs lasting several days or weeks.

**Applying it to this question**

Each option has three components: Fed funds’ key feature, the level of CD and commercial paper rates, and the reason or use. Check each against the table. Option A gets all three right. Options B, C and D each change exactly one component: B the level of CD and commercial paper rates, C the key feature of Fed funds, D the short-run popularity.

**Fragile fact.** Fed funds: advantage is availability, disadvantage is rate volatility (settlement day); CDs and commercial paper: slightly higher but more stable rates.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Discuss factors affecting the choice of nondeposit funding sources. **GARP:** Chapter 13, Section 13.4, “Relative Costs”. **GARP vs Schweser:** none of substance; Schweser condenses the same points and omits the marketing-cost reason (GARP used).

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-12 c, where it is Q2 of 11.

a.reason: A is correct because it restates GARP: Fed funds’ key advantage is ready availability with maturities as short as a few hours or as long as several months, and CD and commercial paper rates are “somewhat more stable” and slightly above Fed funds because of longer average maturity and marketing costs.

b.reason: (Polarity flip). B says CD and commercial paper rates sit slightly below Fed funds. GARP says they hover close to and slightly above the Fed funds rate; the stated reasons (longer maturity, marketing costs) push the rate up, not down. B would be correct only if the comparison were with a source priced above Fed funds, such as primary credit.

c.reason: (Polarity flip). C names a stable rate as Fed funds’ key advantage. GARP says the rate is volatile, fluctuating around the target with often wide swings especially on settlement day, and calls this the key disadvantage. C would describe CD and commercial paper rates, not Fed funds.

d.reason: (Polarity flip). D reverses short-run popularity. GARP says CDs and commercial paper are usually less popular than Fed funds and the discount window when money is needed right away, and better for needs stretching over several days or weeks. D would be correct if “in the short run” were replaced by “for needs lasting several days or weeks”.

questions.source: High quality paper LTR-12 c Q3
questions.question:
A treasury analyst at a US savings bank is estimating the annualized effective cost rate of raising funds by selling negotiable CDs. Management’s estimates are:

| Item | Estimate |
|---|---|
| Negotiable CDs to be sold | USD 60 million |
| Current interest rate on the CDs | 5.20% |
| Noninterest costs (staff time, facilities, transaction costs) | 0.80% of amount raised |
| Funds placed in nonearning assets | USD 1.5 million |
| Deposit insurance assessment | USD 0.0030 per dollar of deposits |
| Effective Federal funds rate today | 4.90% |
| Shareholders’ required after-tax return | 12.0% |

Which of the following is closest to the effective cost rate of the CD funding?
questions.solution:
Effective cost rate of USD 60 million of negotiable CDs with noninterest costs, nonearning assets and deposit insurance.

**Concept and theory**

The quoted interest rate understates what a source really costs. GARP says the rate of interest is usually the principal expense of borrowing nondeposit funds, but noninterest costs (including the time management and staff spend finding the best source each time new money is needed) cannot be ignored. And not every dollar raised can be put to work: some is absorbed by reserve requirements, deposit insurance assessments, or diversion into nonearning assets such as excess cash reserves or fixed assets. GARP therefore compares sources on an effective cost rate, the dollar cost of attracting the funds divided by the dollars that can actually be invested:

Effective cost rate $= \frac{\text{Current interest cost} + \text{Noninterest costs to access funds}}{\text{Net investable funds raised}}$

Current interest cost $= \text{r} \times$ B, Noninterest costs $= \text{c} \times$ B

Net investable funds $= \text{B} -$ reserve requirements $- \text{deposit insurance} -$ nonearning assets

where B is the total amount borrowed, r the prevailing money market rate on the source and c the estimated noninterest cost rate (staff time, facilities, transaction costs). For CDs, which are legally deposits, the deposit insurance fee equals the assessment rate times the full face amount of deposits received, not just the insured portion, and GARP deducts it from net investable funds. The result is the minimum annualized return the institution must earn on the loans and investments financed by that source just to break even. GARP’s illustration shows the deduction matters: a CD costing 8.07% before the insurance fee costs 8.10% after it, still above Fed funds at 6.51%.

**Applying it to this question**

Formula first, then one step per line (USD millions):

Interest cost = 0.0520 × 60 = 3.12

Noninterest costs = 0.0080 × 60 = 0.48

Numerator = 3.12 + 0.48 = 3.60

Deposit insurance fee = 0.0030 × 60 = 0.18

Net investable funds = 60 − 1.5 − 0.18 = 58.32

Effective cost rate = 3.60/58.32 = 0.06173 ≈ 6.17%

The bank must earn at least 6.17% annualized on the assets financed by the CDs to break even, 97 basis points above the 5.20% quoted rate. Two inputs are irrelevant. The 4.90% Fed funds rate belongs to a different source; it is useful only for a later comparison. The 12% shareholders’ required return enters the historical average cost of capital in LO 77.d, not the effective cost of a single source. No reserve requirement is given, so none is deducted.

**Fragile fact.** The deposit insurance fee reduces the denominator (net investable funds) and is charged on the full face amount of the CDs, not just the insured portion.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Discuss factors affecting the choice of nondeposit funding sources. **GARP:** Chapter 13, Section 13.4, “Relative Costs”, Equations 13.4 to 13.8 and the Fed funds and CD worked examples. **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser lists reserve requirements and insurance fees among “noninterest costs”, blurring the numerator and denominator; GARP deducts them from net investable funds (GARP used).

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-12 c, where it is Q3 of 11.

a.reason: (Dropped term). 5.35% omits the noninterest costs: 3.12/58.32 = 5.35%. GARP stresses that noninterest costs cannot be ignored. A would be correct only if the stem said accessing the CD market involved no staff, facilities or transaction costs.

b.reason: (Dropped term). 6.00% divides by the gross amount raised: 3.60/60 = 6.00%, which is simply r + c. It ignores both deductions that create net investable funds. B would be correct only if every dollar raised could be placed in earning assets and no insurance were charged.

c.reason: (Dropped term). 6.15% deducts the nonearning assets but forgets the insurance fee: 3.60/(60 − 1.5) = 3.60/58.5 = 6.15%. C would be correct for a source that carries no deposit insurance assessment, such as Fed funds or commercial paper, or for a CD issuer in a regime with no insurance fee.

d.reason: D is correct because it applies GARP’s formula in full: interest plus noninterest costs in the numerator, and the amount raised reduced by both nonearning assets and the deposit insurance assessment in the denominator.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Discuss factors affecting the choice of non-deposit funding sources.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-12 c Q4
questions.question:
An internal auditor at a Singapore-headquartered bank is validating the spreadsheet that the bank’s US branch uses to compare the effective cost rates of alternative nondeposit funding sources. The model documentation makes the following statements:

I. Noninterest costs, such as staff time, facilities and transaction costs, are added to the current interest cost on the amount borrowed to form the numerator.

II. Legal reserve requirements on the funds raised are added to the numerator as a noninterest cost of accessing the funds.

III. The denominator is net investable funds: the total amount borrowed less legal reserve requirements (if any), deposit insurance assessments (if any) and funds placed in nonearning assets.

IV. Whenever part of the borrowed funds is diverted into nonearning assets, the effective cost rate exceeds the sum of the market interest rate and the noninterest cost rate.

Which of the statements are consistent with the effective cost rate formula?

options.text: I and III only
I, III and IV only
II, III and IV only
I, II, III and IV

questions.solution:
Model validation: four statements on the components of the effective cost rate formula.

**Concept and theory**

The effective cost rate puts every nondeposit source on a common footing, so a cheap-looking source with heavy fees, or one whose funds cannot all be invested, is not mistakenly preferred. GARP builds it from three parts:

| Component | Contents (GARP Equations 13.5 to 13.7) |
|---|---|
| Numerator: current interest cost | Prevailing money market rate × amount borrowed |
| Numerator: noninterest costs | Cost rate for staff time, facilities and transaction costs × amount borrowed |
| Denominator: net investable funds | Total borrowed less legal reserve requirements (if any), deposit insurance assessments (if any) and funds placed in nonearning assets |

The logic of the base is explained in GARP: net investable funds is used “as the borrowing base” because the aim is to compare the dollar cost paid to attract funds with the dollar amount that can actually be used to acquire earning assets and cover the cost of fund-raising. Deductions such as reserve requirements and insurance therefore work by shrinking the base, not by adding to the numerator.

A useful algebraic consequence follows when both costs are proportional to the amount borrowed B and net investable funds are N \< B:

Effective cost rate $= \frac{(\text{r} + \text{c}) \text{B}}{\text{N}} = (\text{r} + \text{c}) \times\frac{\text{B}}{\text{N}} > \text{r} +$ c.

Any diversion of funds into nonearning assets (or any reserve or insurance deduction) grosses up the combined rate. In GARP’s Fed funds example, (6.00% + 0.25%) × 25/24 = 6.51%.

**Applying it to this question**

Statement I places staff time, facilities and transaction costs in the numerator: consistent.

Statement II places legal reserve requirements in the numerator as a noninterest cost: inconsistent, because Equation 13.7 deducts them from the amount borrowed to obtain net investable funds.

Statement III reproduces Equation 13.7: consistent. Statement IV follows from the algebra above: if any funds go to nonearning assets, B/N > 1 and the effective rate exceeds r + c: consistent. The statements consistent with the formula are I, III and IV.

**Fragile fact.** Staff, facilities and transaction costs go in the numerator; reserve requirements, deposit insurance and nonearning assets shrink the denominator (net investable funds).

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Discuss factors affecting the choice of nondeposit funding sources. **GARP:** Chapter 13, Section 13.4, “Relative Costs”, Equations 13.4 to 13.7 and the paragraph on net investable funds as the borrowing base. **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser lists “deductions for reserve requirements, insurance fees” and nonearning assets among noninterest costs; GARP treats them as reductions of net investable funds (GARP used; the Schweser wording is a condensation, not a different formula, since Schweser’s own formula still divides by net investable funds).

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-12 c, where it is Q4 of 11.

a.reason: (Scope or condition error). A rejects statement IV, treating the gross-up as optional. Because the base is net investable funds rather than the amount borrowed, any diversion into nonearning assets raises the effective rate above r + c (6.51% versus 6.25% in GARP’s example). A would be correct only if IV had claimed the effective rate exceeds r + c even when every dollar borrowed is invested.

b.reason: B is correct because GARP’s formula puts interest and noninterest (staff, facilities, transaction) costs over net investable funds, defined as the amount borrowed less reserve requirements, insurance assessments and nonearning assets; this makes I and III true and implies IV.

c.reason: (Role misassignment). C accepts statement II, which treats legal reserve requirements as a numerator cost. GARP assigns them to the denominator, as a deduction in arriving at net investable funds. C also drops statement I, which is true. C would be correct only under a convention that books reserves as a cost and excludes noninterest costs, which is not GARP’s formula.

d.reason: (Role misassignment). D accepts all four statements, including II. Reserve requirements cannot be both a numerator cost and a denominator deduction without double counting; GARP uses them only in the denominator. D would be correct only if II described staff time or transaction costs instead of reserve requirements.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Discuss factors affecting the choice of non-deposit funding sources.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-12 c Q5
questions.question: A senior risk analyst at a UK retail bank is preparing a board paper on whether the bank should increase its reliance on money market borrowing relative to its deposit base. Which of the following statements best describes how nondeposit funds compare with deposits?

options.text: Nondeposit funds tend to be less expensive than checkable deposits but more expensive than time and savings deposits, and their costs and profits tend to be more volatile from year to year than those of deposits.

Nondeposit funds tend to be more expensive than checkable deposits but less expensive than time and savings deposits, and their costs and profits tend to be less volatile from year to year than those of deposits.

Nondeposit funds tend to be more expensive than checkable deposits but less expensive than time and savings deposits, and although quickly available, they are not as stable a funding source as time and savings deposits.

Nondeposit funds tend to be more expensive than checkable deposits but less expensive than time and savings deposits, and they are a more stable funding source than time and savings deposits because the borrower sets amount and term.

questions.solution:
Board paper: cost and stability of nondeposit funds compared with deposits.

**Concept and theory**

After comparing nondeposit sources with each other, GARP steps back and places nondeposit funding as a whole against deposit funding. The comparison has three dimensions:

| Dimension | GARP’s statement about nondeposit funds |
|---|---|
| Level of cost | Generally moderate: more expensive than checkable deposits, less expensive than thrift (time and savings) deposits |
| Volatility of cost and profit | Costs and profits tend to be more volatile from year to year than the cost and profitability of deposits |
| Availability and stability | Quick availability compared with most deposits, but clearly not as stable a funding source as time and savings deposits |

The reasoning is intuitive. Checkable deposits pay little or no interest, so purchased money market funds cost more; time and savings deposits pay higher contractual rates and carry their own servicing costs, so nondeposit funds can be cheaper. But nondeposit funds are priced in open markets every day; GARP’s discussion of liability management notes that money market suppliers respond elastically to rate changes, and that if the borrower is unwilling to pay higher rates, funds “will be gone in minutes”. Hence their cost and profitability swing more from year to year, and their stability is lower even though they can be raised quickly. Flexibility is real (the borrower decides how much and for how long), but flexibility in raising funds is not the same as stability in keeping them.

**Applying it to this question**

All four options share the cost-level clause or a variant of it, and differ in one further claim. A reverses the cost ordering. B keeps the ordering but reverses the volatility claim. D keeps the ordering but reverses the stability claim. Only C keeps both the ordering (more than checkable, less than time and savings) and the availability-versus-stability trade-off as GARP states it.

**Fragile fact.** Cost order: checkable deposits $< \text{nondeposit funds} <$ time and savings deposits; nondeposit funds are quicker to raise but less stable, with more volatile year-to-year costs.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Discuss factors affecting the choice of nondeposit funding sources. **GARP:** Chapter 13, Section 13.4, “Relative Costs” (closing paragraph on nondeposit versus deposit funding); flexibility point from Section 13.2. **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser omits the comparison with checkable and time and savings deposits (GARP-only content; GARP used). Schweser’s Section 77.a note that nondeposit funds carry more interest rate risk than deposits is consistent.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-12 c, where it is Q5 of 11.

a.reason: (Polarity flip). A reverses the cost ordering, placing nondeposit funds below checkable deposits and above time and savings deposits. Its volatility clause is true. A would be correct only if checkable deposits paid market rates and time and savings deposits were the cheapest funds, which is the opposite of GARP’s statement.

b.reason: (Polarity flip). B says nondeposit costs and profits are less volatile than those of deposits. GARP cautions that they tend to be more volatile from year to year. B would be correct if it compared deposits with nondeposit funds rather than the reverse.

c.reason: C is correct because GARP states that nondeposit funds tend to be more expensive than checkable deposits but less expensive than time and savings deposits, and that despite quick availability they are not as stable a funding source as time and savings deposits.

d.reason: (Polarity flip). D concludes that nondeposit funds are more stable than time and savings deposits. The premise (the borrower sets amount and term) is GARP’s flexibility point from Section 13.2, but GARP says nondeposit funds are clearly not as stable as time and savings deposits. D would be correct if “more stable” were replaced by “more flexible”.

questions.question: The CRO of a US commercial bank owned by a Chinese parent is reviewing an ALCO proposal to fund a 90-day corporate loan of USD 75 million by rolling overnight Federal funds each day, instead of selling a 90-day negotiable CD, because the Fed funds rate is currently lower than the CD rate. Which of the following statements best describes the interest rate risk dimension of this choice?

options.text: Rolling overnight Fed funds exposes the bank to the most volatile of the nondeposit market rates, because the shorter the term of a loan, the more volatile the prevailing market rate tends to be.
Interest rate risk is similar under both plans, because the Fed funds rate and the CD rate are both set administratively by the central bank around its target, rather than by supply and demand.
The 90-day CD carries the greater interest rate risk, because the longer the term of a loan, the more volatile the prevailing market rate tends to be, so overnight funding reduces cost volatility.
The main risk of the Fed funds plan is that the Fed funds market is especially sensitive to lenders rationing credit, a risk from which the negotiable CD market is largely insulated.

questions.solution:
ALCO proposal to roll overnight Fed funds for a 90-day loan instead of selling a 90-day CD.

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s second factor is risk, described as the volatility and dependability of each funding source. Managers must consider at least two types. The first, interest rate risk, is defined as the volatility of credit costs. All the money market rates in GARP’s Table 13.9, except most central banks’ discount rates, are set by demand and supply in the open market and so are subject to erratic fluctuations. GARP then states the key regularity: the shorter the term of the loan, the more volatile the prevailing market rate tends to be. Because most Fed funds loans are overnight, the Fed funds rate tends to be the most volatile of all.

This explains why a source can be cheapest and riskiest at the same time. The low Fed funds rate comes with the widest swings, especially on reserve settlement days, which GARP says makes planning difficult. A borrower who rolls overnight money to finance a longer asset re-prices its funding every day at whatever that volatile market delivers; a borrower who uses a longer-term instrument faces a rate that, being set for a longer term, tends to fluctuate less. GARP’s Relative Costs discussion adds the companion fact: CD and commercial paper rates are usually somewhat more stable than Fed funds, though slightly higher.

The second risk, credit availability risk (whether lenders will be willing and able to lend at all), is a different dimension and is tested separately; confusing the two is a classic sibling swap.

**Applying it to this question**

The proposal saves on today’s rate but finances a 90-day asset with overnight money. The question asks only for the interest rate risk dimension. Apply GARP’s rule: shorter term means a more volatile rate, and the overnight Fed funds rate is the most volatile. Rolling daily for 90 days therefore exposes the bank to that volatility on every renewal, whereas the 90-day CD is priced off a longer-term, more stable market rate. The USD 75 million size is irrelevant: both markets are open to a bank needing that amount.

**Fragile fact.** Shorter term means a more volatile rate, so the overnight Fed funds rate is the most volatile; discount rates are the exception because they are administered.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Discuss factors affecting the choice of nondeposit funding sources. **GARP:** Chapter 13, Section 13.4, “The Risk Factor” (interest rate risk) and “Relative Costs” (stability of CD and commercial paper rates). **GARP vs Schweser:** none; Schweser states the same rule (“Rates are more volatile for shorter-term loans”).

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-12 c, where it is Q6 of 11.

a.reason: A is correct because it states GARP’s rule (the shorter the term, the more volatile the rate) and its conclusion (Fed funds, mostly overnight, tend to have the most volatile rate of all).

b.reason: (Scope or condition error). B claims both rates are administered by the central bank. GARP says all the Table 13.9 rates except most central banks’ discount rates are set by demand and supply. B would be correct only for comparing two discount window credit rates, which are administered.

c.reason: (Polarity flip). C reverses the maturity rule, claiming longer-term rates are more volatile. GARP says the shorter the term, the more volatile the rate, so overnight funding increases cost volatility. C would be correct only if the rule in the source ran the other way.

d.reason: (Sibling swap). D substitutes credit availability risk for interest rate risk and attaches it to the wrong market. GARP identifies the negotiable CD, Eurodollar and commercial paper markets, not the Fed funds market, as especially sensitive to credit availability risk. D would describe the CD plan, not the Fed funds plan, if the stem had asked about availability rather than rate volatility.

questions.question: A risk consultant is reviewing the funding of the US branch of a Brazilian bank. The branch funds itself mainly by selling negotiable CDs, borrowing Eurodollars and issuing commercial paper through an affiliate. General credit conditions are tightening, and the branch’s spread over market rates has widened. Which of the following statements best describes the credit availability risk that the consultant should highlight?

options.text: Credit availability risk is the volatility of credit costs, which is greatest for overnight Fed funds, so the branch’s CD, Eurodollar and commercial paper funding carries little of it.

Credit availability risk is the risk that lenders will not accommodate a borrower, and experience shows it is concentrated in the Fed funds market and at the discount window rather than in the branch’s markets.

Credit availability risk is the risk that lenders will not accommodate a borrower; in tight conditions lenders ration credit, but they never refuse a borrower that is willing to pay the going market rate.

Credit availability risk is the risk that lenders will not accommodate a borrower; the CD, Eurodollar and commercial paper markets are especially sensitive to it, so the branch must be ready to switch sources and pay more.

questions.solution:
US branch of a Brazilian bank funded by CDs, Eurodollars and commercial paper as credit conditions tighten.

**Concept and theory**

The second risk GARP asks managers to weigh is credit availability risk: there is no guarantee in any credit market that lenders will be willing and able to accommodate every borrower. It is about the dependability of a source, whereas interest rate risk is about the volatility of its price. GARP describes how it shows up:

- When general credit conditions are tight, lenders may have limited funds and may ration credit, confining loans to their soundest and most loyal customers.
- A financial firm may appear so risky to money market lenders that they deny credit outright, or make the price so high that the borrower’s earnings suffer.
- Experience shows that the negotiable CD, Eurodollar and commercial paper markets are especially sensitive to credit availability risk.
- The management response is preparedness: funds managers must be ready to switch to alternative sources of credit and, if necessary, pay more for the funds they receive.

The 2007 to 2009 crisis is GARP’s background illustration elsewhere in the chapter: the repo market contracted over collateral concerns, and the inability to obtain support in the RP market contributed to the troubles of Bear Stearns and Lehman Brothers. The lesson for funding choice is that a source’s price today says nothing about whether it will be there tomorrow; a funding mix concentrated in the markets most prone to rationing needs a plan for substitution, and that plan will usually cost more.

**Applying it to this question**

The branch relies on exactly the three markets that GARP flags as especially sensitive to credit availability risk, and the stem gives two warning signs: tightening general credit conditions (when lenders ration) and a widening spread (lenders pricing the borrower higher, which GARP lists as an alternative to outright denial). The consultant should therefore stress that availability, not just price, is at risk, and that the branch must be ready to switch to alternative sources and pay more.

**Fragile fact.** Credit availability risk is about whether lenders will lend at all; the CD, Eurodollar and commercial paper markets (not Fed funds) are the ones GARP flags as especially sensitive.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Discuss factors affecting the choice of nondeposit funding sources. **GARP:** Chapter 13, Section 13.4, “The Risk Factor” (credit availability risk); crisis background from Section 13.3, “Repurchase Agreements as a Source of Funds”. **GARP vs** **Schweser:** Schweser adds that “Fed funds are generally more reliable”; GARP does not state this explicitly, so no option relies on it.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-12 c, where it is Q7 of 11.

a.reason: (Sibling swap). A gives the definition of interest rate risk (volatility of credit costs, greatest for overnight Fed funds) under the name of credit availability risk. A would be a correct description of interest rate risk if the stem had asked about the volatility of the branch’s funding costs.

b.reason: (Sibling swap). B uses the right definition but attaches the sensitivity to the wrong markets. GARP singles out the negotiable CD, Eurodollar and commercial paper markets, while the Fed funds market and the discount window are the sources GARP describes as able to lend in small amounts to smaller institutions. B would be correct only if the markets named were swapped.

c.reason: (Absolute claim). C asserts lenders never refuse a borrower willing to pay the market rate. GARP says a firm may appear so risky that lenders deny credit, or set a price so high that earnings suffer. C would be correct only if “never refuse” were softened to “may ration or charge more”.

d.reason: D is correct because it combines GARP’s definition (lenders may be unwilling or unable to accommodate a borrower), its empirical finding (CD, Eurodollar and commercial paper markets are especially sensitive) and its prescription (be prepared to switch sources and, if necessary, pay more).

questions.question:
The treasurer of a US regional bank with USD 6 billion of total assets faces two funding needs. The bank’s dividend payout ratio is 40%.

| Need | Amount | Timing |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Cover a reserve deficiency | USD 35 million | Funds required this afternoon |
| 2. Fund a loan disbursement | USD 120 million | Starts in five days; outstanding for eight weeks |

Which of the following funding plans is most consistent with the role of the length of time for which funds are needed?

options.text: Need 1: borrow in the Fed funds market. Need 2: borrow overnight Fed funds on day five and roll them daily for eight weeks, because the Fed funds rate is the most stable short-term rate.
Need 1: borrow in the Fed funds market. Need 2: because the funds are not needed for a few days, sell longer-term debt, such as negotiable CDs maturing in about eight weeks.
Need 1: sell one-day negotiable CDs to institutional investors this afternoon. Need 2: sell negotiable CDs maturing in about eight weeks.
Need 1: issue commercial paper through an affiliate this afternoon. Need 2: sell negotiable CDs maturing in about eight weeks.

questions.solution:
Two needs: a same-afternoon reserve deficiency and an eight-week loan starting in five days.

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s third factor is the length of time (maturity or term) for which funds are needed. It has two parts: how soon the money must arrive, and how long it must stay.

On immediacy, some sources are difficult to access immediately, notably commercial paper and long-term debt capital. GARP’s illustration is direct: a manager in need of loanable funds “this afternoon” would be inclined to borrow in the Fed funds market, whose key advantage is ready availability through a simple phone call or online request. On term, GARP says that if funds are not needed for a few days, selling longer-term debt becomes a more viable option. The Relative Costs discussion supports the same match: CDs and commercial paper are usually better for longer-term needs stretching over several days or weeks, and CDs have the advantage of being available for several days, weeks, months or years, whereas Fed funds loans must often be repaid in 24 hours.

Rolling overnight money to fund a multi-week asset is technically possible but conflicts with the risk factor, because the overnight Fed funds rate is the most volatile market rate. Regulation also interacts with maturity: in the United States CDs must be issued with maturities of at least seven days, so a CD cannot serve a one-day need.

| Need profile | Source GARP points to |
|---|---|
| Money required today, short need | Fed funds (immediately available) |
| Need starting in a few days, lasting weeks | Longer-term debt such as negotiable CDs (at least seven days) |

**Applying it to this question**

Need 1 must be met this afternoon, which rules out commercial paper (hard to access immediately) and one-day CDs (below the seven-day minimum), and points to Fed funds. Need 2 starts in five days and lasts eight weeks, so a term instrument matched to about eight weeks is viable and avoids eight weeks of daily repricing at the most volatile market rate. Irrelevant inputs: the 40% dividend payout ratio has no bearing on the funding choice, and the USD 6 billion asset size only confirms the bank is large enough for USD 1 million trading units; it does not change the maturity reasoning.

**Fragile fact.** “This afternoon” means Fed funds; “not needed for a few days” makes longer-term debt viable; CDs need a maturity of at least seven days.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Discuss factors affecting the choice of nondeposit funding sources. **GARP:** Chapter 13, Section 13.4, “The Length of Time Funds Are Needed”, “Relative Costs” and “Regulations”. **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser’s maturity example (longer-term funding for fixed-rate mortgages versus overnight funds for reserves) is Schweser-only; not used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-12 c, where it is Q8 of 11.

a.reason: (Polarity flip). A justifies rolling Fed funds for eight weeks by calling the Fed funds rate the most stable short-term rate. GARP says it tends to be the most volatile of all, which is why CDs are better for needs lasting several weeks. A would be defensible only if the need lasted a day or two.

b.reason: B is correct because it follows GARP: borrow Fed funds when funds are needed this afternoon, and, when funds are not needed for a few days, sell longer-term debt, with CDs suited to needs stretching over days or weeks.

c.reason: (Scope or condition error). C proposes one-day CDs for Need 1, ignoring the regulatory condition that US CDs must be issued with maturities of at least seven days. C’s Need 2 leg is fine. C would be correct only if the reserve deficiency needed funding for seven days or more and the CDs could be placed in time.

d.reason: (Sibling swap). D attributes Fed funds’ immediate availability to commercial paper. GARP names commercial paper (with long-term debt capital) as a source that may be difficult to access immediately. D’s Need 2 leg is fine. D would be correct only if Need 1 arose a few days ahead of time.

questions.question: A risk consultant is reviewing the funding plan of a small, unrated US community bank with total assets of USD 95 million. The plan proposes to cover a recurring funding need of about USD 400,000 by selling large negotiable CDs to institutional investors and by borrowing Eurodollars through a London correspondent. Which of the following critiques is most accurate?

options.text: The plan is unsuitable mainly because of size: money market trading units of USD 1 million exceed the need, Eurodollar borrowings usually go only to top-rated money-center firms, and investors prefer the large CDs of the largest banks.

The plan is suitable for the CDs, because investors prefer the large CDs of small banks, which pay higher yields, but the Eurodollar leg should be dropped, because such borrowings usually go only to top-rated money-center firms.

The plan is unsuitable mainly because of interest rate risk: negotiable CD and Eurodollar rates are the most volatile of all nondeposit rates, so the bank should instead fund itself in the Fed funds market.

The plan is unsuitable mainly because of regulation: banks with total assets below USD 100 million are prohibited from issuing negotiable CDs, so the bank must instead fund itself at the discount window.

questions.solution:
Small unrated community bank planning to fund USD 400,000 via large negotiable CDs and Eurodollars.

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s fourth factor is the size of the borrowing institution (in its summary, the size of the institution and its funding needs). Size matters for two reasons: the denomination in which money market funds trade, and the credit standing that investors require.

| Source | Size and access (GARP Section 13.4) |
|---|---|
| Most money market loans | Standard trading unit of USD 1 million, which may exceed the needs of the smallest institutions |
| Eurodollar borrowings | Multiples of USD 1 million; usually available only to money-center firms with the highest credit ratings |
| Large negotiable CDs | Investors prefer those of the largest institutions because of the active secondary market for prime-rated CDs; smaller institutions may lack the credit standing to sell the largest CDs |
| Commercial paper | Same constraint as large CDs |
| Discount window, Fed funds | Can make relatively small-denomination loans suitable for smaller institutions |

The economics are straightforward. Wholesale lenders deal in large round lots, and buyers of negotiable CDs value the ability to resell them before maturity, which exists for prime-rated paper from large issuers. A small, unrated bank therefore faces both a denomination mismatch and an access problem in these markets. GARP’s data on usage confirm the pattern: the smallest US banks support only about 4% of assets with nondeposit borrowings, against about 16% at the largest banks.

**Applying it to this question**

The bank is small (USD 95 million), unrated, and needs about USD 400,000, well below the USD 1 million trading unit. Eurodollars are usually reserved for top-rated money-center firms, and investors prefer the large CDs of the largest institutions. Size is the decisive factor; GARP’s alternatives for such a bank are the Fed funds market and the discount window, which make small-denomination loans.

**Fragile fact.** Investors prefer the large CDs of the largest banks (active secondary market for prime-rated CDs); small banks turn to Fed funds and the discount window.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Discuss factors affecting the choice of nondeposit funding sources. **GARP:** Chapter 13, Section 13.4, “The Size of the Borrowing Institution”; usage percentages from Section 13.3 (Table 13.3). **GARP vs Schweser:** none; Schweser says the same in condensed form.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-12 c, where it is Q9 of 11.

a.reason: A is correct because each of its three reasons is a size statement from GARP: the USD 1 million trading unit exceeding small needs, Eurodollar access limited to the highest-rated money-center firms, and investor preference for large CDs of the largest institutions.

b.reason: (Role misassignment). B assigns the investor preference to small banks’ CDs. GARP says investors prefer large CDs from the largest institutions, because of the active secondary market for prime-rated CDs, and smaller institutions may lack the credit standing to sell them. B’s Eurodollar point is true. B would be correct only if the issuer were a prime-rated money-center bank.

c.reason: (Sibling swap). C attributes the greatest rate volatility to CDs and Eurodollars. GARP says the overnight Fed funds rate tends to be the most volatile of all, and CD rates are usually somewhat more stable. C’s recommended destination (Fed funds) is reasonable, but for the wrong reason. C would be correct if “most volatile” were replaced by “traded in USD 1 million units”.

d.reason: (Scope or condition error). D invents a legal prohibition tied to an asset threshold. GARP says smaller institutions may not have the credit standing to sell the largest CDs, a market-access constraint, not a regulatory ban. D would be correct only if a regulation in the stem explicitly barred such issuance.

questions.source: High quality paper LTR-12 c Q10
questions.question: The chief compliance officer of a US bank owned by an Australian group is drafting the “regulatory constraints” section of the bank’s nondeposit funding policy. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Regulation affects only the cost of nondeposit funds and not their risk; for example, legal reserve requirements reduce net investable funds and therefore raise the effective cost rate.
In the United States, negotiable CDs must be issued with maturities of no more than seven days, which confines CD funding to the shortest-term funding needs.

Regulations may limit the amount, frequency and use of borrowed funds; for example, the Federal Reserve banks may limit discount window borrowing by institutions that appear to display significant risk of failure.
The legal reserve requirements imposed in the late 1960s and early 1970s on Fed funds borrowing, repurchase agreements and affiliate-issued commercial paper remain in force today.

questions.solution:
Funding policy: how regulation constrains the choice of nondeposit sources.

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s fifth factor is regulation. Federal and state regulations may limit the amount, frequency and use of borrowed funds, and so can rule a source in or out regardless of its cost. GARP gives three examples:

- Minimum maturity: in the United States, CDs must be issued with maturities of at least seven days.
- Access limits: the Federal Reserve banks may limit borrowings from the discount window, particularly by depository institutions that appear to display significant risk of failure.
- Reserve requirements: the central bank may subject other forms of borrowing to legal reserve requirements. During the late 1960s and early 1970s, when the Federal Reserve was fighting inflation with tight-money policies, it imposed reserve requirements for a time on Fed funds borrowing, repurchase agreements and commercial paper issued to purchase assets from affiliated lending institutions.

Those particular requirements are not currently in force (GARP notes elsewhere that there are currently no legal reserve requirements on Fed funds borrowings). But GARP warns that in times of national emergency policymakers would move swiftly to impose new controls, affecting both the costs and the risks of nondeposit borrowing. The chapter summary adds that among the most important regulations are central bank reserve requirements and rules dictating the content of contractual agreements when one financial institution lends to another. Regulation links to the cost factor through the effective cost formula, since reserve requirements reduce net investable funds, and to the risk factor, since sudden controls change availability.

**Applying it to this question**

The CCO needs a statement that is accurate as of today and complete in scope. Test each option for the direction of the CD rule, the current status of the 1960s and 1970s requirements, and whether regulation touches cost only or cost and risk. Only C states GARP’s general principle (amount, frequency, use) with a correct example.

**Fragile fact.** CDs: maturity of at least seven days; the 1960s and 1970s reserve requirements on Fed funds, RPs and affiliate commercial paper are no longer in force; new controls would hit both cost and risk.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Discuss factors affecting the choice of nondeposit funding sources. **GARP:** Chapter 13, Section 13.4, “Regulations”; chapter Summary; current absence of reserve requirements on Fed funds from Section 13.3, “Federal Funds Market”. **GARP** **vs Schweser:** Schweser says the Fed imposed reserve requirements on “commercial paper” generally; GARP specifies commercial paper issued to purchase assets from affiliated lending institutions (GARP used).

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-12 c, where it is Q10 of 11.

a.reason: (Scope or condition error). A confines regulation to cost. Its example is true (reserve requirements shrink net investable funds), but GARP says new controls would affect both the costs and the risks of nondeposit borrowing, for example by limiting access. A would be correct if “only the cost” were replaced by “the cost and the risk”.

b.reason: (Polarity flip). B turns the seven-day rule into a maximum. GARP says US CDs must be issued with maturities of at least seven days, which is why CDs cannot meet an overnight need. B would be correct only if “no more than” were replaced by “at least” and the conclusion reversed.

c.reason: C is correct because it restates GARP’s principle that regulations may limit the amount, frequency and use of borrowed funds, and its example that the Federal Reserve banks may limit discount window borrowing by institutions that appear to display significant risk of failure.

d.reason: (Scope or condition error). D extends a historical episode to the present. GARP says these particular requirements are not currently in force, while warning that similar controls could return in a national emergency. D would be correct only for the late 1960s and early 1970s.

questions.source: High quality paper LTR-12 c Q11
questions.question:
A member of the board risk committee of the US subsidiary of a Canadian banking group asks the treasurer to recommend a source for the following need:

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| Institution | Money-center bank, assets USD 180 billion, rated AA |
| Funding need | USD 250 million, starting in ten days, for four months |
| Market conditions | Commercial paper investors rationing credit to bank affiliates |
| Overnight Fed funds rate | 4.30% |
| Four-month negotiable CD rate | 4.55% |
| Four-month affiliate commercial paper rate | 4.70% |
| Parent group CET1 ratio | 13.1% |

Which of the following recommendations is best supported by the factors that affect the choice of nondeposit funding sources?

options.text: Roll overnight Fed funds for the four months, because the source with the lowest quoted rate should be chosen whatever the term of the need.
Sell four-month negotiable CDs, because the bank’s size and rating give it access, the need is not immediate, and CDs avoid the rationed commercial paper market at a modestly higher rate.
Borrow primary credit at the discount window, because primary credit is normally priced below market rates and is available to institutions in sound financial condition.
Issue four-month commercial paper through the affiliate, because the bank’s size and rating give it access and the commercial paper market is among the least sensitive to credit availability risk.

questions.solution:
Board question: choosing a source for USD 250 million, starting in ten days, for four months, at a large AA bank.

**Concept and theory**

GARP frames the choice among nondeposit sources as a second question that follows the available funds gap: once management knows how much it must borrow, which sources are best given its goals? The answer depends largely on five factors:

| Factor | What GARP asks the manager to weigh |
|---|---|
| 1. Relative cost | Market rate plus noninterest costs over net investable funds; Fed funds among the cheapest, CDs and Eurocurrency slightly higher, commercial paper slightly higher again, primary credit among the highest |
| 2. Risk | Interest rate risk (shorter term, more volatile rate; Fed funds most volatile) and credit availability risk (CD, Eurodollar, commercial paper markets especially sensitive) |
| 3. Maturity | How soon and for how long: Fed funds for today; longer-term debt viable when funds are not needed for a few days |
| 4. Size | USD 1 million trading units; Eurodollars and large CDs favour the largest, highest-rated institutions |
| 5. Regulation | Limits on amount, frequency and use; CD minimum maturity of seven days; possible reserve requirements |

The factors interact, and cost alone never decides: GARP says managers would prefer the cheapest sources “although other factors do play a role”, and its own CD example concludes that CDs, though dearer than Fed funds, have the advantage of being available for weeks or months whereas Fed funds must often be repaid in 24 hours. The right source is the one that best satisfies all five factors for the specific need, which often means paying a modest premium over the cheapest quoted rate.

**Applying it to this question**

Apply the factors in turn. Size: a USD 180 billion AA-rated money-center bank has access to the large-CD market, where investors prefer prime-rated issues of the largest institutions. Maturity: the need begins in ten days and lasts four months, so it is not immediate, making a term instrument viable (and four months clears the seven-day CD minimum). Risk: rolling overnight Fed funds would expose four months of funding to the most volatile rate; the commercial paper market is currently rationing, the credit availability risk GARP warns about. Cost: the CD at 4.55% costs 25 basis points more than Fed funds but less than commercial paper at 4.70%. The CET1 ratio of the parent is irrelevant to the choice among nondeposit sources.

**Fragile fact.** No single factor decides: the cheapest quoted source (Fed funds) loses here on term and rate volatility, and commercial paper loses on credit availability.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Discuss factors affecting the choice of nondeposit funding sources. **GARP:** Chapter 13, Section 13.4, “Nondeposit Funding Sources: Factors to Consider” and its five subsections; chapter Summary. **GARP vs Schweser:** none of substance; Schweser’s Key Concepts list for 77.c omits the size factor, which its main text includes.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-12 c, where it is Q11 of 11.

a.reason: (Absolute claim). A lets the lowest quoted rate decide whatever the term. GARP says other factors play a role and that the overnight Fed funds rate is the most volatile, so rolling it for four months maximises interest rate risk. A would be correct only for a need lasting a day or so.

b.reason: B is correct because it is the only recommendation that satisfies every factor simultaneously: access given size and rating, a term matched to a non-immediate four-month need, avoidance of the market currently exhibiting credit availability risk, and only a modest cost premium over Fed funds.

c.reason: (Polarity flip). C says primary credit is priced below market rates. GARP says primary credit is generally among the highest short-term rates because it is priced above the Fed funds target. C’s second clause is true (primary credit is for institutions in sound financial condition). C would describe the Fed’s discount window only before 2003, when the discount rate was often below Fed funds.

d.reason: (Polarity flip). D says the commercial paper market is among the least sensitive to credit availability risk. GARP says the negotiable CD, Eurodollar and commercial paper markets are especially sensitive, and the stem confirms that commercial paper investors are rationing. D’s size point is true. questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Calculate overall cost of funds using both the historical average cost approach and the pooled-funds approach.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-12 d Q1
questions.question:
A treasury analyst at a Singapore commercial bank is applying the historical average cost approach and starts with the funds the bank has raised to date. Her data (SGD millions) are:

| Source of funds drawn upon | Average amount raised | Average interest rate (%) |
|---|---|---|
| Noninterest-bearing demand deposits | 150 | 0.0 |
| Interest-bearing transaction deposits | 250 | 2.4 |
| Savings accounts | 200 | 1.8 |
| Time deposits | 600 | 4.2 |
| Money market borrowings | 300 | 5.0 |

Salaries and overhead are SGD 18 million and earning assets are SGD 1,200 million. Which of the following is closest to the bank’s weighted average interest expense?
questions.solution:
Singapore bank: weighted average interest expense from five funding sources raised to date.

**Concept and theory**

GARP introduces two methods for an overall cost of funds because a bank never funds itself from a single source: it draws simultaneously on deposits, nondeposit borrowings and owners’ equity, so costing each source separately (the effective cost rate of one source) does not tell management what the whole funding mix costs. The first method, the historical average cost approach, looks at the past. It asks what funds the institution has raised to date and what they cost, and it proceeds in three steps:

| Step | Measure | Denominator |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Weighted average interest expense | Total funds raised (deposits and money market borrowings) |
| 2 | Break-even cost rate (interest plus other operating costs) | All earning assets |
| 3 | Weighted average overall cost of capital (adds stockholders) | Earning assets (equity weight) |

Step 1 is a dollar-weighted average:

Weighted average interest expense $= \frac{\text{All interest paid}}{\text{Total funds raised}} = \frac{\sum\text{A}_{\text{i}} \text{r}_{\text{i}}}{\sum^{\text{i}} _{\text{i}} \text{A}_{\text{i}}}$ ,

where $\text{A}_{\text{i}}$ is the average amount raised from source i and $\text{r}_{\text{i}}$ its average interest rate. Every source sits in the denominator, including noninterest-bearing demand deposits: they are part of the funds the bank has raised even though they add nothing to the interest bill, and they dilute the average. In GARP’s illustration, sources totalling \$1,000 million generate \$65 million of interest, giving 6.5%. Note what step 1 leaves out: salaries and overhead (added in step 2), the shift from funds raised to earning assets (step 2), and the stockholders’ required return (step 3).

**Applying it to this question**

Interest paid = 150(0%) + 250(2.4%) + 200(1.8%)

\+ 600(4.2%) + 300(5.0%)

= 0 + 6.0 + 3.6 + 25.2 + 15.0 = SGD 49.8 million

Total funds raised = 150 + 250 + 200 + 600 + 300 = SGD 1,500 million

Weighted average interest expense = 49.8/1,500 = 3.32%

The bank pays, on average, 3.32% in interest on each unit of funds it has raised. The salaries and overhead (SGD 18 million) and earning assets (SGD 1,200 million) are irrelevant to step 1; they become relevant only in the break-even step.

**Fragile fact.** In step 1 the denominator is total funds raised (including zero-cost demand deposits); earning assets appear only from step 2 onward.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 77.d, verbatim):** Calculate overall cost of funds using both the historical average cost approach and the pooled-funds approach.

**GARP:** Chapter 13, “Figuring the Overall Cost of Funds”, subsection “The Historical Average Cost Approach”. **GARP vs Schweser:** none in substance. Caution: in the GARP text extraction the interest rate on interest-bearing transaction deposits is garbled; it is implied by \$14 million on \$200 million (7%).

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-12 d, where it is Q1 of 12.

a.reason: (Calculation slip: unweighted average). 2.68% is the simple average of the five rates, (0 + 2.4 + 1.8 + 4.2 + 5.0)/5. It ignores the fact that time deposits (SGD 600 million at 4.2%) dominate the mix. It would be right only if every source had the same amount raised.

b.reason: (Scope error: dropped source). 3.69% is 49.8/1,350, which drops the SGD 150 million of noninterest-bearing demand deposits from the denominator because they pay no interest. GARP’s table keeps them in total funds raised at 0%. The figure would be right only if the question asked for the average rate on interest-bearing sources alone.

c.reason: GARP defines the weighted average interest expense as all interest paid divided by total funds raised. That is exactly 49.8/1,500 = 3.32%, option C.

d.reason: (Wrong input twin: earning assets for funds raised). 4.15% is 49.8/1,200, which divides by earning assets. Earning assets are the denominator of the break-even rate (step 2), not of the weighted average interest expense. It would be the right number only for a “break-even rate excluding operating costs” question.

questions.loText: Calculate overall cost of funds using both the historical average cost approach and the pooled-funds approach.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-12 d Q2
questions.question:
A junior risk analyst at a Japanese regional bank is preparing the first step of the bank’s historical cost-of-funds report. The data (JPY billions) are:

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Total interest paid on deposits and money market borrowings | 31.8 |
| Other operating costs (salaries and overhead) | 9.2 |
| Total deposits and money market borrowings raised | 900.0 |
| Earning assets | 720.0 |
| Stockholders’ equity | 80.0 |
| Stockholders’ after-tax required return (%) | 10.0 |
| Tax rate (%) | 30.0 |

Which of the following is closest to the bank’s break-even cost rate on borrowed funds invested in earning assets?
questions.solution:
Japanese regional bank: break-even cost rate on borrowed funds invested in earning assets.

**Concept and theory**

Step 1 of the historical approach (the weighted average interest expense) is incomplete for two reasons. First, interest is not the only cost of raising money: salaries, overhead and other operating costs must also be covered. Second, not every unit of funds raised earns a return; part goes into cash reserves, fixed assets and other nonearning assets. GARP therefore moves to a second measure, the break-even cost rate on borrowed funds invested in earning assets:

Break-even cost rate $= \frac{\text{Interest} + \text{Other operating costs}}{\text{All earning assets}}$ .

In GARP’s illustration, \$65 million of interest plus \$10 million of other operating costs over \$750 million of earning assets gives 10%. GARP explains the name: the institution must earn at least this rate on its earning assets (primarily loans and securities) just to meet the total operating costs of raising borrowed funds. Schweser adds that this is the rate needed before considering the required return of equity holders. The break-even rate therefore sits between two neighbours:

| Measure | Numerator | Denominator |
|---|---|---|
| Weighted average interest expense | Interest only | Total funds raised |
| Break-even cost rate | Interest + other operating costs | Earning assets |
| Overall cost of capital | Break-even + equity add-on | Earning assets |

**Applying it to this question**

Numerator = 31.8 + 9.2 = JPY 41.0 billion

Break-even cost rate = 41.0/720 = 5.694% ≈ 5.69%

The bank must earn about 5.69% on its earning assets just to cover the interest and operating costs of its borrowed funds. Stockholders’ equity, the 10% required return and the 30% tax rate are irrelevant here; they enter only in step 3. Total deposits and borrowings raised (JPY 900 billion) are also irrelevant, since the denominator is earning assets.

**Fragile fact.** The break-even rate covers borrowed funds only (interest plus operating costs over earning assets); the stockholders’ return is not in it.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 77.d, verbatim):** Calculate overall cost of funds using both the historical average cost approach and the pooled-funds approach.

**GARP:** Chapter 13, “Figuring the Overall Cost of Funds”, “The Historical Average Cost Approach” (break-even cost rate). **GARP vs Schweser:** none. Schweser states explicitly that the break-even rate is before the equity holders’ required return; GARP implies the same by adding the stockholders’ cost afterwards.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-12 d, where it is Q2 of 12.

a.reason: GARP’s break-even formula is (interest + other operating costs)/all earning assets = 41.0/720 = 5.69%, option A.

b.reason: (Wrong input twin: total funds raised for earning assets). 4.56% is 41.0/900. It divides by total funds raised instead of earning assets, so it ignores the fact that JPY 180 billion of funds are not in earning assets. It would be right only if every unit raised were invested in earning assets.

c.reason: (Dropped term: operating costs). 4.42% is 31.8/720. It leaves out the JPY 9.2 billion of salaries and overhead that GARP adds to interest in the numerator. It would be right only if the bank had no other operating costs.

d.reason: (Sibling swap: overall cost of capital). 7.28% is the step-3 figure: 5.694% + \[10%/(1 − 0.30)\] × 80/720 = 5.694% + 1.587%. The question asks for the break-even rate, which comes before the stockholders’ required return. It would be right if the question asked for the weighted average overall cost of capital.

questions.loText: Calculate overall cost of funds using both the historical average cost approach and the pooled-funds approach.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-12 d Q3
questions.question:
An internal auditor at a US savings institution is reviewing the methodology note for the institution’s historical average cost of funds calculation. The note contains the following statements about the break-even cost rate:

I. It divides the interest paid plus the other operating costs (such as salaries and overhead) of the borrowed funds by the institution’s earning assets.

II. It already incorporates the stockholders’ required rate of return, so it is the minimum return on earning assets that satisfies every provider of funds.

III. When earning assets are smaller than total funds raised, it must exceed the weighted average interest expense, because its numerator is larger and its denominator is smaller.

IV. It is forward looking: it estimates the cost of the new funds the institution expects to raise, so it is the rate that future loans must exceed.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.text: I only
I and II only
II and IV only
I and III only

questions.solution:
US savings institution: auditing four statements about the break-even cost rate.

**Concept and theory**

The break-even cost rate is the middle step of the historical average cost approach, so it carries the properties of that approach and of its own position in the chain.

- **What it includes.** The interest paid on deposits and money market borrowings plus other operating costs such as salaries and overhead. Both are costs of the borrowed funds.
- **What it is measured against.** All earning assets, because only earning assets generate the income that must cover these costs. Funds parked in reserves or fixed assets earn nothing.
- **What it excludes.** The stockholders’ required return. GARP asks, after computing the break-even rate, “but what about the borrowing institution’s stockholders?” and only then adds the before-tax cost of their investment to obtain the weighted average overall cost of capital.
- **Its time orientation.** It is historical: the approach looks at the past and asks what funds the institution has raised to date and what they cost. The forward-looking question (what must future loans earn to cover new funds) belongs to the pooled-funds approach.

A useful algebraic consequence: write I for interest, O for other operating costs, F for total funds raised and E for earning assets. Then the weighted average interest expense is I/F and the break-even rate is $(\text{I} + \text{O})$/E. If E \< F and O > 0, the break-even rate has a larger numerator and a smaller denominator, so it must exceed I/F. GARP’s numbers show this: 6.5% versus 10%.

**Applying it to this question**

Statement I restates GARP’s formula: correct. Statement II attributes to the break-even rate a property of the overall cost of capital: incorrect. Statement III follows directly from the two formulas when E \< F (and operating costs are positive): correct. Statement IV attributes the pooled-funds approach’s forward-looking orientation to a historical measure: incorrect. So I and III only.

**Fragile fact.** Break-even = borrowed funds only, historical, over earning assets; adding the stockholders’ return gives the overall cost of capital.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 77.d, verbatim):** Calculate overall cost of funds using both the historical average cost approach and the pooled-funds approach.

**GARP:** Chapter 13, “Figuring the Overall Cost of Funds”, “The Historical Average Cost Approach”. **GARP vs Schweser:** none. Statement III is a derived inference from GARP’s formulas, not a sentence in either source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-12 d, where it is Q3 of 12.

a.reason: (Scope error: true statement omitted). “I only” rejects III, which is a valid inference from the two GARP formulas. It would be right only if earning assets could exceed total funds raised and operating costs were zero, in which case the break-even rate need not exceed the interest expense.

b.reason: (Sibling swap (in II)). Including II treats the break-even rate as if it were the weighted average overall cost of capital. GARP adds the before-tax cost of stockholders’ investment after the break-even rate. II would be true of the overall cost of capital, not of the break-even rate.

c.reason: (Sibling swap (II) and polarity flip on time orientation (IV)). II is the overall-cost property; IV turns a backward-looking measure into a forward-looking one. IV would describe the pooled-funds hurdle rate, which is the minimum return future loans and investments must earn to cover all new funds.

d.reason: I matches GARP’s definition (interest plus other operating costs over all earning assets). III is the arithmetic consequence of that definition compared with the weighted average interest expense (interest over total funds raised), illustrated by GARP’s 10% versus 6.5%. Option D.

questions.question:
The CRO of an Australian bank asks the treasury team for the minimum before-tax return the bank must earn on its earning assets under the historical average cost approach. The team provides (AUD millions):

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Total interest paid on borrowed funds | 54 |
| Noninterest expenses (salaries and overhead) | 16 |
| Total assets | 1,600 |
| Earning assets | 1,000 |
| Stockholders’ equity | 120 |
| Stockholders’ after-tax required return (%) | 11 |
| Tax rate (%) | 30 |

Which of the following is closest to the bank’s weighted average overall cost of capital?
questions.solution:
Australian bank: weighted average overall cost of capital under the historical approach.

**Concept and theory**

The break-even rate covers creditors and operating costs but ignores the owners. Stockholders have also put money into the bank and require a return on it, so GARP’s final step adds the before-tax cost of the stockholders’ investment, expressed per unit of earning assets:

Overall cost $= \text{Break-even cost} + \frac{\text{k}_{\text{E}}}{1 - \text{t}} \times\frac{\text{S}}{\text{EA}}$ ,

where $\text{k}_{\text{E}}$ is the after-tax cost of stockholders’ investment (their required return after taxes), t is the tax rate, S is the stockholders’ investment and EA is earning assets. The term $\text{k}_{\text{E}}$/(1 $- \text{t}) \times$ S/EA is GARP’s “before-tax cost of the stockholders’ investment in the borrowing institution”. Two adjustments are built in. The tax gross-up: stockholders’ required return is stated after taxes, while the break-even rate and asset yields are before-tax, so the after-tax return is divided by (1 − tax rate) to convert it to the before-tax return the bank must generate. The weight: the equity cost is multiplied by stockholders’ investment over earning assets, which converts it into a rate per unit of earning assets so that it can be added to the break-even rate (also per unit of earning assets). In GARP’s illustration, 10% + \[12%/(1 − 0.35)\] × 100/750 = 10% + 2.46%, which GARP rounds to 2.5% and a total of 12.5%: the lowest rate of return over all fund-raising costs the institution can afford to earn on its assets, given a \$100 million investment by stockholders.

**Applying it to this question**

Break-even = (54 + 16)/1,000 = 7.000%

Before-tax equity return = 11%/(1 − 0.30) = 15.714%

Equity weight = 120/1,000 = 0.12

Equity add-on = 15.714% × 0.12 = 1.886%

Overall cost = 7.000% + 1.886% = 8.886% ≈ 8.89%

The bank must earn at least about 8.89% before tax on its earning assets to cover its borrowed-fund costs and give stockholders their 11% after-tax return. Total assets (AUD 1,600 million) are irrelevant: GARP weights equity by earning assets.

**Fragile fact.** Divide, do not multiply, by (1 − tax rate); weight by stockholders’ investment over earning assets.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 77.d, verbatim):** Calculate overall cost of funds using both the historical average cost approach and the pooled-funds approach.

**GARP:** Chapter 13, “Figuring the Overall Cost of Funds”, “The Historical Average Cost Approach” (weighted average overall cost of capital). **GARP vs Schweser:** none in method. Caution: GARP’s worked example rounds the equity add-on 2.46% to 2.5%; Schweser’s equivalent Orange Tree Bank tables did not survive text extraction.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-12 d, where it is Q4 of 12.

a.reason: (Sign error on the tax adjustment). 7.92% multiplies by (1 − tax rate) instead of dividing: 7.000% + 11% × 0.70 × 0.12 = 7.92%. This converts a before-tax return into an after-tax one, the reverse of what is needed. It would be right only if 11% were a before-tax return and the question asked for an after-tax equivalent, which the method never requires.

b.reason: Applying GARP’s formula with the gross-up and the earning-asset weight gives 8.89%, option B.

c.reason: (Dropped term: tax gross-up). 8.32% is 7.000% + 11% × 0.12. It treats the after-tax return as if it were before-tax. It would be right if stockholders’ required return were stated before taxes (or the tax rate were zero).

d.reason: (Wrong input twin: total assets for earning assets). 8.18% is 7.000% + 15.714% × 120/1,600. The equity weight must use earning assets, the same base as the break-even rate, so that the two rates can be added. It would be right only if all assets were earning assets.
