questions.source: High quality paper LTR-13 a Q8
questions.question:
A senior treasury analyst on an Australian bank’s trading desk (Counterparty A) financed a purchase of Commonwealth Government bonds with a 7-day repo from a money market fund (Counterparty B). No buyer has been found, so the desk rolls the financing by unwinding the repo with B and simultaneously entering a new repo with Counterparty C.

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Face amount of bonds | AUD 60,000,000 |
| Coupon rate on the bonds | 3.75% |
| Cash received from B at initiation | AUD 61,200,000 |
| Repo rate with B (annualized, actual/360) | 4.20% |
| Market value of the bonds on the roll date | AUD 60,850,000 |
| Haircut applied by C | 1% |
| Repo rate agreed with C (annualized) | 4.35% |

The desk’s net cash position from the roll on the roll date is closest to:

options.text: a deficit of AUD 1,008,480
a deficit of AUD 958,500
a deficit of AUD 399,980
a surplus of AUD 1,008,480

questions.solution:
Australian desk rolls a 7-day repo to a new lender: cash surplus or deficit on the roll date.

**Concept and theory**

A financial institution that finances a bond position through repo and does not sell the bond before the repo matures must roll or renew the financing. GARP describes two routes: renew with the same counterparty, or unwind the repo and find a different counterparty (Figure 14.3, back-to-back repo trades). In the second route the desk, still Counterparty A, repays B the amount due and takes back the bonds, then borrows from C and delivers the bonds as collateral.

The two cash flows on the roll date are set differently. The amount due to B is fixed by the old contract:

$\text{D}_{\text{B}} = \text{C}_{\text{B}} ($1 $+ \text{r}_{\text{B}} \frac{\text{d}}{360} )$ .

The cash obtainable from C depends on the bond’s price at the time of the roll, less any haircut C applies:

$\text{C}_{\text{C}} = \text{MV}_{\text{roll}} ($1 $- \text{h}_{\text{C}})$.

GARP’s point is that because one leg is fixed and the other is market-dependent, the renewal may leave the desk with a cash surplus or a deficit, $\text{C}_{\text{C}} - \text{D}_{\text{B}}$. A fall in bond price or a new haircut produces a deficit, which the desk funds from capital; had the desk hedged the price risk of its inventory, the hedge P&L would offset the surplus or deficit. The rate agreed with C matters only for the next settlement, not for the roll-date cash.

**Applying it to this question**

$\text{D}_{\text{B}} =$ 61,200,000 $\times($1 + 0.042 $\times\frac{7}{360} ) =$ 61,200,000 + 49,980 = 61,249,980

$\text{C}_{\text{C}} =$ 60,850,000 × (1 − 0.01) = 60,241,500

$\text{C}_{\text{C}} - \text{D}_{\text{B}} =$ 60,241,500 − 61,249,980 = −1,008,480

The desk has a deficit of AUD 1,008,480, made up of the fall in collateral value (AUD 350,000), interest owed to B (AUD 49,980) and C’s haircut (AUD 608,500). Irrelevant inputs: the face amount, the coupon, and C’s 4.35% repo rate.

**Fragile fact.** Direction: the amount due to the old lender is fixed, the new cash floats with the bond price and the haircut, so a price fall leaves a deficit that the borrower funds.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Describe the mechanics of repurchase agreements (repos) and calculate the settlement for a repo transaction. **GARP:** Chapter 14, Section 14.1, subsection “Repos and Long Financing” (Figure 14.3, back-to-back repo trades). **Schweser:** Reading 78, “Bond Financing” under LO 78.b (Figure 78.3). **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser shows the roll but does not mention the cash surplus or deficit; that point is GARP-only. Boundary call: the motive for financing a long position belongs to LO 78.b; the roll is tested here only as a settlement calculation.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-13 a, where it is Q8 of 8.

a.reason: A is correct because GARP states that cash from C depends on the bond price at the time of the roll while the cash due to B depends on the previously agreed transaction; netting the two, with C’s haircut, gives a deficit of AUD 1,008,480.

b.reason: (Dropped term). Omits B’s repo interest: 61,200,000 − 60,241,500 = 958,500. Correct only if the amount due to B were the original cash with no interest, for example a zero repo rate.

c.reason: (Dropped term). Omits C’s haircut: 61,249,980 − 60,850,000 = 399,980. Correct only if C lent the full market value of the bonds.

d.reason: (Sign error). Right magnitude, wrong direction: the desk owes more to B than it raises from C. Correct only if the bond price had risen enough for C’s advance to exceed the amount due to B by that amount.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Explain how counterparty risk and liquidity risk can arise through the use of repo transactions.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-13 c Q1
questions.question: A senior risk analyst at an Australian money market fund (AUD reporting) is drafting the fund’s credit policy for its reverse repo book, in which the fund lends cash and holds securities as collateral. She must specify the event that produces a counterparty credit loss on a position. Which of the following events would cause the fund to suffer such a loss?

options.text: The borrower is downgraded two notches during the repo term, but it repurchases the collateral at maturity as agreed.
The collateral’s market value falls below the cash lent during the term, but the borrower repurchases the collateral at maturity as agreed.
The borrower fails to repurchase at maturity, and the collateral, when sold, raises less than the cash lent plus the repo interest owed.
The borrower fails to repurchase at maturity, and the collateral, when sold, raises more than the cash lent plus the repo interest owed.

questions.solution:
Which event produces a counterparty credit loss for a money market fund lending cash through reverse repos.

**Concept and theory**

A repo is economically a short-term loan secured by collateral: the borrower of cash sells securities and agrees to buy them back later at a fixed, higher price, the difference being the repo interest. Because a repo involves an exchange of cash and an exchange of collateral, Schweser says both counterparty (credit) risk and liquidity risk are present. GARP defines the counterparty risk of lending money through a repo very precisely, in the lead-in to its JPMorgan and Lehman case: it is the risk that the borrower defaults and the value of the collateral turns out to be insufficient to cover the loan amount. Two conditions must therefore hold together for a credit loss:

| Borrower defaults? | Collateral proceeds vs amount owed | Outcome for cash lender |
|---|---|---|
| No | any | No loss: repurchase at the agreed price |
| Yes | proceeds ≥ cash lent plus interest | No loss: sell collateral, recover all owed |
| Yes | proceeds \< cash lent plus interest | Loss equal to the shortfall |

GARP’s cash management discussion explains why collateral matters: holding collateral makes the lender less vulnerable to the creditworthiness of its counterparty, because on a default it can sell the collateral to recover any amounts owed. That is why, for very short, well-collateralized repos, Schweser says counterparty risk is “less of a concern”. Less of a concern is not zero: the residual risk is precisely the joint event in the last row of the table, which haircuts and margin calls are designed to make unlikely.

**Applying it to this question**

The fund is the cash lender (it does the reverse repo). Option A has a deteriorating borrower who still performs; option B has deteriorating collateral with a borrower who still performs; option D has a default with sufficient collateral. Only option C combines both GARP conditions: default and collateral proceeds below the amount owed (cash lent plus repo interest).

**Fragile fact.** A repo credit loss needs both a borrower default and a collateral shortfall; either alone is not a loss.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Explain how counterparty risk and liquidity risk can arise through the use of repo transactions. **GARP:** Chapter 14, Case Study: JPMorgan Chase’s Repo Exposure to Lehman Brothers (opening definition); Section 14.1, Repos and Cash Management. **GARP** **vs Schweser:** none on this point; Schweser’s shorter definition (“risk of borrower default or non-payment”) is consistent with GARP’s two-condition definition.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-13 c, where it is Q1 of 12.

a.reason: (Scope or condition error). A downgrade alone causes no loss if the borrower repurchases as agreed; collateral exists precisely so that the lender is less vulnerable to changes in the borrower’s creditworthiness. It would be correct only if the stem asked about mark-to-market of an unsecured exposure, not a realized credit loss on a secured repo.

b.reason: (Scope or condition error). A fall in collateral value with no default produces no credit loss, because the borrower pays the agreed repurchase price. This is the collateral value (liquidity) risk that becomes a loss only if a default follows; it would be correct if the borrower had also failed to repurchase.

c.reason: C matches GARP’s definition word for word in substance: the counterparty risk is that the borrower defaults and the collateral turns out to be insufficient to cover the loan.

d.reason: (Scope or condition error (dropped condition)). Default with collateral proceeds above the amount owed leaves the lender whole, because it sells the collateral and recovers everything owed. It would be correct if the proceeds were below cash lent plus interest.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Explain how counterparty risk and liquidity risk can arise through the use of repo transactions.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-13 c Q2
questions.question:
A treasury analyst at an Irish pension fund (EUR reporting) has lent cash to a dealer through a 30-day repo. The details are below.

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Collateral | EUR 50 million face of a euro-area government bond |
| Clean price at initiation | 104.00 per 100 face |
| Haircut | 5% of collateral market value |
| Repo rate (actual/360) | 3.10% |
| Dealer’s long-term credit rating | A+ |
| Clean price the next morning | 101.40 per 100 face |

The margin agreement requires the collateral’s market value to be kept at no less than the cash lent divided by (1 minus the haircut). Ignore accrued interest. Which statement about the margin call the next morning is most accurate?

options.text: The dealer must deliver additional bonds with a market value of EUR 1.300 million.
The fund must return bonds with a market value of EUR 1.300 million to the dealer.
The dealer must deliver additional bonds with a market value of EUR 1.235 million.
No call arises, because the collateral’s market value still exceeds the cash lent.

questions.solution:
Margin call the morning after the bond collateral of a 30-day EUR repo falls in price.

**Concept and theory**

GARP describes two layers of protection for the cash lender against a fall in collateral value. The first is the haircut: the lender requires the borrower to deliver securities worth more than the loan. In GARP’s example, counterparty B lends only EUR 106 million against EUR 111.772 million of bunds. The second is the margin call (repricing): repos are normally subject to margin calls, through which the borrower of cash supplies extra collateral in declining markets but may withdraw collateral in advancing markets. In GARP’s example the bunds fall from EUR 111.772 million to EUR 110 million, so the borrower must put up the EUR 1.772 million difference, and after the drop the investor still holds EUR 111.772 million of collateral against a loan of EUR 106 million. With haircut h, cash lent L and collateral market value V:

L = (1 $- \text{h}) \text{V}_{0}$, $\text{V}_{\text{required}} = \frac{\text{L}}{1 - \text{h}}$ , Call $= \text{max}(\text{V}_{\text{required}} - \text{V}_{\text{t}}$, 0$)$.

If $\text{V}_{\text{t}}$ rises above the requirement, the call reverses and the borrower may withdraw the excess. The haircut is a fixed cushion against the joint event of default and price decline; the margin call refreshes that cushion daily so it is not used up by price moves.

**Applying it to this question**

$\text{V}_{0} =$ 50 × 104.00/100 = EUR 52.000 million

L = (1 − 0.05) × 52.000 = EUR 49.400 million

$\text{V}_{\text{required}} =$ 49.400/0.95 = EUR 52.000 million

$\text{V}_{\text{t}} =$ 50 × 101.40/100 = EUR 50.700 million

Call = 52.000 − 50.700 = EUR 1.300 million, delivered by the dealer

The dealer (borrower of cash) delivers EUR 1.300 million of additional bonds, restoring the fund’s cushion exactly as in GARP’s example. The repo rate (3.10%), the 30-day term and the dealer’s A+ rating are irrelevant: none enters the collateral requirement.

**Fragile fact.** In falling markets the borrower of cash posts collateral; in rising markets the borrower withdraws it. The lender never posts.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Explain how counterparty risk and liquidity risk can arise through the use of repo transactions. **GARP:** Chapter 14, Section 14.1, Repos and Cash Management (haircut and margin call example, EUR 106 million against EUR 111.772 million). **GARP vs** **Schweser:** none; Schweser lists haircuts and margin calls as mitigants of liquidity risk, GARP introduces them against the joint risk of default and collateral decline.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-13 c, where it is Q2 of 12.

a.reason: A applies GARP’s rule that in declining markets the borrower of cash supplies extra collateral, in the amount needed to restore the haircut-adjusted coverage.

b.reason: (Role misassignment (polarity of the call)). Returning collateral to the dealer is what happens in advancing markets, when the borrower may withdraw excess collateral. It would be correct if the price had risen from 104.00 to 106.60.

c.reason: (Wrong input twin (haircut applied to the shortfall)). EUR 1.235 million = 49.400 − 0.95 × 50.700 is the haircut-adjusted shortfall, that is, the cash the dealer would have to repay to reduce the loan. Delivered as bonds at market value, it leaves collateral at 50.700 + 1.235 = 51.935 \< 52.000. It would be correct if the question asked for a cash repayment of the loan rather than additional collateral.

d.reason: (Scope or condition error). Collateral of EUR 50.700 million still exceeds the EUR 49.400 million lent, but the agreement requires coverage of L/(1 $- \text{h})$, not L; treating the haircut as a one-off buffer ignores margining. It would be correct only if the agreement had no margin call provision.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Explain how counterparty risk and liquidity risk can arise through the use of repo transactions.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-13 c Q3
questions.question: A treasurer of a Canadian municipality (CAD reporting) holds tax receipts until scheduled expenditures fall due and currently invests them through overnight and open repos against government collateral. A dealer proposes that the city instead lend for a fixed three-month term at a higher repo rate. Which statement best describes the risk implications of the proposal?

options.text: The term repo lowers the city’s counterparty risk, because a borrower willing to commit for three months signals greater creditworthiness.
The term repo leaves the city’s risk unchanged, because an open repo also cannot be cancelled before an agreed final maturity date.
The term repo removes the city’s liquidity risk, because the haircut fixed at initiation protects the cash for the full three months.
The term repo adds liquidity and counterparty risk, as well as interest rate risk, because the city can no longer reassess or recall daily.

questions.solution:
Risk implications of moving a municipality’s surplus cash from overnight and open repo to a three-month term repo.

**Concept and theory**

GARP explains why cash investors such as money market funds and municipalities use repo: it pays a short-term rate without sacrificing much liquidity or incurring significant default risk. Municipalities run cash surpluses because tax receipts arrive on a different schedule from expenditures; the cash cannot go into risky securities but should not lie idle. Because repo investors place a premium on liquidity, they tend to lend overnight rather than for term (any maturity longer than one day). Investors who plan to lend for an extended period often use an open repo: a one-day repo that renews itself day to day until cancelled by either party. GARP then states the key risk point: investors willing to take on some additional liquidity and counterparty risk, in addition to interest rate risk, do lend through term repos, which are available out to several months, although demand declines rapidly with term. The logic, as Schweser adds, is that after each overnight repo the investor can re-evaluate whether to keep lending.

| Structure | Can lender reassess or recall? | Risk profile |
|---|---|---|
| Overnight | Every day | Lowest liquidity and counterparty risk |
| Open | Every day (either party cancels) | Similar to overnight, rolls automatically |
| Term (e.g., 3 months) | Only at maturity | Adds liquidity, counterparty and rate risk |

**Applying it to this question**

The city moves from structures it can reassess or exit daily (overnight, open) to a fixed three-month commitment. For three months it cannot recall the cash if the borrower weakens (counterparty risk), cannot use the cash for unexpected needs and is exposed to collateral value developments over a longer horizon (liquidity risk), and its rate is locked while market rates move (interest rate risk). The higher repo rate is the compensation for these risks.

**Fragile fact.** Term repo adds risk for the cash lender; open repo is overnight that rolls until either party cancels.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Explain how counterparty risk and liquidity risk can arise through the use of repo transactions. **GARP:** Chapter 14, Section 14.1, Repos and Cash Management (overnight, open and term repos). **GARP vs Schweser:** none; Schweser places the overnight preference under 78.b and lists shorter terms as a liquidity risk mitigant under 78.c.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-13 c, where it is Q3 of 12.

a.reason: (Polarity flip). Lengthening the term increases, not lowers, counterparty risk: the lender is locked in for longer and cannot reassess the borrower. It would be correct only if the stem compared a term repo with an unsecured term loan to the same borrower.

b.reason: (Sibling swap (open repo given term repo’s property)). An open repo renews day to day until cancelled by either party; it has no fixed final maturity that prevents cancellation. It would be correct if the city’s existing book were in fixed term repos.

c.reason: (Absolute claim). A haircut cushions collateral value declines, but it does not remove liquidity risk, and the city still cannot access its cash before maturity. It would be closer to correct if worded “reduces the collateral value risk”.

d.reason: D restates GARP’s statement that term repo lenders take on additional liquidity and counterparty risk, in addition to interest rate risk.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Explain how counterparty risk and liquidity risk can arise through the use of repo transactions.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-13 c Q4
questions.question: A regulator at the Monetary Authority of Singapore (SGD reporting) is preparing a note for the supervisory committee on why periods of stress create tension between repo borrowers and repo lenders over the term of repo financing. Which statement best describes that tension?

options.text: Borrowers want to shorten repo terms to cut their funding costs, while lenders want to extend repo terms to lock in higher repo rates.
Borrowers want to extend repo terms to gain time to refinance, while lenders want to shorten repo terms to limit exposure to borrower defaults.
Lenders shorten repo terms mainly to limit their interest rate risk, since the collateral already removes their exposure to borrower defaults.
Because repo rates allocate terms, the system as a whole can extend secured borrowing maturities while also shortening secured lending maturities.

questions.solution:
Why stress creates tension between repo borrowers and lenders over the term of repo financing.

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s Section 14.2 sets out how the risks of repo funding and the risks of repo investing pull in opposite directions. A borrower that funds itself with short-maturity repo faces the risk that lenders will not roll its financing. To protect itself, it wants to extend the term of its repo borrowing, sometimes at the encouragement of its regulators, so that if refinancing conditions deteriorate it has more time to arrange alternate financing, raise capital or even sell corporate entities. A lender of cash faces the risk that the borrower defaults during the life of the repo. To protect itself, it wants to shorten the term of its repo lending, also sometimes at its regulators’ encouragement, so as to minimize its exposure to borrower defaults. Repo rates (the price) allocate repos of various terms across borrowers and lenders, but GARP stresses a fallacy-of-composition point: the financial system as a whole cannot both extend the maturities of secured financing and contract the maturities of secured lending, because each repo is simultaneously someone’s borrowing and someone’s lending. This tension is how counterparty risk (for lenders) and liquidity risk (for borrowers) arise from the same contract.

| Party | Preferred term in stress | Risk being managed |
|---|---|---|
| Borrower of cash | Longer | Funding liquidity (refinancing) risk |
| Lender of cash | Shorter | Exposure to borrower default |

**Applying it to this question**

The stem asks for the tension in stressed periods. B assigns the correct direction and the correct motive to each side: borrowers extend to buy time to refinance, lenders shorten to limit exposure to borrower defaults.

**Fragile fact.** Borrowers extend, lenders shorten; and the system cannot do both at once.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Explain how counterparty risk and liquidity risk can arise through the use of repo transactions. **GARP:** Chapter 14, Section 14.2, Repo, Liquidity Management, and the Financial Crisis of 2007-2009. **GARP vs Schweser:** GARP-only detail; Schweser does not discuss this tension (Schweser 78.d mentions only the general shortening of repo terms in the crisis).

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-13 c, where it is Q4 of 12.

a.reason: (Role misassignment). The directions and motives are attached to the wrong parties: it is lenders who shorten and borrowers who extend. It would be correct only in a calm market where borrowers chase the cheapest overnight rate, which is not the stressed tension GARP describes.

b.reason: B paraphrases GARP’s statement of the competing desires of borrowers and lenders and their reasons.

c.reason: (Sibling swap (interest rate risk for counterparty risk) plus absolute claim). GARP says lenders shorten to minimize exposure to borrower defaults; collateral reduces but does not remove that exposure. It would be correct only if the lender held riskless collateral with no default concern and cared only about rate moves.

d.reason: (Polarity flip). GARP states the opposite: the system as a whole cannot both extend secured financing maturities and contract secured lending maturities. Prices allocate terms between parties but cannot satisfy both wishes in aggregate.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Explain how counterparty risk and liquidity risk can arise through the use of repo transactions.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-13 c Q5
questions.question: A member of the board of a London-based hedge fund (GBP reporting) is reviewing how the fund finances a leveraged GBP 3 billion portfolio of gilts through overnight repos with several dealers. She asks the CRO how this financing structure can create liquidity risk for the fund itself. Which answer is most accurate?

options.text: If lenders lose confidence in the fund, they can decline to roll maturing overnight repos, so financing can vanish quickly and force fire sales, losses and possibly bankruptcy.
Because the repos are secured by gilts, lenders will keep rolling them even after losing confidence in the fund, so liquidity risk arises only if gilt prices fall.
The liquidity risk sits with the dealers rather than the fund, because the dealers hold the gilts and would have to sell them if the fund were to fail.
Liquidity risk of this kind arises only for broker-dealers that hold inventory for customers, because a fund can always sell its own positions at market.

questions.solution:
How overnight repo financing of a leveraged gilt portfolio creates liquidity risk for a hedge fund.

**Concept and theory**

Liquidity risk in repo arises on both sides. For the lender it is chiefly the risk that collateral becomes illiquid or loses value. For the borrower of cash it is funding liquidity risk, which GARP develops in Section 14.2. Repo markets are relatively liquid and repo rates relatively low, but because of its short maturities repo is on the less stable side of the funding spectrum: more stable than short-term unsecured borrowing such as commercial paper (collateral should prevent lenders from bolting too quickly on unfavorable rumors or news), but less stable than long-term debt and equity. GARP’s key sentence is that if repo investors lose confidence in an institution, its repo financing can disappear as fast as the repos mature, which is mostly overnight. The institution must then sell positions to repay lenders; given their size and public nature, these sales are likely to become fire sales with significant losses. GARP then generalizes beyond banks: the same argument applies to all leveraged investors, such as part of the hedge fund world. To the extent a firm borrows to finance positions, losing the confidence of repo and other secured financing counterparties can result in fire sales, substantial losses and possible bankruptcy.

Overnight maturity ⇒ daily roll decision by lenders

⇒ loss of confidence: no roll ⇒ forced sales at depressed prices.

**Applying it to this question**

The fund borrows overnight against gilts with leverage, so every morning each lender decides whether to roll. A loss of confidence in the fund (not in gilts) is enough to end the financing. The GBP 3 billion size makes any forced sale large and visible, which is exactly GARP’s fire-sale channel.

**Fragile fact.** For the borrower, overnight repo means the financing can vanish overnight; collateral slows lenders but does not bind them.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Explain how counterparty risk and liquidity risk can arise through the use of repo transactions. **GARP:** Chapter 14, Section 14.2, Repo, Liquidity Management, and the Financial Crisis of 2007-2009. **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser defines repo liquidity risk only from the lender’s side (collateral value); the borrower’s funding liquidity risk is GARP content, used here as part of how liquidity risk arises through repo.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-13 c, where it is Q5 of 12.

a.reason: A follows GARP’s chain: overnight maturity, loss of lender confidence, disappearing financing, fire sales, losses and possible bankruptcy, explicitly extended to leveraged investors such as hedge funds.

b.reason: (Absolute claim). GARP says collateral should slow lenders from bolting, but “nevertheless” financing can disappear as fast as repos mature once confidence is lost; good collateral does not guarantee a roll. It would be closer to correct if worded “collateral makes repo more stable than unsecured funding”.

c.reason: (Role misassignment). The funding liquidity risk belongs to the borrower, the fund; the dealers face counterparty and collateral liquidity risk, a different risk. It would be correct if the question asked about the dealers’ exposure as cash lenders.

d.reason: (Scope or condition error). GARP states explicitly that the argument applies to all leveraged investors, including hedge funds; positions cannot be sold at undisturbed market prices in a forced, large, public sale. It would be correct only for an unleveraged fund with no borrowing to repay.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Explain how counterparty risk and liquidity risk can arise through the use of repo transactions.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-13 c Q6
questions.question:
The CRO of a Brazilian investment bank (BRL reporting), which finances most of its trading inventory through overnight repo, is drafting a stress scenario in which repo investors lose confidence in the bank. The draft contains four statements:

I. The bank’s repo financing could disappear as fast as its repos mature, which for most of the book is overnight.

II. The bank could no longer facilitate customer trades by holding inventory or facilitate customer financing, and might cease to be an acceptable counterparty for derivative and even spot trades.

III. Selling inventory and proprietary positions to repay repo lenders would likely turn into fire sales with significant losses, given the size and public nature of the sales.

IV. Because business losses rather than financing are the usual cause of a firm’s difficulties, the loss of repo financing would be a secondary effect that rarely decides whether the bank survives.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.text: I and II only
I, II, III and IV
I, II and III only
II and III only

questions.solution:
Audit of four statements in a stress scenario where repo investors lose confidence in a repo-funded investment bank.

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s Section 14.2 traces what happens to a financial institution that relies on repo when its repo investors lose confidence. The mechanism has three links. First, speed: repo financing can disappear as fast as the repos mature, and most repos are overnight. Second, franchise damage: a beleaguered institution would no longer be able to facilitate customer trades by holding inventory, would not be able to facilitate customer financing, and might not remain an acceptable counterparty for derivative and even spot security transactions. Third, forced sales: the institution would have to sell inventory and proprietary positions to repay repo lenders, and given the size and public nature of these sales they would likely become fire sales with significant losses. GARP then draws the conclusion that matters for risk management: while significant business losses rather than financing are the usual cause of a financial institution’s difficulties, the loss of financing is often the killing blow. In other words, the root cause and the proximate cause of failure are different, and a firm with solvent but illiquid positions can be destroyed by funding withdrawal. This is why liquidity management (balancing the cost of funding against the risk of being caught without financing) matters even for profitable institutions.

**Applying it to this question**

Statement I is GARP’s speed point. Statement II lists GARP’s franchise consequences. Statement III is GARP’s fire-sale point. Statement IV takes GARP’s true premise (business losses are the usual cause) and attaches the reversed conclusion: GARP says the loss of financing is often the killing blow, not a secondary effect. So I, II and III are correct.

**Fragile fact.** Business losses are the usual cause; the loss of financing is often the killing blow.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Explain how counterparty risk and liquidity risk can arise through the use of repo transactions. **GARP:** Chapter 14, Section 14.2, Repo, Liquidity Management, and the Financial Crisis of 2007-2009. **GARP vs Schweser:** GARP-only content (borrower funding liquidity risk); Schweser does not list these consequences.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-13 c, where it is Q6 of 12.

a.reason: (Scope error (true statement III rejected)). Omitting III drops GARP’s fire-sale channel, the step that turns lost financing into losses. A would be correct only if the bank held no inventory or proprietary positions to sell.

b.reason: (Polarity flip (in statement IV)). Accepting IV accepts the reversal of GARP’s conclusion: loss of financing is often the killing blow, not a secondary effect that rarely decides survival. B would be correct only if IV said “the loss of financing is often the killing blow”.

c.reason: C accepts exactly the three statements that reproduce GARP’s consequences and rejects the one that reverses GARP’s “killing blow” conclusion.

d.reason: (Scope error (true statement I rejected)). Statement I is GARP’s direct point that repo financing disappears as fast as the repos mature, mostly overnight. D would be correct only if the bank funded through long-term repo facilities.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Explain how counterparty risk and liquidity risk can arise through the use of repo transactions.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-13 c Q7
questions.question: A junior risk analyst at a Japanese trust bank (JPY reporting) writes in a draft report: “When we lend cash in repo to a large, well-established dealer against the highest-quality government bonds, our main residual exposure is wrong-way risk: if the dealer defaults, the collateral is likely to fall in value at the same time.” Which reviewer comment on the draft is most accurate?

options.text: The draft is right: a major dealer’s default and a fall in top-quality government collateral are positively linked, which is why haircuts exist.
The draft is wrong: this is a right-way risk, and it means haircuts on top-quality government collateral are no longer needed at all.
The draft is wrong: this is a right-way risk, and the label applies equally to lower-quality corporate bond and mortgage-backed collateral.
The draft is wrong: this is a right-way risk, as a dealer default would likely set off a flight to quality that raises top government bond values.

questions.solution:
Whether a dealer default with top-quality government collateral is wrong-way or right-way risk.

**Concept and theory**

GARP notes that even when taking high-quality securities as collateral, a lender of cash faces the risk that a borrower defaults at the same time as those securities decline in value; selling the collateral might then not fully cover the loan, which is why repo agreements often provide haircuts. In a footnote GARP adds an important nuance about the direction of that dependence. Wrong-way risk is the case where exposure or loss rises when the counterparty is more likely to default, so that default and a fall in collateral value tend to occur together. Right-way risk is the opposite. GARP says that in the case of repo, in risk management parlance, this is a right-way risk: if a repo borrower, typically a well-established financial institution, were to default, the market response would probably be a flight-to-quality trade in which securities of the most creditworthy governments increase in value. So, for top-quality government collateral, the lender’s collateral is likely to be worth more, not less, at the moment it needs to be sold. Two limits follow. First, the argument depends on the collateral being the safest government paper; lower-quality collateral (corporate bonds, non-agency mortgage securities) does not benefit from a flight to quality and may fall sharply. Second, right-way dependence does not remove the need for haircuts: GARP still motivates haircuts by the joint risk of default and decline.

**Applying it to this question**

The draft describes lending to a large, well-established dealer against the highest-quality government bonds, exactly GARP’s setting. A dealer default would likely send investors into those bonds, raising their value. So the label is right-way risk, for the reason given in D.

**Fragile fact.** Dealer default plus top government collateral is right-way risk, because a flight to quality raises the collateral’s value.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Explain how counterparty risk and liquidity risk can arise through the use of repo transactions. **GARP:** Chapter 14, Section 14.1, Repos and Cash Management, and footnote 1. **GARP vs Schweser:** GARP-only content; Schweser does not mention right-way risk.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-13 c, where it is Q7 of 12.

a.reason: (Sibling swap (wrong-way for right-way)). It applies the label and mechanism of wrong-way risk where GARP identifies right-way risk. It would be correct if the collateral were securities issued by, or highly correlated with, the borrower itself.

b.reason: (Absolute claim). Right-way dependence lowers the residual risk but does not eliminate it, and GARP still explains haircuts as protection against default coinciding with a decline in collateral value. It would be correct only if the collateral’s price could never fall over the repo term.

c.reason: (Scope or condition error). The flight-to-quality logic applies to the most creditworthy government securities. Lower-quality corporate and mortgage collateral is not bid up in a flight to quality. It would be correct only if the statement were limited to top-quality government collateral.

d.reason: D restates GARP’s footnote: right-way risk, because a default by a well-established financial institution would probably trigger a flight to quality that raises the value of the most creditworthy government securities.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Explain how counterparty risk and liquidity risk can arise through the use of repo transactions.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-13 c Q8
questions.question:
An internal auditor at a U.S. life insurer (USD reporting) is reviewing the insurer’s reverse repo program, in which it lends surplus cash against securities collateral. The draft audit memo contains four statements:

I. Holding collateral makes the insurer less vulnerable to the borrower’s creditworthiness, because on a default it can sell the collateral to recover amounts owed.

II. That protection depends on the insurer’s own expertise and operational ability to take possession of and liquidate collateral, which many repo lenders found they lacked during the 2007 to 2009 crisis.

III. Once collateral has been delivered, the insurer’s exposure to the borrower is replaced entirely by exposure to the issuer of the collateral.

IV. Haircuts charged on the insurer’s repos would normally depend on the creditworthiness and negotiating power of the counterparties concerned.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.text: I and II only
I, II and IV only
I, III and IV only
II and IV only

questions.solution:
Audit of four statements on how collateral mitigates a cash lender’s counterparty risk.

**Concept and theory**

Collateral is the main mitigant of counterparty risk in repo. GARP explains that holding collateral makes the lender less vulnerable to the creditworthiness of its counterparty, because if the borrower defaults the lender can sell the collateral to recover amounts owed. Schweser draws the consequence that, because repos are very short-term and secured, counterparty risk is “less of a concern”. The protection is real but conditional in three ways that GARP identifies. First, the lender must be able to use it: GARP notes that many lenders in the repo market during the 2007 to 2009 crisis realized they were not well positioned, either in expertise or in operational ability, to take possession of and liquidate repo collateral. Second, the collateral must be worth enough when sold, so collateral value risk (liquidity risk) remains with the lender and is addressed with haircuts and margin calls. Third, the terms of protection are negotiated: in describing back-to-back repos, GARP says the haircuts charged on each leg depend on the creditworthiness and negotiating power of the relevant counterparties. Collateral therefore does not convert the lender’s exposure into a pure exposure to the collateral issuer; the lender still has a claim on the borrower, and it loses only if the borrower defaults and the collateral proceeds fall short (a “double” event).

**Applying it to this question**

I is GARP’s core point. II is GARP’s observation about lenders’ expertise and operational ability during the crisis. III overstates the effect of collateral: the exposure to the borrower remains and is merely reduced, and a loss needs both a borrower default and a collateral shortfall. IV is GARP’s statement about haircut determination. So I, II and IV are correct.

**Fragile fact.** Collateral reduces, not removes, exposure to the borrower, and it only helps if the lender can actually seize and sell it.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Explain how counterparty risk and liquidity risk can arise through the use of repo transactions. **GARP:** Chapter 14, Section 14.1, Repos and Cash Management; Repos and Long Financing (haircuts on back-to-back repos). **GARP vs Schweser:** none; the operational-ability point and haircut drivers are GARP-only detail.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-13 c, where it is Q8 of 12.

a.reason: (Scope error (true statement IV rejected)). It rejects GARP’s statement that haircuts depend on counterparty creditworthiness and negotiating power. A would be correct if IV said haircuts were fixed by regulation regardless of the counterparty.

b.reason: B accepts the three statements drawn from GARP and rejects the overstated claim in III.

c.reason: (Absolute claim (statement III accepted) and true II rejected). III claims the exposure to the borrower is replaced entirely, but collateral only reduces vulnerability to the borrower’s credit; II is a true GARP lesson. C would be correct only if II were false and the lender had no claim on the borrower.

d.reason: (Scope error (true statement I rejected)). Statement I is the basic reason collateral mitigates counterparty risk. D would be correct only if collateral could not be sold on default.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Explain how counterparty risk and liquidity risk can arise through the use of repo transactions.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-13 c Q9
questions.question: A treasurer at a Chinese commercial bank (CNY reporting) raises USD 200 million overnight by repoing out U.S. Treasuries with a market value of USD 206 million to a single dealer. The bank’s board asks whether the bank, as the borrower of cash, has any counterparty exposure to the dealer. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: The bank has no counterparty exposure to the dealer, since in a repo only the lender of cash is exposed to the other side’s default.
The bank’s exposure to the dealer falls if the Treasuries rise in value overnight, since its cash then covers more of the collateral.
The haircut protects the bank, because it ensures that the dealer always delivers more cash than the value of the securities received.
The bank is exposed to the dealer failing to return the Treasuries, roughly the excess of their value over the repurchase price owed.

questions.solution:
Counterparty exposure of a bank that borrows cash by repoing out Treasuries with a haircut.

**Concept and theory**

Counterparty risk in repo is usually discussed from the side of the cash lender, but the contract is two-sided: cash goes one way and securities go the other. GARP’s haircut mechanism requires borrowers to deliver securities worth more than the amount of the loan. The cash borrower has therefore handed over more value than it has received, and it relies on the cash lender to return those securities at maturity against the repurchase price. If the cash lender fails, the borrower keeps the cash (and owes no repurchase payment) but loses the securities, so its exposure is roughly

Exposure of cash borrower $\approx\text{max}(\text{V}_{\text{collateral}} - \text{P}_{\text{repurchase}}$, 0$)$,

where $\text{V}_{\text{collateral}}$ is the market value of the securities delivered and $\text{P}_{\text{repurchase}}$ is the cash lent plus repo interest. GARP shows this risk is real in its discussion of general collateral rates: in times of financial stress, willingness to lend Treasury bonds in repo declines as market participants fear that collateral may not be returned, either because a counterparty will fail to return it or because a counterparty’s counterparty will fail to do so. The exposure rises when collateral rises in value (more value is at stake) and with the size of the haircut. A margin agreement lets the borrower withdraw excess collateral in advancing markets, which limits this exposure.

**Applying it to this question**

The bank received USD 200 million and delivered USD 206 million of Treasuries. Its exposure to the dealer is about USD 206 million minus the repurchase price (USD 200 million plus one night’s interest), roughly USD 6 million. That is exactly the risk that the dealer fails to return the Treasuries.

**Fragile fact.** The cash borrower’s exposure equals collateral value minus repurchase price, and it grows when the collateral rises in value.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Explain how counterparty risk and liquidity risk can arise through the use of repo transactions. **GARP:** Chapter 14, Section 14.1, Repos and Cash Management (haircuts); Section 14.3, General and Special Repo Rates (fear that collateral may not be returned). **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser discusses counterparty risk only from the lender’s side; this question uses GARP content.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-13 c, where it is Q9 of 12.

a.reason: (Role misassignment). Both sides of a repo have counterparty exposure; GARP explicitly cites the fear that collateral may not be returned. It would be correct only if the bank had received cash at least equal to the collateral value plus interest (no haircut).

b.reason: (Polarity flip). If the Treasuries rise in value, the bank has more value at stake with the dealer, so its exposure rises. It would be correct if the Treasuries fell in value.

c.reason: (Role misassignment (haircut protects the wrong party)). The haircut protects the cash lender by making the borrower deliver securities worth more than the cash; it increases the borrower’s exposure. It would be correct if the bank were the lender of cash.

d.reason: D identifies the cash borrower’s exposure as GARP describes it (collateral may not be returned) and sizes it correctly as the excess of collateral value over the repurchase price.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Explain how counterparty risk and liquidity risk can arise through the use of repo transactions.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-13 c Q10
questions.question:
A chief compliance officer at a Dutch bank (EUR reporting) is reviewing the risk report of the bank’s repo lending desk, which lends cash against securities collateral. The report contains four statements about the desk’s liquidity risk:

I. Even when collateral makes the desk less concerned about a borrower’s credit, the desk remains exposed to the collateral becoming illiquid or falling in value during the repo term.

II. This exposure is of particular concern to the borrower of cash rather than to the desk, because the borrower has handed over its securities.

III. Accepting only higher-quality collateral and shortening the repo term both reduce this exposure.

IV. A haircut set at initiation fully neutralizes this exposure, which makes daily margin calls redundant.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.text: I and III only
I, III and IV only
I, II and III only
III only

questions.solution:
Audit of four statements on a repo lending desk’s liquidity risk and its mitigants.

**Concept and theory**

Schweser defines liquidity risk in a repo as the risk of an adverse change in the value of the collateral, and says it can be of particular concern to the lender. Even if the lender is less concerned about the counterparty’s credit because it holds collateral, it remains exposed to the collateral becoming illiquid and to its value declining during the repo term. Especially in times of market turbulence, collateral value can fall significantly and its liquidity can dry up, as GARP’s crisis discussion illustrates. Schweser lists four mitigants: haircuts, margin calls, reducing the term of the repo, and accepting only higher quality collateral. GARP supports each one: haircuts make the borrower deliver securities worth more than the loan; margin calls make the borrower supply extra collateral in declining markets; investors who lend for term take on additional liquidity and counterparty risk; and safety-minded investors typically accept only collateral of the highest credit quality.

| Mitigant | How it reduces collateral value and liquidity risk |
|---|---|
| Haircut | Cushion between collateral value and cash lent |
| Margin call | Refreshes the cushion as prices fall |
| Shorter term | Less time for value to fall before the lender can exit |
| Higher-quality collateral | Smaller price falls, more liquid in stress |

A haircut is a fixed cushion: a price fall larger than the haircut, or a sequence of falls, can exhaust it, which is why haircuts and margin calls are used together.

**Applying it to this question**

I is Schweser’s definition from the lender’s side. II assigns the concern to the wrong party: Schweser says it is of particular concern to the lender. III lists two of the four mitigants. IV claims a fixed haircut fully neutralizes the risk, which is false because a fall larger than the haircut exhausts it. So I and III are correct.

**Fragile fact.** Repo liquidity risk (Schweser) is a lender’s concern about collateral value and illiquidity, cut by haircuts, margin calls, shorter terms and better collateral.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Explain how counterparty risk and liquidity risk can arise through the use of repo transactions. **GARP:** Chapter 14, Section 14.1, Repos and Cash Management. **GARP** **vs Schweser:** Schweser’s narrow definition (collateral value risk) is used here; GARP uses “liquidity risk” more broadly, also covering the borrower’s funding risk. The four mitigants are consistent across both sources.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-13 c, where it is Q10 of 12.

a.reason: A accepts the definition and two mitigants and rejects both the role swap and the absolute claim.

b.reason: (Absolute claim (statement IV accepted)). IV says the haircut fully neutralizes the risk; it is only a buffer, and margin calls exist because it can be used up. B would be correct if IV said the haircut “reduces” the exposure.

c.reason: (Role misassignment (statement II accepted)). Collateral value risk is of particular concern to the lender, who must rely on the collateral if the borrower defaults. C would be correct if II referred to the lender.

d.reason: (Scope error (true statement I rejected)). I is the definition of the lender’s liquidity risk in Schweser. D would be correct only if collateral could not lose value or liquidity during the term.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Explain how counterparty risk and liquidity risk can arise through the use of repo transactions.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-13 c Q11
questions.question:
A risk consultant is reviewing a reverse repo in which a Canadian pension plan (CAD reporting) lent cash to a dealer against corporate bond collateral.

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Cash lent at initiation | CAD 95.0 million |
| Collateral market value at initiation | CAD 100.0 million |
| Repo rate (actual/360), term | 4.00%, 30 days |
| Dealer’s 5-year CDS spread at initiation | 180 bp |
| Collateral market value at maturity | 7.0% below its value at initiation |
| Discount needed to sell the collateral quickly | 2.0% below its market value at maturity |

At maturity the dealer defaults and fails to repurchase. Market turbulence means the plan can sell the collateral only at the stated discount. Ignoring legal and transaction costs, which is closest to the plan’s loss?

options.text: CAD 3.86 million
CAD 2.32 million
CAD 4.18 million
CAD 9.19 million

questions.solution:
Pension plan’s loss when a dealer defaults on a CAD reverse repo against corporate bond collateral that has fallen in value and is illiquid.

**Concept and theory**

This numerical combines the two risks the LO names. Counterparty risk is that the borrower defaults and the collateral turns out insufficient to cover the loan (GARP). Liquidity risk, in Schweser’s sense, is that the collateral loses value and becomes illiquid during the term, especially in turbulent markets. At default the lender is owed the repurchase price, that is, the cash lent plus repo interest on the money market convention (actual/360):

P $= \text{L} ($1 $+ \text{r} \frac{\text{d}}{360} )$ , Proceeds $= \text{V}_{0}($1 − ∆)(1 $- \delta)$, Loss $= \text{max}(\text{P} -$ Proceeds, 0),

where L is cash lent, r the repo rate, d the days in the term, $\text{V}_{0}$ the collateral’s initial market value, ∆ the fractional fall in market value and $\delta$ the extra discount needed to sell quickly (the illiquidity cost). The haircut, 1 − $\text{L/V}_{0}$, is the cushion: a loss arises only once the combined value fall and liquidation discount exceed it, after allowing for the interest that has accrued on the loan.

**Applying it to this question**

P = 95.0 $\times($1 + 0.04 $\times\frac{30}{360} ) =$ CAD 95.317 million

$\text{V}_{\text{T}} =$ 100.0 × (1 − 0.07) = CAD 93.000 million

Proceeds = 93.000 × (1 − 0.02) = CAD 91.140 million

Loss = 95.317 − 91.140 = CAD 4.177 ≈ 4.18 million

The dealer’s CDS spread is irrelevant: it describes the probability of default, but the loss given that default has happened depends only on the amount owed and the collateral proceeds. The 5% haircut cushion was overwhelmed by the 7% fall plus the 2% fire-sale discount.

**Fragile fact.** The lender is owed cash lent plus interest (actual/360), and it recovers the stressed, discounted sale price, not the screen price.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Explain how counterparty risk and liquidity risk can arise through the use of repo transactions. **GARP:** Chapter 14, Case Study: JPMorgan Chase’s Repo Exposure to Lehman Brothers (definition of counterparty risk); Section 14.1, Repos and Cash Management (actual/360, haircuts). **GARP vs Schweser:** none.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-13 c, where it is Q11 of 12.

a.reason: (Dropped term (repo interest)). 95.000 − 91.140 = 3.86 uses the cash lent rather than the repurchase price owed. It would be correct if the dealer had defaulted at initiation, before any interest accrued.

b.reason: (Dropped term (illiquidity discount)). 95.317 − 93.000 = 2.32 assumes the collateral can be sold at its market value, ignoring the liquidity risk in turbulent markets. It would be correct if the stem gave no liquidation discount.

c.reason: C applies the correct amount owed (including repo interest) against proceeds that reflect both the fall in value and the illiquidity discount.

d.reason: (Wrong input twin (collateral value used as the loan)). 100.0 × (1 + 0.04 × 30/360) − 91.140 = 9.19 treats the CAD 100 million collateral value as the cash lent, ignoring the haircut. It would be correct only if the plan had lent CAD 100 million with no haircut.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Explain how counterparty risk and liquidity risk can arise through the use of repo transactions.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-13 c Q12
questions.question: A senior treasury analyst at an Australian broker-dealer (AUD reporting) finances a book of lower-quality corporate bonds and mortgage-backed securities through overnight repo at relatively low rates and haircuts. Market conditions deteriorate: the bonds fall in price, lenders raise haircuts, and fewer lenders are willing to take this collateral at all. Which statement best describes how liquidity risk now materializes for the dealer?

options.text: Falling collateral prices allow the dealer to withdraw collateral under its margin agreements, which offsets the cash it must find when haircuts rise.
The dealer must meet margin calls and post more collateral as haircuts rise, and if it cannot replace lost financing, it faces liquidations and capital depletion.
The lenders rather than the dealer bear the liquidity strain, because they must post additional cash to the dealer when the collateral they hold falls in value.
Overnight funding insulates the dealer, because the haircuts agreed on the first trade continue to apply each time the overnight repo is rolled.

questions.solution:
How falling prices, higher haircuts and fewer takers drain the liquidity of a dealer financing lower-quality collateral in repo.

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s Section 14.2 describes how collateral risk turns into liquidity risk for the borrower of cash. Repo is attractive because of relatively low rates and haircuts. Before the 2007 to 2009 crisis, borrowers financed lower-quality collateral, such as lower-quality corporate bonds and mortgage-backed securities, at those low rates and haircuts, and lenders accepted it for somewhat higher rates. When conditions deteriorated, three channels drained the borrowers’ liquidity. First, margin calls: as security values declined, borrowers had to supply extra collateral. Second, rising haircuts: when lenders raised haircuts, borrowers had to post more collateral (or more of their own capital) for the same financing. Third, lost financing: as lower-quality collateral found fewer and fewer takers, borrowers had to replace financing arrangements, and some could not. The worst-hit borrowers suffered collateral liquidations, losses, capital depletion and business failure. The general lesson is that the lender’s protections (margin calls, haircuts, the option not to roll) are exactly the mechanisms that transmit stress to the borrower, and they bite hardest on low-quality, hard-to-value collateral and on short-term (overnight) financing, which reprices every day.

| Lender action | Effect on the borrower of cash |
|---|---|
| Margin call after price falls | Must post extra collateral or cash |
| Higher haircut | Less cash per unit of collateral, more own capital |
| Refusal to roll or accept collateral | Must replace financing or sell assets |

**Applying it to this question**

The dealer is the borrower of cash, financing lower-quality collateral overnight. Falling prices trigger margin calls; higher haircuts require more collateral; fewer takers mean financing may not be replaced. Each draws on the dealer’s liquidity, and failure on the last leads to liquidation and capital depletion, as in B.

**Fragile fact.** In a falling market the borrower posts collateral, and overnight financing reprices every day.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Explain how counterparty risk and liquidity risk can arise through the use of repo transactions. **GARP:** Chapter 14, Section 14.2, Repo, Liquidity Management, and the Financial Crisis of 2007-2009. **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser places this pre-crisis narrative under 78.d; here only the general mechanism (not the Lehman or Bear Stearns case facts) is tested, as part of how liquidity risk arises for repo borrowers.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-13 c, where it is Q12 of 12.

a.reason: (Polarity flip). Borrowers may withdraw collateral in advancing markets; in declining markets they must supply extra collateral. It would be correct if bond prices were rising.

b.reason: B lists GARP’s channels (margin calls, haircut increases, inability to replace financing) and its outcome (liquidations, losses, capital depletion).

c.reason: (Role misassignment). The borrower of cash posts collateral to the lender when collateral value falls; the lender does not post cash to the borrower. It would be correct only if the dealer were the cash lender.

d.reason: (Scope or condition error). Overnight repos are renegotiated each time they roll, so new haircuts apply immediately; short maturity increases, not removes, the dealer’s exposure. It would be correct only for a long term repo with haircuts fixed for its life.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Compare the use of general and special collateral in repo transactions.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-13 e Q1
questions.question: A treasury analyst at a Singapore money market fund (SGD reporting) is documenting the fund’s overnight repo programme for the risk report. The fund lends its surplus cash only against AAA-rated Singapore Government Securities with a remaining maturity of less than three years. Its standing instruction to dealers states that any issue meeting these terms is acceptable as collateral. Which of the following classifications of this collateral arrangement is most accurate?

options.text: Special collateral, because the fund specifies the acceptable securities with precision by issuer, rating and maturity.
Special collateral, because the fund, as lender of cash, initiates the repo in order to take possession of the securities.
General collateral, because the fund restricts the class of securities but does not insist on any particular issue within it.
General collateral, because government securities are always general collateral whatever the lender of cash requests.

questions.solution:
Singapore money market fund lends only against a narrowly specified class of government securities, any issue acceptable.

**Concept and theory**

Every repo is a cash loan secured by securities, but lenders of cash differ in how much they care about which security they receive, and GARP uses this to split the repo market into two segments. Under **general collateral (GC)**, the lender of cash is willing to take any particular security, although the broad categories of acceptable securities might be specified with some precision. GARP’s illustration is a cash investor that will accept only, for example, euro-area government bonds below a given maturity: the investor can be very particular about the class of securities it takes, yet it will not insist on receiving any particular security within that delineated class. Such investors are said to accept general collateral, and their trades take place at GC repo rates.

Under **special collateral** (a specials trade), by contrast, the lender of cash initiates the repo in order to take possession of a particular security. The deciding attribute is therefore not quality, issuer or the precision of the eligibility rules, but whether a particular issue is required.

|  | General collateral | Special collateral |
|---|---|---|
| What the cash lender requires | Any security within stated categories | One particular security |
| Typical initiator and motive | Investor wanting to invest cash safely | Trader wanting to borrow a bond (often to short) |
| Rate | GC rate (highest available for that collateral) | Special rate, typically below GC |

**Applying it to this question**

The fund restricts collateral by issuer (Singapore Government), rating (AAA) and remaining maturity (under three years). Those are class restrictions. The decisive sentence in the stem is that any issue meeting these terms is acceptable: the fund does not ask for one named security. It is a cash investor seeking a safe return on surplus cash, the archetypal GC participant. The SGD reporting currency and the AAA rating are colour and do not affect the classification.

**Fragile fact.** The test is “a particular security required?”, not “how narrow is the class?”: a precisely specified class is still GC.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Compare the use of general and special collateral in repo transactions. **GARP:** Chapter 14, Section 14.1 (Repos and Cash Management) and Section 14.3 (General and Special Repo Rates). **GARP vs Schweser:** none; Schweser’s “only the broad categories of acceptable securities are specified” compresses GARP’s “specified with some precision”.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-13 e, where it is Q1 of 10.

a.reason: (Scope or condition error). It treats the precision of the eligibility criteria as the test. GARP explicitly allows GC categories to be specified with some precision; what makes a trade special is a requirement for a particular security. A would be correct only if the instruction named one specific issue (for example, one ISIN) that had to be delivered.

b.reason: (Sibling swap). It borrows the defining motive of a specials trade (initiating the repo to take possession of a particular security) and attaches it to a cash investor. The fund initiates the repo to invest cash, not to obtain a security. B would be correct if the fund needed a particular bond, for example to cover a short sale.

c.reason: C matches GARP exactly: investors can be very particular about which classes of securities they accept but will not insist on any particular security within the delineated class, so they accept general collateral.

d.reason: (Absolute claim). Government securities are not “always” GC. A particular government bond requested by a cash lender is special collateral, and the most in-demand government bonds are exactly the ones said to trade special. D would be correct only with the condition “when no particular issue is requested”.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Compare the use of general and special collateral in repo transactions.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-13 e Q2
questions.question:
The CRO of a Canadian bank (CAD reporting) with a U.S. Treasury repo desk is reviewing a draft glossary written by the desk. The glossary contains four statements:

I. Any repo in which the lender of cash requests a specific security is a specials trade, even if that security is not in unusual demand.

II. A bond is said to be trading special when it is among the bonds most in demand to be borrowed.

III. There is a single GC rate each day that applies to all Treasury collateral and to all repo terms, while special rates vary by security.

IV. Special rates are quoted only for overnight repos, because a specials trade must be rolled each day until the short is covered.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.text: I and II only
I, II and III only
II and IV only
I, II, III and IV

questions.solution:
CRO audits four glossary statements on specials trades, trading special, GC rates and special rates.

**Concept and theory**

GARP adds three pieces of market terminology to the GC versus special split. First, **any** request for specific collateral is a specials trade. Second, the bonds most in demand to be borrowed are said to be **trading special**. These two ideas are deliberately separated: a cash lender can ask for an unpopular, seasoned issue, and the trade is still a specials trade even though that bond is not “trading special” in the colloquial sense; its special rate would simply sit close to GC.

Third, rates are quoted on a grid, not as single numbers. Each day there is a **GC rate for each** **bucket of collateral and each repo term**; the most commonly cited GC rates are for repos in which any U.S. Treasury collateral is acceptable, and “the” GC rate is the overnight rate for that bucket. For special rates the grid is finer still: there can be **one special rate for each security** **for each term** (GARP’s example quotes one particular Treasury issue to a specific date months ahead). Every special rate is typically below the GC rate.

| Rate | Dimensions along which it varies |
|---|---|
| GC rate | Collateral bucket (e.g., any Treasury) × term |
| Special rate | Individual security × term |

**Applying it to this question**

Statement I restates GARP’s “any request for specific collateral is a specials trade”: true.

Statement II restates the meaning of trading special: true. Statement III collapses the GC grid into one daily number; GARP says there is a GC rate for each bucket and each term: false.

Statement IV denies term special rates, but GARP quotes special rates security by security and term by term: false. Correct set: I and II only.

**Fragile fact.** “Specials trade” = any specific request; “trading special” = most in demand to be borrowed. They are not synonyms.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Compare the use of general and special collateral in repo transactions. **GARP:** Chapter 14, Section 14.3 General and Special Repo Rates. **GARP vs** **Schweser:** Schweser says only that GC rates “can be used for repos with U.S. Treasury collateral” and omits the bucket-by-term grid; GARP followed.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-13 e, where it is Q2 of 10.

b.reason: (Scope or condition error). It accepts Statement III, which drops the “each bucket and each term” condition on GC rates. B would be correct if III had said “There is a GC rate for each bucket of collateral and each repo term”.

questions.loText: Compare the use of general and special collateral in repo transactions.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-13 e Q3
questions.question: An internal auditor at a U.K. bank (GBP reporting) is reviewing a repo desk memo. A hedge fund client sold short one particular 10-year gilt and needs it to make delivery. The client asked the bank’s repo desk for that gilt, and the desk delivered it to the client against GBP 25 million of cash for one week, the cash to be returned with interest at maturity. Which of the following descriptions of this trade is most accurate?

options.text: The bank lent cash to the client and took the gilt as collateral, and the bank initiated the trade in order to invest surplus cash.
The client borrowed cash from the bank against the gilt, so the client pays the repo rate to the bank when the trade unwinds.
The client initiated the trade to invest cash, so it is a general collateral trade even though only one gilt was delivered.
The client initiated the trade to take possession of the gilt, so it is clearer to say the bank lent the gilt and took cash as collateral.

questions.solution:
Auditor reviews a gilt delivered to a hedge fund that needs it to cover a short, against GBP 25 million cash.

**Concept and theory**

Economically, every repo has two legs: cash moves one way and a security moves the other, and both are returned at maturity with interest paid to the cash provider. Which party “lends” and which “borrows” therefore depends on which asset you focus on, and GARP stresses that the description should follow the motive. In a GC trade the cash lender’s motive is to invest cash, so it is natural to say the investor lends cash and takes a security as collateral. In **specials** **trading**, the lender of cash initiates the repo in order to take possession of a particular security. GARP therefore says it makes more sense to describe the trade as “counterparty A is lending a security to counterparty B and taking cash as collateral” rather than “counterparty B is lending cash and taking a security as collateral”, although the two statements are economically equivalent. For the same reason GARP recommends that, when using the words borrow or lend in repo, one should specify whether cash or securities are being borrowed or lent.

The short seller in a specials trade is doing what GARP calls a reverse repo: it delivers cash, receives the bond, delivers the bond into its short sale, and later buys the bond back to return it, receiving its cash plus interest at the (special) repo rate. The holder of the bond receives cash and pays that repo rate.

**Applying it to this question**

The facts: the client sold short and needs one particular gilt; the client asked for it; the desk delivered the gilt and received GBP 25 million. So the client is the lender of cash and the initiator, and its motive is the security, not the investment of cash. This is a specials trade, best described as the bank lending the gilt and taking cash as collateral. The client receives interest on its cash (at the special rate); it does not pay it. The one-week term and amount do not affect the classification.

**Fragile fact.** In a specials trade the cash lender initiates, and it receives (not pays) the low special rate.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Compare the use of general and special collateral in repo transactions. **GARP:** Chapter 14, Section 14.3 General and Special Repo Rates; Section 14.1 Reverse Repos and Short Positions. **GARP vs Schweser:** none; the “lend the security, take cash as collateral” framing is GARP-only detail.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-13 e, where it is Q3 of 10.

a.reason: (Role misassignment). It makes the bank the cash lender and the initiator with an investment motive. In the stem the bank received cash and the client asked for the gilt. A would be correct if a cash-rich investor had approached the bank to invest cash against collateral.

b.reason: (Role misassignment). It reverses who borrows cash. The client provided the GBP 25 million, so it is the cash lender and receives the repo interest; the bank, which received the cash, pays it. B would describe a client that delivered the gilt to raise cash.

c.reason: (Sibling swap). It applies the GC motive (investing cash) to a trade whose purpose was to obtain one specific gilt. Delivery of a required particular security is the definition of a specials trade. C would be right only if the client would have taken any gilt in a class.

d.reason: D identifies the initiator (the client), its motive (to take possession of the gilt), and GARP’s preferred framing (security lent, cash taken as collateral).

questions.loText: Compare the use of general and special collateral in repo transactions.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-13 e Q4
questions.question: A senior risk analyst at a Brazilian broker-dealer (BRL reporting) is presenting to newly hired analysts. She notes that every special repo rate is typically less than the GC rate for the same term and asks the group to explain why. Which of the following explanations is most accurate?

options.text: A specific security is of higher credit quality than the GC basket, so lenders of cash accept a lower return for the extra safety.
A low cash-borrowing rate induces holders of in-demand securities to lend them, and a low cash-lending rate allocates them to borrowers.
Holders of in-demand securities accept a low rate on the cash they lend, which compensates borrowers of the securities for concentration.
Lenders of cash in specials trades are investors seeking the highest rate for their collateral, so competition among them bids the rate down.

questions.solution:
Explain to new hires why every special repo rate is typically below the GC rate.

**Concept and theory**

A specials trade is a two-sided bargain. On one side is the **holder of a security that is in great** **demand**: it gives up the use of that security for the term of the repo (and, for a liquid bond, the liquidity it was holding the bond for) and receives cash. On the other side is the **party that** **wants that particular security**, typically to cover a short, which hands over cash in exchange. The repo rate is the price that clears this bargain, and GARP explains its level through two forces acting at once:

- Inducement: being able to **borrow cash at a relatively low rate** induces holders of securities that are in great demand to lend those securities.
- Allocation: being **forced to lend cash at a relatively low rate** allocates securities that are in great demand to the potential borrowers of those securities, i.e., to those willing to pay most for them.

So the security borrower “pays” for the bond by accepting a below-GC return on its cash, and the security lender “earns” by borrowing cash cheaply. The GC rate, by contrast, is the rate on cash lent against any security in a bucket, with no premium attached to any particular issue, and is the highest rate a cash investor can earn for that collateral. Hence every special rate is typically less than the GC rate; the difference, GC rate minus special rate, is called the special spread (its behaviour belongs to LO 78.f). Note that credit quality plays no role in this explanation: the special issue and the GC basket can be of identical credit quality.

**Applying it to this question**

The stem asks for the mechanism. Option B states both GARP forces with the correct actor on each side: holders lend securities and borrow cash cheaply; borrowers of securities lend cash at a low rate. Every other option either imports a credit-risk argument, puts the low rate on the wrong party, or attributes a GC-investor motive to specials.

**Fragile fact.** Actor check: the security lender borrows cash cheaply; the security borrower lends cash cheaply.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Compare the use of general and special collateral in repo transactions. **GARP:** Chapter 14, Section 14.3 General and Special Repo Rates. **GARP vs** **Schweser:** none; Schweser gives only the demand logic (“lenders have to accept a lower return”); the inducement and allocation mechanism is GARP detail.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-13 e, where it is Q4 of 10.

a.reason: (Sibling swap). It uses the explanation for a different spread: GARP explains why the GC rate is below the unsecured fed funds rate by the extra safety of Treasury collateral. Specialness is about demand for a particular issue, not credit quality. A would answer “why is the GC rate below the fed funds rate?”

b.reason: B paraphrases GARP’s two-part explanation: a low borrowing rate induces holders to lend in-demand securities, and a low lending rate allocates those securities to potential borrowers.

c.reason: (Role misassignment). The holders of in-demand securities do not lend cash; they lend the securities and borrow cash. It is the borrower of the security that accepts the low rate on cash. C would be correct only with the actors swapped.

d.reason: (Sibling swap). Seeking the highest rate for the collateral accepted is GARP’s description of GC investors, not of specials participants, and competition among cash investors would not explain a below-GC rate for one issue. D would describe the GC segment.
