questions.source: High quality paper LTR-13 e Q5
questions.question:
A portfolio manager at an Australian hedge fund (AUD reporting) wants to short one particular U.S. Treasury note for 21 days. To borrow the note, the fund will lend USD cash to a dealer in a specials trade. The dealer and the fund’s screens show the following:

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Cash to be lent by the fund | USD 80,000,000 |
| Face amount of the note to be received | USD 78,500,000 |
| 21-day special repo rate on the note | 0.35% |
| 21-day term GC rate, Treasury collateral | 1.20% |
| Overnight GC rate, Treasury collateral | 1.10% |
| Overnight federal funds rate | 1.35% |

Using the actual/360 convention, which of the following is closest to the interest the fund gives up, relative to lending the same cash as general collateral for the same term, in order to receive the note?
questions.solution:
Hedge fund lends USD 80 million for 21 days in a specials trade at 0.35% versus 21-day term GC of 1.20%; interest given up.

**Concept and theory**

A trader who wants to short a particular bond has to borrow it, and in repo it does so by lending cash against that bond in a specials trade. GARP is explicit that such traders “must decide whether they are willing to lend money at rates below GC rates in order to borrow those securities”; Schweser calls this the trade-off between receiving the desired security and lending at below-GC rates. The natural benchmark is what the same cash would have earned with no requirement for a particular security, that is, in a GC repo for the same collateral bucket and the same term, since GARP notes a GC rate exists for each bucket and each term (and a special rate for each security and each term).

With money market conventions (actual/360, simple interest):

Interest given up $= \text{P} \times(\text{r}_{\text{GC,T}} - \text{r}_{\text{S,T}} ) \times\frac{\text{d}}{360}$

where P is the cash lent, $\text{r}_{\text{GC,T}}$ is the term GC rate for term T, $\text{r}_{\text{S,T}}$ is the special repo rate on the particular security for the same term, and d is the number of days. The bracket is the term special spread for this issue; the cost is borne by the cash lender, while the holder of the note enjoys the mirror-image benefit (the financing value of a bond trading special, LO 78.g).

**Applying it to this question**

Term spread = 1.20% − 0.35% = 0.85%

Interest earned in GC = 80,000,000 × 1.20% × 21/360 = USD 56,000.00

Interest earned in specials = 80,000,000 × 0.35% × 21/360 = USD 16,333.33

Interest given up = 56,000.00 − 16,333.33 = USD 39,666.67

Irrelevant inputs: the face amount of the note (interest accrues on cash lent, not on face), the overnight GC rate (wrong term) and the fed funds rate (an unsecured rate, not the alternative use of cash against Treasury collateral). The fund sacrifices about USD 39.7 thousand of interest over 21 days as the price of obtaining that specific note.

**Fragile fact.** Match terms: compare a term special rate with the term GC rate for the same bucket, never with fed funds or overnight GC.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Compare the use of general and special collateral in repo transactions. **GARP:** Chapter 14, Section 14.3 General and Special Repo Rates (actual/360 convention from Section 14.1). **GARP vs Schweser:** none. Boundary: this is the cash lender’s cost of special collateral (78.e), not the bond holder’s financing value (78.g).

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-13 e, where it is Q5 of 10.

a.reason: A is the cash lent times the 21-day term spread times 21/360.

b.reason: (Wrong input twin). Uses the fed funds rate as the benchmark: 80,000,000 × (1.35% − 0.35%) × 21/360 = 46,666.67. Fed funds is the unsecured interbank rate; the alternative for this cash is a GC repo. B would be correct if the stem asked for the give-up relative to an unsecured overnight interbank loan at 1.35% for 21 days.

c.reason: (Intermediate result). 80,000,000 × 0.35% × 21/360 = 16,333.33 is the interest the fund still earns in the specials trade, not what it gives up. C would be correct if the question asked for interest received on the cash.

d.reason: (Wrong input twin). Uses the overnight GC rate in place of the 21-day term GC rate: 80,000,000 × (1.10% − 0.35%) × 21/360 = 35,000.00. The benchmark must match the term of the special rate. D would be correct if the term GC rate were 1.10%.

questions.loText: Compare the use of general and special collateral in repo transactions.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-13 e Q6
questions.question:
A risk consultant is reviewing the U.S. repo activity of the New York branch of a Chinese bank (CNY reporting). The branch’s activities and the collateral type the branch’s policy assigns to each are listed below.

I. The branch invests surplus USD cash overnight and accepts any U.S. Treasury as collateral: general collateral trade.

II. A hedge fund client must borrow one particular Treasury note to cover a short and lends cash to get it: specials trade, lending cash below the GC rate.

III. The branch finances its inventory of Treasury notes, none of which is trading special: general collateral funding trade.

IV. The branch holds a note that is trading special and needs cash against it: finance the note in a GC trade at the GC rate, because funding trades are GC.

Which of the assignments are consistent with how general and special collateral are used?

options.text: I and II only
I, II and IV only
I, II and III only
I, II, III and IV

questions.solution:
Consultant checks a branch’s assignment of GC or specials to four repo activities.

**Concept and theory**

GARP relates the two collateral types to the market participants introduced earlier in the chapter:

| Participant and motive | Collateral type | Rate consequence |
|---|---|---|
| Repo investor (money market fund, municipality, branch with surplus cash) | General collateral | Earns the highest rate for the collateral it accepts |
| Trader shorting a particular security | Specials trade (must) | Lends cash below GC to borrow the bond |
| Institution financing positions (funding trade) | Predominantly GC | Borrows cash at about the GC rate |
| Institution borrowing cash against a security that is trading special | Specials market | Lends the security, borrows cash below GC |

The last row is the subtle one. Funding trades are predominantly GC because most inventory is not in special demand. But if the security being financed happens to trade special, the owner would be leaving money on the table by delivering it into a GC trade: someone in the specials market is willing to lend cash below GC to get it. GARP therefore says such an institution will lend that security in the specials market and borrow cash at a rate below GC, rather than financing it as part of a GC trade. Put differently, “funding trades are GC” is a default, not a rule.

**Applying it to this question**

I: cash investment against any Treasury is GC: consistent. II: a short seller needing one note must do a specials trade and lend cash below GC: consistent. III: financing inventory that is not trading special is an ordinary funding trade, predominantly GC: consistent. IV: the note is trading special, so the branch should lend it in the specials market and borrow below GC; financing it at the GC rate gives away its specialness: inconsistent. Correct set: I, II and III only.

**Fragile fact.** Funding is GC by default; if the bond being funded trades special, fund it in the specials market below GC.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Compare the use of general and special collateral in repo transactions. **GARP:** Chapter 14, Section 14.3 General and Special Repo Rates (paragraph relating GC and specials trades to market participants). **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser says the specials cash lender wants the security “to finance its inventory or proprietary positions”; GARP says funding trades are predominantly GC and a holder of a special security lends it in the specials market. GARP followed.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-13 e, where it is Q6 of 10.

a.reason: (Scope or condition error). It rejects III, treating inventory financing as a specials activity (the Schweser compression “finance its inventory” read as a specials motive). GARP says funding trades are predominantly GC. A would be correct if the inventory in III were trading special.

b.reason: (Scope or condition error). It accepts IV and rejects III, applying the funding-is-GC default exactly where it fails (a security trading special) and dropping it where it holds. B would be correct only if the labels in III and IV were swapped.

c.reason: C accepts the three assignments that follow GARP and rejects IV, which drops the “trading special” condition.

d.reason: (Scope or condition error). It accepts IV, overextending “funding trades are predominantly GC” to a security trading special. D would be correct if IV read “lend the note in the specials market and borrow cash below GC”.

questions.loText: Compare the use of general and special collateral in repo transactions.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-13 e Q7
questions.question: The treasurer of a U.S. municipality invests surplus tax receipts overnight in repo, accepting general collateral. A council member proposes that the municipality instead insist on receiving one particular on-the-run Treasury note as collateral in every repo, because it is the most liquid issue in the market. Which of the following is the most likely consequence of adopting the proposal?

options.text: The municipality would earn a rate above GC, because dealers must pay a premium to deliver an issue in such demand.
The municipality’s return would be unchanged, because the requested note has the same credit quality as the GC basket.
Dealers delivering the note would accept a rate below GC, so the municipality would earn the special spread over GC.
The municipality would likely have to accept a rate below GC, giving up the highest rate available on general collateral.

questions.solution:
Municipality investing tax receipts considers insisting on one particular on-the-run note as collateral.

**Concept and theory**

Repo investors such as money market funds, municipalities, mutual funds, insurers and pension funds come to the repo market to earn a short-term return on cash with high safety and liquidity. GARP notes that municipalities in particular run cash surpluses from tax receipts that cannot be invested in risky securities but should not lie idle. Such investors care about the quality and class of collateral, but not about which particular bond they receive. That indifference has a price benefit: GARP states that **GC trades suit repo investors because they obtain the highest rate** **for the collateral they are willing to accept**.

Why is GC the highest rate? Because the moment a cash lender insists on one particular security, it becomes a buyer of that security’s “borrowability”, and if the issue is in demand it must compete with traders who need that bond to cover shorts. Those traders lend cash below GC to get the bond. Schweser puts the logic plainly: when lenders look to receive a specific rather than generic security, this creates a demand for that security and lenders have to accept a lower return. On-the-run Treasuries are precisely the issues most in demand to be borrowed, so insisting on one would typically mean earning a special rate, below GC. The liquidity of the collateral does not change who pays whom: the cash lender pays for the privilege of choosing.

**Applying it to this question**

The municipality is a cash investor currently in GC. The proposal turns every repo into a specials trade on an issue that is typically trading special. The consequence is a lower rate on its cash: it gives up the GC rate, the highest rate available for collateral it is willing to accept. Nothing in the proposal improves the credit quality of the collateral relative to the Treasury GC basket, so there is no offsetting benefit to the municipality’s investment objective.

**Fragile fact.** GC = highest rate for the cash investor; asking for a specific in-demand bond lowers the cash lender’s return.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Compare the use of general and special collateral in repo transactions. **GARP:** Chapter 14, Section 14.3 General and Special Repo Rates; Section 14.1 Repos and Cash Management. **GARP vs Schweser:** none.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-13 e, where it is Q7 of 10.

a.reason: (Polarity flip). It reverses the direction of the special rate relative to GC. Demand to receive a specific security lowers, not raises, the rate earned by the cash lender. A would be correct if special rates were above GC, which GARP says they typically are not.

b.reason: (Scope or condition error). It assumes only credit quality sets the repo rate and drops the condition that a request for a particular in-demand issue changes the rate. B would be correct only if the requested note were not in any special demand, so that its special rate equalled GC.

c.reason: (Role misassignment). Dealers delivering the note do borrow cash below GC, but that benefit accrues to the dealers, not to the municipality. The municipality, as lender of cash, receives the lower rate. C would be correct if the municipality were the holder lending the note.

d.reason: D restates GARP’s comparison: GC gives investors the highest rate for acceptable collateral, and lenders who require a specific security must accept rates below GC.

questions.question: A board risk committee member at a Japanese insurer (JPY reporting) that holds USD Treasuries is reading a review of a stressed week in U.S. funding markets. During the week the Federal Reserve had cut its fed funds target to 2.00%, while overnight GC repo on Treasury collateral traded at about 0.40%. Which of the following explanations of this gap is most consistent with the behavior of the fed funds-GC spread?

options.text: The spread narrowed, because lenders of cash demanded more compensation for counterparty risk on Treasury repo in the stress.
The spread widened, as demand to lend cash on Treasury collateral rose and willingness to lend Treasuries fell for fear of non-return.
The spread widened, because Treasuries became scarcer as the government ran surpluses and paid down its outstanding debt.
The spread turned positive for the first time, because in normal markets GC trades above the unsecured fed funds rate.

questions.solution:
Stressed week: fed funds target 2.00%, overnight Treasury GC about 0.40%; explain the gap.

**Concept and theory**

In the United States the GC rate is typically **close to, but below**, the federal funds rate. The fed funds rate is the unsecured rate for overnight loans between banks in the Federal Reserve system; repo loans secured by U.S. Treasury collateral are safer and so should trade at a lower rate. The difference, **fed funds rate minus GC rate**, is the fed funds-GC spread (not to be confused with the special spread, GC minus a special rate).

GARP identifies two forces that widen the fed funds-GC spread by pushing the GC rate down:

- Scarcity of Treasury collateral: when the U.S. government ran surpluses and paid down debt (late 1990s and early 2000s), Treasuries became scarcer and the spread widened.
- Financial stress: (i) in flight-to-quality trades, demand to hold Treasuries and **to lend cash** **on Treasury collateral increases**; (ii) **willingness to lend Treasury bonds in repo declines**, because participants fear collateral may not be returned, either by a counterparty or by a counterparty’s counterparty.

Both stress channels lower the GC rate: more cash chases Treasury collateral, and less Treasury collateral is offered. GARP cites the period after the collapse of Bear Stearns, when GC traded far below a fed funds target the Fed had just cut, and very wide spreads after the failure of Lehman Brothers.

**Applying it to this question**

Here the spread is about 2.00% − 0.40% = 1.60%, i.e., roughly 160 basis points, far above the normal small gap, in a stressed week. So the spread widened, and the stress mechanism is the right explanation: flight-to-quality cash wanting Treasury collateral and holders reluctant to lend Treasuries for fear of non-return. The insurer’s JPY reporting is irrelevant.

**Fragile fact.** Fed funds-GC spread = fed funds minus GC; in stress GC falls and the spread widens.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Compare the use of general and special collateral in repo transactions. **GARP:** Chapter 14, Section 14.3 General and Special Repo Rates. **GARP vs** **Schweser:** none; Schweser’s quiz explanation cites only the falling willingness to lend Treasuries, while GARP adds the flight-to-quality demand to lend cash on Treasury collateral.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-13 e, where it is Q8 of 10.

a.reason: (Polarity flip). It says the spread narrowed. With GC at 0.40% against 2.00% fed funds the spread is unusually wide, and a counterparty-risk premium on Treasury repo would raise, not lower, GC. A would describe a market in which GC rose toward fed funds.

b.reason: B gives both GARP stress channels with the correct direction (widening, GC falling).

c.reason: (Sibling swap). Scarcity from fiscal surpluses and debt paydown is a true cause of widening, but of a different episode (the late 1990s and early 2000s), not a stressed week. C would be correct if the stem described a period of government surpluses.

d.reason: (Polarity flip). GC normally trades below, not above, the unsecured fed funds rate, so the spread is normally positive already. D would be correct only if Treasury-secured lending were riskier than unsecured interbank lending.

questions.question:
A regulator at a European supervisory agency (EUR reporting) is reviewing a briefing note on U.S. repo rates prepared for a cross-border college of supervisors. The note makes four statements:

I. The GC rate is typically close to, but below, the fed funds rate, because repo loans secured by Treasury collateral are safer than unsecured overnight interbank loans.

II. When the U.S. government ran surpluses and paid down debt so that Treasuries became scarcer, the fed funds-GC spread narrowed.

III. “The” GC rate refers to the overnight rate on repos in which any U.S. Treasury collateral is acceptable.

IV. The fed funds-GC spread is another name for the special spread of the on-the-run Treasury.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.text: I and III only
I, II and III only
III and IV only
I and IV only

questions.solution:
Regulator audits four statements on GC versus fed funds, “the” GC rate, scarcity and the special spread.

**Concept and theory**

The GC rate sits inside a small family of short-term dollar rates, and the LO’s comparison of general and special collateral requires keeping three of them apart:

| Rate or spread | Meaning (GARP) |
|---|---|
| Fed funds rate | Unsecured overnight rate between banks in the Federal Reserve system |
| “The” GC rate | Overnight repo rate where any U.S. Treasury collateral is acceptable |
| Special rate | Repo rate for one particular security and term; typically below GC |
| Fed funds-GC spread | Fed funds rate minus GC rate |
| Special spread | GC rate minus the special rate of a given security and term |

Because Treasury-secured loans are safer than unsecured interbank loans, GC is typically close to but below fed funds (GARP quotes an average of about 16 basis points over one sample period). The fed funds-GC spread varies with the demand for Treasury collateral. When Treasuries became scarcer during the government surpluses of the late 1990s and early 2000s, and were expected to become scarcer still, the spread **widened**, reflecting the decreasing supply of Treasury collateral. It also widens in financial stress. The special spread is a different object: it compares GC with the rate on a single issue.

**Applying it to this question**

I: matches GARP’s reasoning on safety: true. II: scarcity widened the spread; “narrowed” reverses it: false. III: the definition of “the” GC rate: true. IV: confuses the fed funds-GC spread (fed funds minus GC) with the special spread (GC minus a special rate): false. Correct set: I and III only. The EUR reporting and the supervisory college are context only.

**Fragile fact.** Two different spreads: fed funds minus GC (collateral-wide) versus GC minus special (one issue).

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Compare the use of general and special collateral in repo transactions. **GARP:** Chapter 14, Section 14.3 General and Special Repo Rates. **GARP vs** **Schweser:** none; Schweser places the special spread definition under LO 78.f. Garbled source caution: GARP’s date range for the 16 basis point average is missing a year in the extraction; not tested.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-13 e, where it is Q9 of 10.

a.reason: A accepts the two statements that match GARP and rejects the polarity error (II) and the sibling confusion (IV).

b.reason: (Polarity flip). It accepts II, which reverses the effect of Treasury scarcity. Scarcer Treasury collateral lowers GC and widens the spread. B would be correct if II said “widened”.

c.reason: (Sibling swap). It accepts IV, swapping the fed funds-GC spread for the special spread, and rejects the true Statement I. C would require IV to define a single spread for both and I to be false.

d.reason: (Sibling swap). It accepts IV and rejects the true definitional Statement III. D would be correct only if the special spread were measured against fed funds and “the” GC rate meant something else.

questions.loText: Compare the use of general and special collateral in repo transactions.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-13 e Q10
questions.question:
A junior risk analyst at a U.S. asset manager (USD reporting) compares two Treasury notes of similar maturity.

| Note | Price relative to neighbouring notes | Ownership |
|---|---|---|
| P | About 20 cents rich | Widely held, actively lent in repo |
| Q | In line | Larger amount outstanding; most held by institutions that, for institutional reasons, do not lend in repo |

Her manager states: “Note P must trade more special in repo than Note Q, because it is richer.” Which of the following assessments of the manager’s statement is most accurate?

options.text: Correct, because a rich note has high demand relative to its supply, and its special rate reflects that same demand.
Not necessarily, because P’s richness reflects demand to own it, while its special rate depends on demand to borrow it.
Not necessarily, but Q cannot trade special, because its larger amount outstanding guarantees a larger supply for borrow.
Not necessarily, because special rates depend on each note’s credit quality relative to the GC basket, which is the same here.

questions.solution:
Manager claims the richer note must trade more special; assess against demand to own versus demand to borrow.

**Concept and theory**

GARP states that special rates for a particular issue to a particular date are determined by the **demand to borrow that issue to that date relative to the supply available for borrow**. The point that matters is that the supply and demand to borrow and lend an issue are not the same as the supply and demand to buy and sell it. Two mechanisms separate them:

- Supply side: some owners of U.S. Treasuries, for institutional reasons, do not lend bonds in repo, so the amount of an issue available for borrow may be somewhat less or very much less than the amount outstanding, depending on how ownership is distributed across institutions.
- Demand side: a bond that trades **rich** relative to neighbouring bonds shows high demand to own it relative to the outstanding supply, but it may or may not trade very special, depending on how much traders want to short it relative to the supply available for borrow.

Schweser makes the same point: a bond in high demand in the market may not be in great demand as collateral for a specials trade, and the reverse can equally be true. GARP concludes that predicting the special spreads of individual bonds is therefore quite difficult. Price richness and repo specialness are linked only through the short base and the lendable supply, not mechanically.

**Applying it to this question**

The manager infers specialness from richness. Note P is rich (demand to own) but widely lent in repo (ample supply for borrow); nothing is said about short demand. Note Q is fairly priced, yet most of it is held by institutions that do not lend in repo, so its lendable supply may be much smaller than its larger outstanding amount suggests. Either note could be the more special one; the statement “must” is unsupported. B identifies exactly why.

**Fragile fact.** Rich means demand to own; special means demand to borrow relative to lendable supply; outstanding is not lendable.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Compare the use of general and special collateral in repo transactions. **GARP:** Chapter 14, Section 14.3 General and Special Repo Rates (paragraph following Table 14.1). **GARP vs Schweser:** none. Boundary: Schweser places this point under 78.e; GARP uses it to lead into special spreads (78.f).

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-13 e, where it is Q10 of 10.

a.reason: (Sibling swap). It treats demand to own and demand to borrow as the same demand. GARP says they are not the same. A would be correct only if the special rate were set by supply and demand to buy and sell the issue.

b.reason: B separates demand to own (richness) from demand to borrow relative to the supply for borrow (specialness), as GARP does.

c.reason: (Absolute claim). A larger amount outstanding does not guarantee a larger supply for borrow, because owners who do not lend in repo remove supply; Q may in fact be scarce for borrow. C would be correct only if all holders of Q lent it freely and short demand were equal across the notes.

d.reason: (Sibling swap). It replaces the demand-and-supply-to-borrow explanation with a credit-quality explanation (the logic for GC versus fed funds). Specialness arises between securities of identical credit quality. D would answer a question about secured versus unsecured rates.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Identify the characteristics of special spreads and explain the typical behavior of U.S. Treasury special spreads over an auction cycle.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-13 f Q1
questions.question:
A junior risk analyst at a Canadian pension plan, which reports in CAD but runs a USD Treasury book, is preparing the daily repo report. The desk’s screen shows the following rates for the same pricing date.

| Rate | Level (%) |
|---|---|
| Overnight GC rate, U.S. Treasury collateral | 1.45 |
| Effective federal funds rate | 1.62 |
| One-month term GC rate | 1.52 |
| OTR 10-year note, overnight repo rate | 0.30 |
| OTR 10-year note, one-month term repo rate | 0.55 |

Which of the following is the overnight special spread of the on-the-run (OTR) 10-year note?

options.text: 132 basis points
115 basis points
122 basis points
−115 basis points

questions.solution:
Overnight special spread of the OTR 10-year from a screen of GC, fed funds and term rates.

**Concept and theory**

In a general collateral (GC) repo the lender of cash accepts any security from a broad class, so it earns the highest repo rate available for that class. In a specials trade the lender of cash initiates the trade to take possession of one particular security, so it is really lending cash in order to borrow a bond. Because securities in great demand to be borrowed can raise cash cheaply, the repo rate on a specific security (its special rate) is typically below the GC rate. GARP defines the special spread as the difference between the GC rate and the special rate for a particular security and a particular term:

Special $\text{spread}_{\text{i,T}} = \text{GC rate}_{\text{T}} - \text{special rate}_{\text{i,T}}$.

Here i is the security and T the term (overnight, one week, to a futures expiry, and so on). Two features matter. First, the spread is security specific: each issue has its own special rate. Second, it is term specific: an overnight special rate must be compared with the overnight GC rate, and a one-month term special rate with the one-month term GC rate (GARP Table 14.2 lists term GC rates next to term special rates for exactly this reason). A positive spread means the special rate is below GC, which is the normal case. Do not confuse the special spread with the fed funds to GC spread, which compares the unsecured overnight interbank rate with the GC rate and belongs to the discussion of GC rates.

**Applying it to this question**

The question asks for the overnight spread, so both inputs must be overnight:

Overnight GC rate = 1.45%

OTR 10-year overnight special rate = 0.30%

Special spread = 1.45% − 0.30% = 1.15% = 115 bp

The fed funds rate (1.62%) is irrelevant to the special spread. The one-month rows would give a one-month term spread of 1.52% − 0.55% = 97 bp, which is not what is asked. The CAD reporting currency is also irrelevant. A spread of 115 bp means the holder of the OTR can borrow cash overnight 115 bp below the GC rate by lending the note.

**Fragile fact.** Spread = GC minus special, same security and same term; positive when the issue trades special.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Identify the characteristics of special spreads and explain the typical behavior of U.S. Treasury special spreads over an auction cycle. **GARP:** Chapter 14, Section 14.3 General and Special Repo Rates (definition of special spreads; Tables 14.1 and 14.2). **GARP** **vs Schweser:** none.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-13 f, where it is Q1 of 12.

a.reason: (Wrong input twin). Using the fed funds rate in place of the GC rate: 1.62% − 0.30% = 1.32% = 132 bp. This would only be right if the stem defined the spread against fed funds, which the special spread never is; fed funds belongs in the fed funds to GC spread.

b.reason: B applies the GARP definition (GC rate minus special rate for the particular security and term) using matching overnight inputs.

c.reason: (Scope or condition error (term mismatch)). Using the one-month term GC rate with the overnight special rate: 1.52% − 0.30% = 122 bp. It would be right only if the overnight GC rate were also 1.52%; a special spread compares rates for the same term.

d.reason: (Sign error). Computing special rate minus GC: 0.30% − 1.45% = −115 bp. It would be right only if the spread were defined the other way round; GARP defines it as GC minus special, so a bond trading special shows a positive spread.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Identify the characteristics of special spreads and explain the typical behavior of U.S. Treasury special spreads over an auction cycle.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-13 f Q2
questions.question:
A board risk committee member at a German bank (EUR reporting) is reviewing a staff paper on the repo market for the OTR 10-year U.S. Treasury. The paper makes four statements about OTR special spreads observed over the long history of the market:

I. They are quite volatile on a daily basis, reflecting the supply of and demand for special collateral each day.

II. They can be quite large, with spreads of hundreds of basis points being quite common.

III. They attain higher levels over some periods than over others, and the level of interest rates is part of the explanation.

IV. Because the auction cycle drives them, they repeat a regular pattern of the same size in every auction cycle.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.text: I, II, III and IV
I and III only
II and III only
I, II and III only

questions.solution:
Audit of four statements on the empirical characteristics of OTR 10-year special spreads.

**Concept and theory**

GARP studies the overnight special spread of the OTR 10-year Treasury from July 1997 to July 2010 (Figures 14.4 to 14.6, with vertical lines marking 10-year auctions) and draws four lessons:

| Lesson | Content |
|---|---|
| 1. Volatility | Special spreads are quite volatile on a daily basis, reflecting supply and demand for special collateral each day. |
| 2. Size | Special spreads can be quite large; spreads of hundreds of basis points are quite common. |
| 3. Regimes | Spreads attain higher levels over some periods than others; the level of interest rates is part of the explanation (Figure 14.8). |
| 4. Cycle | While the cycle is far from regular, spreads tend to be small right after auctions and to peak before them. |

Why does the level of rates matter? Before May 2009 there was no penalty for failing to deliver, so the special rate could not sensibly fall below 0%, which caps the special spread at the GC rate. When rates were low the cap was tight and spreads were small; when rates were high there was more room. The cycle pattern is a tendency visible clearly only on average (Figure 14.7 averages across 13 years of cycles precisely because individual cycles are so noisy). Schweser adds that the level and volatility of the spread can be an important gauge of market sentiment; GARP does not state this, so treat it as Schweser-only (condensed source).

**Applying it to this question**

Check each statement against the lessons. I matches lesson 1. II matches lesson 2. III matches lesson 3 together with the Figure 14.8 discussion of the level of rates. IV takes the true idea that the auction cycle drives spreads and turns it into a promise of a regular, identically sized pattern; GARP says the cycle is far from regular and daily spreads are volatile. So I, II and III are correct and IV is not.

**Fragile fact.** The pattern over the cycle is a tendency, "far from regular"; daily spreads are noisy and can be hundreds of basis points.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Identify the characteristics of special spreads and explain the typical behavior of U.S. Treasury special spreads over an auction cycle. **GARP:** Chapter 14, Section 14.3, Special Spreads in the United States and the Auction Cycle (Figures 14.4 to 14.6) and Special Spreads in the United States and the Level of Rates (Figure 14.8). **GARP vs Schweser:** the "gauge of market sentiment" characteristic is Schweser-only; not used as a deciding fact.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-13 f, where it is Q2 of 12.

a.reason: (Absolute claim). Accepts IV, which promises a regular, same-size pattern each cycle. It would be right only if the stem said the average spread across cycles rises toward the auction, which is a tendency, not a fixed repeating pattern.

b.reason: (Polarity flip (size)). Rejects II, treating special spreads as small. It would be right if spreads were typically a few basis points, as for old and double-old issues, but for the OTR 10-year spreads of hundreds of basis points are common.

c.reason: (Polarity flip (stability)). Rejects I, treating special spreads as stable from day to day. It would be right for a smoothed average such as Figure 14.7, but daily spreads are quite volatile.

d.reason: D is the only option that accepts exactly the three statements GARP supports (volatile, large, period-dependent with the level of rates as part of the explanation) and rejects the regularity claim.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Identify the characteristics of special spreads and explain the typical behavior of U.S. Treasury special spreads over an auction cycle.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-13 f Q3
questions.question: A portfolio manager at a Japanese life insurer (JPY reporting) plans to short the OTR 10-year U.S. Treasury for about one week as a hedge, borrowing the note through a reverse repo. A new 10-year issue was sold on 15 February and the next new issue will be sold on 15 May, with no re-openings in between. She can start the trade on 17 February, 31 March or 12 May. Ignoring day-to-day noise, on which date would she typically expect to give up the most interest relative to the GC rate, and why?

options.text: 12 May, because shorts have migrated to the OTR and many short it to hedge purchases of the to-be-issued next OTR.
17 February, because the new issue is scarce right after the auction since dealers have not yet distributed it.
31 March, because the spread peaks mid-cycle and then falls as shorts shift back into the previous OTR issue.
No date, because the spread stays the same while the note remains the most liquid issue until it is replaced.

questions.solution:
When in the auction cycle a one-week short of the OTR 10-year gives up the most interest relative to GC.

**Concept and theory**

A trader who shorts a Treasury must deliver it, so she borrows it through a reverse repo: she lends cash and receives the specific bond as collateral. Because she needs that particular bond, she lends cash at the special rate rather than the GC rate. Her cost of carrying the short, relative to an ordinary cash investment at GC, is therefore the special spread (GC minus special rate). The higher the spread, the more interest she gives up.

GARP explains how the OTR special spread moves over the auction cycle. Immediately after an auction it tends to be small: a short base takes time to develop, shorts can either stay in the previous OTR or move to the new one (this substitutability depresses the spread), and extra supply after a re-opening depresses it too. As time passes, shorts migrate toward the OTR and its spread tends to rise. Finally, many participants short the current OTR to hedge purchases of the to-be-issued next OTR, so demand to short the OTR, and its spread, can increase dramatically or spike going into the next auction. Figure 14.7 confirms that, on average across 1997 to 2010, the spread rises over the cycle and spikes as the next auction approaches.

| Point in cycle | Typical spread | Main reason |
|---|---|---|
| Just after auction | Small | Short base not built; substitutability |
| Mid-cycle | Rising | Shorts migrate to the OTR |
| Just before next auction | Peak or spike | Hedging of to-be-issued OTR |

**Applying it to this question**

17 February is two days after a new issue (spread small). 31 March is mid-cycle (spread rising). 12 May is three days before the next new issue (spread typically peaks). Her cost relative to GC is highest when the spread is highest, so 12 May. The JPY reporting currency and the one-week length do not change the ranking.

**Fragile fact.** Direction: small right after the auction, highest just before the next one; the short (cash lender) bears the spread.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Identify the characteristics of special spreads and explain the typical behavior of U.S. Treasury special spreads over an auction cycle. **GARP:** Chapter 14, Section 14.3, Special Spreads in the United States and the Auction Cycle (Figures 14.4 to 14.7). **GARP** **vs Schweser:** Schweser attributes the pre-auction widening to "substitutability of the special collateral as shorts change to the new OTR"; GARP uses substitutability to explain the low spread just after the auction and attributes the widening to migration and hedging of the to-be-issued OTR. GARP followed.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-13 f, where it is Q3 of 12.

a.reason: A identifies the pre-auction date and gives GARP’s reasons: migration of shorts to the OTR and shorting the OTR to hedge purchases of the to-be-issued next OTR.

b.reason: (Polarity flip). Places the peak right after the auction and claims the new issue is scarce. GARP says dealers tend to own a lot of a new issue until it seasons, and the spread is small just after the auction. It would be right only if the stem described a squeeze in a newly auctioned issue, which is not the typical pattern.

c.reason: (Sibling swap (timing of substitutability)). Moves the post-auction substitutability effect (shorts able to stay in the previous OTR) to the run-up to the next auction. It would be right only if the question asked why the spread is low right after an auction.

d.reason: (Absolute claim). Treats liquidity as constant and so the spread as constant over the cycle. It would be right only for the bond’s liquidity ranking, not its special spread, which rises on average through the cycle.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Identify the characteristics of special spreads and explain the typical behavior of U.S. Treasury special spreads over an auction cycle.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-13 f Q4
questions.question: A senior treasury analyst at the New York branch of a Brazilian bank (BRL reporting) is presenting to newly hired analysts on why recently issued U.S. Treasuries tend to trade special in the repo market. Which of the following explanations is most accurate?

options.text: Short sellers need the OTR issue as collateral, so they lend cash against it at a repo rate above the GC rate to secure delivery.
OTR collateral carries less credit risk than older Treasury issues, so cash lenders accept a lower return in exchange for the extra safety.
Holders of the OTR for liquidity reasons require compensation to lend it, while shorts are willing to pay for the liquidity of shorting it.
Cash investors such as money market funds prefer the most liquid collateral, so they accept below-GC rates in order to receive the OTR.

questions.solution:
Why OTR U.S. Treasuries tend to trade special: the economics and the actors on each side.

**Concept and theory**

GARP starts from liquidity. Current (OTR) issues tend to be the most liquid: bid-ask spreads are particularly low and large trades can be done quickly. This is partly self-fulfilling: because everyone expects a recent issue to be liquid, investors and traders who need liquidity flock to it, and the dealer community tends to own a lot of a new issue until it seasons and passes to buy-and-hold investors.

That liquidity makes OTR issues ideal for longs and for shorts. Most Treasury shorts are held for brief periods (a dealer hedging inventory, an issuer or underwriter hedging an upcoming bond sale, an investor betting on rising rates), so shorts prefer the most liquid issue, which they can cover quickly and at low transaction cost.

The repo market then prices the two sides:

| Actor | Repo role | Motivation |
|---|---|---|
| Long the OTR for liquidity | Lends the bond, borrows cash | Requires compensation to give up the bond’s liquidity: borrows cash cheaply |
| Short seller | Lends cash, borrows the bond | Willing to pay for the liquidity of shorting this bond: accepts a below-GC rate |
| Repo investor (e.g. money fund) | Lends cash | Accepts GC, earns the highest rate for the collateral class |

The result is a special rate below GC, that is, a positive special spread on OTR issues.

**Applying it to this question**

The stem asks why recently issued Treasuries trade special. The deciding fact is the pairing of motivations: longs need compensation to lend, shorts pay for the liquidity of shorting, and the payment is made by accepting a low rate on the cash lent.

**Fragile fact.** Actors: the short lends cash (accepts the low rate); the long OTR holder lends the bond (borrows cash cheaply).

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Identify the characteristics of special spreads and explain the typical behavior of U.S. Treasury special spreads over an auction cycle. **GARP:** Chapter 14, Section 14.3, Special Spreads in the United States and the Auction Cycle, and the preceding discussion of GC and special trades. **GARP vs Schweser:** none.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-13 f, where it is Q4 of 12.

a.reason: (Polarity flip). Shorts pay by lending cash below GC, not above it. With a rate above GC there would be no special spread. Right only if the question asked about a security that trades cheap in repo, which is not the case described.

b.reason: (Sibling swap). Borrows the explanation for why GC is below fed funds (Treasury collateral is safer than an unsecured loan). OTR and older Treasuries have the same issuer credit quality; specialness is about demand to borrow a particular issue. Right if the stem asked why GC trades below fed funds.

c.reason: C restates GARP’s explanation: holders for liquidity reasons require compensation to lend the OTR, and shorts are willing to pay for the liquidity of shorting it, so OTR securities trade special.

d.reason: (Role misassignment). Repo investors such as money market funds accept general collateral and earn the highest rate for it; the parties who accept below-GC rates for a specific bond are the shorts. Right only if the actor were a trader needing to borrow the OTR.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Identify the characteristics of special spreads and explain the typical behavior of U.S. Treasury special spreads over an auction cycle.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-13 f Q5
questions.question:
A regulator at a U.S. supervisory agency is reviewing representative overnight repo rates for recently issued U.S. Treasuries on one pricing date. The fed funds target rate is 2.25%.

| Issue | Designation | Overnight repo rate (%) |
|---|---|---|
| General collateral | GC | 2.10 |
| 2-year note | OTR | 1.92 |
| 10-year note | OTR | 0.85 |
| 10-year note | Old | 2.02 |
| 10-year note | Double-old | 2.06 |
| 30-year bond | OTR | 1.80 |
| 30-year bond | Old | 2.05 |

Which of the following conclusions is most accurate?

options.text: The OTR 10-year trades more special than the OTR 30-year, a long-standing regularity; 30-year specials activity has been muted since the years before the 2001 halt in issuance.
The OTR 2-year spread is far narrower than the OTR 10-year spread because 2-year notes carry less interest rate risk and are therefore poor instruments for hedging.
The double-old 10-year trades more special than the old 10-year, which is consistent with older issues becoming scarcer for borrowing as they season over time.
The OTR 30-year trading more special than the old 30-year shows that the 30-year is again as liquid, and its spreads as large and volatile, as the 10-year.

questions.solution:
Interpreting a cross-section of overnight special spreads across OTR, old and double-old issues and maturities.

**Concept and theory**

GARP Table 14.1 shows representative overnight repo rates for recent 10-year and 30-year Treasuries and draws cross-sectional regularities. Each issue is designated by how recent it is: the most recent is on-the-run (OTR), the second most recent is the old issue, the third the double-old, and so on (all non-current issues are off-the-run). As a general rule, at each maturity the OTR trades most special, followed by the old, then the double-old. The table also shows the OTR 10-year trading more special than the OTR 30-year, a regularity that has held for some time.

Why? The 30-year was historically as liquid as the 10-year, with spreads as large and volatile, but not since the years leading up to the 2001 discontinuation of 30-year issuance. Apart from active specials trading around the 2005 announcement and 2006 re-introduction of "the bond," 30-year special spreads have been muted relative to shorter maturities. For shorter maturities than the 10-year, the pattern over the cycle is similar but the spreads tend not to be nearly as wide, mainly because more frequent issuance prevents any one issue from becoming far and away the most liquid or most favored short. The 5-year behaves much like the 10-year.

**Applying it to this question**

Compute each spread as GC minus the issue’s rate:

OTR 10-year = 2.10% − 0.85% = 125 bp

OTR 30-year = 2.10% − 1.80% = 30 bp

OTR 2-year = 2.10% − 1.92% = 18 bp

Old 10-year = 2.10% − 2.02% = 8 bp, Double-old 10-year = 2.10% − 2.06% = 4 bp

Old 30-year = 2.10% − 2.05% = 5 bp

OTR 10-year (125 bp) far exceeds OTR 30-year (30 bp), matching GARP. The fed funds target (2.25%) is irrelevant.

**Fragile fact.** Order of specialness: OTR, then old, then double-old; OTR 10-year more special than OTR 30-year.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Identify the characteristics of special spreads and explain the typical behavior of U.S. Treasury special spreads over an auction cycle. **GARP:** Chapter 14, Section 14.3, Table 14.1 and Special Spreads in the United States and the Auction Cycle. **GARP vs Schweser:** none (Schweser omits the maturity comparisons; GARP-only detail).

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-13 f, where it is Q5 of 12.

a.reason: A is consistent with the data and with GARP’s explanation that the 30-year’s specials activity has been muted since the years before the 2001 discontinuation, which is why the 10-year has long traded more special.

b.reason: (Sibling swap (wrong cause)). The narrower 2-year spread is explained by more frequent issuance of shorter maturities, which stops one issue from dominating liquidity, not by interest rate risk. Right if the stem asked for a reason unrelated to the issuance schedule, which GARP does not give.

c.reason: (Polarity flip). Specialness declines with age: OTR, then old, then double-old. The data show 8 bp for the old 10-year versus 4 bp for the double-old. Right only if the double-old rate had been below the old rate.

d.reason: (Scope or condition error (overextension)). The OTR trading more special than the old issue is true at every maturity and says nothing about the 30-year matching the 10-year. With 30 bp against 125 bp, the 30-year is clearly not as special. Right only if the OTR 30-year spread were comparable to the 10-year’s.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Identify the characteristics of special spreads and explain the typical behavior of U.S. Treasury special spreads over an auction cycle.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-13 f Q6
questions.question: An internal auditor at the U.S. broker-dealer subsidiary of a UK bank (GBP reporting) is validating a memo in which the repo desk explains the behavior of the OTR 10-year special spread over the auction cycle. Which of the following statements in the memo is NOT correct?

options.text: Right after the auction of a new OTR, shorts can stay in the previous OTR or move to the new one, and this substitutability tends to depress the new issue’s special spread.
Shorts migrate toward the OTR as the cycle progresses, but hedgers of the to-be-issued next OTR usually cover their shorts early, so the spread typically eases into the auction.
Averaged across many cycles and plotted against the fraction of the cycle elapsed, the OTR special spread increases over the cycle and spikes as the next auction approaches.
It takes some time for a short base to develop in a newly issued OTR security, which is one reason its special spread tends to be small just after the auction.

questions.solution:
Auditing a desk memo on the mechanisms behind the OTR special spread cycle.

**Concept and theory**

GARP gives several mechanisms that together produce the typical cycle in the OTR 10-year special spread:

| Mechanism | Effect | When |
|---|---|---|
| Short base takes time to develop | Depresses | Just after an auction |
| Substitutability: shorts can stay in the previous OTR or shift to the new OTR | Depresses | Just after a new-issue auction |
| Extra supply after a re-opening | Depresses | Just after a re-opening; re-opened issues do not get as special as new issues |
| Migration of shorts toward the OTR | Raises | As time passes |
| Shorting the OTR to hedge purchases of the to-be-issued next OTR | Raises sharply (spike) | Going into the next auction |

Figure 14.7 averages the spread across cycles from 1997 to 2010, with the horizontal axis measured as days since issue divided by days between the previous and next issues. As expected, the average rises over the cycle and spikes as the subsequent auction approaches. The hedging mechanism deserves attention: GARP notes that many market participants short the current OTR to hedge their purchases of the to-be-issued next OTR, so demand to short the current OTR, and its special spread, can increase dramatically or spike going into the auction.

**Applying it to this question**

A, C and D match GARP. B gets the migration right but reverses the hedging effect: hedgers of the to-be-issued OTR add shorts going into the auction, so the spread spikes, it does not ease.

**Fragile fact.** Hedgers of the to-be-issued OTR add shorts into the auction: spread spikes, it does not ease.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Identify the characteristics of special spreads and explain the typical behavior of U.S. Treasury special spreads over an auction cycle. **GARP:** Chapter 14, Section 14.3, Special Spreads in the United States and the Auction Cycle (Figure 14.7). **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser says spreads "widen before auctions due to the substitutability of the special collateral as shorts change to the new OTR security"; GARP ties substitutability to the low post-auction spread. GARP followed; likely a compression in the condensed source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-13 f, where it is Q6 of 12.

a.reason: (Not the answer: true statement). GARP explicitly says that immediately after an auction of a new OTR, shorts can stay in the previous OTR or shift, and this substitutability tends to depress special spreads. It would be the false statement only if it said substitutability widens the spread before the auction. (Schweser compresses this differently; see the reference.)

b.reason: B is the incorrect statement, so it is the answer: GARP states that shorting the OTR to hedge purchases of the to-be-issued next OTR can make demand to short the OTR, and its special spread, increase dramatically or spike going into the auction.

c.reason: (Not the answer: true statement). This is the reading of Figure 14.7: the average spread increases over the cycle and spikes as the next auction approaches. It would be false if it claimed the average declines over the cycle.

d.reason: (Not the answer: true statement). GARP says it takes some time for a short base to develop, which is why spreads tend to be small immediately after auctions. It would be false if it said a short base forms instantly.

questions.source: High quality paper LTR-13 f Q7
questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at the U.S. branch of a Chinese bank (CNY reporting) is reading the term structure of repo rates for the OTR 10-year U.S. Treasury. Day counts are measured from the pricing date and rates use actual/360.

| Term | Days | Term special rate (%) | Term GC rate (%) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Overnight | 3 | 1.20 | 1.55 |
| One month | 30 | 0.95 | 1.58 |
| Futures expiry | 47 | 1.10 | 1.60 |
| Two months | 61 | 1.18 | 1.62 |

Using the approach in the reading, which of the following is closest to the forward special spread from the one-month date to the two-month date?
questions.solution:
Implied forward special spread between two term dates from term special and term GC rates.

**Concept and theory**

Special rates exist for each security for each term, so an individual issue has a term structure of special spreads. Term spreads are the differences between term GC rates and the respective term special rates. GARP Table 14.2 shows the term structure for the OTR 10-year (overnight, one week, futures expiry dates, fixed months). Futures expiries appear because many participants do basis trades, trading the OTR against the futures contract into which it is deliverable.

From term spreads one can back out forward spreads: the forward spread from date $\text{t}_{1} \text{to t}_{2}$ is the spread that makes investing at the term spread to $\text{t}_{1}$ and then at the forward spread to $\text{t}_{2}$ equivalent to investing at the term spread to $\text{t}_{2}$. With simple interest on an actual/360 basis, the day-weighted relationship (GARP Equation 14.2) is

$\text{t}_{1}\text{s}_{1} + (\text{t}_{2} - \text{t}_{1}) \text{s}_{\text{fwd}} = \text{t}_{2}\text{s}_{2} =\Rightarrow\text{s}_{\text{fwd}} = \frac{\text{t}_{2}\text{s}_{2} - \text{t}_{1}\text{s}_{1}}{\text{t}_{2} - \text{t}_{1}}$ ,

where $\text{t}_{1}$, $\text{t}_{2}$ are days to each term date, $\text{s}_{1}$, $\text{s}_{2}$ are the term special spreads (term GC minus term special rate) and $\text{s}_{\text{fwd}}$ is the forward special spread. The 1/360 factor cancels on both sides. Forward spreads are useful because they show when the market expects an issue to be most special, which, for the OTR, lines up with the auction schedule.

**Applying it to this question**

Step 1, the term spreads:

$\text{s}_{1} =$ 1.58% − 0.95% = 0.63% $(\text{t}_{1} =$ 30)

$\text{s}_{2} =$ 1.62% − 1.18% = 0.44% $(\text{t}_{2} =$ 61)

Step 2, the forward spread:

$\text{t}_{2}\text{s}_{2} =$ 61 × 0.44% = 26.84

$\text{t}_{1}\text{s}_{1} =$ 30 × 0.63% = 18.90

$\text{s}_{\text{fwd}} = \frac{26.84 - 18.90}{61 - 30} = \frac{7.94}{31} =$ 0.2561% ≈ 0.26%

The overnight and futures-expiry rows are irrelevant. The forward spread is below both term spreads, so the market expects the issue to be less special in the second month than in the first.

**Fragile fact.** Use spreads (GC minus special), weight by days, divide by the forward-period days $\text{t}_{2} - \text{t}_{1}$.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Identify the characteristics of special spreads and explain the typical behavior of U.S. Treasury special spreads over an auction cycle. **GARP:** Chapter 14, Section 14.3, Special Spreads in the United States and the Auction Cycle (Table 14.2, Equation 14.2). **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser mentions term special spreads but not the forward calculation; GARP-only detail.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-13 f, where it is Q7 of 12.

a.reason: (Unit or time-conversion slip). Divides by the total days to the far date instead of the forward period: 7.94/61 = 0.1302% ≈ 0.13%. Right only if the forward period started on the pricing date.

b.reason: (Intermediate result). Stops at the two-month term spread, $\text{s}_{2} =$ 0.44%. Right if the question asked for the spot two-month term spread.

c.reason: (Wrong input twin). Uses term special rates instead of term spreads: (61 × 1.18% − 30 × 0.95%)/31 = 43.48/31 = 1.4026% ≈ 1.40%. Right if the question asked for the forward special rate.

d.reason: D applies Equation 14.2 to spreads (not rates) and divides by the length of the forward period.

questions.source: High quality paper LTR-13 f Q8
questions.question:
The CRO of a UK asset manager (GBP reporting) is reviewing the implied forward special spreads for the current OTR 10-year U.S. Treasury as of 2 March. The issue will be re-opened at an auction in mid-March, and a new 10-year issue is scheduled for mid-May.

| Forward period | Forward special spread (%) |
|---|---|
| 2 Mar to 9 Mar | 0.18 |
| 9 Mar to 31 Mar | 0.41 |
| 31 Mar to 30 Apr | 0.30 |
| 30 Apr to 31 May | 0.27 |
| 31 May to 30 Jun | 0.12 |
| 30 Jun to 30 Sep | 0.01 |

Which of the following conclusions is most accurate?

options.text: The market projects the spread to fall into the March re-opening as hedgers cover, then to widen after the May new issue as the old issue becomes scarce.
The forward spreads measure the fed funds target minus the GC rate, and so they track flight-to-quality demand for Treasury collateral over the period.
The market projects the spread to rise into the March re-opening, stay special into and somewhat past the May new issue, then dissipate to about GC.
The issue is certain to trade at exactly the GC rate from the day after the May new issue, because only the OTR issue of a maturity can trade special.

questions.solution:
Reading the auction cycle from an issue’s implied forward special spreads.

**Concept and theory**

The auction-driven pattern of special spreads can be seen not only in history (Figures 14.4 to 14.7) but in the term structure of special spreads for an individual issue, which expresses the market’s current view. GARP’s example is the OTR 10-year (the 3½s of May 15, 2020) as of May 28, 2010. The auction schedule then was a re-opening of that issue in mid-June and mid-July, followed by a new OTR issue in mid-August. Given the historical evidence, the special spread would be expected to increase into these auctions, and the forward spreads agreed: the spread was projected to rise into the June re-opening, and the issue was projected to stay special into and somewhat past the July and August auctions. But the forward spread from September 30 to December 31 was only one basis point. So, once the new 10-year had been around for about a month, the specialness of the old issue was projected to have dissipated, with no reason to expect it ever to trade special again.

The lesson for the LO: the term structure of special spreads for an OTR issue has a hump tied to its remaining time as OTR. Forward spreads rise into scheduled auctions while the issue is current, and collapse toward zero once the issue has been replaced and shorts have moved to the new OTR. Schweser states the same idea compactly: term special spreads decline right after the new OTR is issued and increase closer to new auctions.

**Applying it to this question**

Read the table against the calendar. The forward spread rises from 0.18% to 0.41% over the window that contains the mid-March re-opening, remains special at 0.27% to 0.30% through April and May (the May new issue falls inside the 30 Apr to 31 May period), is still 0.12% for June (somewhat past the new issue), and then drops to 0.01% from July to September, which is essentially GC. The fed funds rate is not part of the table and is not needed.

**Fragile fact.** Forward spreads rise into scheduled auctions (including re-openings) and dissipate roughly a month after the issue loses OTR status.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Identify the characteristics of special spreads and explain the typical behavior of U.S. Treasury special spreads over an auction cycle. **GARP:** Chapter 14, Section 14.3, Special Spreads in the United States and the Auction Cycle (Table 14.2 discussion). **GARP** **vs Schweser:** none.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-13 f, where it is Q8 of 12.

a.reason: (Polarity flip). Reverses the direction around both events: the forward spread rises into the re-opening and collapses after the issue is replaced. Right only if the table showed spreads falling into March and rising after May.

b.reason: (Sibling swap). Confuses forward special spreads (term GC minus term special rate for one issue) with the fed funds to GC spread, which reflects Treasury scarcity and flight to quality. Right if the table were labelled fed funds minus GC.

c.reason: C describes exactly GARP’s reading of Table 14.2 applied to this calendar: rising into the re-opening, special into and somewhat past the new issue, then dissipating to about GC.

d.reason: (Absolute claim). The table shows 0.12% in June, so the issue stays special somewhat past the new issue; specialness dissipates gradually, and old issues can still trade a little special. Right only if the June forward spread were zero.

questions.question: A risk consultant is advising the CCO of a U.S. primary dealer. A chart of the overnight OTR 10-year special spread against the fed funds target rate shows that, before May 2009, the special spread appeared to be limited by the level of interest rates. Which of the following explanations is most accurate?

options.text: Holders lending the OTR would refuse to accept a special rate below 0%, since it is the lender of the bond who bears the cost of a negative special rate.
A short who fails to deliver loses a day’s interest on the sale proceeds, the same as lending cash at 0% to borrow the bond, so the spread should not exceed the GC rate.
The special spread could not exceed the fed funds to GC spread, because special collateral cannot be safer than general Treasury collateral of the same issuer.
The GC rate remained the cap on the special spread after May 2009 as well, because the fails penalty adopted then applies only to off-the-run issues.

questions.solution:
Why, before May 2009, the special spread was bounded by the level of rates (0% floor on the special rate).

**Concept and theory**

Plotting spreads rather than rates hides a factor that historically limited special spreads. Until 2009 there was no explicit penalty for a fail, that is, for failing to deliver a bond that had been sold. GARP’s argument: suppose a trader shorted the OTR 10-year and failed to deliver at settlement. The trader would not receive the sale cash and so would lose one day of interest on it. Alternatively, the trader could borrow the bond overnight in repo at a special rate of 0%, that is, lend the sale cash at 0% to get the bond and deliver it. The economics are the same: in both cases no interest is earned on the sale proceeds. So no trader would borrow the bond at a special rate below 0%; failing would be cheaper. Hence:

special rate ≥ 0% $\Leftarrow\Rightarrow\text{special spread} = \text{GC} - \text{special rate} \le$ GC rate.

GARP adds in a footnote that this is not strictly true, because fails carry non-monetary costs such as regulatory capital requirements (negative OTR 10-year special rates did occur in 2003). Figure 14.8 superimposes the fed funds target on the special spread: over all but the most recent period the spread was limited by the level of rates, which helps explain periods of high and low special spreads. From May 1, 2009 a fails penalty changed this cap (see Q10).

**Applying it to this question**

The stem asks why the spread looked bounded by rates before May 2009. The deciding fact is the actor and the comparison: the short, who lends cash to borrow the bond, compares a 0% special rate with simply failing.

**Fragile fact.** Pre-2009: floor 0% on the special rate, cap on the spread = GC rate; the short decides by comparing with failing.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Identify the characteristics of special spreads and explain the typical behavior of U.S. Treasury special spreads over an auction cycle. **GARP:** Chapter 14, Section 14.3, Special Spreads in the United States and the Level of Rates (Figure 14.8, footnote 14). **GARP vs** **Schweser:** none of substance.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-13 f, where it is Q9 of 12.

a.reason: (Role misassignment). The party who refuses a negative special rate is the short (lender of cash, borrower of the bond), who would rather fail; the bond lender borrows cash and would receive interest at a negative rate. Right if the stem were about the short’s decision.

b.reason: B reproduces GARP’s reasoning: failing costs a day’s interest, which equals lending at 0%, so the special rate should not go below 0% and the spread should not exceed GC.

c.reason: (Sibling swap). Swaps in the fed funds to GC spread and its safety logic. The bound on the special spread is the GC rate itself, through the 0% floor on the special rate. Right if the question were about why GC trades below fed funds.

d.reason: (Scope or condition error). After the May 2009 penalty the new upper limit is the penalty rate, and the penalty was adopted precisely because of fails in the OTR 10-year. Right only for the period before the penalty.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Identify the characteristics of special spreads and explain the typical behavior of U.S. Treasury special spreads over an auction cycle.
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-13 f Q10
questions.question:
The treasurer of an Australian bank (AUD reporting) reviews a failed delivery by the bank’s U.S. desk, which had sold the OTR 10-year U.S. Treasury short. The fails penalty adopted in 2009 is in force.

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Face amount that failed to deliver | USD 250 million |
| Fed funds target rate | 1.25% |
| Overnight GC rate, Treasury collateral | 1.10% |
| OTR 10-year clean price | 101.40 |
| AUD/USD spot rate | 0.66 |

Which of the following correctly gives the upper limit on the OTR special spread and the penalty for each day the fail persists (actual/360)?

options.text: 1.75%; USD 12,153 per day
1.10%; USD 7,639 per day
3.00%; USD 20,833 per day
4.25%; USD 29,514 per day

questions.solution:
Upper limit on the special spread and daily fails penalty under the 2009 penalty rule.

**Concept and theory**

In October and November 2008, after the Lehman bankruptcy, fails to deliver the OTR 10-year climbed to record levels (USD 5.311 trillion in the week ending October 22 against a pre-crisis average of USD 165 billion). Regulators viewed this as a threat to the liquidity and efficiency of the Treasury market. With their prodding, an industry group, the Treasury Market Practices Group, adopted a penalty rate for fails effective May 1, 2009:

Penalty rate $= \text{max} ($3% − fed funds target rate, 0) .

When fed funds is near zero the penalty is near 3%; failing to deliver USD 100 million then costs 100mm × 3%/360 = USD 8,333 per day. As fed funds rises the penalty falls, because higher rates already raise the opportunity cost of failing, so heavy penalties are not needed to prevent system-wide fails in high-rate environments. With the penalty in place, the new upper limit for the special spread is the penalty rate rather than the GC rate. Soon after the rule began, demand to short the OTR in June 2009 drove the special spread up to this limit.

Daily penalty $= \text{Face} \times\text{Penalty rate} \times\frac{1}{360}$ .

**Applying it to this question**

Penalty rate $= \text{max}($3% − 1.25%, 0) = 1.75%

Upper limit on special spread = 1.75%

Daily penalty = 250,000,000 × 0.0175/360 = USD 12,152.78 ≈ USD 12,153

The GC rate (relevant only to the pre-2009 cap), the clean price and the AUD/USD rate are irrelevant.

**Fragile fact.** Penalty = max(3% minus fed funds target, 0): it falls as rates rise; it, not GC, is the cap after May 2009. Actor: the Treasury Market Practices Group, prodded by regulators.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Identify the characteristics of special spreads and explain the typical behavior of U.S. Treasury special spreads over an auction cycle. **GARP:** Chapter 14, Section 14.3, Special Spreads in the United States and the Level of Rates. **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser says "regulators adopted" the penalty and uses "federal funds rate"; GARP says the Treasury Market Practices Group adopted it at regulators’ prodding and uses the fed funds target rate. GARP followed.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-13 f, where it is Q10 of 12.

a.reason: A applies the GARP formula with the fed funds target and states that the penalty rate is the new upper limit for the special spread.

b.reason: (Sibling swap (pre-2009 cap)). Uses the GC rate as the cap, the rule before the penalty: 250mm × 1.10%/360 = USD 7,639. Right only for the period before May 2009.

c.reason: (Dropped term). Ignores the fed funds subtraction: 250mm × 3%/360 = USD 20,833. Right only if the fed funds target were zero.

d.reason: (Sign error). Adds fed funds instead of subtracting: 3% + 1.25% = 4.25%, giving 250mm × 4.25%/360 = USD 29,514. It would also wrongly make the penalty rise with rates; it falls.

questions.source: High quality paper LTR-13 f Q11
questions.question: A portfolio manager at a Singapore hedge fund (SGD reporting) notes that an off-the-run 7-year U.S. Treasury is trading rich relative to neighboring bonds in the cash market. A colleague concludes that the bond must therefore trade very special in repo. Which of the following assessments is most accurate?

options.text: The colleague is right: a bond that trades rich must trade special, since demand to buy a bond and demand to borrow it are the same.
The colleague is wrong: holders of a rich bond are keen to lend it in repo, so it should trade at or above the GC rate.
The bond may or may not trade special: that depends on the demand to short it relative to the supply actually available to borrow.
The colleague is right: as an older issue, the bond trades most special just before the next auction of its maturity.

questions.solution:
Whether a bond trading rich in the cash market must trade special in repo.

**Concept and theory**

Special rates for a particular issue to a particular date are set by the demand to borrow that issue to that date relative to the supply available to lend. GARP’s key point is that the demand and supply to borrow and lend an issue are not the same as the demand and supply to buy and sell it.

Two reasons. First, supply for borrowing can be far smaller than the amount outstanding: some owners of Treasuries, for institutional reasons, do not lend bonds in repo, so availability depends on how ownership is distributed across institution types. Second, demand differs: a bond that trades rich relative to neighboring bonds shows high demand to own it relative to its outstanding supply, but it may or may not trade very special depending on how much traders want to short it relative to the supply available to borrow.

So predicting the special spreads of individual bonds is quite difficult. GARP adds that in the United States there is one predominant explanatory factor: the auction cycle, meaning that the most recently issued bonds of each maturity trade special.

| Cash market (rich or cheap) | Repo market (special or GC) |
|---|---|
| Demand to own vs amount outstanding | Demand to short vs supply available to borrow |

**Applying it to this question**

The stem gives an off-the-run 7-year that is rich in the cash market. Richness only says demand to own is high. Whether it trades special depends on short demand and borrowable supply, which the stem does not give. The SGD reporting currency is irrelevant.

**Fragile fact.** Rich (cash market) is not the same as special (repo market): borrowable supply can be much less than the amount outstanding.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Identify the characteristics of special spreads and explain the typical behavior of U.S. Treasury special spreads over an auction cycle. **GARP:** Chapter 14, Section 14.3, General and Special Repo Rates (lead-in to Special Spreads in the United States and the Auction Cycle). **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser places the buy versus borrow distinction under LO 78.e; GARP presents it as the determinant of special spreads, so it is used here as a characteristic of special spreads (boundary call).

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-13 f, where it is Q11 of 12.

a.reason: (Absolute claim). Asserts that rich implies special and that buy and borrow demand are the same, which GARP denies. Right only if demand to short tracked demand to own exactly and all holders lent freely.

b.reason: (Polarity flip). GARP says holders who value a bond’s liquidity require compensation to lend it; nothing makes owners of rich bonds eager lenders, and the bond could trade special. Right only if the bond’s holders were known to lend freely and no one wanted to short it.

c.reason: C states GARP’s conclusion that a rich bond may or may not trade special, depending on demand to short relative to the supply available for borrowing.

d.reason: (Scope or condition error). The auction-cycle pattern applies to the OTR issue of each maturity; an off-the-run bond does not become most special before the next auction, when shorts concentrate in the OTR. Right only if the bond were the current OTR.
