questions.question: The CCO of a French bank (EUR reporting) is reviewing a repo trader’s limit request built around the 10-year U.S. Treasury issued on 15 August. That issue will be re-opened at auctions on 15 September and 15 October, and a new 10-year issue will be sold on 15 November. Which of the following best describes the typical path of the August issue’s special spread?

options.text: It falls into each re-opening as shorts cover, then jumps right after each re-opening because the added supply attracts new shorts.
Each re-opening resets it to a new issue, so after September it trades more special than it did just after its original August auction.
Re-openings have no effect on it, because the August issue remains the OTR until November; only new-issue auctions move its spread.
It rises into the re-openings, is held down by their added supply, rises into November, then loses its specialness once replaced as OTR.

questions.solution:
Typical special spread path of an OTR 10-year that is re-opened twice before being replaced.

**Concept and theory**

U.S. Treasuries are sold on a fixed schedule; a new 10-year issue is sold every three months, and between new issues the Treasury may hold re-openings, auctions that increase the size of an already existing issue. In GARP’s Figures 14.4 to 14.6 the vertical lines mark both kinds of auction: after a new-issue auction a different security becomes OTR, while after a re-opening the same security sits on both sides of the line.

The two auction types affect the spread differently:

| Auction | Typical effect on the current OTR’s special spread |
|---|---|
| Re-opening | Spread tends to rise into it; the extra supply right after it depresses the spread; re-opened issues do not get as special as new issues |
| New issue | Spread tends to spike into it as participants short the current OTR to hedge purchases of the to-be-issued OTR; afterwards shorts move to the new OTR and the old issue’s specialness fades within about a month |

GARP’s own example: the 3½s of May 2020 faced re-openings in mid-June and mid-July and a new issue in mid-August 2010. The spread was expected to increase into these auctions and the issue to stay special into and somewhat past them, but the forward spread from September 30 to December 31 was only one basis point.

**Applying it to this question**

Apply this to the August issue: it is the OTR from 15 August. Its spread tends to rise into the 15 September and 15 October re-openings, is held down right after each by the added supply, and rises into the 15 November new issue. Once the November issue becomes OTR, the August issue becomes the old 10-year and its specialness fades.

**Fragile fact.** Re-openings add supply to the same OTR (depressing the spread); new issues replace the OTR (old issue’s specialness fades).

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Identify the characteristics of special spreads and explain the typical behavior of U.S. Treasury special spreads over an auction cycle. **GARP:** Chapter 14, Section 14.3, Special Spreads in the United States and the Auction Cycle (Figures 14.4 to 14.6 and the Table 14.2 discussion). **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser does not mention re-openings; GARP-only detail.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-13 f, where it is Q12 of 12.

a.reason: (Polarity flip). Reverses both effects: spreads tend to rise into auctions, and the added supply after a re-opening depresses the spread rather than raising it. Right only if the directions were the other way round.

b.reason: (Sibling swap). Gives a re-opened issue the behavior of a new issue. GARP notes that re-opened issues do not get as special as new issues because of the extra supply. Right only if the September auction were a new issue.

c.reason: (Scope or condition error). Drops the re-opening condition: re-openings add supply to the existing OTR and do affect its spread. Right only if there were no re-openings in the cycle.

d.reason: D matches GARP: rising into auctions, extra supply after re-openings depressing the spread, and specialness dissipating once the issue is replaced.

questions.loText: Discuss the process of liquidity transfer pricing (LTP) and identify best practices for the governance and implementation of an LTP process.
questions.reading: LTR-14: Liquidity Transfer Pricing: A Guide to Better Practice
questions.topic: Liquidity Transfer Pricing: A Guide to Better Practice
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-14 a Q1
questions.question:
A junior risk analyst at an Australian bank (AUD reporting) is preparing an induction session for newly hired analysts on what the bank’s liquidity transfer pricing (LTP) process does. Her draft slide contains four statements:

I. LTP attributes the costs, benefits and risks of liquidity to the respective business units, transferring them from those units to a centrally managed pool.

II. LTP charges providers of funds, such as deposit-raising branches, for the cost of liquidity and credits users of funds, such as lending units, for its benefit.

III. LTP recoups the cost of carrying the liquidity cushion by charging contingent commitments, such as lines of credit, on their predicted use of liquidity.

IV. Banks with poor LTP practices typically overprice liquidity, which makes them more likely to under-value stable sources of funding.

Which of the statements should she keep on the slide?

options.text: I and II only
I, III and IV only
I and III only
II and III only

questions.solution:
Induction slide: which statements correctly describe what LTP does.

**Concept and theory**

GARP opens the chapter by defining LTP as a process that attributes the costs, benefits and risks of liquidity to the respective business units within a bank (a footnote adds that LTP forms part of the wider funds transfer pricing, FTP, process). Its purpose is to transfer liquidity costs and benefits from business units to a centrally managed pool. To do this LTP performs three jobs:

| Who | What LTP does to them |
|---|---|
| Users of funds (assets, loans) | Charged for the cost of liquidity they consume |
| Providers of funds (liabilities, deposits) | Credited for the benefit of liquidity they create |
| Contingent commitments (lines of credit etc.) | Charged on their predicted (expected) use of liquidity, which recoups the cost of carrying the liquidity cushion |

The motivation is behavioural. A business unit only behaves as if liquidity is scarce if its profit and loss shows that scarcity. GARP notes that banks with poor LTP practices typically underprice or, even worse, fail to price liquidity. Such banks are more likely to accrue illiquid assets and contingent exposures, and to under-value stable sources of funding, an outcome seen at many banks before the global financial crisis (GFC), when liquidity was plentiful and cheap and many believed it would remain so permanently. The direction of the mispricing matters: the failure was cheap liquidity, not expensive liquidity.

**Applying it to this question**

Check each statement against the definition. I restates the definition and purpose (attribution to business units, transfer to a central pool): true. II reverses the roles: users (loans) are charged and providers (deposits) are credited, so II is false. III is the third job of LTP, charging contingent commitments on predicted use to recoup the cushion’s carrying cost: true. IV says poor LTP banks overprice liquidity; GARP says they underprice or fail to price it, and it is the underpricing that leads them to under-value stable funding: false. Keep I and III.

**Fragile fact.** Direction and actor: users (assets) are charged, providers (liabilities) are credited, contingent commitments are charged on expected use; poor LTP means liquidity is underpriced.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Discuss the process of liquidity transfer pricing (LTP) and identify best practices for the governance and implementation of an LTP process.

**GARP:** Chapter 15, Section 15.1 Introduction and Figure 15.1. **GARP vs Schweser:** none (Schweser LO 79.a gives the same charge and credit logic).

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-14 a, where it is Q1 of 13.

a.reason: (Role misassignment). A keeps II, which swaps charge and credit between users and providers of funds. It would be correct only if the stem described a bank whose deposits used liquidity and whose loans created it, which is the reverse of how a bank’s balance sheet works.

b.reason: (Polarity flip). B keeps IV, which flips “underprice” to “overprice”. A bank that overpriced liquidity would, if anything, over-reward stable funding. B would be right only if IV read “typically underprice or fail to price liquidity”.

c.reason: C (I and III only) matches GARP’s opening description: LTP attributes liquidity costs, benefits and risks to business units and a central pool, charges users, credits providers, and recoups the cushion cost by charging contingent commitments “based on their predicted (expected) use”.

d.reason: (Role misassignment). D keeps the swapped statement II and also drops the true definition in I. It would be correct only if II had the roles the right way round and I were absent from the slide.

questions.question: A treasurer at a Singapore bank (SGD reporting) is drafting the rationale section of the bank’s first LTP policy. The bank funds three- to seven-year SGD corporate loans largely with retail deposits of under one year. Which of the following statements is most accurate for the rationale?

options.text: Funding long-term loans with short-term deposits makes the bank inherently vulnerable to liquidity risk; if LTP prices that risk into product pricing, new product approval and performance assessment, the bank need not be discouraged from this activity.

Funding long-term loans with short-term deposits makes the bank inherently vulnerable to liquidity risk; LTP charges should therefore be set high enough to remove this maturity transformation from the balance sheet entirely.
Funding long-term loans with short-term deposits exposes the bank mainly to interest rate risk; LTP exists to price that risk, which is why the swap curve serves as its reference rate.
Funding long-term loans with short-term deposits creates liquidity risk only in systemic crises; in normal markets liquidity is plentiful, so LTP charges can be set at zero until stress emerges.

questions.solution:
Rationale for LTP at a bank funding long-term loans with short-term deposits.

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s Section 15.3.1 (“Why Banks Need LTP”) starts from how banks make money: they fund long-term loans (assets) with short-term deposits (liabilities), a process called maturity transformation. Quoting the BCBS, GARP says this makes banks inherently vulnerable to liquidity risk, both of an institution-specific nature and the kind that affects markets as a whole.

The key step is what GARP concludes from this. It does not say maturity transformation is bad. It says that, provided banks use LTP to account for the costs, benefits and risks of liquidity in three places, namely product pricing, new product approval processes, and profit and performance assessments, they should not be discouraged from engaging in maturity transformation. LTP is a pricing tool, not a prohibition. The danger is the opposite case: banks with poor LTP practices are more likely to accrue larger amounts of long-term illiquid assets, contingent commitments and shorter-dated volatile liabilities, which substantially increases their vulnerability to funding shortfalls. The Senior Supervisors Group (2009) found that firms that relied most on short-term financing of longer-term illiquid assets suffered the worst funding problems, and that poor LTP, which failed to penalise businesses for embedded liquidity risk, drove those business models.

Two misreadings recur. First, interest rate risk is a separate risk, priced through the swap curve (the “base” rate); LTP is about the liquidity spread above it. Second, the pre-GFC belief that liquidity is a free good in calm markets is precisely the error LTP corrects.

**Applying it to this question**

The bank’s three- to seven-year loans funded by sub-one-year deposits are textbook maturity transformation. The rationale needs two parts: the vulnerability (liquidity risk) and the remedy (price it into pricing, product approval and performance). Only A contains both halves in GARP’s direction.

**Fragile fact.** LTP prices maturity transformation; it does not ban it. The risk created is liquidity risk (both idiosyncratic and market-wide), not mainly interest rate risk.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Discuss the process of liquidity transfer pricing (LTP) and identify best practices for the governance and implementation of an LTP process.

**GARP:** Chapter 15, Sections 15.3.1 “Why Banks Need LTP” and 15.3.2 “An Example of What Can Go Wrong with Poor LTP”. **GARP vs Schweser:** none; Schweser does not discuss maturity transformation under 79.a explicitly (boundary call: kept in 79.a as the rationale for the LTP process).

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-14 a, where it is Q2 of 13.

a.reason: A paraphrases GARP Section 15.3.1: maturity transformation makes banks inherently vulnerable to liquidity risk, but if LTP accounts for liquidity costs, benefits and risks in product pricing, new product approval and profit and performance assessment, banks “should not be discouraged” from it.

b.reason: (Absolute claim). B turns “price the risk” into “eliminate the activity entirely”. GARP explicitly says banks should not be discouraged from maturity transformation when it is properly priced. B would be correct only if the stem asked what a bank wishing to run a perfectly matched balance sheet should do, which GARP does not recommend.

c.reason: (Sibling swap). C attributes interest rate risk, the job of the swap-curve base rate, to LTP. In GARP the swap curve prices interest rate risk and the spread above it is the liquidity charge. C would be correct for a question about the base rate in funds transfer pricing, not about the purpose of LTP.

d.reason: (Scope or condition error). D limits liquidity risk to systemic crises and endorses a zero charge in normal times, which is the “free good” view GARP identifies as the worst practice in the survey. D would describe what some banks believed before the GFC, not better practice.

questions.question:
An internal auditor at a Brazilian bank (BRL reporting) is checking the bank’s LTP process map against the process described in the GARP reading. The map describes the following flows:

I. The retail deposit unit receives credits from treasury based on the commitment of funds it provides, reduced by charges against contingent commitments such as deposit run-off.

II. The corporate lending unit incurs charges from treasury based on the commitment of funds it requires, plus additional charges for contingent commitments such as lines of credit.

III. The markets unit is charged for the funds it uses, credited for funds it provides through the sale of marketable securities, and charged for contingent commitments such as collateral calls on derivatives.

IV. Funding raised in the interbank market is booked to the business unit that arranged it, which on-lends any surplus to the internal treasury at a rate the unit sets.

Which of the flows are consistent with the GARP process?

options.text: I and II only
I and III only
I, II, III and IV
I, II and III only

questions.solution:
Auditing an LTP process map against GARP Figure 15.1.

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s Figure 15.1 is a graphical representation of the LTP process. At its centre sits the internal treasury, which runs a central pool and holds the liquidity cushion. Around it are the flows:

| Participant | Treatment in Figure 15.1 |
|---|---|
| Interbank market | Provides funds to the internal treasury (the central pool) |
| Business unit 1 (provides funds, e.g. deposits) | Receives credits from treasury based on the commitment of funds provided; credits are reduced by charges against contingent commitments, such as deposit run-off |
| Business unit 2 (uses funds, e.g. loans) | Incurs charges from treasury based on the commitment of funds required; additional charges apply to contingent commitments, such as lines of credit |
| Trading business | Uses funds, provides funds (through the sale of marketable securities) and receives charges against contingent commitments, such as collateral calls on derivative positions |

Two subtleties make this diagram examinable. First, a liquidity provider is not simply credited: its credit is net of a charge for the contingent risk it brings (deposits can run off). Second, the trading business is two-sided: it both uses and provides funds, and it also carries contingent liquidity needs from derivatives. Everything flows through treasury, which is consistent with the best practice that wholesale funding be confined to a central treasury function.

**Applying it to this question**

I matches business unit 1 including the run-off reduction. II matches business unit 2 including the contingent line-of-credit charge. III matches the trading business on all three counts. IV puts interbank funding in the hands of the arranging business unit, which then sets its own on-lending rate to treasury; in Figure 15.1 the interbank market supplies funds to the internal treasury. IV is inconsistent, so the answer is I, II and III only.

**Fragile fact.** Deposit-raising units receive credits reduced by a run-off charge; the trading business is charged for collateral calls and credited for securities sales.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Discuss the process of liquidity transfer pricing (LTP) and identify best practices for the governance and implementation of an LTP process.

**GARP:** Chapter 15, Section 15.1 and Figure 15.1 (“A graphical representation of the LTP process”). **GARP vs Schweser:** none; Schweser’s Figure 79.1 describes the same central treasury flows. The GARP figure text is garbled in the two-column extraction and was reconstructed from the readable labels.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-14 a, where it is Q3 of 13.

a.reason: (Scope or condition error). A rejects III, typically because the candidate treats the trading business only as a user of funds, forgetting that it also provides funds through securities sales and is charged for collateral calls. A would be right only if the markets unit’s description omitted one of those flows or misstated it.

b.reason: (Scope or condition error). B rejects II, as if contingent charges applied only to trading. Figure 15.1 explicitly adds charges for contingent commitments such as lines of credit to the fund-using unit. B would be right if II had said lending units are charged only for drawn balances.

c.reason: (Role misassignment). C accepts IV, giving the business unit the treasury’s role of raising and pricing wholesale funds. This is the decentralised arrangement that the survey linked to internal arbitrage. C would be right only for a bank that deliberately runs decentralised funding centres, which GARP does not treat as better practice.

d.reason: D matches every flow in Figure 15.1 and rejects IV, which contradicts both the diagram (interbank funds go to treasury) and the governance principle that wholesale funding is confined to group or subsidiary treasury.

questions.question: The chief compliance officer (CCO) of a Canadian bank (CAD reporting) is preparing a board paper on how the bank’s LTP process should be governed. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Regulation and competition differ most across banks, so they explain most of the variation in LTP governance quality; internal controls matter mainly where regulation is weak.

Regulation and competition affect banks in much the same way, so LTP governance is differentiated largely by internal controls; weak controls leave a bank more prone to moral hazard and adverse selection.
Weak internal controls expose a bank to adverse selection, which arises when a business unit insulated from liquidity risk behaves differently than it would if it were fully exposed to that risk.
Strong internal controls, such as board oversight and risk management, guarantee that group-wide LTP objectives are met, which makes external controls such as regulation redundant.

questions.solution:
Board paper: external versus internal control factors in governing LTP.

**Concept and theory**

GARP Section 15.2 opens with a general point about governance. All policies, processes and practices need governing, and this is normally achieved through a combination of:

- **external control factors**, such as regulation and competition; and
- **internal control factors**, such as board oversight and risk management.

Because external factors affect institutions in much the same way, governance is differentiated largely by the internal control factors a bank employs. How well a bank is governed bears heavily on whether its group-wide objectives are met: institutions with strong internal controls are more likely to achieve their goals, while those with weak internal controls are more prone to moral hazard and adverse selection, which weighs on performance. GARP then says that many poor LTP practices in the survey were the direct result of weak internal controls.

GARP’s footnote defines the two problems, and they are a classic sibling pair:

| Problem | Definition (GARP footnote 10) |
|---|---|
| Moral hazard | A party insulated from risk behaves differently than it would if fully exposed to it (e.g. risky behaviour expecting a bail-out) |
| Adverse selection | Bad results arising from information asymmetries between buyers and sellers (e.g. a used-car seller hiding defects) |

Schweser applies them to LTP: mispriced liquidity produced adverse selection in loan and deposit maturities, and moral hazard in trading units that ignored contingent liquidity costs.

**Applying it to this question**

The board paper needs a statement that ranks internal over external factors for the right reason and links weak controls to the right problems. B does both. A inverts the ranking; C mislabels the moral hazard definition; D promises certainty.

**Fragile fact.** Internal controls differentiate governance because external factors are common to all; moral hazard = insulated from risk, adverse selection = information asymmetry.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Discuss the process of liquidity transfer pricing (LTP) and identify best practices for the governance and implementation of an LTP process.

**GARP:** Chapter 15, Section 15.2 “Governing LTP” and footnote 10. **GARP vs Schweser:** none; Schweser 79.a states the same ranking of internal over external factors.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-14 a, where it is Q4 of 13.

a.reason: (Polarity flip). A reverses GARP’s logic: it is precisely because external factors are common to all banks that they do not differentiate governance. A would be correct only if regulation and competition varied sharply across banks, which is the opposite of GARP’s premise.

b.reason: B follows GARP Section 15.2: external factors affect institutions “in much the same way”, so governance is differentiated largely by internal controls, and weak internal controls leave institutions more prone to moral hazard and adverse selection.

c.reason: (Sibling swap). C gives the definition of moral hazard (a party insulated from risk changing its behaviour) the label adverse selection, which GARP defines through information asymmetries. C would be correct if “adverse selection” were replaced by “moral hazard”.

d.reason: (Absolute claim). D says strong internal controls “guarantee” objectives and make regulation redundant. GARP says only that institutions with strong internal controls are more likely to achieve their goals, and governance combines external and internal factors. D would need “make it more likely” and no redundancy claim.

questions.question: A risk consultant is reviewing the draft LTP policy of a UK bank (GBP reporting) that has never had one. Her fieldwork found that the bank’s retail branches were underpaid for the deposits they raised, while the lending, investment and trading portfolios received unduly cheap liquidity. Which of the following draft provisions is most consistent with better LTP practice?

options.text: The policy applies only to business units that are material users of funding liquidity, because providers are already rewarded through their deposit margins.
The policy is deferred until the liquidity management information system (LMIS) is upgraded, because a written policy adds little before granular systems exist.
The policy defines LTP, states its purpose and sets principles or rules, and applies to all business units that are material users or providers of funding liquidity.
The policy is set and owned by each business unit so that its rules reflect local funding conditions, with the treasury notified of any changes made.

questions.solution:
Reviewing the draft provisions of a bank’s first LTP policy.

**Concept and theory**

GARP Section 15.2.1.1 found that few banks in the survey had an effective LTP policy. As a result, LTP was not defined, and there were no principles or rules to help businesses understand how LTP should operate. GARP calls having no LTP policy “clearly poor practice”. Banks had traditionally used internal transfer pricing to manage interest rate risk in the banking book and to assess product and business performance, with no or only minimal adjustment for liquidity; pricing liquidity internally was a new concept for most, brought to light by the breakdown of wholesale funding markets. GARP accepts that it will take time to establish adequate LTP policies and procedures, but calls this “a necessary first step” towards better practice.

The consequence of having no policy is spelled out in Section 15.1.1.1: liquidity generators (such as retail branches raising deposits) were underpaid for the liquidity they created, and liquidity users (lending, investment and trading portfolios) received free or unduly cheap liquidity.

GARP’s better-practice list (Conclusion, “Governing LTP”) sets out what the policy should contain:

- it defines LTP and states the purpose of LTP;
- it provides principles and/or rules so LTP achieves its intended purpose;
- it applies to all business units that are material users or providers of funding liquidity.

The policy sits alongside, not instead of, central management of LTP by group or subsidiary treasury applied consistently across the group.

**Applying it to this question**

The consultant’s fieldwork shows both symptoms of a missing policy: providers (branches) underpaid, users (portfolios) overly cheap. The provision must therefore cover both sides and set out the definition, purpose and rules. C does exactly this. A drops providers, B postpones the first step, D decentralises ownership.

**Fragile fact.** The policy covers material users and providers of funding liquidity, and it is the first step, not the last.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Discuss the process of liquidity transfer pricing (LTP) and identify best practices for the governance and implementation of an LTP process.

**GARP:** Chapter 15, Sections 15.1.1.1 “Governance of the LTP process”, 15.2.1.1 “LTP Policies”, and 15.5 Conclusion (“Governing LTP”). **GARP vs Schweser:** none; Schweser’s wording is “a well-defined LTP process with guiding principles and rules ... that apply to all business units that use funding liquidity or provide funding liquidity”.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-14 a, where it is Q5 of 13.

a.reason: (Scope or condition error). A drops providers from the policy’s scope, yet underpaid deposit-raising branches are one of the two failures GARP associates with having no policy. A would be correct only if the policy’s stated scope were “material users or providers”.

b.reason: (Scope or condition error). B makes the policy conditional on an LMIS upgrade. GARP calls establishing LTP policies and procedures a necessary first step; LMIS improvement supports the policy but does not precede it. B would be correct only if GARP ranked the system before the policy, which it does not.

c.reason: C reproduces GARP’s better-practice description of the policy: define LTP, state its purpose, provide principles or rules, and apply it to all business units that are material users or providers of funding liquidity.

d.reason: (Role misassignment). D gives policy ownership to each business unit. GARP’s better practice is that LTP is managed centrally within group or subsidiary treasury and applied consistently across the group; unit-by-unit regimes are the inconsistency the survey criticised. D would be correct only for a decentralised design that GARP does not endorse.

questions.question:
A treasury analyst at a Japanese bank (JPY reporting) that operates decentralised funding centres is investigating a funding transaction booked by its prime brokerage unit.

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Wholesale funding raised externally by prime brokerage (JPY billion) | 40 |
| Spread paid to external lenders over the reference rate (bps) | 18 |
| Spread charged when on-sold to treasury and to the equity derivatives unit (bps) | 31 |
| Reference rate (%) | 0.45 |

Neither treasury nor the equity derivatives unit knew what spread the prime brokerage unit had paid. Which of the following statements best describes this case?

options.text: The unit earned an internal arbitrage profit that was risk-free to it but added possibly badly managed risk for the bank; decentralised funding, poor oversight and weak risk controls jointly enabled it.
The unit earned an internal arbitrage profit, but because the funds never left the group, the bank as a whole took on no additional liquidity risk from the transaction.
The arbitrage was caused solely by the decentralised structure, so confining wholesale funding to treasury would remove it whatever the quality of oversight and controls.
The arbitrage shows that treasury was charging too much for funds; better practice is to let every business unit raise its own wholesale funding at market rates.

questions.solution:
Prime brokerage unit on-sells externally raised wholesale funds at a higher spread.

**Concept and theory**

GARP Section 15.2.1.2 frames a genuine debate: should a bank have a centralised funding centre, where wholesale funding is restricted to a group or subsidiary treasury, or decentralised funding centres, where certain business units raise funding from their own sources to cover their own needs? GARP accepts there are reasonable academic and economic arguments for both. However, the survey found that banks with decentralised funding centres, particularly those with large prime brokerage businesses, were more susceptible to poor LTP practices.

The mechanism is internal arbitrage. Some business units that could raise wholesale funds externally then sold the funds to treasury, and in some cases to other business units, at a higher rate. This produced a “risk-free” profit to the business unit at the cost of more, and possibly badly managed, risk for the bank as a whole.

GARP adds an important qualification: decentralised funding structures were not the sole cause of internal arbitrage. Poor oversight and inadequate risk controls also played a role. Jointly, these factors limited the ability of treasury and business units to know what price other units had paid for external funds, which is what made the arbitrage possible. Most decentralised banks also ran inconsistent LTP regimes and relied on manual off-line processes to update funding costs. The response GARP observed is a move to having wholesale funding managed centrally by treasury, “in part” to restrict arbitrage between business units and treasury and between business units themselves.

**Applying it to this question**

The unit borrowed at 18 bps and on-sold at 31 bps, a 13 bp internal margin, while the buyers did not know its true cost. This is GARP’s internal arbitrage example. The margin is a profit to the unit, but the bank bears the funding risk of the raised money. The information gap (nobody knew the price paid) points to poor oversight and controls alongside decentralisation.

Irrelevant inputs: the JPY 40 billion size, the 13 bp margin (about JPY 52 million a year) and the 0.45% reference rate. The question asks for a characterisation, not a profit figure, and the reference rate level plays no role.

**Fragile fact.** Decentralisation was not the sole cause of arbitrage: oversight and risk controls failed jointly; the profit is risk-free only to the unit.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Discuss the process of liquidity transfer pricing (LTP) and identify best practices for the governance and implementation of an LTP process.

**GARP:** Chapter 15, Sections 15.1.1.1 and 15.2.1.2 “Internal Funding Structure: Centralised vs Decentralised”. **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser says “most problems identified in the banking survey stemmed from a decentralized funding structure”; GARP says only a small proportion of surveyed banks were decentralised and that decentralisation was not the sole cause of arbitrage. GARP followed.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-14 a, where it is Q6 of 13.

a.reason: A matches GARP: a “risk-free” profit to the business unit at the cost of more and possibly badly managed risk for the bank as a whole, made possible jointly by decentralised funding, poor oversight and inadequate risk controls.

b.reason: (Polarity flip). B says the bank took on no additional risk because funds stayed in the group. GARP says the arbitrage profit came at the cost of more and possibly badly managed risk for the bank as a whole. B would be correct only if the unit’s profit had no counterpart risk anywhere in the bank.

c.reason: (Absolute claim). C makes decentralisation the sole cause and centralisation a complete cure. GARP states decentralised structures were not the sole cause; poor oversight and inadequate risk controls also played a role. C would be correct if it said centralisation “helps restrict” arbitrage.

d.reason: (Role misassignment). D concludes that every unit should raise its own wholesale funding, handing treasury’s role to business units. Better practice confines wholesale funding to group or subsidiary treasury. D would describe the decentralised structure GARP found more susceptible to poor LTP, not a fix.

questions.question: The chief risk officer (CRO) of a Chinese banking group (CNY reporting) with subsidiaries in Hong Kong and Singapore is redesigning the group’s internal funding structure after an internal review found inconsistent LTP regimes across entities. Which design is most consistent with better LTP practice?

options.text: Each business line raises its own wholesale funding and reports its funding cost to group treasury monthly, and group treasury then aligns the LTP rates across the lines.
Only group treasury may manage LTP; subsidiary treasuries are barred from managing LTP or raising wholesale funding, even for their own local entities.
Each subsidiary sets its own LTP regime tailored to local conditions, because academic and economic arguments clearly favour decentralised funding centres.
LTP is managed centrally within group treasury or a subsidiary treasury and applied consistently across the group, with wholesale funding confined to that function.

questions.solution:
Group CRO redesigns the internal funding structure across subsidiaries.

**Concept and theory**

Once GARP has shown how decentralised funding centres enabled internal arbitrage and inconsistent LTP regimes, it sets out the better practice in its Conclusion (“Governing LTP”): LTP should be managed centrally, within group treasury or a subsidiary treasury, and applied consistently across the group, and wholesale funding should be confined to this function. In the survey, the small proportion of banks operating decentralised funding centres were all moving towards having wholesale funding managed centrally by a treasury function, in part to restrict arbitrage between business units and treasury and between business units themselves.

Three features of the recommendation are each examinable:

| Feature | What GARP requires |
|---|---|
| Who manages LTP | A treasury: group treasury or a subsidiary treasury |
| Consistency | One LTP regime applied consistently across the group |
| Wholesale funding | Confined to that treasury function, not raised by business lines |

Note what GARP does not say. It does not ban subsidiary treasuries; a subsidiary treasury is an acceptable home for LTP and wholesale funding. Nor does it claim the academic debate is settled: it acknowledges reasonable arguments on both sides, but bases its recommendation on what the survey observed. Schweser’s shorter wording (“centrally managed by a group treasury”) can mislead candidates into thinking subsidiary treasuries are excluded.

**Applying it to this question**

The CRO’s problem is inconsistent LTP regimes across entities. The fix must centralise wholesale funding in a treasury, keep subsidiary treasuries as acceptable hosts, and apply one regime group-wide. D contains all three. A leaves wholesale funding with business lines; B over-centralises beyond GARP’s wording; C both decentralises and misstates the debate.

**Fragile fact.** Group or subsidiary treasury; applied consistently across the group; wholesale funding confined to that treasury.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Discuss the process of liquidity transfer pricing (LTP) and identify best practices for the governance and implementation of an LTP process.

**GARP:** Chapter 15, Sections 15.2.1.2, 15.2.1.5 “Towards Better LTP Practice” and 15.5 Conclusion (“Governing LTP”). **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser 79.a says “a group treasury should centrally manage all wholesale funding” and later “a group or subsidiary treasury”; GARP’s “group treasury or a subsidiary treasury” followed.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-14 a, where it is Q7 of 13.

a.reason: (Role misassignment). A leaves wholesale fundraising with business lines and gives treasury only an after-the-fact alignment role, which preserves the arbitrage channel. A would be correct only if business lines were barred from raising wholesale funds.

b.reason: (Scope or condition error). B overextends the rule by barring subsidiary treasuries. GARP explicitly allows LTP and wholesale funding to sit in a subsidiary treasury. B would be correct only if GARP said “group treasury only”.

c.reason: (Polarity flip). C claims the arguments clearly favour decentralisation and endorses entity-specific regimes. GARP says there are reasonable arguments for both, but the survey found decentralised banks more susceptible to poor LTP and better practice requires consistency across the group. C would describe the pre-reform state of the minority of decentralised banks.

d.reason: D restates GARP’s better practice: LTP managed centrally within group treasury or a subsidiary treasury, applied consistently across the group, with wholesale funding confined to that function.

questions.question: A senior risk analyst at a German bank (EUR reporting) is reviewing the trading book funding policy. The policy assumes every trading asset is held for 180 days or less and charges short-term funding rates on that basis. A long-term funding charge applies only when a position is transferred to the banking book. Treasury cannot see individual desk balance sheets, so it funds the trading businesses on their total net funding requirement. Which assessment of this policy is most accurate?

options.text: The 180-day assumption is prudent because trading assets are marketable by definition, and funding on the net requirement across trading units correctly captures their liquidity risk.
Long-term charges apply only when positions roll to the banking book, whatever their likely holding period, and funding the net requirement in effect gives the trading book a line of credit.
The main weakness is that funding on the total net requirement overcharges the trading book, because netting across desks inflates the requirement attributed to each desk.
The policy is weak only because the 180-day threshold is too short; extending it to 360 days would align funding charges with the liquidity risk of traded assets.

questions.solution:
Assessing a trading book funding policy with a 180-day assumption and net funding.

**Concept and theory**

GARP calls the LTP practices around trading and investment banking “probably the worst” identified in the survey, blaming poorly designed trading book policies, inadequate risk controls and limits, and lack of oversight (Section 15.2.1.3). Three weaknesses stand out:

(1) **The 180-day assumption.** Most surveyed banks had trading book funding policies, but nearly all assumed assets were held only short-term (180 days or less). Irrespective of whether assets were likely to be held beyond 180 days, long-term funding charges applied only when assets rolled from the trading book to the banking book. This gave little incentive to build controls and limits to measure liquidity risk in traded assets, and showed up as a build-up of highly illiquid positions.

(2) **No line of sight; net funding.** Many larger banks lacked a line of sight to individual business balance sheets and could not identify the funding requirements of individual desks. Trading and investment banking were funded on the total net funding requirement across related units. GARP says this “essentially provides a line of credit to the trading book” and ignores embedded liquidity risk, so it is poor practice.

(3) **Haircuts and margin calls.** Insufficient haircuts were applied to traded assets, and nobody had priced the liquidity cost of potential margin calls, which then strained banks when prices fell.

Section 15.1.1.1 adds that treasuries charged trading businesses on net funding requirement “with no add-ons” for the risk of a blow-out in liquidity needs.

**Applying it to this question**

The German bank’s policy reproduces weaknesses (1) and (2) exactly: a 180-day holding assumption, long-term charges only on transfer to the banking book, and treasury funding the net requirement without desk visibility. The correct assessment names both mechanisms and their effect, which is B.

**Fragile fact.** Long-term charges kicked in only on rolling to the banking book; funding on net requirement acts like a free line of credit to trading.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Discuss the process of liquidity transfer pricing (LTP) and identify best practices for the governance and implementation of an LTP process.

**GARP:** Chapter 15, Sections 15.1.1.1 and 15.2.1.3 “Trading Book Funding Policies and Identifying Funding Requirements”. **GARP vs Schweser:** none of substance; Schweser condenses this to “trading book funding policies and principles should be clearly set” and does not mention the 180-day assumption (GARP-only detail).

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-14 a, where it is Q8 of 13.

a.reason: (Polarity flip). A calls the assumption prudent and the net approach correct. GARP calls both poor practice that allowed illiquid positions to build up. A would be correct only if traded assets stayed reliably liquid in stress, which the GFC disproved.

b.reason: B paraphrases GARP: long-term funding charges apply only when assets roll to the banking book, irrespective of likely holding period, and funding on the total net requirement in effect provides a line of credit to the trading book.

c.reason: (Polarity flip). C says netting inflates the requirement and overcharges the trading book. Netting across units reduces the measured requirement, and GARP’s criticism is that it undercharges by ignoring desk-level and contingent liquidity risk. C would be correct only if netting increased funding needs.

d.reason: (Scope or condition error). D blames only the threshold length and proposes 360 days. A longer threshold would delay long-term charges further; GARP’s fixes are desk-level funding, line of sight, higher charges on stale positions and limits. D would be correct only if GARP’s criticism were the length of the threshold rather than the roll-to-banking-book trigger and the net funding method, which it is not.

questions.question:
A banking regulator is reviewing the trading book remediation plans of two banks against the better practices drawn from the international LTP survey. Bank X’s trading book is small relative to its main business activities; Bank Y’s trading book is large relative to its main business activities.

I. Bank Y will rely mainly on higher funding charges on its net funding requirement when funding limits are breached, rather than on desk-level charges.

II. Bank X will impose higher funding charges on its net funding requirement when certain funding limits are breached, to curb over-trading behaviour.

III. Both banks will apply higher funding charges to positions more likely to become stale, that is, more likely to roll from the trading book to the banking book.

IV. Both banks will provide funding at the trading book level rather than the desk level, so that netting across desks keeps funding charges low.

Which of the statements are consistent with the better practices?

options.text: I, II and III only
II and IV only
II and III only
II, III and IV only

questions.solution:
Regulator compares trading book remediation plans of a small-book and a large-book bank.

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s Section 15.2.1.5 (“Towards Better LTP Practice”) reports how surveyed banks were repairing trading book funding, and the Conclusion turns this into better practice. The survey’s remediation differs by the relative size of the trading book:

| Bank type | Remediation observed in the survey |
|---|---|
| Trading book small relative to main business | Curb over-trading by imposing higher funding charges on net funding requirements when certain funding limits are breached |
| Trading book large relative to main business | Devote more attention to the funding requirements of individual trading desks and apply charges on a more granular basis |

Across banks, the most notable enhancement was higher funding charges on trading positions more likely to become “stale”, meaning positions with a higher probability of rolling from the trading book to the banking book. Haircuts were also being widened for more severe and prolonged disruptions.

The better-practice list then states: trading book funding policies should exist and, where appropriate, funding should be provided at the most granular level, for example at the trading desk level rather than the trading book level, which requires treasury to have full line of sight to individual business balance sheets. Banks should apply higher funding charges to positions more likely to become stale, or that present significantly greater funding liquidity risk, and should have limits and adequate controls to curb over-trading. The pairing of bank type with remedy is a sibling-swap trap: limit-breach charges belong to the small-book banks; desk-level granularity to the large-book banks.

**Applying it to this question**

I gives Bank Y (large book) the small-book remedy and explicitly rejects desk-level charges: inconsistent. II gives Bank X (small book) the limit-breach charge: consistent. III applies higher charges to stale positions: consistent. IV funds at book level to keep charges low through netting, the reverse of the granularity principle: inconsistent. Answer: II and III only.

**Fragile fact.** Small book: limit-breach charges on net funding; large book: desk-level granular charges; stale positions get higher charges.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Discuss the process of liquidity transfer pricing (LTP) and identify best practices for the governance and implementation of an LTP process.

**GARP:** Chapter 15, Section 15.2.1.5 “Towards Better LTP Practice” and 15.5 Conclusion (“Governing LTP”). **GARP vs Schweser:** none; this detail is GARP-only (Schweser does not distinguish small and large trading books).

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-14 a, where it is Q9 of 13.

a.reason: (Sibling swap). A accepts I, which attaches the small-book remedy to the large-book bank and rejects desk-level charges. A would be correct if statement I described Bank X instead of Bank Y.

b.reason: (Polarity flip). B rejects III (as if stale positions deserved lower charges because the banking book would fund them later) and accepts book-level funding in IV. GARP wants higher charges on likely-stale positions and desk-level funding. B would require both directions reversed.

c.reason: C matches GARP: small-book banks curb over-trading with higher charges when funding limits are breached, and all banks should apply higher charges to positions more likely to become stale, while funding at desk level rather than book level.

d.reason: (Scope or condition error). D accepts IV, which uses trading book level funding and netting to keep charges low. GARP’s better practice is funding at the most granular level, such as the desk. D would be correct only if granularity were “where appropriate” judged inappropriate for both banks, which the stem does not say.

questions.question: A board risk committee member at a US bank (USD reporting) learns that the bank’s trading account holds USD 6 billion of highly rated collateralised debt obligation (CDO) tranches funded with overnight to 90-day liabilities. LTP oversight currently rests with the heads of the business lines, and funding costs are reviewed semi-annually. Which recommendation is most consistent with better LTP practice?

options.text: Business-line heads, who best understand their products, keep oversight of LTP, and monthly meetings with ALCO, senior management and treasury discuss changes in funding costs.
Independent risk and financial control staff oversee LTP with senior management involved, and meetings with ALCO, senior management and treasury on funding costs are held quarterly.
Independent risk and financial control staff oversee LTP with senior management involved, and the CDO funding can stay unchanged because the high rating ensures the tranches sell quickly.
Independent risk and financial control staff oversee LTP with senior management involved, and monthly meetings with ALCO, senior management and treasury discuss changes in funding costs.

questions.solution:
Board recommendation on LTP oversight after finding short-funded CDO holdings.

**Concept and theory**

GARP Section 15.2.1.4 says ineffective oversight of the LTP process contributed to many of the problems found in the survey. Oversight at nearly all participating banks was “poor to nonexistent”, especially by risk and financial control functions. Two consequences follow:

- the accrual of long-term illiquid assets and short-term volatile liabilities created a large and poorly understood maturity mismatch, raising structural liquidity risk;
- the “most striking example”: some banks’ LTP processes let them accumulate significant amounts of highly rated, yet highly illiquid, CDO tranches in their trading accounts, assumed to be safely funded with much shorter-term liabilities, typically overnight to 90-day funds.

A high rating is a credit attribute, not a liquidity attribute; GARP’s phrase “highly rated, yet highly illiquid” is the lesson.

The repair has two dimensions, who and how often:

| Dimension | Better practice |
|---|---|
| Who | Oversight by independent risk and financial control personnel; senior management also involved; meetings include stakeholders such as ALCO, senior management and treasury functions |
| How often | Meetings to discuss changes in funding costs held more regularly, for example monthly instead of quarterly or semi-annually as before the crisis |

GARP also links independence to remuneration: oversight staff paid on the results of the businesses they oversee cannot be relied on to charge those businesses fully.

**Applying it to this question**

The bank has both failures: oversight by business-line heads (not independent) and semi-annual reviews (pre-crisis frequency), plus the CDO symptom. The recommendation must fix both dimensions. D does; A fixes frequency but not independence; B fixes independence but keeps a pre-crisis frequency; C fixes independence but endorses the CDO funding on a false liquidity premise.

Irrelevant input: the USD 6 billion size of the holding does not change the governance recommendation.

**Fragile fact.** Independent risk and financial control staff (not business heads, not treasury alone); monthly, not quarterly or semi-annual.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Discuss the process of liquidity transfer pricing (LTP) and identify best practices for the governance and implementation of an LTP process.

**GARP:** Chapter 15, Sections 15.1.1.1, 15.2.1.4 “Oversight”, 15.2.1.5 and 15.5 Conclusion. **GARP** **vs Schweser:** Schweser states “hold monthly meetings” as a rule; GARP’s better-practice list says meetings should be held “regularly”, citing monthly as the example of the improvement. No conflict in this question because the alternative offered is the pre-crisis quarterly cycle.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-14 a, where it is Q10 of 13.

a.reason: (Role misassignment). A leaves oversight with the business-line heads whose units generate the liquidity risk, which is not independent oversight. A would be correct if oversight passed to independent risk and financial control personnel.

b.reason: (Scope or condition error). B keeps a quarterly cycle, which GARP lists as the pre-crisis frequency being replaced by monthly meetings. B would be correct with “monthly”.

c.reason: (Absolute claim). C says a high rating “ensures” the CDOs can be sold quickly. GARP’s case is that such tranches were highly rated yet highly illiquid and their short-term funding disappeared. C would be correct only if rating guaranteed market liquidity.

d.reason: D matches GARP: oversight by independent risk and financial control personnel with senior management involved, and regular meetings including ALCO, senior management and treasury, held for example monthly rather than quarterly or semi-annually.

questions.question: An internal auditor at an Irish bank (EUR reporting) finds that the bank’s liquidity management information system (LMIS) applies one bank-wide liquidity adjustment and cannot attribute liquidity costs, benefits and risks to individual products. Management argues that a replacement would cost about EUR 40 million and take three years. Which conclusion is most accurate?

options.text: Reported business-unit profits, and the bonuses based on them, may not reflect actual performance, so the upgrade is warranted because the benefits of granular attribution far outweigh its cost.
Because upgrading an LMIS in a large bank is costly and slow, a basic LMIS applying one bank-wide liquidity adjustment is an acceptable long-run substitute for granular attribution.
The LMIS matters mainly for regulatory reporting; the internal pricing of liquidity is set by treasury independently, so the weakness does not affect business-unit performance figures.
The weakness distorts only the charges made to asset-generating units; deposit-raising units are unaffected because their credits are calculated outside the LMIS.

questions.solution:
Audit finding: an LMIS that cannot attribute liquidity costs at a granular level.

**Concept and theory**

GARP Section 15.2.2 explains why the liquidity management information system (LMIS) is part of LTP governance. LMIS are widely used by management as a primary source for measuring and monitoring business performance, and they support strategic liquidity decisions. One application is to support internal pricing mechanisms: in LTP, the LMIS is what lets the costs, benefits and risks of liquidity be attributed to the appropriate business activities.

The survey found that many pre-2009 LMIS were simplistic, inflexible and too basic. Two weaknesses recur:

- some business activities failed to receive a charge for the cost of liquidity or, conversely, a credit for its benefit, so the error ran on both sides of the balance sheet;
- costs, benefits and risks could not be attributed at a sufficiently granular level, causing product mispricing that distorted profit and performance assessments.

The Senior Supervisors Group made similar findings, stressing better-quality and more timely liquidity reporting during a crisis.

The implication GARP draws is about performance and pay: businesses reported performance, and employees claimed bonuses, on a basis that might not reflect actual performance, limiting management’s ability to separate good from poor performers. GARP accepts that upgrading an LMIS in a large bank is “a costly and long-term process”, but says the benefits of charging business activities at a sufficiently granular level will far outweigh the costs and limitations of basic LMIS. Better practice: an LMIS advanced enough to attribute, at a sufficiently granular level, all relevant costs, benefits and risks of liquidity.

**Applying it to this question**

The Irish bank’s LMIS applies one bank-wide adjustment and cannot attribute by product: the textbook granularity failure. Management’s objection is cost and time. GARP concedes both but concludes the upgrade is worth it, and the consequence of not upgrading is distorted performance and bonuses. That is A.

Irrelevant input: the EUR 40 million cost and three-year horizon do not change the conclusion, since GARP accepts the cost is high and still favours upgrading.

**Fragile fact.** Weak LMIS misstate both charges and credits; upgrading is costly and slow, yet GARP says the benefits far outweigh the costs.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Discuss the process of liquidity transfer pricing (LTP) and identify best practices for the governance and implementation of an LTP process.

**GARP:** Chapter 15, Sections 15.1.1.1 and 15.2.2 “Liquidity Management Information Systems (LMIS)”, and 15.5 Conclusion. **GARP vs Schweser:** none.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-14 a, where it is Q11 of 13.

a.reason: A follows GARP: weak LMIS meant reported performance and bonuses might not reflect actual performance, and the benefits of granular attribution “far outweigh” the costs of upgrading.

b.reason: (Polarity flip). B uses GARP’s admission that upgrading is costly to conclude the basic LMIS is acceptable. GARP draws the opposite conclusion. B would be correct only if the costs of the upgrade exceeded its benefits, which GARP rejects.

c.reason: (Sibling swap). C treats the LMIS as a regulatory reporting tool and separates it from internal pricing. GARP says one application of LMIS is to support internal pricing mechanisms and attribute liquidity costs to business activities. C would describe a regulatory reporting system, not the LMIS’s role in LTP.

d.reason: (Scope or condition error). D limits the damage to charges on assets. GARP says some activities failed to receive a charge or, conversely, a credit, so deposit-raising units are equally affected. D would be correct only if the LMIS calculated credits correctly, which the stem does not say.

questions.question:
A board risk committee member at an Australian bank (AUD reporting), who also sits on the remuneration committee, reviews four proposals on remuneration and LTP:

I. Profit pools set as a simple percentage of accrued revenues encourage revenue maximisation rather than risk-adjusted earnings and should be replaced.

II. Paying risk-control staff on the performance of the front-line businesses they oversee weakens their independence and their incentive to attribute full liquidity costs.

III. Consistent with FSB Principle 3, risk-control staff should be paid in line with the profits of the business areas they oversee, to align their interests with those businesses.

IV. Profit pools used to set short-term incentives such as bonuses should be adjusted for the cost of liquidity through the LTP process.

Which proposals are consistent with better LTP practice?

options.text: I and IV only
I, II and IV only
I, II, III and IV
I and II only

questions.solution:
Remuneration committee proposals on profit pools and pay for risk-control staff.

**Concept and theory**

GARP Section 15.2.3 treats remuneration as part of LTP governance because incentive pay decides how people react to the prices LTP sets. Well-designed incentive pay encourages behaviour consistent with the institution’s culture; poorly designed pay can promote perverse behaviour such as excessive risk-taking. The FSB (2009) named poor remuneration as one contributor to the GFC, and the SSG found pay largely insensitive to the risks taken and to the costs of long-term funding commitments needed to hold illiquid assets.

Two remuneration failures are specific to LTP:

| Failure | Mechanism and fix |
|---|---|
| Profit pools | Derived from a simple percentage of accrued revenues, with no regard to the cost of liquidity (or capital); this emphasised revenue maximisation over risk-adjusted earnings. Fix: adjust profit pools for the cost of liquidity through LTP |
| Oversight staff pay | Many oversight staff were paid on the performance of the front-line businesses they oversaw; charging full liquidity costs would cut their own pay, impairing independence. Fix: FSB Principle 3 |

FSB Principle 3 states that staff engaged in financial and risk control should be compensated in a manner that is independent of the business areas they oversee and commensurate with their key role. GARP says many larger banks are redesigning pay for risk control positions along these lines, which should promote a more appropriate attribution of liquidity costs and restore independence. Banks are also developing LTP so that profit and performance measures include the relevant costs of liquidity.

**Applying it to this question**

I describes the profit-pool failure correctly. II describes the oversight-pay failure and its effect on independence correctly. III inverts FSB Principle 3: pay should be independent of, not aligned with, the overseen businesses. IV is GARP’s fix for profit pools. Consistent: I, II and IV.

**Fragile fact.** FSB Principle 3: control staff pay is independent of the businesses they oversee; profit pools are adjusted for liquidity costs via LTP.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Discuss the process of liquidity transfer pricing (LTP) and identify best practices for the governance and implementation of an LTP process.

**GARP:** Chapter 15, Sections 15.1.1.2 and 15.2.3 “Remuneration Practices”, and 15.5 Conclusion. **GARP vs Schweser:** none; Schweser condenses this to “employee bonuses and remuneration practices should factor in the cost of liquidity” and omits FSB Principle 3 (GARP-only detail).

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-14 a, where it is Q12 of 13.

a.reason: (Scope or condition error). A omits II, missing GARP’s second remuneration failure, the dependence of oversight staff pay on front-line results. A would be correct only if II had misstated the effect, for example by saying such pay strengthened independence.

b.reason: B matches GARP: revenue-based profit pools encouraged revenue maximisation, oversight-staff pay tied to front-line results impaired independence, and profit pools should be adjusted for the cost of liquidity through LTP.

c.reason: (Polarity flip). C accepts III, which reverses FSB Principle 3. Risk-control staff should be compensated independently of the business areas they oversee. C would be correct only if III read “independent of” instead of “in line with”.

d.reason: (Scope or condition error). D omits IV, the fix GARP explicitly recommends. Rejecting IV leaves the diagnosis without the cure. D would be correct only if IV had proposed adjusting pools by something other than the cost of liquidity.

questions.question:
A treasury analyst at a Singapore bank (SGD reporting) is recomputing the corporate lending unit’s bonus pool for the year after the bank adopted better LTP practice. The pool is 12% of the unit’s profit measure. Under the old practice the profit measure was accrued revenues; under the new practice it must be adjusted for the cost of liquidity through the LTP process. The unit has 140 staff.

| Item | SGD million |
|---|---|
| Accrued revenues of the corporate lending unit | 80.0 |
| LTP charge for funds used by the unit’s loans | 9.0 |
| LTP charge for the unit’s contingent commitments (undrawn credit lines) | 2.5 |
| LTP credit for deposits raised by the retail deposit unit | 4.0 |

What is the corporate lending unit’s bonus pool under the new practice?

options.text: SGD 9.60 million
SGD 8.52 million
SGD 8.22 million
SGD 8.70 million

questions.solution:
Corporate lending unit’s bonus pool after adjusting for LTP charges (SGD).

**Concept and theory**

Before the GFC, profit pools used to set short-term incentives were derived from a simple percentage of accrued revenues, with no regard to the cost of liquidity taken to generate them (GARP Sections 15.1.1.2 and 15.2.3). GARP’s better practice is that profit pools “should be adjusted for the cost of liquidity through the LTP process”. Which amounts enter that adjustment follows from the LTP process in Figure 15.1: a fund-using unit incurs charges based on the commitment of funds it requires, and additional charges apply to its contingent commitments such as lines of credit. Credits for the benefit of liquidity go to the unit that provides funds, such as a deposit-raising unit, not to the lending unit. GARP also states that charges and credits should not be borne by central treasury but attributed, at a sufficiently granular level, to the business activities that use or provide liquidity.

Writing k for the pool rate, R for the unit’s accrued revenues, $\text{C}_{\text{funds}}$ for the LTP charge for funds used and $\text{C}_{\text{cont}}$ for the LTP charge on contingent commitments, the two regimes are:

$\text{Pool}_{\text{old}} = \text{k} \times$ R

$\text{Pool}_{\text{new}} = \text{k} \times(\text{R} - \text{C}_{\text{funds}} - \text{C}_{\text{cont}})$

The arithmetic is trivial; the interpretation is the test. Leaving out the contingent charge repeats the pre-GFC habit of not charging undrawn commitments; adding another unit’s deposit credit misassigns the actor.

**Applying it to this question**

Total LTP charges = 9.0 + 2.5 = 11.5 (SGD million)

Adjusted profit measure = 80.0 − 11.5 = 68.5 (SGD million)

$\text{Pool}_{\text{new}} =$ 0.12 × 68.5 = 8.22 (SGD million)

$\text{Pool}_{\text{old}} =$ 0.12 × 80.0 = 9.60 (SGD million)

The pool falls by 0.12 × 11.5 = 1.38 (SGD million): the unit’s bonus now reflects the liquidity it consumes and the contingent liquidity it commits the bank to. Irrelevant inputs: the SGD 4.0 million credit belongs to the retail deposit unit (a provider of funds), and the headcount of 140 does not enter the pool.

**Fragile fact.** Fund users bear charges for funds used and contingent commitments; provider credits belong to the unit that raised the funds.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Discuss the process of liquidity transfer pricing (LTP) and identify best practices for the governance and implementation of an LTP process.

**GARP:** Chapter 15, Sections 15.1 (Figure 15.1), 15.2.3 “Remuneration Practices” and 15.5 Conclusion. **GARP vs Schweser:** none. Note: GARP gives no explicit profit-pool formula; the pool definition (rate times the liquidity-adjusted profit measure) is set in the stem and applies GARP’s stated principle.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-14 a, where it is Q13 of 13.

a.reason: (Intermediate result). SGD 9.60 million = 0.12 × 80.0 is the old, unadjusted pool: the starting point of the calculation, and exactly the revenue-based profit pool GARP criticises. It would be correct only if the stem asked for the pool under the old practice.

b.reason: (Dropped term). SGD 8.52 million = 0.12 × (80.0 − 9.0) omits the SGD 2.5 million contingent-commitment charge, repeating the error of not charging undrawn lines. It would be correct only if the unit had no contingent commitments.

c.reason: C (SGD 8.22 million) applies both LTP charges that Figure 15.1 assigns to a fund-using unit, and excludes the provider credit, consistent with GARP’s call to adjust profit pools for the cost of liquidity.

d.reason: (Role misassignment). SGD 8.70 million = 0.12 × (80.0 − 11.5 + 4.0) credits the lending unit with the deposit unit’s liquidity credit. Credits go to the provider of funds. It would be correct only if the SGD 4.0 million were a credit for deposits raised by the corporate lending unit itself.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Compare the various approaches to liquidity transfer pricing (zero cost, average cost, and matchedmaturity marginal cost).
questions.reading: LTR-14: Liquidity Transfer Pricing: A Guide to Better Practice
questions.topic: Liquidity Transfer Pricing: A Guide to Better Practice
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-14 c Q1
questions.question: A member of the board risk committee at a Canadian bank is reading an internal postmortem of the bank’s pre-crisis transfer pricing. Before the crisis, lending units were charged the swap rate matching each loan’s maturity and deposit-gathering units were credited the swap rate matching each deposit’s maturity, with no spread added on either side. Interest rate risk was fully hedged through the swap curve. Which of the following statements about this approach is most accurate?

options.text: The rate charged to users of funds is the swap rate plus a single average liquidity spread that is the same for every maturity.
A zero spread above the swap curve implies a zero charge for funding liquidity, which exacerbated maturity transformation to the largest degree possible.
Supervisors may tolerate the approach in calm markets, since a one-year LIBOR/swap spread near 0.5 bp shows that funding liquidity risk is then zero.
Its main weakness is that it lags changes in the bank’s actual market cost of funds, because its charges are built from historical average funding costs.

questions.solution:
Canadian bank: pre-crisis transfer pricing at the swap rate with no liquidity spread.

**Concept and theory**

Liquidity transfer pricing (LTP) attributes the costs, benefits and risks of liquidity to business units: users of funds (assets, loans) are charged for the liquidity they consume and providers of funds (liabilities, deposits) are credited for the liquidity they supply. Every approach in the 2009 survey of 38 banks used the swap curve as the reference rate for pricing interest rate risk; they differ only in what, if anything, is added on top for liquidity.

| Approach | Spread over swap curve | Main effect |
|---|---|---|
| Zero cost | None | Liquidity treated as free; worst practice |
| Average cost (pooled or separate) | One average spread, same for all maturities | Long assets undercharged, long liabilities under-credited; lags market |
| Matched-maturity marginal cost | Term liquidity premium for the maturity | Best practice; uses actual market cost of funds |

GARP calls the zero cost approach the most striking and worst practice found in the survey. Banks came to view funding liquidity as essentially free and funding liquidity risk as essentially zero, so some assets received no charge for using funding liquidity and some liabilities no credit for providing it. If interest rate risk is properly handled by the swap curve, a zero spread above the curve means a zero charge for liquidity. GARP’s conclusion is that this "exacerbated maturity transformation to the largest degree possible": banks hoarded long-term, highly illiquid assets and had very few long-term stable liabilities to meet funding demands as they fell due. Why did banks do this? Funding conditions before the crisis were ideal: in June 2005 the one-year LIBOR/swap spread was only 0.5 bp, so banks read spreads as pure credit risk adjustments and believed funding would always be available cheaply. GARP’s summary is blunt: failing to price liquidity is unacceptably poor practice and supervisors should not tolerate it.

**Applying it to this question**

The stem describes charges and credits at the swap rate of matching maturity with nothing added. Matching the swap maturity handles only interest rate risk; the liquidity component is zero for every maturity. That is the zero cost approach, and the hedged interest rate risk detail is the condition under which GARP says a zero spread equals a zero liquidity charge. The question then asks which statement about it is accurate, so each option must be checked against GARP’s description of this approach rather than of its neighbours.

**Fragile fact.** Ranking by encouragement of maturity transformation: zero cost is the worst (largest), average cost next, matched-maturity marginal cost the least; a zero spread over swaps means zero liquidity charge, not zero rate.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 79.c, verbatim):** Compare the various approaches to liquidity transfer pricing (zero cost, average cost, and matched-maturity marginal cost).

**GARP:** Chapter 15, Section 15.3.3 “Zero Cost of Funds Approach: Liquidity as a Free Good” and 15.3.3.1; Section 15.3.7 “Summary”. **GARP vs Schweser:** none in substance. Schweser dates the 0.5 bp spread as “2005 through the first quarter of 2007” and adds that it exceeded 120 bps in 2008; GARP’s text cites June 2005 (the 120 bps figure appears only on GARP’s chart axis).

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-14 c, where it is Q1 of 13.

a.reason: (Sibling swap). A single average spread over the swap rate for every maturity is the pooled average cost of funds approach. Under the zero cost approach there is no spread at all. The option would be right if the stem had described a bank adding one fixed spread for all maturities.

b.reason: GARP states that a zero spread above the swap curve implies a zero charge for funding liquidity, and that this exacerbated maturity transformation to the largest degree possible, leading to hoarding of long-term illiquid assets. Option B restates both points.

c.reason: (Scope or condition error). The 0.5 bp spread of June 2005 is GARP’s explanation of why banks wrongly viewed liquidity as free, not a condition under which the practice is acceptable. GARP says supervisors should not tolerate failing to price liquidity. The statement would be a fair description only of the pre-crisis belief, not of supervisory policy.

d.reason: (Sibling swap). Lagging the actual market cost of funds because rates are historical averages is the second defect of the average cost approach. The zero cost approach uses no average at all; its defect is that it prices liquidity at zero. Correct if the stem described an average cost approach.
