questions.question: A senior risk analyst at a Brazilian bank (BRL reporting) is summarising for the risk committee the core mechanism that turned European banks’ chronic US dollar funding needs into an acute shortage. Which of the following combinations best describes that mechanism?

options.text: Effective holding period of dollar assets lengthened; effective maturity of dollar funding shortened; maturity mismatch rose endogenously and was difficult to hedge ex ante.
Effective holding period of dollar assets lengthened; effective maturity of dollar funding shortened; maturity mismatch rose but could have been fully hedged ex ante with FX swaps.
Effective holding period of dollar assets unchanged; effective maturity of dollar funding shortened; maturity mismatch rose only because suppliers of funds withdrew.
Effective holding period of dollar assets shortened; effective maturity of dollar funding shortened; maturity mismatch unchanged because both sides moved together.

questions.solution:
Senior risk analyst states the core mechanism that turned chronic dollar needs into an acute shortage.

**Concept and theory**

The funding gap is the amount of dollars invested in longer-horizon assets that is not supported by longer-term dollar liabilities, and so must be rolled over before the assets mature. Its size depends on two effective maturities:

$$\text{Rollover need} \uparrow \text{ when } \underbrace{\text{T}_{\text{A}}}_{\text{effective holding period of assets}} \uparrow \text{ and/or } \underbrace{\text{T}_{\text{L}}}_{\text{effective maturity of funding}} \downarrow.$$

In the crisis both moved the wrong way at once:

- $\text{T}_{\text{A}}$ lengthened: assets such as structured products could not be sold in illiquid markets, vehicles came back and credit lines were drawn, so assets intended to be held for a while had to be held longer.
- $\text{T}_{\text{L}}$ shortened: suppliers of funds withdrew, so banks relying on wholesale funding and short-term FX swaps had to roll over more often, which became difficult to maintain.

GARP calls this an endogenous rise in maturity mismatch: it was produced by the crisis itself, not chosen by the banks. Because it arises from market conditions that change both sides at once, it was “difficult to hedge ex ante”. A bank could hedge its currency exposure with swaps, but it could not lock in the future liquidity of its assets or the future willingness of funders to roll. This endogenous rise in maturity mismatch, GARP says, generated the global US dollar shortage.

**Applying it to this question**

The matrix asks for three items. The source gives: holding period lengthened, funding maturity shortened, mismatch rose endogenously and was difficult to hedge ex ante. Only A has all three.

**Fragile fact.** Assets longer, funding shorter, at the same time, and endogenously: memorise the two directions.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Identify the causes of the U.S. dollar shortage during the Great Financial Crisis. **GARP:** Chapter 16, Section 16.1 Introduction and Section 16.4 The US Dollar Shortage. **GARP vs Schweser:** none; Schweser omits “difficult to hedge ex ante”.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-15 a, where it is Q6 of 12.

a.reason: A restates GARP Section 16.4: the effective holding period of assets lengthened just as the maturity of funding shortened, and this endogenous rise in maturity mismatch, difficult to hedge ex ante, generated the shortage.

b.reason: (Absolute-claim trap). The first two cells are right, but “could have been fully hedged ex ante with FX swaps” contradicts the source. FX swaps were themselves the short-term funding that had to be rolled. It would be correct only if the risk were currency risk rather than funding risk.

c.reason: (Scope or condition error (dropped term)). It drops the asset side: the holding period did lengthen because assets could not be sold. It would describe a pure funding run on a bank whose assets remained fully liquid.

d.reason: (Polarity flip). It reverses the asset side to “shortened”, implying banks could liquidate assets, which contradicts the hampered deleveraging. It would fit a bank able to sell assets as fast as funding ran off.

questions.question:
A regulator at a US supervisory agency (USD reporting) is reviewing the US branch of a large European bank over the year before the failure of Lehman Brothers. The branch has access to Federal Reserve facilities.

| Item (USD bn) | Start of period | End of period |
|---|---|---|
| Local US dollar liabilities, incl. Fed facility borrowing | 318 | 359 |
| Local US dollar claims on US residents | 352 | 353 |
| Parent group’s euro retail deposits (EUR bn) | 210 | 214 |

Which of the following best explains the pattern, consistent with the reading?

options.text: The branch used the additional local US dollar funding mainly to expand its lending to US households and firms.
The branch raised local US dollar liabilities and channelled the funds to its head office via inter-office transfers to replace lost market funding.
The head office transferred US dollars to the branch to cover withdrawals by US depositors, so local liabilities rose to match.
The branch obtained its additional dollars mainly through the Fed swap lines with the ECB and auctioned them to related offices.

questions.solution:
Regulator interprets the rise in a European bank’s US branch liabilities before Lehman.

**Concept and theory**

Before turning to central bank swap lines, banks reacted to the dollar shortage with their own internal tools. GARP describes what European banks did prior to the Lehman collapse: they tapped funds in the United States. Their US offices’ local US dollar liabilities, which included borrowing from Federal Reserve facilities, grew by USD 329 billion (13%) while their local assets remained largely unchanged. Banks with an established US presence could borrow against collateral from the Fed facilities open to depository institutions, and some had more access as primary dealers.

If liabilities rise and local assets do not, the extra dollars must go somewhere. GARP shows they were channelled out of the United States through inter-office transfers to related offices, presumably to help head offices replace dollar funding previously obtained from the market. This is an internal capital market: the group uses its US branch as a dollar-raising arm for the whole consolidated balance sheet.

| Channel | Who can use it |
|---|---|
| Fed facilities via US offices (this question) | Banks with US offices and eligible collateral, before and around Lehman |
| Fed swap lines via home central banks (LO 80.c) | Any bank in the home jurisdiction, through local dollar auctions, even without US subsidiaries or collateral |

**Applying it to this question**

Working from the table:

∆Local liabilities = 359 − 318 = USD 41 bn (+12.9%)

∆Local claims on US residents = 353 − 352 = USD 1 bn (+0.3%)

Liabilities rose by about 13%, while local lending was flat, so the funds were not lent locally. They were sent to related offices. The parent’s euro retail deposits are irrelevant: they concern euro funding at home, not the branch’s dollar flows.

**Fragile fact.** Direction: dollars raised in the US were sent out to head offices; the local balance sheet did not grow on the asset side.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Identify the causes of the U.S. dollar shortage during the Great Financial Crisis. **GARP:** Chapter 16, Section 16.4 The US Dollar Shortage (Figure 16.6 discussion) and footnote 28. **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser dates the Lehman collapse to “the second quarter of 2008” and says the pattern “created a U.S. dollar funding gap”. GARP places Lehman’s failure in September 2008 (the data run up to end-Q2 2008) and presents the pattern as a response to the shortage. GARP followed. The GARP quarter labels here are OCR-garbled, so no quarter is tested.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-15 a, where it is Q7 of 12.

a.reason: (Polarity flip). Local claims on US residents were flat (+USD 1 billion), so the money did not go into US lending. It would be correct if local claims had risen by about USD 41 billion.

b.reason: B matches GARP Section 16.4: local dollar liabilities, including Fed borrowing, grew while local assets were unchanged, allowing European banks to channel funds out of the United States via inter-office transfers to replace market funding.

c.reason: (Polarity flip (direction of transfer)). Funds flowed from the US office to the head office, not the reverse, and nothing in the data shows US deposit withdrawals. It would fit a branch facing a local deposit run.

d.reason: (Sibling swap). Swap lines are the LO 80.c policy response: the Fed lends to the ECB, which auctions dollars in the euro area. A US branch borrows directly from Fed facilities. It would be correct for a euro area bank without a US office in late 2008.

questions.question:
A treasurer at a European banking group (EUR reporting, USD figures shown) is estimating the group’s US dollar funding gap at end-Q1 2009. The group measures the gap by its net US dollar claims on non-banks (the lower-bound estimate) and has gathered the following data:

| Item | USD bn |
|---|---|
| Net US dollar claims on non-banks, mid-2007 | 96 |
| Net US dollar claims on non-banks, end-Q1 2009 (as reported) | 51 |
| Cumulative asset writedowns, mid-2007 to end-Q1 2009, all assets | 38 |
| of which on US dollar non-bank assets | 30 |
| US dollars obtained at ECB dollar auctions, end-Q1 2009 | 12 |

Assuming the group did not close out, but rolled over, the funding positions that supported the written-down assets, what is the best estimate of its US dollar funding gap at end-Q1 2009?

options.text: USD 21 billion
USD 51 billion
USD 81 billion
USD 89 billion

questions.solution:
Treasurer estimates the end-Q1 2009 dollar funding gap when funding behind written-down assets was rolled over.

**Concept and theory**

During the crisis the measured lower-bound gap (net dollar claims on non-banks) fell by nearly 50%. GARP warns that this decline is hard to interpret because writedowns reduce the reported stock of dollar claims, and so reduce net claims on non-banks, even though the funding that supported those assets may still be outstanding.

GARP’s two cases:

| Bank behaviour | Effect on funding | Gap estimate |
|---|---|---|
| Closed out the funding (e.g. bought dollars spot) | Funding gone with the asset value | Observed estimate is correct |
| Rolled the funding over | Funding still needs rollover | Observed estimate understates the true gap by the writedowns |

Formula under the roll-over assumption:

$\text{G}^{\text{true}} = \text{G}^{\text{obs}} + \text{W}_{\text{USD,NB}}$,

where $\text{G}^{\text{obs}}$ is the reported net dollar claim on non-banks and $\text{W}_{\text{USD,NB}}$ is the writedowns on dollar non-bank assets. In GARP’s aggregate figures, the observed USD 583 billion becomes about USD 880 billion once the bulk of European banks’ writedowns is assumed to relate to dollar non-bank assets.

**Applying it to this question**

$\text{G}^{\text{obs}} =$ USD 51 bn

$\text{W}_{\text{USD,NB}} =$ USD 30 bn

$\text{G}^{\text{true}} =$ 51 + 30 = USD 81 bn

Irrelevant inputs: the mid-2007 gap of USD 96 billion only shows the misleading measured decline, (96 − 51)/96 = 46.9%, close to GARP’s “nearly 50%”. The ECB auction dollars are policy support (LO 80.c), not part of net claims on non-banks. Total writedowns of USD 38 billion include non-dollar assets, which do not affect the dollar gap.

The group still needed to roll over about USD 81 billion of dollar funding, far more than the reported figure suggests.

**Fragile fact.** Rolled over means understated: add back the dollar non-bank writedowns, not total writedowns.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Identify the causes of the U.S. dollar shortage during the Great Financial Crisis. **GARP:** Chapter 16, Section 16.4 The US Dollar Shortage (paragraphs on the decline in the lower-bound estimate). **GARP vs Schweser:** none of substance; Schweser places this under LO 80.a. Caution: Schweser later reuses USD 583 billion as the swap-line peak (a coincidence of numbers in GARP); not tested here.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-15 a, where it is Q8 of 12.

a.reason: (Sign error). USD 21 billion = 51 − 30 subtracts the writedowns instead of adding them. It would require that the observed measure overstated the gap.

b.reason: (Wrong condition (intermediate result)). USD 51 billion is the observed figure, which is correct only if the group closed out the funding behind the written-down assets. The stem assumes roll-over.

c.reason: C applies GARP’s rule: if funding positions are rolled over, the observed measure underestimates the true gap by the writedowns on the dollar non-bank assets.

d.reason: (Wrong input twin). USD 89 billion = 51 + 38 adds total writedowns, including those on non-dollar assets. It would be correct only if all writedowns were on dollar non-bank assets.

questions.question: A portfolio manager at a Chinese asset manager (CNY reporting) holds senior unsecured paper of several European banks and is assessing which suppliers of US dollar funding to those banks proved unstable during the crisis. Which of the following statements about official monetary authorities’ US dollar placements is most accurate?

options.text: A portion of the reserves central banks had placed with commercial banks was withdrawn less abruptly than money fund funding, some emerging market authorities withdrawing to support their own banks.
A portion of the reserves central banks had placed with commercial banks was withdrawn by advanced-economy authorities only, while emerging market authorities kept their placements in place.
Central bank deposits with commercial banks rose during the crisis as reserve managers sought the safety of large banks, partly offsetting the withdrawal of money fund funding.
The Federal Reserve recalled US dollar deposits it had placed with foreign commercial banks in order to finance its swap lines with other central banks.

questions.solution:
Portfolio manager identifies how central banks’ dollar reserve placements behaved during the crisis.

**Concept and theory**

Central banks hold large US dollar foreign exchange reserves, and part of those reserves had been placed as deposits with commercial banks. For the receiving banks these deposits were a non-bank source of dollar funding. GARP explains that European banks’ difficulties were compounded by instability in non-bank funding, and that, “less abruptly” than the money fund withdrawal, a portion of these central bank placements was withdrawn during the crisis.

Evidence and motive:

- Data from 63 monetary authorities reporting to the IMF show central bank deposits with commercial banks dropped by USD 257 billion between mid-2007 and end-2008.
- Some emerging market monetary authorities reportedly withdrew placements in support of their own banking systems, which needed dollars.

This shows how a dollar shortage spreads: a central bank whose own banks are short of dollars draws down the reserves it keeps with foreign banks. Central banks cannot create dollars (only the Fed can), so their ability to help their banks is limited to the FX reserves they hold. Pulling deposits from commercial banks abroad shifts the shortage onto those banks.

Compare speeds: money funds (Q4) withdrew abruptly after Lehman; central bank placements were withdrawn gradually over the crisis.

**Applying it to this question**

The deciding facts are speed (less abrupt), extent (a portion) and actor and motive (including emerging market authorities supporting their own banks). Only A has all three.

**Fragile fact.** Actor: reserve-holding (including emerging market) central banks; speed: less abrupt than money funds; direction: deposits fell.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Identify the causes of the U.S. dollar shortage during the Great Financial Crisis. **GARP:** Chapter 16, Section 16.4 The US Dollar Shortage and footnote 23. **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser says central banks “withdrew a sizable portion of their U.S. dollar foreign exchange reserves”, omitting that these were placements with commercial banks and that the withdrawal was less abrupt. GARP followed.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-15 a, where it is Q9 of 12.

a.reason: A paraphrases GARP Section 16.4: a portion of the reserves central banks had placed with commercial banks was withdrawn less abruptly, some emerging market authorities withdrawing in support of their own banking systems.

b.reason: (Scope or condition error). It removes the emerging market authorities that GARP names. It would be correct only if GARP had attributed the withdrawals to advanced-economy central banks alone.

c.reason: (Polarity flip). Central bank deposits with commercial banks fell by USD 257 billion, not rose. It would describe a flight-to-quality inflow, which the source does not report.

d.reason: (Role misassignment). The withdrawing actors were reserve-holding central banks, not the Fed. The Fed supplied dollars through swap lines (LO 80.c); it did not fund them by recalling deposits.

questions.question:
A junior risk analyst at a London-based bank (GBP reporting) is preparing a chart of the bank’s gross US dollar claims for a report on the dollar shortage. The bank, like its peers, did not show signs of deleveraging until the fourth quarter of 2008.

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Gross US dollar claims, mid-2007 (USD bn) | 410 |
| Gross US dollar claims, end-Q3 2008, as reported (USD bn) | 422 |
| Writedowns on US dollar assets over the period (USD bn) | 14 |
| Growth in sterling retail deposits over the period (GBP bn) | 6 |

Which of the following best states the change in the bank’s US dollar claims before writedowns, and its explanation?

options.text: An increase of USD 12 billion; deleveraging was hampered as vehicles returned to the balance sheet, commitments were drawn and structured products were hard to sell.
A decrease of USD 2 billion; the bank had begun to deleverage by selling structured products as soon as the funding pressure began.
An increase of USD 26 billion; deleveraging was hampered as vehicles returned to the balance sheet, commitments were drawn and structured products were hard to sell.
An increase of USD 26 billion; the bank chose to expand its dollar lending because dollar funding remained plentiful until the fourth quarter of 2008.

questions.solution:
Junior analyst computes the pre-writedown change in gross dollar claims and explains it.

**Concept and theory**

If banks are short of dollar funding, one would expect them to shed dollar assets. GARP shows the opposite in the first phase of the crisis: the estimated stock of European banks’ US dollar claims actually rose slightly (by USD 248 billion, about 3%), despite writedowns of USD 280 billion by end-Q3 2008. Signs of deleveraging emerged only in Q4 2008.

Writedowns lower the reported stock of claims without any sale. So the underlying change in claims, before writedowns, is

$$\Delta\text{C}^{\text{pre-WD}} = \underbrace{(\text{C}_{1} - \text{C}_{0})}_{\text{reported change}} + \underbrace{\text{W}}_{\text{writedowns}}.$$

A reported rise despite writedowns means that underlying holdings grew by more than the reported figure. GARP’s explanation is not a strategic choice to expand. Deleveraging was hampered: structured finance products could not be sold into illiquid markets without large losses, off-balance sheet vehicles were brought back onto balance sheets, and prearranged credit commitments were drawn. Assets therefore stayed on the books longer than intended, and the dollar funding need persisted while funding markets were already stressed (from August 2007).

**Applying it to this question**

$\text{C}_{1} - \text{C}_{0} =$ 422 − 410 = USD 12 bn (+2.9%)

W = USD 14 bn

$\Delta\text{C}^{\text{pre-WD}} =$ 12 + 14 = USD 26 bn (+6.3%)

The growth in sterling retail deposits is irrelevant: it concerns domestic currency funding, not dollar claims. Before writedowns the bank’s dollar claims rose by USD 26 billion because it could not shed them.

**Fragile fact.** Dollar claims rose before they fell: deleveraging began only in Q4 2008, and writedowns hid part of the rise.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Identify the causes of the U.S. dollar shortage during the Great Financial Crisis. **GARP:** Chapter 16, Section 16.4 The US Dollar Shortage, footnotes 24 to 26. **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser omits the rise in claims and the Q4 2008 timing; content from GARP. Some GARP quarter labels are OCR-garbled; the Q4 2008 deleveraging statement is unambiguous.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-15 a, where it is Q10 of 12.

a.reason: (Intermediate result). USD 12 billion is the reported change, which ignores that writedowns had already reduced the stock. It would be correct only if there were no writedowns.

b.reason: (Sign error). 12 − 14 = −2 subtracts the writedowns, and the explanation follows from that error. GARP says deleveraging appeared only in Q4 2008.

c.reason: C has the correct pre-writedown figure and GARP’s explanation: hampered deleveraging through vehicles, drawn commitments and illiquid structured products.

d.reason: (Scope or condition error). The number is right but the explanation is wrong: dollar funding was not plentiful; interbank and swap funding were stressed from August 2007. It would fit a bank expanding in a calm market.

questions.question:
The chief credit officer of an Irish bank (EUR reporting) notes that the lower-bound estimate of European banks’ US dollar funding gap fell by nearly 50% between the onset of the crisis and end-Q1 2009, and asks whether this shows the shortage had largely resolved itself. A risk analyst prepares four statements:

I. Writedowns reduce the reported stock of US dollar claims and hence net claims on non-banks, which lowers the estimated gap.

II. Because net FX swap positions are backed out as a residual, any asset writedown automatically shows up as a lower estimated net FX swap position.

III. If banks closed out the funding behind the written-down assets, for example by buying US dollars in the spot market, the observed estimate is accurate.

IV. If banks instead rolled over that funding, the observed estimate overstates the true funding gap by the amount of the writedowns.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.text: I and III only
I, II and III only
II and IV only
I, II, III and IV

questions.solution:
Chief credit officer asks whether the near 50% fall in the lower-bound gap means the shortage resolved itself.

**Concept and theory**

The lower-bound funding gap is estimated as net dollar claims on non-banks. In principle one could measure the gap directly from the funding side, as the sum of net interbank funding, net FX swap positions and net liabilities to monetary authorities. But FX swaps are off-balance sheet and unobserved, so GARP backs out the net FX swap position as a residual: whatever is needed to equate gross dollar assets and liabilities.

That method has a consequence. When an asset is written down:

1. the reported stock of dollar claims falls, so net claims on non-banks (the gap estimate) fall;
2. the residual net FX swap position falls automatically, even if no swap was unwound.

Whether the lower estimate is right depends on what banks actually did with the funding behind the written-down assets:

- closed out (for example by buying dollars spot): the observed estimate is correct;
- rolled over: the observed estimate underestimates the true gap by the amount of the writedowns.

GARP’s numbers: about USD 583 billion if positions were closed, about USD 880 billion if rolled over, still below the pre-crisis peak. So the measured fall overstates the improvement, and the shortage was not resolving itself.

**Applying it to this question**

I is true (writedowns cut net claims on non-banks). II is true (residual FX swaps absorb writedowns). III is true (close-out makes the observed estimate correct). IV is false: roll-over makes the observed estimate understate the gap, not overstate it. Correct set: I, II and III.

**Fragile fact.** Rolled over means the observed gap is too small (understated), not too large.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Identify the causes of the U.S. dollar shortage during the Great Financial Crisis. **GARP:** Chapter 16, Section 16.4 The US Dollar Shortage and footnote 30; equation (16.2) in Section 16.2. **GARP vs Schweser:** none; Schweser omits the residual FX swap mechanism (GARP-only detail).

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-15 a, where it is Q11 of 12.

a.reason: (Scope or condition error (incomplete set)). It omits II, the mechanism by which writedowns pass automatically into the estimated FX swap positions. It would be correct only if FX swaps were observed directly.

b.reason: B is the only option containing I, II and III and excluding IV, as in GARP Section 16.4.

c.reason: (Polarity flip (accepts IV)). It accepts IV’s “overstates” and drops the true statements I and III. It would be correct only if writedowns raised the reported claims.

d.reason: (Polarity flip (accepts IV)). It accepts all four, including the reversed direction in IV. With “understates” in IV, D would be correct.

questions.question: A member of the risk committee of a Canadian pension fund (CAD reporting) asks a consultant how the 2007 to 2009 US dollar shortage differed from earlier international funding episodes cited in the reading. Which of the following best identifies what, according to the reading, pushed the system to the brink in this crisis?

options.text: Japanese banks paying a premium for dollar funding after financing their global expansion in the eurodollar and euroyen markets.
The lengthening maturity of Latin American dollar debt, which raised concerns about a maturity mismatch on European banks’ balance sheets.
Cross-currency funding per se, since any bank that funds in one currency and invests in another must eventually face a dollar shortage.
Too many large banks employing funding strategies in the same direction, the funding equivalent of a crowded trade, which seized up the global interbank and FX swap structure.

questions.solution:
Risk committee member asks what distinguished the 2007 to 2009 shortage from earlier episodes and pushed the system to the brink.

**Concept and theory**

GARP places the GFC dollar shortage alongside earlier international funding episodes:

| Episode | Lesson in the reading |
|---|---|
| Early 1980s Latin American dollar debt | Lengthening maturity raised concerns about maturity mismatch on European banks’ balance sheets |
| 1990s “Japan premium” | Japanese banks that financed global expansion in eurodollar and euroyen markets paid a funding premium |
| Emerging market bank runs | Depositors convert to foreign currency until FX reserves are exhausted |
| 2007 to 2009 | Exposures to other industrialised countries deteriorated and the global interbank and FX swap funding structure seized up |

The concluding remarks make a precise point about the cause. Cross-currency funding was central to the build-up, but GARP says what pushed the system to the brink was not cross-currency funding per se. It was too many large banks using funding strategies in the same direction: the funding equivalent of a “crowded trade”. Each bank’s strategy might look manageable alone; together they created a one-way demand for short-term dollars through interbank and FX swap markets. When credit risk compromised short-term funding, the chronic dollar needs became acute, especially after Lehman.

A further lesson is that such vulnerabilities can only be identified at the aggregate level, by tracking cross-currency funding and reliance on short-term interbank and FX swap positions across consolidated balance sheets.

**Applying it to this question**

The stem asks what pushed this system to the brink. Options A and B are true lessons of other episodes; C names the build-up channel but in the form GARP rejects. D states GARP’s conclusion.

**Fragile fact.** Not cross-currency funding per se, but everyone doing it in the same direction (the crowded trade).

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** Identify the causes of the U.S. dollar shortage during the Great Financial Crisis. **GARP:** Chapter 16, Section 16.1 Introduction (earlier episodes) and Section 16.6 Concluding Remarks. **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser does not discuss the crowded trade or earlier episodes; GARP-only content within the LO’s causes.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-15 a, where it is Q12 of 12.

a.reason: (Sibling swap (other case)). This is the 1990s Japan premium, a true lesson of an earlier episode. It would be correct if the stem asked about Japanese banks in the 1990s.

b.reason: (Sibling swap (other case)). This is the early 1980s Latin American episode. It would be correct if the stem asked about that maturity mismatch.

c.reason: (Absolute-claim trap). GARP explicitly says the trigger was not cross-currency funding per se; “must eventually face” turns a channel into a certainty. It would be closer if it said cross-currency funding raised reliance on short-term FX swaps.

d.reason: D paraphrases GARP Section 16.6: the cause was not cross-currency funding per se but too many large banks employing funding strategies in the same direction, a “crowded trade”, with the global interbank and FX swap funding structure seizing up.

questions.question:
A treasury analyst at a Japanese bank is presenting to newly hired analysts. The bank wants to acquire USD 2 billion of US corporate loans and is comparing three ways of financing them: (1) borrow JPY and convert it in a straight FX spot transaction; (2) use FX swaps to convert JPY liabilities into USD; (3) borrow USD directly from the interbank market, non-bank lenders or central banks. Her slides contain the following statements:

I. Under option 1 the bank has no subsequent need to deliver US dollars, but the on-balance-sheet mismatch between its USD assets and JPY liabilities leaves it exposed to currency risk.

II. Under option 2 the currency risk is hedged and, because the swap is an off-balance-sheet contract, the bank faces no foreign currency funding risk.

III. The second leg of the swap in option 2 is not very different from option 3: in both cases the bank must deliver US dollars when the contractual obligation comes due.

IV. Option 3 leaves the bank with a positive net USD position that is mirrored by net borrowing in JPY.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.text: I, II and III only
I and III only
I only
I, III and IV only

questions.solution:
Japanese bank financing USD loans: auditing statements on the three funding options.

**Concept and theory**

GARP opens its framework (Section 16.2) with a bank that diversifies internationally and must finance a portfolio of foreign currency loans and securities, for example a German bank buying US dollar structured finance products. There are three ways to do this:

| Option | Mechanics | Currency risk | Later foreign currency needs |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Spot | Borrow domestic currency, convert spot, buy the asset | Yes: unhedged on-balance-sheet mismatch | None |
| 2. FX swap | Convert domestic liabilities into foreign currency via an FX swap | Hedged | Must deliver foreign currency when the swap matures |
| 3. Direct | Borrow foreign currency (interbank, non-banks, central banks) | None: currencies matched | Must deliver foreign currency when the liability matures |

GARP’s working assumption is that banks use FX swaps and forwards to hedge any on-balance-sheet currency mismatch, so a bank funding in domestic currency (option 1 or 2) is likely to end up as in option 2. In balance sheet terms, with $\text{A}_{\text{i}}$ the assets and $\text{L}_{\text{i}}$ the liabilities in currency i (i = 0 domestic, $\text{L}_{0}$ including equity): option 1 produces a long position $\text{A}_{\text{i}} >$ 0 financed by $\text{L}_{0} = \text{A}_{\text{i}}$; option 2 couples the same on-balance-sheet positions with an off-balance-sheet promise to repay $\text{A}_{\text{i}}$ when the swap comes due; option 3 matches foreign funding to foreign assets, leaving a zero net position $\text{A}_{\text{i}} - \text{L}_{\text{i}} =$ 0. The key insight is that hedging currency risk does not remove funding risk: the second leg of the swap requires the bank to “deliver” foreign currency at maturity, which is economically close to repaying a foreign currency loan.

**Applying it to this question**

Statement I restates option 1: no later foreign currency need, but an unhedged mismatch. True.

Statement II is false: the swap hedges currency risk, but being off-balance sheet does not remove the obligation to deliver USD at maturity, and GARP says the various funding options expose the bank to funding risk, the risk that funding (including FX swaps) cannot be rolled over.

Statement III paraphrases GARP’s comparison of the swap’s second leg with option 3. True.

Statement IV is false: option 3 leaves a zero net USD position; the positive net position mirrored by domestic borrowing is the outcome of options 1 and 2. Correct set: I and III.

**Fragile fact.** Hedging currency risk (option 2) does not remove funding risk; only option 1 carries currency risk, and options 2 and 3 both require delivering foreign currency later.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 80.b, verbatim):** Evaluate the importance of assessing maturity/currency mismatches across the balance sheets of consolidated entities.

**GARP:** Chapter 16, Section 16.2 “Banks’ International Positions: Concepts and Data”. **GARP vs** **Schweser:** none; Schweser LO 80.b “Global Balance Sheets and Funding Risk” lists the same three options.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-15 b, where it is Q1 of 13.

a.reason: (Absolute claim). Option A accepts statement II, which promises that an off-balance-sheet swap carries no funding risk. GARP’s whole funding gap framework includes FX swaps among the short-term funding that must be rolled over. II would be true only if the swap’s maturity matched the asset’s investment horizon, and even then it would describe a zero gap, not the absence of a delivery obligation.

b.reason: GARP: the first option produces no subsequent foreign currency needs but leaves the on-balance-sheet mismatch unhedged, and the swap’s second leg “is not that different” from foreign currency borrowing because in both cases the bank must deliver foreign currency when the liability comes due. Only option B selects exactly I and III.

c.reason: (Scope error). Option C rejects statement III, treating the swap leg as fundamentally different from direct foreign currency borrowing. GARP says the opposite. C would be right only if the question asked which statement describes option 1 alone.

d.reason: (Sibling swap). Option D accepts statement IV, which attributes the long net position of options 1 and 2 to option 3. Option 3 leaves $\text{A}_{\text{i}} - \text{L}_{\text{i}} =$ 0. IV would be true if it described option 1 or 2.

questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a Swiss banking group (domestic currency CHF) is preparing a report on the group’s on-balance-sheet currency positions. Equity is included in CHF liabilities. Worldwide consolidated positions, in USD billions equivalent, are:

| Currency | Assets | Liabilities |
|---|---|---|
| USD | 900 | 620 |
| EUR | 400 | 460 |
| JPY | 150 | 120 |
| GBP | 80 | 80 |

The share of the group’s foreign claims booked by offices outside Switzerland is 82%. Using the balance sheet identity, which of the following best describes the group’s implied net position in CHF?

options.text: A net long CHF position of USD 250 billion equivalent
Net borrowing in CHF of USD 310 billion equivalent
Net borrowing in CHF of USD 280 billion equivalent
Net borrowing in CHF of USD 250 billion equivalent

questions.solution:
Swiss banking group: implied net CHF position from the balance sheet identity.

**Concept and theory**

Every balance sheet balances, so if a bank is long some currencies it must be short others. GARP writes this as a balance sheet identity across currencies. Let $\text{A}_{\text{i}} \text{and L}_{\text{i}}$ be assets and liabilities in currency i, with i = 0 the domestic currency and $\text{L}_{0}$ including equity. Because total assets equal total liabilities plus equity,

$\sum_{\text{i}} (\text{A}_{\text{i}} - \text{L}_{\text{i}}) =$ 0 $=\Rightarrow\sum_{\text{i}\not=0} (\text{A}_{\text{i}} - \text{L}_{\text{i}}) = \text{L}_{0} - \text{A}_{0}$. (16.1)

In words: net foreign currency positions, if positive, are mirrored in net borrowing in domestic currency. “Long” denotes a positive net on-balance-sheet position and “short” a negative one. This identity is how GARP infers banks’ net positions vis-à-vis home residents: the BIS statistics do not report banks’ “strictly domestic” gross positions (domestic currency positions booked by home offices with home residents), so their net value is backed out as a residual. Its economic meaning is important for the LO: European banks built up long US dollar positions after 2000 and funded them largely by borrowing in their domestic currency from home residents, consistent with universal banks using their retail arms to fund dollar-heavy investment banking. Combined with GARP’s working assumption that open currency positions are small, the net foreign currency positions then measure how much the bank relies on FX swaps.

**Applying it to this question**

USD: 900 − 620 = +280

EUR: 400 − 460 = −60

JPY: 150 − 120 = +30

GBP: 80 − 80 = 0

$\sum_{\text{i}\not=0}(\text{A}_{\text{i}} - \text{L}_{\text{i}}) =$ 280 − 60 + 30 + 0 = +250

$\text{L}_{0} - \text{A}_{0} =$ 250 $\Rightarrow\text{A}_{0} - \text{L}_{0} = -$250

The group is a net borrower in CHF of USD 250 billion equivalent: its net long foreign currency book is financed by net CHF borrowing. The 82% share of foreign claims booked abroad is irrelevant to the identity; it matters for where positions are booked, not for their consolidated sum.

**Fragile fact.** Long foreign currency (positive net) is mirrored by net borrowing (negative net) in domestic currency; sum all currencies, including the short ones.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 80.b, verbatim):** Evaluate the importance of assessing maturity/currency mismatches across the balance sheets of consolidated entities.

**GARP:** Chapter 16, Section 16.2 (equation 16.1) and Section 16.3.3 “Cross-Currency Funding Positions”. **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser does not show equation 16.1 but states that long foreign currency positions were financed by domestic currency borrowing at home. Caution: equation 16.1 is garbled in the GARP text extraction; it is reconstructed here from GARP’s verbal statement of the identity.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-15 b, where it is Q2 of 13.

a.reason: (Sign error). Option A has the right magnitude but the wrong sign: it sets $\text{A}_{0} - \text{L}_{0} = +$250. A net long foreign currency book must be mirrored by a net short domestic position. A would be right if the group were net short foreign currencies by 250.

b.reason: (Dropped term). 310 is the sum of the long positions only (280 + 30), dropping the −60 short EUR position. 310 would be right only if the EUR book were balanced.

c.reason: (Intermediate result). 280 is the USD net position alone, ignoring EUR and JPY. It would be right only if USD were the group’s only foreign currency.

d.reason: Equation 16.1 sets the net domestic position equal to minus the sum of net foreign currency positions: −250, that is, net CHF borrowing of USD 250 billion equivalent, option D.

questions.question:
An internal auditor at a Canadian bank is reviewing the methodology note for the bank’s US dollar foreign currency funding gap. The note contains the following statements:

I. A foreign currency funding gap exists when the investment horizon of the bank’s foreign currency assets exceeds the maturity of its foreign currency funding or FX swaps.

II. Because FX swaps hedge currency risk, USD obtained through swaps can be excluded from the short-term funding liabilities used to measure the gap.

III. The investment horizon of the assets depends on the desired holding period, the maturity of the underlying assets and their market liquidity.

IV. The gap equals the bank’s net on-balance-sheet USD position (USD assets minus USD liabilities), since that is the amount the bank funds through FX swaps.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.text: I and III only
I, II and III only
I only
I, III and IV only

questions.solution:
Canadian bank: auditing a methodology note on the foreign currency funding gap.

**Concept and theory**

Funding risk is the risk that funding liabilities cannot be rolled over. Its size depends on the degree of maturity transformation in the balance sheet. GARP says a bank faces a foreign currency funding gap if the investment horizon of its foreign currency assets $\text{A}_{\text{i}}$ exceeds the maturity of its foreign currency funding or FX swaps. Three things set the portfolio’s investment horizon:

- the desired holding period;
- the maturity of the underlying assets;
- market liquidity (an illiquid asset cannot be turned into cash early without loss).

If the contractual liabilities $\text{(L}_{\text{i}}$ or swaps) cannot be rolled over, assets that were meant to be held must instead be sold, possibly in distressed conditions. When the bank fully hedges currency risk, $\text{A}_{\text{i}} = \text{L}_{\text{i}} + \text{S}_{\text{i}}$, where $\text{S}_{\text{i}}$ is foreign currency obtained via swaps. Short-term funding is then $(\text{L}_{\text{i}} - \text{L}^{\text{LT}}_{\text{i}} ) + \text{S}_{\text{i}}$, which includes the swaps. Note the difference between the gap and the net on-balance-sheet position: $\text{A}_{\text{i}} - \text{L}_{\text{i}} = \text{S}_{\text{i}}$ tells you how much is funded through swaps (a currency concept), while the gap $\text{A}^{\text{LT}}_{\text{i}} - \text{L}^{\text{LT}}_{\text{i}}$ tells you how much long-horizon investment is not supported by long-maturity funding (a maturity concept).

**Applying it to this question**

Statement I is GARP’s definition. True. Statement II is false: swaps are explicitly part of the short-term funding that must be rolled over; GARP names them alongside foreign currency funding in the definition. Statement III lists GARP’s three drivers of the investment horizon. True. Statement IV is false: it confuses the net position (equal to swap usage) with the gap, which depends on maturities. Correct set: I and III.

**Fragile fact.** Direction: the gap exists when the asset horizon is longer than the funding maturity, and FX swaps count as funding.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 80.b, verbatim):** Evaluate the importance of assessing maturity/currency mismatches across the balance sheets of consolidated entities.

**GARP:** Chapter 16, Section 16.2 “Banks’ International Positions: Concepts and Data”. **GARP vs** **Schweser:** none; Schweser defines the gap the same way (also in Module Quiz 80.1).

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-15 b, where it is Q3 of 13.

a.reason: GARP defines the gap by comparing the investment horizon of foreign currency assets with the maturity of foreign currency funding or FX swaps, and says that horizon depends on the desired holding period, the maturity of the underlying assets and market liquidity. Option A.

b.reason: (Scope error). Option B accepts statement II, which drops FX swaps from the funding that must be rolled over. In the crisis it was precisely short-term FX swap funding that became hard to roll. II would be true only for swaps whose maturity matched the asset horizon.

c.reason: (Scope error). Option C rejects statement III, implicitly equating investment horizon with contractual maturity alone. GARP adds holding period and market liquidity, which is why illiquid structured products lengthened effective horizons in the crisis.

d.reason: (Sibling swap). Option D accepts statement IV, which substitutes the net open position $\text{A}_{\text{i}} - \text{L}_{\text{i}}$ for the gap $\text{A}^{\text{LT}}_{\text{i}} - \text{L}^{\text{LT}}_{\text{i}}$. IV would describe the bank’s reliance on FX swaps, not its funding gap.

questions.question:
A treasurer at a French banking group is estimating the group’s US dollar funding gap. The group fully hedges the currency risk of its USD book, so USD assets equal USD on-balance-sheet liabilities plus USD obtained through FX swaps. Consolidated data (USD billions) are:

| Item | Amount |
|---|---|
| Total USD assets | 600 |
| of which: long investment horizon | 420 |
| USD on-balance-sheet liabilities | 350 |
| of which: long effective maturity | 140 |
| USD obtained through FX swaps | 250 |
| EUR retail deposits (USD equivalent) | 900 |

Which of the following is closest to the group’s US dollar funding gap?

options.text: USD 460 billion
USD 250 billion
USD 280 billion
USD 30 billion

questions.solution:
French banking group: computing the US dollar funding gap with FX swap funding.

**Concept and theory**

GARP builds the funding gap from the hedging equality. Let $\text{A}_{\text{i}}$ be foreign currency assets, $\text{L}_{\text{i}}$ on-balance-sheet foreign currency liabilities and $\text{S}_{\text{i}}$ foreign currency obtained via FX swaps, with full hedging $\text{A}_{\text{i}} = \text{L}_{\text{i}} + \text{S}_{\text{i}}$. Let $\text{A}^{\text{LT}}_{\text{i}}$ $\text{(L}^{\text{LT}}_{\text{i}}$) be the assets (liabilities) with a long investment horizon (long effective maturity).

- Short-term funding liabilities, including swaps: $(\text{L}_{\text{i}} - \text{L}^{\text{LT}}_{\text{i}} ) + \text{S}_{\text{i}}$. Because swaps are usually off-balance sheet and unobserved, GARP substitutes the hedging equality to write this as $\text{A}_{\text{i}} - \text{L}^{\text{LT}}_{\text{i}}$.
- These can be met with liquid or maturing assets worth $\text{A}_{\text{i}} - \text{A}^{\text{LT}}_{\text{i}}$.

The difference is the foreign currency funding gap:

$\text{Gap}_{\text{i}} = (\text{A}_{\text{i}} - \text{L}^{\text{LT}}_{\text{i}} ) - (\text{A}_{\text{i}} - \text{A}^{\text{LT}}_{\text{i}} ) = \text{A}^{\text{LT}}_{\text{i}} - \text{L}^{\text{LT}}_{\text{i}}$. (16.2)

Schweser states the same result: the gap is the difference between long-term USD assets and long-term USD liabilities, the amount of dollars that must be rolled over before the assets mature.

**Applying it to this question**

Check hedging: L $+ \text{S} =$ 350 + 250 = 600 = A

Short-term funding $= (\text{L} - \text{L}^{\text{LT}} ) + \text{S} = ($350 − 140) + 250 = 460

Liquid or maturing assets $= \text{A} - \text{A}^{\text{LT}} =$ 600 − 420 = 180

Funding gap = 460 − 180 = 280 (= 420 − 140)

The group must roll over USD 280 billion of short-term dollar funding before its long-horizon dollar assets mature. EUR retail deposits are irrelevant: they are domestic currency funding and do not enter the USD gap.

**Fragile fact.** FX swaps are short-term funding; the gap is long-horizon assets minus long-maturity liabilities, not assets minus liabilities.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 80.b, verbatim):** Evaluate the importance of assessing maturity/currency mismatches across the balance sheets of consolidated entities.

**GARP:** Chapter 16, Section 16.2 (equation 16.2). **GARP vs Schweser:** none in substance. Caution: equation 16.2 is garbled in the GARP text extraction and is reconstructed from GARP’s verbal derivation; Schweser’s “long-term assets minus long-term liabilities” confirms it.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-15 b, where it is Q4 of 13.

a.reason: (Intermediate result). 460 is the short-term funding liabilities A $- \text{L}^{\text{LT}}$, before deducting the USD 180 billion of liquid or maturing assets that can meet them. It would be the gap only if no USD assets were liquid or maturing $\text{(A}^{\text{LT}} =$ A).

b.reason: (Sibling swap). 250 is the net on-balance-sheet position A − L, which equals swap usage S. That measures cross-currency funding, not the maturity gap. It would be the answer to “how much USD does the group raise through FX swaps?”.

c.reason: Equation 16.2 gives $\text{A}^{\text{LT}} - \text{L}^{\text{LT}} =$ 420 − 140 = 280, option C.

d.reason: (Dropped term). 30 is $(\text{L} - \text{L}^{\text{LT}} ) - (\text{A} - \text{A}^{\text{LT}} ) =$ 210 − 180, which omits the FX swaps from short-term funding. It would be right only if the group used no swaps (S = 0).

questions.question: A member of the board risk committee of an Australian bank asks why the bank’s liquidity stress test applies a harsher assumption to an AUD 5 billion maturity mismatch in its US dollar book than to a maturity mismatch of the same size in its AUD book. Which of the following justifications is most accurate?

options.text: Maturity transformation is not an essential function of banking in the domestic currency, so the bank can cheaply eliminate its AUD mismatch whenever it wishes.
The Reserve Bank of Australia can act as lender of last resort in AUD but cannot create US dollars, so the bank’s USD needs may have to be met from international sources.
The Reserve Bank of Australia’s support for AUD funding is limited by its FX reserves, whereas USD funding can always be raised in international markets at short notice.
Because FX swaps hedge the USD book, its mismatch creates currency risk rather than funding risk, and currency risk requires the harsher stress assumption.

questions.solution:
Australian bank: why a USD maturity mismatch is stressed more harshly than an AUD one.

**Concept and theory**

Banks face maturity transformation risk in every currency, so why does GARP single out foreign currency funding risk? The argument has three steps.

- **Maturity transformation is normal.** It is an essential function of banking, and banks would find it unprofitable to eliminate maturity mismatch altogether. A domestic mismatch is therefore not a flaw to be removed.
- **Domestic currency has a backstop.** In a purely domestic context the central bank can act as lender of last resort and provide enough liquidity to eliminate a domestic funding shortage. GARP calls this both time-honoured practice (Bagehot) and optimal policy.
- **Foreign currency does not.** Central banks cannot create foreign currencies. Their ability to meet banks’ demand for foreign currency is constrained by the exchange rate regime or limited to available FX reserves. Foreign currency requirements may therefore have to be met from international sources.

This is why GARP focuses its analysis on foreign currency, and particularly US dollar, funding gaps, and why the crisis response needed a central bank that can create dollars (the Federal Reserve swap lines, LO 80.c). Schweser summarises: domestic funding risk is significantly reduced by the lender of last resort, while foreign currency needs must be met directly in international markets.

**Applying it to this question**

The committee member’s question is about the asymmetry between two equal-sized mismatches. The deciding fact is the asymmetry of the backstop: the Reserve Bank of Australia can supply AUD without limit but has no power to create USD. The size (AUD 5 billion) is the same in both books, so it plays no role.

**Fragile fact.** The lender of last resort works only in the currency the central bank issues; its foreign currency capacity is limited by the exchange rate regime or FX reserves.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 80.b, verbatim):** Evaluate the importance of assessing maturity/currency mismatches across the balance sheets of consolidated entities.

**GARP:** Chapter 16, Section 16.2 (“Why is funding risk in foreign currencies of special interest?”). **GARP vs Schweser:** none.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-15 b, where it is Q5 of 13.

a.reason: (Polarity flip). GARP says maturity transformation is an essential function of banking and that eliminating mismatch altogether would be unprofitable. A would be right only if domestic mismatches were costless to remove, which the source denies.

b.reason: Option B restates GARP’s reason: a domestic central bank can be lender of last resort in its own currency but cannot create foreign currencies, so foreign currency needs may have to be met from international sources.

c.reason: (Role misassignment). Option C attaches the FX reserve constraint to the wrong currency. Reserves limit a central bank’s ability to supply foreign currency; in AUD it faces no such limit. It also wrongly assumes USD markets are always open, the opposite of the crisis experience. C would be right if the two currencies were swapped.

d.reason: (Sibling swap). Option D confuses currency risk with funding risk. A swap-hedged USD book has little currency risk; its exposure is funding risk, the risk that the swaps or USD borrowing cannot be rolled over. D would describe an unhedged option 1 position.

questions.question: A regulator at the Central Bank of Brazil is designing a data template to identify vulnerabilities in the foreign currency funding of internationally active banks. Which of the following statements about measuring foreign currency funding risk is least accurate?

options.text: Published accounts of individual banks, such as those collected in BankScope and Bloomberg, contain the counterparty, maturity and currency breakdowns that are needed.
Measurement should be on a consolidated basis, preferably at the level of the decision-making economic unit, that is, the individual bank.
Ideal data would break down both assets and liabilities by currency, maturity and counterparty type, together with risk characteristics and off-balance-sheet positions.
Information collected by bank examiners during supervision may contain the needed detail, but it is not included in publicly available data sources.

questions.solution:
Brazilian regulator: least accurate statement on measuring foreign currency funding risk.

**Concept and theory**

GARP states that funding risk is inherently tied to stresses across the global balance sheet: mismatches between the maturity, currency and counterparty of assets and liabilities. Measuring it therefore requires:

- **The right unit:** banking activity on a consolidated basis, preferably at the level of the decision-making economic unit, the individual bank.
- **The right breakdowns:** ideally, for both assets and liabilities, a complete breakdown by currency, maturity and counterparty type, plus risk characteristics and off-balance-sheet positions.

Available data fall short of this ideal in three ways:

| Source | Limitation |
|---|---|
| Published accounts (BankScope, Bloomberg) | Consolidated, bank level, but lack the counterparty, maturity and currency breakdowns |
| Supervisory data from bank examiners | May hold the detail, but not public; bank-level focus may miss macroprudential issues (many banks with the same funding patterns) |
| National statistics (authorities, IMF, OECD) | Residency based, so insufficient for a globalised national banking system |
| BIS international banking statistics | Most comprehensive: consolidated foreign assets and liabilities, gross and net positions by currency, and sources of financing by counterparty |

Schweser adds that banks do not publicly disclose important details of their international positions, making supervisory oversight more challenging.

**Applying it to this question**

The question asks for the least accurate statement, so three options are true and one corrupts the source. B, C and D paraphrase GARP. A claims that published accounts contain the needed breakdowns; GARP says they lack exactly these breakdowns.

**Fragile fact.** Bank-level published accounts are consolidated but lack the counterparty, maturity and currency breakdown; the BIS statistics supply it, at the national banking system level.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 80.b, verbatim):** Evaluate the importance of assessing maturity/currency mismatches across the balance sheets of consolidated entities.

**GARP:** Chapter 16, Section 16.2 (paragraph on funding risk and stresses across the global balance sheet, and data sources). **GARP vs Schweser:** none; Schweser condenses this to banks’ non-disclosure and the BIS data.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-15 b, where it is Q6 of 13.

a.reason: Option A reverses GARP’s statement that published accounts, while available for individual consolidated banks, “lack the essential breakdowns” of counterparty, maturity and currency. It is the least accurate statement (built by a polarity flip of the source).

b.reason: (True statement (qualifier: least accurate)). GARP says quantifying funding risk requires measurement on a consolidated basis, preferably at the decision-making economic unit, the individual bank. Choosing B means misreading the qualifier. B would be the answer only if it named residency-based offices as the preferred unit.

c.reason: (True statement (qualifier: least accurate)). This is GARP’s ideal data set: currency, maturity and counterparty breakdowns for assets and liabilities, with risk characteristics and off-balance-sheet positions. It would be false only if it omitted liabilities or off-balance-sheet positions and claimed completeness.

d.reason: (True statement (qualifier: least accurate)). GARP notes such information may be collected by bank examiners but is not in public sources. It would be false if it claimed examiner data were published.

questions.question:
A risk consultant is reviewing a German banking group’s US dollar book. On-balance-sheet USD positions by booking office, excluding inter-office claims and liabilities, are (USD billions):

| Booking office | USD assets | USD liabilities |
|---|---|---|
| London | 310 | 140 |
| New York | 220 | 330 |
| Singapore | 60 | 75 |
| Frankfurt (home office) | 45 | 70 |

The group’s total assets are EUR 1,900 billion. Which of the following best describes the group’s consolidated on-balance-sheet US dollar position?

options.text: A net long US dollar position of USD 170 billion
A net short US dollar position of USD 150 billion
A net short US dollar position of USD 20 billion
A net long US dollar position of USD 20 billion

questions.solution:
German banking group: consolidating office-level USD positions.

**Concept and theory**

Internationally active banks have offices in many countries, but GARP stresses that their currency and maturity positions are managed across the consolidated global entity rather than office by office. Consequences:

- A large measured “mismatch” at one office may be hedged off-balance sheet or offset by on-balance-sheet positions booked by offices elsewhere, leaving a matched book for the bank as a whole.
- Foreign offices are a large part of the picture: in most banking systems less than half of foreign claims are booked by home offices (French and Japanese banks are the exceptions). Swiss banks had more than USD 3 trillion of foreign claims, over 80% of their total assets, with only 18% booked in Switzerland.
- An office-level or host-country view can therefore signal a mismatch that does not exist for the bank, or hide one that does. Vulnerabilities can only be measured on the entire balance sheet of the consolidated global entity.

Consolidation itself is mechanical: sum each office’s positions in the currency (after removing inter-office positions, which net to zero across the group), then take assets minus liabilities. The analytical point is which number is meaningful for the group’s risk.

**Applying it to this question**

London: 310 − 140 = +170

New York: 220 − 330 = −110

Singapore: 60 − 75 = −15

Frankfurt: 45 − 70 = −25

Consolidated: 635 − 615 = +20

The group is net long only USD 20 billion, although London alone shows a long position of USD 170 billion. A UK host-country view would overstate the group’s USD position by a factor of more than eight. The EUR 1,900 billion of total assets is irrelevant to the net USD position.

**Fragile fact.** Office-level mismatches can offset within the group; read the consolidated net, and keep the sign (assets minus liabilities, positive is long).

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 80.b, verbatim):** Evaluate the importance of assessing maturity/currency mismatches across the balance sheets of consolidated entities.

**GARP:** Chapter 16, Section 16.3.1 “The Structure of Banks’ Operations”. **GARP vs Schweser:** minor: Schweser says Swiss foreign claims are 80% of total assets with nearly 80% booked abroad; GARP says over 80% (Table 16.1: 89%) with only 18% booked in Switzerland. Use GARP.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-15 b, where it is Q7 of 13.

a.reason: (Intermediate result). 170 is the London office alone, the figure a UK host-country data set would show. It would be correct only if London were the group’s only office with a USD book.

b.reason: (Dropped term). −150 sums the three short offices (−110 − 15 − 25) and drops the long London office. It would be right only if the London book were balanced.

c.reason: (Sign error). Option C has the right magnitude but treats the group as net short. Assets (635) exceed liabilities (615), so the position is long. C would be right if the asset and liability columns were swapped.

d.reason: Summing across booking offices gives USD assets of 635 and liabilities of 615, a consolidated net long position of USD 20 billion, option D. This is GARP’s point that offices’ long or short positions offset each other on the consolidated balance sheet.

questions.question:
An economist at a UK financial stability authority is reviewing the UK’s net external position before the crisis. She notes the following (USD billions, change in net cross-border positions from Q4 2000 to Q2 2007):

| Booked by offices in the UK of | Change |
|---|---|
| Foreign-headquartered banks | −490 |
| UK-headquartered banks | −190 |

Offices of foreign banks also account for nearly 40% of the UK’s external assets. Which of the following conclusions is most appropriate?

options.text: The swing driven by foreign banks’ UK offices signals a matching rise in the currency and maturity mismatches borne by UK residents.
Because the offices are located in the UK, their UK-booked positions are the best unit for measuring the funding risk of the banks that own them.
The swing may be only loosely related to UK residents’ vulnerabilities, since positions booked in London may be offset or hedged elsewhere on the parent banks’ global balance sheets.
The swing must be matched by an equal and opposite change in the parent banks’ home countries’ external positions, so netting the two countries’ data reveals the vulnerability.

questions.solution:
UK host-country view: interpreting a swing in the national external position.

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s Tables 16.1 and 16.2 show that “bank nationality” and “bank residency” are fundamentally different concepts. Positions booked by offices in any one country are generally a small part of a banking system’s global consolidated balance sheet, yet the cross-border positions booked by banks’ offices in one country can be large relative to that host country’s external assets. In five countries (BE, CH, DE, JP, UK) banks’ cross-border positions were almost half of the country’s external assets at end-2007, and offices of foreign banks alone accounted for nearly 40% of the UK’s. GARP gives two reasons why the “national balance sheet” may be a poor indicator of residents’ vulnerabilities. The first (the host-country view) is tested here:

- Changes in a country’s external position can be driven largely by foreign banks’ offices, and so be only loosely related to residents’ vulnerabilities. If banks headquartered in country A double their balance sheet through their foreign offices, other countries’ external positions swing without country A’s external position necessarily changing.
- Swiss, German and Dutch banks’ expansion was driven largely by positions booked by their UK offices; before the crisis, foreign banks’ offices in the UK changed their net cross-border positions by −\$490 billion against −\$190 billion for UK-headquartered banks.
- A long or short net position in a currency booked by foreign banks’ offices in a host country may be offset or hedged elsewhere on those banks’ global balance sheets, so the host-country “mismatch” may not exist at all.

**Applying it to this question**

The data show the swing was driven mostly by foreign-headquartered banks (\$490 billion against \$190 billion), which also hold nearly 40% of UK external assets. The decisive fact is GARP’s statement that such positions may be offset or hedged elsewhere on the parent banks’ global balance sheets, so the swing says little about UK residents and the right unit is the consolidated parent.

**Fragile fact.** Host-country data overstate what is “UK” risk: positions booked in London by foreign banks belong to, and may be offset within, their parents’ consolidated balance sheets.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 80.b, verbatim):** Evaluate the importance of assessing maturity/currency mismatches across the balance sheets of consolidated entities.

**GARP:** Chapter 16, Section 16.3.1 “The Structure of Banks’ Operations” and Tables 16.1 and 16.2. **GARP vs Schweser:** none in substance; Schweser condenses the same points (foreign offices contributed to changes in UK, Italian and Spanish net external positions).

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-15 b, where it is Q8 of 13.

a.reason: (Absolute claim). Option A treats the swing as a one-for-one signal of UK residents’ mismatches. GARP says such changes may be only loosely related to residents’ portfolios. A would be right only if the positions were booked by UK residents and not offset elsewhere.

b.reason: (Sibling swap). Option B swaps residency for nationality as the unit of analysis. GARP argues the opposite: funding risk should be measured on the consolidated (nationality) balance sheet, preferably at the level of the individual bank. B would describe the BIS locational statistics by residency, which GARP says are insufficient alone.

c.reason: Option C restates GARP’s interpretation: host-country positions booked by foreign banks may be offset elsewhere, so the national balance sheet change is only loosely related to residents’ vulnerabilities, which must be assessed on the consolidated entities.

d.reason: (Absolute claim). Option D asserts an equal and opposite change in the home countries’ external positions. GARP’s example says the balance sheet adjustment in foreign offices can swing other countries’ positions without necessarily affecting the home country’s. D would be right only if every foreign office were funded cross-border from home.

questions.question:
A portfolio manager at a Singapore asset manager is assessing the banking system of Country N, whose large banks are headquartered there. She gathers the following data:

| Indicator | Value (%) |
|---|---|
| Domestic banks’ cross-border claims / Country N’s external assets | 35 |
| Assets booked by offices outside Country N / banks’ total worldwide assets | 45 |
| Country N’s annual GDP growth | 2 |

She plans to judge the banks’ vulnerabilities from Country N’s external position and domestic credit data. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Because a large share of the banks’ assets is booked abroad, their vulnerabilities may not be visible in Country N’s external position, even when combined with domestic credit data.
Combining Country N’s external position with its domestic credit aggregates reproduces the banks’ worldwide consolidated balance sheet, so no further data are needed.
Vulnerabilities on the banks’ consolidated balance sheets translate one for one into vulnerabilities of Country N’s residents, whatever exposures those residents hold.
Bank residency and bank nationality are essentially the same concept for internationally active banks, so either basis gives a similar picture of the banks’ vulnerabilities.

questions.solution:
Country N: judging a home banking system’s vulnerabilities from national data.

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s second reason why national balance sheets mislead is the converse of the host-country problem: it is generally difficult to identify a particular banking system’s vulnerabilities from the home country’s domestic and external positions data.

- In at least six countries (BE, CH, DE, FR, JP, NL), domestic banks’ cross-border positions account for a third or more of the home country’s external position.
- Yet assets booked by offices outside the home country account for a quarter or more of these banking systems’ total worldwide assets (Japanese banks are the exception, at about 6 to 7%).
- So the vulnerabilities of these banks may not be visible in the home country’s external position, even when combined with data on their domestic positions such as domestic credit aggregates.
- Vulnerabilities can only be measured by taking into account the entire balance sheet of the consolidated global entity. Moreover, they relate to domestic residents only to the extent that residents hold exposures in the national banking system.

The two reasons together are GARP’s case for the consolidated, nationality-based approach:

| View | Problem |
|---|---|
| Host country | Foreign banks’ offices drive external positions; their mismatches may be offset elsewhere |
| Home country | Positions booked abroad are missing from home external and domestic data |

**Applying it to this question**

Country N fits GARP’s description: domestic banks’ cross-border claims are 35% of its external assets (a third or more), and 45% of the banks’ assets are booked abroad (a quarter or more). Her plan to use home external and domestic credit data will miss the positions booked abroad. GDP growth is irrelevant to whether the data capture the banks’ balance sheets.

**Fragile fact.** Even combined home external and domestic credit data miss positions booked abroad; and bank vulnerabilities become residents’ vulnerabilities only through residents’ exposures.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 80.b, verbatim):** Evaluate the importance of assessing maturity/currency mismatches across the balance sheets of consolidated entities.

**GARP:** Chapter 16, Section 16.3.1 “The Structure of Banks’ Operations”. **GARP vs Schweser:** none in substance. Caution: GARP’s text gives Japanese banks’ share booked abroad as 6% while the extracted Table 16.1 shows 7; not tested.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-15 b, where it is Q9 of 13.

a.reason: Option A states GARP’s conclusion that vulnerabilities in these banks’ balance sheets may not be visible in the home country’s external position, even when combined with domestic data.

b.reason: (Absolute claim). Option B claims home external plus domestic data reproduce the consolidated balance sheet. They omit the local and cross-border positions booked by offices abroad (45% here). B would be right only for a bank with no foreign offices.

c.reason: (Scope error). Option C drops GARP’s condition that vulnerabilities relate to domestic residents only to the extent residents hold exposures in the national banking system. C would be right only if residents owned all of the banks’ exposures.

d.reason: (Polarity flip). GARP says nationality and residency are fundamentally different concepts. D would be right only for purely domestic banks.

questions.question: A junior risk analyst at a UK banking group is interpreting its worldwide consolidated net on-balance-sheet positions by currency (USD billions equivalent): USD +120 (on gross USD claims of 1,100), EUR +60, other currencies +20, and implied net sterling position vis-à-vis UK residents −200. Assuming the group’s on-balance-sheet open currency positions are small, which interpretation is most accurate?

options.text: The net long dollar position of USD 120 billion is the group’s US dollar funding gap, the amount it must roll over before its dollar assets mature.
The group carries an unhedged currency exposure of USD 200 billion, because its net sterling borrowing is not matched by any sterling assets.
The group’s long foreign currency positions are funded mainly by borrowing dollars and euros in the interbank market rather than in sterling.
The net positions measure the group’s reliance on FX swaps that convert sterling funding into foreign currency, exposing it to swap rollover risk.

questions.solution:
UK banking group: interpreting net cross-currency positions.

**Concept and theory**

Cross-currency funding is the extent to which banks invest in one currency and fund in another. GARP measures it from a currency breakdown of banks’ gross and net foreign positions (Figures 16.2 and 16.3). Key findings and logic:

- Foreign currency assets often exceed funding in the same currency, so banks hold long foreign currency positions.
- By the balance sheet identity, these are mirrored in net borrowing in domestic currency from home residents. UK banks, for example, borrowed (net) about \$550 billion in sterling to fund long positions in USD, EUR and other currencies; their long USD position was about \$200 billion on some \$2 trillion of gross USD claims.
- If on-balance-sheet open currency positions are small, these net cross-currency positions are a measure of banks’ reliance on FX swaps. Thus as cross-currency funding grew, so did hedging requirements and FX swap transactions, which are subject to funding risk when they have to be rolled over.
- The net position is not the funding gap: the gap needs a maturity dimension (long-horizon assets versus long-maturity funding), which GARP proxies with counterparty data.

In aggregate, European banks’ long USD positions reached about \$700 billion by mid-2007, funded by short positions in sterling, euros and Swiss francs.

**Applying it to this question**

The group is long foreign currencies by 120 + 60 + 20 = 200, mirrored by net sterling borrowing of 200. Under the stated assumption of small open positions, the 200 is swapped into foreign currency, so the group depends on rolling those swaps. The gross USD claims of 1,100 are irrelevant to the interpretation asked; they would matter for an upper-bound gap estimate, which needs counterparty data not given.

**Fragile fact.** Net long foreign currency + small open position = reliance on FX swaps (a funding risk), not a funding gap and not currency risk.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser LO 80.b, verbatim):** Evaluate the importance of assessing maturity/currency mismatches across the balance sheets of consolidated entities.

**GARP:** Chapter 16, Section 16.3.3 “Cross-Currency Funding Positions”. **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser says German and Swiss banks’ long USD positions were “a combined \$300 billion”; GARP’s wording (“approached \$300 billion”) is ambiguous between each and combined. Not tested.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-15 b, where it is Q10 of 13.

a.reason: (Sibling swap). Option A equates the net long USD position with the funding gap. The gap is a maturity measure, $\text{A}^{\text{LT}} - \text{L}^{\text{LT}}$; the net position measures swap reliance. A would be right only if every dollar asset were long-horizon and every swap were the only short-term funding.

b.reason: (Scope or condition error). Option B ignores the stated condition that open currency positions are small, treating the sterling borrowing as an unhedged exposure. B would be right without that assumption, that is, under option 1 funding.

c.reason: (Polarity flip). If the long positions were funded by borrowing dollars and euros, the net positions in those currencies would be close to zero, not long. GARP says they are mirrored in net domestic currency borrowing. C would be right if the net foreign positions were flat.

d.reason: Option D matches GARP: with small open positions, net cross-currency positions measure reliance on FX swaps, the long positions are mirrored in domestic currency borrowing, and swaps carry funding (rollover) risk.
