questions.question:
A treasury analyst at a German insurer that hedges its US dollar bond portfolio is comparing the cost of obtaining US dollars through a one-year EUR/USD FX swap with the cost of borrowing US dollars directly in the cash market. She collects the following data:

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Spot rate, S (USD per EUR) | 1.0800 |
| One-year forward rate, F (USD per EUR) | 1.1060 |
| One-year USD interest rate, r (%) | 4.50 |
| One-year EUR interest rate, $\text{r}^{*}$ (%) | 2.50 |
| Three-month EUR interest rate (%) | 2.10 |

Which of the following is closest to the FX swap implied one-year US dollar interest rate?
questions.solution:
German insurer’s treasury analyst computes the FX swap implied one-year US dollar rate from EUR/USD spot, forward and the EUR rate.

**Concept and theory**

A party that holds euros and needs dollars can get them without a cash loan. It gives euros at spot and receives S dollars per euro. At maturity it pays the pre-agreed F dollars per euro to get its euros back. Lending the euros in the swap means giving up the euro interest $\text{r}^{*}$ they could have earned, and the dollars to be repaid are fixed at the forward rate. Per dollar received, the gross cost of the swapped dollars is

1 $+ \text{r}_{\text{swap}} = \frac{\text{F}}{\text{S}} ($1 $+ \text{r}^{*})$,

which GARP calls the FX swap implied US dollar rate. Here S and F are in USD per EUR, and $\text{r}^{*}$ is the euro (foreign currency) rate for the swap tenor.

Under CIP this equals the cash-market dollar rate, 1 + r. GARP’s point is that since the GFC the US dollar has tended to command a premium in FX swaps, so $\frac{\text{F}}{\text{S}} ($1 $+ \text{r}^{*}) >$ 1 + r: a party borrowing dollars through the swap, for example to hedge a dollar asset as this insurer does, effectively pays a higher rate than in the cash market. The gap is what a cross-currency basis swap expresses as the basis paid by the dollar borrower.

The rate has to match the swap tenor. A one-year swap uses the one-year foreign rate, not a shorter one.

**Applying it to this question**

Formula: $\text{r}_{\text{swap}} = \frac{\text{F}}{\text{S}} ($1 $+ \text{r}^{*}) -$ 1.

$\frac{\text{F}}{\text{S}} = \frac{1.1060}{1.0800} =$ 1.024074

$\frac{\text{F}}{\text{S}} ($1 $+ \text{r}^{*}) =$ 1.024074 × 1.025 = 1.049676

$\text{r}_{\text{swap}} =$ 1.049676 − 1 = 4.97%

$\text{r}_{\text{swap}} - \text{r} =$ 4.97% − 4.50% ≈ 0.47% (47 bp)

The swap route costs about 47 bp more than the 4.50% cash rate, so the dollar is at a premium in the FX swap. The three-month EUR rate (2.10%) is irrelevant: the swap is one year, so the one-year rate applies. The USD rate is needed only for the comparison, not to compute the implied rate.

**Fragile fact.** The implied dollar rate multiplies F/S by (1 $+ \text{r}^{*})$, the foreign rate, with S and F in USD per foreign currency.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** LO 81.a: Differentiate between the mechanics of foreign exchange (FX) swaps and cross-currency swaps.

**GARP:** Chapter 17, Covered Interest Parity Lost: Understanding the Cross-Currency Basis, Box 17.1 (FX swap implied US dollar rate). Schweser 81.a, Foreign Exchange (FX) Swaps. **GARP vs** **Schweser:** none (Schweser does not state the implied-rate expression; content from GARP).

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-16 a, where it is Q3 of 11.

a.reason: (Intermediate result (dropped term)). $\frac{\text{F}}{\text{S}} -$ 1 = 2.41% is the forward premium alone. It omits the euro interest the party gives up, (1 $+ \text{r}^{*})$. It would be correct only if $\text{r}^{*} =$ 0.

b.reason: (Unit or quote inversion). $\frac{\text{S}}{\text{F}} ($1 $+ \text{r}^{*}) -$ 1 = 0.976492 × 1.025 − 1 = 0.09% inverts the exchange-rate ratio, as if S and F were quoted in EUR per USD. It would be correct only if the rates were given as EUR per USD and the formula were left unchanged.

c.reason: (Wrong input twin). $\frac{\text{F}}{\text{S}} ($1 $+ \text{r}) -$ 1 = 1.024074 × 1.045 − 1 = 7.02% uses the USD rate in place of the EUR rate. The rate given up when lending euros in the swap is the euro rate.

d.reason: Applying GARP’s implied US dollar rate, $\frac{\text{F}}{\text{S}} ($1 $+ \text{r}^{*})$, gives 4.97%. D is correct.

questions.question:
The CRO of a Japanese life insurer that funds US dollar bond holdings through FX swaps notes that the one-year USD/JPY forward points, F − S (with S in US dollars per yen), have been persistently wider than the value implied by the cash-market interest rates,

S $( \frac{1 + \text{r}}{1 + \text{r}^{*}} -$ 1$)$ .

Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: A party lending US dollars via the FX swap sells the yen forward at a lower dollar price than CIP warrants, so it earns less than the cash-market dollar rate.
A party borrowing US dollars via the FX swap effectively pays a higher interest rate on the swapped dollars than it would pay in the dollar cash market.
A party borrowing US dollars via the FX swap effectively pays a lower interest rate on the swapped dollars, because the wide points are paid by the dollar lender.
The wide points are consistent with CIP holding, because the forward points of an FX swap always equal the value implied by the cash-market rates.

questions.solution:
CRO of a Japanese life insurer interprets USD/JPY forward points that are persistently wider than CIP implies.

**Concept and theory**

Rearranging CIP with S and F in US dollars per foreign currency gives the forward points CIP warrants:

F $- \text{S} = \text{S} ( \frac{1 + \text{r}}{1 + \text{r}^{*}} -$ 1$)$ .

GARP explains that, typically, the US dollar has tended to command a premium in FX swaps, so that

F $- \text{S} > \text{S} ( \frac{1 + \text{r}}{1 + \text{r}^{*}} -$ 1$)$ .

Two equivalent readings follow.

- Lender of dollars: it receives the foreign currency at spot and, at maturity, sells the foreign currency forward at a higher dollar price F than the interest differential warrants. It earns more than the cash-market dollar rate.
- Borrower of dollars: for example a hedger of a dollar asset, such as a Japanese insurer holding US bonds. It effectively pays a higher interest rate on the swapped dollars than is paid in the cash market.

These are the same fact seen from the two sides of one contract. GARP adds that CIP arbitrageurs pass their balance sheet costs on to hedgers through wider forward points, and that hedgers pay those points to hedge their US dollar assets. The FX swap itself carries no open currency position by construction, so the gap is an interest-cost gap, not a currency bet.

**Applying it to this question**

“Wider than implied” is the “wide” F − S case in GARP. With S in USD per yen, a high F means the yen is dear and the dollar cheap in the forward market. So the dollar lender gains and the dollar borrower (the insurer) pays more than the cash rate. Option B states the borrower’s side correctly.

**Fragile fact.** Direction and actor: wide F − S (USD per foreign currency) means the dollar borrower pays above cash, and the dollar lender earns above cash.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** LO 81.a: Differentiate between the mechanics of foreign exchange (FX) swaps and cross-currency swaps.

**GARP:** Chapter 17, Covered Interest Parity Lost: Understanding the Cross-Currency Basis, Box 17.1. Schweser 81.a, Foreign Exchange (FX) Swaps. **GARP vs Schweser:** none.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-16 a, where it is Q4 of 11.

a.reason: (Polarity flip). Wide points mean the dollar lender sells the foreign currency forward at a higher, not lower, dollar price, so it earns more than the cash rate. A would be correct if the points were narrower than CIP implies.

b.reason: GARP: a positive (“wide”) value of F − S means a party borrowing US dollars via an FX swap is effectively paying a higher interest rate on the swapped dollars than in the cash market. B matches.

c.reason: (Role misassignment). The cost falls on the dollar borrower (the hedger pays the forward points), not on the dollar lender. C would be correct only if the forward points were narrower than CIP warrants.

d.reason: (Absolute claim). Forward points equal the CIP value only when CIP holds. Wider points are the signature of a CIP failure. D would be correct only if the points matched the CIP value.

questions.question:
The treasurer of an Australian bank arranges a five-year USD/AUD cross-currency basis swap with a US dealer. At inception the bank delivers Australian dollars and receives USD 250 million. The following data are available:

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Spot rate at inception (USD per AUD) | 0.6400 |
| Five-year outright forward rate at inception (USD per AUD) | 0.6215 |
| Spot rate prevailing at maturity (USD per AUD) | 0.7050 |
| Cross-currency basis (bp) | 12 |

At maturity, the bank repays the USD 250 million. Which of the following is closest to the amount of Australian dollars the bank receives in that final exchange?

options.text: AUD 390.63 million
AUD 402.25 million
AUD 354.61 million
AUD 160.00 million

questions.solution:
Australian bank’s five-year USD/AUD cross-currency basis swap: AUD received in the final exchange.

**Concept and theory**

A cross-currency swap is a longer-term contract, typically above one year, in which the parties simultaneously borrow and lend equivalent amounts of two currencies. The principal is exchanged at the start at the spot rate S, and at maturity the borrowed amounts are exchanged back at the initial spot rate S. The interest differential, and any deviation from CIP, is handled by the periodic interest payments, which in a basis swap are each currency’s Libor rate plus the basis b on one leg.

This is the key mechanical contrast with an FX swap, which has no interim payments and therefore must reverse at a pre-agreed forward rate F that already embeds the interest differential. In a cross-currency swap, using F for the final exchange would charge the interest differential twice, once through the coupons and again through the reversal rate. Using the spot rate at maturity would leave the principal unhedged.

The final exchange simply reverses the initial one. With S in USD per AUD, the AUD principal is

$\text{N}_{\text{AUD}} = \frac{\text{N}_{\text{USD}}}{\text{S}_{0}}$ ,

and the same two amounts change hands, in the opposite direction, at maturity whatever the market rate is then.

**Applying it to this question**

$\text{N}_{\text{AUD}} = \frac{\text{N}_{\text{USD}}}{\text{S}_{0}} = \frac{250}{0.6400}$

= AUD 390.625 million ≈ AUD 390.63 million

At maturity the bank pays USD 250 million and receives AUD 390.63 million. The five-year forward rate (0.6215) belongs to an FX swap and is irrelevant. The spot rate at maturity (0.7050) is irrelevant because the rate is fixed at inception. The 12 bp basis affects the periodic interest payments, not the principal re-exchange.

**Fragile fact.** The cross-currency swap reverses at the initial spot rate. Only the FX swap reverses at F.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** LO 81.a: Differentiate between the mechanics of foreign exchange (FX) swaps and cross-currency swaps.

**GARP:** Chapter 17, Covered Interest Parity Lost: Understanding the Cross-Currency Basis, Box 17.1. Schweser 81.a, Cross-Currency Basis Swaps. **GARP vs Schweser:** none.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-16 a, where it is Q5 of 11.

a.reason: GARP: at maturity the borrowed amounts are exchanged back at the initial spot rate S. A follows.

b.reason: (Sibling swap). 250/0.6215 = 402.25 uses the forward rate, which is how an FX swap reverses. It would be correct if the contract were a five-year FX swap reversing at 0.6215.

c.reason: (Scope or condition error). 250/0.7050 = 354.61 uses the spot rate at maturity, which would make the hedge useless because the amount would be unknown at inception. It would be correct only for a later spot conversion with no swap.

questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a Brazilian bank is projecting the cash flows of a three-year cross-currency basis swap in which the bank borrows USD 150 million and lends the equivalent amount of Brazilian reais. Interest is exchanged semiannually (use the annual rate divided by two). The US dollar commands a premium in the swap market. Current data:

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| USD Libor, current fixing (%) | 4.20 |
| BRL reference rate, current fixing (%) | 10.50 |
| Cross-currency basis, b (bp) | 35 |
| Spot rate (USD per BRL) | 0.18 |

Which of the following is closest to the amount the bank pays on the US dollar leg at the next semiannual payment date?

options.text: USD 3.1500 million
USD 6.8250 million
USD 3.4125 million
USD 2.8875 million

questions.solution:
Brazilian bank borrowing USD in a cross-currency basis swap: next semiannual USD-leg payment.

**Concept and theory**

During the life of a cross-currency swap the counterparties periodically exchange interest payments. Each party pays interest in the currency it has borrowed, on the principal of that currency. In a cross-currency basis swap the reference rates are the respective Libor rates plus the basis, b.

Which leg carries the basis? GARP Box 17.1 sets up the case where the US dollar commands a premium (forward points wider than CIP warrants). There, the FX swap implied dollar rate exceeds dollar Libor, and parity between the two instruments holds if the party borrowing US dollars in the cross-currency swap pays b on top of US dollar Libor. Whenever CIP fails, one party pays the basis on top of the cash market rate to borrow its currency, while the other in effect gets an equivalent discount when borrowing the other currency. Schweser puts it the same way: the USD borrower pays the USD rate plus the basis.

For one payment period of length $\tau$ years, the dollar borrower pays

$\text{Payment}_{\text{USD}} = \text{N}_{\text{USD}} \times(\text{L}_{\text{USD}} + \text{b}) \times\tau$,

where $\text{N}_{\text{USD}}$ is the dollar principal borrowed, $\text{L}_{\text{USD}}$ is the dollar Libor fixing and $\tau=$ 0.5 for semiannual payments under the stated convention.

**Applying it to this question**

The bank borrows USD, and the dollar is at a premium, so the bank pays USD Libor plus b:

$\text{L}_{\text{USD}} + \text{b} =$ 4.20% + 0.35% = 4.55%

Annual amount = 150 × 4.55% = USD 6.825 million

Semiannual payment = 6.825 × 0.5 = USD 3.4125 million

The BRL reference rate (10.50%) sets the payment the bank receives on the real leg and is irrelevant to what it pays. The spot rate only fixed the principal at inception.

**Fragile fact.** Actor: with the dollar at a premium, the dollar borrower pays Libor plus b. Payments are per period ($\tau=$ 0.5 here).

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** LO 81.a: Differentiate between the mechanics of foreign exchange (FX) swaps and cross-currency swaps.

**GARP:** Chapter 17, Covered Interest Parity Lost: Understanding the Cross-Currency Basis, Box 17.1. Schweser 81.a, Cross-Currency Basis Swaps. **GARP vs Schweser:** none on who pays (both: USD borrower pays the basis). Schweser adds that the FC borrower pays less than the FC rate by the basis; GARP calls this an “equivalent discount”. The stem applies the basis to the USD leg only, to avoid double counting.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-16 a, where it is Q6 of 11.

a.reason: (Dropped term). 150 × 4.20% × 0.5 = 3.15 omits the basis. It would be correct if CIP held (b = 0), when the swap is a plain floating-for-floating currency swap.

b.reason: (Time-conversion slip). 150 × 4.55% = 6.825 is the annual amount, not the semiannual payment. It would be correct for annual payment dates.

c.reason: The USD borrower pays the basis on top of dollar Libor, on the dollar principal, per period. That gives USD 3.4125 million, so C is correct.

d.reason: (Sign error). 150 × (4.20% − 0.35%) × 0.5 = 2.8875 subtracts the basis. With the dollar at a premium the dollar borrower pays the basis, it does not receive it. D would fit a case where the bank lent dollars and the discount were applied to the dollar leg.

questions.question:
A risk consultant advising a UK building society wants to express the deviation from covered interest parity in the one-year GBP/USD market as a cross-currency basis. Assuming a one-period maturity, she uses the relationship

F $- \text{S} = \text{S} \frac{1 + \text{r} + \text{b}}{1 + \text{r}^{*}} -$ S

and the following data:

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Spot rate, S (USD per GBP) | 1.2600 |
| One-year forward rate, F (USD per GBP) | 1.2740 |
| One-year USD Libor, r (%) | 4.40 |
| One-year GBP Libor, $\text{r}^{*}$ (%) | 3.60 |

Which of the following is closest to the basis, b?
questions.solution:
Risk consultant converts a one-year GBP/USD CIP deviation into a cross-currency basis using the one-period parity relationship.

**Concept and theory**

The cross-currency basis translates the FX swap’s deviation from CIP into an interest rate spread. GARP Box 17.1: if the forward points F − S are greater than warranted by CIP then, assuming a one-period maturity, the basis b is the amount by which the interest rate on one of the legs has to be adjusted so that parity with the pricing of FX swaps holds:

F $- \text{S} = \text{S} \frac{1 + \text{r} + \text{b}}{1 + \text{r}^{*}} -$ S,

with S and F in USD per foreign currency, r the US dollar rate, $\text{r}^{*}$ the foreign rate and b added to the dollar leg. Rearranging:

1 $+ \text{r} + \text{b} = \frac{\text{F}}{\text{S}} ($1 $+ \text{r}^{*}) =\Rightarrow\text{b} = \frac{\text{F}}{\text{S}} ($1 $+ \text{r}^{*}) - ($1 $+ \text{r})$.

The first term is the FX swap implied dollar rate. So b is the gap between the swap-implied and the cash-market cost of dollars, and it is zero when CIP holds. A positive b in this setup means the dollar borrower pays b on top of dollar Libor.

GARP also writes the deviation in the simpler form b $\approx\frac{\text{F}-\text{S}}{\text{S}} - (\text{r} - \text{r}^{*})$, in its discussion of the factors that move the basis, where it assumes $\text{r}^{*}$ is small so that 1 $+ \text{r}^{*} \approx$ 1. That is an approximation. When the stem specifies the one-period relationship, the exact rearrangement must be used.

**Applying it to this question**

$\frac{\text{F}}{\text{S}} = \frac{1.2740}{1.2600} =$ 1.011111

$\frac{\text{F}}{\text{S}} ($1 $+ \text{r}^{*}) =$ 1.011111 × 1.036 = 1.047511

b = 1.047511 − 1.044 = 0.003511 ≈ 35.1 bp

The forward points are about 35 bp per year wider than CIP warrants: the dollar is at a premium, and the dollar borrower in a cross-currency basis swap would pay about 35 bp over dollar Libor.

**Fragile fact.** b $= \frac{\text{F}}{\text{S}} ($1 $+ \text{r}^{*}) - ($1 $+ \text{r})$ with S in USD per foreign currency. Multiply by (1 $+ \text{r}^{*})$, the foreign gross rate, before subtracting (1 $+ \text{r})$.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** LO 81.a: Differentiate between the mechanics of foreign exchange (FX) swaps and cross-currency swaps.

**GARP:** Chapter 17, Covered Interest Parity Lost: Understanding the Cross-Currency Basis, Box 17.1 (one-period parity between FX swap and cross-currency basis swap). Schweser 81.a, Cross-Currency Basis Swaps (formula image missing in the text extraction). **GARP vs Schweser:** none in content. Sign convention caution: GARP’s text calls the post-2007 dollar basis against the euro and yen negative (a quoting convention), while the Box 17.1 algebra, and Schweser, treat b as positive when paid by the dollar borrower. This question uses the Box 17.1 algebra.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-16 a, where it is Q7 of 11.

a.reason: (Dropped term (linear approximation)). $\frac{\text{F}-\text{S}}{\text{S}} - (\text{r} - \text{r}^{*}) =$ 1.1111% − 0.80% = 31.1 bp drops the (1 $+ \text{r}^{*})$ factor. It would be correct if the stem had specified GARP’s approximation b $= \frac{\text{F}-\text{S}}{\text{S}} - (\text{r} - \text{r}^{*})$, or if $\text{r}^{*} \approx$ 0.

b.reason: Solving GARP’s one-period parity equation exactly gives 35.1 bp. B is correct.

c.reason: (Intermediate result). $\frac{\text{F}-\text{S}}{\text{S}} =$ 1.1111% = 111.1 bp is the forward premium before deducting the interest rate differential. It ignores the interest rate differential entirely, which is acceptable only if the two interest rates were equal.

d.reason: (Sign error). $\frac{\text{F}-\text{S}}{\text{S}} + (\text{r} - \text{r}^{*}) =$ 1.1111% + 0.80% = 191.1 bp adds the differential instead of subtracting it, as if the GBP rate exceeded the USD rate by 0.80%.

questions.question: A member of the board risk committee at a Japanese bank is reviewing a five-year cross-currency basis swap in which the bank borrows US dollars from a top-rated European supranational and lends it the equivalent amount of yen. At the time of the trade, covered interest parity does not hold and the US dollar commands a premium in the swap market. Which of the following statements best describes the economics of the swap?

options.text: The supranational, as the party borrowing yen, pays the basis on top of yen Libor, while the bank pays US dollar Libor flat on the dollars it borrows.
Neither party bears the basis, because re-exchanging the principal at the initial spot rate removes any deviation from covered interest parity.
The bank receives the basis on top of US dollar Libor, so its swapped-dollar funding is cheaper than borrowing dollars directly in the cash market.
The bank pays the basis on top of US dollar Libor, so its swapped-dollar funding is dearer than direct cash-market funding, and the supranational in effect borrows yen at a discount.

questions.solution:
Japanese bank borrows USD from a supranational in a five-year cross-currency basis swap with the dollar at a premium: who bears the basis?

**Concept and theory**

GARP defines the cross-currency basis as the amount by which the interest paid to borrow one currency by swapping it against another differs from the cost of borrowing that currency directly in the cash market. A non-zero basis is therefore a violation of CIP.

Box 17.1 shows how a cross-currency basis swap absorbs that violation. If the dollar commands a premium (forward points wider than CIP warrants), the FX swap implied dollar rate exceeds dollar Libor. Parity between the two instruments then holds if the party borrowing US dollars in the cross-currency swap pays the basis b on top of dollar Libor. GARP concludes that failure of CIP has implications for the relative cost of funding in the cash and swap markets: whenever CIP fails, one party pays the currency basis on top of the cash market rates to borrow the corresponding currency, while the other counterparty in effect receives an equivalent discount when borrowing the other currency.

The roles in the reading’s examples line up with this. Japanese banks have funded overseas dollar lending heavily through swaps, and dollar borrowing via swaps has been in higher demand and more costly than in the cash market. Top-rated supranationals, with their funding cost advantage, can issue in dollars and swap the proceeds back into their home currency, “collecting the currency basis”. They are the side that obtains the other currency at an effective discount.

**Applying it to this question**

The Japanese bank is the dollar borrower, and the dollar is at a premium. So the bank pays b on top of dollar Libor, and its swapped dollars cost more than direct cash-market dollars. The supranational, borrowing yen, is the counterparty that in effect borrows yen at a discount. Option D states both halves.

**Fragile fact.** Actor and direction: dollar at a premium, so the dollar borrower pays b on top of Libor and the other side borrows its currency at an equivalent discount.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** LO 81.a: Differentiate between the mechanics of foreign exchange (FX) swaps and cross-currency swaps.

**GARP:** Chapter 17, Covered Interest Parity Lost: Understanding the Cross-Currency Basis, opening section and Box 17.1; Section 17.3 (Tighter Limits to Arbitrage and the Basis), on supranationals collecting the basis. Schweser 81.a, Cross-Currency Basis Swaps. **GARP vs** **Schweser:** none in substance. Schweser phrases the discount as the FC borrower paying less than the FC rate by the basis.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-16 a, where it is Q8 of 11.

a.reason: (Role misassignment). It puts the basis on the yen borrower. With the dollar at a premium, the dollar borrower pays. A would be correct if the yen, not the dollar, commanded the premium.

b.reason: (Scope or condition error). Re-exchanging at the initial spot rate is standard cross-currency swap mechanics and does not remove the basis. b = 0 only if CIP holds, and the stem says it does not. B would be correct if CIP held.

c.reason: (Polarity flip). The dollar borrower pays the basis, it does not receive it, so its swapped funding is dearer, not cheaper. C would be correct only if the dollar traded at a discount in the swap market.

d.reason: GARP: the party borrowing US dollars pays the basis on top of dollar Libor, and the other counterparty in effect receives an equivalent discount on the other currency. D matches.

questions.question: The treasurer of a Canadian non-financial company has two US dollar needs. Need 1: USD for three months to bridge a seasonal working capital gap, funded by surplus Canadian dollar cash. Need 2: USD for seven years, funded by the proceeds of a new seven-year Canadian dollar floating-rate bond, with the currency exposure hedged over the life of the bond. Which of the following choices and reasons is most accurate?

options.text: FX swap for need 1, as it exchanges at spot and reverses at a pre-agreed forward rate; cross-currency swap for need 2, as it is longer-term, exchanges periodic interest and re-exchanges at the initial spot rate.
Cross-currency swap for need 1, as it is typically under one year and has no interim payments; FX swap for need 2, as it is longer-term and exchanges periodic interest payments.
FX swap for both needs, as FX swaps are typically longer than one year and include periodic interest payments that can match the coupons on the floating-rate bond.
Cross-currency swap for both needs, as only a cross-currency swap fixes the final exchange rate in advance; an FX swap reverses at the spot rate prevailing at maturity.

questions.solution:
Canadian corporate treasurer chooses between an FX swap and a cross-currency swap for a three-month and a seven-year USD need.

**Concept and theory**

The two instruments do the same basic job: simultaneous borrowing of one currency and lending of another, with no open currency position. They are built for different horizons and cash flow profiles.

|  | FX swap | Cross-currency swap |
|---|---|---|
| Horizon | Short-term | Longer-term, typically above one year |
| Cash flows | Two exchanges only | Two exchanges plus periodic interest |
| Reversal rate | Pre-agreed forward F | Initial spot S |
| Cost shown in | Forward points F − S | Libor plus basis b |

A short, one-off funding gap suits an FX swap. One spot exchange and one forward reversal fix the round trip at inception, and the implicit interest sits in F − S. A long-dated liability with periodic interest suits a cross-currency swap. Its periodic interest payments can be matched to the liability’s coupons, and its principal re-exchange at the initial spot rate fixes the currency value of the repayment. GARP’s reverse yankee example is exactly this: US firms issuing long-term euro bonds (average maturity around 10 years) and swapping the proceeds into dollars, which increases demand for cross-currency swaps.

Both instruments fix the reversal rate at inception. The difference is which rate (forward versus initial spot) and whether interest flows separately.

**Applying it to this question**

Need 1 is three months with no interim coupon: FX swap. Need 2 is seven years with floating coupons to service: cross-currency swap, with periodic interest exchanged and principal re-exchanged at the initial spot rate. Option A gives both the right pairing and the right reasons.

**Fragile fact.** Both swaps fix the far-leg rate at inception: the FX swap at F, the cross-currency swap at the initial S. The tenor distinction is short versus typically above one year.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** LO 81.a: Differentiate between the mechanics of foreign exchange (FX) swaps and cross-currency swaps.

**GARP:** Chapter 17, Covered Interest Parity Lost: Understanding the Cross-Currency Basis, Box 17.1; Box 17.2 (Reverse yankee issuance in the euro and the EUR/USD basis). Schweser 81.a. **GARP vs Schweser:** none. Boundary: Box 17.2 is used only for the instrument-choice illustration; hedging demand as a driver of the basis belongs to LO 81.c.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-16 a, where it is Q9 of 11.

a.reason: GARP: an FX swap exchanges at S and repays at the pre-agreed F. A cross-currency swap is longer-term, typically above one year, exchanges periodic interest and re-exchanges at the initial S. A uses exactly these attributes.

b.reason: (Sibling swap). It swaps the two instruments’ attributes, giving the cross-currency swap a sub-one-year tenor with no interim payments and the FX swap periodic interest. It would be correct only if the labels in B were interchanged.

c.reason: (Sibling swap). Long tenor and periodic interest belong to the cross-currency swap, not the FX swap. C would describe a cross-currency swap used for both needs, with a weaker fit for need 1.

d.reason: (Polarity flip (fixed versus floating reversal rate)). An FX swap reverses at the pre-agreed forward rate, not the spot rate at maturity, so it also fixes the final exchange in advance. D would be correct only if an FX swap’s far leg were left open.

questions.question: A portfolio manager at a US hedge fund observes that the US dollar is cheaper in terms of yen in the one-year forward market than covered interest parity stipulates. The fund can borrow US dollars at prevailing cash-market rates and can trade USD/JPY FX swaps. Which of the following strategies would exploit the deviation?

options.text: Borrow yen in the cash market, and enter an FX swap that sells yen for dollars at spot today and repurchases the yen at the forward rate.
Borrow dollars in the cash market, sell them for yen at spot today, and buy the dollars back at the spot rate prevailing in one year.
Borrow dollars in the cash market, and enter an FX swap that sells dollars for yen at spot today and repurchases the dollars at the forward rate.
Borrow dollars in the cash market and enter the same FX swap, which earns a profit only if the yen spot rate appreciates against the dollar by maturity.

questions.solution:
Hedge fund portfolio manager exploits a USD/JPY CIP deviation in which the dollar is cheap in yen terms forward.

**Concept and theory**

CIP says there are two equivalent ways to hold dollars for a period: invest them at the dollar rate r, or convert them to the foreign currency at S, invest at $\text{r}^{*}$, and lock in the conversion back at F. If the two routes give different results, a riskless profit exists in principle. Schweser introduces FX swaps and cross-currency swaps under this LO as the two ways to exploit such a violation.

GARP’s opening gives the FX swap version directly. If the dollar is cheaper in terms of yen in the forward market than CIP stipulates, anyone able to borrow dollars at cash market rates could profit by entering an FX swap: selling dollars for yen at the spot rate today and repurchasing them cheaply at the forward rate. The FX swap does the two currency legs in one contract. Because both legs are fixed at inception, the trade carries no open currency position. The profit per dollar, ignoring frictions, is $\frac{\text{F}}{\text{S}} ($1 $+ \text{r}^{*}) - ($1 $+ \text{r})$, the same quantity as the basis in the one-period parity relationship.

GARP then explains why, in practice, this does not close the gap: the trade needs balance sheet, credit lines and capital, and those costs are now priced (LO 81.c). The mechanics, however, are as above.

**Applying it to this question**

The dollar is cheap forward, so you want to buy dollars forward. You get yen to fund that purchase by selling dollars at spot, and those dollars are borrowed in the cash market. That is option C: borrow dollars, enter an FX swap that sells dollars for yen at spot and repurchases them at the forward rate.

**Fragile fact.** Cheap forward dollar: borrow dollars cash, sell them spot, buy them back forward. The profit is fixed at inception.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** LO 81.a: Differentiate between the mechanics of foreign exchange (FX) swaps and cross-currency swaps.

**GARP:** Chapter 17, Covered Interest Parity Lost: Understanding the Cross-Currency Basis, opening section (FX swap example) and Box 17.1. Schweser 81.a (introduction: FX swaps and cross-currency swaps as two ways to exploit CIP violations). **GARP vs Schweser:** none. Boundary: why arbitrage does not close the basis is LO 81.c and is not tested.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-16 a, where it is Q10 of 11.

a.reason: (Polarity flip). Borrowing yen and buying the yen back forward means buying the expensive leg forward. That locks in a loss. A would be correct if the dollar were dearer in yen terms forward than CIP stipulates.

b.reason: (Scope or condition error). Reversing at the future spot rate drops the forward leg, so the position becomes an open currency bet with no arbitrage profit locked in. B would describe an uncovered carry trade, not CIP arbitrage.

c.reason: This is GARP’s own example: borrow dollars at cash market rates, sell dollars for yen at spot through an FX swap, and repurchase the dollars cheaply at the forward rate. C is correct.

d.reason: (Scope or condition error). The trade legs are right, but the profit is locked in at inception by the pre-agreed forward rate. It does not depend on the yen’s later moves. D would be correct only for an unhedged position.

questions.question: A banking supervisor at a Hong Kong regulator is reviewing a bank’s internal training material on cross-currency basis swaps against the US dollar. Which of the following statements in the material is NOT correct?

options.text: In a cross-currency basis swap, the reference rates on the two legs are the respective Libor rates plus the basis.
The cross-currency basis is the same quantity as the forward points, F − S, quoted on the matching FX swap.
A non-zero basis means borrowing a currency by swapping another currency into it costs a different amount than borrowing it directly in the cash market.
If covered interest parity holds over the life of the contract, the basis is zero and the swap is a plain floating-for-floating currency swap.

questions.solution:
Hong Kong supervisor reviews training material on cross-currency basis swaps: identify the statement that is NOT correct.

**Concept and theory**

The basis and the forward points measure the same CIP deviation through different instruments, but they are different quantities.

- Forward points, F − S, are the FX swap’s quote. They are an exchange rate difference, in USD per unit of foreign currency, and they contain the whole interest differential. Under CIP they equal S $( \frac{1+\text{r}}{1+\text{r}^{*}} -$ 1$)$, which is generally non-zero.
- The basis, b, is the cross-currency basis swap’s quote. It is an interest rate spread on one leg: the reference rates are the respective Libor rates plus the basis. In GARP’s one-period relationship, F $- \text{S} = \text{S} \frac{1+\text{r}+\text{b}}{1+\text{r}^{*}} -$ S, it is the adjustment that makes the cross-currency swap consistent with FX swap pricing.

GARP defines the cross-currency basis as the amount by which the interest paid to borrow one currency by swapping it against another differs from the cost of directly borrowing it in the cash market. So a non-zero basis is a violation of CIP, and when CIP holds the basis is zero. Schweser adds that, in that case, the cross-currency basis swap is simply a straightforward floating-for-floating currency swap.

The forward points, by contrast, are zero only if the two interest rates are equal. They can be large while CIP holds exactly.

**Applying it to this question**

Check each statement. A matches GARP’s description of the reference rates. C is GARP’s definition of the basis. D is the zero-basis case (Schweser wording on floating-for-floating). B equates the basis with the forward points. That is false: points are the FX swap’s exchange rate quote containing the full interest differential, while the basis is only the deviation from CIP, expressed as an interest spread.

**Fragile fact.** Forward points ̸= basis. Points contain the whole interest differential; the basis is only the deviation from CIP, as a spread on one leg.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** LO 81.a: Differentiate between the mechanics of foreign exchange (FX) swaps and cross-currency swaps.

**GARP:** Chapter 17, Covered Interest Parity Lost: Understanding the Cross-Currency Basis, opening section and Box 17.1. Schweser 81.a, Cross-Currency Basis Swaps. **GARP vs Schweser:** none. “Floating-for-floating currency swap” wording in D is Schweser-only (condensed source).

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-16 a, where it is Q11 of 11.

a.reason: (True statement, not the exception). GARP: in a cross-currency basis swap the reference rates are the respective Libor rates plus the basis b. It would be the answer only if it said the legs paid Libor flat with the basis exchanged at maturity.

b.reason: Forward points are an exchange rate quote. The basis is the interest-rate adjustment that reconciles the cross-currency swap with FX swap pricing. They are not the same quantity, so B is the incorrect statement and the answer.

c.reason: (True statement, not the exception). This paraphrases GARP’s definition of the cross-currency basis. It would be the answer only if it claimed the swap and cash-market costs are always equal.

d.reason: (True statement, not the exception). With CIP holding, b = 0 and the contract is a plain floating-for-floating currency swap (Schweser wording; consistent with GARP’s statement that a non-zero basis signals a CIP violation). It would be the answer only if it claimed the basis could be non-zero while CIP holds.

questions.loText: Identify key factors that affect the cross-currency swap basis.

questions.question: A senior risk analyst at a Canadian pension fund is preparing a training session for newly hired analysts on why the cross-currency basis can move away from zero. She drafts four candidate statements for her opening slide. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Deviations from covered interest parity (CIP) arise mainly because cash-market interest rates adjust to imbalances in FX swap demand, while the forward rate is taken as given.
In the textbook framework, CIP arbitrage is treated as riskless because the arbitrageur holds an open currency position that is fully collateralised.
Because the cash and spot markets are much larger than FX derivatives markets, it is mainly shifts in demand for FX swaps or currency swaps that push the forward rate away from CIP.
Once credit, counterparty, market and liquidity risks become non-negligible, the basis is guaranteed to be negative for every currency against the US dollar.

questions.solution:
Training slide: what pushes the basis away from zero in the CIP framework.

**Concept and theory**

Covered interest parity (CIP) says that once currency risk is hedged with a forward, the interest rates on two otherwise identical assets in two currencies must be equal. With S and F quoted in US dollars per unit of foreign currency (FC), r the USD rate and $\text{r}^{*}$ the FC rate,

$\frac{\text{F}}{\text{S}} = \frac{1 + \text{r}}{1 + \text{r}^{*}}$ .

The cross-currency basis b is the amount by which the interest rate on one leg must be adjusted so that parity with observed FX swap prices holds; a non-zero basis means CIP has failed. GARP’s framework starts from the question of which price moves. Cash-market interest rates and the spot exchange rate can be taken as given because those markets are far larger than the markets for FX derivatives. It is therefore primarily shifts in the demand for FX swaps or currency swaps that push the forward rate away from CIP and create a non-zero basis. In an ideal world any such gap would be closed instantly by arbitrage, because CIP arbitrage is treated as riskless: by construction an FX swap entails no open currency position, and the credit, counterparty, market and liquidity risks involved are assumed negligible, with unimpaired access to cash and derivatives markets. The key factors in this LO (market illiquidity and risk premia) are precisely the real-world breaches of those assumptions.

| Element | Role in the framework |
|---|---|
| r, $\text{r}^{*}$, S | Taken as given (large markets) |
| F | Moves with demand for FX swaps or currency swaps |
| Arbitrage | Riskless only if risks are negligible and access is unimpaired |

**Applying it to this question**

The question asks for the statement that correctly describes the mechanism. Only one statement places the adjustment in the forward rate and gives the reason (relative market size).

**Fragile fact.** The variable that moves is F (the forward leg), not S or the cash interest rates.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** LO 81.b: Identify key factors that affect the cross-currency swap basis.

**GARP:** Chapter 17, Section 17.1 A Framework and Box 17.1 (CIP, FX swaps, cross-currency swaps and the factors that move the basis); introduction (sign of the basis by currency). **GARP** **vs Schweser:** none on this point; Schweser does not discuss which price adjusts.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-16 b, where it is Q1 of 11.

a.reason: (Role misassignment). It assigns the adjustment to the wrong variable: in GARP the cash-market rates are taken as given and the forward rate is what moves. It would be correct only in a world where FX derivatives markets dwarfed cash money markets.

b.reason: (Polarity flip). GARP says FX swaps do not entail an open currency position; that is why textbook arbitrage is riskless. The statement would be correct only if the arbitrage were an unhedged (uncovered) trade.

c.reason: GARP states that cash rates and spot can be taken as given because those markets are much larger, so shifts in demand for FX swaps or currency swaps drive forward rates away from CIP. Option C restates this.

d.reason: (Absolute claim). Non-negligible risks can cause CIP to fail, but nothing guarantees a sign: GARP notes the basis has been negative against the euro and yen yet positive for the Australian dollar. It would be correct only as a statement about some currencies over some periods.

questions.question: A treasury analyst at a Singapore bank is reviewing a stress episode in which the bid-ask spreads on SGD/USD spot and forward transactions widened sharply. Over the same period, interbank credit spreads and sovereign CDS spreads were essentially unchanged, yet a CIP deviation computed from mid quotes persisted for several weeks. The analyst must explain to the head of treasury why arbitrageurs lending US dollars did not close the deviation. Which of the following explanations is most accurate?

options.text: Market liquidity has fallen; the arbitrageur buys SGD at the spot ask and sells SGD forward at the forward bid, so wider spreads raise transaction costs and can eliminate the apparent profit.
Market liquidity has fallen; the arbitrageur buys SGD at the spot bid and sells SGD forward at the forward ask, so wider spreads add to the arbitrage profit and the basis should close faster.
A risk premium has emerged; the wider bid-ask spreads signal higher counterparty credit risk in the interbank market, so the deviation is best measured with the Libor-OIS spread.
Market liquidity has fallen; wider bid-ask spreads affect the basis only once the hedging demand for SGD exceeds the credit limits that arbitrageurs set on their counterparties.

questions.solution:
SGD/USD stress episode: wider bid-ask spreads and why arbitrageurs did not close the gap.

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s Box 17.1 lists the factors that can make CIP fail. The first is market liquidity in the underlying instruments. If market liquidity evaporates, the difference between bid and ask prices for spot and forward transactions becomes non-trivial. A CIP deviation computed from mid quotes then overstates what an arbitrageur can actually earn, because the arbitrageur must trade at the unfavourable side of each quote. Take the USD-lending arbitrage in USD per FC terms: the arbitrageur sells dollars for FC spot, which means buying FC at the spot ask $\text{S}^{\text{a}}$, and simultaneously agrees to sell the FC forward, which means dealing at the forward bid $\text{F}^{\text{b}}$. GARP denotes exactly these two prices when it writes the deviation attributable to a drop in market liquidity. Schweser condenses the same idea: the lack of liquidity in the underlying forward and spot FX contracts, typically caused by a financial crisis, widens bid-ask spreads, raises the transaction costs of executing the FX swap and eliminates the arbitrage opportunity. The basis therefore stays away from zero not because anyone is mispricing risk, but because the round trip costs more than the deviation pays.

| Factor | Source of friction | Typical measure |
|---|---|---|
| Market liquidity | Bid-ask on spot and forward FX | Bid-ask spreads |
| Counterparty risk premium | Interbank (Libor) borrowing and lending | Libor-OIS spread |
| Sovereign risk premium | Government bonds used in the arbitrage | Sovereign CDS spreads |

**Applying it to this question**

The stem isolates the liquidity channel: bid-ask spreads widened while interbank credit spreads and sovereign CDS were unchanged, which rules out the two risk-premium channels. The deciding facts are (i) which side of each quote the USD lender trades on and (ii) that wider spreads add cost.

**Fragile fact.** The USD lender (buyer of FC spot, seller of FC forward) deals at $\text{S}^{\text{a}} \text{and F}^{\text{b}}$; wider spreads always hurt the arbitrageur.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** LO 81.b: Identify key factors that affect the cross-currency swap basis.

**GARP:** Chapter 17, Box 17.1, paragraph beginning “A number of factors can cause CIP to fail”. **GARP vs Schweser:** consistent; Schweser ties the liquidity factor to times of financial crisis, while GARP states it generally.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-16 b, where it is Q2 of 11.

a.reason: Option A names the factor (fall in market liquidity), the correct executable prices (spot ask, forward bid) and the effect (higher transaction costs that can wipe out the apparent profit), matching Box 17.1 and Schweser LO 81.b.

b.reason: (Polarity flip). It reverses the sides of the quotes and the sign of the effect. A buyer pays the ask and a seller receives the bid, so wider spreads reduce profit. It would be correct only for a market maker who earns the spread rather than an arbitrageur who pays it.

c.reason: (Sibling swap). It attributes the liquidity factor to the counterparty-risk sibling. Libor-OIS measures interbank counterparty credit risk, which the stem says was unchanged. It would be correct if Libor-OIS had jumped while FX bid-ask spreads stayed tight.

d.reason: (Scope or condition error). It adds a condition the source does not impose. Illiquidity is a stand-alone factor that works through transaction costs; hedging demand and credit limits relate to the risk-premium channel. It would be correct only if the question concerned balance sheet costs rather than bid-ask spreads.

questions.question:
A junior risk analyst at an Australian asset manager is checking whether a EUR/USD CIP deviation is exploitable by an arbitrageur who lends US dollars (buys EUR spot and sells EUR forward). Quotes are in USD per EUR; interest rates are three-month rates expressed for the three-month period (not annualised).

| Item | Bid | Ask |
|---|---|---|
| Spot rate | 1.0840 | 1.0860 |
| Three-month forward rate | 1.0905 | 1.0935 |

- USD three-month rate r: 0.55%; EUR three-month rate $\text{r}^{*}$: 0.05%
- EUR sovereign CDS spread: 45 bp; trade notional: EUR 50 million

Following the GARP reading, the analyst computes b $= \frac{\text{F}-\text{S}}{\text{S}} - (\text{r} - \text{r}^{*})$, replacing mid quotes with the executable quotes for this trade. Which of the following is closest to the deviation available to the arbitrageur, and what does it imply?

options.text: +37.6 bp, so the arbitrage remains profitable after transaction costs
+14.5 bp, so the arbitrage remains profitable after transaction costs
+41.4 bp, so the arbitrage remains profitable after transaction costs
−8.6 bp, so the apparent opportunity is eliminated by transaction costs

questions.solution:
EUR/USD deviation from mid quotes versus executable quotes for a USD-lending arbitrageur.

**Concept and theory**

When market liquidity is good, bid and ask are close and the deviation computed from mid quotes is a fair guide to the arbitrage profit. GARP’s general deviation expression is

b $= \frac{\text{F} - \text{S}}{\text{S}} - (\text{r} - \text{r}^{*})$,

where S and F are USD per FC, r is the USD rate and $\text{r}^{*}$ the FC rate for the period. When liquidity evaporates, GARP rewrites the deviation using the prices at which the arbitrage can actually be executed, the spot ask $\text{S}^{\text{a}}$ and the forward bid $\text{F}^{\text{b}}$ (and simplifies by assuming $\text{r}^{*}$ is small). The intuition is the cost of a round trip: the arbitrageur lending dollars buys FC at the higher spot price and sells it forward at the lower forward price, so each widening of the spreads eats into the forward premium $(\text{F} - \text{S})$/S that the arbitrageur earns relative to the interest differential. If the executable deviation is zero or negative, the apparent mispricing cannot be harvested, and the basis can persist even though nothing about credit risk has changed. This is why Schweser describes the illiquidity factor as one that eliminates the arbitrage opportunity through transaction costs. Note that the formula is linear in the forward premium; it is an approximation of the exact parity condition, adequate for short periods and small rates.

**Applying it to this question**

Formula first: $\text{b}_{\text{exec}} = \frac{\text{F}^{\text{b}} - \text{S}^{\text{a}}}{\text{S}^{\text{a}}} - (\text{r} - \text{r}^{*})$.

Interest differential r $- \text{r}^{*} =$ 0.55% − 0.05% = 0.50% = 50.0 bp

Executable forward premium $= \frac{1.0905 - 1.0860}{1.0860} = \frac{0.0045}{1.0860} =$ 0.4144% = 41.4 bp

$\text{b}_{\text{exec}} =$ 41.4 − 50.0 = −8.6 bp

Mid quotes (for comparison): $\text{S}^{\text{m}} =$ 1.0850, $\text{F}^{\text{m}} =$ 1.0920

$\text{b}_{\text{mid}} = \frac{1.0920 - 1.0850}{1.0850} -$ 0.50% = 64.5 − 50.0 = 14.5 bp

The mid-quote deviation of +14.5 bp looks like an opportunity, but at executable prices the USD lender earns 8.6 bp less than the interest differential, so there is no profit. The EUR sovereign CDS spread and the EUR 50 million notional are irrelevant: CDS spreads matter only for arbitrage using government bonds, and the deviation is a rate, independent of size.

**Fragile fact.** The USD lender buys FC at the spot ask and sells it forward at the forward bid; always subtract $(\text{r} - \text{r}^{*})$ from the forward premium.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** LO 81.b: Identify key factors that affect the cross-currency swap basis.

**GARP:** Chapter 17, Box 17.1 (market liquidity paragraph, “Denoting by $\text{S}^{\text{a}}$ the spot ask rate and by $\text{F}^{\text{b}}$ the forward bid rate”). **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser gives no formula. **Garbled-source** **caution:** the right-hand side of GARP’s liquidity formula is garbled in the extraction; this question relies only on the stated substitution of $\text{S}^{\text{a}} \text{and F}^{\text{b}}$ into the general deviation expression, which the stem specifies.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-16 b, where it is Q3 of 11.

a.reason: (Wrong input twin). Uses the spot bid and forward ask, the other side of each quote: (1.0935 − 1.0840)/1.0840 − 0.50% = 87.6 − 50.0 = 37.6 bp. It would be correct for an arbitrageur who could sell FC spot at the bid and buy it forward at the ask, which is not the USD-lending trade.

b.reason: (Wrong input twin). Uses mid quotes: 64.5 − 50.0 = 14.5 bp. This ignores the bid-ask spreads that are the whole point of the liquidity factor. It would be correct only if spreads were negligible, as in liquid markets.

c.reason: (Dropped term). Computes only the executable forward premium, 41.4 bp, and forgets to subtract the interest differential r $- \text{r}^{*}$. It would be correct only if the two interest rates were equal.

d.reason: Using the prices the USD lender actually trades at gives −8.6 bp; the liquidity factor has removed the opportunity, exactly the mechanism in Box 17.1 and Schweser LO 81.b.

questions.question: The CRO of a Japanese bank is reviewing a past episode for the board. At the time, the bank’s CIP arbitrage desk funded and invested by borrowing and lending unsecured in the USD and JPY Libor markets. Within a few weeks the three-month Libor-OIS spread rose from about 10 bp to about 150 bp, while bid-ask spreads on USD/JPY spot and forward quotes and sovereign CDS spreads on both governments were broadly stable. The cross-currency basis moved sharply away from zero. Which of the following best identifies the factor at work and how it is measured?

options.text: Reduced market liquidity in the underlying FX instruments, best measured by spot and forward bid-ask spreads
A risk premium from higher counterparty credit risk in interbank markets, best measured by the Libor-OIS spread
A risk premium from higher sovereign credit risk in the two bond markets, best measured by sovereign CDS spreads
A fall in the risk premium, because a higher Libor-OIS spread raises the return to interbank lending and narrows the basis

questions.solution:
Libor-OIS jump while FX bid-ask and sovereign CDS are stable: which factor moved the basis.

**Concept and theory**

The second family of factors in GARP’s Box 17.1 is credit risk in the instruments used to carry out the arbitrage. CIP arbitrage is not done in a vacuum: the arbitrageur must borrow one currency and lend the other. If the arbitrage is conducted by global banks borrowing and lending in the respective Libor (unsecured interbank) markets, then a rise in counterparty credit risk in those interbank markets makes the lending leg risky, and arbitrageurs demand a risk premium before committing funds. GARP notes that this counterparty risk is typically captured using Libor-OIS spreads: Libor is an unsecured term rate that embeds bank credit risk, while the overnight indexed swap (OIS) rate is close to risk-free, so their difference isolates interbank credit and funding stress. GARP’s introduction records that the first explanation for post-2007 CIP violations was exactly this channel: heightened concerns about counterparty risk and constrained bank access to wholesale dollar funding inhibited arbitrage during the Global Financial Crisis and again during the euro area sovereign debt crisis. Schweser summarises the factor as risk premia arising from increases in counterparty credit risk, alongside sovereign credit risk measured by sovereign CDS spreads. The key skill is matching the instrument used in the arbitrage to the risk measure.

| Arbitrage carried out via | Risk premium measured by |
|---|---|
| Interbank (Libor) borrowing and lending | Libor-OIS spread |
| Government bonds in both currencies | Sovereign CDS spreads |

**Applying it to this question**

The desk used unsecured Libor borrowing and lending; Libor-OIS jumped from 10 bp to 150 bp; FX bid-ask spreads and sovereign CDS spreads were stable. This isolates the counterparty-risk premium as the factor, measured by Libor-OIS.

**Fragile fact.** Libor-OIS goes with interbank (Libor) arbitrage by banks; sovereign CDS goes with government-bond arbitrage.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** LO 81.b: Identify key factors that affect the cross-currency swap basis.

**GARP:** Chapter 17, Box 17.1 (“CIP can also fail because of credit risks in the underlying investments”); introduction (GFC and euro area crisis). **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser locates counterparty risk “in the underlying FX markets”; GARP locates it in the interbank (Libor) markets used for the arbitrage and names Libor-OIS. GARP is followed.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-16 b, where it is Q4 of 11.

a.reason: (Sibling swap). It names the market-liquidity sibling. Bid-ask spreads were stable in the stem. It would be correct if FX bid-ask spreads had widened while Libor-OIS stayed flat.

b.reason: Option B matches GARP’s statement that if banks arbitrage in Libor markets, a rise in interbank counterparty credit risk, captured by Libor-OIS spreads, can produce CIP deviations.

c.reason: (Sibling swap). It names the sovereign-risk sibling. Sovereign CDS spreads matter when the arbitrage uses government bonds, and they were stable here. It would be correct for a bond-based arbitrage during a sovereign spread shock.

d.reason: (Polarity flip). Higher counterparty risk raises, not lowers, the premium arbitrageurs require, so it pushes the basis away from zero. It would be correct only if Libor-OIS had fallen sharply.

questions.question:
An internal auditor at a UK insurer is reviewing a risk consultant’s note that pairs each type of CIP arbitrageur with the indicator that best captures its risk premium or cost of arbitrage, rp:

I. A global bank arbitraging by borrowing and lending in the respective Libor markets: the Libor-OIS spread.

II. A bank or asset manager arbitraging with government bonds in the two currencies: sovereign CDS spreads.

III. A hedge fund relying on collateralised markets to fund the arbitrage: the price and availability of repo funding.

IV. A top-rated supranational issuing USD bonds and swapping the proceeds: bid-ask spreads on spot FX transactions.

Which of the pairings are consistent with the GARP reading?

options.text: I and II only
I, II, III and IV
I, II and III only
II and III only

questions.solution:
Pairing arbitrageur types with the indicator of their risk premium or cost of arbitrage.

**Concept and theory**

GARP generalises the credit-risk factors with a single symbol. If r and $\text{r}^{*}$ are risk-free rates and rp is the risk premium for the underlying investment over the life of the swap, the deviation measured with risk-free rates is b $= \frac{\text{F}-\text{S}}{\text{S}} - (\text{r} - \text{r}^{*}) =$ rp. The important point for this LO is that what rp represents depends on who is doing the arbitrage and with which instruments. GARP gives four cases. Global banks arbitraging through the Libor markets face interbank counterparty risk, captured by Libor-OIS spreads. Banks or asset managers arbitraging with government bonds face differences in sovereign credit risk, measured by sovereign CDS spreads. Highly rated supranational and quasi-government agencies arbitrage the long-term basis by issuing US dollar bonds at attractive rates and swapping them out; for them rp is more closely related to the costs of placing bonds in different currencies. Hedge funds, which rely on collateralised markets to fund CIP arbitrage, face an rp in which the price and availability of repo funding play a significant role. Bid-ask spreads on spot FX belong to the separate market-liquidity factor, not to any arbitrageur’s risk premium.

| Arbitrageur | What drives rp |
|---|---|
| Global bank (Libor markets) | Interbank counterparty risk (Libor-OIS) |
| Bank or asset manager (government bonds) | Sovereign credit risk (sovereign CDS) |
| Top-rated supranational or agency | Costs of placing bonds in different currencies |
| Hedge fund | Price and availability of repo funding |

**Applying it to this question**

Check each pairing against the table: I matches, II matches, III matches, IV pairs the supranational with a liquidity measure instead of bond placement costs, so IV is wrong.

**Fragile fact.** Supranationals: bond placement costs; hedge funds: repo. Bid-ask spreads are a liquidity factor, not anyone’s rp.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** LO 81.b: Identify key factors that affect the cross-currency swap basis.

**GARP:** Chapter 17, Box 17.1 (credit risk paragraph and “The specific constraints . . . will also depend on the players acting as arbitrageurs”). **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser mentions only counterparty and sovereign credit risk; the supranational and hedge fund cases are GARP-only.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-16 b, where it is Q5 of 11.

a.reason: (Scope or condition error). It drops III, treating rp as purely a credit-risk measure. GARP explicitly says that for hedge funds the price and availability of repo funding plays a significant role. It would be correct if the note were restricted to credit risk premia.

b.reason: (Sibling swap). It accepts IV, which swaps in the market-liquidity measure for the supranational’s actual cost driver, the cost of placing bonds in different currencies. It would be correct only if IV named bond placement costs.

c.reason: Pairings I, II and III reproduce GARP’s Box 17.1 statements, so “I, II and III only” is the answer.

d.reason: (Scope or condition error). It rejects I, as if interbank counterparty risk were irrelevant to banks arbitraging in Libor markets. GARP names Libor-OIS for exactly that case. It would be correct only if the bank arbitraged with secured or government-bond funding.

questions.question:
A portfolio manager at a Brazilian multi-asset fund wants to isolate the risk premium embedded in the one-year GBP/USD basis. Quotes are in USD per GBP.

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Spot rate S | 1.2500 |
| One-year forward rate F | 1.2610 |
| One-year USD risk-free rate r (%) | 4.20 |
| One-year GBP risk-free rate $\text{r}^{*}$ (%) | 3.50 |
| One-year USD Libor (%) | 4.60 |
| One-year GBP Libor (%) | 3.75 |

Using b $= \frac{\text{F}-\text{S}}{\text{S}} - (\text{r} - \text{r}^{*}) =$ rp, which of the following is closest to the risk premium rp for the underlying investment over the life of the swap?

options.text: 18 bp
3 bp
88 bp
158 bp

questions.solution:
One-year GBP/USD quotes: backing out the risk premium using risk-free rates.

**Concept and theory**

GARP shows that a measured CIP deviation is not necessarily a free lunch. Suppose r and $\text{r}^{*}$ are the risk-free rates in the two currencies and rp is the risk premium on the underlying investment over the duration of the swap. Measured with risk-free rates, the deviation is

b $= \frac{\text{F} - \text{S}}{\text{S}} - (\text{r} - \text{r}^{*}) =$ rp,

where S and F are in USD per FC (here GBP), $(\text{F} - \text{S})$/S is the forward premium of the FC, and $(\text{r} - \text{r}^{*})$ is the risk-free interest differential. The interpretation is that the arbitrageur who appears to earn b is actually being paid for bearing the risk of the instruments used (interbank lending, government bonds and so on). If the arbitrage could be executed in genuinely risk-free instruments, rp would be zero and so would b. A consequence for the analyst is that the choice of rates matters: if risky rates such as Libor are used for r and $\text{r}^{*}$, part of the risk premium is already embedded in the differential and the computed b no longer isolates rp. GARP also gives the exact version F $- \text{S} = \text{S} \frac{1+\text{r}+\text{b}}{1+\text{r}^{*}} -$ S; the linear form above is the approximation specified in the question.

**Applying it to this question**

Forward premium $\frac{\text{F} - \text{S}}{\text{S}} = \frac{1.2610 - 1.2500}{1.2500} = \frac{0.0110}{1.2500} =$ 0.88% = 88 bp

Risk-free differential r $- \text{r}^{*} =$ 4.20% − 3.50% = 0.70% = 70 bp

rp $= \text{b} =$ 88 − 70 = 18 bp

The USD and GBP Libor rates are deliberately irrelevant: the formula equates b to rp only when r and $\text{r}^{*}$ are risk-free. (The exact form, 1.0088 × 1.035 − 1.042, gives about 21 bp, still closest to 18 bp.) A positive 18 bp means the forward premium exceeds what the risk-free differential warrants by 18 bp, which compensates for the risk of the underlying investment.

**Fragile fact.** b = rp only when r and $\text{r}^{*}$ are risk-free rates; with Libor the premium is partly hidden in the differential.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** LO 81.b: Identify key factors that affect the cross-currency swap basis.

**GARP:** Chapter 17, Box 17.1 (“More generally, suppose r and $\text{r}^{*}$ are the respective risk-free rates. . . ”). **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser does not give this expression; GARP-only.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-16 b, where it is Q6 of 11.

a.reason: Option A applies GARP’s expression with risk-free rates, as the question specifies.

b.reason: (Wrong input twin). Uses the Libor rates instead of the risk-free rates: 88 − (4.60 − 3.75) × 100 = 88 − 85 = 3 bp. It would be correct only if the question asked for the deviation measured against Libor, which does not isolate rp.

c.reason: (Dropped term). Reports only the forward premium, 88 bp, forgetting to subtract the interest differential. It would be correct only if r $= \text{r}^{*}$.

d.reason: (Sign error). Adds the differential instead of subtracting it: 88 + 70 = 158 bp. It would be correct only if the deviation were defined as $(\text{F} - \text{S})$/S $+ (\text{r} - \text{r}^{*})$, which no source uses.

questions.question:
A risk consultant advising a Japanese life insurer models the three-year USD/JPY CIP deviation as proportional to the per-dollar balance sheet cost of arbitrageurs (rp) multiplied by net FX hedging demand. The deviation currently has a magnitude of 30 bp.

| Expected change over the next year | Value |
|---|---|
| Per-dollar balance sheet cost of arbitrageurs, rp | rises by 25% |
| Net FX hedging demand vis-a-vis the US dollar | rises by 40% |
| USD/JPY spot rate | JPY 150 per USD (unchanged) |

Assuming the proportionality factor is unchanged, which of the following is closest to the expected magnitude of the deviation?
questions.solution:
Three-year USD/JPY deviation scaled by changes in balance sheet cost and hedging demand.

**Concept and theory**

A small risk premium does not by itself explain a large or persistent basis. GARP’s insight is that the premium is scaled by the amount of balance sheet arbitrageurs must commit. Drawing on Sushko et al (2016), the reading states that the CIP deviation can be proportional to FX hedging demand multiplied by the per-dollar balance sheet cost of FX derivatives exposures:

b $= \frac{\text{F} - \text{S}}{\text{S}} - (\text{r} - \text{r}^{*}) \propto\text{rp} \times$ FX hedging demand.

Here rp is the per-dollar balance sheet cost of the arbitrageurs who take the other side of hedgers’ trades, and FX hedging demand is the net amount hedgers want to swap. Because markets must clear, arbitrageurs’ aggregate position equals hedgers’ aggregate net position, so a larger hedging demand forces arbitrageurs to expand their balance sheets, and every extra dollar carries the cost rp. A multiplicative relation has a practical consequence: changes in the two drivers compound. A rise in either factor widens the deviation in proportion, and simultaneous rises multiply. This is why the basis can be large in non-crisis times when risk premia are modest but hedging demand is big and one-sided, and why it can widen when balance sheet costs rise around reporting dates even with unchanged demand.

**Applying it to this question**

With the proportionality factor k fixed, $\text{b}_{1}$/b$_{0} = (\text{rp}_{1}$/rp$_{0}) \times(\text{D}_{1}$/D$_{0})$.

rp factor = 1 + 0.25 = 1.25

Demand factor = 1 + 0.40 = 1.40

Combined factor = 1.25 × 1.40 = 1.75

$\text{b}_{1} =$ 30 × 1.75 = 52.5 bp

The spot rate of JPY 150 per USD is irrelevant: the relation links the deviation to rp and demand, not to the level of the exchange rate.

**Fragile fact.** The relation is multiplicative: rp times hedging demand, so percentage changes compound rather than add.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** LO 81.b: Identify key factors that affect the cross-currency swap basis.

**GARP:** Chapter 17, Box 17.1 (“CIP deviation can be proportional to the hedging demand multiplied by the per-dollar balance sheet costs”). **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser states only that small risk premia matter when hedging demand is large; the proportional form is GARP-only.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-16 b, where it is Q7 of 11.

a.reason: (Sign error). Treats the 25% change in rp as a fall: 30 × 0.75 × 1.40 = 31.5 bp. It would be correct if balance sheet costs had declined by 25%.

b.reason: (Intermediate result). Stops after applying the rp factor: 30 × 1.25 = 37.5 bp. It would be correct only if hedging demand were unchanged.

c.reason: (Dropped term). Ignores the change in rp and applies only the demand factor: 30 × 1.40 = 42.0 bp. It would be correct only if balance sheet costs were unchanged.

d.reason: Applying GARP’s multiplicative relation, both drivers rise and the deviation scales by 1.75 to 52.5 bp.

questions.question: A member of the board risk committee at a Canadian bank argues: “Market illiquidity and credit risk premia are crisis phenomena. In calm markets, when these premia are small, the cross-currency basis against the US dollar should be close to zero.” Which of the following responses by the bank’s treasurer is most accurate?

options.text: The member is right: as long as Libor-OIS spreads and bid-ask spreads are within normal ranges, the risk premia are too small to sustain a non-zero basis.
Even small risk premia can have big effects on the basis when they are scaled by the large balance sheet exposures needed to meet a large demand to hedge one currency.
Even small risk premia can have big effects on the basis, but only when the demand for currency hedges is balanced across the two currencies of the pair.
Even small risk premia can have big effects on the basis, but only on the three-month basis, because long-term swap pricing is insensitive to hedging demand.

questions.solution:
Board challenge: is the basis close to zero in calm markets because premia are small?

**Concept and theory**

Schweser’s summary of this LO says the two key factors, declining market liquidity and rising risk of the underlying instruments, cause the basis to change and depart from zero in times of financial crisis. GARP goes further and explains why a basis can persist outside crises. Its argument in Box 17.1 is that even when risk premia in the underlying transaction are low, CIP deviations can arise if the demand to hedge one of the currencies is large: small risk premia can have big effects when scaled by the large balance sheet exposures needed to meet hedgers’ demand. Schweser echoes this in one line: even small increases in risk premia can significantly affect arbitrageurs’ ability to execute the trades if hedging demand for one currency is sufficiently large. The framework’s conclusion is that CIP deviations look set to stay even in non-crisis times as long as the demand for currency hedges is sufficiently high and imbalanced across currencies. Two conditions therefore matter: the size of hedging demand and its one-sidedness. Balanced demand nets out and needs little arbitrage capital; one-sided demand forces arbitrageurs to expand their balance sheets. GARP also documents that the basis widened after 2014 despite fading concerns about bank credit quality, the empirical puzzle this framework resolves.

**Applying it to this question**

The member’s premise (small premia imply a near-zero basis) ignores the scaling by hedging demand. The deciding fact is that the effect of the premium is multiplied by the balance sheet needed to meet a large, one-sided demand.

**Fragile fact.** Small premium times large one-sided demand can mean a large basis; “crisis only” is Schweser’s compression, not GARP’s full argument.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** LO 81.b: Identify key factors that affect the cross-currency swap basis.

**GARP:** Chapter 17, Box 17.1 (“Even if risk premia in the underlying transaction are low. . . ”); introduction; Section 17.3 Regression Results. **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser frames the factors as operating in times of financial crisis; GARP stresses they also operate in non-crisis times via hedging demand. GARP is followed.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-16 b, where it is Q8 of 11.

a.reason: (Absolute claim). It asserts that normal Libor-OIS and bid-ask spreads guarantee a negligible basis. GARP shows the basis widening after 2014 with credit strains faded and volatility within normal ranges. It would be correct only if hedging demand were small or balanced.

b.reason: Option B restates GARP’s Box 17.1 point that small risk premia can have big effects when scaled by the large balance sheet exposures needed to meet hedgers’ demand to hedge one currency.

c.reason: (Scope or condition error). It inverts the condition: the effect arises when demand is large and imbalanced, not balanced. It would be correct if “balanced” were replaced with “one-sided”.

d.reason: (Polarity flip). GARP finds the long-term basis is the more direct barometer of hedged-flow imbalances, with hedging demand having a direct effect on the two-year basis. It would be correct if “three-month” and “long-term” were swapped and the claim were about sensitivity to funding strains.

questions.question:
The chief compliance officer at a Hong Kong dealer bank is reviewing a desk memo on the real-world counterparts of rp, the per-dollar cost of CIP arbitrage, in non-crisis times. The memo states:

I. In aggregate, rp reflects the costs that banks and other participants assign to deploying their balance sheet in CIP arbitrage, which in turn reflect their risk management practices.

II. For individual players, these practices may include absolute credit limits that cap exposures to the underlying instruments and counterparties.

III. Even without strict limits, the funding cost of the capital allocated to the arbitrage, notably to current and potential future derivatives exposures, can stop the basis from closing.

IV. Because rp is a per-dollar cost, its effect on the basis does not depend on the size of the aggregate hedging positions that arbitrageurs must absorb.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.text: I, II and III only
I and III only
II, III and IV only
I, II, III and IV

questions.solution:
Desk memo audit: real-world counterparts of the per-dollar arbitrage cost rp.

**Concept and theory**

In crises the risk premium has obvious sources: interbank counterparty risk and sovereign risk. GARP then asks what plays the role of rp in non-crisis times. Its answer is about balance sheet use. In aggregate, rp reflects any costs that banks or other participants assign to deploying their balance sheet in CIP arbitrage, and those costs in turn reflect their risk management practices. For individual players, these practices can include absolute credit limits that set a maximum for exposures to the underlying instruments and counterparties. Even without strict limits, the funding cost of the capital allocated to the arbitrage, notably to the current and potential future derivatives exposures involved, will prevent the basis from closing when it opens up because of changes in hedging demand. Crucially, rp is a per-dollar cost, so its total impact depends on how many dollars of balance sheet arbitrageurs must commit, which is set by the aggregate hedging positions they absorb. GARP describes the resulting constraint as one that becomes more binding as the size of aggregate FX hedging positions grows.

| Level | Counterpart of rp |
|---|---|
| Aggregate | Cost assigned to deploying balance sheet (risk management practices) |
| Individual | Absolute credit limits on instruments and counterparties |
| Without limits | Funding cost of capital for current and potential future exposures |

**Applying it to this question**

Statements I, II and III are close paraphrases of Box 17.1. Statement IV denies the scaling of a per-dollar cost by position size.

**Fragile fact.** rp is per dollar; the basis effect is rp times the dollars committed, so size matters.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** LO 81.b: Identify key factors that affect the cross-currency swap basis.

**GARP:** Chapter 17, Box 17.1 (“What are some of the real-world counterparts to rp in non-crisis times?”); Section 17.1 A Framework (constraint becomes more binding as positions grow). **GARP** **vs Schweser:** Schweser does not discuss the counterparts of rp; GARP-only content.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-16 b, where it is Q9 of 11.

a.reason: I, II and III are each supported by Box 17.1; IV contradicts it, so “I, II and III only” is correct.

b.reason: (Scope or condition error). It omits II, as if credit limits were not part of rp. GARP explicitly lists absolute credit limits for individual players. It would be correct only if the memo were restricted to aggregate pricing effects.

c.reason: (Scope or condition error). It drops I and accepts IV, which ignores that a per-dollar cost scales with the balance sheet committed; the constraint becomes more binding as aggregate hedging positions grow. It would be correct only if arbitrage capacity were unlimited.

d.reason: (Absolute claim). It accepts all four, including the false claim that size does not matter. It would be correct only if IV were rewritten to say the effect grows with aggregate hedging positions.
