questions.question: A regulator at a euro area central bank is explaining to a parliamentary committee how arbitrageurs’ costs show up in FX swap prices when euro area investors hedging US dollar assets create a large one-sided demand and the US dollar trades at a premium in FX swaps. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Arbitrageurs pass on their balance sheet costs through the spot rate S, because the spot leg is the price that is actually set in FX derivatives.
Arbitrageurs absorb their balance sheet costs, so the forward points narrow below the CIP level and hedgers pay less than the interest differential.
Arbitrageurs pass on their balance sheet costs as wider forward points $(\text{F} - \text{S})$; since markets clear, their aggregate position equals the hedgers’ net position.
Arbitrageurs pass on their balance sheet costs as wider forward points $(\text{F} - \text{S})$, which the arbitrageurs then pay to the hedgers who are lending US dollars.

questions.solution:
How arbitrageurs’ balance sheet costs appear in FX swap prices under one-sided hedging demand.

**Concept and theory**

GARP stresses that in FX derivatives the price that is actually set is that of the forward leg of the swap, F. When hedgers create a large one-sided demand, for example euro area investors who want to hedge their US dollar assets and therefore borrow dollars via FX swaps, someone must take the other side. That someone is the CIP arbitrageur, who lends dollars through the swap and funds the position in the cash market. Doing so uses balance sheet, which is costly (the per-dollar cost rp). GARP states that CIP arbitrageurs pass on these balance sheet costs of taking the other side of FX hedging demand as wider forward points, $(\text{F} - \text{S})$, than warranted by CIP. Because markets have to clear, the aggregate position of CIP arbitrageurs when the dollar is at a premium in FX swaps equals the aggregate net position of currency hedgers, and the hedgers are the ones paying the forward points to hedge their US dollar assets. Equivalently, a party borrowing US dollars via an FX swap effectively pays a higher interest rate on the swapped dollars than in the cash market.

| Party | Swap position | Pays or receives |
|---|---|---|
| Hedger (USD asset holder) | Borrows USD via swap | Pays wide forward points |
| Arbitrageur | Lends USD via swap | Receives them, covering rp |

**Applying it to this question**

The stem fixes the direction: dollar at a premium, hedgers borrowing dollars. The deciding facts are which price carries the cost (F, hence forward points) and who pays (hedgers).

**Fragile fact.** Hedgers borrowing dollars pay the wide forward points; arbitrageurs lend dollars and collect them to cover rp.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** LO 81.b: Identify key factors that affect the cross-currency swap basis.

**GARP:** Chapter 17, Box 17.1 (“In each of the above examples, the price that is actually set in FX derivatives is that of the forward leg of the swap”). **GARP vs Schweser:** none; Schweser does not discuss pass-through. Sign convention: GARP’s Box treats a “wide” $(\text{F} - \text{S})$ as a positive b, while its charts show the dollar basis against EUR and JPY as negative; this question avoids the sign.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-16 b, where it is Q10 of 11.

a.reason: (Sibling swap). It swaps the forward leg for the spot leg. GARP says the price actually set in FX derivatives is the forward leg F; spot is taken as given. It would be correct only if the spot market were smaller than the swap market.

b.reason: (Polarity flip). Arbitrageurs pass costs on, so forward points widen, not narrow, and hedgers pay more than the differential. It would be correct only if arbitrage were costless and supply exceeded hedging demand.

c.reason: Option C states both GARP facts: costs passed on as wider forward points, and market clearing that equates arbitrageurs’ aggregate position with hedgers’ net position.

d.reason: (Role misassignment). Right mechanism, wrong payer: the hedgers (who borrow dollars) pay the forward points, and the arbitrageurs lend the dollars. It would be correct with the roles reversed.

questions.question: A senior risk analyst at a Japanese life insurer is summarising the regression evidence on the JPY/USD basis in the GARP reading. The standard specification relates the basis to counterparty risk (Libor-OIS spread), funding liquidity (repo spreads) and market liquidity (FX bid-ask spreads); the researchers then add an indicator of FX hedging demand, on its own and interacted with the Libor-OIS spread. Which of the following conclusions is most accurate?

options.text: For the three-month basis, the Libor-OIS spread on its own remains the main significant driver after the hedging demand indicator is added.
For the two-year basis, hedging demand has a direct effect, with 1% higher demand associated with roughly a 1 bp wider basis.
For the two-year basis, the interaction of hedging demand and the Libor-OIS spread dominates, at about 45 bp per 1% rise in each.
The short-term basis is the more direct barometer of hedged flow imbalances, while the long-term basis is more sensitive to funding strains.

questions.solution:
Regression evidence on the JPY/USD basis: which drivers matter at which tenor.

**Concept and theory**

Section 17.3 tests the factors econometrically. The standard specification, used in earlier research, models the basis as a function of three market-friction factors: counterparty risk (Libor-OIS spread), funding liquidity (repo spread differentials) and market liquidity (currency market bid-ask spreads). For the three-month basis this specification performs reasonably well, with all coefficients economically and statistically significant. The authors then add a quantitative indicator of FX hedging demand, both on its own and interacted with the Libor-OIS spread. Results differ by tenor:

| Tenor | What matters once demand is added | Size |
|---|---|---|
| Three-month | Interaction of Libor-OIS and demand; Libor-OIS alone insignificant | About 45 bp per 1% rise in each |
| Two-year | Hedging demand directly (linear); interaction insignificant | About 1 bp per 1% higher demand |

GARP interprets this as follows: the cost of long-term cross-currency swaps is the more direct barometer of imbalances in cross-currency flows hedged for currency risk, whereas the cost of short-term FX swaps is much more sensitive to risk premia and bank funding strains, especially in crises. Higher hedging demand works together with market dislocations to drive the basis. So the key factors identified in the LO show up in different combinations across the maturity curve.

**Applying it to this question**

Each option makes a claim about one tenor. Only the two-year claim of a direct effect of roughly 1 bp per 1% higher demand matches the reading (coefficient about −0.91).

**Fragile fact.** Short tenor: risk premia and funding strains (interaction with demand); long tenor: hedging demand directly.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** LO 81.b: Identify key factors that affect the cross-currency swap basis.

**GARP:** Chapter 17, Section 17.3 (Regression Results; Table 17.1). **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser does not cover the regression; GARP-only. **Garbled-source caution:** Table 17.1 columns are scrambled in the extraction; the figures used (45 bp, −0.913, about 1 bp) are taken from the narrative text. **Boundary call:** included because the standard specification names the factors that affect the basis; the wider post-crisis story belongs to LO 81.c.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-16 b, where it is Q11 of 11.

a.reason: (Polarity flip). GARP reports that once hedging demand is added, money market strains alone (Libor-OIS) no longer exert a significant impact on the three-month basis; it is the interaction that matters. It would be correct for the original standard specification before demand is added.

b.reason: Option B matches GARP: for the two-year basis, hedging demand has a direct linear effect, about 1 bp wider per 1% higher demand, while the interaction term is no longer significant.

c.reason: (Sibling swap). It moves the three-month result (interaction worth about 45 bp) to the two-year basis, where the interaction is insignificant. It would be correct if “two-year” read “three-month”.

d.reason: (Polarity flip). It reverses the tenors: the long-term basis is the direct barometer of hedged-flow imbalances and the short-term basis is more sensitive to risk premia and funding strains. It would be correct with the tenors swapped.

questions.topic: Covered Interest Parity Lost: Understanding the Cross-Currency Basis
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-16 c Q1
questions.question: A member of the risk committee of a German bank is preparing a briefing on why covered interest parity (CIP) has been violated systematically since the Great Financial Crisis (GFC), including the widening of the basis after 2014, when banks had strengthened their balance sheets and regained easy access to funding. Which of the following statements best describes the assessment in the GARP reading?

options.text: Strains in interbank markets, namely counterparty risk concerns and constrained access to wholesale dollar funding, explain the violations, so the basis is expected to close once these strains have dissipated.
Growing demand for currency hedges explains why the basis opens up, while tighter limits to arbitrage, reflecting tighter risk management and balance sheet constraints, explain why it does not close.
Tighter limits to arbitrage, reflecting tighter risk management and balance sheet constraints, explain why the basis opens up, while growing demand for currency hedges explains why it does not close.
Growing demand for currency hedges and tighter limits to arbitrage explain the violations, so CIP deviations are expected to disappear in non-crisis periods once banks restore their balance sheets.

questions.solution:
Risk committee briefing: what explains persistent CIP violations since the GFC, including after 2014.

**Concept and theory**

Covered interest parity says that the interest rate differential between two currencies in the cash money markets should equal the differential between forward and spot exchange rates; otherwise an arbitrageur could earn a seemingly riskless profit. With S and F in US dollars per unit of foreign currency, r the US dollar rate and $\text{r}^{*}$ the foreign rate,

$\frac{\text{F}}{\text{S}} = \frac{1 + \text{r}}{1 + \text{r}^{*}}$ .

A non-zero cross-currency basis measures how far the cost of borrowing a currency by swapping it against another differs from the cost of borrowing it directly in the cash market, so a non-zero basis is a CIP violation. GARP’s puzzle is that the basis has been non-zero since 2007, and has even widened since 2014, although bank credit concerns had faded and wholesale funding had recovered.

Initially, violations were read as a sign of strains in global interbank markets: counterparty risk concerns and constrained access to wholesale dollar funding inhibited arbitrage during the GFC and again during the euro area sovereign debt crisis. That explanation cannot account for persistence after these strains dissipated. GARP’s framework has two parts:

| Component | Role |
|---|---|
| FX hedging demand (banks, institutional investors, non-financial issuers) | Why the basis opens up: large, imbalanced demand that is insensitive to the size of the basis |
| Limits to arbitrage (tighter risk management, balance sheet constraints) | Why the basis does not close: balance sheet space is costly, so arbitrage stops short |

If these are the right factors, CIP deviations look to be here to stay even in non-crisis times, as long as hedging demand is sufficiently high and imbalanced across currencies.

**Applying it to this question**

The stem stresses that the basis widened after 2014, when banks were strong and funding was easy. That rules out the pure interbank-strain story and points to the two-part framework. The deciding fact is the assignment of roles: demand opens the basis; limits to arbitrage stop it from closing.

**Fragile fact.** Direction of the roles: demand opens, limits to arbitrage keep open; and the violations persist in non-crisis times.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** LO 81.c: Assess the causes of covered interest rate parity violations after the financial crisis of 2008.

**GARP:** Chapter 17, introduction and Section 17.1 (A Framework). **GARP vs Schweser:** none on this point; Schweser (LO 81.c, Why the Basis Opens Up / Why the Basis Does Not Close) gives the same two-part structure in condensed form.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-16 c, where it is Q1 of 12.

a.reason: (Scope or condition error). This is the initial explanation, valid for crisis episodes (GFC, euro area sovereign debt crisis). Extending it to the whole post-crisis period predicts that the basis closes once strains fade, but GARP stresses that violations persisted and even widened after 2014. It would be correct if the stem asked only how violations were explained during the 2008 to 2009 crisis.

b.reason: Option B matches GARP’s statement that the evolving demand for FX hedges explains why the basis opens up, and new constraints on arbitrage, reflecting lower balance sheet capacity from tighter management of risks, explain why it does not close.

c.reason: (Sibling swap). The two causes are attached to the wrong roles. Hedging demand is what pushes the forward rate away from parity (opens the basis); limits to arbitrage are what prevent arbitrageurs from pushing it back (keep it open). It would be correct with the two roles exchanged back.

d.reason: (Polarity flip). GARP concludes the opposite: CIP deviations look to be here to stay even in non-crisis times, as long as hedging demand is sufficiently high and imbalanced. Stronger bank balance sheets do not remove the cost of deploying balance sheet. It would be correct only if hedging demand were small and balanced across currencies.

questions.question:
A junior risk analyst at a Singapore insurer is presenting to newly hired analysts on the sources of FX hedging demand that put pressure on the cross-currency basis after the GFC. She drafts four statements:

I. Banks are a structural source: a banking system that is short a foreign currency relative to its core deposit base closes the remaining gap between its assets and liabilities in that currency with currency derivatives such as FX swaps.

II. Institutional investors such as insurers and pension funds hedge strategically, and their hedge ratios adjust quickly to hedging costs, so their demand fades as soon as the basis widens.

III. Non-financial firms issue debt opportunistically where credit spreads are narrower; a US firm issuing in euros and swapping the proceeds into dollars effectively borrows dollars and lends euros through the swap market.

IV. Firms’ hedging of trade receivables and speculative positions such as yen carry trades form a fourth source in the framework, because they are the largest sources of pressure on the basis.

Which of the statements are consistent with the GARP reading?

options.text: I and II only
II and IV only
I, III and IV only
I and III only

questions.solution:
Training slide audit: the three sources of FX hedging demand that open the basis.

**Concept and theory**

Hedging of open FX positions is the main proximate driver of demand for FX swaps. GARP focuses on three sources that are rather insensitive to the size of the basis and so exert sustained pressure on it even when it is non-zero:

| Source | Mechanism in GARP |
|---|---|
| Banks | Structural: business models leave banking systems short or long specific currencies given their core deposit base; a foreign currency funding shortfall is managed with cash borrowing, and the remaining asset-liability gaps are closed with currency derivatives such as FX swaps. |
| Institutional investors | Strategic hedging by insurers and pension funds of foreign currency investments; hedge ratios are quite insensitive to hedging costs and move slowly; term and credit spread compression from unconventional monetary policy boosted these flows. |
| Non-financial firms | Opportunistic issuance where credit spreads are narrower (for example US firms issuing in euros and swapping into dollars: they borrow dollars and lend euros through the swap market). |

GARP explicitly excludes other possible sources, such as firms’ hedging of trade receivables or subsidiary cash flows and speculative FX positions (for example yen carry trades), because of data limitations, not because they are large. Indeed GARP notes speculation could push the basis the other way, since carry trades can push down the forward rate even as hedging demand pushes it up. The key property of the three sources is insensitivity to price: because demand does not shrink much as the basis widens, it keeps pressure on the forward rate.

**Applying it to this question**

Check each statement against the table. I matches the bank source. II reverses the key property of institutional demand. III matches the non-financial issuer source, including the direction of the swap. IV turns an exclusion into an inclusion. So I and III only.

**Fragile fact.** Hedging demand is insensitive to the size of the basis; that insensitivity, not its price responsiveness, is why it opens the basis and keeps it open.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** LO 81.c: Assess the causes of covered interest rate parity violations after the financial crisis of 2008.

**GARP:** Chapter 17, Section 17.1, Demand for Currency Hedges: Why the Basis Opens Up. **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser lists institutional investors as “insurance companies and banks” and says US firms swap proceeds back “using FX swaps”; GARP says insurers and pension funds, and Box 17.2 refers to cross-currency swaps for long-term reverse yankee issuance. GARP followed.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-16 c, where it is Q2 of 12.

a.reason: (Polarity flip (in statement II)). Statement II says institutional hedge ratios adjust quickly to hedging costs. GARP says they are quite insensitive to hedging costs and move slowly over time, which is exactly why they keep pressure on the basis. A would be correct if II said hedge ratios are insensitive to costs and slow-moving.

b.reason: (Polarity flip (statement II)). B rests on statement II, which reverses the price sensitivity of institutional demand, and it also adds IV, which brings in sources GARP excludes, while leaving out the two true statements I and III. B would be correct only if II described slow-moving, cost-insensitive hedge ratios and IV were replaced by a true statement.

c.reason: (Scope or condition error (statement IV)). Trade receivable hedging and speculative positions are left out of GARP’s framework because of data limitations, and GARP does not claim they are the largest. C would be correct if the framework had added them as a fourth source, which it does not.

d.reason: Option D is the only combination containing exactly the two true statements. GARP describes banks as running currency mismatches managed mainly via swaps, and US firms issuing in euros and swapping into dollars, which in effect borrow dollars and lend euros.

questions.question:
The treasurer of a BBB-rated US telecoms company is deciding whether to issue in euros (a reverse yankee bond) and swap the proceeds into US dollars with a cross-currency swap, or to issue directly in US dollars. In the swap the company borrows US dollars and lends euros, and because the US dollar trades at a premium it pays the currency basis shown below on top of the reference rates. All figures are in basis points per year.

| Tenor | USD spread over swap rate | EUR spread over swap rate | Basis paid by the company |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3-year | 110 | 75 | 48 |
| 10-year | 145 | 80 | 30 |

Planned issue size is EUR 750 million and the 10-year US Treasury yield is 4.10%. Taking the currency swap into account, which of the following is closest to the all-in saving from issuing in euros rather than in US dollars (a negative figure means euro issuance is more expensive)?

options.text: 10-year: +35 bp; 3-year: −13 bp
10-year: +65 bp; 3-year: +35 bp
10-year: +95 bp; 3-year: +83 bp
10-year: +17 bp; 3-year: +5 bp

questions.solution:
Reverse yankee decision: all-in saving from euro issuance after paying the basis, 3-year versus 10-year.

**Concept and theory**

Box 17.2 explains the non-financial source of hedging demand. ECB bond purchases compressed euro corporate credit spreads relative to US dollar spreads. US firms that need dollars therefore found it cheaper to issue in euros (reverse yankee bonds) and swap the proceeds into dollars. Through the swap they borrow dollars and lend euros, which adds to demand for cross-currency swaps. GARP’s example: a BBB-rated US telecoms firm yields 100 bp over the swap rate in dollars but only 50 bp in euros; if CIP held, it would save 50 bp by issuing in euros and swapping back, and would do so for all its new debt. The widening of the basis can be seen as tending to reconcile the different spreads in the two markets.

When CIP fails, the party borrowing the premium currency pays the basis on top of the reference rate. So the all-in comparison is

All-in saving $= (\text{USD spread} - \text{EUR spread}) -$ b,

where both spreads are over the respective swap rates and b is the basis paid by the dollar borrower, all in bp per year. GARP notes that reverse yankee issuance has been long-term (average maturity about 10 years, with 15- and 20-year tenors common). Short maturities are rare because the all-in cost of short-term euro debt is still higher than issuing short-term dollar debt, owing to the wider basis relative to the spread differential at the short end.

**Applying it to this question**

Apply the formula tenor by tenor.

10-year spread differential = 145 − 80 = 65 bp

10-year all-in saving = 65 − 30 = +35 bp

3-year spread differential = 110 − 75 = 35 bp

3-year all-in saving = 35 − 48 = −13 bp

At 10 years, euro issuance saves 35 bp a year; at 3 years, the basis more than absorbs the spread advantage and euro issuance costs 13 bp a year more. The issue size (EUR 750 million) and the 10-year Treasury yield (4.10%) are irrelevant: the comparison is in spreads over the swap rate per year, so neither the notional nor the level of Treasury yields changes it.

**Fragile fact.** The dollar borrower in the swap pays the basis, so it is subtracted from the spread advantage; and the basis is wider relative to the spread gap at the short end.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** LO 81.c: Assess the causes of covered interest rate parity violations after the financial crisis of 2008.

**GARP:** Chapter 17, Section 17.1, Box 17.2 (Reverse Yankee Issuance in the Euro and the EUR/USD Basis). **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser gives only a one-line version (US firms issue foreign currency debt when credit spreads narrow abroad and swap back); the all-in cost logic and tenor point are GARP-only. Numbers in the question are original.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-16 c, where it is Q3 of 12.

a.reason: Option A applies the reading’s logic: the spread differential is the gross saving and the basis is the cost of swapping back. The result reproduces GARP’s observation that long-tenor issuance is attractive while short-tenor issuance is not.

b.reason: (Dropped term). It reports only the spread differentials, 65 and 35 bp, ignoring the basis paid in the swap. This is GARP’s “if CIP held” saving. It would be correct if the basis were zero at both tenors.

c.reason: (Sign error). It adds the basis instead of subtracting it: 65 + 30 = 95 and 35 + 48 = 83 bp. That treats the company as receiving the basis, as the dollar lender in the swap would. It would be correct only if the company received the basis on top of the reference rates instead of paying it.

d.reason: (Wrong input twin). It uses the other tenor’s basis: 65 − 48 = 17 and 35 − 30 = 5 bp. It would be correct only if the 3-year and 10-year basis figures were exchanged in the table.

questions.question:
A portfolio manager at an Australian superannuation fund is comparing two banking systems against the US dollar. Use the convention of the charts in the GARP reading, under which a negative basis means that borrowing US dollars through the FX swap market is more expensive than borrowing them in the cash market.

- Country X: banks have a surplus of domestic currency deposits over domestic currency loans and use it to fund lending abroad, mainly in US dollars, via FX swaps. Domestic life insurers hedge large US dollar bond holdings.
- Country Y: banks have a large domestic currency mortgage book relative to their domestic deposit base and rely on the FX swap market for funding. Domestic institutional investors hedge their foreign assets.

Which of the following best describes the signs of the basis against the US dollar that the reading’s framework predicts?

options.text: Both bases negative, because the institutional investors’ hedging demand fixes the sign of the basis whatever the position of the banking system.
X positive and Y negative, because banks in X supply dollars to domestic investors while banks in Y compete with them to borrow dollars.
X negative, because banks compete with investors to borrow dollars via swaps; Y positive, because banks offset investors’ demand by lending dollars in swaps.
X negative and Y positive, because banks in Y, with a surplus of domestic deposits over loans, lend dollars in the FX swap market to investors.

questions.solution:
Two banking systems: do banks add to or offset institutional investors’ dollar hedging demand?

**Concept and theory**

Section 17.2 tests whether the framework explains the sign and size of the basis across currencies. GARP builds sector indicators: for banks, the US dollar “funding gap”, the difference between consolidated on-balance sheet assets and liabilities in dollars, which, assuming banks hedge currency risk, indicates the size of their off-balance sheet position, largely managed with FX swaps; for institutional investors, hedged foreign assets; for non-financial firms, foreign currency bonds issued by US firms. A positive bar in GARP’s Graph 2 means net borrowing of dollars against local currency via swaps (positive net FX hedging demand), a negative bar net dollar lending.

The key finding concerns banks versus institutional investors:

| Case | Bank position | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| Japan | Surplus of domestic deposits over domestic loans; banks borrow dollars via swaps to fund dollar lending, competing with institutional investors | Negative |
| Australia | Large domestic mortgage book relative to deposits; banks rely on the FX swap market for funding and lend dollars in swaps, offsetting investors | Positive |

In GARP’s chart convention, a negative basis means dollar borrowing via the FX swap market is in higher demand and so more costly than in the cash market. Where banks are on the opposite side to institutional investors, their needs are typically larger, so banks are the swing factor.

**Applying it to this question**

Country X is the Japanese pattern: deposit surplus, dollar lending abroad funded by swaps, plus insurers hedging dollar bonds. Both sectors want to borrow dollars through swaps, so the basis is negative. Country Y is the Australian pattern: banks need domestic currency funding, so they lend dollars in swaps, offsetting investors’ hedging demand, and the basis is positive.

**Fragile fact.** Deposit surplus means banks borrow dollars via swaps and add to demand (negative basis); mortgage book above deposits means banks lend dollars via swaps and offset demand (positive basis).

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** LO 81.c: Assess the causes of covered interest rate parity violations after the financial crisis of 2008.

**GARP:** Chapter 17, Section 17.2 (The Currency Basis in the Cross Section; Quantitative Indicators of Hedging Demand; Graphs 2 and 3). **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser does not cover the cross-section evidence; GARP-only. Sign caution: Schweser describes the post-crisis basis as greater than zero (dollar premium convention), whereas GARP’s charts show the dollar basis against EUR and JPY as negative; the stem fixes the GARP chart convention.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-16 c, where it is Q4 of 12.

a.reason: (Scope or condition error). It drops the banking sector from the analysis. GARP finds that banks’ positions are consistent with the sign of the basis and that banks are typically the swing factor when they oppose investors. It would be correct if banks in Y also needed to borrow dollars, or held no net currency position.

b.reason: (Polarity flip). Both signs and both bank roles are reversed. Banks in X compete with investors to borrow dollars; banks in Y supply dollars. It would be correct if the descriptions of X and Y were exchanged.

c.reason: Option C states both signs and the correct mechanism for each, matching GARP’s comparison of Japan and Australia.

d.reason: (Sibling swap). The signs are right but the mechanism is borrowed from the other system: a surplus of domestic deposits over loans is the Japanese (X) feature that leads banks to borrow dollars. Y’s banks lend dollars because their domestic mortgage book exceeds their deposit base. It would be correct if “surplus of domestic deposits over loans” read “large domestic mortgage book relative to deposits”.

questions.question: An internal auditor at a Swedish bank is reviewing a consultant’s report. The report notes that Swedish banks, like Australian banks, have a large krona mortgage book relative to their krona deposit base and rely on FX swaps for funding, yet the SEK/USD basis has been negative while the AUD/USD basis has been positive. The report asks how this fits the hedging demand framework. Which of the following explanations is most consistent with the GARP reading?

options.text: The FX swap market in euros, not in dollars, is the marginal funding source for excess krona lending, and the SEK/EUR basis is positive, so Sweden resembles Australia once the right currency pair is chosen.
The hedging needs of Swedish institutional investors exceed those of Swedish banks, so investors rather than banks are the swing factor that fixes the sign of the SEK/USD basis.
Swedish banks add to institutional investors’ demand to borrow dollars through FX swaps, as Japanese banks do, so the negative SEK/USD basis is what the framework predicts.
Banks’ currency positions cannot explain the sign of the basis for any Swedish currency pair, so the negative SEK/USD basis must reflect interbank counterparty risk.

questions.solution:
Swedish banks look like Australian banks, yet the SEK/USD basis is negative: how does the framework explain it?

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s cross-section analysis treats banks as the swing factor. When banks are on the opposite side of the market to domestic institutional investors, banks’ hedging needs are typically larger, so the sign of the basis follows the banks’ position. The framework only works, however, if the right currency pair is chosen: the pair that matters is the one in which banks actually do their marginal swap funding.

Sweden is GARP’s instructive exception. Swedish banks are in the same position as Australian banks: a large krona mortgage book relative to the krona deposit base, so they rely on the FX swap market for funding. Yet the dollar/krona basis is negative. GARP’s explanation is that the FX swap market in euros, rather than in dollars, is the marginal funding source for excess krona lending, since swapping out of euros is more expensive than swapping out of dollars. The euro/krona basis is positive. So the Swedish picture resembles Australia’s once the correct currency pair is chosen, and in GARP’s Graph 3 Sweden is plotted with net euro liabilities and the SEK/EUR basis. GARP also notes that Australian and Swedish banks are exceptional: banks typically add to resident institutional investors’ hedging needs rather than offset them.

| Pair | Swedish bank position | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| SEK/USD | Not the marginal funding market | Negative |
| SEK/EUR | Marginal funding source for excess krona lending | Positive |

**Applying it to this question**

The puzzle in the stem is resolved by changing the currency pair, not by abandoning the bank-position logic. Swedish banks offset investors’ demand in the euro market, so the basis consistent with their position is the positive SEK/EUR basis.

**Fragile fact.** For Sweden the relevant pair is SEK/EUR (positive basis), not SEK/USD; banks remain the swing factor.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** LO 81.c: Assess the causes of covered interest rate parity violations after the financial crisis of 2008.

**GARP:** Chapter 17, Section 17.2 (The Currency Basis in the Cross Section; Graph 3 and footnote 18). **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser does not cover the cross section; GARP-only. **Garbled-source** **caution:** Graph 3 is unreadable in the extraction; the facts used come from the narrative text and the graph note.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-16 c, where it is Q5 of 12.

a.reason: Option A restates GARP’s explanation: the FX swap euro market is the marginal funding source, the euro/krona basis is positive, and Sweden then resembles Australia.

b.reason: (Role misassignment). It hands the swing role to institutional investors. GARP finds that when banks are opposite institutional investors, banks’ needs are typically larger, so banks are the swing factor. B would be correct if Swedish investors’ hedging needs were larger than banks’ needs, which GARP does not report.

c.reason: (Sibling swap). It gives Swedish banks the Japanese banks’ role. Swedish banks, like Australian banks, rely on FX swaps to fund excess domestic currency lending and so offset investors’ demand. C would be correct for Japan, where banks fund dollar lending through swaps and compete with investors.

d.reason: (Absolute-claim trap). It asserts that bank positions explain no Swedish pair. GARP shows the bank-position logic works once the euro pair is used. D would be correct only if the SEK/EUR basis were also inconsistent with banks’ positions.

questions.question: A treasury analyst at a Japanese bank is studying how the cross-currency basis reacts to central bank announcements. In the run-up to a meeting, markets expected a large new ECB stimulus package; the stimulus actually announced was clearly smaller than expected. According to the GARP reading, which of the following best describes the likely reaction of the basis and its cause?

options.text: The basis widens, because any easing announcement raises the expected hedged outflows from the euro area, whether or not it falls short of market expectations.
The basis narrows, because a smaller stimulus lowers bank counterparty risk as measured by the Libor-OIS spread, which reduces the cost of arbitraging the basis.
The basis narrows, because swap dealers revise down the expected volume of hedged cross-currency outflows from the euro area and lower their prices for currency hedges.
The basis narrows, because the ECB supplies the extra dollars through its central bank swap lines, so dealers no longer need to provide currency hedges to euro area banks.

questions.solution:
ECB stimulus smaller than expected: likely reaction of the basis and its cause.

**Concept and theory**

Box 17.3 links monetary policy to hedging demand through price and quantity effects. Easing lowers the yield curve and compresses the term premium and credit spreads. That encourages investors to seek return and duration in foreign currency bonds, and foreign issuers to sell bonds in the currency with cheaper funding. Large-scale asset purchases strengthen these effects by withdrawing securities from the market, and so do negative policy rates. The resulting outflows are often hedged for currency risk, which raises demand for FX swaps and cross-currency swaps.

Much of the widening of the dollar basis since 2014 coincided with easing announcements by the ECB and the Bank of Japan (for example the 5 June 2014 negative rate announcement and the 22 January 2015 ECB quantitative easing announcement, which also affected USD/JPY). GARP’s explanation runs through dealer expectations: swap dealers who provide currency hedges expect hedged outflows from the euro or yen to rise when the ECB or BoJ eases, so they set higher prices for hedges, widening CIP deviations. The mechanism is symmetric. On 3 December 2015 the ECB announced less stimulus than expected; dealers revised down the hedging demand coming their way, lowered prices and helped narrow the basis.

| Announcement versus expectations | Dealer reaction | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| More easing than expected | Expect larger hedged outflows; raise hedge prices | Widens |
| Less easing than expected | Revise expected flows down; lower hedge prices | Narrows |

**Applying it to this question**

What matters is the surprise relative to expectations, since dealers price expected hedging demand. A smaller than expected package lowers the expected volume of hedged outflows from the euro area, so the basis narrows through the dealer-pricing channel.

**Fragile fact.** Direction depends on the surprise: less easing than expected narrows the basis; dealers, not central banks, reprice the hedges.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** LO 81.c: Assess the causes of covered interest rate parity violations after the financial crisis of 2008.

**GARP:** Chapter 17, Section 17.1, Box 17.3 (CIP Deviations and Monetary Policy Announcements); footnote 1 on central bank swap lines. **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser does not cover monetary policy effects; GARP-only.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-16 c, where it is Q6 of 12.

a.reason: (Scope or condition error). It drops the condition that the announcement is judged against expectations. In GARP, a disappointing easing narrowed the basis. A would be correct if the announced stimulus had exceeded expectations.

b.reason: (Sibling swap). It substitutes the counterparty-risk channel (Libor-OIS), which GARP associates with crisis episodes, for the hedging-demand channel GARP uses to explain announcement effects. B would be correct for a question about interbank strains during the GFC or the euro area sovereign debt crisis.

c.reason: Option C matches GARP’s account of the December 2015 episode: dealers revised down expected hedging demand, lowered their prices and helped narrow the basis.

d.reason: (Role misassignment). It makes the central bank the supplier of hedges. GARP notes that, unlike earlier dollar funding stress episodes, banks have drawn very little on central bank swap lines; the price change comes from dealers’ revised expectations. D would be correct only if banks had switched to central bank swap lines for their dollar needs.

questions.question: The CRO of a UK bank is reviewing a trading desk’s proposal to commit GBP 2 billion of balance sheet to arbitraging the USD/GBP cross-currency basis. Which of the following statements about the limits to such arbitrage is most accurate?

options.text: Because an FX swap entails no open currency position, CIP arbitrage remains riskless after the crisis, and its only cost to the bank is the bid-ask spread paid on the spot and forward legs.

Arbitrage requires enlarging the balance sheet, incurring credit risk in both borrowing and investing, and possibly facing mark-to-market and liquidity risk; these risks existed before the GFC but were not fully priced.

Arbitrage requires enlarging the balance sheet, incurring credit risk in both borrowing and investing, and possibly facing mark-to-market and liquidity risk; these risks did not exist before the GFC and arose from new regulation.

Since the crisis, pressure from shareholders, creditors and prudential authorities has raised dealer leverage, increasing their willingness to deploy balance sheet for activities such as arbitraging the basis.

questions.solution:
CRO review of a basis arbitrage proposal: what limits arbitrage after the GFC?

**Concept and theory**

In the textbook view, any CIP deviation should immediately trigger arbitrage that brings the basis back to zero, because CIP arbitrage is treated as riskless: FX swaps by construction carry no open currency position, and credit, counterparty, market and liquidity risks are assumed negligible. GARP explains why, after the GFC, the basis does not close. Arbitrage can be both costly and risky. It typically requires the arbitrageur to:

- enlarge its balance sheet;
- incur credit risk in both borrowing and investing;
- possibly face mark-to-market and liquidity risk in the valuation of the positions (the need to transfer collateral or take paper gains or losses).

These risks and costs exist all the time. What changed is how they are managed and priced. Before the GFC they were not fully priced, and partly as a result dealer banks raised leverage to dangerous levels. The crisis brought them to light. Since then, pressure from shareholders, creditors and prudential authorities has reinforced and hard-wired participants’ awareness. Leverage has declined and there is less willingness to deploy the balance sheet for activities that make heavy demands on it, such as arbitraging the basis. In GARP’s phrase, balance sheet space is rented, not free: arbitrage now incurs a cost per unit of balance sheet, passed on to the pricing of FX swaps, so the spot-forward relationship goes out of line with CIP.

**Applying it to this question**

The desk proposal would expand the bank’s balance sheet by GBP 2 billion; the notional is context only. The decision turns on recognising that the risks are permanent features of the trade but have been priced and managed more tightly since the crisis.

**Fragile fact.** The risks of CIP arbitrage are old; their pricing and management are new; leverage went down, not up.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** LO 81.c: Assess the causes of covered interest rate parity violations after the financial crisis of 2008.

**GARP:** Chapter 17, Section 17.1, Limits to Arbitrage: Why the Basis Does Not Close. **GARP vs** **Schweser:** none; Schweser (Why the Basis Does Not Close) gives the same list in condensed form and attributes the pressure to regulators, shareholders and creditors.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-16 c, where it is Q7 of 12.

a.reason: (Absolute-claim trap). It asserts the arbitrage is riskless with only bid-ask costs. No open currency position does not make the trade riskless: it carries balance sheet, two-sided credit, mark-to-market and liquidity risk. A would describe the idealised textbook world, not the post-crisis market.

b.reason: Option B lists the costs and risks GARP names and correctly dates the change: the risks always existed, but were not fully priced before the GFC.

c.reason: (Polarity flip). It says the risks did not exist before the GFC. GARP says these risks and costs exist all the time; what changed is that they were not fully priced before the crisis and are managed more actively since. C would be correct if “did not exist” read “were not fully priced”.

d.reason: (Polarity flip). Post-crisis pressure from shareholders, creditors and prudential authorities has reduced leverage and reduced willingness to deploy the balance sheet for arbitrage. D would describe the pre-GFC period, when leverage rose to dangerous levels.

questions.question: A risk consultant at a Canadian bank is preparing a report for the board on how regulatory changes have reinforced market pressure for tighter management of balance sheet risks, and so on the cost of CIP arbitrage. Which of the following statements should the consultant include in the report?

options.text: Changes related to credit value adjustments require dealers to hold capital in proportion to their derivatives exposures, while potential future exposure charges push dealers to price counterparty risk more accurately.

Potential future exposure charges under Basel III and US leverage ratios apply only to on-balance sheet cash exposures, so the FX swaps used in CIP arbitrage attract no additional capital requirement.
Regulatory capital charges have replaced banks’ internal credit limits on counterparties, so the basis now reflects only the regulatory cost of capital and no longer any internal limits on exposures.
Changes related to credit value adjustments push dealers to price counterparty risk more accurately, while potential future exposure charges require capital in proportion to derivatives exposures.

questions.solution:
Board report: how regulation reinforced balance sheet discipline and raised the cost of CIP arbitrage.

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s limits-to-arbitrage argument has a market part and a regulatory part. Market discipline came from shareholders and creditors after the crisis exposed unpriced risks. Regulation then reinforced market pressure for tighter management of balance sheet risks. GARP gives two examples, each with its own function:

| Regulatory change | Effect named in GARP |
|---|---|
| Changes related to credit value adjustments (CVA) | Incentivise dealers to price the counterparty risk in their derivatives portfolios more accurately |
| Potential future exposure (PFE) add-on charges in Basel III and US leverage ratios | Require market participants to hold capital in proportion to their derivatives and other exposures |

The combined effect is that arbitrage now incurs a cost per unit of balance sheet. GARP adds that this need not come from individual pricing decisions: internal credit limits may constrain individual balance sheets and, in aggregate, be reflected in a larger basis. Box 17.1 makes the same point: for individual players, risk management practices may even include absolute credit limits on exposures, and even without strict limits, the funding cost of capital allocated to the arbitrage, notably to current and potential future derivatives exposures, prevents the basis from closing. Because FX swaps and cross-currency swaps are derivatives, these regimes bite directly on CIP arbitrage.

**Applying it to this question**

The question asks which statement correctly pairs each regulatory change with its effect and keeps the link to derivatives exposures. Only one option does both.

**Fragile fact.** CVA: price counterparty risk accurately; PFE add-on: hold capital against derivatives exposures. Do not swap them.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** LO 81.c: Assess the causes of covered interest rate parity violations after the financial crisis of 2008.

**GARP:** Chapter 17, Section 17.1, Limits to Arbitrage (including footnote 10); Box 17.1 on credit limits and capital funding costs. **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser mentions only “pressure from regulators”; the CVA and PFE details are GARP-only.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-16 c, where it is Q8 of 12.

a.reason: (Sibling swap). The two effects are exchanged: capital in proportion to exposures is the PFE add-on charge, while more accurate counterparty risk pricing is the CVA-related change. A would be correct with the regulatory labels exchanged.

b.reason: (Scope or condition error). It limits the charges to cash exposures. GARP says PFE add-on charges require capital in proportion to derivatives and other exposures, so FX swaps are squarely caught. B would be correct only if derivatives were outside the leverage ratio and Basel III exposure measures.

c.reason: (Absolute-claim trap). It claims regulation has replaced internal credit limits and that the basis reflects only regulatory costs. GARP notes internal credit limits may themselves constrain balance sheets and, in aggregate, widen the basis. C would be correct only if banks had abolished internal limits, which the reading does not say.

d.reason: Option D matches GARP: CVA-related changes target accurate pricing of counterparty risk, and PFE add-on charges in Basel III and US leverage ratios require capital in proportion to derivatives exposures, which together raise the cost per unit of balance sheet.

questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a Brazilian bank is reviewing evidence that tighter limits to arbitrage have kept the yen/dollar basis from closing. She lists four observations:

I. Since mid-2014, increased Bank of Japan government bond purchases, while the Federal Reserve stopped its net purchases, have made dollar repo funding more expensive relative to yen repo funding, and the basis has widened even with the VIX in normal ranges.

II. Since 2014, the basis has shown quarter-end spikes along with repo rates, coinciding with the greater importance attached to quarter-end reporting and regulatory ratios after regulatory reforms.

III. As the basis widened, foreign banks cut their claims on the Japanese official sector, so Standard & Poor’s 2015 downgrade of Japan had no visible effect on the yen/dollar basis.

IV. After the GFC, many arbitrageurs switched from secured repo funding to unsecured funding, which increased their flexibility to arbitrage the basis.

Which of the observations are consistent with the GARP reading?

options.text: I and III only
II and IV only
I and II only
I, II and III only

questions.solution:
Evidence that tighter limits to arbitrage kept the yen/dollar basis open.

**Concept and theory**

GARP argues that the sudden break in the basis during the GFC points to new limits to arbitrage, then asks for more direct evidence of balance sheet constraints. It lists four developments for the yen/dollar basis:

| Development | What GARP reports |
|---|---|
| Shift to secured funding | After the GFC raised awareness of counterparty risk, many participants switched from unsecured to secured funding, notably repo. Repo constrains flexibility, because funds cannot be obtained without a security to pledge. Since mid-2014, BoJ bond purchases (making collateral scarce) while the Fed stopped net purchases made dollar repo more expensive relative to yen repo; the basis widened even with the VIX in normal ranges. |
| Quarter-end spikes | Since 2014 the basis has spiked at quarter-ends along with repo rates, coinciding with the greater importance of quarter-end reporting and regulatory ratios. |
| Official sector exposure | As the basis widened, BIS reporting banks (especially big US, French and UK banks) increased claims on the Japanese official sector from about USD 200 billion to USD 323 billion, 10% to 19% of their equity. The widening after the 2015 S&P downgrade of Japan highlights internal limits on such exposures. |
| Related markets | Supranationals’ issuance arbitrage slowed when USD swap spreads inverted in Q3 2015. |

Each item is evidence that arbitrage capacity is constrained even when market volatility is normal, consistent with balance sheet costs rather than crisis-type funding strains.

**Applying it to this question**

Statements I and II restate the first two developments. Statement III reverses the direction of banks’ official sector claims and the effect of the downgrade. Statement IV reverses the direction of the funding switch and its effect on flexibility. So I and II only.

**Fragile fact.** Funding moved to secured repo (less flexibility); foreign banks’ Japanese official sector claims went up; the downgrade widened the basis.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** LO 81.c: Assess the causes of covered interest rate parity violations after the financial crisis of 2008.

**GARP:** Chapter 17, Section 17.3, Tighter Limits to Arbitrage and the Basis (Graphs 5 and 6). **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser does not cover this evidence; GARP-only. **Garbled-source** **caution:** Graphs 5 and 6 are unreadable in the extraction; only narrative figures are used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-16 c, where it is Q9 of 12.

a.reason: (Polarity flip (statement III)). A pairs the true statement I with III, which says banks cut their claims and the downgrade had no effect; GARP reports claims rising to USD 323 billion and the basis widening after the downgrade. A also omits the true statement II. A would be correct only if foreign banks had reduced their claims and the basis had ignored the downgrade, and if quarter-end spikes had not been observed.

b.reason: (Polarity flip (statement IV)). B pairs the true statement II with IV, which reverses the funding switch: participants moved from unsecured to secured (repo) funding, and this constrained their flexibility. B also omits the true statement I. B would be correct only if arbitrageurs had moved away from repo and gained flexibility, and if the repo collateral channel had not been observed.

c.reason: Option C contains exactly the two observations GARP reports: the repo collateral channel with the VIX in normal ranges, and quarter-end spikes linked to reporting and regulatory ratios.

d.reason: (Polarity flip (statement III)). D adds the false statement III to the two true statements. It would be correct only if foreign banks had reduced their Japanese official sector claims and the downgrade had left the basis unchanged, the opposite of GARP’s account.

questions.source: High quality paper LTR-16 c Q10
questions.question:
The treasurer of a top-rated European supranational agency explains to its board why the agency’s US dollar issuance, which it swaps back into euros, slowed after the third quarter of 2015. The data below were tabled at the meeting.

| Item (USD billion) | Amount |
|---|---|
| Euro bonds outstanding, end of 2013 | 660 |
| Dollar bonds outstanding, end of 2013 | 355 |
| Dollar bonds issued in the following six quarters | 192 |
| Euro bonds issued in the following six quarters | 178 |

Which of the following explanations is most accurate?

options.text: The USD interest rate swap rate fell below the US Treasury yield; since such issuers must issue above Treasury yields, this sharply raised their cost of placing 7- to 10-year dollar bonds and swapping them into euros.

The USD interest rate swap rate rose above the US Treasury yield; since such issuers must issue above Treasury yields, this sharply raised their cost of placing 7- to 10-year dollar bonds and swapping them into euros.
The agencies act as hedgers rather than arbitrageurs, so their dollar issuance had been widening the basis; once swap rates fell below Treasury yields, their need to hedge euro assets declined.
The agencies lost the top credit rating that lets them issue dollar bonds at attractive rates, so the funding cost advantage they use to harvest the basis disappeared after mid-2015.

questions.solution:
Supranational dollar issuance swapped into euros slowed after Q3 2015: why?

**Concept and theory**

Arbitrageurs differ, and so do their constraints. For highly rated supranational and quasi-government agencies, CIP arbitrage takes the form of “issuance arbitrage”: thanks to their top credit rating they issue bonds in US dollars at attractive rates and swap the proceeds back into euros, thus collecting the currency basis. In Box 17.1 terms, their cost of arbitrage rp is more closely related to the cost of placing bonds in different currencies. GARP observes the rising share of US dollar bond liabilities of major euro area supranationals relative to their euro bond liabilities. In footnote 17 GARP notes that such institutions in effect operate as arbitrageurs, actively harvesting the basis, in the dollar/euro pair and also in the Australian dollar market.

GARP cites this as an example of how developments in related markets can impede arbitrage. Issuance arbitrage slowed when the USD interest rate swap rate fell below the US Treasury yield in Q3 2015. Supranationals have to issue at rates above US Treasury yields; the inversion of USD swap spreads therefore sharply increased their cost of placing a 7- to 10-year bond in dollars and swapping it into euros. With a smaller gain from issuing in dollars, less arbitrage capacity flowed into closing the EUR/USD basis.

| Item | Implication |
|---|---|
| Swap rate above Treasury yield (normal) | Issue just above Treasuries, swap at a rate above that: cheap to harvest the basis |
| Swap rate below Treasury yield (inverted) | Issue above Treasuries but swap off a lower swap rate: placement cost rises sharply |

**Applying it to this question**

The table is context. From end-2013 the agencies issued USD 192 billion in dollar bonds and only USD 178 billion in euro bonds over six quarters, a shift of over USD 10 billion per quarter from euro to dollar, showing they had been harvesting the basis. These figures do not explain the slowdown; the deciding fact is the swap spread inversion in Q3 2015.

**Fragile fact.** Inversion means the swap rate fell below the Treasury yield; supranationals are arbitrageurs, not hedgers.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** LO 81.c: Assess the causes of covered interest rate parity violations after the financial crisis of 2008.

**GARP:** Chapter 17, Section 17.3, Tighter Limits to Arbitrage and the Basis (footnotes 17 and 22; Graph 6); Box 17.1 on supranationals’ rp. **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser does not cover this example; GARP-only.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-16 c, where it is Q10 of 12.

a.reason: Option A gives GARP’s explanation: the swap rate fell below the Treasury yield, and because supranationals must issue above Treasury yields, the cost of placing 7- to 10-year dollar bonds and swapping them into euros rose sharply.

b.reason: (Polarity flip). It reverses the direction of the move. A swap rate above the Treasury yield is the normal configuration that makes issuance arbitrage cheap; it was the fall of the swap rate below the Treasury yield that raised costs. B would be correct if “rose above” read “fell below”.

c.reason: (Role misassignment). It casts the supranationals as hedgers that widen the basis. GARP says they in effect operate as arbitrageurs, actively harvesting the basis, which narrows it. C would describe US non-financial reverse yankee issuers, who add to hedging demand.

d.reason: (Sibling swap). It replaces the related-market channel (swap spread inversion) with a credit-standing channel GARP never mentions. The agencies’ funding advantage rests on their top rating, which the reading does not say they lost. D would be correct only if the agencies had been downgraded.

questions.question:
A portfolio manager at a Chinese asset manager is analysing the sources of US dollar hedging demand behind the yen/dollar basis, using estimates from the GARP reading.

| Item | Estimate |
|---|---|
| Aggregate USD hedging needs (Japanese banks, institutional investors, US issuers) | USD 0.9 trillion (2009) to over USD 1.2 trillion (2015) |
| Japanese banks’ estimated dollar funding gap | about USD 0.6 trillion to USD 0.9 trillion |
| Japanese life insurers’ average hedge ratio on USD bonds | 60% to 70% |
| Unsecured share of Japanese banks’ USD 600 billion New York liabilities | about two thirds |

Which of the following conclusions is most accurate?

options.text: Life insurers were the main driver of the rise in hedging demand, since the banks’ dollar funding gap was broadly unchanged over the period.
Japanese pension funds, dominated by a public fund with high hedge ratios, added most to the demand to borrow dollars through FX swaps.
Samurai bond issuance by US firms was a major contributor, mirroring the role of reverse yankee issuance in the EUR/USD basis.
Banks were the main driver, and their heavier reliance on FX swaps for dollar funding reduced their capacity to serve as counterparties to non-bank hedgers and to arbitrage the basis.

questions.solution:
Sources of dollar hedging demand behind the yen/dollar basis: which sector drove the rise?

**Concept and theory**

Section 17.3 tests the framework over time on the yen/dollar basis, the most extreme and persistent non-zero basis among the major currencies, with banks and institutional investors both bidding for hedges. GARP’s measure of the aggregate dollar hedging needs of Japanese banks, institutional investors and US non-financial firms (samurai bond issuers) rose from USD 0.9 trillion in 2009 to over USD 1.2 trillion in 2015.

The composition matters:

| Sector | GARP’s assessment |
|---|---|
| Banks | Main driver: estimated dollar funding gap grew from about USD 0.6 trillion to USD 0.9 trillion, to finance overseas loan expansion and hedge their own foreign bond holdings. Since 2015 more reliance on FX swaps as US money market fund reform cut wholesale dollar funding. |
| Life insurers | Search for yield raised FX-hedged USD bond holdings; average hedge ratios 60% to 70%. |
| Pension funds | Hedge ratios low (dominated by the unhedged Government Pension Investment Fund), so they ought not to affect the basis. |
| Samurai bonds | No significant role, owing to the thin corporate bond market in Japan. |

GARP draws the limits-to-arbitrage link explicitly: Japanese banks’ reliance on swaps to fund foreign assets reduced their capacity to serve as counterparties to non-bank hedgers in cross-currency markets and to arbitrage the basis. Banks thus play the dual role noted in Section 17.2: they put pressure on the basis and could also arbitrage it, and the balance sheet hedging motive dominates.

**Applying it to this question**

Compare the change in the total with the change in the banks’ component, using the table:

Rise in aggregate hedging needs ≈ 1.2 − 0.9 = 0.3 trillion (at least)

Rise in banks’ funding gap ≈ 0.9 − 0.6 = 0.3 trillion

The banks’ increase accounts for essentially all of the aggregate rise, so banks were the main driver. The unsecured share of Japanese banks’ New York liabilities (about two thirds of USD 600 billion) is background to the money market fund story; it does not change which sector drove the rise. The insurers’ hedge ratio shows they hedge heavily, but not that they drove the increase.

**Fragile fact.** In USD/JPY, banks (not insurers, not pension funds, not samurai issuers) drove the rise in hedging demand.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** LO 81.c: Assess the causes of covered interest rate parity violations after the financial crisis of 2008.

**GARP:** Chapter 17, Section 17.3, The Currency Basis in the Time Series: The Yen/Dollar Case; Demand for Currency Hedges and the Basis (footnotes 19 to 21; Graph 4). **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser does not cover the yen/dollar evidence; GARP-only. **Garbled-source caution:** Graph 4 is unreadable in the extraction; figures come from the narrative.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-16 c, where it is Q11 of 12.

a.reason: (Sibling swap). It gives the main-driver role to life insurers and misreads the bank data: the funding gap rose by about USD 0.3 trillion. A would be correct if the banks’ gap had been flat while insurers’ hedged holdings rose by about USD 0.3 trillion.

b.reason: (Polarity flip). Japanese pension funds have low hedge ratios, being dominated by the unhedged Government Pension Investment Fund, so GARP says they ought not to affect the basis. B would be correct if the public fund hedged most of its foreign assets.

c.reason: (Sibling swap). It transfers the euro area’s reverse yankee story to Japan. GARP says samurai bond issuance has not played a significant role, owing to the thin corporate bond market in Japan. C would be correct for the EUR/USD basis after 2014.

d.reason: Option D matches GARP: the banking sector has been the main driver, and its reliance on swaps reduced its capacity to act as counterparty to non-bank hedgers and to arbitrage the basis.

questions.question: A regulator at a Singapore authority is reviewing a market commentary which claims: “The post-GFC yen/dollar basis was driven by counterparty risk in 2008 to 2009 and in 2011 to 2012; hedging demand only became relevant after 2014, once market tensions had subsided.” Which of the following assessments of the commentary is most consistent with the GARP reading?

options.text: The commentary is accurate: the econometric evidence shows that hedging demand had no role in the basis before 2014 and became significant only after the crisis episodes ended.

The commentary is incomplete: heightened counterparty risks did influence the basis in 2008 to 2009 and 2011 to 2012, but demand for dollar hedging was at work throughout and has continued to matter since.
The commentary is wrong: counterparty risk never influenced the basis, and hedging demand alone explains every post-GFC episode, including the widening in 2008 to 2009 and 2011 to 2012.
The commentary is incomplete: before the crisis the basis tracked hedging volumes closely, whereas after the crisis it has been small and stable regardless of hedging volumes.

questions.solution:
Assessing a commentary that hedging demand mattered only after 2014.

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s conclusion brings both parts of the framework together. The systematic and persistent violation of CIP since the GFC reflects the combination of FX hedging demand and limits to arbitrage arising from lower balance sheet capacity, due to tighter risk management and balance sheet constraints. GARP stresses that even at the height of market tensions, hedging demand played an important but underappreciated role.

Two pieces of evidence support this. First, in the yen/dollar time series, the relationship between hedging demand and the basis changed at the GFC:

| Period | Relationship between basis and hedging volumes |
|---|---|
| Pre-crisis | Basis very small and stable, regardless of hedging volumes |
| Post-crisis | Basis tracks hedging demand remarkably closely; higher demand coincides with a basis further into negative territory |

Second, the regression evidence for December 2007 to December 2015: adding hedging demand to the standard specification (counterparty risk, funding liquidity, market liquidity) improves the fit. For the short tenor, hedging demand works together with money market strains; for the long tenor it has a direct effect. GARP concludes that, while generally ignored, hedging demand played a role even before the widening of the basis from 2014, when market tensions were subdued. Heightened counterparty risks did influence the basis in 2008 to 2009 and again in 2011 to 2012, but the demand for dollar hedging has been at work throughout and has continued to play a significant role since.

**Applying it to this question**

The commentary gets the crisis-time role of counterparty risk right but wrongly confines hedging demand to the post-2014 period. The correct assessment keeps both causes and dates hedging demand to the whole post-GFC period.

**Fragile fact.** Pre-crisis: basis small and stable regardless of hedging volumes; post-crisis: it tracks them. Hedging demand mattered throughout, not only after 2014.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** LO 81.c: Assess the causes of covered interest rate parity violations after the financial crisis of 2008.

**GARP:** Chapter 17, Section 17.3 (Demand for Currency Hedges and the Basis; Regression Results) and Conclusions. **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser’s summary (hedging demand opens the basis, limits to arbitrage keep it open) is consistent but does not cover this evidence; GARP-only. **Boundary call:** the regression coefficients by tenor were tested under LO 81.b; here only the overall assessment of causes is tested.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-16 c, where it is Q12 of 12.

a.reason: (Polarity flip). GARP finds the opposite: hedging demand played a role even before the post-2014 widening and even at the height of market tensions. A would be correct if the regressions had found hedging demand insignificant before 2014.

b.reason: Option B paraphrases GARP’s conclusion: counterparty risk did matter in 2008 to 2009 and 2011 to 2012, but hedging demand was at work throughout and has continued to matter since.

c.reason: (Absolute-claim trap). It denies any role for counterparty risk. GARP explicitly says heightened counterparty risks did influence the basis in 2008 to 2009 and 2011 to 2012. C would be correct only if the counterparty risk terms had no explanatory power in any period.

d.reason: (Polarity flip). It reverses the pre-crisis and post-crisis patterns. Pre-crisis the basis was small and stable regardless of hedging volumes; post-crisis it has tracked them closely. D would be correct with “before” and “after” exchanged.

questions.topic: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-17 a Q1
questions.question:
A member of the board risk committee at a Singapore commercial bank is reviewing a briefing note that explains why the bank adopted an asset-liability management (ALM) framework. The note contains the following statements:

I. Decisions on which customer credit requests to fulfil are closely related to the bank’s ability to raise funds to support the requested new loans.

II. The amount of risk the bank accepts in its portfolio is closely related to the adequacy and composition of its capital, which protects stockholders and creditors against loss.

III. ALM techniques are purely defensive: they help the bank withstand business cycles and seasonal pressures, but they are not used to shape the portfolios of assets and liabilities.

IV. Under ALM, each specialist department takes sole responsibility for optimising its own side of the balance sheet, and the asset and liability portfolios are evaluated separately against the bank’s goals.

Which of the statements in the note are accurate?

options.text: I and IV only
II and III only
I and II only
I, II, and III only

questions.solution:
Board risk committee member audits four statements on why a bank adopts an ALM framework.

**Concept and theory**

GARP opens the chapter (Section 18.1) by describing the modern financial institution as a complex organisation with many departments, each staffed by specialists who make different kinds of decisions: which customers receive credit, which securities are added to or removed from the portfolio, what terms are offered on loans and other services, and which sources of funding to draw upon. The key observation is that these decisions are intimately linked. GARP gives two illustrations. First, the decision on which credit requests to fulfil is closely related to the firm’s ability to raise funds to support the new loans. Second, the amount of risk the firm accepts is closely related to the adequacy and composition of its capital (net worth), which protects stockholders and creditors; even as the firm takes on more risk it must protect net worth from erosion that could end in failure.

Because the decisions are linked, they must be coordinated across the whole institution so that they do not clash and produce inconsistent actions that damage earnings and net worth. Managers therefore look at their asset and liability portfolios as an integrated whole, asking how the whole portfolio contributes to the broad goals of adequate profitability and acceptable risk. This coordinated, integrated decision making is ALM. GARP adds that ALM techniques give institutions two kinds of tool:

|  |  |
|---|---|
| Defensive weapons | handle challenging events such as business cycles and seasonal pressures |
| Offensive weapons | shape portfolios of assets and liabilities to promote the institution’s goals |

Schweser condenses the same idea: the two sides of the balance sheet are seen, for both profitability and risk, as an integrated whole, managed by the asset-liability committee.

**Applying it to this question**

Statement I is GARP’s first illustration of linked decisions (credit decisions depend on funding capacity), so it is accurate. Statement II is GARP’s second illustration (risk taken depends on capital adequacy and composition), so it is accurate. Statement III says ALM is purely defensive; GARP explicitly lists offensive weapons as well, so it is false. Statement IV says each department optimises its own side and the two portfolios are evaluated separately, which is the opposite of the integrated whole that defines ALM, so it is false. The accurate set is I and II.

**Fragile fact.** ALM is both defensive (business cycles, seasonal pressures) and offensive (shaping portfolios), and its essence is coordination across departments, not separate optimisation.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** LO 82.a: Discuss how asset-liability management strategies can help a bank hedge against interest rate risk.

**GARP:** Chapter 18, Section 18.1 Introduction. **Schweser:** Reading 82, Asset-Liability Management Strategies. **GARP vs Schweser:** none; Schweser omits the defensive and offensive framing (condensed).

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-17 a, where it is Q1 of 13.

a.reason: (Polarity flip). Includes IV, which reverses the defining feature of ALM: GARP says decisions must be coordinated across the whole institution and the portfolios viewed as an integrated whole, not optimised department by department. IV would describe the pre-ALM world, in which separate groups made credit, investment and funding decisions without coordination. It also omits II, which is true.

b.reason: (Absolute claim). Includes III, which restricts ALM to “purely defensive” uses. GARP describes ALM as providing defensive weapons for business cycles and seasonal pressures and offensive weapons to shape portfolios in ways that promote the institution’s goals. III would be correct only if the stem asked about the defensive role alone. It also omits I, which is true.

c.reason: GARP states that credit decisions are closely related to the ability to raise funds and that risk accepted is closely related to the adequacy and composition of capital, and that ALM coordinates such decisions as an integrated whole. Only I and II survive, which is option C.

d.reason: (Absolute claim). Adds the false statement III to the two true ones. A candidate who remembers the defensive role but forgets the offensive role chooses this. It would be right only if the source described ALM as a protective tool only.
