questions.question: An internal auditor at a Singapore thrift institution is checking a duration gap report. The thrift reports total assets of SGD 900 million with an average duration of 2.2 years and total liabilities of SGD 820 million with an average duration of 3.1 years. Its one-year IS gap is +SGD 45 million and its net interest margin is 2.4%. Market interest rates on all assets and liabilities are expected to fall from 5.50% to 4.75%. Which of the following is closest to the expected change in the value of the thrift’s net worth?

options.text: An increase of SGD 4.0 million
A decrease of SGD 4.0 million
A decrease of SGD 4.2 million
A decrease of SGD 5.8 million

questions.solution:
Internal auditor estimates the change in a thrift’s net worth when rates fall with a negative leverage-adjusted gap.

**Concept and theory**

The sign of the net worth change is set jointly by the sign of the leverage-adjusted duration gap and the direction of the rate move. GARP’s summary table reads:

| Leverage-adjusted gap | Rates rise | Rates fall |
|---|---|---|
| Positive $\text{(D}_{\text{A}} > \text{D}_{\text{L}} \times$ L/A) | Net worth decreases | Net worth increases |
| Negative $\text{(D}_{\text{A}} < \text{D}_{\text{L}} \times$ L/A) | Net worth increases | Net worth decreases |
| Zero | No change | No change |

With a negative gap, GARP explains that a parallel change in all rates produces a larger change in liability values than in asset values; if rates fall, liabilities increase more in value than assets and net worth declines. The calculation itself is unchanged (Equation 18.22):

$\Delta\text{NW} = \left[-\text{D}_{\text{A}} \frac{\Delta\text{i}}{1 + \text{i}} \text{A}\right] - \left[-\text{D}_{\text{L}} \frac{\Delta\text{i}}{1 + \text{i}} \text{L}\right]$ .

A falling rate makes ∆i negative, so both bracketed terms become value increases; the question is which increase is larger. Candidates often anchor on “rates fall, bond values rise, so net worth rises”, which is true only for a positive gap. Thrift institutions with long-duration liabilities relative to leverage-scaled assets, or any bank whose funding has lengthened relative to its assets, sit in the negative-gap row. The IS gap and net interest margin are income measures; the first describes NII exposure and is irrelevant to the value of net worth.

**Applying it to this question**

$\frac{\Delta\text{i}}{1 + \text{i}} = -$0.0075/1.055 = −0.0071090

$\Delta\text{A} = -$2.2 × (−0.0071090) × 900 = +14.08 SGD million

$\Delta\text{L} = -$3.1 × (−0.0071090) × 820 = +18.07 SGD million

$\Delta\text{NW} =$ 14.08 − 18.07 = −3.995 ≈ −4.0 SGD million

Check: gap = 2.2 − 3.1 × 820/900 = 2.2 − 2.8244 = −0.62 years

Liabilities gain more value than assets, so net worth falls by about SGD 4.0 million. The positive IS gap and the 2.4% NIM are irrelevant to the value of net worth.

**Fragile fact.** Negative gap plus falling rates means net worth falls: liabilities rise in value by more than assets.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** LO 82.c: Describe duration gap management and apply this strategy to protect a bank’s net worth.

**GARP:** Chapter 18, Section 18.6, Using Duration to Hedge against Interest Rate Risk (Equation 18.22 and the summary table of gap, rates and net worth). **GARP vs Schweser:** none.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-17 c, where it is Q9 of 12.

a.reason: (Sign error). Right magnitude, wrong direction. An increase of SGD 4.0 million would follow if rates rose by 75 basis points from 5.50%, since a negative gap gains when rates rise.

b.reason: With a negative leverage-adjusted gap and falling rates, Equation 18.22 gives a decrease of about SGD 4.0 million, option B.

c.reason: (Dropped term). Omits the 1 + i divisor: −(1,980 − 2,542) × (−0.0075) = −4.215, about −4.2. It would be right only under a convention without the relative rate change.

d.reason: (Dropped term). Uses the unadjusted gap: −(2.2 − 3.1) × 900 × (−0.0071090) = −5.76, dropping the L/A factor. It would be correct only if liabilities were also SGD 900 million.

questions.question: The treasurer of a Canadian bank reports to the ALCO that the bank’s leverage-adjusted duration gap is −0.45 years. The bank’s economists now forecast a significant decline in market interest rates over the coming quarter, and the ALCO wants to protect the value of net worth. Which of the following actions and rationales is most appropriate?

options.text: Lengthen asset duration and shorten liability duration, because with a negative gap a fall in rates raises liability values by more than asset values.
Shorten asset duration and lengthen liability duration, because with a negative gap a fall in rates raises asset values by more than liability values.
Leave the balance sheet unchanged, because with a negative gap a fall in rates raises asset values by more than liability values.
Shift funding toward liabilities that reprice beyond one month, because a negative gap exposes net interest income rather than net worth to falling rates.

questions.solution:
Treasurer chooses the ALCO action for a negative leverage-adjusted gap when rates are forecast to fall.

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s summary table links the gap, the rate forecast and the management response. It reads, in condensed form:

| Gap | Forecast | Action |  | Outcome if forecast correct |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Positive | Rates will rise | Reduce $\text{D}_{\text{A}}$, increase $\text{D}_{\text{L}}$ ward a negative gap) | (to- | Net worth increases |
| Negative | Rates will fall | Increase $\text{D}_{\text{A}}$, reduce $\text{D}_{\text{L}}$ ward a positive gap) | (to- | Net worth increases |
| Zero | Any | None needed |  | No change (immunized) |

The logic follows from Equation 18.22. With a negative gap, liability values are more rate-sensitive in currency terms than asset values. When rates fall, liabilities rise in value by more than assets and net worth declines. To protect net worth, management must reverse that imbalance by lengthening assets (raising $\text{D}_{\text{A}}$), shortening liabilities (lowering $\text{D}_{\text{L}}$), or both. Moving all the way to zero immunizes net worth; GARP notes that more aggressive managers may dislike this “wimpy” strategy and may push beyond zero to profit from their rate forecast, accepting the risk that the forecast is wrong. Section 18.6 also lists hedging tools such as futures, options and swaps as alternatives. The IS gap framework has its own table of actions for buckets and NII; it is a sibling tool and does not address the value of net worth.

**Applying it to this question**

The bank’s gap is −0.45 years and the forecast is for falling rates. From the table, the bank is in the negative-gap row and will lose net worth if it does nothing. The required action is to increase $\text{D}_{\text{A}}$ and reduce $\text{D}_{\text{L}}$, which matches option A, together with the correct mechanism (liability values rise by more).

**Fragile fact.** Negative gap: falling rates hurt net worth; the cure is longer assets and shorter liabilities.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** LO 82.c: Describe duration gap management and apply this strategy to protect a bank’s net worth.

**GARP:** Chapter 18, Section 18.6, Using Duration to Hedge against Interest Rate Risk (summary table of gap, rate forecast and management action). **GARP vs Schweser:** none (Schweser’s three-case list gives the same directions).

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-17 c, where it is Q10 of 12.

a.reason: GARP’s table pairs a negative gap and a forecast of falling rates with increasing $\text{D}_{\text{A}}$ and reducing $\text{D}_{\text{L}}$; the rationale in A is the one GARP gives for a negative gap.

b.reason: (Polarity flip). Reverses both the action and the mechanism. Shortening $\text{D}_{\text{A}}$ and lengthening $\text{D}_{\text{L}}$ is GARP’s response for a positive gap when rates are forecast to rise.

c.reason: (Polarity flip). Reverses the outcome: with a negative gap, falling rates raise liability values by more than asset values, so net worth falls. Doing nothing would be appropriate if the gap were negative and rates were forecast to rise.

d.reason: (Sibling swap). Treats the exposure as an IS gap (net interest income) problem and proposes a repricing-bucket action. The stem’s gap is a leverage-adjusted duration gap, which measures exposure of net worth. D would describe an IS gap response for a liability-sensitive bank expecting rates to rise.

questions.question: An internal auditor at a Japanese bank is reviewing the ALCO’s written description of how the bank’s exposure of net worth to interest rate changes is determined and managed. Which of the following statements in the description is NOT correct?

options.text: Exposure can be reduced by closing up the duration gap, that is, by changing the average duration of assets, of liabilities, or of both.
Exposure can be reduced by changing the relative amounts of total assets and total liabilities outstanding, even if item durations are unchanged.
For the same duration gap and the same change in rates, a smaller institution experiences a larger change in net worth than a larger one.
Remaining exposure can be covered with hedging tools such as financial futures, options, or swaps instead of restructuring the balance sheet.

questions.solution:
Internal auditor identifies the incorrect statement about the drivers of net worth exposure and the levers to reduce it.

**Concept and theory**

After the worked examples in Section 18.6, GARP draws out what Equation 18.22 implies. The impact of rate changes on the market value of net worth depends on three size factors:

| Factor | Effect on exposure |
|---|---|
| Size of the duration gap | Larger gap, greater exposure |
| Size of the institution (A and L) | Larger institutions experience a greater change in net worth for any given rate change |
| Size of the rate change | Larger rate changes, greater exposure |

Writing the formula as $\Delta\text{NW} = -(\text{D}_{\text{A}} - \text{D}_{\text{L}}$ L/A$) \times\text{A} \times\Delta$i/(1 $+ \text{i})$ makes all three visible: the gap, the scale A and the relative rate change multiply together. (GARP labels the first factor as $\text{D}_{\text{A}} - \text{D}_{\text{L}}$; the leverage-adjusted form is what enters the formula.) GARP then states that management can reduce exposure by closing up the duration gap, changing $\text{D}_{\text{A}}$, $\text{D}_{\text{L}}$ or both, or by changing the relative amounts of assets and liabilities outstanding, which alters L/A. Earlier in the section GARP adds that a bank may hedge the remaining gap with financial futures, options or swaps, discussed in the following chapter, and Schweser notes that derivatives can move the leverage-adjusted gap toward zero. These levers are complements: balance sheet restructuring changes the gap at source, while derivatives offset it.

**Applying it to this question**

Options A, B and D each restate one of GARP’s levers. Option C contradicts the size-of-institution factor: holding the gap and the rate change fixed, a larger A produces a larger currency change in net worth, not a smaller one.

**Fragile fact.** Bigger is riskier: a larger institution, a larger gap or a larger rate move each enlarge the currency change in net worth.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** LO 82.c: Describe duration gap management and apply this strategy to protect a bank’s net worth.

**GARP:** Chapter 18, Section 18.6, Using Duration to Hedge against Interest Rate Risk (three size factors following the Table 18.4 example; hedging tools in the asset duration discussion). **GARP** **vs Schweser:** none.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-17 c, where it is Q11 of 12.

a.reason: (True statement (not the exception)). GARP lists closing up the duration gap by changing $\text{D}_{\text{A}}$, $\text{D}_{\text{L}}$ or both as a way to reduce exposure. Choosing A treats a stated lever as false; A would be the exception only if duration changes could not move the gap.

b.reason: (True statement (not the exception)). GARP lists changing the relative amounts of A and L as a separate lever; it works through the L/A factor even with item durations fixed. It would be the exception only if the gap did not depend on L/A.

c.reason: GARP says larger institutions experience a greater change in net worth for any given change in rates. C reverses this, so C is the statement that is NOT correct.

d.reason: (True statement (not the exception)). GARP’s Section 18.6 names futures, options and swaps as tools to cover a duration gap. D would be the exception only if hedging were restricted to on-balance-sheet restructuring.

questions.question: A risk consultant is presenting the duration gap experience of the Federal National Mortgage Association (Fannie Mae) in the early 2000s to newly hired analysts at a US bank. Fannie Mae reports its duration gap monthly. Which of the following statements best describes what happened and its lesson for net worth?

options.text: Expecting falling rates, Fannie Mae bought unusually large amounts of government bonds; rates rose instead and the resulting loss of about USD 500 million forced it to sell its headquarters.
Falling rates lengthened Fannie Mae’s assets relative to its liabilities, opening a positive duration gap of about 14 months, so a rebound in rates would have reduced the value of its net worth.
Fannie Mae’s duration gap of about negative 14 months stayed inside its target band of negative 18 to positive 18 months, so investors treated the disclosure as evidence of sound hedging.

Falling rates shortened Fannie Mae’s assets relative to its liabilities, opening a negative duration gap of about 14 months, so further declines in rates would have reduced the value of its net worth.

questions.solution:
Risk consultant explains Fannie Mae’s negative duration gap and its lesson for net worth.

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s “Real Banks, Real Decisions” box describes duration gap management at the Federal National Mortgage Association (Fannie Mae), which reports its duration gap on a monthly basis. Fannie raises funds by issuing notes and bonds and uses the proceeds to buy residential mortgages. As market rates plummeted early in the 21st century and home mortgage financings soared, the average maturity of its assets and liabilities shifted: its liabilities lengthened and its assets became shorter-term. The result was a negative duration gap of about 14 months at the close of 2002; assets were rolling over into cash more than a year sooner than liabilities. With a negative gap, continued declines in rates would have continued to reduce net worth, because the longer-term liabilities would rise in value relative to the shorter-term assets. Investors reacted negatively to the announcement of a widening negative gap and the stock price fell for a time. Fannie’s stated objective is a duration gap between negative 6 months and positive 6 months; GARP reports that it later brought the gap to negative 6 months and, by September 2007, within negative 1 to positive 1 month. The case shows the mechanics of the negative-gap row of GARP’s table in a real balance sheet, and why disclosure of the gap matters to investors.

| Case in Chapter 18 | True lesson |
|---|---|
| Fannie Mae (2002) | Shorter assets, longer liabilities: negative gap, net worth hurt by further rate falls |
| First Bank System, Minneapolis | Bought large bond holdings on a forecast of falling rates; rates rose, loss of about USD 500 million, headquarters sold |

**Applying it to this question**

The stem asks what happened and what it means for net worth. The deciding facts are the direction of the maturity shift (assets shorter, liabilities longer), the sign and size of the gap (negative, about 14 months) and the consequence (further rate declines reduce net worth). Only option D has all three.

**Fragile fact.** Fannie Mae’s gap was negative (assets shorter than liabilities), so it was hurt by falling rates; the target band was plus or minus 6 months.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** LO 82.c: Describe duration gap management and apply this strategy to protect a bank’s net worth.

**GARP:** Chapter 18, Section 18.6, Real Banks, Real Decisions: Duration Gap Management at the World’s Largest Mortgage Bank. **GARP vs Schweser:** Schweser does not cover the case (GARP-only). Source caution: the GARP box dates both the negative 14 month gap and the return to negative 6 months to 2002; no question depends on the year of the return.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-17 c, where it is Q12 of 12.

a.reason: (Case swap (sibling swap)). This is the true lesson of First Bank System of Minneapolis in GARP’s Section 18.3, which bought large amounts of government bonds on a forecast of falling rates and lost about USD 500 million when rates rose. It would be correct if the stem asked about First Bank System.

b.reason: (Polarity flip). Reverses the maturity shift and the sign of the gap: Fannie’s assets shortened and liabilities lengthened, giving a negative gap. B would describe a bank whose assets lengthened relative to its liabilities, which is exposed to rising rates.

c.reason: (Scope or condition error). Fannie’s band is negative 6 to positive 6 months, so a gap of about negative 14 months was well outside it, and investors reacted negatively. C would require a band three times as wide and a different market reaction.

d.reason: GARP reports that lengthening liabilities and shorter-term assets produced a negative gap of about 14 months, and that if rates had continued to fall, net worth would have continued to decline. Option D states this.

questions.question:
A member of the board risk committee at an Australian regional bank is reviewing a treasury proposal. The treasurer is confident that rates will rise and proposes to shade the bank’s interest-sensitive (IS) gap strongly toward asset sensitivity in every bucket out to one year, arguing that the plan “can only help the bank” if the forecast is right. The committee member asks which limitation of IS gap management the proposal overlooks.

Which of the following statements best describes that limitation?

options.text: An aggressive IS gap position cannot widen the net interest margin even if the forecast proves correct, because IS gap management can only freeze the margin at its current level.
The proposal relies on duration, which is a linear measure that is reasonably accurate only for small, parallel shifts in the yield curve, so a large rise in rates would distort the gap reading.

The position may widen the net interest margin if rates rise, but IS gap analysis ignores the effect of rate changes on net worth, and the policy raises earnings volatility and can reduce the value of the owners’ investment.
The position is free of interest rate risk as long as the cumulative gap over one year is positive, because a positive cumulative gap guarantees that net interest income rises when rates rise.

questions.solution:
Board risk committee reviews an aggressive asset-sensitive IS gap proposal; which limitation is overlooked?

**Concept and theory**

Interest-sensitive (IS) gap management is the income-side tool of asset-liability management. Management groups repriceable assets and liabilities into maturity buckets and computes, for each bucket, the dollar IS gap $= \text{IS assets} -$ IS liabilities. Its purpose is to protect, or deliberately widen, the net interest margin, NIM $= (\text{interest income} -$ interest expense)/total earning assets.

GARP describes two styles. A defensive policy sets the IS gap as close to zero as possible to reduce the expected volatility of net interest income. An aggressive policy shades the gap toward asset sensitivity (when management confidently forecasts rising rates) or liability sensitivity (falling rates). GARP warns that such a strategy creates greater risk, that consistently correct rate forecasting is impossible, and that rates moving the wrong way magnify losses.

The deeper limitation, stated at the end of GARP’s list of problems with IS gap management, is one of scope: IS gap management does not consider the impact of changing rates on the owners’ position as represented by net worth. A manager pursuing an aggressive gap policy may expand the NIM, but at the cost of increasing the volatility of net earnings and reducing the value of the stockholders’ investment. Effective ALM therefore requires managers to target desirable levels of both net interest income and net worth, which is why GARP then introduces duration gap management. Schweser’s summary words the same point as: an aggressive approach may increase earnings volatility, which may in turn hurt the stock price.

| Tool | What it protects | What it leaves exposed |
|---|---|---|
| IS gap | Net interest income and NIM | Market value of net worth |
| Duration gap | Market value of net worth | Relies on duration’s own assumptions |

**Applying it to this question**

The treasurer’s claim that the plan “can only help” focuses on the upside to the margin if the forecast is right. The committee member’s question is what the IS gap framework itself fails to capture. The deciding fact is GARP’s statement that IS gap management ignores net worth and that an aggressive gap policy, while possibly widening the NIM, raises earnings volatility and can reduce the value of the owners’ investment. Only option C states both halves.

**Fragile fact.** The cost of aggressive gapping falls on earnings volatility and net worth, not on the margin’s upside: the NIM may widen, yet the owners’ value can fall.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** LO 82.d: Discuss the limitations of interest-sensitive gap management and duration gap management. **GARP:** Chapter 18, Section 18.4, “Problems with Interest-Sensitive GAP Management” (final paragraph) and the aggressive versus defensive gap discussion. **GARP vs Schweser:** none in substance; GARP says “reducing the value of the stockholders’ investment (net worth)”, Schweser says “negatively affect the bank’s stock price”.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-17 d, where it is Q1 of 12.

a.reason: (Absolute claim). GARP says an aggressive policy may expand the NIM, and lists “increase the NIM” as one of management’s target choices alongside freezing it. Saying the gap “cannot widen” the margin turns one option into a universal rule. It would be correct only for a purely defensive policy whose stated target is to freeze the NIM at its present level.

b.reason: (Sibling swap). Reliance on a linear measure that works best for small, parallel shifts is a limitation of duration gap management (GARP 18.7). The proposal concerns repricing buckets, not duration. The option would be correct if the treasurer had proposed immunizing net worth by setting the leverage-adjusted duration gap to zero.

c.reason: C paraphrases GARP’s closing limitation of IS gap management: an aggressive gap policy may expand the NIM, but at the cost of more volatile net earnings and a lower value of the stockholders’ investment, because the IS gap does not consider the effect of rate changes on net worth.

d.reason: (Absolute claim). A positive gap benefits from rising rates only if the forecast is right and if asset and liability rates move together; GARP stresses that aggressive gapping creates greater risk and that interest rates attached to assets and liabilities are not perfectly correlated. Nothing is “guaranteed” or “free of risk”. The direction would be correct under the textbook assumption of equal rate changes on all items (positive gap, rising rates, higher NII).

questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a Singapore commercial bank is preparing a note for the asset-liability committee (ALCO). After a rebalancing exercise, the bank’s dollar IS gap is zero in every maturity bucket, and the ALCO chair states that the net interest margin is now “fully protected regardless of which way rates go”. The bank funds a large share of its SGD loan book with money market borrowings. The economy is entering an expansion and market rates are expected to rise steadily.

Which of the following outcomes is most consistent with the limitations of IS gap management described in the reading?

options.text: Net interest income is likely to fall, because loan rates tend to lag money market borrowing rates, so interest revenues tend to grow more slowly than interest expenses during expansions.
Net interest income is likely to rise, because money market borrowing rates tend to lag loan rates, so interest expenses tend to grow more slowly than interest revenues during expansions.
Net interest income is likely to stay unchanged, because a zero IS gap in every bucket removes all interest rate risk from the margin whatever the speed of individual rate changes.
Net interest income is likely to fall, because rising rates lower the market value of the long-term loans, and that loss of asset value flows directly into the net interest margin.

questions.solution:
Zero IS gap in every bucket, money-market funded bank, expansion with rising rates: what happens to NII?

**Concept and theory**

In theory a zero IS gap protects the NIM whichever way rates move, because repriceable revenues and repriceable costs change together. GARP immediately qualifies this: as a practical matter a zero gap does not eliminate all interest rate risk, because the interest rates attached to assets and liabilities are not perfectly correlated in the real world. The gap counts dollars that reprice in a period; it says nothing about how far or how fast each rate moves when they do.

GARP gives specific directions, which must be kept apart:

| Pair of rates | Which moves faster (GARP) |
|---|---|
| Loan rates vs money market borrowing rates | Money market borrowing rates; loan rates lag behind |
| Deposit rates vs loan rates | Loan rates; deposit rates typically lag |
| Liability rates (mostly short term) vs asset rates (many long term) | Liability rates tend to move faster |

From the first pair GARP draws the cycle result: interest revenues often grow more slowly than interest expenses during economic expansions, while interest expenses fall more rapidly than interest revenues during downturns. Schweser summarizes the general point as “rates on assets and liabilities may not move together” and gives a deposit example (banks may be slow to raise savings rates but quick to adjust loan rates). The two sources are consistent once the specific pair of rates is identified.

**Applying it to this question**

The stem gives three facts: a zero gap in every bucket, heavy money market funding of the loan book, and an expansion with rising rates. The ALCO chair’s claim that the margin is “fully protected” ignores imperfect correlation. Because loan rates lag money market borrowing rates, the bank’s expenses rise faster than its revenues during the expansion, so net interest income tends to fall even though the gap is zero.

**Fragile fact.** Direction check: money market borrowing rates lead, loan rates lag, deposit rates lag loans; so in an expansion expenses outrun revenues and a zero-gap bank still loses NII.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** LO 82.d: Discuss the limitations of interest-sensitive gap management and duration gap management. **GARP:** Chapter 18, Section 18.4, discussion of the zero gap (after the ISR) and “Problems with Interest-Sensitive GAP Management”. **GARP** **vs Schweser:** none; Schweser uses a savings-versus-loan example, GARP adds the loan-versus-money-market lag and the cycle result.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-17 d, where it is Q2 of 12.

a.reason: A restates GARP: a zero gap does not remove all risk; loan rates lag money market borrowing rates, so interest revenues grow more slowly than interest expenses in expansions.

b.reason: (Polarity flip). It reverses the lag: GARP says loan rates lag money market borrowing rates, not the other way round. The option’s conclusion (NII rises) would be correct in the opposite phase of the cycle: in a downturn with falling rates, GARP says interest expenses fall more rapidly than interest revenues, so NII tends to rise.

c.reason: (Absolute claim). GARP explicitly says a zero gap “does not eliminate all interest rate risk”. The option would be correct only under the textbook assumption that rates on all repriceable assets and liabilities change by the same amount at the same time.

d.reason: (Sibling swap). The fall in the market value of long-term fixed-rate loans is a net worth (price risk) effect, measured by duration gap, not a driver of net interest income. The option would be correct if the question asked about the market value of net worth for a bank with a positive leverage-adjusted duration gap when rates rise.

questions.question:
A treasury analyst at a Canadian bank is testing the ALCO’s one-year earnings forecast. The forecast applies the standard rule, change in net interest income equals the change in rates times the IS gap, to a 100 basis point rise in market rates. The analyst’s repricing study shows that the bank’s rates do not move one for one with market rates.

| Item (one-year bucket) | Amount (CAD m) | Rate change for a 100 bp market move (bp) |
|---|---|---|
| IS assets | 820 | 60 |
| IS liabilities | 700 | 90 |
| Total assets | 1,500 | n/a |

Using the repricing study, the expected change in annual net interest income is closest to:

options.text: CAD +3.18 million
CAD +1.20 million
CAD −6.30 million
CAD −1.38 million

questions.solution:
Canadian bank: positive one-year gap, but asset rates move 60 bp and liability rates 90 bp for a 100 bp market move.

**Concept and theory**

The standard gap rule (GARP Eq. 18.13) is

∆N I I $\approx\Delta\text{r} \times$ IS gap, IS gap $= \text{ISA} -$ ISL,

where ISA and ISL are the dollar amounts of interest-sensitive assets and liabilities in the period and ∆r is the change in rates. Schweser stresses that this equation is accurate only when interest rates on all assets and liabilities change by the same amount, “but this is an unlikely outcome”. The first limitation of IS gap management in both sources is precisely that rates on assets and liabilities may not move together.

When they do not, go back to the definition of net interest income (GARP Eq. 18.12): income is the yield on rate-sensitive assets times their volume plus the yield on fixed assets times their volume, less the matching cost terms for liabilities. Holding fixed-rate items constant, only the repriceable items change, so

∆N I I $= \text{ISA} \times\Delta\text{r}_{\text{A}} - \text{ISL} \times\Delta\text{r}_{\text{L}}$,

with $\Delta\text{r}_{\text{A}}$ and $\Delta\text{r}_{\text{L}}$ the actual changes in the average rates on IS assets and IS liabilities. This is exactly how GARP’s Table 18.1 recomputes NII when rate-sensitive asset yields and liability costs both rise by two points. If $\Delta\text{r}_{\text{A}} = \Delta\text{r}_{\text{L}}$ the expression collapses to the gap rule; if liability rates move further or faster (which GARP says is typical, since liabilities are mostly short term), a positive gap can still lose income. This is the same idea that motivates the weighted gap: the dollar gap alone hides basis risk.

**Applying it to this question**

Formula first: ∆N I I $= \text{ISA} \times\Delta\text{r}_{\text{A}} - \text{ISL} \times\Delta\text{r}_{\text{L}}$.

Change in interest income = 820 × 0.0060 = 4.92 (CAD m)

Change in interest expense = 700 × 0.0090 = 6.30 (CAD m)

∆N I I = 4.92 − 6.30 = −1.38 (CAD m)

Gap rule (for comparison) = (820 − 700) × 0.0100 = +1.20 (CAD m)

Total assets of CAD 1,500 million are irrelevant: they would be needed only for the relative IS gap (120/1,500 = 8%), which does not change the answer. Meaning: although the bank is asset sensitive on a dollar basis, its liability rates move one and a half times as far as its asset rates, so a rate rise cuts annual NII by about CAD 1.38 million instead of raising it by CAD 1.20 million.

**Fragile fact.** The gap rule is exact only when every repriceable rate moves by the same amount; with liability rates moving further, a positive gap can still lose income.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** LO 82.d: Discuss the limitations of interest-sensitive gap management and duration gap management. **GARP:** Chapter 18, Section 18.4, Eq. 18.12, Eq. 18.13, Table 18.1 and “Problems with Interest-Sensitive GAP Management”. **GARP vs Schweser:** none; the accuracy condition on the gap rule is stated in Schweser (LO 82.b text) and is the first limitation in Schweser LO 82.d.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-17 d, where it is Q3 of 12.

a.reason: (Wrong input twin). It swaps the two adjustment speeds: 820 × 0.0090 − 700 × 0.0060 = 7.38 − 4.20 = +3.18. It would be correct if the study had found asset rates moving 90 bp and liability rates 60 bp.

b.reason: (Dropped term (assumes equal moves)). It applies the gap rule 120 × 0.01 = +1.20, discarding the repricing study. It would be correct only if both asset and liability rates moved by the full 100 bp, the condition under which Schweser says the rule is accurate.

c.reason: (Intermediate result). −6.30 is the increase in interest expense alone (700 × 0.009), with the CAD 4.92 million rise in interest income left out. It would be the answer if the question asked only for the change in interest expense.

d.reason: D applies the actual rate responses to each side, as the limitation requires, instead of assuming that all rates move with the market by the same amount.

questions.question:
A junior risk analyst at a UK building society is asked to adjust the IS gap for basis risk using rate-sensitivity weights estimated by the ALCO. The weights measure how far each item’s rate moves for a one-point move in the overnight interbank rate.

| Rate-sensitive item | Amount (GBP m) | Weight |
|---|---|---|
| Interbank loans | 80 | 1.00 |
| Government securities | 60 | 1.20 |
| Loans and leases | 140 | 1.40 |
| Interest-bearing deposits | 220 | 0.80 |
| Money market borrowings | 100 | 0.95 |
| Total assets (all items) | 900 | n/a |

If the overnight interbank rate rises by 150 basis points, which of the following correctly states the weighted IS gap and the predicted change in net interest income?

options.text: Weighted gap GBP −40 million; net interest income changes by GBP −0.60 million
Weighted gap GBP +77 million; net interest income changes by GBP +1.155 million
Weighted gap GBP +77 million; net interest income changes by GBP −1.155 million
Weighted gap GBP +28 million; net interest income changes by GBP +0.42 million

questions.solution:
UK building society: unweighted gap −40; weight each item; predict NII for a 150 bp rise in the interbank rate.

**Concept and theory**

Because rates on different assets and liabilities change by different amounts and at different speeds (GARP calls this basis risk), some institutions use a **weighted interest-sensitive gap**. Each rate-sensitive item is multiplied by an interest rate sensitivity weight that measures how much its rate moves for a one-point move in a reference market rate (GARP uses the federal funds rate with a weight of 1.0). More rate-volatile items weigh more heavily in the refigured balance sheet:

Weighted gap $= \sum_{\text{i}} \text{w}_{\text{i}} \text{A}_{\text{i}} - \sum_{\text{j}} \text{w}_{\text{j}} \text{L}_{\text{j}}$, ∆N I I $\approx\text{Weighted gap} \times\Delta\text{r}_{\text{ref}}$,

where $\text{A}_{\text{i}} \text{and L}_{\text{j}}$ are the dollar amounts of rate-sensitive assets and liabilities, w their weights, and $\Delta\text{r}_{\text{ref}}$ the change in the reference rate. In GARP’s example, securities carry 1.3 and loans and leases 1.5 (moving more than federal funds), while deposits carry 0.86 and money market borrowings 0.91 (moving less). The unweighted gap of −\$23 million becomes a weighted gap of +\$75 million: the bank looked liability sensitive but would actually benefit from rising rates, and a 2-point rise changes NII by +\$1.50 million rather than −\$0.46 million. GARP’s lesson: “things are not always as they appear”. Schweser makes the same point with weights of 1.0 for federal funds, 0.5 for savings rates set at the bank’s discretion and 1.4 for a highly volatile security.

**Applying it to this question**

Formula first: weighted gap $= \sum\text{w}_{\text{i}} \text{A}_{\text{i}} - \sum\text{w}_{\text{j}} \text{L}_{\text{j}}$, then ∆N I I $= \text{weighted gap} \times\Delta$r.

Unweighted gap = (80 + 60 + 140) − (220 + 100) = 280 − 320 = −40

Weighted IS assets = 80(1.00) + 60(1.20) + 140(1.40) = 80 + 72 + 196 = 348

Weighted IS liabilities = 220(0.80) + 100(0.95) = 176 + 95 = 271

Weighted gap = 348 − 271 = +77 (GBP m)

∆N I I = 77 × 0.015 = +1.155 (GBP m)

Total assets of GBP 900 million are irrelevant; the weighted gap uses only rate-sensitive items. Meaning: the society looks liability sensitive on a simple count but behaves as asset sensitive, gaining about GBP 1.155 million of annual NII from the rise instead of losing GBP 0.60 million.

**Fragile fact.** A weight above 1.0 means the item’s rate moves more than the reference rate; weighting can flip the sign of the gap.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** LO 82.d: Discuss the limitations of interest-sensitive gap management and duration gap management. **GARP:** Chapter 18, Section 18.4, “Problems with Interest-Sensitive GAP Management” and the table “The Weighted Interest-Sensitive Gap: Dealing with Basis Risk”. **GARP vs Schweser:** none; the illustrative weights differ (GARP 1.3, 1.5, 0.86, 0.91; Schweser 0.5 and 1.4). GARP’s extracted table shows rounded products (\$137 and \$58).

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-17 d, where it is Q4 of 12.

a.reason: (Dropped term (weights ignored)). −40 × 0.015 = −0.60 is the unweighted gap result, the very measure the weighted approach is designed to correct. It would be correct only if every weight were 1.00.

b.reason: B weights both sides and applies the reference-rate change to the weighted gap, exactly as in GARP’s weighted-gap table.

c.reason: (Sign error). The weighted gap of +77 is right, but a positive gap gains when the reference rate rises. −1.155 would be correct if the interbank rate fell by 150 bp.

d.reason: (Dropped term (liability weights omitted)). Weighting assets only gives 348 − 320 = +28 and 28 × 0.015 = +0.42. It would be correct only if both liability weights were 1.00.

questions.question:
A risk consultant is presenting the weighted interest-sensitive gap to newly hired analysts at a Swiss cantonal bank and lists four statements:

I. The weighted gap is designed to deal with basis risk, the tendency of rates on different assets and liabilities to change by different amounts and at different speeds.

II. Interest-bearing deposits usually receive a weight below 1.0 because the rates on them tend to change more slowly than market rates.

III. A weight of 1.4 on a security portfolio means that the portfolio’s average yield moves by 40% less than the reference market rate.

IV. Because the weights only rescale balance sheet items, the weighted gap must always have the same sign as the unweighted gap.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.text: I and II only
I and III only
II and IV only
I, II, and IV only

questions.solution:
Statement audit on the weighted IS gap: basis risk, deposit weights, meaning of a 1.4 weight, sign of the weighted gap.

**Concept and theory**

The weighted gap exists because of the first limitation of simple gap analysis: the simple gap implicitly assumes that every repriceable rate moves one for one with market rates. GARP observes that rates attached to assets of various kinds often change by different amounts and at different speeds than many of the rates attached to liabilities, “a phenomenon called basis risk”, and that some institutions therefore developed a weighted interest-sensitive gap that takes into account the tendency of interest rates to vary in speed and magnitude relative to each other and with the business cycle.

Reading a weight correctly is the whole skill:

| Weight | Meaning | GARP and Schweser examples |
|---|---|---|
| 1.0 | Moves one for one with the reference rate | Federal funds loans |
| Above 1.0 | Moves more than the reference rate | Securities 1.3, loans and leases 1.5; volatile security 1.4 |
| Below 1.0 | Moves less or more slowly | Deposits 0.86, money market borrowings 0.91; savings 0.5 |

Deposit rates and some money market borrowings change more slowly than market rates (Schweser: savings rates are changed at the bank’s discretion), so they receive weights below 1.0. Multiplying each item by its weight rebuilds the balance sheet in “effective” rate-sensitive dollars, and the weighted gap can differ from the simple gap not only in size but in sign. GARP’s worked example turns a gap of −\$23 million into +\$75 million.

**Applying it to this question**

Check each statement against the source. I: GARP’s definition of basis risk and the purpose of the weighted gap; true. II: GARP assigns deposits 0.86 because their rates change more slowly than market rates; true. III: a weight of 1.4 means the yield moves 40% more, not less; false. IV: GARP’s own example changes sign; false. Correct set: I and II only.

**Fragile fact.** Weight above 1.0 means more volatile than the reference rate; deposits sit below 1.0; and the weighted gap can change sign.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** LO 82.d: Discuss the limitations of interest-sensitive gap management and duration gap management. **GARP:** Chapter 18, Section 18.4, “Problems with Interest-Sensitive GAP Management” and “The Weighted Interest-Sensitive Gap: Dealing with Basis Risk”. **GARP vs Schweser:** none; illustrative weights differ.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-17 d, where it is Q5 of 12.

a.reason: A selects exactly the two statements that match the source: the weighted gap targets basis risk (I), and deposits carry weights below 1.0 because their rates lag market rates (II).

b.reason: (Polarity flip). It includes III, which reverses the meaning of a weight above 1.0. GARP gives loans and leases 1.5 because they are “half again as volatile” as federal funds. III would be correct for a weight of 0.6.

c.reason: (Absolute claim). It includes IV and drops I. IV claims the sign can never change, yet GARP’s example moves from −\$23 million to +\$75 million. IV would be correct only if every weight were the same number, so that weighting rescaled both sides equally.

d.reason: (Absolute claim). It accepts I and II but adds the false “must always have the same sign” in IV. D would be correct only if the question asked about a balance sheet where all weights equalled 1.0.

questions.question:
An internal auditor at a Brazilian bank is reviewing its IS gap process. The bank measures the gap over a single 12-month planning period. Checkable deposits and savings accounts are slotted into the bucket that contains the next scheduled central bank policy meeting, on the grounds that the bank changes those rates only after a policy move. Several medium-sized BRL loan pools reprice just after the 12-month cut-off.

Which recommendation is most consistent with the limitations of IS gap management described in the reading?

options.text: Exclude checkable deposits and savings accounts from the gap report, since items without a contractual repricing date cannot be classified as interest sensitive.
Replace the gap report with duration gap analysis, since duration requires no assumptions about the cash flow pattern of checkable deposits and savings accounts.

Recognize that these deposit rates can be changed at any time, not only after policy moves, and measure the gap over several planning periods, since a single period is arbitrary and items can fall between the cracks.
Keep the single 12-month period, since a zero cumulative gap over the year keeps net interest income immunized in every sub-period within the year.

questions.solution:
Auditor reviews a single 12-month bucket with deposits slotted by policy-meeting dates; best recommendation?

**Concept and theory**

IS gap analysis depends on knowing when each asset and liability will reprice, because the gap is built by placing items into maturity buckets. GARP lists two related problems with this step.

First, the point at which certain assets and liabilities can be repriced is not always easy to identify. GARP’s example is checkable deposits and savings accounts, whose rates may be adjusted up or down at any time. Schweser sharpens it: banks may adjust rates on interest-bearing demand deposits and savings accounts at any time, “not just when the Fed increases or decreases the target fed funds rate”. Slotting such accounts by the calendar of policy meetings is therefore an assumption, not a fact.

Second, the choice of planning periods over which to balance interest-sensitive assets and liabilities is highly arbitrary. Some items always fall between the cracks in setting planning periods, and they could cause trouble if rates move against the firm. GARP’s remedy is practical: wise asset-liability managers use several different lengths of planning periods (“maturity buckets”) in measuring their exposure. Schweser adds the within-period version of the same problem: rates may change at different speeds inside one bucket, so a cumulative gap of zero over a year can coexist with NII that varies through the year.

Note that the answer to these problems is better bucketing and judgment about deposit behavior, not dropping the accounts: GARP lists savings accounts, money market deposits and interest-bearing checkable deposits among repriceable liabilities, and Schweser notes that banks must estimate the sensitivity even of noninterest-bearing demand deposits.

**Applying it to this question**

The auditor sees two flaws: deposits are slotted by the assumption that their rates change only after policy moves, and a single 12-month period lets loan pools just past the cut-off “fall between the cracks”. Option C addresses both with the remedies GARP gives.

**Fragile fact.** The repricing date of savings and checkable deposits is a judgment call, since the bank can reset them at any time; the fix is several bucket lengths, not exclusion.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** LO 82.d: Discuss the limitations of interest-sensitive gap management and duration gap management. **GARP:** Chapter 18, Section 18.4, “Problems with Interest-Sensitive GAP Management” (paragraph beginning “Moreover, the point at which certain assets and liabilities can be repriced”). **GARP vs Schweser:** none; the “not just when the Fed moves” wording and the zero-cumulative-gap example are Schweser’s elaborations.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-17 d, where it is Q6 of 12.

a.reason: (Scope error). GARP and Schweser treat savings and checkable deposits as rate-sensitive items whose sensitivity must be estimated, not as items to exclude. Exclusion would be appropriate only for genuinely nonrepriceable items, such as equity capital or buildings and equipment.

b.reason: (Sibling swap). Duration gap analysis faces the same problem: GARP 18.7 says checkable deposits and passbook savings have cash flow patterns that are not well defined, making duration difficult to calculate. B would be correct only if the question asked which tool measures the effect of rate changes on net worth.

c.reason: C restates GARP: deposit rates can be changed at any time, planning periods are arbitrary and items fall between the cracks, so managers should use several lengths of planning periods.

d.reason: (Absolute claim). A zero cumulative gap over a year does not immunize every sub-period: Schweser’s example of variable-rate loans repricing annually funded by daily-repricing funds shows NII varying through the year despite a zero cumulative gap. D would be correct only if all items in the bucket repriced on the same date.

questions.question:
A treasury analyst at a Japanese regional bank reviews the following position. The bank holds JPY 50 billion of variable-rate business loans whose next rate reset falls exactly 12 months from today, funded entirely by JPY 50 billion of overnight borrowings that reprice daily. The current loan yield is 1.9% and the current overnight funding cost is 0.3%. Because both items reprice within one year, the one-year cumulative IS gap is zero. Market rates rise by 80 basis points at the end of month 3 and then stay unchanged.

Ignoring compounding, the change in the bank’s net interest income over the next 12 months is closest to:

options.text: JPY 0
JPY −300 million
JPY −400 million
JPY +300 million

questions.solution:
Japanese bank: loans reset in 12 months, funding reprices daily, rates up 80 bp after month 3; NII change over 12 months?

**Concept and theory**

The cumulative gap is “a useful overall measure” (GARP): it sums IS assets minus IS liabilities over a designated period, and GARP’s Eq. 18.13 approximates the change in NII as the change in rates times the cumulative gap. The measure is blind to when within the period each item reprices. Two items can both “reprice within one year” yet one resets tomorrow and the other in twelve months.

Schweser states this limitation with an example that matches this question: a bank with variable-rate loans that reprice annually, financed with short-term funds that reprice daily, has a cumulative IS gap of zero and appears immunized, but NII will vary over the year as the cost of funding adjusts with market rates. GARP’s version is that rates change at different speeds, the choice of planning periods is highly arbitrary, and items fall between the cracks; hence its advice to use several bucket lengths.

For a horizon of length H, a repriceable item of amount X whose rate changes by ∆r after it reprices at time $\tau$ contributes approximately

∆(interest over H$) \approx\text{X} \times\Delta\text{r} \times\text{max}($0, H $- \tau_{\text{eff}})$,

with H and $\tau_{\text{eff}}$ measured in years and $\tau_{\text{eff}}$ the later of the date of the rate change and the item’s first repricing date after it. Put simply: income or expense changes only for the part of the horizon after both the market move and the item’s own reset have happened.

**Applying it to this question**

Formula first: ∆N I I $= \Delta(\text{interest income}) - \Delta(\text{interest expense})$, each measured only for the months after the item reprices at the new rate.

Loans: reset at month 12 ⇒ ∆(income over 12 months) = 0

Funding: reprices daily, rate up from end of month 3 $\Rightarrow\text{months affected} =$ 12 − 3 = 9

$\Delta(\text{interest expense}) =$ 50,000 × 0.0080 $\times\frac{9}{12} =$ 300 (JPY m)

∆N I I = 0 − 300 = −300 (JPY m)

Cumulative-gap rule = 0 × 0.0080 = 0

The current loan yield (1.9%) and funding cost (0.3%) are irrelevant: they set the level of NII, but the question asks for the change, which depends only on the rate change, the amounts and the timing. Meaning: the zero one-year gap suggests no exposure, but the bank loses about JPY 300 million of NII because its funding reprices nine months before its loans.

**Fragile fact.** “Reprices within one year” is not “reprices at the same time”: a zero cumulative gap can hide a nine-month funding mismatch.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** LO 82.d: Discuss the limitations of interest-sensitive gap management and duration gap management. **GARP:** Chapter 18, Section 18.4, cumulative gap (Eq. 18.13) and “Problems with Interest-Sensitive GAP Management”. **GARP vs Schweser:** none; the specific zero-cumulative-gap example is Schweser-only (condensed source); GARP supports it through “rates change at different speeds” and “items fall between the cracks”.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-17 d, where it is Q7 of 12.

a.reason: (Scope error). JPY 0 is the cumulative-gap rule applied to a gap that is zero over the whole year. It would be correct if the loans also repriced daily (or if both items reset on the same date).

b.reason: B charges the higher funding cost for the nine months during which it applies while loan income stays fixed until the reset, which is exactly the within-bucket mismatch that a zero cumulative gap conceals.

c.reason: (Time-conversion slip). 50,000 × 0.008 = 400 charges the higher funding cost for the full 12 months. It would be correct if rates had risen today rather than at the end of month 3.

d.reason: (Sign error). +300 has the right size but the wrong direction: funding costs rise while loan income is fixed, so NII falls. It would be correct if rates fell by 80 bp at the end of month 3.

questions.question:
The treasurer of a Chinese joint-stock bank is explaining to newly hired analysts why finding CNY assets and liabilities with matching durations is often frustrating, and why it would be easier if every loan’s maturity equalled its duration.

Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: For loans and securities that pay out gradually over time, duration usually exceeds calendar maturity, so assets that look short can carry long durations.
A five-year amortizing commercial loan has a duration equal to its five-year maturity, because it is a single loan contract with one final maturity date.
The less frequently an instrument pays interest or repays principal, the shorter its duration, other things being equal.
Duration equals calendar maturity only for instruments such as zero-coupon securities, single-payment loans and Treasury bills, and the match improves as maturity shortens.

questions.solution:
Treasurer explains why matching durations is frustrating: duration versus calendar maturity.

**Concept and theory**

Duration is a value- and time-weighted measure of maturity: the present-value-weighted average time at which an instrument’s cash flows arrive (GARP Eq. 18.15),

D $= \frac{\sum^{\text{n}}_{\text{t}=1} \text{CF}_{\text{t}} \text{t/}(1 + \text{YTM})^{\text{t}}}{\sum^{\text{n}}_{\text{t}=1} \text{CF}_{\text{t}}\text{/}(1 + \text{YTM})^{\text{t}}}$ ,

where $\text{CF}_{\text{t}}$ is the expected cash flow in period t and the denominator equals the current market price. Duration gap management requires assembling assets and liabilities whose dollar-weighted durations offset each other.

GARP’s first limitation of duration gap management is practical: finding assets and liabilities of the same duration that fit into the institution’s portfolio is often a frustrating task. It would be much easier if an instrument’s maturity equalled its duration, but for instruments that pay out gradually over time, duration is always less than calendar maturity, because early interest or principal payments pull the weighted-average time forward. Only for instruments such as zero-coupon securities, single-payment loans and Treasury bills (one cash flow at maturity) does duration equal calendar maturity. Two further facts follow:

- The more frequently an instrument pays interest or principal, the shorter its duration.
- The shorter the maturity, the closer the match between maturity and duration (Schweser: the duration of shorter-term securities and loans is closer to their maturities than that of longer-term ones).

GARP’s own five-year 10% loan illustrates the gap: priced at par, its duration is 4.17 years, not 5. Schweser adds the managerial consequence: it may not be possible to match asset and liability durations even if managers prefer a zero gap.

**Applying it to this question**

The treasurer’s “it would be easier if maturity equalled duration” is GARP’s framing. Test each option against the duration-versus-maturity facts: only D states the zero-coupon, single-payment and Treasury bill exception and the narrowing gap at short maturities.

**Fragile fact.** Duration is below maturity for anything that pays before maturity; equality holds only for single-payment instruments, and the gap shrinks as maturity shortens.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** LO 82.d: Discuss the limitations of interest-sensitive gap management and duration gap management. **GARP:** Chapter 18, Section 18.7, “The Limitations of Duration Gap Management” (opening paragraph); duration formula and loan example in Section 18.5. **GARP vs Schweser:** none.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-17 d, where it is Q8 of 12.

a.reason: (Polarity flip). GARP says duration is always less than calendar maturity for instruments paying out gradually. A would be correct if “exceeds” were replaced by “is less than” (and the conclusion reversed: assets that look long carry shorter durations).

b.reason: (Scope error). Being one contract does not matter; the number and timing of cash flows do. An amortizing loan pays principal over its life, so its duration is below five years. B would be correct for a five-year single-payment loan with all interest and principal paid at maturity.

c.reason: (Polarity flip). GARP: the more frequently an instrument pays interest or principal, the shorter its duration. C would be correct with “more frequently” in place of “less frequently”.

d.reason: D combines GARP’s two statements: duration equals maturity only for single-cash-flow instruments, and the shorter the maturity, the closer the match.

questions.question:
A risk consultant is validating the duration model of a German savings bank. Most EUR funding comes from checkable deposits and passbook savings accounts. On the asset side, borrowers may prepay residential mortgages at any time, and defaults in the small-business loan book have been rising. The consultant drafts four statements on the reliability of the bank’s duration estimates:

I. The cash flow pattern of checkable deposits and passbook savings accounts is not well defined, so their durations are difficult to calculate.

II. Customer prepayments distort the expected cash flows from loans and therefore the measured asset duration.

III. Prepayments and defaults matter only for IS gap buckets and not for duration, because duration weights promised rather than expected cash flows.

IV. Customer defaults distort the expected cash flows from loans when expected cash flows do not happen.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.text: I and II only
II and IV only
I, II, and IV only
I, II, III, and IV

questions.solution:
Validating a savings bank’s duration model: deposits with undefined cash flows, prepayable mortgages, rising SME defaults.

**Concept and theory**

Duration is built from expected cash flows: GARP’s Eq. 18.14 weights “Expected CF in Period t” by time and present value. Any feature that makes those cash flows uncertain or ill-defined weakens the duration estimate and hence the duration gap.

GARP 18.7 names three such features:

| Feature | Why it hurts duration |
|---|---|
| Checkable deposits, passbook savings | Their pattern of cash flows is not well defined, so duration is difficult to calculate. |
| Customer prepayments | Distort the expected cash flows from loans (borrowers repay early). |
| Customer defaults (credit risk) | Distort expected cash flows when expected cash flows do not happen. |

Schweser’s version lists the deposit problem and adds that prepayments on loans, which affect duration, may be uncertain; it does not mention defaults. A candidate who studies only the condensed list may wrongly reject the default statement, which is why it is tested here.

These problems are not confined to one technique. The IS gap also struggles with deposits (their repricing point is hard to identify), but that does not remove the problem from duration analysis: in duration analysis the issue is the timing and size of cash flows, in gap analysis it is the repricing date.

**Applying it to this question**

Statement I is GARP’s deposit limitation (true). II is GARP’s prepayment limitation (true). IV is GARP’s default limitation (true). III claims duration uses promised cash flows and is unaffected; GARP’s formula uses expected cash flows and explicitly lists prepayments and defaults as distortions, so III is false. Correct set: I, II and IV.

**Fragile fact.** Duration uses expected cash flows; GARP names deposits, prepayments and defaults (Schweser omits defaults).

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** LO 82.d: Discuss the limitations of interest-sensitive gap management and duration gap management. **GARP:** Chapter 18, Section 18.7, “The Limitations of Duration Gap Management” (second paragraph); Eq. 18.14 in Section 18.5. **GARP vs Schweser:** GARP adds customer defaults; Schweser lists deposits and prepayments only. Resolved from GARP.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-17 d, where it is Q9 of 12.

a.reason: (Scope error). It omits IV, matching Schweser’s shorter list but not GARP, which states that customer defaults distort expected cash flows. A would be correct if the question asked which features appear in Schweser’s summary.

b.reason: (Scope error). It omits I, the first and most prominent duration limitation in both sources. B would be correct only if statement I were corrupted, for example by claiming that these deposits have well-defined cash flows.

c.reason: C picks the three limitations GARP lists for duration measurement: undefined deposit cash flows, prepayments and defaults.

d.reason: (Sibling swap). It accepts III, which moves the cash flow problem onto IS gap buckets and away from duration. Duration uses expected cash flows, so prepayments and defaults do distort it. D would be correct only if every statement were true.

questions.question:
The CRO of a US bank holding company reports that the leverage-adjusted duration gap has been brought to approximately zero, so net worth is “immunized”. A board member asks under which scenario this protection would be least reliable.

Which of the following best combines the scenario and the reason?

options.text: Short-term rates rise by 175 basis points while long-term rates rise by 25 basis points, because the change is large and the yield curve does not shift in parallel.
All rates rise by 30 basis points in parallel, because duration misstates the sensitivity of asset and liability values to any change in rates, however small.
All rates fall by 30 basis points in parallel, because the linear relation that duration assumes between value and rates breaks down only when rates fall.
All rates rise by 40 basis points in parallel, because the convexity effect that duration ignores is largest when rates change by small amounts.

questions.solution:
Zero leverage-adjusted duration gap: under which scenario, and why, is the protection least reliable?

**Concept and theory**

Duration gap management estimates the change in net worth as

∆NW $\approx\left[ - \text{D}_{\text{A}} \frac{\Delta\text{i}}{1 + \text{i}} \text{A}\right] - \left[ - \text{D}_{\text{L}} \frac{\Delta\text{i}}{1 + \text{i}} \text{L}\right]$,

with $\text{D}_{\text{A}}$, $\text{D}_{\text{L}}$ the dollar-weighted durations of assets and liabilities, A and L their values, i the original rate and ∆i the change. Two assumptions are built into this formula: a single ∆i applies to every asset and liability, and value changes are linear in ∆i.

GARP 18.7 explains how both can fail. Duration gap models assume a linear relationship between the market values of assets and liabilities and interest rates, “which is not strictly true”; the related problem is convexity, the nonlinear relation between price and yield. Duration gap analysis is reasonably effective if the yield curve changes by relatively small amounts and moves in parallel steps, with short-term and long-term rates changing by about the same proportion. If there are major changes in rates and different rates move at different speeds, accuracy and effectiveness decrease. Real yield curves do not usually shift in parallel: short-term rates tend to move over a wider range than long-term rates, and a big change in market rates (say one or two percentage points) can give a distorted reading of the true exposure. Schweser compresses this to: the duration gap is more effective for small changes and for changes that affect the entire yield curve than for large changes and/or slope changes.

**Applying it to this question**

The question asks for the least reliable case. Scenario A combines both failure conditions GARP names: a large move (175 bp at the short end, within GARP’s “one or two percentage points”) and a non-parallel move (short rates up far more than long rates, the pattern GARP describes). The other scenarios are small parallel shifts, the conditions under which GARP says duration works reasonably well, each paired with a wrong reason.

**Fragile fact.** Duration works for small, parallel shifts; it is least reliable for large moves (one or two points) with short rates moving more than long rates.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** LO 82.d: Discuss the limitations of interest-sensitive gap management and duration gap management. **GARP:** Chapter 18, Section 18.7, “The Limitations of Duration Gap Management” (convexity and non-parallel shift paragraph); Eq. 18.22 in Section 18.6. **GARP vs Schweser:** none.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-17 d, where it is Q10 of 12.

a.reason: A matches GARP: effectiveness falls when rate changes are large and different rates move at different speeds, so a single ∆i no longer describes the balance sheet.

b.reason: (Absolute claim). GARP says duration is reasonably effective for small parallel changes; it does not misstate sensitivity for “any” change. B would be correct if the stem described a large non-parallel shift and the reason were limited to such moves.

c.reason: (Scope error). The linearity problem is not restricted to falling rates; GARP ties the inaccuracy to the size of the change and to non-parallel moves, not to direction. C would be correct if “only when rates fall” were replaced by “especially when rates change by large amounts”.

d.reason: (Polarity flip). Convexity matters most for large changes in rates (Schweser: duration is more accurate for small changes, less accurate for larger ones due to convexity). D would be correct with “large” in place of “small” and a large rate move in the scenario.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Discuss the limitations of interest-sensitive gap management and duration gap management.
questions.reading: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
questions.topic: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-17 d Q11
questions.question:
A bank supervisor in Singapore is reviewing a bank that set its leverage-adjusted duration gap to zero twelve months ago and has not rebalanced since. The supervisor drafts statements for the examination report on the limitations of duration gap management.

Which of the following statements is NOT correct?

options.text: Duration itself can shift as market interest rates move, so a duration gap set to zero may not remain at zero after rates change.
The durations of different financial instruments can change at differing speeds with the passage of time, even if rates do not move.
Research suggests that duration balancing can still be effective even when the technique’s underlying assumptions are moderately violated.
Once the gap is set to zero, net worth stays immunized without rebalancing, because asset and liability durations always drift at the same speed.

questions.solution:
Supervisor reviews a bank that zeroed its duration gap a year ago and never rebalanced: which statement is NOT correct?

**Concept and theory**

A zero leverage-adjusted duration gap, $\text{D}_{\text{A}} - \text{D}_{\text{L}} \times$ L/A = 0, immunizes net worth only at the moment it is set. GARP closes its list of duration limitations with two dynamic problems. First, duration itself can shift as market interest rates move, so a balanced position becomes unbalanced after rates change. Second, the durations of different financial instruments can change at differing speeds with the passage of time, so even with rates unchanged, asset and liability durations drift apart as instruments age and pay down. Schweser lists the first as “duration shifts as rates change”.

The practical consequence is that duration gap management is a continuing process, not a one-off trade: the bank must re-measure durations and adjust its balance sheet or hedges. A bank that zeroed its gap twelve months ago and did nothing since cannot assume it is still immunized.

GARP balances the limitations with two positive points. Research suggests duration balancing can still be effective even with moderate violations of the technique’s underlying assumptions. And duration gap analysis helps managers manage the value of the firm to its shareholders (its net worth), so it remains a valuable managerial tool despite its limitations. Schweser’s closing words agree: duration gap analysis remains a valuable tool for estimating the impact of rate changes on capital. A NOT-correct question on this target therefore tests two opposite overreactions: believing a zero gap lasts forever, and believing the limitations make the tool useless.

**Applying it to this question**

Read each option for the qualifier “NOT correct”. A, B and C are close paraphrases of GARP 18.7. D asserts that immunization persists without rebalancing because durations “always drift at the same speed”, which contradicts GARP’s statement that durations change at differing speeds. D is the incorrect statement.

**Fragile fact.** A zero duration gap decays: durations move with rates and drift at different speeds over time, yet duration balancing remains useful under moderate violations.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** LO 82.d: Discuss the limitations of interest-sensitive gap management and duration gap management. **GARP:** Chapter 18, Section 18.7, “The Limitations of Duration Gap Management” (final two paragraphs). **GARP vs Schweser:** none; GARP’s “differing speeds with the passage of time” is not in Schweser’s list.

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-17 d, where it is Q11 of 12.

a.reason: (True statement (qualifier misread)). GARP: “Duration itself can shift as market interest rates move”. Selecting A means treating a stated limitation as false. A would be the answer only if the question asked for a statement that is correct.

b.reason: (True statement (scope error in the reader)). GARP: durations of different instruments “can change at differing speeds with the passage of time”. A candidate who believes duration changes only when rates move would wrongly reject B. B would be the answer if it claimed durations change only when rates move.

c.reason: (True statement (absolute-claim reflex)). GARP cites research that duration balancing can still be effective with moderate violations of its assumptions. A candidate who thinks the limitations make duration useless would wrongly pick C. C would be the answer if it claimed duration balancing fails whenever any assumption is violated.

d.reason: D is the only false statement: GARP says the durations of different instruments change at differing speeds over time and that duration shifts as rates move, so a zero gap decays without rebalancing.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Discuss the limitations of interest-sensitive gap management and duration gap management.
questions.reading: LTR-17: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
questions.topic: Risk Management for Changing Interest Rates: Asset-Liability Management and Duration Techniques
questions.source: High quality paper LTR-17 d Q12
questions.question:
A junior risk analyst at a CAD-reporting bank is preparing a slide that sorts limitations under the technique to which they belong:

I. An aggressive approach to managing NII and NIM with this tool may increase earnings volatility, which may in turn hurt the bank’s stock price.

II. It may not be possible to match the relevant measure for assets and liabilities, even if managers prefer a zero gap.

III. Rates may change at different speeds within a single maturity bucket.

IV. The tool is more effective for small rate changes that affect the entire yield curve than for large changes or changes in the slope of the curve.

Which of the following classifications is accurate?

options.text: IS gap: I and II; duration gap: III and IV
IS gap: I and III; duration gap: II and IV
IS gap: III and IV; duration gap: I and II
IS gap: I, III, and IV; duration gap: II

questions.solution:
Sorting four limitations between IS gap management and duration gap management.

**Concept and theory**

The LO asks for the limitations of two sibling techniques, and the exam regularly tests whether a candidate can attribute each limitation to the right one. The cleanest way is to ask what each tool measures. IS gap management uses repricing buckets to protect net interest income and the NIM, so its limitations concern repricing: rate speeds, repricing dates, bucket boundaries, and its blindness to net worth. Duration gap management uses durations of asset and liability portfolios to protect net worth, so its limitations concern duration: matching, cash flow patterns, linearity and parallel shifts, and drift.

| IS gap limitations (Schweser 82.d list, GARP 18.4) | Duration gap limitations (Schweser 82.d list, GARP 18.7) |
|---|---|
| Asset and liability rates may not move together | Matching durations may not be possible even if a zero gap is preferred |
| Rates may change at different speeds within a bucket | Duration of shorter instruments is closer to maturity |
| Repricing point is not easy to identify | Cash flow patterns of demand and savings deposits are hard to define |
| Aggressive gapping may raise earnings volatility and hurt the stock price | More effective for small, whole-curve changes than for large or slope changes Duration shifts as rates change |

Some limitations echo across both tools (both struggle with deposits, and both assume rates move together in some sense), which is exactly why the exam uses them as sibling traps. Use the source lists as the tie-breaker.

**Applying it to this question**

I mentions NII and NIM management and earnings volatility: IS gap. II speaks of matching a measure for assets and liabilities under a preferred zero gap: duration gap (Schweser’s first duration limitation; GARP’s “finding assets and liabilities of the same duration”). III refers to a maturity bucket: IS gap. IV refers to small changes affecting the whole curve versus large or slope changes: duration gap. So IS gap: I and III; duration gap: II and IV.

**Fragile fact.** Bucket, repricing date, NIM or earnings volatility points to IS gap; matching durations, cash flow patterns, parallel shifts or convexity points to duration gap.

**Reference**

**LO wording (Schweser, verbatim):** LO 82.d: Discuss the limitations of interest-sensitive gap management and duration gap management. **GARP:** Chapter 18, Section 18.4, “Problems with Interest-Sensitive GAP Management”, and Section 18.7, “The Limitations of Duration Gap Management”. **GARP vs Schweser:** none; the stock price wording in I is Schweser’s (GARP: reduced value of the stockholders’ investment).

**Source:** High quality question set, Liquidity and Treasury Risk: the paper for LTR-17 d, where it is Q12 of 12.

a.reason: (Sibling swap). It swaps II and III. A maturity bucket belongs to gap analysis, and matching durations belongs to duration gap. A would be correct if II said “rates may change at different speeds within a bucket” and III said “it may not be possible to match durations”.

b.reason: B reproduces the Schweser 82.d key-concept lists, which match GARP’s sections 18.4 (IS gap problems) and 18.7 (duration limitations).

c.reason: (Sibling swap). It reverses I and IV: earnings volatility from aggressive NII management is an IS gap problem, and the small, parallel-shift condition is a duration problem. C would be correct only if I and IV traded places, that is, if I described a duration problem and IV a repricing-bucket problem.

d.reason: (Sibling swap). It moves IV to IS gap. Although simple gap analysis also assumes rates move in lockstep (Schweser LO 82.b), the “small changes affecting the entire yield curve versus large and slope changes” limitation is listed under duration gap. D would be correct if IV instead read “rates on assets and liabilities may not move together”.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Explain and calculate liquidity trading risk via cost of liquidation and liquidity-adjusted VaR (LVaR).
questions.question: A manager at an asset management firm requests that an analyst calculate the cost of liquidation of one of the fund’s stock positions. The position consists of 100,000 shares of company ABC and the stock has a current bid price of USD 53.5 and an offer price of USD 54.5. The mean and standard deviation for the stock’s proportional bid-offer spread is 0.0185 and 0.0250 respectively. The analyst calculates the cost of liquidation for this entire stock position under a stressed market scenario based on a 99% confidence level. What is the correct cost of liquidation for this stock position?
questions.solution:
**Concept**

Cost of liquidation in normal markets is half the proportional spread times the position value, $\frac{1}{2} s \alpha$. In a stressed market the spread is replaced by its mean plus a number of standard deviations: $\frac{1}{2} (\mu+ \lambda\sigma) \alpha$, with $\lambda= 2.326$ at 99%.

**Working**

**Mid price and position value:** $\frac{53.5 + 54.5}{2} = 54$, so $\alpha= 54 \times100{,}000 = \text{USD} 5{,}400{,}000$

**Stressed spread:** 0.0185 + 2.326 × 0.0250 = 0.07665

**Cost of liquidation:** $\frac{1}{2} \times5{,}400{,}000 \times0.07665 = \text{USD} 206{,}955$

**Exam trap.** Two switches, four options: normal versus stressed, and with or without the one half. The question says stressed, and the one half always applies.

**Source:** 2026 PE2 Q29 (All past year questions, Question 197).

a.reason: USD 49,950 is the cost in a normal market: $\frac{1}{2} \times5{,}400{,}000 \times0.0185$.

b.reason: USD 99,900 is the normal-market cost without the one half.

c.reason: Correct.

d.reason: USD 413,910 is the stressed cost without the one half.

questions.subject: Liquidity Risk
questions.loText: Explain and calculate liquidity trading risk via cost of liquidation and liquidity-adjusted VaR (LVaR).
questions.source: GARP past 10-year papers book, Q52.3
